London’s most famous shopping street is now pedestrianised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:57:37 UTC
15:57:37 KST

Ahead of the holiday season, cars, buses and bikes are banned from nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street.
For first-time visitors to London, there are certain addresses you need to tick off, like Leicester Square, Brick Lane, or Abbey Road.
And while the latter is most famous for its zebra crossing – thanks to The Beatles, whose album cover of the same name was shot here – one popular tourist location is making sure marked crosswalks are no longer necessary: Oxford Street.
That’s because the world-famous shopping street is now closed to cars, buses and bicycles as of 26 October.
Nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street, between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, is now traffic-free, with vehicles diverted onto surrounding roads.
The move is the first step in a makeover of the storied shopping precinct, with plans to plant trees, install seating and add two new public squares.
Oxford Street still sees about half a million visitors a day, with shoppers bustling between retailers such as Selfridges, Zara and John Lewis.
But city officials say pedestrianising the street will put it back into the league of top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.
“This is a momentous day for London, a momentous day for Oxford Street,” London Mayor Sadiq Khan told the BBC. “It’s a new era.”
Why now?
While local officials began discussing the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street more than a decade ago, momentum began to build over the last two years when the mayor’s office created the Oxford Street Development Corporation to shepherd the project.
That helped overcome opposition from local residents who complained that diverting vehicles from Oxford Street would clog their neighbourhoods with traffic.
A public consultation later determined that removing traffic would attract new shops and visitors to Oxford Street, making it “an iconic destination”.
The project also got a boost from the new Elizabeth Line, which runs through the heart of the city, with a stop on Oxford Street.
Further work on the makeover will begin in the new year, with city officials refining their plans based on feedback from visitors, Khan told reporters.
“In advance of Christmas, you know, I want people to come here and shop and enjoy the experience,” he added.
Oxford Street’s famed lights
As hinted at by Khan, one of the best times to visit (or worst, if you hate crowds) is during the holiday season when lights line Oxford Street, a tradition first started in 1959.
According to the official website, this year the Christmas lights will be Harry Potter themed to mark the opening of the UK’s largest official Harry Potter store as well as the launch of the controversial new HBO series.
Previous years have seen the street lit up with 5,000 stars glowing thanks to the help of 300,000 LED bulbs.

‘10% Now’: Ukraine Asks 5 European Allies for Patriot Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:52:18 UTC
15:52:18 KST

Ukraine has asked five European partners to provide 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T air defense systems to help protect the country against Russian attacks, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said.
The request was directed to the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. Khmara said Ukraine had already signed contracts for future deliveries of interceptor missiles and proposed an exchange that would allow Kyiv to receive ammunition immediately.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine already has contracts in place for future deliveries of interceptor missiles, so it is proposing an exchange: partners would provide a portion of their current stocks now, in return for the shipments that are scheduled to arrive in Ukraine later,” he said on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces (AFU) also urgently need additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), he added.
“Ukraine is counting on funding for new acquisitions, as well as the transfer of systems from the existing stockpiles of its partners,” Khmara said.
The minister added Ukraine could double its drone production by 2027 if funding arrived on time. Kyiv is proposing not only to increase procurement but also to expand joint production of Ukrainian drones abroad.
“We are proposing not only to increase procurement but also to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries,” Khmara said. He added that the approach would help Ukraine obtain the drones it needs while strengthening the defensive capabilities of partner countries.
Ukraine Confirms It Is Honoring US-Brokered Truce in Russian-Occupied Oleshky
European allies prepare winter aid
Following a meeting in Paris with defense ministers from the UK, France, Italy and Poland, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the participating countries had already prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine.
“Moreover, we will do everything in our power to ensure that the United States continues to support Ukraine – through its own shipments, and, above all, by providing intelligence and satellite data,” Pistorius said.
He added that European countries were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was preparing to intensify attacks on major Ukrainian cities.
Senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Moscow planned to paralyze Kyiv before the onset of colder weather in an effort to destabilize the political situation. According to the officials, Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered attacks on civilian infrastructure across the capital.
Separately, Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times (FT) that Moscow intended to increase pressure on Kyiv in hopes of forcing Ukraine to accept Russian demands, including surrendering territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.
Ukraine has waited nearly a month for US approval of Patriot missiles
Ukraine will again raise the issue of delayed air defense missile deliveries with the US, as Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky added that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington again. Ukraine is also seeking PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from EU countries and other partners holding existing stocks.
The shortage comes as Ukraine struggles to secure enough ammunition to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky previously said Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite requiring around 350 per month.
He has also asked European partners to provide 300 interceptors for the winter, but efforts to obtain missiles from existing stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Air Force official Yuriy Ihnat said that missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukraine’s Patriot systems for several years.
He said Ukrainian crews had developed more efficient tactics, typically using one interceptor per target and employing ambushes before quickly relocating systems. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight interceptors at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
Zelensky also called for faster implementation of decisions expected to support Ukraine’s air defense, as officials prepare for the next Ramstein-format meeting in November. “Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” he said.

Creepy Cat in the Hat videos reach Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:51:19 EET
15:51:19 KST

Viral images that purport to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character roaming the streets after dark are sparking fear and confusion among children.
The so-called Cat in the Hat phenomenon is spreading on social media. In frightening videos, the black-and-white feline, familiar from 1950s children's books, turns up in various towns and cities.
Over the past few days, the phenomenon has also reached Finland. The police in Oulu told Yle that they have been contacted about it. They said they have searched the streets but have not found anyone sneaking around in a cat costume.
Jyrki Mikkonen, principal of Koivuhaka School in Kokkola, says he is aware that content featuring the hat-wearing feline is circulating on social media. The school learned about it from parents.
"There were posts on social media warning that the figure would show up in this area. According to messages from guardians, this is worrying kids," he says.
The phenomenon centres on videos, shared especially on TikTok, that portray the cat character as menacing and claim it has been 'spotted' in various places or is 'on its way' to a particular town or school.
Kaisa Rissanen, of Someturva, a Finnish service that helps victims of online harassment and bullying, says the pattern is familiar. About ten years ago, people dressed up as clowns sparked similar worry.
"The threat is specific to videos created with AI, not to real dangerous situations," she notes.
But even if the threat isn't real, Rissanen says children's fear is genuine.
She also points out that digital security skills are becoming increasingly important as AI-generated content on social media keeps growing.
"This is a good wake-up call that we need to address these topics more broadly," she says.

China brings legacy of Tokyo Trial to UN Headquarters with exhibition marking 80th anniversary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:50:18 CST
15:50:18 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday.
Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II.
"The Tokyo Trial cements the post-war world order, upholds fairness and justice, and advances international rule of law. It is a landmark victory of peace over war, civilization over barbarism, and justice over evil, with far-reaching political and historical significance," said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, at the opening ceremony.
"The Tokyo Trial put Japanese militarism in the dock. It's essential for Japan to bear in mind what is at the core of the trial, make a clean break with militarism, and commit itself to peace once and for all," he said.
"Regrettably, right-wing forces in Japan keep questioning the legitimacy of the Tokyo Trial under various pretexts, and try to gloss over Japan's history of aggression. From worshiping Class-A war criminals to hollowing out the pacifist Constitution, from easing controls on arms exports to lifting the ban on the right to collective self-defense, Japan is going further away from the Tokyo Trial and tearing up its 'pacifist' rulebook."
"History, if not forgotten, can serve as a guide for the future," said Fu. "We need to guard against rising neo-militarism, and together uphold the post-war order and international peace and security."
Qi Dahai, director-general of the Department of Treaty and Law of China's Foreign Ministry, Zhou Feng, curator of the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, and officials from Russia and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea addressed the opening ceremony. Permanent representatives to the United Nations from Spain, Nicaragua and other countries attended the ceremony.
Speakers highlighted the Tokyo Trial's role in upholding peace through the rule of law and bringing Japan's wartime aggression to justice. They stressed the need to learn from history, remember the suffering caused by war, and work together to prevent the resurgence of militarism and aggression.
Organized by China's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, the exhibition is being held during the UN International Law Week. ■

World Insights: Japanese firm under fire over Mongolia wildfire, ecological damage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:50:13 CST
15:50:13 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A subsidiary of a Japanese telecom firm is under fire and facing legal consequences after its executives' activities sparked a massive wildfire in Mongolia near the Chinese border, which burned an area more than twice the size of Tokyo.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, one of eastern Mongolia's best-preserved natural ecosystems and a habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including rare and endangered species. It was extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports.
The wildfire burned for more than eight days, sweeping across approximately 530,000 hectares, destroying about 80 percent of the protected nature reserve, according to the country's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change.
Some wild animals, among them rare and endangered species, fled across the border into China. More than 2,000 personnel were deployed in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region to contain a grassland fire spreading from Mongolia. As Chinese firefighters worked to contain the blaze, they also left a passage open for the fleeing animals to escape.
OUTRAGE AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS
Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI did not admit until Oct. 20, almost two weeks after the fire broke out, that the disaster was linked to the activities of its subsidiary, Mobicom.
According to Mongolian media, a five-vehicle Mobicom convoy led by senior Japanese executives and carrying 13 people entered the restricted area. Dry grass beneath one vehicle caught fire, and strong winds quickly spread the flames across the grassland.
Mobicom claimed the trip was an official survey for telecom infrastructure construction, describing the fire as an operational accident.
However, Mongolian government officials and local media have strongly questioned the explanation, pointing out that the proposed fibre-optic project lacked technical and economic justification.
Local media reports said the convoy may have entered the area for illegal hunting and fishing involving critically endangered species. Such activities are prohibited under Mongolian criminal law in specially protected areas, where starting a forest or steppe fire can also carry criminal penalties.
Although the company apologized for the fire, it did not directly address the allegations.
The incident has sparked widespread public outrage in Mongolia, with questions raised over whether the convoy had obtained the necessary permits to enter the ecologically sensitive reserve during the high-risk fire season.
Amid mounting public anger over the delayed apology from the Japanese side and the lack of a plan and compensation to address the damage, Mongolia's Deputy Prime Minister Nyamtaishiryn Nomtoibayar said, "Strictly protected areas are not places that anyone can simply enter at will ... Mobicom's empty 'apology' means nothing to me."
Temuulen Ganzorig, Mongolia's minister of justice and internal affairs, said those involved, along with personnel from relevant border-port administrations, would be held accountable and ordered to compensate for the losses.
The incident was "not merely a private matter for one company," Kazuya Shimba, secretary-general of Japan's Democratic Party for the People, told a press conference, noting that "Japan as a nation must take it seriously."
"No one should be allowed to escape accountability for the damage. The investigation must establish who authorized entry into the protected area, for what purpose, who was responsible for ensuring fire safety, and what measures were taken after the fire broke out," said Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral.
"Any issues related to Mobicom's operations must also be investigated in accordance with the law and based on evidence," he stressed.
ECOLOGICAL DAMAGE
Beyond the immediate damage, the fire's long-term ecological consequences could be far more difficult to assess.
A Mongolian government working group is assessing damage to the Numrug Strictly Protected Area. The country's environment ministry said the assessment should examine the fire's impacts on soil, water, air, vegetation, wildlife and ecosystem functions, as well as its long-term ecological consequences.
The grasslands in eastern Mongolia form a vital ecological barrier in Northeast Asia, Liu Zhiyan, a senior research fellow at the Research Institute for Eco-civilization of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the media.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, said Wang, stressing that further assessment is needed to determine whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether ash, sediment or smoke from the fire has crossed national borders.
The wildfire also released smoke and particulate matter that could be carried across borders by air currents, said Liu.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects warrant further investigation, including whether ash and sediment could enter rivers and wetlands through surface runoff and whether smoke had crossed national borders, Wang said.
Citing research in Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fires occurring from autumn through the following spring were associated with the number of dust storm days in spring. Reduced vegetation cover leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion, making surface materials more susceptible to being carried away by the wind, he said.
Regular international cooperation on fire warnings, emergency response and ecological restoration is essential to containing cross-border disasters and reducing environmental risks, Liu said.
Kazuo Yawata, a former senior official at Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry and a history writer, reiterated that Mobicom should offer a sincere apology for the disaster, stressing that the fire had caused "a significant impact on the local ecosystem." ■

A missing link to Australia's newest airport comes with a $55 sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:50:12 UTC
15:50:12 KST

in brief
- Western Sydney International Airport travellers face public transport stop gaps.
- The promised metro line to the airport may not be operational until mid 2028.
Western Sydney International Airport (WSI)'s opening marks Australia's first major new aviation gateway in over half a century, yet it will be a long time before visitors will be able to take a train to or from the terminal.
From its outset, state and transit authorities had promised that WSI would come complete with a high-speed, driverless metro line to connect passengers to the wider Sydney rail network.
However, disputes with contractors, corruption allegations, and deadline blowouts have left staff and travellers forced to use stop-gap methods to reach the airport, with alternative arrangements unlikely to materialise for well over a year.
In June, the NSW government was forced to concede that the delays to the metro line opening could continue until mid-2028 — some 18 months after the grand opening of WSI.
While construction delays continue, travellers and staff face limited public transport options, with private firms' alternatives costing up to $55 per person.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Temporary transport measures
While the NSW government and Sydney Metro maintained that the metro line connecting Badgerys Creek to Bradfield and St Marys would open on schedule, planning for an emergency alternative began in early 2025, internal policy documents later revealed.
After spending $11 billion on an incomplete metro line, the NSW government announced earlier this month that the WSI Link free shuttle service would ferry passengers the 20km shortfall between the terminal and St Marys railway station on the T1 Western Line.
Five suburban bus routes have also been re-routed to the airport precinct to deliver travellers to Mount Druitt, Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown and Leppington at standard rates.
Other travel options to the city
Private operator Super Shuttle WSI offers an express coach service to Parramatta, the Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport (Kingsford Smith). A single adult ticket to Parramatta costs $25 and a return $45, the single/return adult fares to the Sydney CBD are $55/$80 and for Sydney Airport they are $65/$90.
One of the primary advantages of WSI over Sydney's original Kingsford Smith Airport is its lack of curfew, allowing passengers to arrive and depart 24 hours a day. However, current public transport services keep to standard operational hours, potentially leaving some passengers and staff with limited early-morning options.
Transport for NSW defended the interim transit arrangements, stating operating hours reflect current scheduling.
"There are currently no passenger flights operating or at this moment planned between 1 and 4.30am through Western Sydney International Airport," a Transport for NSW spokesperson told SBS News. "Transport for NSW continues to monitor service demand as the airport grows."
The department said travellers arriving during the overnight window have access to private shuttles, rideshares, and vehicle parking.
While current schedules favour daytime hours, international and budget carriers are scheduled to scale up through early 2027.
Western Sydney International's limitations 'understood'
Adam Leto, CEO of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, told SBS News that the airport ought to be seen in its broader context and that initial concerns over transport pale in comparison to the benefit it brings.
"Rome wasn't built in a day," Leto said. "We've understood what the airport was going to look like when it opened, and it's not going to be the full picture. I think most people in western Sydney understood that and accepted that."
Leto noted that the surrounding road network, including the newly opened M12 motorway, was always expected to carry the bulk of early passenger movements but that it will need to adapt as passenger numbers swell.
"This is about what's happening over the next 20 — 30 years, not what happens over the next 20 — 30 days," he said. "I think there's going to be more infrastructure that will be required to support the growth of the airport."
Round-the-clock transport will take time to mature, Leto said.
"We've never had a 24-hour airport, so it's a new thing for Sydney to grapple with and understand and learn how to leverage."
However, local government leaders have warned that interim solutions must not displace long-term public transport commitments.
Penrith mayor Todd Carney said the completed metro line to St Marys would eventually be a "gamechanger", but called on the state government to fund the full north-south rail link. The route linking St Marys to Tallawong and Bradfield to Macarthur remains in the early planning stages.
"Ours is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country and with that growth comes enormous opportunity," Carney said. "However, communities can only benefit from opportunity if they can access it.''
The rail delivery timeline blew out after lead contractor Webuild lodged claims for around $2.2 billion in contract variations, slowing station works.
The dispute was compounded when an independent probity investigation uncovered invoicing and payroll irregularities among subcontractors, triggering referrals to the police, the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, and the National Anti-Corruption Commission.
Commercial passenger services on the airport metro line are now not expected to run until late 2027 at the earliest, with Premier Chris Minns revealing in June that services may not open until mid 2028.

By the time Mongolian emergency teams fully extinguished the fire on Oct. 16 after eight days of round-the-clock efforts, it had scorched about 530,000 hectares of land, according to preliminary figures from Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. Some 470,000 hectares of that lie within the Numrug reserve, accounting for 79.8 percent of its total area.
Initial investigations suggest the fire may have been sparked by a vehicle convoy operated by Mobicom, the Mongolian subsidiary of Japanese telecom giant KDDI. On Oct. 20, KDDI acknowledged that the fire was linked to Mobicom's activities and that Japanese executive Yasuhiro Ochi was present at the time.
The disaster has drawn widespread anger and criticism among Mongolian and Japanese social media users, and Mongolian authorities have vowed to identify those responsible and seek compensation.
However, it was not until Monday, more than two weeks after the fire broke out, that the Japanese government responded for the first time, with Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara saying the government takes the matter seriously and will maintain close communication with Mongolia and cooperate in efforts to restore the damaged area.
"Only now?! The government should've said it two weeks ago. Where were they back then?" one Japanese netizen wrote in the comments under a news post on X about Kihara's remarks. Another criticized the government's inaction: "Up until today, both the government and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi completely ignored it."
Many other netizens expressed anger and heartbreak over the fire's large-scale damage to local ecosystems and biodiversity, calling for a thorough investigation and accountability for those responsible.
"I heard the area burned is about 2.4 times the size of Tokyo? That's shocking! The impact on wildlife, plants and the wider ecosystem is still unclear, and it shouldn't be taken lightly," one Japanese social media user commented.
"The grassland has been burned to a wasteland. Who knows how long it will take to recover. Poor animals..." another wrote.
"There should be a thorough investigation, and whoever is responsible should face serious consequences," said another. "Countless creatures lived there. Just seeing those images is heartbreaking."
Others stressed corporate responsibility. "Complying with local environmental regulations and nature conservation rules is the basic responsibility of Japan-linked companies," one user wrote. "The natural environment cannot recover overnight just through apologies or compensation payments."
Questions also persisted about the convoy's purpose in entering the strictly protected reserve and whether it had obtained proper approval.
Meanwhile, not only the government but also Japan's mainstream media were slow to report, initially giving the fire little coverage and only stepping it up after public discussion and outrage gained traction on social media.
Some Japanese netizens pointed to an apparent double standard, noting that Japanese public discourse routinely plays up cases of foreigners behaving badly and damaging Japan's environment, yet fell largely silent when a Japan-linked company caused large-scale ecological harm abroad.
Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral said on Monday that the damage caused by the fire is not simply a matter of land being burned but a serious loss of Mongolia's pristine natural environment, rare wildlife and plant species, and natural heritage that must be preserved for future generations.
"No one should be allowed to escape accountability for the damage. The investigation must establish who authorized entry into the protected area, for what purpose, who was responsible for ensuring fire safety, and what measures were taken after the fire broke out. Any issues related to Mobicom's operations must also be investigated in accordance with the law and based on evidence," he stressed. ■

The stakes extend beyond bilateral trade. As the world's second- and third-largest economies, China and Germany, which are all-around strategic partners, share an interest in global economic stability, climate mitigation and multilateral cooperation.
As protectionism and uncertainty rattle global supply chains, the two countries can ease the strain by keeping economic channels open, addressing trade concerns through dialogue and working under the auspices of the World Trade Organization. A more stable and balanced economic relationship would benefit businesses and consumers in both nations while supporting broader global growth.
Steinmeier's visit offers an opportunity to consolidate mutual trust, strengthen mutual understanding and maintain the momentum of practical cooperation. In a world of growing uncertainty, a stable and constructive China-German relationship can bolster global economic growth and help create a more predictable international environment. ■

====================================================================================================

Deadly parasite: how fox tapeworm warns of pandemic X
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:41:31 UTC
15:41:31 KST

The WHO has developed an early warning system to spot looming pandemics. Tropical medicine expert Dr Carsten Köhler from Tübingen explains the background to Euronews.
The warning about fox tapeworm is something almost everyone in Germany has heard if they have ever wanted to pick berries or collect mushrooms in the forest. The concern is that the tapeworm eggs could be stuck to them - a parasite that attacks the liver and can cause a potentially life-threatening disease.
This disease is one of 21 illnesses that the World Health Organization WHO has placed on its list of NTDs. These so-called "Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs)", known in German as "vernachlässigte Tropenkrankheiten", are regarded as a global early-warning system.
"Wherever NTDs occur, they mark the weak points in the global health system, precisely because there is no system in place there," explains Dr. Dr. Carsten Köhler from the University of Tübingen in an interview with Euronews. He heads, among other things, the Institute of Tropical Medicine, Travel Medicine and Human Parasitology and is president of the German Society for Tropical Medicine, travel medicine and global health.
NTDs can therefore show where medical care, disease surveillance and reliable data are lacking. Precisely in such places, infectious diseases may remain undetected for a long time - with consequences that can reach far beyond the regions directly affected.
Fox tapeworm: Is it still a threat?
The parasite measures only two to six millimetres but can cause severe liver disease in humans. The medical term is alveolar echinococcosis. Adult tapeworms live in the small intestine of foxes and occasionally also in the intestines of dogs and cats.
These animals are then the so-called "definitive hosts" of the tapeworms.
To explain: in biology and medicine, a definitive host is the organism in which a parasite reaches sexual maturity and reproduces. Many parasites have a complex life cycle and change their host - their "home" - during their lifetime. Example: a mouse (intermediate host) ingests the tapeworm eggs. Larvae develop inside the mouse. A fox (definitive host) eats the mouse. In the fox's intestine, the larvae develop into adult tapeworms, which then mate and produce new eggs. The fox is therefore the definitive host.
According to the Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL), the most important definitive host in central Europe is the red fox. Infection in humans is very rare but, if it occurs, can be life-threatening.
In 2024, 52 infections were recorded at the Robert Koch Institute (RKI); in previous years the number in humans mostly lay between 40 and 45 cases. According to the German Liver Aid, the majority of cases come from the southern federal states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. Depending on the region, between 33 and 50 percent of foxes are infected with the parasite.
Echinococcosis is one of the neglected tropical diseases that occur in Germany. But according to Köhler, leishmaniases are now also knocking at the door. This infectious disease can present in different ways and is transmitted by tiny sandflies.
"Many Germans like to travel to the Mediterranean region on holiday and can then bring it back with them," Köhler explains in the interview with Euronews. According to the health magazine of the AOK health insurer, the disease is often curable if it is detected and treated early. The WHO estimates that around 700,000 to one million people worldwide fall ill with leishmaniases every year.
However, most of the 21 neglected tropical diseases occur above all in parts of the world whose health systems are less developed than Germany's.
New neglected disease identified
For example, in 2026 the state of Gabon in Central Africa submitted an application to the World Health Organization WHO to have another disease added to the list of NTDs. "Only endemic countries are allowed to submit applications," Köhler explains. In this case it concerns Loa loa disease, a so-called eye worm. According to Köhler, the WHO will deliberate on the request.
The parasite is transmitted by horseflies. The worms can move through the subcutaneous tissue and sometimes become visible under the conjunctiva of the eye. Infection may be accompanied by itching, swelling and other complaints.
In Köhler's view, the WHO should consider the application. However, in October 2026 the responsible WHO advisory committee recommended a temporary pause in adding new diseases. First, the criteria and procedures for inclusion on the list are to be fundamentally reviewed.
"NTDs occur in regions where the health system does not exist or is only rudimentary," Köhler continues. The diseases themselves are not automatically a danger to the global population. What matters far more is what they reveal about the conditions under which infections can spread: lack of medical care, inadequate monitoring and gaps in the recording of disease cases. There is also a risk that illnesses with pandemic potential may emerge and spread there.
NTDs as an early-warning system for potential endemics
So-called community health workers operate in such regions. They go from community to community, inform the population and observe the local health situation. "A community health worker who is looking out for a worm infection that itself has no pandemic potential would still notice if, all of a sudden, an entire family had died and could report that immediately," says tropical medicine specialist Köhler.
They can recognise illnesses, refer people to medical facilities and report unusual developments to the responsible authorities. "That is why we say these structures can be used as an early-warning system if such basic services have already been set up for NTDs," he explains in his interview with Euronews at the World Health Summit.
The advantage is that helpers are already present in the communities. If NTD programmes are already running in these regions, diseases with pandemic potential are likely to be detected earlier.
Emergency structures do not have to be created from scratch when a new infectious disease appears. If staff are already supporting people with neglected tropical diseases, they can at the same time observe changes that point to other health threats. The work of health workers is also about collecting data as comprehensively as possible.
For this reason, in its strategy to combat neglected tropical diseases up to 2030 the WHO is also relying on integrated approaches: measures are to be more firmly embedded in existing health systems and linked with other areas of public health.
Ebola outbreak: data gap noticed too late
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo showed exactly how problematic missing data can be, says Köhler. "In fact we had expected an outbreak in other hotspots," explains the director of the Centre for Tropical Medicine. "Then we had to realise that the data for the Democratic Republic of Congo were out of date."
When up-to-date information from a region is lacking, health authorities may misjudge the risk. Contact tracing and the targeted deployment of medical staff and supplies also become more difficult.
Local health workers are therefore not only vital for the treatment of individual diseases; they also help to detect outbreaks earlier and to coordinate the response more effectively.
In some cases, the withdrawal of the USA from health promotion has also made data collection in affected areas more difficult. "Because funding from the USA has fallen so sharply, the community health worker structures that were built up over recent decades have collapsed dramatically," Köhler explains.
The missing funds meant, among other things, that former health workers had to give up their jobs. According to UNAIDS, as a result of US funding cuts, thousands of community health workers in Malawi were affected by contract terminations in 2025. The organisation also reported restrictions in the electronic recording of health data.
A study published in 2026 from Zambia likewise describes how cuts in international development aid undermined the work of health facilities. Staff reported lay-offs, a lack of diagnostic tests and difficulties in using electronic patient records. The result: less comprehensive health data.
The next pandemic: Disease X
A new pandemic triggered by Ebola is not considered likely, as the risk varies greatly from disease to disease. While in the case of coronavirus, for example, droplet infection was enough, Ebola mainly threatens people who come into contact with the body fluids of infected patients.
Neglected tropical diseases likewise do not automatically have pandemic potential. A high number of NTD cases is rather a possible indication that medical care and surveillance in a region need to be strengthened.
"We should prepare for the next pandemic, which the WHO calls Disease X, whatever it turns out to be," warns Köhler. It is assumed that Covid-19 will not have been the last pandemic; only the timing cannot be predicted.
Preparation therefore means not only developing vaccines and medicines. It also includes having laboratories, specialist staff, data infrastructures and international networks in place that can work together quickly in an emergency. Köhler points to the importance of European and international cooperation.
"That is why I very much hope that programmes such as the European Vaccine Hub for Pandemic Preparedness (EvH) or the European & Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP) continue to receive support," Köhler says in his Euronews interview. These programmes bring together research structures, laboratory capacity and experts.
"It is important to create a platform now that enables very rapid action and to have functioning cooperative structures in place when this Disease X arrives," Köhler stresses. "For that you need a network. Health has no borders, and neither do pathogens."

Delhi traders sought Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s intervention over losses allegedly caused by the October 10 protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), demanding compensation from those responsible for the disruption.The Automotive Parts Merchants Association (Regd.), Delhi, said customers stayed away from markets for four to five days before and after the protest call, resulting in heavy business losses.The association had said October, November and December were crucial for traders because of the festive season, including Navratri, Dhanteras and Diwali. It warned that repeated disruptions during this period could threaten the livelihoods of shopkeepers and their employees.
The trade body called for a transparent assessment of the losses and sought full compensation from the principal organisers and participants responsible for the disruption, arguing that traders should not bear the financial burden.It said shop earnings were used to support traders’ families and employees, pay rent, fund children’s education and cover medical expenses for elderly parents.The association also flagged the absence of basic emergency arrangements, including ambulances, fire services and first aid, at protests, warning that such gaps could lead to serious accidents.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Goldman Sachs has raised its forecast for Taiwan's economic growth in 2026 to 11.7%.
In a report released on Saturday, Goldman Sachs economists also raised their 2027 GDP growth forecast to 3.3%, up from 2.9%. The firm expects the Central Bank to begin raising interest rates in December, citing stronger domestic demand, per CNA.
The bank said domestic demand was strengthening broadly, prompting it to revise its monetary policy outlook from an expectation that rates would remain unchanged to a forecast of a rate-hiking cycle beginning in December.
Goldman Sachs now expects the policy rate to reach 2.125% by the end of 2026 and 2.375% by the end of 2027, compared with its previous forecast of 2% for both years.
The bank also maintained its bullish outlook for the New Taiwan dollar, citing stronger economic growth, a large current account surplus, the AI boom, and its assessment that the currency remains undervalued.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 11.05% in August, citing stronger-than-expected exports, investment, and consumption. The estimate was 1.41 percentage points higher than its previous projection, per a press release.
The Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research also raised its forecast for this year to 12.16% on Oct. 16, marking its third upward revision and the highest estimate among major forecasting institutions cited in its report. CIER attributed the outlook to robust AI-related demand and stronger domestic investment and consumption.
The think tank expects Taiwan's economy to grow 5.97% in 2027, compared with Goldman Sachs' projection of 3.3%. Forecasts vary because institutions use different assumptions about trade, investment, domestic demand, and the AI boom.
DGBAS is scheduled to release its preliminary estimate of third-quarter GDP growth this week. Its latest official forecast put full-year 2026 growth at 11.05%, while the Central Bank's September projection was reported at 11.48%.
The third-quarter release will provide a fresh indication of whether economic activity is running ahead of official expectations, per CNA.

Former US official says Taiwan’s value goes beyond strategic location
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:31:27 UTC
15:31:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Thomas J. Christensen warned that emphasizing Taiwan's strategic location could weaken efforts to deter a Chinese attack.
In an essay published Wednesday by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Christensen said Washington should focus on Taiwan's democracy, economic importance, and regional security rather than geography alone. He argued that focusing on Taiwan's location could imply unconditional US support for its defense, increasing tensions with China.
Taiwan sits at the center of the first island chain, which stretches from Japan to the Philippines. Christensen acknowledged its military importance but said preventing a Chinese attack matters more than denying Beijing control of a strategic location.
He said an attack on Taiwan would damage US credibility among Asian allies, regardless of any military advantage China might gain. A successful invasion could also encourage Beijing to use force in future disputes with neighboring countries.
Christensen noted that the Trump administration's 2025 National Security Strategy highlighted Taiwan's location as a key US defense concern. However, citing US Naval War College scholar Jonathan Caverley, he questioned how much additional military advantage China would gain from controlling Taiwan, given its growing military capabilities.
He warned that placing too much emphasis on geography could undermine Washington's policy of strategic ambiguity. Under this policy, the US does not explicitly state the circumstances under which it would intervene militarily to defend Taiwan.
Christensen argued that an unconditional US defense commitment could weaken support for peaceful unification within Chinese policy circles, increasing the risk of conflict. He also warned that stronger US guarantees could encourage Taiwanese politicians to pursue formal independence, further raising tensions with China.
Taiwanese officials have emphasized the country's strategic position as they seek stronger regional security cooperation. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) has warned about China's expanding military reach, while National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) has said Beijing's military activities threaten countries beyond Taiwan.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) has also called for closer security cooperation with Japan and the Philippines to counter Chinese threats. Christensen said Taiwan's emphasis on the first island chain reflects efforts to secure stronger defense support from Washington and Tokyo.
Christensen said strategic ambiguity has helped prevent major conflict in the Taiwan Strait for decades. He cited the Taiwan Relations Act and the Six Assurances as key parts of US policy that support Taiwan's security without guaranteeing military intervention.
He urged Washington to maintain its current approach and continue helping Taiwan deter a Chinese attack. He argued that protecting Taiwan's democracy and preserving regional peace offer stronger reasons for US support than geography alone.

India’s privacy law threatens newsrooms, media groups tell top court

By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court on Tuesday, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources, Reuters reported on Monday.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) told the judges.
“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission…it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The Supreme Court posted the case for next month.
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.

Europe must prepare for a 3°C warmer world, EU climate chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:30:44 UTC
15:30:44 KST

As Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, new EU rules will require governments to clarify who is responsible for climate preparedness – but no new funding is being offered to help households adapt.
The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
The move comes as Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, including scenarios involving 3°C of global warming by 2100.
Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said.
While the EU continues to pursue emissions reductions, the costs of adapting to a hotter world are becoming harder to ignore, from rebuilding after wildfires and floods to protecting homes, roads and public infrastructure.
The Dutch Commissioner estimated the economic damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion.
Asked what a 3°C rise above pre-industrial temperatures could mean for Europeans, Hoekstra pointed to heat plans for cities and the need to prepare infrastructure for a hotter future, rather than relying on historical weather patterns.
The reference trajectory is based on scientific research, including work by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and advanced European climate modeling, he said.
The Commission's projections envisage 2°C of global warming by 2050 and 3°C by 2100 for Europe, reflecting Brussels' assessment that Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average.
The trajectory is intended to be translated into national and local risk assessments, taking account of the uneven distribution of climate impacts.
“Even if we get all of this right, we have no way to avoid more summers than the one we saw last year,” the Commissioner said, arguing that readiness, resilience and preparedness must become the priority alongside emissions cuts.
The proposed legislation would require EU countries to specify whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for preparing for climate disasters.
Governments would retain flexibility over how they allocate responsibilities, but would have to specify who is accountable — an attempt to prevent political disputes over who failed to prepare when floods or wildfires destroy homes.
The Commission also wants climate scenarios to be considered when planning new roads, bridges and neighbourhoods, recognising that infrastructure designed for past weather conditions may no longer be fit for purpose.
"We want to introduce a culture of preparedness and resilience by design, rather than dealing with the damages in the aftermath, which is often very ad hoc and doesn't always build back better," a senior Commission official said on Monday on condition of anonymity.
No new money
However, the question of how to pay for climate adaptation remains unresolved.
No new financial commitment to household support is expected from the Commission's climate resilience strategy, despite concerns that ordinary citizens may struggle to afford the investments needed to adapt.
Hoekstra pointed to the Commission's proposal to devote 35% of the EU budget to climate and nature.
But the strategy's effectiveness will depend partly on the outcome of ongoing negotiations over the EU's next multiannual budget, with climate spending competing against priorities such as defence, security, competitiveness and agricultural support.
The Commission is also counting on the recently announced €30 billion from the European Investment Bank for climate adaptation through 2030.
Nonetheless, the lack of new funding is a potential weakness in the Commission's ambition.
The Commissioner argued that preventive investment is economically worth it but did not announce a new household support scheme or explain how the EU would ensure that lower-income households could afford necessary improvements.
In an attempt to fill the bloc's climate protection gap, Brussels wants to work with the insurance sector, as Commissioner Hoekstra pointed out that many areas in Europe are underinsured against climate disasters.
According to the senior Commission official, only around 25% of assets exposed to climate impacts are insured, leaving governments and property owners vulnerable to substantial losses.
“The fact that so many areas are underinsured” is one of the issues the Commission will examine, Hoekstra said.
The strategy could therefore expose another fault line between Brussels' climate ambitions and the cost-of-living pressures facing European voters.

North Korean artillery pointed south stirs concern at border observatory
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:30:44 CET
15:30:44 KST

By Hyun Young Yi and Brenda Goh
GIMPO, South Korea, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Visitors to a South Korean observatory that overlooks North Korea said on Tuesday that the appearance of artillery pieces with their barrels pointed south on the border was worrying, as tensions between the two countries intensify.
The two Koreas have traded barbs and strengthened their postures along the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating them since September, after a mine blast there wounded three South Korean soldiers. South Korea has demanded that North Korea apologise, while Pyongyang has accused Seoul of fabricating the incident.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, said last Thursday that Pyongyang would place loudspeakers that can blast anti-South Korean propaganda on standby along the entire border within days and had put unspecified new countermeasures on alert.
On Friday, South Korean media photographed an armoured vehicle in clear view near the frontier. By Monday, there were three with their gun barrels pointed south, according to a Reuters witness.
“I’d only seen on TV that North Korea had deployed 122-mm artillery, but seeing the area in person makes me realise just how real the danger is,” Jang Gil-seong, an 83-year-old war veteran who fought in the Vietnam War, said outside the Aegibong observatory, which overlooks North Korea’s Kaephung county from about 1.4 km away.
“I’m really concerned about how much South Korea will need to do to prepare for and respond to this threat in the future.”
The DMZ remains a draw for foreign and local tourists despite periodic flare-ups in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
Hannah Robbins, a 28-year-old tourist from Canada, said her tour group had only found out about the artillery pieces after their guide told them about the weapons at the observatory.
“We’re a bit scared obviously,” she said. “The tour guide was like ‘don’t worry, they won’t shoot’ but then it’s a bit of a worry that we have right now.”
Analysts identified the weapons as M-1981 122-mm self-propelled howitzers, an older North Korean artillery system believed to have entered service in the late 1970s.
They have a maximum range of about 24 km (15 miles), putting areas such as the South Korean town of Gimpo where the observatory is located within reach, although they are less powerful than newer artillery systems, said Yang Uk, a military expert at Seoul’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies.
“I would view this more as a display of firepower than a meaningful increase in combat capability,” Yang said.
“The fact that it was positioned where it can be easily seen suggests it was deployed to be noticed.”
South Korea’s military also described the weapons as an older system.
“While North Korea has mentioned new weapons systems in its recent statements, we believe that this cannot be considered as such,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young told a briefing on Tuesday.
(Reporting by Hyunyoung Yi, Brenda Goh, Daewoung Kim in Gimpo and Kyu-seok Shim in SeoulEditing by Ed Davies)

Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:28:13 UTC
15:28:13 KST

Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the polls
Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign wrapped up.
While Israelis go to the polls this week in one of the most consequential elections in years, many Palestinians in the West Bank have been confined to their homes or neighbourhoods as a wave of Israeli military operations around Hebron continues.
The West Bank city has been in a state of lockdown since two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at an army checkpoint at Hebron’s northern entrance on Friday, killing two Israeli soldiers and wounding three. After the suspects were killed, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the isolation of Hebron and said troops would go house to house in the gunmen’s neighbourhood. “We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.
What followed has been a mass displacement operation in the Hebron area, echoing last year’s military expulsions of three refugee camps, alongside widespread destruction in the neighbourhoods targeted by the army, evoking scenes out of Gaza.
During the weekend, soldiers ordered residents of al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods out by loudspeaker, according to residents. Thousands have been forced out of their homes already, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying people would not be allowed back “until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron”. By Monday, the governorate’s fourth day under closure, at least 3,171 Palestinians from 488 families had been forced out, according to Hebron Municipality data cited by the Wafa news agency. Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said Israeli forces had searched more than 500 homes, arrested more than 70 people and fragmented the city with 128 closed gates and 120 checkpoints.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society says the displaced include 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, and that at least 47 people have been detained in Hebron since Friday.
Bulldozers razed a three-apartment building belonging to Riyad Amrish, as well as a tile and ceramics factory, an auto-parts shop and other businesses in Farsh al-Hawa. Israel’s Channel 12 said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich ordered the demolitions.
Israeli NGO B’Tselem warned the operation amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
Sieges at every scale
But Hebron is only the most prominent of multiple sieges happening at different scales, with years-long efforts to strategically encircle Palestinian communities in the West Bank now being employed to devastating effect:
- Homes: The three-week siege by Israeli settlers of the family of Yusuf Shanaran in Wadi al-Rakheem, Masafer Yatta continues, with the family unable to leave or receive aid for days at a time without army coordination, Shanaran told Al Jazeera on Monday. In Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, village Mayor Marwan Sabah said Mohammad al-Obaiyat’s 1954 house received a demolition order with a November 11 deadline after months with a gate blocking its road. Settlers have since been filmed attempting to break into the family home, which has been besieged for nearly a month, with few supplies entering during that time.
- A village: Madama, south of Nablus, is only just emerging from a two-week siege of its four entrances, with heavy restrictions remaining at its just-opened northern entrance, according to villagers. A kindergarten principal there told Al Jazeera she lifts children over the barrier one by one.
- A region: Twelve Masafer Yatta communities in the southern West Bank were cut off for several days, with about 50 teachers unable to reach their schools, and Wafa reported that Bethlehem governorate’s roads were closed for several days.
- A territory: The Israeli army barred Palestinian workers from illegal Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday and will close all crossings on election day.
The only Palestinians who can vote – Palestinian citizens of Israel – may face issues at the polls, too; Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu’s Likud party was preparing to challenge results from Arab polling stations before a vote had been cast.
Olive harvest attacks
This year’s olive harvest has drawn unprecedented levels of settler pogroms, theft and closed-military-zone orders. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission has counted 482 attacks on the harvest by Sunday across nine governorates, Wafa reported.
At the same time, Israel released nine of 10 settlers arrested following last week’s attacks on a foreign journalist and diplomats. The attacks have continued undeterred. Wafa reported 17 attacks on farmers and their property on Thursday, and the commission documented 21 in 12 hours on Friday. The past week’s harvest-related incidents fall into a handful of repeating patterns:
- Theft of olives and equipment in at least a dozen villages, including Sinjil, Silwad, Berin, Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya, Kafr Malek, Ein Arik and Deir Ballut, according to Wafa and local reports. Near Immatin, at least 25 masked settlers sent three tractors and two trailers rolling down a hillside, destroying the equipment and olives on board.
- Assaults in at least 15 places, among them Burin, where stones left three farmers with head wounds; Ein Arik, where The Times of Israel reported a farmer suffered fractures; and Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya and Kafr Malek, where pickers were pepper-sprayed. Settlers fired live rounds at pickers in Berin and Osarin, and smashed cars and trucks in Marda, Wad Qaddoum and Sinjil, Wafa and local monitors reported.
- Detentions and expulsions in at least a dozen places. Fifteen farmers were detained in as-Sawiya on Sunday. In Beit Iksa, where the harvest had been coordinated with the Israeli Civil Administration, Mohammed al-Kiswani was pepper-sprayed and detained; settlers told farmers they would never harvest “with or without coordination”. Land at Deir Jarir and Turmus Aya was declared a closed military zone without orders shown, Ayed Jafry reported – and far-right influencers were brought to film the expulsions for campaign content.
- Damage to olive trees in at least 10 locations. Settlers burned dozens of trees in Burqa on Friday, keeping Palestinian Civil Defence crews out, according to Wafa; trees were set on fire in Immatin, Salem and Beit Furik; and a bulldozer uprooted hundreds in Madama, according to villagers. Soldiers uprooted dozens more in Deir Qaddis for a settler road and posted a notice at al-Mughayyir ordering hundreds of trees uprooted and in Khirbet Abu Falah for a “security buffer zone”, giving residents 24 hours to object, Jafry reported.
- Arson. In Burqa, settlers set fire on Tuesday to a memorial to Palestinian residents killed and, an hour later, to the home of Jamal Bajes, a Palestinian-American – the second arson at his house in recent months, according to local reports. Local activist networks reported a home was burned in Deir Abu Mishal, and Wafa said settlers tried to set another ablaze in Burin under army protection.
Those joining the harvests in solidarity were targeted, too. United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was among about 80 volunteers detained near Nahalin on Wednesday and released with a “warning”; Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused him of “harvesting headlines”.
Gaza: Managed scarcity as killings continue
The last week in Gaza saw at least 37 more Palestinians killed as Israel’s daily attacks continued. Monday’s daily report from the Gaza Ministry of Health alone recorded 11 deaths – eight newly killed, three recovered from rubble – and 35 wounded, taking the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,559 killed and 5,608 wounded, with a cumulative toll of 74,555.
Among those killed this week:
- Akram Yassin and his wife, Dina Abu Bakr, in a strike on their apartment behind al-Shifa Hospital on Tuesday.
- Majdi Mohammad Fakhri Hassan, a child, shot near the Happy City resort south of Khan Younis; Rafif Raed Lubad, 17, shot in the head in Jabalia; and Fatima Abu Laban, killed in Tal al-Dhahab, northwest of Beit Lahiya on Saturday, according to Wafa.
- Three security guards – Sami Baroud, Ashraf Dahlan and Shadi Abu Ataya – at the Islamic University in Gaza City on Sunday, after an earlier strike wounded seven students. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas operative.
For days, hunger worsened with crossings into Gaza shut: Flour stocks ran out, leaving seven of 20 commercial bakeries open, Abdul Nasser al-Ajrami of the bakers’ association told Wafa, and a tray of eggs reached a price of 60 shekels ($19.50).
The pressure began to ease somewhat on the evening of October 23, as Israel told traders that commercial goods would resume and an Egyptian committee delivered flour, Mohammad Abu Warda of the private sector’s emergency committee said.

Blood test could reveal prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:28:08 UTC
15:28:08 KST

Proteins present in men’s blood could give clues to prostate cancer risk years before diagnosis.
Distinctive proteins in men’s blood can signal a higher risk of prostate cancer more than 15 years before diagnosis, Oxford researchers have found.
“Finding proteins linked to known prostate cancer driver genes in blood collected years before diagnosis gives us new insights into the earliest stages of the disease,” said Karl Smith-Byrne, corresponding author of the study at Oxford.
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the European Union and second worldwide, after lung cancer. About 330,000 new cases are diagnosed every year and about 75,000 men die of the disease annually, in the EU alone.
Researchers at Oxford University analysed blood samples collected between 1992 and 2000 from more than 2,500 men. They compared baseline samples from 982 men who went on to develop prostate cancer with those from 1,573 men who did not.
The team measured more than 6,000 different proteins in each participant’s blood plasma. Because the samples were taken years before any diagnosis, sometimes more than 15 years, the researchers could look for early chemical warning signs — changes in proteins.
Some proteins were linked to a higher overall risk of prostate cancer, while others were associated specifically with aggressive or fast-growing forms of the disease. At the same time, men with higher levels of certain immune-system proteins, like GZMK and ANXA2, showed a lower long-term risk of prostate cancer, according to the study, published in the journal European Urology
“Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” said Zhe Huang, first author of the study and a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health.
“Ultimately, we hope this will help us understand the biology of aggressive prostate cancer and identify markers that could improve how we assess risk in the future,” Huang said.
The findings are not yet a screening test and need further validation, the researchers noted.
“Together with existing and future genetic evidence, these findings may help us identify biological pathways that could be targeted to prevent aggressive prostate cancer”, said Smith-Byrne.

At least 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in separate attacks on October 20 and 24 in Ethiopia’s Oromia region, with more than 20 others seriously wounded and 20 homes burned down, church officials said in a statement late on Monday.
“We have heard with deep sorrow the report submitted by the Diocese Office,” the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s Holy Synod said, describing the killings as “extremely tragic cruelty and suffering inflicted on our citizens”.
The church said 14 people were killed on October 20 in Gora Silingo, Angada Kebele, in Merti district, while another 46 were killed on October 24 in Tereta, Chole and Birbo in Shirka district.
Both districts are located in the Arsi Zone of central Ethiopia’s Oromia region.
The Holy Synod condemned the killings, saying the violence violated constitutional protections for life and religious freedom and threatened Ethiopia’s tradition of peaceful coexistence among different faiths.
It called on government institutions to publicly condemn the attacks, strengthen civilian protection and ensure those responsible are brought to justice.
The church also urged security agencies to provide additional protection to affected communities and take preventive measures against further violence.
The Oromia regional government has pledged to pursue those responsible for the killings.
According to local media reports, a local official accused a newly formed rebel alliance that includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) of carrying out the attacks. The OLA has previously denied allegations of targeting civilians.
The killings come amid continuing insecurity in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest regional state, where government forces have been battling armed groups for years.
In July, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi between 2021/2022 and June 1.
The Holy Synod said it would seek discussions with senior government officials to address the security crisis.
It also announced prayers for the victims on Monday and directed Orthodox churches and monasteries worldwide to hold similar services on Tuesday, following the Divine Liturgy.
The church expressed condolences to the bereaved families and called for urgent measures to ensure its followers could live and worship without fear.

Kazakhstan allocates over 122 billion tenge in recycling fees to waste management projects

Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan allocates over 122 billion tenge in recycling fees to waste management projects
Kazakhstan has allocated 122.6 billion tenge in recycling fees to finance 34 projects aimed at developing modern waste management infrastructure across the country, Qazinform News Agency reports via the country’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
With the ministry’s support, Zhasyl Damu joint-stock company is funding initiatives that include the construction of new recycling facilities, the establishment of waste sorting complexes, and the purchase of specialized equipment.
A total of 67 projects, worth 440 billion tenge, have been approved by the Investment Headquarters under the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Of these, 34 have already received funding.
Among the funded initiatives, six projects involve the construction of municipal solid waste sorting facilities with a combined annual capacity of 650,000 tons. Another 18 projects focus on expanding recycling capacity by a total of 435,000 tons per year, while 10 projects provide for the purchase of 177 units of specialized equipment.
As of now, 15 projects have been commissioned. Their implementation has resulted in the purchase of 131 units of specialized equipment, the launch of waste sorting lines with a combined annual capacity of 290,000 tons, and the commissioning of recycling facilities capable of processing 19,300 tons of waste annually.
The largest share of funding has been allocated to projects in Almaty, North Kazakhstan, Pavlodar, Aktobe, and Kostanay regions. Initiatives are also being implemented in Atyrau, Akmola, Mangistau, East Kazakhstan, Abai regions, as well as Astana, Shymkent, and other parts of the country.
The projects cover nearly all major areas of the waste management sector, including the recycling of waste paper, PET bottles, used car tires, and other waste materials. They also involve modernizing existing facilities and upgrading fleets of specialized equipment.
Work on new projects is ongoing. Several initiatives are currently at different stages of review, approval, and preparation for funding in accordance with established procedures.
Under Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code, recycling fee revenues are allocated to support such initiatives. Their implementation is expected to strengthen the country’s waste management infrastructure, increase recycling volumes, reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills, and promote the reuse of secondary raw materials in the economy.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan would build waste-to-energy plants.

A storm is set to sweep into southern Israel on Election Day, bringing a risk of significant flash flooding and road disruptions. Moisture from a Red Sea trough, a low-pressure system that extends north from the Red Sea, will move into the south by Tuesday afternoon.
