Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:48 UTC
15:15:48 KST

Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect change
Elections cannot stop the accelerated process of ‘recolonisation’ of 1948 Palestinian communities.
For the majority of Israelis, the general election on October 27 is a choice between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the forces that oppose him, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot. But for the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the population, the upcoming polls present a different dilemma.
As the political mainstream in Israel continues to shift to the far right, Palestinian citizens face growing threats to their political and collective rights. Palestinian communities in Israel experience increased violence, while settlers are encroaching on their boundaries. The recent push to expand policing and militarisation of civilian life is another source of growing anxiety within the Palestinian population.
In this context, the anti-Netanyahu bloc does not seem to offer the prospect of policy reversal or change. Therefore, the question on many Palestinian minds is whether voting in the Israeli elections can make any difference at all.
Recolonisation of 1948 Palestine
Since the Nakba of 1948, the Palestinians who managed to remain in their homes in what was declared as territory of the new State of Israel have had a different fate than the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. In 1952, they were granted Israeli citizenship, and in 1966, the martial law under which they were forced to live was lifted.
Although Palestinian citizens of Israel have the right to vote and participate in politics, citizenship has not shielded them from the broader system of dispossession and attempts to reshape their Palestinian identity and national belonging.
Through land confiscation and the regulation of education and culture, the Israeli state has sought to detach Palestinians from their historical roots and collective past, promoting instead a model of the “Arab Israeli” as a citizen whose identity is separate from its Palestinian and Arab national context.
Formal citizenship has not secured substantive equality for Palestinians as they face discriminatory laws, systemic underfunding of basic services, and political and socioeconomic marginalisation.
Instead of engaging in direct violence towards Palestinian citizens – as it has done in the West Bank and Gaza – the Israeli state has instead “outsourced” brutality to criminal networks.
As a result, Palestinian communities have faced killings, shootings, bombings and arson while Israeli law enforcement has largely ignored the problem. More recently, this problem has escalated, as organised crime groups obtained advanced weapons reportedly stolen from Israeli army stockpiles or smuggled across borders. This growing militarisation of organised crime has claimed hundreds of lives.
In parallel, Israeli settlements next to Palestinian communities have expanded, accompanied by accelerated seizure of land. This process of “recolonisation” began in mixed cities, such as Jaffa and Lydd, where religious-nationalist settler groups started establishing themselves in Palestinian neighbourhoods in 2021.
Since October 2023, this process has accelerated. In August, Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich unveiled his party’s plan to “Judaise” the Naqab and northern Israel. He proposes to add one million Jewish residents to the two regions, establishing 40 new settlements and dozens of farms, expanding existing settlements, and creating hundreds of thousands of new housing units.
The idea is to extend the model of territorial control from the occupied West Bank into the Naqab and northern Israel, where Palestinian communities are concentrated.
There are also indications that the policing of Palestinian towns and villages could increasingly fall under the National Guard, established under National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The idea of creating the force was prompted by the May 2021 protests, known as the Dignity Uprising, which spread across Palestinian communities in Lydd, Haifa, Umm al-Fahm, and dozens of other towns and villages.
Ben-Gvir has advocated expanding the state’s capacity to suppress such unrest. Although the National Guard’s precise role and operational framework remain under development, its potential deployment against mass protests raises serious concerns about the right to protest and the protection of democratic freedoms.
The government has strengthened settler security squads and integrated them into a broader security framework, raising concerns about the growing role of armed civilian groups in enforcing control over Palestinian communities.
At the same time, Ben-Gvir has widened access to personal firearms, issuing 300,000 gun licences since taking office.
Together, these measures normalise civilian policing and deepen the militarisation of everyday life, reinforcing the unequal distribution of coercive power in a society structured on the dispossession and subordination of Palestinians.
The Palestinian response
Parties seeking to represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, such as the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, have long argued that parliamentary participation and support for the anti-Netanyahu camp can help remove the far right from power and halt its settler-colonial agenda. But the party’s own track record proves this premise wrong.
Ra’am joined the coalition government formed after the elections in 2021, which excluded Netanyahu, but it failed to bring about fundamental changes in the conditions of Palestinian citizens. The coalition was fragile and often rocked by deep ideological contradictions.
In 2022, Mazen Ghnaim, a member of Ra’am, publicly acknowledged that he could not push through policies that would benefit the Palestinian population, despite his party being part of the ruling coalition and despite promises being made that such policies would be accepted. He also lamented the heavy criticism he faced whenever he was visiting Palestinian communities.
Ra’am’s experience in that coalition illustrated the challenge of sustaining Palestinian political participation in a government whose other constituent parties uphold exclusionary nationalist policies.
The problem, therefore, extends beyond Netanyahu himself: Palestinian support for the anti-Netanyahu camp cannot translate into meaningful policies that challenge the broader structures of discrimination and dispossession Palestinian citizens of Israel face.
Voting may offer a way to slow down this project, but it cannot reverse the deeper transformation taking place within Israeli society. The cultural shift towards fascism extends beyond the government and its political leadership, becoming increasingly embedded in social attitudes and everyday life.
That said, I believe another four years of far-right rule would pose an immediate threat to Palestinian communities and their rights. Therefore, I will vote in Tuesday’s election.
But Palestinians need to recognise that electoral participation must be accompanied by a more radical political response capable of confronting the structures and ideologies driving this transformation. This requires, among other things, reforming the High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel and rooting it more firmly in Palestinian society through popular committees and grassroots organising.
It also demands a broader commitment to democratisation and de-Zionisation across historic Palestine, as part of a larger political project aimed at building a different future through alternative institutions, mechanisms, and forms of collective action.
Whatever the Israeli state might claim, the fate of the Palestinian citizens of Israel is tied to the fate of the rest of the Palestinian population. That is a realisation that Palestinian political leaders must finally embrace.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

How you can access free public transportation to get to polling booths on Election Day - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:44 UTC
15:15:44 KST

Free intercity public transportation is available across Israel on Tuesday, Election Day for the 26th Knesset, with the benefit extending to all passengers, not just eligible voters, according to Walla. The service is funded by the Central Elections Committee.
Free travel began at 8 p.m. on Monday and will continue until public transportation services conclude Tuesday night.
The benefit applies to about 660 intercity bus routes longer than 15 kilometers, up from 600 routes during the 2022 elections, as well as all Israel Railways lines.
However, city buses, light rail services, the Metronit bus rapid transit system, and Haifa's Carmelit underground railway will continue to charge regular fares.
Passengers can check whether a specific intercity bus route is included in the arrangement by calling the Transportation Ministry's information hotline at \*8787.
How can passengers travel for free?
Intercity buses: Passengers can board eligible buses free of charge without presenting identification, obtaining a ticket, or validating a Rav-Kav public transportation card.
Israel Railways: Passengers must obtain a special paper ticket from station ticket counters or ticket machines. To avoid unnecessary charges, they should not use tickets or passes loaded onto their Rav-Kav cards or public transportation apps.
Additional trains on Jerusalem-Tel Aviv route
Due to anticipated demand, Israel Railways will run three trains per hour in each direction between Jerusalem's Yitzhak Navon Station and Tel Aviv from noon until 8 p.m. Tuesday, up from the usual two trains per hour.
Some of the additional services will begin and end at Tel Aviv's HaHagana Station.
In addition, police have restricted the number of passengers traveling to and from Jerusalem. Passengers are therefore required to obtain a personal travel voucher in advance for their selected train.
Due to expected congestion, railway staff will enforce the voucher requirement. Vouchers can be obtained free of charge through the Israel Railways website.
Will travel to Eilat also be free?
Different eligibility requirements apply to passengers traveling to and from Eilat.
Free travel on these routes is subject to an eligibility check based on the passenger's registered residential address and advance registration through Egged's information center at \*2800.
Rail passenger numbers could break 2022 election record
During the previous elections for the 25th Knesset on November 1, 2022, Israel Railways recorded a roughly 33% increase in passenger numbers, rising from 249,146 on a typical weekday to 331,706 on Election Day.
That record is expected to be broken this year.
The free transportation initiative is estimated to cost NIS 3.5 million and will be funded by the Central Elections Committee through the Transportation Ministry.
Passengers are advised to check updated schedules and service changes through the Israel Railways website, its official app, the \*5770 information hotline, or the railway's official WhatsApp channel.

Finance Ministry prepares plan to prevent increase in deficit, fund defense, for next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:15:36 UTC
15:15:36 KST

Even before the exit poll results of today's elections are known, the Finance Ministry has already prepared a plan that includes a series of harsh economic measures, intended, among other things, to finance the defense budget and prevent an increase in the deficit and the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Some of the measures were planned in cooperation with the Bank of Israel. The next government will be responsible for implementing the policy.
In addition, after Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich subsidized gasoline prices by NIS 1 per liter over the past two months to prevent price increases, the subsidy, which has cost more than half a billion shekels, will end Saturday night. As a result, gasoline prices will surge by at least NIS 1 per liter at midnight on Saturday, and may rise further as global fuel prices climb.
The price of a liter of self-service 95-octane gasoline is expected to reach NIS 8.90. However, the dollar's roughly 1% decline against the shekel yesterday will help moderate the increase.
Higher fuel prices are expected to trigger price increases across a range of other goods and services whose rates have so far been frozen at the government's initiative, including electricity, water, and public transportation. This is expected to drive up the Consumer Price Index.
The freeze on adjustments to income tax brackets, tax credit points, and National Insurance contributions, along with the current VAT rate, will remain in place in 2027 under existing automatic budgetary provisions.
Revenue from these measures is estimated at NIS 10 billion. In addition to ending the gasoline subsidy, further tax measures will be proposed to boost state revenue.
These include mandatory reporting of income from residential property rentals and taxation of rental income from the first shekel earned. Currently, rental income of up to NIS 5,654 per month is exempt from tax. Some of these legislative initiatives have been held up in the Knesset Finance Committee.
Another proposal would impose a tax on international content providers operating in Israel, commonly referred to as the "Netflix tax." Another measure expected to be implemented is a reduction in tax benefits on pension contributions, along with a recommendation to eliminate VAT exemptions for sectors that currently benefit from them.
Economic measures aim to fund increased defense budget
Broader macroeconomic measures are aimed at finding sources of funding for the required increase in the defense budget, which is expected to reach NIS 187 billion.
One almost certain source of funding will be sharp cuts to coalition funds, alongside sweeping efficiency measures across government ministry budgets.
The main challenge facing the coalition forming the next government will be the immediate need to pass a 2027 budget, or potentially a two-year budget covering 2027 and 2028. The budget must include comprehensive reforms under the Economic Arrangements Law.
As a result, the Finance Ministry is unlikely to secure approval by the end of 2027, so it will need to prepare a continuing budget.
The timetable for implementing these measures is tight, and the parties that make up the new coalition will have to begin taking action even before the next government is formed.
Stock exchange unfazed by Netanyahu crypto economy warning
Meanwhile, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange appeared unfazed yesterday by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's dire economic warnings over the weekend concerning the crypto economy.
Trading opened lower yesterday, the final trading day before the elections, against the backdrop of Netanyahu's statements warning of possible sanctions, cuts to US aid, and the prospect of a shift toward a shadow economy.
However, the trend quickly reversed, and the stock market moved into positive territory, with the exception of banking stocks.
The stock exchange has declined since the beginning of the month amid uncertainty over the elections. Now, however, traders appear to be cautiously optimistic about the possibility of change.

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:12:04 UTC
15:12:04 KST

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Majd al-Krum’s peaceful protests have forced settlers to withdraw, but fears of further provocations loom after elections.
Majd al-Krum, Israel – The police closed the road to al-Rus, so the villagers found other ways up there.
Beginning on September 13, local Palestinian citizens of Israel made the steep climb to the pine-covered hilltop above Majd al-Krum using horses, off-road vehicles and on foot. A couple of weeks earlier, settlers from the occupied West Bank had begun building an outpost there, on village land – one of the first such attempts on this side of the Green Line, the name used for the boundary between Israel and the occupied West Bank.
The young Israeli settlers said they were there to graze livestock with a Jewish National Fund (JNF) permit. But there was no livestock, noted Hussein Mannaa, 50, a lawyer and member of the town’s Popular Committee. Within a week, the camp had grown from a handful of people to between 25 and 30, according to villagers, with a kitchen, a toilet, a water line and electricity.
Villagers rushed to the scene, so police closed the road to the site. Yet local Palestinians came in droves nonetheless.
Anas Sgaier, a 21-year-old law student and youth organiser, made the nearly hour-long climb up the mountain. “I remember one moment: I’m going up and it’s hard for me to breathe,” he said. “And to my right, I saw an older woman, in her 80s, with her husband … walking up 50 minutes, just to show her presence.”
After almost a week of peaceful protests that saw hundreds of Palestinians from Majd al-Krum and across the region come every day, the JNF ordered the settler tents removed. By September 16, the site was cleared out.
The village had won, for now.
A ‘pilot’ experiment
A little more than a month later, Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, and Palestinian villagers fear al-Rus was a prelude to what may come next. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is campaigning on a promise to “Judaise” the Galilee, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up a large proportion of the population, and says he will repeat there “the revolution we carried out in [the occupied West Bank]”.
“The al-Rus experiment is like a pilot … experiment: ‘come on, let’s see the reaction’,” said Husein Khalaily, 50, an economic consultant, while sitting at his home in Majd al-Krum.
Reaction was swift: the village’s Popular Committee met as soon as the rumours of the settler outpost were confirmed and, with the local council, called daily demonstrations. “The popular struggle alongside the legal track is what bore fruit,” said Mannaa, a mainstay at the weeklong demonstrations at the site.
It was young people who drove the protests, villagers said. “Bring your coffee and come,” beckoned Sgaier in Instagram posts alongside his cousin. “We’re only going up to drink coffee, because that’s our land.”
“Not only the people of Majd al-Krum: Deir al-Asad, al-Bi’na, Sakhnin, Arrabeh … from the Naqab they came,” recalled Mannaa. Some left-leaning residents of nearby Jewish communities also turned up. “There was this incredible solidarity,” said Khalaily.
Hanan, a Palestinian Christian from a nearby village, said the outposts she read about in the occupied West Bank had felt far away – until Majd al-Krum. “I never saw the Arab community so united and really fighting for their lands,” she said.
Smotrich came to Majd al-Krum, a village long known for its political activism, to campaign with a police force and a water cannon. “The young people were hot-blooded and wanted to go out and confront him,” Khalaily said, but the local committees and political parties talked them down.
But the targeting continued. On September 18, police announced the arrest of a 32-year-old Majd al-Krum resident over alleged contact with a Lebanese agent. Smotrich seized on it, saying Galilee residents were “in the atmosphere of October 6”, a reference to the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
‘The language is clear’
On August 27, Smotrich posted a plan promising one million more Jews and 40 new Jewish communities in the Galilee and al-Naqab, another area of Israel where many of the residents are Palestinian. His party then released an AI-generated video in which a West Bank Palestinian frantically warns a relative in the Galilee that “the Jews are coming” to “do to you what they did to us”.
Sgaier said he and his friends laughed at the absurdity of the video. Then they watched it come to life at al-Rus.
“He came here and said it clearly: ‘I want to Judaise the Galilee,’” said Khalaily. “Back in the day, they used to say, ‘we want to develop the Galilee.’ Today – the language is clear.”
Villagers believe the recent provocations are intended to create a pretext for making that happen, where Palestinian citizens hold rights that Palestinians under military occupation in the West Bank do not, making dispossession a harder proposition. “Building the outposts, they wanted to lead the people into a confrontation,” said Mannaa. “They want to impose a state of chaos because chaos benefits them.”
The settlers pointed to a grazing permit granted on the land of al-Rus from the quasi-governmental JNF. But according to Khalaily, the plot, about 8.4 dunams (roughly two acres), is half privately owned by his cousin, and half administered by the Israel Land Authority, which has long refused to partition it so the owner can tell which part is his.
“They chose Majd al-Krum because it’s hard to break,” said Mannaa, pointing to the village’s history of defiance since the Nakba in 1948, when many villagers were expelled from their homes. “If they break Majd al-Krum,” said Khaled Kewan, 27, a singer from the village, “[it’s] going to happen all over the Galilee”.
The JNF later said the “grazing” initiative would move to another plot about 500 metres away on land villagers consider theirs. But the village rejects any relocation, “even one tent”, Mannaa said.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the JNF, the Israeli police and the Israeli Finance Ministry for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
‘Coming not just for Majd al-Krum’
Whether Smotrich remains in power depends on the election results on Tuesday – where the Palestinian vote will likely figure prominently. Polls suggest neither of the main Zionist blocs can reach 61 seats without support from the Arab parties.
Turnout by Palestinian citizens of Israel has hovered between 45 and 65 percent in recent years. However, organisers believe the demographic’s turnout may hit 70 to 75 percent, a level last seen in 1999.
After the settlers’ attempts and provocations in Majd al-Krum, Mannaa boldly predicted the town “will go past 80 percent”.
Khalaily, a longtime boycotter who has only ever voted once, now urges turnout at every talk he gives. “These prominent racists who are there now have to be removed, even if just for a stage,” he said. He sees little difference between Netanyahu’s government and its likely replacement, “except that Smotrich and [far-right National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir won’t be in it”.
After October 7, fear kept Palestinian citizens away from demonstrating. “People got busy with other things,” said Khalaily. “Busy with fear, with making a living.” Crime in the town made it worse. “I’ll be sitting here at night and I hear the sound of shooting,” said Khalaily, who has children who witnessed three men murdered. “Nothing moves. It’s become normal.”
Palestinian citizens have more rights than those in the West Bank, leaving them caught between a system they oppose but must live in. “We here have the most to lose,” he said, “because we’re settled on our land and we stayed on it.”
As a result, many stayed quiet in recent years. “We left Gaza alone, left the West Bank alone, left Lebanon alone,” said Sgaier. “I said after that our time is coming.”
“I just didn’t expect it to come this early.”
However, after Smotrich’s rhetoric and the settlers’ local incursions, “the people who were indifferent about the elections, who didn’t want to take part or vote: the matter provoked them,” said Mannaa. “They know well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”
Some, like Sgaier, will still boycott. “What happened in Majd al-Krum, we solve it by going out [to] the street – not through the Knesset [parliament] and the laws,” said Sgaier, who sees little difference between the two Zionist political blocs. “They don’t want Palestinians here.”
Sgaier believes there was a real change where it counts: on the streets. During the protests at al-Rus, he saw people he never expected. “They are not politically engaged,” he said, “but they came, too”.
The settlers’ tents are gone, leaving only sparse remains and Hebrew graffiti proclaiming “the nation of Israel lives”. Nonetheless, villagers keep trekking up the mountain every day. Families barbecue there, and schoolchildren draw and play music.
During the weeklong protests, Khaled Kewan would leave al-Rus in the evenings to go to a recording studio. He and fellow musicians from the town made the song “Ibn Bladi”:
“Oh, land of mine, land of my ancestors!” he sings. “No matter how many walls they build across my country … I am a son of this land, a son of my own country.”
The inspiration was clear, but Kewan deliberately chose not to name Majd al-Krum explicitly. “Haifa’s my town too, Akka’s my town too, Sakhnin’s my town too, Arraba’s my town too … I love the whole homeland,” he said.
The settlers’ “Judaisation” efforts, he said, “are coming not just for Majd al-Krum, but for the whole Galilee.”

Centre to train 10,000 healthcare workers in drug de-addiction by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:08:41 UTC
15:08:41 KST

The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme (Representative Image)
NEW DELHI: With the Centre targeting a drug-free India by 2029, the health ministry has launched a nationwide capacity-building programme to train 10,000 healthcare professionals in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of substance use disorders, including addiction to alcohol, opioids and other drugs.Union health minister J P Nadda launched the programme on Monday under the Vision Document on Narcotic Control 2026-2029, stressing that tackling substance abuse requires coordinated action by healthcare, social welfare and law enforcement agencies. The ministry aims to train 2,000 personnel in the current financial year, followed by 3,000 in 2027-28 and 5,000 in 2028-29.The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme, with the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS, serving as the coordinating centre. The other institutions are NIMHANS, Bengaluru; PGIMER, Chandigarh; Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi; Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Delhi; and AIIMS Bhubaneswar.The training will combine live online sessions, self-paced courses and in-person programmes. Doctors and medical officers will undergo a 12-week online training course featuring lectures and clinical case discussions, while nurses, community health officers, auxiliary nurse midwives, counsellors and psychologists will have access to specialised modules.
The curriculum will cover substances ranging from alcohol and cannabis to opioids, sleeping tablets and inhalants, as well as addiction among vulnerable groups, including women and adolescents.More than 800 nominations have already been received through the health ministry and the National Health Mission for online and offline training. Around 150 personnel from de-addiction centres supported by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment are also expected to undergo in-person training over the next two months.Nadda said fragmented efforts among government departments had created gaps in coordination and service delivery. Effective implementation of the narcotic control strategy, he said, would require clearly defined responsibilities, sustained inter-ministerial coordination and collective accountability. He also stressed the need to strengthen de-addiction centres through training, institutional support and adequate resources.
At the launch, Nadda released the second edition of Substance Use Disorder: Manual for Physicians (Management of Addictive Disorders). First published in 2005, the revised manual incorporates advances in the understanding and treatment of addiction and is intended to help doctors manage substance use disorders in both specialised facilities and general healthcare settings.The initiative follows the Vision Document on Narcotic Control unveiled by Union home minister Amit Shah in June 2026. Besides enforcement against drug trafficking, the strategy assigns the health ministry the task of expanding access to evidence-based addiction treatment by strengthening the skills of medical and allied healthcare personnel.Officials said the programme would draw on the clinical expertise and training infrastructure of the six institutions to improve the availability and quality of addiction care across states and Union territories.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Russia's assault on Ukraine's energy grid is a war crime, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:05:16 UTC
15:05:16 KST

The United Nations has determined that Russia's frequent and intentional attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure constitute a war crime, a U.N. inquiry report said on Oct. 26.
In recent months, Russian forces have strategically escalated attacks on Ukraine's energy grid in the lead up to the freezing winter months to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure, despite U.S. President Donald Trump having called for an energy ceasefire.
"Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter," a report from the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concludes.
Last winter, the Kremlin also focused its attacks on energy sources, leaving millions of Ukrainians without power in temperatures as low as minus 21°C.
Based on interviews with 255 people who endured these conditions across Ukraine, the commission concluded that "Russian authorities have committed the crimes against humanity of other inhumane acts."
One interviewed man described how, during winter, he would attempt remain awake through the night out of fear of falling asleep and dying from the cold. "The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up; it was like torture to be scared of dying from cold," he said.
"The waves of attacks by Russian authorities against Ukraine's energy infrastructure were carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering," the report outlines.
In addition, the report outlines how Russia's recruitment of soldiers from third countries also violates human rights law. Recruitment from 29 other countries through lies and coercion counts as human trafficking, the report finds.

Court rejects eastern border bunker procurement tender appeal
The Supreme Court of Estonia on Monday rejected a company's appeal challenging the tender to procure concrete bunkers to be installed along Estonia's eastern border.
The court decided on Monday not to hear a cassation appeal by Nordic Shield Group AB, in which the company sought to challenge a tender organized by the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) for the procurement of concrete bunkers.
RKIK's Baltic Defense Line project manager Armin Siilivask told ERR that Monday's court decision means the procurement process can now proceed.
"Now that the court has made its decision, our aim is to continue with the procurement according to the planned schedule, so that we can, if possible, reach the signing of a contract as early as March next year. To do this, the necessary procurement procedures must be carried out: conducting bidding rounds, holding negotiations, carrying out checks and evaluations and, if everything goes smoothly, signing a contract with a suitable bidder," Siilivask said.
Nordic Shield Group's appeal focused on the tender's production quality standard and the required ISO certificate.
RKIK said the certificate submitted by Nordic Shield Group did not meet the requirements set out in the tender conditions.
Estonia's aim is to install 600 concrete bunkers along its eastern border by the end of 2027 as part of the Baltic Defense Line. RKIK announced a tender for the procurement of the bunkers in 2025.

====================================================================================================

Animal panic and air pollution: Why Switzerland is set to vote on a nationwide firework ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:02:12 UTC
15:02:12 KST

Fireworks have already been banned in the Netherlands earlier this year on safety and environmental grounds.
Swiss citizens are gearing up for an explosive vote: whether to ban noisy fireworks.
Spurred on by animal welfare and environmental groups, the citizen-proposed ‘popular initiative’ will be put to the ballot on 29 November.
“For pets, wild animals, and farm animals, fireworks are not a celebration, but pure stress,” says non-profit Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection), which is supporting the initiative.
The proposal also calls for better protection for people and the natural environment against noise, air pollution, litter, accidents and fires caused by fireworks.
An initial Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) poll released on Friday (23 October) showed promising support for the ban, with 69 per cent of voters backing it.
While the proposal proved most popular among left-wing voters, it received majority support across the political spectrum, and particularly among women.
Votes like these are common in Switzerland, where any citizen or group can launch an initiative by gaining 100,000 valid signatures from eligible voters. Recent examples include the neutrality initiative, rejected in September, and the pending nuclear disarmament initiative.
Would it mean a complete ban on fireworks in Switzerland?
The proposal seeks to “significantly restrict particularly loud and disruptive fireworks” in private settings by banning the sale of noisy pyrotechnics. Quieter alternatives would still be permitted, such as sparklers and fountain-style volcano fireworks.
It would also allow ‘cantons’ (local areas) to grant exemptions for events of “supra-regional significance”, such as 1 August (Swiss National Day) and New Year’s Eve, but still with a focus on quieter alternatives.
Currently, Swiss cantons and communes may restrict or ban the sale and use of fireworks on a local level. Age limits and licensing requirements also govern their use.
STS says the initiative, ‘For a restriction on fireworks’, would create a clear rule for the entire country.
But industry association the Swiss Fireworks Coordination Office (SFK) argues that the proposal is a “threat to Swiss tradition”, while some politicians have said that it would infringe on citizens’ personal freedoms and should be left up to the cantons to govern.
The Swiss People’s Party, the Centre Party and the Swiss Trade Association have launched a campaign to vote against the measure, warning of its impact on business owners and potential to fuel a "prohibition culture".
After initially being submitted in 2023, the proposal received over 137,000 signatures. A failed counter-proposal in summer means it will now be followed by a public vote.
If successful, it could see Switzerland follow in the footsteps of the Netherlands, where a broader firework ban came into force this summer, primarily for safety reasons but also on animal and environmental welfare grounds. Other countries in Europe have their own rules and restrictions, such as Belgium where the use of large, powerful fireworks is restricted to professionals only.
How do fireworks impact the environment?
When fireworks explode, they release tiny dust particles, which are rich in toxic metals from the gunpowder and colouring compounds they contain.
According to the Swiss Federal Office of Police, between 1,000 and 2,000 tonnes of fireworks – three-quarters of which is made up of packaging – are used annually in Switzerland, producing between 200 and 400 tonnes of particulate matter per year.
This accounts for two-to-three per cent of the country’s annual particulate matter emissions, according to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).
As well as contributing to air, water and soil pollution, these fine particles can be inhaled with harmful health impacts, particularly for vulnerable people with existing conditions.
Unfavourable weather conditions can heighten the harms, such as fog which can trap particles in the air for longer, or hot and dry conditions which can increase wildfire risk.
FOEN urges responsible disposal of used fireworks, which can be placed in regular household waste once cooled down, while packaging should be recycled as normal.
Fireworks trigger ‘fear, panic and disorientation’
Animal welfare groups have been vocal in their support of a firework ban.
“The sudden noise triggers fear, panic, and disorientation [in animals],” says STS. “The consequences range from flight behaviour and acute stress to injuries or even death. Protecting animals from unnecessary noise is therefore a central concern of animal welfare.”
Speaking in a campaign video for the initiative, Swiss veterinarian Maruschka Blaser says that animals hear high-pitched sounds and loud bangs more acutely than humans. Giving horses as an example, she says “things can become dangerous very quickly when they run uncontrollably because of fireworks”, either for people in crowds or other animals in fields.
“When it comes to domestic animals such as cats and dogs, they sometimes need to be given medication to calm them down days in advance” of firework displays, says Blaser. “I also know families who spend the night in an air-raid shelter with their pets, but somehow that isn’t a solution either,” she adds.
“Millions of pets live in Switzerland. For many of them, fireworks trigger stress or panic,” says Casimir von Arx, President of the Bern branch of Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection SAP) in a campaign video. “We can only protect them if, as a society, we show consideration for one another.”

Dating costs in Europe: Which cities are cheapest and most expensive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Dating can be costly across Europe. Some cities are incredibly expensive, but the picture changes when salaries are taken into account.
Do you think about money when planning a date? And does your financial situation affect whether you feel ready to start a relationship?
Romance is not only about feelings. Dating also costs money. A coffee, a drink or a dinner can put pressure on your wallet. And for some people, money may affect not only where they go on a date, but whether they want to start a relationship at all.
So, how much does dating cost across Europe? The answer varies widely from city to city according to the Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute.
What is included in the Cheap Date Index?
The Cheap Date Index includes one bottle of wine, one pair of jeans, one dress, two coffees, one meal for two people in a mid-range restaurant, two cinema tickets, two one-way public transport tickets and a 5km taxi trip.
As the index includes a pair of jeans and a dress, clothing can account for a large share of the total cost. So, it may not reflect only the cost of the date itself.
The prices come from Numbeo, which is not an official data source. Its prices are crowdsourced from users.
Switzerland most expensive, Turkey cheapest
Among 28 European cities, two Swiss cities rank at the top. The cost of this date basket is €407 in Geneva, and Zurich closely follows at €400.
Istanbul is the cheapest city for a date, but the basket still costs €168. It also costs less than €200 in the Italian capital, Rome (€195).
The simple average across the 28 cities is €270. The figures reflect prices in mid-2026.
Dating is also quite expensive in the Nordic countries. Oslo and Copenhagen share third place at €323. Stockholm ranks sixth at €310, while Helsinki is eighth at €296.
The UK is more expensive than other major economies
Among Europe’s largest economies, London is the most expensive city at €317. Another British city, Birmingham, is also in the top 10 at €290.
Paris is close to the European average at €279. In Italy, the date basket costs €278 in Milan but just €195 in Rome, showing significant differences within countries.
The three German cities on the list are all below the European average and very close to each other. A date costs €260 in Munich and €254 in both Berlin and Frankfurt.
The two Spanish cities are also among the cheapest. The date basket costs €219 in Madrid and €213 in Barcelona.
Among other cities, the cost is €294 in Dublin, €290 in Edinburgh, €271 in Brussels, €263 in Amsterdam, €250 in Vienna, and €225 in Warsaw and Lisbon. It is €222 in Athens and €214 in Prague.
Europe at the top
Eight of the 10 most expensive cities are in Europe. Europe also has 14 of the top 20 and 20 of the top 30. Istanbul is the only European city among the 20 cheapest.
A cheap date costs €270 on average across the 28 European cities whereas it costs €195 in the other 41 cities.
Globally, Tel Aviv-Yafo ranks third at €365 and is the only non-European city in the top five.
New York ranks eighth (€308), Los Angeles 13th (€288) and San Francisco 14th (€281). Sydney (€270) is close to Amsterdam (€263), while Dubai (€243) is close to Berlin (€254). Singapore and Madrid both cost €219.
Tokyo (€161) and Seoul (€163) are cheaper than Istanbul (€168). Hong Kong (€196) is also close to Rome (€195).
When income is considered, the rankings reverse
The nominal prices alone tell only half the story. Zurich and Geneva have the most expensive cheap dates, but they also have the highest salaries. That means a date takes the smallest bite out of pay there: 5.6% of a monthly net salary in Zurich and 6.4% in Geneva.
Luxembourg (6.6%), Amsterdam (6.7%) and Frankfurt (7.2%) follow.
The picture reverses in southern and central Europe. A cheap date in Athens costs €222. This is just over half the price in Zurich. Yet it takes 19.6% of an average monthly net salary of €1,132, the highest share among the 28 European cities. Istanbul (16.7%), Lisbon (16.3%) and Budapest (15.6%) come next.
The salary figures are city-level estimates from Numbeo cited by Deutsche Bank. Still, they are broadly in line with the shares calculated using Eurostat’s annual net earnings for a single person without children earning the average wage. Eurostat figures are national averages, rather than city-level data.
Using Eurostat data, the share of the date cost would be 7.2 percentage points lower in Athens at 12.4%. In Lisbon, it would be 12.6%, rather than 16.3% using Numbeo’s salary estimate.
Examining the link between income and readiness for a relationship using US data, Johanna Peetz and Geoff MacDonald found that the financial well-being of young adults is linked with romantic desire, perceived readiness for relationships, and actual transitioning into intimate partnerships.
Chen-Hao Hsu and Henriette Engelhardt also found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.
Another study found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.

Seeking guaranteed snow? These are Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:32 UTC
15:00:32 KST

A new study has ranked Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions. Here are the top destinations to consider for your next active winter getaway.
Choosing where to go on a ski holiday involves more than finding a great resort, especially if you have a need for speed, slopes and adventure.
Snow conditions, the reliability of snowfall throughout the season and whether lifts and slopes are open can make a huge difference to your ski holiday.
Although no destination can completely promise perfect conditions, Inghams Ski has analysed more than 100 popular ski resorts and regions in the Northern Hemisphere to create the “Reliable Ski Score” ranking, with scores out of 100.
The travel operator measured each resort for mountain running (35%), which looked at the average percentage of lifts and slopes operating during the core season; and for snow adequacy (25%), which looked at the percentage of core-season days with 30cm or more at the base station.
Other factors included consistency (20%), or how steady mountain running was from season to season; downside protection (12%), which is the gap between the average season and the worst one; as well as average snow depth of the mountain (8%).
Each resort and region’s historical performance was studied during the core season period of 5 January to 20 March across seven Northern Hemisphere winter seasons between 2017-2018 and 2025-2026, with the exception of the seasons impacted by Covid-19.
The results see Italian, Austrian and French destinations dominate the top 10 ranking of Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions.
Top 10 most reliable ski resorts and regions in Europe
How the destinations scored out of 100 in the study:
- 1. Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy: 93.1
- 2. Obertauern, Austria: 92.9
- 3. Les Arcs, France: 92.2
- 4. Les 3 Vallées, France: 91.1
- 5. Alpe d’Huez, France: 90.5
- 6. Kitzsteinhorn, Austria: 89.6
- 7. Filzmoos, Austria: 89.5
- 8. Tignes-Val d'Isère, France: 89.4
- 9. Espace San Bernardo (La Rosière/La Thuile), France: 89.2
- 10. Damüls Mellau, Austria: 89.1
A look at the top three most reliable ski resorts and regions
Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy
According to the Inghams study, Pontedilegno-Tonale in northern Italy is Europe’s most reliable region for skiing.
The mountainous area between Valle Camonica in Lombardy and Val di Sole in Trentino is a standout destination for its glaciers, nature reserves and high-altitude areas. It was highlighted for its consistent performance across reliability factors, giving skiers “practically hiccup-free exploring alongside snow-sure slopes”.
The ski area is home to 46 slopes, with the highest point of the resort sitting at 3,016 metres above sea level. Ponte di Legno’s slopes take skiers through dense pine and spruce forest, while Passo del Tonale sits at the foot of the Presena glacier and the skiing area features more than 44km of slopes.
During selected dates of the ski season, Inghams recommends taking advantage of the “Alba in Quota”, or “dawn at high altitude” window of opportunity. Here, lifts open earlier for skiers to experience sunrise skiing before the slopes officially open for the day.
Obertauern, Austria
In Austria’s Salzburg region, at 1,752 metres, the Obertauern ski resort emerged as the second most reliable in Europe.
It offers beginners and advanced skiers alike more than 100km of slopes across a long season from November through to May. And, as Inghams highlighted, the area is made up entirely of ski-in/ski-out hotels, giving visitors direct access to pistes from their accommodation.
Obertauern is also replete with cross-country ski trails, with routes ranging from six to 23km, including the medium-difficulty Gnadenalm. At an altitude of 1,350 metres, the trail sits halfway between Obertauern and Untertauern, earning the name "snow basin" because of its unique location.
Les Arcs, France
Rounding up the top three is Les Arcs. The French ski resort nestled in the heart of the Alps is set amid alpine meadows, glaciers and a peak that reaches 3,226 metres.
The mountain resort features 200km of ski trails with a winter season set to start on 12 December this year and will last until 24 April 2027.
Part of Paradiski, one of the world’s largest interconnected ski areas, Les Arcs is described as an “excellent choice for both freestyle enthusiasts as well as those looking for reliable conditions”. Les Arcs is also connected to Peisey-Vallandry and La Plagne via the iconic Vanoise Express cable car. Paradiski features 425km of slopes and 258 ski runs between the three linked resorts.

Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall could make or break the next EU budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

Brussels faces a highly charged mix as the fight over the next EU budget overlaps with the efforts to plug Ukraine's €70 billion gap.
The fight over the European Union's next seven-year budget has entered a critical new phase, one that could make or break the deal.
In a striking coincidence, the heated negotiations have overlapped with the effort to fill Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall for 2027.
Brussels had long suspected that Kyiv's accounts would show a sizable gap next year, as Russia escalates its war and devastates the levers of the domestic economy. But it was not until this month's summit that the €70 billion figure was validated.
Leaders then asked the European Commission to present possible options for providing the additional financing, with joint debt immediately emerging as the most feasible path.
The bloc is expected to cover two-thirds of the request, roughly €46 billion. Other allies, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan, should take up the rest.
The vast scale of the deficit prompted a change of agenda in next month's special summit, which was originally planned to focus exclusively on the draft budget.
The meeting has been extended to two days, 26 and 27 November, to accommodate discussions on Ukraine. Fresh proposals are expected on both fronts.
Technically, the two issues remain separate files. But politically, diplomats and officials say, they are becoming rapidly intertwined.
"These are the most pressing issues for the remainder of the year, definitely," a diplomat said, cautioning it was still too early to talk about one big package.
Two key reasons explain the entanglement.
First, the two are about money.
The budget battle pits the so-called “Frugals”, or “Sensible Six”, against the “Friends of Cohesion”, with the two camps clashing over which budget envelopes should be cut and by how much. The "Frugals", which happen to be the net payers, demand steep reductions across the board, while the "Friends" want to preserve bigger volumes.
Second, the two face a pressing deadline set by the French election.
Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far-right National Rally, who is firmly ahead in polls, has vowed to cap her country's contribution to the budget at €5 billion a year and warned sealing a deal before the election would be a "democratic scandal".
The incumbent, Emmanuel Macron, told his fellow leaders that reaching a deal between January and April would be "complicated".
The same logic now applies to Ukraine. As part of her programme, Le Pen has promised to halt all French support for the war-weary country.
"This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell (Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) the truth," she said earlier this month.
Easier or harder?
The prospect of a Le Pen win in the spring weighs heavily on officials and diplomats in Brussels, who admit both open issues – the budget and Ukraine – must be resolved by the end of the year before the window of opportunity closes.
The closer the election, the narrower the space for high-stakes decisions.
"Our internal cohesion is fragile. If that starts to unravel, the consequences for Ukraine could be even greater than anything Trump says or does," a national official said, referring to the US president's recent shift to Russia.
"We need a structural solution for financing Ukraine. We can't keep scrambling at the end of every year under pressure. Support for Kyiv needs to be properly built into the next budget. It's good that these discussions are coming together in November."
However, it is not yet clear whether Ukraine would make it easier or harder to agree on the budget, which remains stuck in maximalist red lines from the opposing camps.
One school of thought holds that reaching a deal may be easier because the “Frugals” includes some of Ukraine's largest bilateral donors – Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany – who have a vested interest in locking in the fresh funding.
A strong collective decision on Ukraine could make it more politically palatable for them to accept – or rather, tolerate – a bigger budget than they might have wished.
"It might be helpful to get it done," another diplomat said.
But an alternative view is that the “Frugals’” continued push to cut funding for agriculture and cohesion policies could make it impossible for some “Friends of Cohesion” to back a deal on Ukraine without triggering a backlash at home.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are signalling they will exempt themselves from any joint debt to support Kyiv. Bulgaria, a vocal critic of weapons deliveries, is expected to follow suit. All of them sit in the cohesion group.
Making matters more difficult, the talks will unfold against a bleak backdrop of elevated energy prices, high borrowing costs and public discontent across Europe.
"It would be very dangerous, and I want to make this absolutely clear, if anyone tried to link the financing of Ukraine to the budget," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said.
"It would be a miracle if we reached an agreement in December."

Ukrainian media face pressure as they step up scrutiny of authorities in wartime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

Ukrainian media face pressure as they step up scrutiny of authorities in wartime
President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, on April 22, 2025. The president has not had a major press conference open to all media since February 2025. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Over the past year, Ukrainian independent media have stepped up investigations into corruption among top officials and abuse in the military, despite the constraints and risks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Yet this work is coming at a cost. Ukrainian media have faced a wave of lawsuits, controversial court rulings, threats, and smear campaigns on social media.
"An environment is gradually taking shape in which it is becoming increasingly difficult for journalists to do their jobs," Inna Vedernikova, a journalist at the Ukrainian newspaper Dzerkalo Tyzhnia, told the Kyiv Independent. "The space for freedom of speech is shrinking."
Despite the pressure and nearly five years of working under the full-scale invasion and martial law, the journalistic community remains robust. In the Reporters Without Borders' 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Ukraine climbed seven places to 55th worldwide — above the U.S. and some European countries.
But Ukrainian journalists and editors describe a less optimistic reality, pointing to persistent threats that make it difficult to hold power to account.
From wartime consensus to scrutiny
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Ukrainian journalists put the criticism of the government on hold, as the country rallied behind the war effort.
"(The war) has led to an unprecedented rise in self-censorship," Yurii Nikolov, a journalist at the media outlet Nashi Hroshi, told the Kyiv Independent.
In their turn, the authorities were expected to play by the rules and act responsibly.
At the same time, to unify the nation’s media policy amid the invasion, the authorities also merged all major television channels into one state-controlled pool. It has stayed that way ever since.
But several months into the invasion, the wartime consensus began to unravel. The first corruption investigations appeared before the end of 2022.
In recent years, a series of major corruption scandals has erupted, prompting independent journalists to step up their scrutiny of the government and bringing criticism of the authorities back into the public sphere.
Vedernikova said, despite the invasion, "it quickly became clear that a journalist's role — asking direct questions and pointing out problems — had not gone away."
As independent media resumed their investigations, those under scrutiny began to retaliate.
After a series of scandals in 2023-2024, when some journalists faced surveillance and persecution by law enforcement, the pressure shifted toward other arenas, including the courts and online smear campaigns.
Inna Biletska, head of investigations at the public broadcaster Suspilne, said that “the underreformed law enforcement sector and judiciary create fertile ground for those implicated in investigative reporting to push back."
There is also a growing number of SLAPP lawsuits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation), according to Kateryna Dyachuk, head of freedom of speech monitoring at the Institute of Mass Information, a non-profit watchdog tracking press freedom.
Courts and lawmakers
The most direct pushback has come through the courts and parliament, and it risks changing what journalists can publish.
One of the defining moments came in July, when a Ukrainian court banned the Anti-Corruption Action Center, the media outlet Slidstvo.info, and journalist Alina Stryzhak from publishing a specific investigative report. The report focused on the brother of Oleksiy Sukhachov, head of the State Investigation Bureau. It exposed him as the owner of a staggering real estate portfolio.
Although courts had previously upheld libel lawsuits against Ukrainian media, a ban on an investigative report before publication appeared to be unprecedented.
Maksym Savchuk, a journalist at Slidstvo.info and a co-author of the report, said the ban did not apply to him, so he sent the investigation to other media for publication. It was published by 27 other outlets in an organized effort.
"The investigation that the court tried to suppress went on to receive 4 million views, and I doubt it would have reached anything close to that number had it not been for the court order and the publicity surrounding it,” Savchuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Libel suits have long been a tool of pressure. Hromadske’s head of investigations, Yaroslava Volvach, said the outlet faced enormous pressure from the late Andriy Portnov, a former ally of pro-Russian ex-President Viktor Yanukovych who was widely seen as wielding immense influence over Ukraine’s judiciary.
In 2023-2024, Portnov sued both Hromadske and the Kyiv Independent’s editor-in-chief for libel. Lower courts initially upheld the suits, but the Supreme Court rejected them in May 2026. Portnov was shot dead in Madrid in May 2025.
Another blow to free speech came in October 2025, when the Supreme Court restricted what media can report about criminal cases. Back then, the court banned Dzerkalo Tyzhnia from naming a suspect in a criminal case and ordered the outlet to remove his name.
In August, Dzerkalo Tyzhnia reported that Dmytro Borzykh, a lawyer and former prosecutor, was also seeking a court order barring the publication of his name as a suspect until a guilty verdict against him enters into force.
"This approach is fundamentally at odds with European standards," Dzerkalo Tyzhnia’s Vedernikova said. "A journalist cannot declare someone guilty of a crime before a court has convicted them. But informing the public that a specific person has formally been named a suspect by law enforcement… is an entirely different matter."
Parliament may add to the pressure.
In April 2026, the Ukrainian parliament approved a draft of a new Civil Code in the first reading. The draft would allow individuals to request the removal of information about them from search engines and databases if it has "ceased to be of public interest."
A separate clause would introduce the concept of a company's “digital image" and require the company’s consent for data processing. This could make due diligence harder and limit corporate transparency.
"If journalists once investigated something — a corruption case, for example — all of that material would eventually have to be removed from the internet altogether," Dyachuk said.
The draft of the new Civil Code was met with public outcry over several controversial provisions. It is still being revised, and no final vote has been scheduled.
Risks of investigating the military
Investigating abuse in the military has brought a different kind of pressure: direct threats, often with little response from law enforcement.
In February, the Kyiv Independent and the Brazilian TV channel SBT published an investigation into alleged abuse and torture within a Brazilian unit of Ukraine’s International Legion, which led to the death of a Brazilian recruit. The same month, the unit’s commander threatened journalists from both outlets, accusing them of taking money from Russia and saying they would be “identified” and “located.” Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR), which oversees the unit, said in March that the unit’s command had ordered a probe into the threats.
In a separate incident, a Security Service (SBU) official came to Kyiv Independent CEO Daryna Shevchenko’s apartment building in September 2025 and attempted to collect information about her. The SBU said the official’s activities were not linked to Shevchenko, and that it was a misunderstanding. A month earlier, the Kyiv Independent published an investigative story about Fire Point, Ukraine’s biggest new defense producer, and the company’s management threatened to report journalists to the SBU over it.
Other outlets have faced the same and more.
In June, the Ukrainian media outlet Babel published a report on alleged excessive battlefield losses, inadequate medical care, coercion, and physical abuse at the Skelia assault unit.
Following the publication, Mykola Kharkhan, a soldier at the unit, released a video accusing the author of the report of working for Russian money and saying such reports would not stay "unpunished.” Skelia's press office said that such threats are unacceptable.
Kateryna Kobernyk, Babel's chief editor, told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet is mostly afraid not of Skelia's leadership but of "retaliation and unpredictable behavior by specific individuals within Skelia."
Babel said in July that it had reported the threat to the State Investigation Bureau and the police, who initially failed to react and open a criminal case. The bureau later said it had opened an investigation.
"I believe that, from what I know, law enforcement agencies are currently working very slowly and somewhat unprofessionally," Kobernyk said about the case.
Also in July, the State Investigation Bureau searched the facilities of drone maker Vyriy, whose co-founder Oleksii Babenko holds a 75% stake in Babel. Some interpreted the searches as an effort to pressure Babel, although Babenko himself denied this.
Kobernyk said that Babel's editorial operations are independent of Babenko but "Babel's reporting may have served as a trigger" in an attempt to deal a blow to Vyriy.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from the State Investigation Bureau.
Ukrainian freelance journalist Anna Kaliuzhna, who covers the front line, has faced pressure over her investigations of the military.
Kaliuzhna said she had received death threats in 2024 from a battalion commander at the 3rd Assault Corps, after she accused the brigade's leadership of using its political influence to get better battlefield conditions.
The police investigation into the threats "is not making any progress," she said.
"They haven't questioned any of these people or ordered any forensic examinations to confirm that the messages were actually sent from those phones," Kaliuzhna told the Kyiv Independent. "No one has been charged."
In March 2026, Kaliuzhna published a post criticizing alleged violations at the Skelia and 225th Assault Regiments. She said she had received around 150 messages pressuring and insulting her from fighters of the two regiments.
In July, the Ukrainian outlet Texty published her investigation into the 225th, alleging soldiers were beaten, shot at, jailed, and even killed. Both regiments said they could not comment. The police told the Kyiv Independent they are investigating the threats, but no charges have been brought yet.
The Kyiv Independent has also requested comment from the 3rd Assault Corps.
"I just hate the fact that I don't feel any safer behind the front lines than I do at the front," Kaliuzhna said.
Conscription as leverage
The authorities also have quieter tools, and conscription is one of them. A number of media outlets, including independent ones, have the “critically important” status, granted by the government, which allows them to obtain draft exemptions for their staff. So far no independent media outlet has lost that status, but some fear it could become a pressure tool.
“We have seen the fact that Ukrainska Pravda has critical infrastructure status… increasingly used in the rhetoric of Telegram channels and bloggers affiliated with the authorities, as well as by bots on social media,” Andriy Boborykin, CEO of the Ukrainska Pravda media outlet, told the Kyiv Independent. “It was entirely predictable that the conscription exemptions granted to journalists at independent media outlets would become a target for manipulation.”
In the past, officials have used conscription as a means of exerting pressure on the media.
In 2024, military enlistment officials attempted to draft Yevheniy Shulhat, then a journalist at Slidtsvo.Info who was investigating the wealth of a top SBU official. The media outlet identified that the enlistment officers were getting instructions from a subordinate of the SBU official Shulhat was investigating.
A green light to disregard media
President Volodymyr Zelensky and his office have also come under fire for failing to communicate with the media about policy changes, corruption scandals, and other pressing domestic issues.
The president and his office often ignore journalists’ requests for comment, and Zelensky does not give interviews to independent Ukrainian media. Instead, the president opts to send voice messages via a WhatsApp group chat with reporters run by his team and to hold closed-door briefings with groups of journalist. (Editor's note: The Kyiv Independent is often invited to these briefings). After a briefing, Zelensky’s team picks which quotes can be published, with the rest being off-limits.
According to two people who have long worked with the president, he doesn’t want to face anticipated questions about corruption, domestic political crises, and reforms that would arise in a sit-down interview with independent Ukrainian media.
The last time Zelensky held a major press conference was in February 2025. In August, Ukrainian journalist Danylo Mokryk, a reporter with the Kyiv Independent’s War Crimes Investigations Unit, filed a petition for Zelensky to hold a press conference and invite independent media. The petition was blocked for unclear reasons. Several more petitions were filed by Mokryk’s followers, until eventually one was accepted and published. It gathered the necessary 25,000 votes in late September, giving the president 10 working days to respond. Zelensky ignored the petition.
“The country’s current leadership is trying to create an environment in which the doors are closed to journalists who criticize the government and point out its mistakes,” Savchuk said.
Yevhen Buderatskyi, a deputy chief editor at Ukrainska Pravda, said that the outlet “has no access to government officials.”
“They keep telling us that the President’s Office doesn’t really allow them to talk to us,” he added. “It’s difficult to obtain information. It’s hard to speak of any real progress for freedom of speech.”
The President’s Office has not responded to the Kyiv Independent’s request for comment.
Smear campaigns online
Another threat to journalists comes from social media.
Telegram, one of the most popular sources of news for Ukrainians, is often used for smear campaigns against journalists and activists, and some of the channels are reportedly linked to the authorities and top officials.
“Telegram channels can reach huge audiences and say virtually anything they want,” Dyachuk said. “They can take money to publish paid-for content, while at the same time facing no real accountability for the information they put out.”
Sevgil Musayeva, chief editor of Ukrainska Pravda, also told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet “is very often targeted by online bots or supporters of various political parties.”
Difficulties with funding
Financing independent journalism is another challenge.
A major blow to Ukrainian journalism came in 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended most of the projects of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). USAID had been a major source of funding for many Ukrainian independent media.
Journalists interviewed by the Kyiv Independent said, however, that they had adapted by shifting their focus to European grants and other sources of funding.
Another source of funding — the advertising market — has shrunk due to the war. But advertisers have also faced political pressure.
Musayeva said in 2024 that the President’s Office had been pressuring advertisers to stop dealing with her outlet. In June 2026 she said that the pressure had ceased after Andriy Yermak, then Zelensky’s chief of staff, was forced to resign in November 2025.
The ousting of Yermak revealed one of the stranger attempts to pressure journalists. At his arrest hearing in 2026, prosecutors revealed that the former head of Zelensky’s office texted his psychic the names of Musayeva and another Ukrainska Pravda journalist, in what appeared to be a request to curse them.
Musayeva also said in 2024 that Ukrainska Pravda’s owner Tomas Fiala had received offers to sell the outlet, and that she believed it to be a form of pressure by the authorities.
“The pressure (on the media) is growing, and the most frightening thing is that it is becoming the norm,” Musayeva told the Kyiv Independent.
“You don’t even take these threats seriously anymore because they are essentially constant.”

Landowners could scupper free Land Registry access plans, campaigners warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

Plans by the government to give the public free access for the first time to information on who owns England’s land are at risk of being scuppered by landowners, campaigners have said.
On Tuesday the government set out its proposals to lift the paywall on the Land Registry, arguing that opening it would help the UK build more houses, protect nature and improve strategic planning. The plans will be open to public consultation for eight weeks.
The Guardian has previously revealed that there are internal rifts between the government and the Land Registry – an “arm’s length body” that comes under the oversight of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government but acts largely independently – over how far to open it to scrutiny.
Guy Shrubsole, author of Who Owns England?, urged people to get involved. “The government has put forward a bold but sensible proposal to open up the Land Registry and reveal who owns the vast majority of land in England and Wales – a question that goes back to the Domesday Book and has always been entwined with wealth and power,” he said.
“But the country’s biggest landowners may still try to scupper these plans at the last hurdle. It’s up to us peasants to stage the most gentle of revolts, by submitting our views to this public consultation.”
The proposals would for the first time allow public sector bodies, including government departments and local authorities, to access the information free of charge. This should make it easier for councils to identify sites for new homes, schools, hospitals, environmental assets, water infrastructure and public transport.
A new free public dataset would identify the owners of significant land-holdings, covering the vast majority of land in England and Wales, but excluding ordinary homeowners. More sensitive information might also be available to investigators, civil society groups and regulators who can demonstrate a clear public interest.
A government spokesperson said: “We are improving access to the Land Registry’s database to help fill in the gaps on who really owns land in England – with at least 10% currently unknown. By driving up land transparency we can make smarter decisions on building the homes and infrastructure we need, while delivering a crucial win-win for the economy and nature.”
Campaigners welcomed the move. Roger Mortlock, chief executive of the Campaign to Protect Rural England, said: “Our finite land supply is facing an unprecedented squeeze. Making it easier to find out who owns what will help us make the most of every hectare, whether for homes, infrastructure, food or nature’s recovery.”
Gavin Lane, president of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents landowners and rural businesses, warned of the possible impact of opening the register further.
“Making more personal information public could leave families vulnerable to fraud and other risks, especially as AI makes it easier to steal and misuse people’s identities,” Lane said. “Greater transparency should not come at the expense of people’s privacy, security and safety.”
Many landowners have been reluctant to have their holdings made public, and are likely to fight the proposals. Shrubsole said: “Centuries of secrecy over who owns our land might finally be coming to an end – but only if enough members of the public respond to this consultation.”
