Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:47:36 UTC
14:47:36 KST

Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington?
Pakistan has gained diplomatic visibility under Trump, but analysts question how much the relationship has delivered.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Addressing a mixed crowd of the diaspora and policy experts in New York late in September, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar was asked about challenges in New Delhi’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump.
“Well, I think if I stand back and look at the relationship … I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” Jaishankar responded.
Pakistan – perhaps uncomfortably for rival India – is an exception.
Trump’s tumultuous second term has seen him rock the global economy with tariffs and the Iran war, upend decades of trust with traditional US allies, and attempt to shred international law and the institutions that govern it. From Europe to the Middle East to East Asia, allies that counted on a US security umbrella are scrambling to build alternative partnerships, unable to rely on Washington for help if they are attacked. Leaders of nations that have been staunch US supporters have instead found themselves targeted – often personally – by Trump.
Yet amid this churn, Pakistan has managed to turn what was a deeply troubled relationship with the US into a partnership that Trump repeatedly touts, even as the government in Islamabad has faced mounting criticism domestically over allegations that it is crushing political opposition and entrenching military rule in all but name.
As the US holds its midterm elections on November 3, with the power in the House of Representatives and Senate at stake, Pakistan is one country that will prefer success for Trump and his Republican Party, which at present is expected to lose critical seats in both chambers.
“The prime minister of Pakistan – terrific man – said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that,” the US president said, addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September, referring to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif – and to a war that appears to have endeared Islamabad to Trump.
A closer relationship
After decades of strong ties, US-Pakistan relations had plummeted in recent years, as successive US presidents built close ties with rival India, and Islamabad was seen in Washington as duplicitous over its role in supporting both the US and, at the time, the Afghan Taliban.
As presidents, Trump in his first term and then Joe Biden used harsh words to describe Pakistan.
But two months into his second term, in March 2025, Trump thanked Pakistan in his address to Congress for helping arrest a suspect in the 2021 Abbey Gate bombing at Kabul airport.
Then, in May, came a major turning point. India and Pakistan fought an intense, four-day war after armed fighters killed 26 tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir. The war ended in a ceasefire on May 10. Trump announced it first, and Pakistan thanked him for mediating it, but India rejects his account, insisting that the war was ended through bilateral talks.
Since then, Pakistan’s top leadership has been welcomed at the White House, tariffs on its exports have been cut, and Islamabad has mediated between Washington and Tehran in their ongoing war.
Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for lunch at the White House – the first time for a Pakistani army chief who is not the country’s president. Trump has described Munir as his “favourite field marshal”.
Pakistan also nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. On October 9, the day the Nobel Peace Prize was announced for South African jurist Navi Pillay, Sharif posted on X: “President Donald Trump played a historic role in advancing peace in South Asia. His timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire, that is holding till today.”
Analysts say Islamabad’s relevance to Washington extends beyond South Asia.
“Pakistan is now an important player that must be seen within the Middle East security framework,” Qamar Cheema, executive director of the Islamabad-based Sanober Institute, told Al Jazeera.
A trade deal in July 2025 cut US tariffs on Pakistani goods from 29 to 19 percent. Memorandums of understanding with US firms on minerals, cryptocurrency and drones have followed.
Imran Khan, a geopolitical analyst and former Pakistan country director at the United States Institute of Peace, said Islamabad’s closeness to Trump had significantly raised its diplomatic profile.
“But at the same time, you could say that Pakistan has not gained anything directly from the Americans, apart from some intangibles: Its diplomatic profile and its geopolitical relevance,” he told Al Jazeera.
Mediation and the Gulf
Following the US-Israel attacks on Iran in February, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran on April 8 and hosted the highest-level direct talks between the two sides since 1979.
In June, the US and Iran agreed to the 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. “Pakistan was able to bring the United States and Iran under one roof after 47 years,” Cheema said.
But the 60-day period for further talks expired in mid-August without an extension.
Munir returned to Tehran on October 20, his fifth visit since the war began. Iranian officials said they had nothing new to offer Washington. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said threats and military manoeuvres would not influence Iran’s decisions. No breakthrough was announced.
“The Iran war continues to loom large in the Gulf, especially as there are increased indications that the US, possibly again with Israel, will relaunch attacks after their respective elections,” Grace Wermenbol, a former US national security official and senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, told Al Jazeera. Israel’s elections are scheduled for October 27.
The congressional test
Trump goes into the midterms with historically low popularity numbers. His approval rating stood at 30 percent in a Pew Research Center survey conducted between September 28 and October 4, down from 37 percent in January.
Khan, the analyst, said Democrats would prioritise treaty alliances such as NATO if they won both chambers.
“[In that case], the Senate and the House of Representatives, where the Democrats would have a majority, would lean more towards India than Pakistan,” he said.
Wermenbol, who is also an executive director of the Paris-based advisory firm Boussole Mondiale, said allies and partners were asking whether the midterms could shape US foreign policy in the short term.
In the longer term, she said, the result could foreshadow a change in the White House in 2028 or 2029.
For Pakistan, the question is how to position itself.
Cheema said Pakistan should not shape its approach around whether Trump’s influence grows or weakens. Its strength, he said, lay in its Middle East relevance and role in protecting US interests.
“It is not just a question of Trump’s weakening influence. It is a question of how Pakistan can stay relevant,” he said.
Khan said a weaker Trump might change little in the short term but warned that it could mark the beginning of the end of Pakistan’s current importance.
“But what it does not change is Pakistan’s amplified geopolitical profile globally, and its increasing national security and defence relevance in West Asia,” Khan told Al Jazeera. “That is not going to change whether the Trump administration is strong or weak, or whether Trump is around or not.”

Spanish language learning surges in China but teachers are in short supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:45:43 UTC
14:45:43 KST

Spanish language teaching is booming in China, with enrolments up 12.6% between 2023 and 2025. But the Cervantes Institute says there's a shortage of teachers to meet rising demand.
The number of children choosing to learn Spanish in China is growing at an incredible rate, according to new figures from the Cervantes Institute.
Enrolments in Philology degrees, optional subjects and Spanish as a foreign language courses have soared by 12.6% between 2023 and 2025. However, this post-pandemic surge has coincided with a shortage of staff.
In a speech in Beijing to launch the "Spanish in the World 2026" yearbook, Luis García Montero, director of the Cervantes Institute said: "Teachers tell us that demand for Spanish keeps rising in the wake of the pandemic, which is why we are prioritising teacher training: quite simply, more teachers are needed."
The document was presented at the symposium 'Spanish in China: Evolution and new dynamics', organised to mark the 20th anniversary of the institution in Beijing. The second part of the yearbook pays tribute to this milestone with several analyses of the impact, evolution and reach of the language in the education system of the Asian giant.
Between the market and the humanities
China is approaching 98,000 potential Spanish speakers, a group made up of more than 18,000 native residents and some 66,000 students of the language. This boom in Spanish is reflected in data from the Global Spanish Observatory: the language is now offered in 31 Chinese cities and up to 98% of universities in the country already teach a degree in Hispanic Philology.
García Montero spoke of the "essential dialogue between China and the Spanish-speaking world", driven decisively by Latin America, but he did not hide his misgivings about teaching that is increasingly geared towards the market. Although the language is gaining ground in business, engineering and science, he warned that philology is losing weight: "In the current dynamic of commercialisation, the humanities are in decline, and that is something that worries us."
The map of Spanish in China counts 55,000 university graduates after "an expansion at extraordinary speed", as explained at the event by SISU vice-dean Yang Ming. However, the professor highlighted the new demands of the business sector: the market no longer looks only for translators, but for multidisciplinary professionals able to master the language alongside law, accounting or business management.
The world’s third native language
Globally, Spanish now has 640 million users with some degree of proficiency, after growing by 1.5% in the last year, which means 10 million more Spanish speakers. The "Spanish in the World" yearbook also underlines the weight of the language in migration flows: one in ten native speakers already lives in non-Spanish-speaking countries.
In its 27th edition, the report explores the role of the language in strategic areas such as machine translation, digital media and the presence of Spanish in Europe. With more than 520 million native speakers (second only to Mandarin Chinese and Hindi) and 95 million speakers with limited skills (+3.3%), Spanish is consolidating its position among the most widely spoken languages in the world. Within the Spanish-speaking sphere, the report counts around 460 million native speakers and more than 20 million people with partial knowledge.
Without including students, Spanish has more than 137 million potential users in countries where it is not an official language. The United States leads this group with the largest pool of speakers outside the Spanish-speaking world, driven largely by its native community.
From AI to challenges in the classroom
With almost 50 million potential speakers in the EU, the yearbook also points to the fragile state of creole and contact varieties, which together do not reach one million people (0.2% of the global total).
Among the more than 24 million students of Spanish worldwide (+7% in two years), the contrast between continents is striking: while Brazil has suffered a 46% decline due to changes in legislation affecting public schools, Africa is seeing vigorous growth, driven by formal teaching in countries such as Cameroon, Ivory Coast, Benin, Morocco and Tunisia.
In the digital environment, Spanish stands out as the second language with the strongest presence on websites and has 72 million learners on Duolingo (two thirds of them English speakers). Digital reading leads in Spain (31.7%), Mexico (21%) and Argentina (20%), while audiobooks are gaining ground.
In artificial intelligence, Ibero-America accounts for 14% of global traffic for AI solutions, above its share of total internet users (11%). This growing demand, according to the yearbook, is reshaping the consumption of information and securing the language’s weight in the new era of virtual assistants.
Two decades of the Cervantes Institute in Beijing
The programme opened with a debate around the exhibition 'Truths and Lies. The power of fiction', with the participation of journalists, curators and renowned local artists such as Xu Bing and Zhang Peili. Several round tables focused on methods for teaching Spanish, updating textbooks and the pedagogical application of artificial intelligence.
Following the presentation of the yearbook, Inmaculada González Puy, director of the Cervantes Institute in Beijing, and Hispanist Lu Jingsheng held a discussion titled 'Spanish in China'. The sessions were rounded off with contributions from ambassador Marta Betanzos Roig, Chinese education official Chang Fuliang and prestigious academics such as Carme Riera and Darío Villanueva.

SPK raises investor thresholds, extends fund deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:38:49 UTC
14:38:49 KST

Türkiye’s Capital Markets Board (SPK) raised financial thresholds for qualified investors on Oct. 26 and extended the deadline for investment funds to comply with portfolio and investment limits to Jan. 31, 2027.
For clients applying for professional status, the total financial asset threshold rose from 10 million Turkish Liras to 50 million liras.
The trading volume threshold increased from 5 million liras to 25 million liras.
The changes also apply to qualified investor requirements linked to professional client rules.
An exemption for investors buying units in real estate and venture capital investment funds was abolished, making them subject to the general thresholds.
Existing investors who obtained their status through financial criteria must provide written or electronic evidence to their investment firm that they meet the requirements.
Those who fail to do so will be limited to selling their holdings in instruments reserved for qualified investors.
Citing recent market developments, the SPK also scrapped interim compliance deadlines of Oct. 31 and Nov. 30 for funds’ portfolio and investment limits.
Full compliance, previously required by Dec. 31, is now due a month later.
The board removed a provision in its fund guide covering exemptions for financial instruments of public institutions and their affiliates, while preserving corresponding provisions in the underlying regulations.
Separately, the SPK temporarily suspended the capital market activities of Tera Portföy and Pusula Portföy and expanded the liquidation of their funds.
The decision covers investment funds, including real estate and venture capital funds, outside the liquidation orders issued on Sept. 17.
Türkiye İş Bankası will handle the liquidation of Tera’s funds, while Ziraat Bank will oversee Pusula’s.

Voting began on Tuesday in Israel’s parliamentary elections, with more than 7.3 million people eligible to elect the 120-member Knesset.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000 GMT), according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
A total of 12,018 polling stations and around 18,000 ballot boxes have been prepared nationwide, with approximately 100,000 election workers deployed.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing, with at least 61 seats needed to form a governing coalition.

Palestinian-led parties include the Joint List, headed by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas.
First general vote since October 7
The elections are Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 7 2023.
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm local time (2000 GMT), when Israeli television channels are expected to release exit polls.
Initial results are expected overnight, while the official results are scheduled to be published by November 4, according to the Central Elections Committee.
Separately, 4,218 Israelis cast ballots during early voting at 101 polling stations across 99 diplomatic missions abroad on October 15–16.
The turnout represented 86.7 percent of the 4,863 eligible overseas voters, according to the Central Elections Committee.

Rare ermine spotted in Kazakhstan's Kaindy Gorge
A small and agile ermine has been captured on video in Kaindy Gorge, located in the Karabulak forestry area of Kazakhstan's Kolsai Lakes National Park, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The footage was recorded by Koishybayev, a state inspector with the Karabulak forestry service.
“Small but incredibly agile! Just look at this adorable little creature!” the national park said in a statement.
The ermine (Mustela erminea) is a small predator belonging to the weasel family. Despite its tiny size, it is remarkably fast, agile, and cautious. It feeds mainly on small rodents, helping maintain the natural balance of the ecosystem.
The animal also changes its coat with the seasons. Its fur is reddish-brown in summer but turns snow-white in winter, providing natural camouflage that helps it avoid predators and approach prey unnoticed.

World’s climate pledges would cut emissions a tenth of what’s needed: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

World’s climate pledges would cut emissions a tenth of what’s needed: UN
- The UN said current climate pledges would cut global emissions by only 6% by 2035, far below the 60% needed to keep warming near 1.5 deg C.
- The report covered 154 countries’ NDCs and said even full delivery, including conditional targets, would cut emissions by just 9%.
- UN climate chief Simon Stiell said COP31 in Turkey can help close gaps, while climate finance rose to US$1.9 trillion a year but still falls short.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The latest climate pledges put forth by nations will cut global greenhouse gas emissions by just 6% by 2035, a UN report said on Oct 27, weeks before COP31 talks in Turkey.
That is a tenth of the roughly 60% reduction from 2019 levels that scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5 deg C, significantly down from the estimate in 2025 after the US withdrew from the Paris Agreement.
The report by UN Climate Change is a synthesis of 154 countries’ nationally determined contributions – obligatory submissions under the 2015 Paris deal – received between January 2024 and August 2026, covering 71% of global emissions.
It found that if the countries fully implemented their plans and also met conditional targets, emissions cuts would still amount to just 9%.
The UN in 2025 estimated a 10% cut by 2035, but that was before a large number of nationally determined contributions had come in, leaving it to model the missing pledges, and before the US was taken out of the equation.
Under President Donald Trump, the US left the Paris Agreement for a second time and is pursuing policies that heavily favour fossil fuels.
Last week, the UN Environment Programme found that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions put the world on course for 2.6 deg C warming this century.
“With its focus on practical measures to support greater implementation”, the COP31 meeting in Turkey “can help address some of the key gaps”, UN climate chief Simon Stiell said in a statement.
To have a reasonable chance of limiting warming to 1.5 deg C by 2100, compared with pre-industrial levels, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates that global greenhouse gas emissions need to fall by 60% from 2019 levels by 2035.
For pathways to limiting warming to below 2 deg C – the Paris Agreement’s fallback goal – emissions would need to fall by 37% by 2035.
Scientists warn that every extra fraction of a degree above 1.5 deg C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed by roughly 1.4 deg C relative to pre-industrial times, and crossing 1.5 deg C is expected in a matter of years.
In another report released on Oct 27, the UN found that progress has been made in increasing financing to curb warming, but it still falls far short of what is required.
Global climate finance flows reached an average of US$1.9 trillion (S$2.4 trillion) a year in 2023 and 2024 – a 32% increase compared with 2021 and 2022 – driven largely by private investment in low-emission technology, including renewable electricity generation, and private household investment in electric vehicles and heat pumps. Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:29:24 UTC
14:29:24 KST

Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections
The 50 biggest contributors have poured $2.77bn into the race, led by Elon Musk’s $446m for Republican-aligned groups.
The 2026 US midterms are on track to be the most expensive in the country’s history. Spending on political advertising alone is projected to reach $11.6bn, more than in any previous election cycle, including the 2024 presidential race, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
Much of that money comes from wealthy donors, political nonprofits and businesses seeking to shape Washington’s priorities, and some of it passes through networks of organisations before it is spent.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera uses Federal Election Commission data to trace the billionaires, financiers and companies behind the largest contributions ahead of the November 3 vote.
The 50 largest donors contributed $2.77bn
The 50 largest donors and organisations have so far contributed a combined $2.77bn during the 2026 midterm election cycle.
Republican-aligned contributors accounted for $1.67bn, or about 60 percent of donations, double the $832m (30 percent) from Democratic-aligned contributors.
The remaining $264m, about 10 percent, came from contributors classified as bipartisan or special interest, including groups backing sports betting and cryptocurrency.
Individuals can donate up to $3,500 per election to a US federal candidate’s campaign in the 2025–26 election cycle. Yet some of the people on this list have given hundreds of millions of dollars.
That is legal because most of the money went not to candidates but to super political action committees, or super PACs, which can accept donations of any size.
What is a super PAC?
A super PAC is a group that can raise and spend unlimited sums to support or oppose candidates, mainly through advertising. The main condition is that it must not coordinate its spending with candidates or their campaigns.
They emerged in 2010 after two court rulings paved the way for unlimited spending on elections by groups independent of candidates.
Super PACs must report their donors to the Federal Election Commission (FEC), the US agency that oversees federal elections. But some major contributors, including One Nation and Majority Forward, are nonprofit groups that do not have to disclose their own donors.
This can hide where political money originally comes from, a practice known as “dark money”.
But Lawrence Lessig, a professor of law and leadership at Harvard Law School and a campaign finance reform advocate, argues that the money is hidden only from voters.
“It’s not dark to the politicians. It’s dark to us,” he told Josh Rushing on Al Jazeera’s Let’s Focus, in a debate on money in US elections with Bradley Smith, a former chairman of the Federal Election Commission. “Nobody’s confused from the politician’s side about where this money is coming from, and they know what they need to do.”
Who are the biggest individual donors?
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and head of Tesla and SpaceX, is the largest individual contributor of the cycle, with $446m, according to Federal Election Commission data.
He is followed by Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein, founders of the shipping supplies company Uline, and Jeff and Janine Yass. Jeff Yass cofounded the trading firm Susquehanna International Group.
All three have given to Republican-aligned groups.
Republican-aligned top donors:
- Elon Musk: $446 million
- Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein: $150 million
- Jeff and Janine Yass: $110 million
The largest Democratic-aligned donors are George Soros, the billionaire investor and founder of the Open Society Foundations; Mike Bloomberg, the former New York City mayor and founder of the financial data company Bloomberg; and LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and his wife, Michelle Yee.
Democratic-aligned top donors:
- George Soros: $102 million
- Mike Bloomberg: $84 million
- Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee: $41 million
Four individual donors have each given more than $100m. For Lessig, that concentration, not the overall cost of elections, is the real concern.
“The problem isn’t the spending. The problem is the concentration of donors,” he said. “If you don’t have $100 million to put on the table, you’re not going to matter in the way that we think that people ought to matter in a democracy.”
Which organisations contributed the most?
Political nonprofits led the organisational rankings, alongside cryptocurrency firms and an industrial conglomerate.
On the Republican side, the largest was One Nation, a nonprofit aligned with Senate Republican leadership, followed by American Action Network, which is linked to House Republican leadership. On the Democratic side, Majority Forward and House Majority Forward, nonprofits allied with the party’s Senate and House leadership, led the way.
Republican-aligned organisations:
- One Nation: $133 million
- American Action Network: $64.3 million
- American Prosperity Alliance: $50.7 million
Democratic-aligned organisations:
- Majority Forward: $102 million
- House Majority Forward: $93.7 million
- Economic Opportunity Fund: $41.5 million
Cryptocurrency companies also featured prominently. Coinbase, the largest US crypto exchange, gave $57.8m, followed by Ripple, the blockchain payments company, with $49.6m, and Foris DAX, the company behind Crypto.com, with $39m.
The industrial conglomerate Koch gave $46.8m, while the sports betting company DraftKings contributed $40.4m.

The 'growing' health threat now responsible for one in 10 Australian deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:29:18 UTC
14:29:18 KST

In Brief
- Dementia caused more than 10 per cent of deaths in Australia last year.
- The figure increased by almost 40 per cent in the past decade, while deaths due to heart diseases decreased.
Dementia now accounts for more than one in 10 Australian deaths for the first time as advocates warn of a continued surge in the condition as the population ages.
More than 19,000 people (10.1 per cent) died from dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, in 2025, according to analysis released on Tuesday as part of the Australian Bureau of Statistics' (ABS) Causes of Death report.
Dementia has been the leading cause of death for women in Australia since 2016, and in 2024 it overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's leading killer nationally.
This is the first time dementia deaths have exceeded 10 per cent, more than double the rates reported in 2006, when dementia was the fourth-leading cause of death nationally.
Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, professor Tanya Buchanan, said the new data reinforced the urgent need to raise awareness of the condition as a leading public health issue affecting Australians.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers," Buchanan said in a statement.
"Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention has not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues. This needs to change."
Buchanan said that with nearly 500,000 Australians living with dementia, without "significant intervention", the figure was expected to increase to more than one million by 2065.
A gendered killer
In 2025, women accounted for more than 60 per cent of all deaths attributed to dementia in Australia.
The report found that there were almost twice as many deaths from dementia as from ischaemic heart diseases, which is the second leading cause of death for women.
The ABS said that in 2025, there were just 2,791 deaths separating the top two leading causes of death, with that gap continuing to widen as dementia deaths increase over time, and deaths from ischaemic heart disease continued to decline.
Between 2016 and 2025, the number of deaths due to dementia increased by 37 per cent, while deaths due to ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases decreased by 16.2 per cent and 12.1 per cent, respectively.
The mortality rate for ischaemic heart diseases was the lowest on record since its peak in 1968.
After ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases, lung cancer and chronic lower respiratory diseases rounded the top five leading causes of death, which in 2025 represented more than 30 per cent of all registered deaths.

Scammers target major holiday parks across Australia in cybersecurity breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:24:30 UTC
14:24:30 KST

Major holiday park operators warn guests about fraudulent emails, messages seeking credit card details
In short:
BIG4 and other major holiday park operators are warning guests about fraudulent messages following a breach involving a third-party booking platform.
Scammers are using booking details to target travellers with fake payment requests.
What's next?
Travellers are being urged not to click suspicious links or share payment details.
Australian travellers are being warned their personal information may have been exposed following a cybersecurity breach involving an accommodation software company.
Major holiday park operators, including Reflections, BIG4 and G'day Parks, are understood to have been affected through Australian booking management software provider RMS Cloud.
The company provides cloud-based property management and booking systems to more than 6,000 hotels, holiday parks and serviced apartments around the world, according to its website.
RMS said it is investigating reports of phishing messages sent by WhatsApp, SMS and email that "reference genuine booking information" and request payment details.
"Our teams are actively investigating the activity and taking steps to contain it, protect customer information and support affected customers and integration partners," the website said.
"No payment card information has been exposed from RMS."
One of Australia's biggest holiday parks, BIG4, said guests had been targeted by scammers following a breach.
"We've been made aware of a breach of a third-party platform which is used by some of the parks within our network, as well as a number of other accommodation providers and groups. This has resulted in some guests receiving fraudulent messages asking for credit card or payment details," a Big4 spokeswoman said.
"While RMS is undertaking investigations, we have been in touch with parks who may have been affected and provided them with preliminary information and advice for their customers which includes not clicking on suspicious links or providing payment information."
Reflections Holidays, which runs caravan holiday parks across NSW, has sent guests messages warning them of the scam.
"Our booking system provider RMS has made us aware that there are phishing emails being sent to future Reflections Holidays guests from RMS, claiming booking payments have failed," the text message reads.
"Please don't click links or share payment details."
Cherie Midson, who manages a holiday park in Victoria's East Gippsland, said concerned guests began contacting the business after the messages started circulating.
"The messages started going out last night and the calls started coming in today," Ms Midson said.
"Some of the details, like names and dates of stay, are correct."
Ms Midson said she had reported the matter to the federal government's Scamwatch site.
"It's very worrying. Our details are being used, which reflects on us as a business," she said.
"We're concerned our guests could fall victim to the scam, and if they do, our business will be associated with that. That's a real worry for us."
Summerstar Tourist Parks, which operates dozens of caravan parks across Western Australia, has also warned guests of the "cybersecurity breach" on social media.
"We have recently been notified of a cybersecurity breach from RMS, our external booking system provider," the post says.
"Fraudulent emails and WhatsApp messages that appear to be from Summerstar Tourist Parks are circulating asking you to click a link to verify your booking details."
Travellers being targeted
It is not the first cybersecurity breach to target travellers.
Earlier this year, the ABC revealed Booking.com guests had been targeted in a phishing scam involving fake hotel messages on WhatsApp and emails, with their personal details.
Cybersecurity expert Professor Daswin de Silva said travel data was "highly valuable" because it contained detailed information about a traveller's identify.
"There's an assumption that people who travel have financial capacity, which makes them appealing targets for cybercriminals," he said.
Scamwatch, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's scam reporting service, said it received more than 13,000 reports of phishing scams in the first three months of 2026.

Why has France struggled to address students’ demands?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:22:22 UTC
14:22:22 KST

Why has France struggled to address students’ demands?
Protesters demand more spending in education and social services but the government has struggled amid fiscal crisis.
Young people in France continued their nationwide protests over the weekend, demanding better education facilities and a promising future amid the rising cost of living in the country.
France’s Ministry of Interior said 410,000 people protested nationwide on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, as the government has struggled to address the issues raised by the student-led protests.
France was also roiled by nearly two years of protests beginning in 2018 over the high cost of living and opposition to French President Emmanuel Macron’s economic policies. Those protests, which were led by the Yellow Vests movement, demanded that the government address the rising economic inequality, boost welfare and public services, and tax the rich.
As the young protesters take to the streets, many of the old demands remain unfulfilled. So, why have French politicians been unable to address the issues facing the country?
Here’s what we know:
Why are young people in France protesting now?
The youth-led protests in France erupted last month amid deteriorating conditions in schools, broader economic anxieties and opposition to government budget cuts.
The protests began in mid-September after high school students blockaded campuses over overcrowded classrooms (often 32–35 pupils per room), unreplaced teacher absences, and dilapidated building infrastructure.
Protesters have waved placards reading statements like “We have a future to build, not to endure”, as they expressed frustration with shrinking public resources and state investment.
Teachers have also joined the students protesting over low salaries. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries like Germany, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Education at a Glance 2026 report.
School teachers in France earn a gross salary of 41,968 euros ($46,900) per annum compared with 69,453 euros ($77,700) for their German counterparts. Social taxes, high pension contributions and the rising cost of living eat into their monthly income.
What started as a localised strike over school resources has since drawn in trade unions as well as civil servants, and the protests have evolved into a broader economic and political crisis.
This is due to discontent over the government’s proposed 54-billion-euro ($60bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures for the 2027 budget, which includes civil servant salary freezes.
Students and youth fear bearing the brunt of public spending reductions amid a multidecade high in poverty rates and rising costs of living, exacerbated by the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Currently, according to Amine Snoussi, a journalist for Le Media TV and a former parliamentary assistant at the French National Assembly, the condition of public high schools is dire since government money is being spent elsewhere.
“Students are studying in cold, dirty buildings, some of them infested with rats. In some schools, absent teachers haven’t been replaced for over six months. And all of this is happening while thousands of teaching jobs are being cut, and while public money keeps flowing to private schools. That’s what lit the fuse,” he told Al Jazeera.
What has been the government’s response?
The French government has responded to the mass protests by imposing curfews and deploying police across the country to crack down on protesters.
President Macron has blamed ultra-left groups for trying to “bring down the Republic” and threatened accountability for those involved in violence.
On Friday, the French leader met representatives of the student movement for the first time since the protests began.
But the meeting failed to defuse tensions, with student representatives calling for further mobilisation until the government presents concrete actions.
On Monday, during a visit to Marseille, Macron said he has “asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement”.
The government is also expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France’s national online university admissions platform, according to French media reports.
Why is the French government struggling to address protesters’ demands?
Analysts say the French government is struggling to address students’ demands due to a severe fiscal crisis and planned budget cuts, which have led to a drop in the country’s education budget.
According to data published by French economist and co-director of the World Inequality Lab Lucas Chancel, “The public budget for higher education, student life, and research (relative to the total number of students in France, once inflation is taken into account) has decreased by 20 percent since 2017.”
The French government has defended the budget cuts.
In an address to the nation on October 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu acknowledged that “the anger among young people didn’t come out of nowhere” and promised the government would present a plan to address the crisis by the end of October.
The French prime minister has also asked his ministers to check spending as France’s national debt has ballooned to about 3.6 trillion euros ($4 trillion), which is equivalent to 119 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP).
Of greater concern to markets than the total debt is France’s growing deficit, however, which is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 – far above the European Union average of just more than 3 percent. This is the amount by which a government’s spending exceeds its income.
But in a report, French economist and professor Thomas Piketty noted that while public debt has increased, the country’s private wealth has also grown from “300 percent to 600 percent of GDP, with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes”.
“In other words, France has never been richer. The problem to solve is simply one of distribution,” he added.
Does France have a wealth distribution problem?
France has relatively low to moderate income inequality, but wealth redistribution has been an issue of debate, particularly in left-wing political groups.
People aged 60 and older, who form a quarter of the population, own 60 percent of the country’s wealth (non-financial and financial), according to a January 2026 review by prominent French economic policy think tank OFCE.
A huge chunk of government funds go to service social security.
A government report seen by the Reuters news agency earlier this month also noted that nearly one-third of some French ministries’ budgets pay for the pensions of retired civil servants, which reduces spending on education and other priorities.
Snoussi told Al Jazeera that the wealth distribution question has always been central to current French politics.
“Macron is called the rich people’s president for a reason. He always supports rich people and has never managed to create a form of equality between classes,” he said.
Macron has been branded “the president of the rich” for cutting the wealth tax. He has also faced criticism for his economic policies aimed at modernising the economy and creating jobs. His decision to impose a fuel tax triggered the 2018 so-called Yellow Vests protests, a grassroots movement seeking government intervention to address inequality.
Critics say his policies resulted in redistribution of wealth upward and affected the working-class population. But Macron has defended his policies, particularly his decision on wealth tax, saying that forcing the wealthy out of the country won’t help the poor.
“I don’t believe in this French jealousy which says, ‘There are rich people; let’s tax them and we will all feel better,’” he told The New York Times in a 2017 interview.
Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, France, told Al Jazeera: “France has a more redistributive system than other European countries – at least similar”.
He explained that redistribution is a set of programmes of taxes and transfers that redistribute income from high-income individuals towards lower-income individuals.
The real issue, Fatas said, is deeper.
“France’s growth has been limited for years. With low growth, it is not hard to imagine parts of the population that are unhappy with the progress they see, and this leads to demands for a solution in the form of government support or redistribution,” he said.
France is currently facing significant fiscal stress, with its annual budget deficit forecast at 5.4 percent of its GDP, well above the standard European Union ceiling of 3 percent. The country also remains heavily backed by its public sector, with state expenditures consuming roughly 57 percent of its total GDP – including a notable 14 percent allocated strictly towards worker pensions.
“The assumption is that someone out there is rich enough that they can be taxed. While I can imagine in a more progressive system in France, one has to be careful about the limitations of these apparent solutions,” Fatas added.
So how should the government respond?
In his opinion column for the French newspaper Le Monde, Piketty wrote that reinvesting in sectors like education and health should be the government’s priority.
“Reinvesting in these sectors today is not simply a matter of equality between regions or social classes,” he wrote, highlighting that such reinvestment would help an economy produce greater output by using fewer resources.
Snoussi shared a similar view.
“The government has a simple choice: invest, or step aside,” he said.
“But the real question is whether Macron even wants a way out. Or is he hoping the situation gets worse, so he can crush the movement through police and judicial repression?”
Fatas, the economics professor, noted that while there are a lot of good things people in France want the government to do, it is important to prioritise which sector requires funding.
“The government spending [in France] is the largest among advanced economies, so there is little room to just spend the way out of this.
“France faces a political paralysis when it comes to reform decisions, and this is the reason why they are in a more difficult situation than others,” he added.

Israelis head to the polls in parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:17:34 UTC
14:17:34 KST

Sahin Demir and Abdel Raouf Arnaout
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Voting began Tuesday in Israel’s parliamentary elections, with more than 7.3 million people eligible to cast ballots to elect the 120-member Knesset.
 
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000GMT), according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
 
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in the elections, which are being held amid intense competition between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc and the opposition bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
 
A total of 12,018 polling stations and approximately 18,000 ballot boxes have been prepared nationwide, with around 100,000 election workers deployed.
 
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing in the elections, with at least 61 seats required to form a governing coalition.
 
Recent opinion polls suggest that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition parties may secure the 61 seats needed to form a government.
 
Israeli television networks expect a high voter turnout amid the closely contested election.
 
The main contenders include Netanyahu’s Likud party, Eisenkot’s Yashar party and the Together alliance led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
 
Other prominent parties include the Democrats led by Yair Golan, Yisrael Beiteinu, headed by Avigdor Lieberman, and Jewish Power, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
 
Arab parties include the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen and the United Arab List (Ra’am) led by Mansour Abbas.
 
The elections are the first in Israel since 1988 to be held on schedule following the completion of a full four-year parliamentary term.
 
Under Israeli law, parliamentary elections are held every four years, although the Knesset can dissolve itself earlier through legislation supported by at least 61 members.
 
Early elections can also be triggered by a failure to form a government or approve the state budget within the legally prescribed period.
 
The elections represent Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
 
The vote also comes amid Israel’s military offensives against Lebanon, Iran and Yemen, as well as its continued occupation of parts of Syria, Lebanon and Gaza and escalating attacks by illegal Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank.
 
Netanyahu faces an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel’s war on Gaza.
 
The elections are also seen as crucial for the political future of Netanyahu, 76, who is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if convicted.
 
Netanyahu has headed Israel’s current right-wing government since late December 2022, which has been described as the most far-right in the country’s history.
 
Tight elections
 
According to the prime minister’s office, Netanyahu is expected to cast his ballot Tuesday afternoon at a school in West Jerusalem.
 
Eisenkot is also scheduled to vote at a school in the central Israeli city of Herzliya after visiting several polling stations.
 
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state despite UN resolutions supporting a two-state solution.
 
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm local time (2000GMT), when Israeli television channels are expected to release exit polls.
 
Initial results are expected to emerge overnight, while the official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
 
Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to begin consultations with parties elected to the Knesset a week after the elections to determine which lawmaker will be tasked with forming the next government.
 
Meanwhile, Israeli police announced the deployment of 20,000 officers across the country to maintain public order, protect voters and ensure the integrity of the electoral process.
 
Police said uniformed and undercover officers would be stationed at thousands of polling locations and surrounding areas to prevent disruptions and ensure voting proceeds in accordance with the law.
 
Separately, 4,218 Israelis cast their ballots during early voting at 101 polling stations established at 99 diplomatic missions abroad on Oct. 15–16, representing 86.7% of the 4,863 eligible overseas voters, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee.

Passengers traveling through Copenhagen Airport could face longer waits at security checkpoints during busy periods over the weekend, with delays potentially continuing into next week.

“I understand the curiosity about there being some changed security considerations right now, but we cannot go further into details about our security procedures. But it is important to say that security is always top-notch, and that it is safe to fly,” she said.
Trafikstyrelsen will determine when normal security operations can resume or whether the airport must make permanent changes to its procedures.

Danish tax assessments for 2027 to open two weeks later than usual
Around 5.5 million people in Denmark will be able to check their preliminary tax assessments for 2027 from Tuesday, November 24, the Danish Tax Agency (Skattestyrelsen) has announced.
The assessment, known as forskudsopgørelsen, shows a person’s expected income, deductions and tax payments for the coming year.
Taxpayers can update the information to reflect changes in their finances and reduce the risk of receiving an unexpected tax bill later.
Ulrick Junge, deputy director at the Danish Tax Agency, advises people to review their assessments particularly carefully if they have changed jobs, received a pay increase or experienced changes in interest payments.
“The preliminary income assessment is the overview of your finances next year, and this is where you can ensure that you use your deductions and pay the correct tax,” he said.
The assessment is based on financial information from previous years, meaning changes may not automatically be reflected.
Last year, around 800,000 taxpayers owed additional tax averaging 9,850 DKK each, totaling approximately 7.9 billion DKK.
This year’s assessment will become available two weeks later than usual because the Danish Parliament, known as the Folketing, is expected to consider several proposed changes to tax deductions in November.
These include deductions for exercise and music lessons, higher employment deductions for seniors and increased standard deductions for childminders.
“We know that many citizens are looking forward to the amended deductions. Therefore, we have chosen to postpone the opening of the preliminary income assessment by a few weeks so that we can incorporate the deductions,” Junge said.
The agency will provide further guidance when the assessments become available.
University of Copenhagen hit by second cyberattack days after first
The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.

New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.

AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.

Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.

Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.

The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

The Ministry of Immigration and Integration writes this in a press release.

The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.
Most recently, the Danish People’s Party entered the debate because the party wants a Pakistani man removed from an upcoming bill that next year will make 2,055 foreigners Danish citizens.
DF’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, has found a Facebook post from 2016 in which the man, according to DF, supported an Islamic execution.
– The government should strip him of the opportunity to obtain citizenship. If they are not willing to do that, they must at the very least be willing to let us meet this man eye-to-eye so we can see the matter for ourselves, Mikkel Bjørn told DR on Thursday.
Last week, Liberal Alliance found a woman who, according to the party, has repeatedly praised Hamas and the former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Therefore, the party wants the person summoned for an interview with the Folketing’s Naturalisation Committee.
The central element in the debate regarding a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 new individuals has been whether they have been sufficiently investigated for anti-democratic views.
Every six months, a bill is introduced in the Folketing granting new individuals Danish citizenship after an often lengthy and comprehensive application process.
This also applied to the then SVM government.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Data on 525,000 people compromised in KU cyberattack
The University of Copenhagen (KU) has been subjected to a cyberattack.
The hackers have gained access to information on approximately 525,000 individuals. Among this is information such as full name, CPR number, work telephone number, private telephone number, and private email address.
The university stated this in a press release on Friday evening.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, just as “other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed”.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness and the Agency for Public Security write in a press release Friday evening that the authorities are monitoring the cyber incidents at the University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University.
The ministry and the agency are working closely with the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalisation and other relevant authorities on the handling, it is stated.
– The incidents emphasize once again that the cyber threat against Denmark is serious, states Minister for Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen (SF) in a written comment to Ritzau and continues:
– The Agency for Public Security generally assesses that universities in Denmark are exposed to the threat of cyberattacks. Among other things because they are leaders within a range of research areas. I know that the universities are working actively to counter that threat.
The minister states that “relevant higher education institutions have been informed about the incidents and have received advice from the Agency for Public Security.”
The attack against the University of Copenhagen was discovered on Tuesday and “was subsequently brought under control”.
The university is in the process of analyzing the exact scope and preventing similar or further attacks from taking place, it is stated.
KU further writes in the press release that at present they have no further comments on the cyberattack, but that “there will be follow-up with further information when a clearer picture of the incident is available”.
Aarhus University stated on Thursday that the educational institution had been subjected to a hacker attack.
The hacker gained access to one of the university’s servers.
Afterwards, the hacker attempted to gain access to and change passwords for approximately 1,700 users – both current and former employees and students.
This did not succeed, as the unauthorized access to the system was discovered.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Retail sales in Denmark rose by 0.4 percent in September compared with August, despite growing pessimism among consumers, according to figures from Statistics Denmark.
The increase is adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, price changes and the number of trading days.
For the third quarter, covering July through September, retail sales rose by 1.6 percent compared with the previous quarter.
Sales trends varied across industries in September. The largest increases were recorded among retailers selling second-hand goods, household equipment, furniture and building materials.
By contrast, sales fell the most at gas stations and pharmacies. Danish supermarkets also recorded a slight decline.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said the increase in retail sales was encouraging given the growing pessimism among Danish consumers.
On Thursday, Statistics Denmark’s consumer confidence indicator stood at minus 17.2, down from minus 13.7 in September.
A negative reading indicates that consumers have a pessimistic view of the country’s current and future economic situation.
Despite the decline in confidence, Morten Granzau, deputy director at the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri), believes retail sales could continue to grow in the coming months.
“Consumers’ purchasing power is fundamentally good. High employment, growth in real wages, and the lower electricity tax provide breathing room in many households’ budgets. This creates good opportunities for retail sales to maintain progress through the autumn,” he wrote in a comment.
Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.
