In Islamophobic rant, Trump seeks to stir Republican base in Michigan
David E. Sanger and Bayliss Wagner
- Trump used Islamophobic claims at a Michigan rally to attack Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and boost Republican turnout.
- He called El-Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and questioned his loyalty, while praising Republican rival Mike Rogers as “apple pie”.
- The race is close and important for Senate control, but Trump’s low approval in Michigan may also hurt Republicans, despite strong crowd support.
AI generated
PORT HURON, United States – US President Donald Trump turned to Islamophobic stereotypes to motivate Michigan Republicans on Oct 25, claiming at a rally that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, if elected, would bring a wave of jihadis to the country.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump told more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron, a working class, waterfront city in a deep-red congressional district about 95km north-east of Detroit.
Trump called El-Sayed, 41, whose family emigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” – a baseless claim.
He then contrasted El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the US, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the US.
“I call him apple pie,” Trump said of Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”
Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch.
And, while he has often used crude and racist language, Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.
But a broader question about Trump’s rally here – which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops – is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president.
His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.
Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory.
While Trump carried Michigan by 2 points in 2024, just 34% of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.
Polls indicate that El-Sayed has a narrow edge over Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.
Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed on Oct 25, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.
Speaking in a town on the Canadian border, Trump did not dwell on his battle with Prime Minister Mark Carney, one of the few world leaders who has directly confronted him on tariffs and other issues, and he did not repeat his frequent call for Canada to give up its independence and become the 51st state.
Instead, he focused on El-Sayed, his religion and his relatives. Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for El-Sayed.
“Any Jewish person who supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy”.
Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.
Trump made the statement after claiming that El-Sayed’s half sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Oct 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis by Hamas fighters.
She posted a video on the first anniversary of the attack that said that “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner”, but did not mention the massacre directly and did not celebrate the violence.
El-Sayed’s campaign told Fox News that he disagreed with her “on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use”.
El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.
But his opponents have raised an open letter he signed in 2012, when he was a medical student.
It was addressed to Mohammed Morsi, then the new Egyptian president, from a party that represents the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood.
It asked him to “purge the media and police” of loyalists to the government that was overturned during the Arab Spring.
El-Sayed has not discussed the letter. But his spokesperson, Cole Wozniak, said, “Abdul remains laser-focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington”.
“Michigan knows Trump is on the ballot on Nov 3,” he added, “and they will vote like it by rejecting Trump’s rubber stamp Mike Rogers and sending Abdul to the Senate.”
Trump deepened his critique as the day went on, saying that someone with El-Sayed’s background “would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane”.
“They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate,” he added.
He also said that El-Sayed should not be given access to classified information.
At his own rally on Oct 25 in Grand Rapids, El-Sayed said the Republican strategy was “to point at me and my name and my faith”.
“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” he said.
In Michigan, Trump also veered into a discussion of Greenland. He insisted, “Oh, you know we did get Greenland”, suggesting that it was now owned by the US.
In fact, Trump was forced to drop that demand and instead signed a new treaty with Denmark, which handles Greenland’s foreign affairs, that envisions opening two new US bases on the island and bars similar arrangements with foreign powers, notably China. But it does not change Denmark’s sovereignty, as Trump initially insisted.
He also drew cheers when he insisted Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and vaguely said the war with Iran would be resolved soon.
But he largely steered clear of discussing how his decision to attack Iran led directly to high gas and diesel prices.
Rogers has sought distance from the war, calling for it to “end quickly”, and from the President’s tariffs on Canadian goods, saying “Canada is not our enemy” in a campaign ad. He has also backed a one-year moratorium on data centres, creating a contrast with Trump’s support for them.
Like other Republicans, Rogers has largely avoided talking about Trump in ads and on the campaign trail.
Speaking at the rally in Port Huron, Rogers again accused El-Sayed of having family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. He said that watching El-Sayed try to tell the truth is like “watching an octopus put his socks on in the morning”. And he said the country “can’t risk his extreme ideology and thinking”.
On NBC News’ Meet The Press on the morning of Oct 25, Rogers did not endorse Trump’s baseless claim that El-Sayed is “a terrorist”, but did not condemn it outright.
“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers said of El-Sayed.
El-Sayed has become a central villain in Republicans’ narrative of the midterms.
In western Iowa on Oct 22, more than 1280km from Port Huron, Trump railed against El- Sayed, drawing some of the loudest applause of the night. He did the same in North Carolina and Ohio last week.
After holding forth on the potential demise of the nation in Michigan on Oct 25, Trump spent five full minutes admiring the body and physicality of Senator Jon Husted, the Republican running for re-election in Ohio, and rapper Nicki Minaj, who traveled with Trump to the rally.
“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj,” Trump said. “Hard to miss it.” NYTIMES

Ceasefire takes effect in frontline town – Russia
A temporary ceasefire around the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia has taken effect to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians, the Russian Defense Ministry announced.
According to a brief statement by the ministry, the ceasefire began at 4:00 AM Moscow time on Tuesday “in preparation for a humanitarian operation.”
General Valery Gerasimov, Russia’s chief of the General Staff, said last week that military engineers would conduct reconnaissance and ensure “the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy” into the town. The Ukrainian General Staff also confirmed last week that it would observe the truce.
The Russian authorities estimate that 1,500 to 2,000 civilians remain trapped in Alyoshki, on the left bank of the Dnieper River opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. The town has been largely cut off from supplies for months, with Ukrainian shelling and drone strikes preventing regular aid deliveries, according to Russian officials.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town. However, people who escaped told RT earlier this month that Alyoshki was effectively under siege by Ukrainian forces, which they said carried out constant attacks.
From October 19-26 alone, Ukrainian forces carried out 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone strikes on Alyoshki and its main access roads, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.
Russian officials also said Ukrainian forces used drones to drop mines on roads leading to Alyoshki, further hampering supply deliveries.
The ceasefire was brokered with the help of Pope Leo XIV and US First Lady Melania Trump, who warned that the town was “on the brink of disaster.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that the humanitarian truce, if successful, “could set a precedent” for other areas.

Providence poised to become largest US city to mandate divestment from Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:15:22 UTC
10:15:22 KST

Providence, Rhode Island, is on the brink of becoming the largest city in the United States to enact legislation mandating divestment from Israel, as supporters and opponents anticipate a binding ballot measure on November 3.
The initiative, designated Question 7, asks voters to approve an ordinance divesting municipal funds from foreign states committing severe human rights violations—such as genocide, apartheid, ethnic cleansing, or illegal military occupation—alongside corporate entities that knowingly enable them.
The measure's divestment triggers link to formal determinations issued by the International Court of Justice, United Nations bodies, or American federal courts.
Campaigners cite a 2025 UN Human Rights Council commission report concluding Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Political shifts
Activists turned to a charter clause permitting citizens to place ordinances directly before the electorate by gathering signatures from 5 percent of registered voters.
The move bypassed Mayor Brett Smiley, who previously pledged to veto an Israel bond prohibition introduced by City Council President Rachel Miller.
The grassroots coalition — uniting Jewish Voice for Peace, the Democratic Socialists of America, and local student movements — aims to establish a repeatable model for municipal divestment nationwide.
"We're excited to work with fellow activists around the country interested in learning from our work and replicating it in their own communities," said Zach Kligler, a lead organiser with Providence for Palestine.
The political environment favours the initiative.
David Morales, a 27-year-old democratic socialist critical of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, defeated Smiley in September's mayoral primary, and the incoming council is expected to hold a pro-Palestinian majority.
Community friction
Opponents, led by the Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island and local rabbis, argue Question 7 is overly broad, financially impractical, and damaging to communal harmony among the city’s 15,000 Jewish residents.
Rabbi Sara Mack noted that the campaign "feels antisemitic to many people" and fosters alienation, while Rabbi Michael Fel departed from non-partisan tradition to lobby against it.
"There are a whole host of potential legal challenges that we would probably be engaging with national Jewish organisations that specialise in this," said Stephanie Hague, the Alliance’s chief strategy officer.
Financial assessments vary.
Municipal records indicate pension funds hold no direct Israeli bonds, though up to $119,000 may exist in mutual funds.
Providence for Palestine argues the city holds $2.5 million in complicit corporations.
While City Treasurer Shomari Husband acknowledged implementation poses a "daunting task", municipal officials have engaged a retired federal judge to evaluate potential challenges under state anti-boycott laws.

- A 15-year-old, Anthony Rivers III, will be tried as an adult after an Oct 24 Tallahassee shooting left 11 people shot and six in hospital, one critically ill.

AI generated
Tallahassee, Florida – A 15-year-old boy who was arrested in the shooting of 11 people after a college football game in Tallahassee, Florida, will stand trial as an adult, a Florida prosecutor said on Oct 26.
The teenager, Anthony Rivers III, was ordered to remain in custody at a juvenile court hearing on Oct 26 after his arrest the day before. The shooting took place in a crowded, closed-off street on Oct 24 about an hour after Florida A&M University’s (FAMU) homecoming game. A crowd of just over 20,000 attended the event.
The shooting left six people hospitalised as of Oct 25, one of whom was in critical condition. A spokesperson for Leon County School District said four of its students were wounded, including the one in critical condition.
Six of the 11 people shot were minors, the Tallahassee Police Department said. A 12th person was injured but not shot, officials said.
Lawrence Revell, chief of the Tallahassee Police, said at a news conference on Oct 26 that the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a physical altercation among people who knew one another and that none of the victims appeared to be intended targets. He said more arrests were possible.
Judge Andrew Sheeran, who presided over the hearing on Oct 26, said he would grant the request of the top prosecutor in Tallahassee to try Rivers as an adult, which Florida law allows in certain cases. He will be charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, officials said.
“It’s our discretion because of the severity of the offence,” said prosecutor Jack Campbell.
In a phone interview, he added that he had discussed the decision with juvenile-case prosecutors before asking his prosecutors to review the case. “Ultimately, it was my decision,” he said.
Rivers, dressed in a white T-shirt, grey gym shorts and sandals and his hair pulled up into a bun, stood quietly at the hearing on Oct 26 with his hands clasped behind his back as the public defender who was representing him addressed the court.
The public defender said she had previously represented Rivers. Her office did not reply to a request for comment. Efforts to reach relatives of Rivers were not immediately successful.
According to court records, Rivers has been arrested previously on charges including burglary and theft of a gun, but it was unclear what the outcome was. He was arrested on Sept 6 for violating his probation and had been sentenced to a juvenile home.
According to a police affidavit, Rivers was arrested after surveillance cameras and an ankle monitor he was wearing identified him at a Tallahassee mall where gunfire had erupted in an underground carpark.
The police identified another 15-year-old who was with Rivers as the shooter, according to the affidavit. Nobody was injured in the shooting, which occurred after an altercation in the mall.
Campbell declined to discuss anything about Rivers’ criminal record. But he said if someone was a repeat offender, “that’s something we consider” when determining whether to charge a juvenile as an adult.
The shooting echoed others in Tallahassee in recent years. Nine people were shot – one fatally – outside a liquor store in 2022 that Campbell said was connected to a homecoming event at Florida A&M.
In 2025, two people were killed and six others were wounded in a shooting at Florida State University, which is near Florida A&M.
Campbell is seeking the death penalty against the shooter in that case, Phoenix Ikner, who has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.
The shooting on Oct 24 could have been much worse, Campbell said.
It happened in Perry Street, a residential street that runs alongside Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the football team plays. The street was blocked off for vendors selling food and T-shirts, and is a popular place before and after games.
“If you go to FAMU, you’ve spent time in Perry Street,” Campbell said. NYTIMES

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's surprise win in Brazil's presidential vote "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro, has refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party's head, Valdemar Costa Neto.
"We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
"I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange."
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded."
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
Markets roiled by Lula win
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil's real BRL= fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
"The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

====================================================================================================

Mice in folklore beliefs and traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:04:43 UTC
16:04:43 KST

Author
Albena Bezovska
Tuesday 27 October 2026 08:25
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 08:25
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
It is an established fact that before converting to Christianity, proto-Bulgarians used a 12-year East Asian calendar cycle in which every year was named after a given animal. Studies of the so-called Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans have found that the calendar of the proto-Bulgarians coincides fully with the Chinese calendar we know today. The months are even named after the same animals – the first year is samor (mouse), the second – shegor (ox) and so on. The Bulgarian folk calendar includes special days dedicated to appeasing this cunning and troublesome little creature. One of them falls on October 27, a day traditionally known by our ancestors as Mouse Day (Mishinden).
In the folklore of our ancestors, the mouse was seen as a symbol of impure chthonic forces. There is even a legend that mice can be inhabited by unclean spirits and demonic creatures. This applied to both house mice and field mice, which damaged crops, roamed through barns and cupboards, ate stored food, and gnawed on fabrics and clothing.
PHOTO Pixabay
Not being able to find any way to fight this mischievous animal, peasants turned their attention to the spiritual sphere, writes renowned Bulgarian ethnographer Dimitar Marinov and adds that it was believed the mouse was a “tiny spirit which cannot be vanquished except by supplication and appeasement”. In honour of mice, people once organized so-called Mouse Days, lasting one, three or, more rarely, seven days. Most often the Mouse Days are around 27 October, the day of St. Nestor, or in some parts of the country the 24 November, the day of St. Catherine, who is, according to popular belief, the patron saint of rats.
Saint Martyr Nestor of Thessalonica
PHOTO pronewsdobrich.bg
For the ruptsi ethnographic group in Strandzha and the Rhodopes, as well as the migrants coming to Dobroudzha, the mouse days fall on Trifuntsi (1,2 and 3 February), in some towns and villages of the same regions – on Dog Monday (the first day of Lent and St. Todor’s day week). The rituals performed on these days are intended to ward off and drive away harmful rodents. With their eyes closed, women smear mud over the floor around the hearth, the mice’s holes, and the four corners of the room, symbolically “sealing the mice’s eyes.”
To “sew up” the lips of the vermin, people in Eastern Thrace would make stitches on a piece of cloth and then throw it into the fire. On Mouse Days no animal names should be said out loud, people would call them “lads”, “grouse” etc. There are other prohibitions as well – working with wool or sharp objects is not allowed, nor is opening chests of clothes, the lard keg or the flour box. “Mouse weddings” were once put on during Mouse Days or at another time of the year. Two women with the same name would catch a male and a female mouse, “dress them up” as bride and groom, tie them to one another and put them inside a basket or wooden bowl. The whole village would follow the “newlyweds” to the sound of wedding music. They would go to the forest, next to a river or up a hill and would let the mice loose. It was believed all other mice would follow and the homes and the village would be rid of them. After that the villagers would all sit down to a festive dinner.
PHOTO Pixabay
It was once said that mice would never infest a home where Mouse Days were observed. If mice did appear, it was taken as a sign that someone in the family was stealing or secretly taking things out of the house, that daughters-in-law were disobeying their mothers-in-law, sons were defying their fathers, or that there was discord among family members.
In folk tales, the mouse is often brave and cunning, but also overconfident. The expression "as poor as a church mouse" refers to someone who is extremely poor. We use the phrase "blinking like a mouse in bran" to describe a person who has been unpleasantly surprised and does not know how to react.
According to the folklore dream book if you dream of a mouse you shall have worries, friends will leave you… If you dream you are chasing a mouse – good things shall enter your life, and if you catch it – some kind of gain awaits you.
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov
This publication was created by: Kostadin Atanasov

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:01:53 UTC
10:01:53 KST

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
US appeals court blocks government effort to stop California from tabulating ballots from list of alleged non-citizens.
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.
In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.
But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.
In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.
The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.
The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.
Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.
California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.
The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.
The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.
Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.
But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.
It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.
But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.
The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.
Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.
In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.
Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.
Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.
Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.
Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.
But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.
Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.
In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

CAR: Special Criminal Court, the last hope of justice for thousands, on the brink of collapse – new report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

- Special Criminal Court at risk of closure by 2028 with thousands of victims awaiting justice
- Other than the UN and the EU, no state providing financial support to SCC at the moment
- ICC closed investigations; National courts lack resources and independence to take on SCC cases
Suspected perpetrators of crimes under international law in the Central African Republic (CAR), including some of the country’s highest-ranking officials, are at risk of escaping justice unless the Special Criminal Court (SCC) receives the funding it requires to continue investigating and prosecuting cases, Amnesty International said in a new report.
“The perpetrators are still here” – The Central African Republic’s Special Criminal Court on borrowed time, as victims await justice examines the progress and challenges faced by the SCC, which has tried six cases since its inauguration on 22 October 2018, resulting in 19 people being convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity. However, victims of the most serious crimes committed during some of the bloodiest periods in CAR’s history, including during the 2003 coup led by François Bozizé and the 2012–2014 internal armed conflict, are still waiting for all perpetrators in positions of high authority to be prosecuted.
Yet the court, which relies solely on voluntary contributions from states and international organizations, is at risk of closure by 2028. After an initial sense of hope, survivors and victims are beginning to lose faith.
“Victims’ right to justice, truth, and reparations must not depend on the shifting priorities of donors. Thousands of civilians were killed, raped, abducted, maimed, injured, displaced, or had their homes burned down during waves of violence and armed conflict over the last 25 years. Each one of them deserves justice,” said Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa.
“Amnesty International calls on the Central African authorities, the United Nations, the European Union, and all partner states to provide – or continue to provide – financial support to the Special Criminal Court to meet its operating budget.”
The Special Criminal Court was established at the request of the Central African people and civil society. If the court does not receive the resources it needs to continue its essential work, it will fail them.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
‘Victims want justice [to be done]’
Of the six cases tried by the SCC, verdicts have been handed down in the first four at least in the first instance, resulting in the conviction of 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity. In one case, victims also received reparations. The verdict in the fifth trial relating to attacks in Guen, western CAR, in 2014, is expected next December, while the Bossembélé trial, which lists former president Bozizé among the accused, is currently underway.
Despite the remarkable progress in fighting impunity in the CAR, numerous grave crimes still remain unpunished. These include widespread campaigns of murder, rape, and looting committed in 2002–2003, in particular by security forces of former president Ange-Félix Patassé and fighters from Jean-Pierre Bemba’s armed group that he enlisted to try to crush François Bozizé’s coup; as well as many crimes of killings, rapes, torture, and enforced disappearances committed between 2012 and 2014, in the context of conflict between Seleka and Anti-balaka armed groups.
Despite a significant improvement in the enforcement of arrest warrants issued by the SCC in the last few years, dozens of individuals are currently still wanted, and significant obstacles to their arrest remain. François Bozizé resides in Guinea-Bissau, while other suspects subject to arrest warrants are in Chad.
The SCC has tried a number of individuals, such as Bozizé, in their absence, but these in absentia trials significantly undermine the process and defence rights, and fall short of victims’ needs.
“Victims want justice [to be done]. When their perpetrators are brought to justice their hearts will be at peace, when they see them in prison,” said a representative from a Central African organization that supports victims. Other victims said they are satisfied with judgments in absentia.
An unprecedented financial crisis
In 2025, the United States withdrew its financial support for the SCC, leaving it to face an unprecedented funding crisis with more than US$4.15 million in commitments that remain unpaid. The United Nations and the European Union are currently the sole financial contributors to the court.
Funding cuts forced the court to lay off a quarter of its staff, including foreign experts, between August and September 2025. Its witness protection unit has lost more than half of its staff, which has the potential to compromise its ability to limit reprisals against witnesses. Due to the lack of staff and resources, the Office of the Prosecutor can no longer open any new investigations, while cases before the various Chambers suffer delays.
To the best of Amnesty International’s knowledge, with the exception of the UN and EU, no state or organization has committed to future voluntary financial contributions to the SCC, raising the prospect of the SCC’s closure at the end of its mandate in 2028.
States and international organizations must providing urgent funding, preferably through multi-year commitments, so that justice can be served as long as it is necessary.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
No alternative for trying the worst crimes in the CAR
Despite progress, CAR’s national courts currently lack the human and material resources, as well as the necessary independence, to handle cases currently before the SCC. “If the cases are transferred to the national courts, it will mean that they will be before our judges, and their superiors will influence them,” a representative of victims said.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) also has jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in the CAR since 2002. It has opened two investigations at the request of the Central African government. However, in December 2022, the ICC Prosecutor’s Office announced that it was closing its investigations.
An essential jurisdiction amid persistent conflict
In the CAR, the intensity of the violence has decreased since its peak in 2021, but all parties to the conflict continue to commit serious human rights violations and crimes under international law in the northeast and southeast of the country.
“The SCC was established at the request of the Central African people and civil society. If the court does not receive the resources it needs to continue its essential work, it will fail them and embolden those who continue to commit atrocities today,” said Marceau Sivieude.
“The Central African authorities must support and protect the SCC, and extend its mandate beyond October 2028 until the Court’s mission has been accomplished. They must help to secure additional funding for its budget.”
“States and international organizations must fully cooperate by executing the SCC’s arrest warrants and providing urgent funding, preferably through multi-year commitments, so that justice can be served as long as it is necessary.”
Background
This report builds on the research work that Amnesty International has been conducting for a decade on issues of justice, truth and reparation for crimes under international law in the CAR. For this report, the organization conducted a mission in April 2026 to Bangui, the capital, and interviewed 63 people. It also reviewed court decisions, legal texts, reports from international organizations, NGOs and donors, academic works, official statements, and news articles.
The report’s findings were shared with the Central African authorities on 6 October 2026. Amnesty International had not received a response at the time of publication.
The SCC has a mandate to investigate and prosecute crimes under international law committed during conflicts in the Central African Republic since 2003. It is a hybrid court supported by the UN, composed of Central African and foreign prosecutors and judges. It began its second five-year term on 22 October 2023, due to end in October 2028.

'I felt like I had Jew stamped on my forehead': BBC settles antisemitism dispute with producer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:58:35 UTC
09:58:35 KST

The BBC has agreed to pay more than £400,000 (about $534,000) to Jewish producer Lucie Kon, who alleged that she faced antisemitic remarks from colleagues and was pushed out of her job after complaining about the treatment of Jewish employees following the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023. The settlement was reached without an admission of liability by the British broadcaster, after Kon threatened legal action over alleged discrimination and unfair dismissal.
Kohn, 57, worked at the BBC for 22 years and was involved in documentary productions that won prestigious awards. She was among the executive producers of "We Will Dance Again," a documentary about the Hamas attack on the Nova music festival, and "Mr. Nobody Against Putin," which won this year's Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature.
In an interview with The Telegraph, Kon said her Jewish identity had never been an issue at work for many years, but that the atmosphere changed dramatically after October 7. She described a conversation with a colleague in which she said Hamas terrorists were evil, only to receive the response, "So are Zionists." On another occasion, she said, a colleague told her to consider what had driven Hamas to carry out the attack.
"I really did feel like I had Jew stamped on my forehead," Kon said, describing the change she experienced. According to her account, instead of being regarded as a journalist and producer who happened to be Jewish, she began to feel that colleagues viewed her primarily through her Jewish identity and the political positions they attributed to her.
One of the central disputes involved Kon's efforts to advance a documentary about the Hamas attack at the Nova music festival. She said there were demands for the film to present the events in a broader context and examine the reasons behind the attack. Kon alleged that her ability to cover the subject objectively was questioned because she was Jewish, and that she was told she could not oversee the project because she was biased.
Kon also recalled a colleague telling her that if she wanted to describe Hamas members as terrorists, she should apply the same label to Israel. Following these and other remarks, she said she raised concerns about the treatment of Jewish employees with BBC management and established a support group for Jewish staff members.
In January 2024, Kon filed a formal internal complaint. After an investigation lasting approximately five months, she was informed that her complaint had not been upheld. Her subsequent appeal was also rejected.
Kon said the stress later affected her health, forcing her to take sick leave. The broadcaster subsequently informed her that her position was at risk because of organizational restructuring. Her employment with the BBC ended in April 2026, shortly after a documentary she had helped produce won an Oscar.
Kon pursued legal action alleging discrimination, harassment and unfair dismissal. The BBC ultimately agreed to pay her more than £400,000 but did not admit liability for her allegations. According to reports, the settlement also included a correction concerning how her name appeared in the credits for "Mr. Nobody Against Putin."
Kohn also sought a formal apology and a meeting with the BBC's new director-general, Matt Brittin, but said both requests were rejected.
A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster does not comment on individual personnel matters and that antisemitism of any kind is not tolerated within the organization.
In a separate statement cited in reports, the BBC said its internal investigation had not upheld Kon's allegations of antisemitism, but acknowledged that the handling of the matter had revealed shortcomings and had a personal impact on her. The broadcaster also expressed appreciation for her years of service and contributions.
Kon stressed that she does not believe the BBC as a whole is antisemitic. However, she argued that antisemitism and groupthink remain problems within the organization, making it difficult for employees to express views that differ from those prevailing in their workplace.
She said that even after leaving the BBC, she had spoken with Jewish employees who continued to feel uncomfortable and were afraid to speak openly about their Jewish identity or identify themselves as Zionists.

MOLD punctures terracotta-colored greek island ‘M residence’ with seven open-air courtyards

MOLD punctures terracotta-colored greek island ‘M residence’ with seven open-air courtyards
curved passages and planted courtyards create a sheltered interior within the rose-colored home on serifos.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a solid square carved open to the sky
On the Greek island of Serifos, Athens-based MOLD Architects shapes its M Residence around seven open-air courtyards carved into a square volume. From above, the terracotta-colored home looks almost like a diagram. Its flat roof is punctured by irregular openings, revealing planted gardens and shaded passages within the building’s compact outline. The residence occupies an exposed site in Lia, where its geometric silhouette stands against the dry, rocky hills overlooking the Aegean Sea.
The project has an unusually long history. Architect Iliana Kerestetzi first developed the design in 2011, during the early years of her practice, though it remained unbuilt for more than a decade. When new owners revived the scheme, the architect returned to the original drawings with a different perspective. The central concept remained, while the rooms opened more generously toward the courtyards and the material palette grew warmer. Completed in 2026, the house retains the graphic strength of its original design, with a more fluid layout inside.
seven courtyards shape the interior
MOLD Architects’ M residence takes its exterior form from the enclosed architecture of Cycladic monasteries, whose solid walls shelter spaces within. The team combines this reference with the cubic buildings of traditional island settlements and the softer geometry of rural stone structures. The house maintains a strict square perimeter, though inside, curved walls bend around the rooms and connect a sequence of seven courtyards. Each opening introduces a different relationship with the landscape, bringing daylight deep into the plan.
Moving through the house, enclosed rooms give way to pockets of open sky. Some courtyards become small gardens planted with grasses, while others offer shaded places to sit with views toward the Aegean. Broad passages connect these spaces beneath the continuous roof, whose irregular cutouts form curved edges overhead. The sea appears between the walls, disappears around a corner, and returns through another opening.
a pink monolith hovering above the rocky terrain
From the surrounding hillside, the house presents a very different character. Its exterior walls are largely solid, interrupted by recessed windows and occasional perforated brick screens. The entire volume sits on a raised plinth, with a narrow shadow line separating the terracotta-colored mass from the uneven ground. A rectangular swimming pool extends beyond the building’s footprint which introduces a long, straight edge alongside the more irregular geometry of the roof.
The warm plaster continues throughout the residence, covering the walls and ceilings in earthy pink tones. Inside, rounded corners soften the transitions between spaces, while pale wood cabinetry brings a change in texture. The kitchen faces the water through a broad opening, and large sliding glass panels connect the rooms to their neighboring courtyards. Even the bedrooms and bathrooms maintain a close relationship with the surrounding terrain, where windows frame glimpses of the sea.
shifting light across the curved walls
Across the courtyards, the architecture changes considerably with the movement of the sun. Roof openings cast broad shadows that travel over the rounded walls, while the perforated screens filter daylight into smaller patches. The planting adds another layer of texture against the plaster surfaces. In some spaces, the architecture almost entirely frames the sky, leaving the surrounding coastline momentarily out of view.
The residents have already begun making their own additions. Beneath one of the roof openings, they have suspended a piece of white fabric that filters the sunlight and moves with the breeze. It is a small intervention within an otherwise strongly defined composition. For a house conceived around a single geometric figure, M Residence contains a surprising variety of places to occupy, each shaped by the changing light and its particular opening to the outdoors.
project info:
name: M Residence
architect: MOLD Architects | @moldarchitects
location: Serifos, Greece
lead architect: Lia, Serifos Island, Greece

The US-negotiated cease-fire aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the eastern Ukrainian city of Oleshky took effect in the early hours of October 27, shortly after Russian air attacks struck Kyiv, hitting a university dormitory and other civilian sites and killing at least one person.
The start of the cease-fire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump last week and confirmed by Moscow and Kyiv, comes amid what she described as a dire situation in Oleshky, a frontline city on the brink of disaster, where the remaining population consists primarily of elderly residents urgently in need of medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.
"The cease-fire has begun, and the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, wrote on Telegram on October 27.
"Today, at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time and 4:00 a.m. Moscow time, a cease-fire was introduced in designated areas associated with the humanitarian mission," he added.
The Russian Defense Ministry said it had halted fire in the Kherson direction and introduced a "cease-fire regime" ahead of a planned humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
Oleshky lies on the Russian-occupied bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the regional capital of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the city had approximately 24,000 residents.
Melania Trump's office estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 people remain, including about 50 children. Most are believed to be elderly residents who have been unable or unwilling to leave. There has been no formal demographic count since 2022.
The city has endured years of fighting, displacement, and isolation. The destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 compounded the devastation, with an estimated 90 percent of Oleshky's territory flooded.
Russian Strikes Hit Kyiv As Zelenskyy Seeks Air Defenses
Russian air attacks struck Kyiv late on October 26, hitting a university dormitory and other civilian sites and killing at least one person. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Ukraine's partners to provide the "proper tools" for the country to defend itself.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 10 people were injured in the strikes, "most of whom were students from a university dormitory."
"It is precisely under such circumstances, when the threat is constant, when strikes can come at any moment and target cities and villages directly, that artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.
"It is important that our partners understand that Ukraine needs the proper tools to destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers. This would be the most effective way to save lives. It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war. "
US lawmakers have been challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they have said in recent days that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
For several months, Zelenskyy has also called on the US and other allies to step up supplies of critical defense systems such as Patriot missiles amid almost nightly barrages of Russian ballistic missiles and drones.
He said last week that Ukraine was still waiting for previously agreed deliveries of interceptors for Patriot air-defense systems.
Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, Russian officials deny targeting civilian infrastructure in the conflict, which has raged since the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
The university hit in the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), one of Kyiv's largest schools with more than 15,000 students.

What is celebrated on October 27 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:52:46 EET
09:52:46 KST

What is celebrated on October 27 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Ukrainian Writing and Language Day is celebrated, and Nestor the Chronicler is honored. Around the world, people commemorate audiovisual heritage, occupational therapy, and black cats.
On October 27, Ukraine observes Ukrainian Writing and Language Day, while around the world, under the auspices of the UN and international organizations, World Day for Audiovisual Heritage and World Occupational Therapy Day are held. According to the church calendar under the new style, Saint Martyr Nestor of Thessalonica and Venerable Nestor the Chronicler of the Caves are commemorated, while under the old style, Venerable Paraskeva of Serbia and Venerable Nicholas Sviatosha are remembered, UNN reports.
World Day for Audiovisual Heritage
An official international UN date proclaimed by UNESCO in 2005 during the 33rd session of the General Conference. The event is intended to draw the global community’s attention to the importance of preserving films, video recordings, radio programs, sound recordings, and photographs, which constitute the unique documentary heritage of humanity. The day emphasizes the need to digitize archival materials, as a significant portion of the magnetic and film media of the 20th century is threatened with irreversible deterioration and loss.
World Occupational Therapy Day
Established in 2010 at the initiative of the World Federation of Occupational Therapists. This professional observance highlights the importance of rehabilitation medicine, which is aimed at restoring the functional skills lost through illness, injury, or disability that are necessary for independent daily living, education, and professional activity.
International Black Cat Awareness Day
Established by environmental and animal-protection organizations with the aim of overcoming superstitions, prejudices, and myths associated with black-colored animals. The event draws attention to statistics showing that black cats are the least likely to find owners in shelters and are more often subjected to cruelty because of mystical superstitions.
Ukrainian Writing and Language Day
An official state holiday in Ukraine established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 1997. Following the calendar reform of the Ukrainian churches, the date of observance was moved from November 9 to October 27 in order to preserve the historical and spiritual connection with the commemoration day of Venerable Nestor the Chronicler. The day is dedicated to promoting the native language, preserving cultural identity, and strengthening civic consciousness. Traditionally, on this day, Suspilne Broadcasting holds the All-Ukrainian Radio Dictation of National Unity live on air, bringing together millions of Ukrainians around the world.
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Martyr Nestor of Thessalonica — a young Christian warrior who was a disciple of Saint Great Martyr Demetrius. Nestor challenged the gladiator Lyaeus to a duel; Lyaeus had been killing Christians in the arena for the entertainment of Emperor Maximian, and Nestor defeated him with the blessing of Saint Demetrius. For this, Nestor was executed by beheading in 306. On this day, Venerable Nestor the Chronicler of the Caves is also remembered — a monk of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a prominent Old Rus historian and writer, and the author of the "Tale of Bygone Years," who is considered the father of Ukrainian historiography and writing.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Venerable Paraskeva of Serbia — an ascetic and religious devotee who spent many years in strict fasting and prayer in the Jordanian Desert. Venerable Nicholas Sviatosha is also remembered — the first of the Rus princes to renounce power and wealth and accept monastic tonsure at the Kyiv-Pechersk Monastery, becoming renowned for his humility and for building the Trinity Gate Church.

US-Brokered Truce Begins in Russian-Occupied Oleshky Amid Uncertainty Over Evacuations

Ukraine confirmed that a US-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky took effect early Tuesday, Oct. 27, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, although uncertainty remains over monitoring and whether residents can safely leave the devastated southern Ukrainian city.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said the localized truce began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (4 a.m. Moscow time), following negotiations mediated and coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments,” Lubinets wrote on X.
He said the arrangements were agreed with Yana Lantratova, who headed the Russian negotiating delegation.
Lubinets pledged to continue updating the public, emphasizing that the safety of civilians in Oleshky and compliance with the agreement remained Ukraine’s priorities.
Neither Kyiv, Moscow nor Washington has publicly identified an independent monitoring mechanism or disclosed detailed arrangements for the humanitarian operation.
The truce is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and prepare for the evacuation of civilians from Oleshky, where an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain under Russian occupation, many of them elderly.
While Ukraine has confirmed its compliance, officials have not yet reported that humanitarian convoys have entered the city or that evacuations have begun.
Russian attack disrupts Kyiv’s South Bridge and metro service
Questions also remain over the operation’s duration, safe passage for residents and whether both sides will maintain the ceasefire in an area devastated by years of fighting, flooding and severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine warns against sharing evacuation details
In a Telegram statement, Ukraine’s General Staff said the ceasefire would apply exclusively to designated areas involved in the humanitarian operation, including aid deliveries and preparations for civilian departures.
The military urged the public to rely on official information and refrain from circulating unverified details about evacuation routes, convoy movements or the timing and location of humanitarian operations.
Ukrainian forces were taking all possible measures to assist residents and protect civilians, the General Staff said.
Ukraine’s military has previously used drones to deliver food and medicine to residents stranded in Oleshky and surrounding settlements.
The Russian military has said it would facilitate the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy, including engineering reconnaissance of the route, according to AFP.
However, Ukrainian officials have not yet announced when humanitarian supplies will reach residents or when the first evacuations will take place.
Ukrainian ombudsman confirms agreement with Russia
Lubinets said the arrangements followed direct negotiations with Russia’s representative, Yana Lantratova, coordinated through the US first lady’s humanitarian initiative.
The agreement covers several stages, including a localized cessation of hostilities, demining of routes, humanitarian aid deliveries and the voluntary departure of civilians.
“We have recorded all the agreements and signed an agreement,” Lubinets said in an earlier Telegram statement.
He warned that implementing the arrangements would be difficult and would require a gradual approach.
His latest confirmation that Ukraine is honoring the ceasefire marks a new stage in the operation, though the success of aid deliveries and evacuations has yet to be established.
Ukrainian authorities have emphasized that residents must be free to choose whether and where they evacuate.
It remains unclear how their preferred destinations will be verified or whether international humanitarian organizations will participate directly in the operation.
Melania Trump says civilians can choose where to go
Announcing the agreement Friday, Oct. 23, Melania Trump said Ukrainian and Russian civilian officials would visit residents in their homes to assess their humanitarian needs.
Those wishing to leave would receive transportation and support to reach their preferred destinations, she said.
“I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said in a White House statement.
The White House originally announced Oct. 29 as the start date, but Ukrainian and Russian authorities subsequently agreed on Oct. 27.
Melania Trump also said an American media organization would accompany the humanitarian mission to document conditions and the treatment of civilians.
US television network Newsmax said it had secured exclusive access to accompany observers entering Oleshky on Thursday.
However, neither side has publicly explained who would independently monitor compliance with the ceasefire or oversee the evacuation process.
Residents ‘forgotten what bread is’
Oleshky, situated across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the opening stages of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The city’s prewar population of approximately 24,000 has fallen to an estimated 1,700 to 2,000, including around 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Conditions deteriorated further following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, which caused widespread flooding along the lower Dnipro River and severely damaged local infrastructure.
Former residents told AFP that people still living in Oleshky were surviving on garden produce or hunting pigeons as food supplies dwindled.
“They’ve forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there’s not even flour left,” Olga, who remained in contact with two families in the city, told AFP.
Residents have also faced severe shortages of medicine, drinking water and reliable electricity.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly reported that Russian occupation forces prevented civilians from leaving Oleshky, restricting evacuation routes and leaving residents stranded amid worsening humanitarian conditions.
Russian representative Lantratova claimed Monday that most residents wishing to leave had already done so voluntarily.
However, Ukrainian officials and volunteers have warned that remaining residents face significant obstacles to evacuation through Russian-controlled territory.
Fears over evacuation and monitoring remain
Despite confirmation that the ceasefire has taken effect, the humanitarian mission faces considerable challenges because Oleshky remains under Russian military control and lies close to the active front line.
Years of fighting have left roads and surrounding areas damaged or potentially mined, complicating the safe movement of humanitarian convoys and civilians.
Ukrainian Pravda reported Monday that the initial stages of the operation were expected to include demining routes and delivering essential supplies before evacuations could begin.
Lubinets said Ukrainian officials intended to monitor implementation of the agreement and verify conditions inside the city.
However, neither Ukraine nor Russia has announced how long the ceasefire will last or provided a public timetable for completing the humanitarian mission.
The localized truce comes as broader US-mediated negotiations between Ukraine and Russia are expected to resume in November after months without substantive progress.
For residents still stranded in Oleshky, the ceasefire offers a potential opportunity to receive desperately needed supplies and leave the occupied city, but its humanitarian impact remains uncertain.

Luxurious baths, statues of gods, and precious objects – archaeologists have found the likely residence of a Roman military commander
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:35:31 EET
09:35:31 KST

Luxurious baths, statues of gods, and precious objects – archaeologists have found the likely residence of a Roman military commander
Kyiv • UNN
At the Novae fortress, archaeologists discovered a building covering more than 418 m² with private baths, statues, and precious artifacts. Scientists assume that the legion’s commander lived there.
Polish archaeologists have discovered the remains of a luxurious building in northern Bulgaria that may have been the residence of a Roman legion commander. The finds include private baths, ancient sculptures, bronze furniture and valuable ceramics. Science in Poland reports this, citing researchers from the University of Warsaw, according to UNN.
Details
The monumental structure was found on the territory of the ancient Roman fortress of Novae. Its area exceeded 418 square metres, while the interior decoration indicates the high status of its former residents.
Archaeologists discovered the remains of a colourful floor, painted plaster, sculptures and two altars with inscriptions. However, the researchers were most intrigued by the private baths, which were extremely rare in Roman military fortifications.
Why archaeologists believe that a legion commander lived here
The head of the study, Piotr Dyczek of the University of Warsaw, explained that ordinary legionaries used communal baths, while only high-ranking military commanders could afford their own large bathhouses.
"Few people in Roman forts had private baths. There were communal baths for the entire legion. In fact, only a legate could have his own large bathhouse,"
Other finds include bronze furniture fittings, statuettes, a marble head of the god Mithras, a fragment of an imperial portrait and a decorative architectural element in the shape of a pine cone.
Of particular interest is a statuette that researchers associate with ancient religious cults. According to archaeologists, such objects may indicate contacts between the fortress's inhabitants and other regions of the Roman Empire, particularly the Middle East.
Scientists are continuing their research to definitively establish the building's purpose and confirm whether it was indeed the residence of a legion commander.

Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory

Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory
Authorities say the fire in Brasov in September is part of a broader Russian campaign against European countries that support Ukraine.
Romanian authorities say they have uncovered a network “coordinated” by Russia that they believe was responsible for a fire at an industrial site near a state-owned weapons factory in September.
Romania’s Intelligence Service said on Monday that the blaze in the central city of Brasov on September 14 was “part of a wider campaign of sabotage operations coordinated” by Russia amid its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The agency said the operations were aimed at arms manufacturers and “other targets of military and industrial interest”.
“These actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken the contribution of the targeted states to European and regional security,” it said in a statement.
There was no immediate comment from Russia on Romania’s claim. Moscow has previously repeatedly denied such accusations.
Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, said three people had been involved in the Brasov fire – two Belarusians and a Ukrainian, all living in European Union countries.
Two were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offenses”, the directorate said.
The third remains at large in Poland.
According to Romania’s Intelligence Service, recruits for such networks are often found on social media and are first offered money “for a seemingly harmless task”, such as “observing or photographing certain targets”.
Over time, “the tasks become increasingly serious, potentially involving acts of vandalism, arson or even murder”, it said.
‘Hybrid’ war
Romania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border of more than 600km with Ukraine.
Its centrist president, Nicusor Dan, has said the country is a target of a hybrid war that Russia is waging to destabilise nations backing Kyiv, citing drone incursions into Romanian airspace, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and sabotage.
Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said the fire in Brasov was “part of a broader campaign of sabotage across Europe” targeting military production.
“Hybrid attacks will not hold us back from strengthening our resilience and defense,” he wrote on X.
The accusation follows a string of incidents at defence sites across Europe in recent weeks.
In September, explosions and a fire erupted at an ammunition storage site in Bulgaria, weeks after a blaze at another munitions facility in the country. Both sites are operated by the Bulgarian arms maker EMCO, whose munitions are used in Ukraine.
That same month, firebombs were thrown near the offices of a defence company in Munich, and Romanian authorities said they had detained a Russian citizen accused of filming and photographing military sites in preparation for sabotage.
In August, a blast struck an ammunition factory near Rome in Italy operated by the arms maker KNDS.
At sea, at least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks, and about 34 sailors have been reported dead or missing.
Dan, the Romanian president, has called the attacks on ships in Romanian waters “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”.
A year ago, Poland and Romania also detained eight people suspected of taking part in a Russian plot to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.

More than 40 sets of World War II remains exhumed in Mlyniv, Rivne region
Oleksii Zlatohorskyi, director of the specialized institution “Volyn Antiquities” and an archaeologist, told Ukrinform about this.
“During search operations in July of this year, 15 coffins containing remains were discovered on the grounds of the Memorial of Glory in the center of the village. The Soviet monument itself bears the names of 347 people who are supposedly reburied there. These are not local residents, but Soviet soldiers who died during World War II, who were originally buried on the outskirts of the village and later reburied in the center of Mlyniv. However, this figure has not been confirmed. “Preliminarily, during the exhumation, we discovered 47–48 sets of remains. The final figure will be known after a more detailed examination,” the archaeologist said.
1 / 12
Zlatohorskyi is a member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. While on leave, together with his fellow archaeologists Artur Alyoshin, Nazariy Romanyuk, and Dmytro Demianchuk, he conducted the exhumation of this burial site at the request of the Mlyniv community leadership.
As the search team discovered, based on the accompanying documentation, it can be concluded that most of the remains belong to military personnel. In particular, the remains of six women were found among them. The remains of two children were also discovered.
"I suspect that, perhaps, while excavating World War II-era graves near the local cemetery, they unearthed remains from a civilian burial site. That is why children were found buried at the memorial. As for the women, according to the accompanying materials found, they were military personnel,” Zlatohorskyi said.
Along with the remains, archaeologists found spoons engraved with their owners’ initials. They say this usually indicated military status. They also found pieces of leather belts, boots, fragments of eyeglasses, and a razor. Materials that may be important for identification will be transferred to the Rivne Regional Museum of Local History after processing and cleaning. Samples were also collected during the examination of the remains for DNA analysis.
According to Zlatohorskyi, working during the exhumation in Mlyniv was difficult because, during the reburial, the remains of 10–15 people had simply been dumped into a coffin, covered with clay, and placed in brick-lined crypts.
“For the Soviet authorities, the ideological significance of this memorial was more important than respect for the people they supposedly wanted to honor,” the archaeologist added.
The remains exhumed in Mlyniv were reburied at the local cemetery.
Previously, the memorial in Mlyniv was included in the list of 100 monuments to be dismantled as part of the decommunization process by the “Decolonization. Ukraine” project.
Suspilne. Rivne reported that, in order to dismantle the sculpture of a Soviet soldier and renovate the complex, the village council appealed to the Ministry of Culture to have the memorial’s status as a historical monument revoked. Subsequently, in coordination with the Ministry of Culture, search operations were conducted to locate the remains of World War II victims for their subsequent reburial. After obtaining all necessary permits and completing the exhumation and reburial of the Soviet soldiers, the plan is to transfer portraits of soldiers from the Mlyniv community who died in the Russian-Ukrainian war to the memorial grounds.
As reported by Ukrinform, a Ukrainian expedition completed search operations in Laskowo, Poland, where the remains of more than 40 people were discovered.

A US federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s move to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters that the justice department claims are non-citizens.
The court on Monday ruled 2-1 against Donald Trump’s justice department in the dispute, denying the administration’s demand that election officials segregate the thousands of ballots until people on the list could verify their citizenship. The justice department had given the California secretary of state 48-hours to carry out the order, which state election officials refused – leading to the lawsuit.
The decision by the San Francisco-based ninth US circuit court of appeals marks a setback in Trump’s attempts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the 3 November midterms. Voting rights groups and Democrats have criticized the effort, saying the Trump administration is attempting to create uncertainty around the upcoming election results as Republicans vie to retain control of Congress.
The ruling is also the latest development in a conflict between California and Trump’s justice department. The DoJ additionally filed criminal charges against 28 green-card holders in California earlier this month over alleged voter fraud – including several people who court papers suggested were confused about their eligibility and agreed to voluntary interviews with investigators.
There is uncertainty over how the justice department developed its list of 20,000 non-citizen registered voters and its accuracy. Court filings from last week showed that Los Angeles election officials analyzed a sample of 200 people on the list and found that a “high percentage” were born in the United States.
The justice department claims about non-citizen voting in California have also faced backlash from state officials, who have said that the DoJ has not provided data or methodology to back up its allegations. California secretary of state Shirley Weber called the department’s claims “vague and unsubstantiated” in a letter earlier this month. Weber also stated that the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year claimed that California had 190,000 registered voters that “may be” non-citizens, but provided no further details on how it reached that number.
California’s attorney general Rob Bonta touted Monday’s decision as a victory for voting rights and rejection of the Trump administration’s “unlawful overreach”, while Governor Gavin Newsom accused Trump of carrying out an “assault on democracy”.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the constitution and our country’s democracy,” Newsom said in a statement.
Trump has personally advocated for his supporters to seek out voter fraud in the midterm elections, posting on his Truth Social platform on Monday that he would issue a $1m reward for anyone whose report led to an arrest or conviction. He has long made unfounded claims that ineligible voting such as non-citizen voting is rampant, despite experts and data having shown it is exceedingly rare.

Explainer-Israel election: What happens after polls close?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:23:53 CET
09:23:53 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Israel holds a parliamentary election on Tuesday, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.
WHEN WILL WE KNOW WHO WON?
It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.
Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and ends at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT), when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.
A clear picture may emerge quickly but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.
The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
WHY IS IT SO COMPLICATED?
Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be held every four years but early elections have been frequent.
The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE RESULTS ARE PUBLISHED?
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell, Editing by Timothy Heritage)
