Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:23:11 CET
09:23:11 KST

By Steven Scheer and Pesha Magid
JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel’s election on Tuesday, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel’s deepening international isolation.
Yet Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel’s fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.
Opinion polls show a close race between Netanyahu’s Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT). The polls close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT). Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran. Netanyahu said on Sunday that Trump was prepared to act again to “finally” remove the Iranian threat, but only if Netanyahu remained in power.
Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of “relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats,” and said he was confident Trump would work “in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people.”
Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next year.
The Israeli Central Election Committee said 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote, some 330,000 of them for the first time.
THE OCTOBER 7 RECKONING
The election follows one of Israel’s most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Israel’s subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing government.
For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel’s deadliest day.
Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and Eisenkot supporter, said “the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that’s where our healing will come from.”
Lisa Tortor said she hoped Netanyahu would go and “they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel’s image.” Bibi is Netanyahu’s nickname.
But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Netanyahu was to blame for October 7 and called him “the right man for the state of Israel.”
“Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way,” Gabay said.
THE WARTIME RECORD
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after October 7, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks killed 74,000 people.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year’s joint US-Israeli war.
Eisenkot has said Israel’s next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an “arrangement” such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.
THE COALITION MATH
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.
A high turnout among voters from Israel’s Arab minority, Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage, could help nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.
Though Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
“My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide,” said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.
(Additional reporting by Maayan Lubell; Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Howard Goller)

Russia committed war crimes in Ukraine by attacking its energy grid, UN-backed inquiry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:21:17 UTC
09:21:17 KST

Russia committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine by intentionally attacking energy infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity and heat in freezing temperatures, a U.N.-backed inquiry reported Monday.
The inquiry also found evidence that Russia recruited men from 29 countries into its armed forces “through deception or coercion” to fight in Ukraine in violation of international law. The men, age 18 to 60, “came mostly from vulnerable and marginalized communities, with a poor economic background and a low education level,” it said.
The independent commission of inquiry was authorized by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council to investigate human rights violations shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its report to the U.N. General Assembly’s human rights committee on Monday was its first focusing on the impact of Russia’s wide-ranging attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The electricity cuts have left millions of civilians suffering in frigid winter darkness, the elderly without elevators to get to shelters during missile and drone attacks, and hospital patients without critical devices to keep them alive, the report said.
The commission concluded that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constituted war crimes because they were intentionally directed against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity for “inflicting great suffering to civilians,” commission chair Erik Mose said at a U.N. news conference, speaking by video.
Mose, a former Norwegian judge, said the intensifying attacks as this winter approaches raise serious concerns about the threats posed to civilians.
The commission said it based its findings on the accounts of 255 Ukrainians who endured winter conditions in Kyiv and eight other regions in 2025-26 as well as government officials, doctors and civic organizations.
Mose said the Russians have not responded to requests for comment on any of the commission’s reports, including this one.
Russia’s U.N. Mission said Monday that Russia does not recognize the mandate of the commission and claimed its findings were based on “falsified data.”
Throughout the war, Russia has consistently maintained that its forces are only striking military or military-related targets in Ukraine, or targets that are used in the interest of the Ukrainian armed forces, despite multiple reports and evidence indicating otherwise.
Russian authorities have been openly and actively recruiting foreigners into the army, offering perks such as accelerated Russian citizenship or making enlisting in the army mandatory for certain foreigners seeking permanent residency in Russia. Official rhetoric usually underscores the voluntary nature of such enlistments.
The report, however, said the men were recruited through deception and coercion in coordination with agents operating in other countries who presented themselves as legitimate and government-endorsed businesses.
The agents arranged visas and sometimes traveled with the men, who soon after arrival were forced to sign documents in Russian with the Defense Ministry that they didn’t understand, the commission said.
“The recruits were shocked to discover that they would be serving for the Russian armed forces,” it said.
The commission said it investigated the recruitment of nationals from 48 countries and found evidence that men from 29 countries were recruited into Russia’s armed forces as a result of deception or coercion. It named the 29 countries: Azerbaijan, Bangladesh, Belarus, Bolivia, Brazil, Botswana, Cameroon, Colombia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Ghana, Honduras, India, Jordan, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Tunisia, Turkey, Uganda, Uzbekistan, Yemen and Zimbabwe.

Libya says international aviation restrictions lifted

Breadcrumb
Libya says international aviation restrictions lifted after 11 years
Libya's Ministry of Transport said on Monday that the UN's International Civil Aviation Organisation removed airspace restrictions it issued in 2015 during the country's civil war.
The ministry said ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar announced the decision, formally issued on 23 October, at the opening of a meeting of civil aviation officials from the Middle East in Doha.
"This measure comes as a result of the notable progress made and the confidence placed in the capabilities of the Libyan civil aviation sector in recent times," the Tripoli-based Ministry of Transport said in a statement on its verified Facebook page.
In a separate statement, the ministry said the North African country has received requests for permits to transit Libyan airspace, which it characterised as "unprecedented demand from international airlines".
"The total number of permits registered for 2026-2027 winter season has surged to 61,968 flights per month, effective from this November," the ministry said, calling it a significant jump from an average of 2,000 transit flights per month during the 2025-2026 season.
"Such an increase will generate substantial financial revenues using Libyan airspace," it added.
Libya slid into chaos after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011. Three years later, a civil war broke out between armed factions vying for power, dividing the country between eastern and western administrations.
The war caused damage to up to 20 aircraft, including Airbus models, at Tripoli International Airport in 2014.
Few airlines currently operate flights in and out of Libya, and they have long been limited to destinations such as Tunisia, Jordan, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Sudan.
The ministry added that ICAO's decision would be circulated to all 193 member states for implementation.

Five years after AUKUS was signed, the first submarine has been named
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:18:47 UTC
09:18:47 KST

In brief
- The first US submarine bound for Australia under AUKUS has been revealed.
- Its arrival marks a major milestone in the defence pact.
The United States has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.
The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia's HMAS Stirling from late 2027, Defence Minister Richard Marles revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.
It's the first of up to four US submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.
But Colorado's arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in late May over revelations that the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.
The original AUKUS plans were for Australia to receive two used vessels and a new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The fact the US would now be sending second-hand vessels was described as "trash" by Tasmanian independent senator and army veteran Jacqui Lambie, but ministers and top military brass at the time insisted used subs were the best option.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the time assured the public AUKUS was going "full-steam ahead" despite tweaks being made to the mega-money deal, which US defence secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated on Tuesday along with Marles and UK defence secretary Wes Streeting.
Colorado is a "fast-attack" submarine, reaching speeds of more than 46km/h, compared with Australia's Collins-class subs' underwater top speed of 37km/h.
While second-hand, the Virginia class is the US' most advanced line of attack submersibles.
The higher-speed, longer-range vessels are needed to help Australia defend its sea trade, Marles has said.
"The selection of USS Colorado ... is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific," the joint statement read.
Australia's own nuclear subs will be conventionally armed, but the US has maintained a policy of ambiguity about whether or not assets rotating through the country are carrying nuclear weapons.
Being nuclear-powered means its range is effectively limited only by its crew's need for food and water.
Tuesday's statement says the AUKUS rotation arrangement will abide by all relevant non-proliferation treaties.

Addressing the Real AI Challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:18:18 UTC
09:18:18 KST

Adaptive feedback at scale. Conversational practice before high-stakes human interactions. Exposure to dialectal and pragmatic variation that a single instructor could never provide. Robust analytics for many learners. Each is just one example of the ways in which AI is transforming how language is understood, taught, and learned. To shape this transformation, we must move past the familiar debates around AI toward bigger questions. Drawing from years of working as an academic researching second-language acquisition and pragmatics, as a director of a grant-funded, national research center, and as a CEO of a company building responsible learning technology, I am confident we cannot answer any of these questions alone.
The real AI challenge is not technical. It is structural. Education and industry have long been trying to solve shared problems on parallel tracks. This parallel work is further heightened by the pressures AI is placing on all areas. The opportunity in front of us is to bring those tracks together by pairing the energy and speed of industry with depth of learning and teaching expertise. My hope is that our next phase merges historically parallel work into something that genuinely inspires and transforms how we learn language.
Three Key Areas for Collaboration
Collaboration is the answer, and it is well within our reach. Three areas of focus have the potential to facilitate the kind of teamwork that produces real, lasting outcomes:
- Sustainable funding models
- Research-driven decision-making
- Technological expertise
Here are ideas and examples on each area designed to catalyze future models.
Sustainable Funding Models
Meaningful collaboration cannot run on goodwill and unpaid evenings. Research that informs product development takes time, infrastructure, and people. Furthermore, the timelines of grant cycles rarely match the timelines of a release schedule. Sustainable funding models enable researchers and builders to work in genuine partnership over the long term, rather than treating academic input as a one-time consultation or occasional opportunity. Examples include:
- Funding models that utilize both commercial funding and grant dollars in parallel instead of creating contexts that compete with one another (e.g., OER developers partnering with commercial systems for low-cost materials development and scalability instead of an OER versus publisher model)
- Reward structures that promote collaborative work (e.g., guidelines that account for transformational research work in tenure and promotion cases; bonuses to incentivize innovative academic collaboration)
Research-Driven Decision-Making
Going forward, research must shape what is built commercially, even when it complicates the development road map. That means striking a clear balance between what the research tells us is best practice and what is commercially viable. I have seen these two priorities come into conflict many times. Despite what some believe, this is not because all commercial companies want to cut corners and maximize profit, but rather because what works in language-learning research does not always lead to a commercially viable product. Central to moving forward is a shared perspective on what questions to ask and how to utilize the key data. This could happen in any number of ways, including:
- Research time during which commercial companies share current problems they are attempting to solve with the research teams in the position to investigate them, along with commitment by both to answer those questions (e.g., a weekly research challenge meeting with a stable team investigating key problems)
- Shared values and parameters for making decisions collaboratively when timeline, best practices, and cost are in conflict (e.g., a list that a commercial development team always consults when making decisions about tech and development timelines)
Technical Expertise
Researchers cannot guide what they do not understand. Building real fluency with the capabilities, limits, and fail states of core technologies is now part of the job for anyone serious about language education. Industry has the responsibility to ensure any systems are legible enough to be studied, questioned, and improved. This requires curiosity, detailed documentation, and support for expertise to be shared among developers, academic partners, and learners themselves. Some of my favorite problems have even been solved by student interns with the technical expertise necessary to try a different approach to a development problem we face.
A Shared Responsibility
Focusing on these three areas requires rethinking some things we have treated as settled. For example, it means reconsidering how products are developed, with educators and researchers in the room from the first design decision rather than brought in to validate the last one. It means rethinking how time for educators and researchers can be reallocated and valued to ensure there is an opportunity to prioritize collaborative industry work. Moreover, it means accepting a model of shared responsibility, where neither sector gets to point at the other when things go wrong.
The future of language education will not be decided by AI. It will be decided by the choices we make about how to build, study, and deploy it and whether we are willing to make those choices together.
Julie M. Sykes, PhD, is the CEO of Lingro Learning (https://lingrolearning.com) and a professor of Linguistics at the University of Oregon. Her work bridges industry and academic partnerships, responsible and ethical AI, content development, and games with research in second language acquisition, specifically intercultural pragmatics and technological innovation for teaching and learning.

Moldova has offered Ukraine a new export route to Europe with a 50% discount
Kyiv • UNN
Moldova has offered Ukrainian businesses rail transit to Romania with a 50% discount. The countries plan to modernize the routes.
Moldova has offered Ukrainian businesses the use of its railway to export goods to Romania and other countries in the Balkan region. A 50% transit discount has already been provided for Ukrainian cargo. Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan stated this during the Kyiv International Economic Forum, UNN reports.
Details
According to Tofan, Moldova could become an important logistics corridor for Ukrainian exporters seeking to expand their presence in European markets.
He emphasized that Romania's economy exceeds $480 billion, while Moldova itself already directs about 30% of its exports to that country. In his view, Ukrainian enterprises could also make more active use of similar routes.
How the new export route will operate
The Moldovan prime minister acknowledged that the decision to cut tariffs on the rail transit of Ukrainian cargo by 50% was not easy.
Among the main difficulties, he cited the limited capacity of the state budget, the interests of local farmers, and the unsatisfactory condition of certain sections of the railway infrastructure.
Despite this, Chișinău is ready to work with Kyiv to modernize transport routes, simplify border crossings, and develop new routes for transporting goods.
Such cooperation is expected to help Ukrainian producers gain additional opportunities to supply products to Romania and other European countries.

Venezuelan officials allowed Maria Corina Machado to return, Rubio says

Venezuelan officials allowed opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to return, Rubio says
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Venezuela's interim government told the U.S. "weeks and weeks" earlier that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado could return to the country without interference, as the Trump administration pushes for a political transition that hinges on the cooperation of senior figures from Nicolás Maduro's former government.
"We spoke to the interim authorities and just said, 'Look, our expectation is that she's a Venezuelan. She belongs in her country. That's the country she's from. She should be allowed to return, and she should be allowed to return unperturbed, having no problems,'" Rubio told reporters. "And they told us that she could fly into the airport if she wanted to. And we communicated that to her team."
The disclosure came a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, and amid U.S.-backed efforts for an overhaul of the country's judicial and electoral institutions that Rubio argued are required before credible presidential elections can be held.
Machado snuck out of Venezuela in late 2025 to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, after spending nearly a year in hiding. Roughly one month after she departed the country, U.S. military forces captured Maduro and left his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, in control. The Trump administration has collaborated with Rodriguez on oil extraction and other issues, though the U.S. has said it expects Venezuela to eventually transition to a democratically elected government. Machado has suggested that she could run for president herself.
No election date has been announced, but Rubio insisted that the interim government was adhering to agreed-upon deadlines for replacing the country's Supreme Court and electoral council, institutions long used by Maduro's government to control political competition.
"We have timelines that are agreed to. And so far, they've met every one of the timelines," Rubio said, dismissing the possibility that Venezuelan authorities could indefinitely delay elections.
"You've got to change the infrastructure of the elections, not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years," he added. "It needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established."
Rubio cited what he described as compliance with U.S. national security demands to diminish Iranian and Cuban influence, pursue criminal organizations and extradite individuals wanted by American authorities, including former Maduro associate Alex Saab.
He also pointed to the administration's ability to grant or withhold sanctions relief and licenses permitting economic activity as an incentive for the interim government to cooperate.
"The United States has significant influence over the direction that these talks go and the results that we get from them," Rubio said.
Asked by CBS News whether Rodriguez and her brother Jorge, who leads Venezuela's National Assembly, had been offered incentives to facilitate the transition — including immunity from prosecution — Rubio said there was "definitely no talk about prosecutions or anything of this nature." He did not directly address whether immunity had been offered.
Rubio said the only time he personally discouraged Machado from returning was immediately after a devastating earthquake, citing the need to prioritize humanitarian relief operations.
"And the reason why it was very simple, because right at that moment, the only thing we were focusing on from a logistical standpoint was getting as many planes with relief aid as possible into the country," Rubio said.
Machado has criticized aspects of the Trump administration's economic deals with Venezuela's interim government, including a U.S.-backed oil deal announced by President Trump earlier this year. Rubio defended the agreement as a means of attracting private investment, saying her objections were separate from the question of democratic elections.
"She doesn't have to agree with it or like it," he said of the oil deal.
Rubio warned that failure to reach a negotiated transition could result in a return to an authoritarian system – or to armed conflict – but expressed confidence that the interim authorities would continue cooperating.
"If that's the interim authorities that try to do harm to this process or stop complying, then we're gonna have a problem," he said. "But I don't expect that. I really, really don't."
Since Maduro's ouster, the Trump administration has suggested Cuba is also in its sights, urging the island's government to make sweeping political and economic changes. Rubio said hours after the Venezuela operation that "if I lived in Havana and I was in the government, I'd be concerned, at least a little bit," pointing to Cuba's alliance with Venezuela. Mr. Trump has mulled "taking Cuba in some form," and hasn't ruled out military action.
Last week, Rubio and the CIA urged Cubans in social media posts to work with the agency if they want to see "positive change."
Asked why he encouraged Cubans to work with the CIA rather than pursue peaceful political change, Rubio said, "I can't answer that."
He added that Cuba needed "very dramatic change" and was "a totally different case from Venezuela."

Israel election: What happens after polls close?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:06:05 UTC
09:06:05 KST

Israel election: What happens after polls close?
- Israel votes on Oct 27 in its first election since the Hamas attack on 7 October 2023, with Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power under pressure.
- Exit polls are due when voting ends at 10pm, but the result may take days or weeks because seats are shared by proportional representation.
- After results, President Isaac Herzog will pick a prime ministerial nominee, who has 42 days to build a coalition or face another election.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israel is holding a parliamentary election on Oct 27, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.
When will we know who won?
It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.
Voting starts at 7am local time (1pm Singapore time) and ends at 10pm, when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.
A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.
The final tally is expected by Oct 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov 4.
Why is it so complicated?
Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be held every four years, but early elections have been frequent.
The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
What happens after the results are published?
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government. REUTERS

Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes
Unknown

2026-10-27

Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes
JERUSALEM - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel’s election on Oct 27, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel’s deepening international isolation.
Yet Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel’s fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.
Opinion polls show a close race between Netanyahu’s Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7am (1pm Singapore time). The polls close at 10pm (4pm Singapore time on Oct 28).
Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran.
Netanyahu said on Oct 25 that Trump was prepared to act again to “finally” remove the Iranian threat, but only if Netanyahu remained in power.
Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of “relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats,” and said he was confident Trump would work “in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people”.
Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government.
Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held in 2027.
The Israeli Central Election Committee said 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote, some 330,000 of them for the first time.
The Oct 7 reckoning
The election follows one of Israel’s most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Israel’s subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing government.
For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct 7, Israel’s deadliest day.
Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and Eisenkot supporter, said “the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that’s where our healing will come from”.
Lisa Tortor said she hoped Netanyahu would go and “they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel’s image”. Bibi is Netanyahu’s nickname.
But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Netanyahu was to blame for Oct 7 and called him “the right man for the state of Israel”.
“Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way,” Gabay said.
The wartime record
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after Oct 7, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage. The Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks killed 74,000 people.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and the joint US-Israeli war in 2026.
Eisenkot has said Israel’s next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an “arrangement” such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.
The coalition math
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.
A high turnout among voters from Israel’s Arab minority, Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage, could help nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.
Though Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
“My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide,” said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute. REUTERS

Just 23% of adults polled nationwide approve of his handling of the economy.

====================================================================================================

The Rise of Electrostates Could Redraw The Global Economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:01:02 UTC
09:01:02 KST

When shipping through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a halt in March, energy importers relearned an old lesson: a country that buys its energy as fuel, cargo by cargo, also imports every price shock. The consequences of how governments respond to this truth will soon reverberate beyond energy markets.
Decisions made today to secure more reliable energy may help determine where factories are built, which countries manufacture the technologies powering the global economy, and how vulnerable nations remain to the next disruption in oil and gas supplies. These decisions will define which countries emerge as electrostates, with the power to shape and control future economies.
New analysis by We Mean Business Coalition published today looking at electrification across 16 countries reveals how unevenly this transformation is progressing. The United States is doubling down on domestic oil and gas production, while China is rapidly electrifying its economy and consolidating its lead in electric technology manufacturing. Others are now moving in China's direction. France plans to lift electricity's share of final energy from 27% to 38% by 2035, Canada to double its electricity supply by 2050, and Europe wants to become the world's first “electro-continent.”
Rather than simply ranking countries, the Electrification Competitiveness Index maps two dimensions: the deployment and market uptake of electric technologies, and the policies and conditions supporting further progress.
Across the 16 economies, the median score for enabling conditions is 67%, compared with 45% for deployment and market conditions. In other words, in most countries, policy is running ahead of the market. Part of that gap is a time lag, but it also shows the distance between preparing for electrification and achieving it at scale. Successful electrification requires not simply more policies, but better-aligned policies that reinforce one another and give businesses the confidence to invest.
China scores highest on deployment, with extensive electric vehicle adoption and an industrial base producing much of the equipment the world needs to electrify. It already manufactures more than 80% of global battery cells. But its transition extends well beyond transport: electricity's share of China’s final energy consumption has doubled since 2005, with electrification spreading across industry, buildings, and transport. Although much of its electricity (54%) is still generated from coal, the plan is to replace that with clean power. What’s more, given China’s manufacturing dominance, as other countries electrify, they must make a choice: where to compete in electric technology manufacturing and where they might gain more from cheaper imported equipment.
Europe is one region trying to revive industrial competitiveness while reducing its exposure to imported fossil fuels, a vulnerability the Hormuz crisis has brought sharply back into focus. Electrification is central to both ambitions. Brussels wants to double electricity's share of final energy to 46% by 2040, yet that share has been stuck at around 23% for a decade, and the economics of switching remain difficult for many businesses. In Britain, industrial electricity costs over five times as much as gas per unit of energy, while factories in Germany and the U.K. face significant grid-connection constraints. France and Spain are better positioned in several respects, with more favourable electricity prices and stronger deployment, but across Europe the challenge is increasingly one of turning established policy frameworks into commercially viable investment.
Businesses deciding where to build factories, expand production, or replace equipment must also weigh electricity costs and grid access alongside skills, suppliers, and markets. If electrification remains difficult or expensive, businesses may postpone modernisation, continue investing in fossil-fuel equipment or direct new investment towards locations offering better conditions. Over time, this could reshape Europe's industrial geography, influencing where manufacturing capacity, jobs, and technological expertise develop.
In the U.S., existing deployment provides a foundation for further electrification, but policy reversals and infrastructure constraints raise questions about momentum. More than two terawatts of generation and storage are waiting in interconnection queues. Washington's focus on expanding fossil-fuel production risks leaving American manufacturers competing in a global market whose growth is increasingly driven by demand elsewhere.
For developing economies, electrification offers a different prospect: the opportunity to build modern energy and transport systems without first replicating the fossil-fuel infrastructure that wealthier countries are now spending heavily to replace. Ethiopia is already showing what is possible, with rapid electric vehicle adoption despite electricity reaching only around 60% of its population. Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Africa face greater barriers, including limited grid investment and electricity systems still dominated by fossil fuels.
Seizing those opportunities will depend on access to finance, reliable grids, and policies suited to each country's circumstances. Without them, emerging economies risk investing scarce capital in infrastructure that may become increasingly expensive to operate or eventually replace.
As this global shift evolves, economies powered increasingly by domestically generated electricity become less exposed to global fuel markets, but more dependent on access to batteries, electrical equipment, minerals, and the technologies needed to build and maintain their infrastructure. The concentration of manufacturing capacity in a handful of countries creates vulnerabilities of its own. Yet a dependency on equipment you buy once is very different from a dependency on fuel you buy every month. When a shipping lane closes, a fuel-importing economy feels it within days. If solar panel exports stopped tomorrow, the panels already installed would keep generating for decades.
Electrified economies also need far less energy in the first place. Burning fuel in engines, boilers, and power stations wastes around two-thirds of the energy that goes in, mostly as heat. Electric motors and heat pumps do the same work with a fraction of the input. So electrification does not simply swap one import for another; it can shrink the energy bill. The European Commission estimates that meeting its 2040 target could cut E.U. spending on fossil fuels by up to €260 billion a year.
This presents governments with a different industrial and energy-security challenge: not simply how quickly they can replace fossil fuels, but whether they can build the electricity systems, industrial capabilities, and trading relationships that make the transition economically resilient. Climate policy and industrial strategy are becoming impossible to separate, as the technologies needed to cut emissions also become central to economic competitiveness.
When governments meet in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31 in November, the U.N. climate conference president will push for a global goal to raise electricity's share of final energy from around 20% today to 35% by 2035. That shift deserves greater attention than it is getting. The transition from fossil fuels to electricity will not end competition over energy resources and technologies. It will change what countries compete for, what they need to import, and where economic power is concentrated. The electrostates of 2035 are being built now.

UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:01:02 UTC
09:01:02 KST

Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:01:02 UTC
09:01:02 KST

AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.
Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).
It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.
Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.
The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.
It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.
The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.
Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.
It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.
Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”
Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.
“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”

In parts of Southeast Asia, unsold homes are piling up as developers struggle to clear housing stock – yet young buyers hoping to land their first property still cannot find an affordable home.

Ex-FBI chief and Trump critic James Comey hit with fresh charges

Unknown Publisher

Ex-FBI chief and Trump critic James Comey hit with fresh charges
WASHINGTON – Former FBI director James Comey has been charged with allegedly disclosing national defence information, the third criminal case brought against the outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump.
In a criminal complaint unsealed on Oct 26, Comey is accused of communicating the information in October 2016, when he was head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, to a “person not entitled to receive it”.
Comey was charged in September 2025 with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding in what was widely seen as retribution by the Republican president against a political opponent.
A federal judge threw out the case on the grounds that the US attorney handpicked by Trump who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was indicted again in April, this time for allegedly threatening Trump’s life in an Instagram post that showed the numbers “86 47” spelt out in seashells.
The Trump administration’s Justice Department has claimed that “86 47” constitutes a threat to the president – “86” meaning to kill and “47” a reference to Trump being the 47th president.
Comey has denied threatening the president’s life.
‘I’m still innocent’
In the latest case, Comey is accused of directing an unidentified individual to “disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication”.
“They’re back again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack in response to the latest charges.
“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice,” he said. “I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
In a statement to US media, Comey’s attorney Patrick Fitzgerald said the charges in the latest case had been investigated by prosecutors during the first Trump administration and “the government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone”.
“Mr Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” Fitzgerald said.
The unsealing of the court documents came just hours after a US federal judge ruled that the July 2025 firing of Comey’s daughter Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor in New York, was unlawful.
Maurene Comey filed suit against the Department of Justice claiming she had been dismissed “solely or substantially” because of her father’s criticism of Trump or “because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs”.
In ruling against the Department of Justice, District Judge Jesse Furman said the younger Comey had been deprived of her due process rights and ordered that she be reinstated.
Since taking office, Trump has taken a number of punitive measures against his perceived enemies, purging government officials deemed to be disloyal, targeting law firms involved in past cases against him and pulling federal funding from universities. AFP

Jordan launches air strikes in Syria in response to a fatal church shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:50:11 UTC
08:50:11 KST

Jordan strikes Syria after church attack, killing at least seven people
Syria closes border crossings with Jordan after air strikes kill seven people in Deraa and Suweyda, including children.
Jordan attacks Syria in response to Karak church attack
Jordan has carried out air strikes in Syria in “retaliation” for last week’s deadly church attack, with Syrian authorities saying the raids killed at least seven people, including three children and a woman.
The attacks on Monday prompted Syria to close its main crossing with Jordan.
Jordan’s Armed Forces said in a statement that it targeted “hideouts” of armed groups in southeastern Syria in response to the gun attack at a church in its Karak governorate on Friday. At least nine people were killed and dozens more wounded in the shootings.
The Jordanian military said the strikes on Syria were launched “in coordination with the Syrian government”.
It said the raids “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”.
Syria, however, denied any coordination with Jordan.
In a statement, the Syrian government said “the military operation was conducted without prior coordination or notification” and said it has launched an investigation.
Syria’s Civil Defence service said at least four sites in rural Deraa and Suweyda provinces were hit on Monday evening, and that its crews had recovered the bodies of seven people: three men, a woman and three children.
Five of the dead – a man, a woman and three children – were members of one family killed in a strike on a tent in the village of Al-Tai in Deraa Province, the service said. Three other family members, including a child, were wounded.
A second strike hit Al Shayyah, also in Deraa, killing an 80-year-old man. A third hit a residential building in Muzayrib, in the Ain al-Basal area of Deraa, causing no casualties.
A fourth struck a residential building in the town of Shahba in Suweyda province, killing a 60-year-old man.
After the strikes, Syria’s border authority closed the Nassib crossing, suspending traffic in both directions. Nassib is the only crossing for passengers and commercial goods between Jordan and Syria.
A Syrian Foreign Ministry official called the strikes a “treacherous attack” and told Al Jazeera that the ministry would try to manage the fallout in a way that preserved Syrian sovereignty.
Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law on suspicion of involvement in the church attack. The arrests took place in the village of Al-Jadeeda, after a shootout with authorities.
A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the suspects sustained serious injuries during the confrontation, which lasted for about three hours.
The arrests and air strikes in Syria come after Jordan’s King Abdullah II pledged a stern response to the church attack. During the incident, three gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90km south of the capital, Amman.
The king said those responsible would face the “harshest penalties” and ordered a review of the country’s security procedures.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population, which makes up about 300,000 of Jordan’s 11.5 million people.

Russian dictator Vladimir Putin instructed the government to change how search engines operate in order to limit users’ access to information about abortions. Details

Russia is tightening restrictions on abortion
Russian authorities have already begun restricting the dissemination of information about terminating pregnancies. In particular, courts granted prosecutors’ lawsuits and ordered several private clinics to remove materials about medical abortions from their websites.
In addition, Russian television has begun censoring the word "abortion," although there is no legislative ban on its use. Officials are also increasingly replacing it with the phrase "negative choice during pregnancy."
Following the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine, the anti-abortion campaign in Russia intensified. As many as 30 regions have already adopted laws banning so-called inducement to abortion, and 24 of them provide for fines for violations.
Despite the Kremlin’s attempts to increase the birth rate, the demographic situation in the country remains difficult. According to Russia’s Ministry of Health, the number of abortions decreased by 5% in 2025, to 321,000 cases.

Harry Kane, Alexia Putellas win 2026 Ballon d'Or awards in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:43:23 UTC
08:43:23 KST

Halis Sünnetci
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane won the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or on Monday, becoming the first English player to claim football's most prestigious individual award since Michael Owen in 2001, while Spain's Alexia Putellas secured her third Women's Ballon d'Or.
The awards were presented at the 70th Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium, marking the first time the prestigious event was held in the British capital.
Kane, 33, claimed the award for the first time after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025-26 campaign, including 61 goals in 51 matches for the German side, which won a domestic double.
The England captain also scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup, helping his country finish third.
Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second in the Men's Ballon d'Or voting, while Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal took third place.
Kane became the fifth English player to win the award, joining Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, who last claimed the prize in 2001.
He succeeded Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele, who won the award in 2025.
Meanwhile, Putellas, 32, claimed her third Women's Ballon d'Or following her previous victories in 2021 and 2022, equaling former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati's record.
The Spanish midfielder captained Barcelona to a quadruple during the 2025-26 season, winning Liga F, Copa de la Reina, the Spanish Super Cup and Women's Champions League.
She was also named the Champions League Player of the Season and helped Spain win the Women's Nations League.
Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after her trophy-laden spell with Barcelona.
- Other award winners
Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal won Men's Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year, while Barcelona forward Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second successive year.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente was named Men's Coach of the Year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu received the women's coaching award.
Athletic Bilbao's Unai Simon won Men's Goalkeeper of the Year, with Barcelona's Cata Coll claiming the women's honor.
Bayern Munich's Kane also received the Men's Striker of the Year award following his prolific campaign, while Mexican forward Charlyn Corral became the first Mexican to win the Women's Striker of the Year award.
Barcelona were named Women's Club of the Year, while Paris Saint-Germain claimed the men's club award.

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens
- A US appeals court blocked Trump’s bid to stop California counting mail ballots from over 20,000 registered voters the government says may be non-citizens.
- The 9th Circuit said federal action would upset state election powers and risk “disorder and confusion” before the Nov 3 midterms.
- California called the case a “reckless political stunt” that could “disenfranchise thousands”, while evidence says non-citizen voting is very rare.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A US appeals court on Oct 26 ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely non-citizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in.
The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Oct 27 in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged non-citizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent votes from being counted by a state, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people allegedly registered to vote in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on Oct 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives – 52 – than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its so-called “sanctuary state” policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including non-citizen voting, is exceedingly rare.
A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which non-citizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state’s safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data”.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing.
“At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinising state voter lists to identify non-citizens risk wrongly flagging naturalised US citizens for removal from the rolls.
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney-General Rob Bonta, a Democrat. REUTERS

US Justice Department charges former FBI Director James Comey again

Rabia Iclal Turan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The US Justice Department has filed criminal charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time, accusing him of leaking national defense information in October 2016, according to court records unsealed Monday.
 
The two-count criminal information, filed under seal on Oct. 5 in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted and caused that information to be communicated, delivered and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
 
Prosecutors allege that on Oct. 5, 2016, Comey, “through one and more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
 
The information ended up in a New York Times article, according to The Wall Street Journal.
 
The filing was signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter.
 
The department said the filing, made exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure, was meant to preserve the case before the statute of limitations expired while it seeks a grand jury indictment.
 
Comey has moved to dismiss the case in sealed proceedings, arguing that an indictment is required within 10 years and the filing does not suffice.
 
“An indictment fundamentally differs from an information,” his lawyers said in a court filing.
 
In a video posted on social media, Comey said: “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
 
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” he said.
 
Asked about the charges as he arrived at Joint Base Andrews after a rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know too much about it. I just heard about it.”
 
“I think he’s a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it,” he said.

Trump says Brazil election looked ‘rigged’, defeated Bolsonaro’s party recognizes Lula win
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:37:31 CET
08:37:31 KST

By Oliver Griffin and Eduardo Simões
SAO PAULO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote ”looked like another rigged election,” although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in Sunday’s presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded.”
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.
(Reporting by Oliver Griffin, Luciana Magalhaes, Gabriel Araujo, Eduardo Simoes, Lisandra Paraguassu and Andre Romani in Sao Paulo, Ricardo Brito in Brasilia, and Trevor Hunnicutt and Costas Pitas in Washington; editing by Brad Haynes, Gabriel Stargardter, Andrea Ricci, Rosalba O’Brien and Lincoln Feast.)

Harry Kane completed his long quest for football's highest individual honor on Monday, with the Bayern Munich and England striker winning the Ballon d'Or after a record-breaking season that cemented his status as one of the game's greatest goalscorers.
Kane is the first Englishman to win the prestigious award in 25 years, after Michael Owen won it in 2001.
"Wow, wow, wow!" Kane said after taking the stage. "I am almost speechless. Being here in London makes it extra special. It feels like a good omen for me tonight. Thank you to everyone who voted for me. I can imagine it was tough this year.
"Some world-class players in the room tonight. Congratulations to all the winners and nominees tonight, and an impressive showing of determination and hard work can really achieve."
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Féminin for the third time.
Kane's move to Bayern in 2023 brought the team trophies that had long eluded him. In 2025-26, he coupled that success with goalscoring numbers that made him the leading Ballon d'Or candidate.
The England captain produced the most prolific campaign of his life, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German giants completed a domestic league and cup double.
By the end of the season, Kane had established himself as Europe's leading goalscorer, turning every competition into a showcase of his finishing ability.
His influence stretched far beyond club football. As England embarked on another attempt to end decades of hurt at the World Cup, Kane once again emerged as the team's driving force.
He scored six goals during the tournament and led England to the semi-finals, combining his clinical finishing with the leadership and composure that have defined his international career.
In many ways, the award represents the culmination of a remarkable journey. Few players have experienced a career arc quite like Kane's.
Once struggling to establish himself at Tottenham Hotspur as a youngster, being sent out on numerous loans, he developed into one of the most complete center forwards of his generation, capable of scoring every type of goal while also functioning as a playmaker.
The Ballon d'Or has often rewarded players whose success was built on flair and spectacle, but Kane's triumph is a tribute to consistency, intelligence and productivity on an exceptional scale.
Week after week, he delivered. Match after match, he decided contests. There were no prolonged slumps and few quiet nights.
His numbers were almost impossible to ignore.
Kane finished the campaign with 73 goals for club and country, a total rarely seen in the modern era. More importantly, those goals arrived in moments of genuine significance, helping Bayern collect trophies and driving England deep into the biggest tournament in the sport.
Fierce competition
The competition for this year's award was fierce. Kylian Mbappe broke World Cup scoring records. Lamine Yamal helped Spain to World Cup glory. Yet voters ultimately chose Kane, whose excellence lasted the entire season.
At 33, Kane has finally claimed the game's highest individual honor, adding a Ballon d'Or to a legacy that already places him among football's greatest strikers as England's all-time leading marksman and their record World Cup scorer.
Putellas was presented with the women's award after winning the treble with Barcelona in the 2025-26 campaign, in addition to the Spanish Super Cup. She moved to Women's Super League side London City Lionesses in July after 14 years at Barca.

China steps up snow leopard protection as population reaches 5,000

China steps up snow leopard protection as population reaches 5,000
China has continued to strengthen its network of protected areas in key habitats, establishing two national parks and 78 other protected areas in key regions, TV BRICS reported.
Since systematic conservation efforts began in 2013, China’s snow leopard population has doubled, rising from approximately 2,500 to around 5,000, whilst its range has expanded to approximately 2.08 million square kilometres.
According to China Daily, a TV BRICS partner, citing data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration, China is currently home to more than 60 per cent of the global snow leopard range and is the country with the largest snow leopard distribution area and population in the world.
The snow leopard, often hailed as the "King of the Mountains", is a Class I specially protected animal in China; its presence is regarded as a key indicator of the integrity, stability and health of mountain ecosystems. Two national parks and 78 other key protected areas have been established in critical habitats, with over 800,000 square kilometres of habitat under strict protection – meaning nearly 40 per cent of the species’ potential habitat is now under regulatory control.
Significant progress has been made in restoring populations in areas where snow leopards had previously disappeared. In the Helan Mountains region, China launched the country’s first snow leopard reintroduction.

The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.
It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defence alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.
The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.
But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital Tehran were "very good", according to state television.
"I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Read moreTrump says US may launch ‘another little Epic Fury’ attack on Iran
He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention", saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Prince Khalid, Pakistan's powerful army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.
Regional tensions have risen ahead of Israel's pivotal elections on Tuesday and next week's US midterms, where US President Donald Trump's Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.
As the talks in Tehran began, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said it was "essential to stop any escalation" in the Middle East.
"The risk to have the combination of an overwhelming military attack on Iran, and an overwhelming military attack by Iran on the countries of the Gulf, needs to be avoided at all costs," he told a press conference in Cairo.
Hesham Alghannam, a Saudi security analyst and researcher, posted on X, that "this historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control".
