Key Event
ASX closes higher
The S&P/ASX 200 closed up Tuesday, gaining 40.20 points or up 0.46 per cent to 8,850.1 points.
The local gains came after the US share market rose overnight off the back of Anthropic's IPO prospectus filing and Meta announcing plans for a $US95 billion stock offering to fund its spending on artificial intelligence.
Renaissance Capital senior strategist Matt Kennedy called Anthropic the "most highly anticipated IPO of the year".
The Claude developer's market debut will serve as a major test of investor demand for artificial intelligence companies.
Kennedy says it has also opened up wider questions about the need for greater regulation of AI players.
"Anthropic feels a lot of optimism and a lot of worry," he said.
"This could turn out to be, you know, the golden age, or, you know, these cyber incidents could multiply, and they bring up the idea of a worst-case scenario. Hopefully we don't get there, but I'm hopeful."
The geopolitical situation also remains uncertain. Michael Every at Rabobank notes Israel is about to hold its parliamentary elections where Prime Minster Netanyahu is behind in the polls but can't be written off.
"Over the weekend, the PM tweeted imagery of a nuclear attack on Tel Aviv and warned Israel may need to use crypto to avoid global sanctions, shocking Israel's public, its banks, and its high-tech export industries," he said.
The risk of a wider regional war also remains.
Every notes CNN reported the PM had planned to attack Iran again recently but was held off by Trump, who finally endorsed him to keep him quiet, and the IDF chief, who also blocked a move that would likely have meant we would already be deep into a new regional war at this moment.
Reuters also reports that Hezbollah is rearming for a new war with Israel backed by Iran, as Jordan just carried out an airstrike on Syria in response to a terror attack on one if its churches.
"Add that to the shuttle diplomacy being seen in the region, and escalation rather than deescalation seems likely — and imminently," Every said.
Key Event
More risks when investing in AI companies
There are so many more risks that AI businesses could be exposed to.
These risks are not, of course, unique to Anthropic, but the IPO filing with the SEC in the United States nevertheless details the uncertainty surrounding such rapid technological advancement.
Some of these spelled out for investors include the risk of third parties suing them:
"… there is an increasing number of open-source software license types, almost none of which have been tested in a court of law, resulting in a dearth of judicial guidance regarding the proper legal interpretation of such license types. If a third party makes a claim against us alleging that we have not complied with the conditions of the applicable open-source license, we could incur significant legal expenses defending against such allegations, expend substantial time and resources to re-engineer some or all of our software, and could be subject to significant damages …"
It also warns that as competition for AI talent continues to heat up, the company has hired employees who may have previously worked for its competitors. They hold all the secrets. What if they spill?
"These employees may have had access to proprietary or confidential information, including trade secrets, of their former employers. Although we require employees to comply with confidentiality and intellectual property obligations, we may nonetheless be subject to claims that we or our employees have misappropriated or improperly used trade secrets or other intellectual property of competitors or other companies. Such claims may be asserted even if we believe they are without merit and even in the absence of any intentional misconduct. Defending against these claims could be costly, time-consuming, and disruptive, and could divert management attention and resources away from our business."
Key Event
How is Anthropic monitoring the risk that Claude could go rogue?
More from Anthropic's IPO filing on that. It says:
"Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user's accounts. …We also maintain public reporting channels, including a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty program for testing our safety defenses."
Feel safer now?
Key Event
Anthropic IPO reinvites the perennial question: Might AI pose a risk to humanity?
I've just taken a closer look at the Anthropic IPO filing.
Here's my favourite quote, which plays on the idea that AI, or robots going rogue, poses a risk to humans.
"Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy. We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research and these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote about this existential threat this year, saying: "It is clear that, if for some reason it chose to do so, this [hypothetical] country [through AI] would have a fairly good shot at taking over the world — either militarily or in terms of influence and control — and imposing its will on everyone else—or doing any number of other things that the rest of the world doesn't want and can't stop."
Key Event
Qantas workers to strike tomorrow
Hundreds of Qantas ground workers will hold further strikes for 24 hours tomorrow across major airports, with workers from Qantas subsidiaries QGS, AAE and QantasLink demanding an urgent reset on pay, job security and safety.
"These workers are calling for fair pay, more secure full-time jobs and an end to the fragmentation of critical aviation work across multiple subsidiaries," the Transport Workers Union (TWU) said in a statement.
"The action follows years of wage suppression, outsourcing and declining standards across Australian aviation, including the tragic death of a Qantas Freight worker last year."
Qantas has said it has contingency plans in place and is not expecting disruption from the upcoming action.
"We are aware of planned industrial action by some of our freight and regional workgroups in Sydney and we have contingency plans in place. Importantly there will be no disruption to our customers," a Qantas spokesperson said.
"We remain committed to reaching agreements with our employees that deliver substantial pay increases and reflect the priorities they have told us are important to them."
Key Event
Universal Music Group reportedly discussed going private with buyout firms
The world's second largest record company, Universal Music Group, held preliminary discussions with private equity firms earlier this year about going private, Bloomberg News has reported.
The music label's management held preliminary talks with private equity firms including Apollo Global Management, TPG and Blackstone, according to the report.
But talks have not progressed and Universal has not started a sale process, the report said, adding that the company's board is aware of the discussions.
A deal would require the backing of the billionaire Bolloré family, which controls more than 30% of Universal between Vivendi SE and family holdings.
The report comes months after Universal's board unanimously rejected an unsolicited takeover proposal from Bill Ackman's Pershing Square Capital Management.
Hot chips when you fly?
Virgin Australia has introduced hot chips to its economy menu in what it says is an Australian airline first.
Overseas airlines including United, Ryanair and Brussels Air already offer hot chips on some flights.
Virgin Australia chief customer officer Andrew Cleary said the airline had worked to overcome the challenges of serving hot chips mid-flight and had developed a cooking process to keep the chips crispy at 35,000 feet.
A serve of hot chips onboard, with a side of aioli, will cost passengers $12 or 2,400 Velocity points, and will be restricted to flights of 1.5 hours or more.

Anthropic eyes biggest ever IPO as AI funding starts drying up
Anthropic is the next cab off the rank for mega-tech initial public offerings (IPOs), and is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history.
An IPO involves a company asking big financial institutions and "mum and dad" investors for cash via the stock exchange.
Elon Musk's SpaceX played this game in June, raising $US85.7 billion, with a listing price of $US135.
It hit the boards of the Nasdaq and subsequently shot up to $US161, with unprecedented investor interest pushing the company to a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

Key Event
Superannuation complaints on the rise
Superannuation complaints rose sharply in 2025-26, with the financial ombudsman receiving 8,755 complaints, up 42% on the previous financial year.
The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) says across all complaints areas, it received the highest number in its history, with almost 120,000 complaints lodged by consumers and small businesses.
Scams and unauthorised transactions were the top two issues in banking and finance, with 6,580 scam complaints and 6,038 unauthorised transactions complaints.
For general insurance, 36,022 complaints were lodged, marking a fifth year of growth for the industry. The most complained about product was motor vehicle insurance with 14,430 complaints lodged.
Complaints about super funds refusing to pay claims rose by 80%.
"As more Australians move into and through retirement, their relationship with their superannuation fund becomes increasingly important," AFCA chief ombudsman and CEO David Locke said.
"For many people, these funds represent a lifetime of work and financial security in retirement. Funds must take care to respond to members' concerns and focus on achieving good outcomes wherever they can."
He said large-scale collapses were the main driver of investments and advice complaints, with complaints from investors who lost retirement savings as a result of the Shield and First Guardian Master fund collapses, which I investigated in the article provided below, making up the bulk.
Financial difficulty complaints rose 17% to 5,566, with financial firms failing to respond to requests for assistance remaining as the top issue.
Key Event
Jim Chalmers introduces changes to CGT rules for startups
The May budget announced that the government would be removing the 50% CGT discount for indexation and that the change would include startups.
But after heavy campaigning from the startup and tech sector, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the tax break would be retained for them.
He said the Innovative Business Capital Gains Tax concession (IBCC) introduced to parliament today "supports early investment in innovative businesses by providing eligible founders, employees and investors with access to a 50% capital gains tax discount on equity investments".
"This means early investors in innovative startups that begin with a low or zero cost base still receive a significant discount on a future capital gain," he said.
"This will support investment in innovative Australian startups, and the continued growth of Australia's startup and venture capital system."
The legislation also includes changes to the Research and Development Tax Incentive by increasing core R&D offset rates by up to 50%.
Chalmers noted it "extends access to the refundable offset for young, growing firms for longer by increasing the turnover threshold from $20 million to $50 million, reduces the R&D intensity threshold so that firms that invest more substantially in core R&D can benefit from higher offset rates, and increases the maximum expenditure threshold".

Key Event
Woodside Energy to sell interest in Sunrise Joint Venture
Woodside Energy formally agreed to sell its participating interest in the Sunrise Joint Venture to Timor-Leste's state-owned energy company, TIMOR GAP, for up to $US200 million.
TIMOR GAP currently holds a 56.6% interest in the Sunrise Joint Venture.
Following completion, expected in 2027, Woodside will no longer hold a participating interest in the Sunrise Joint Venture.
On September 2 it announced it had entered into an agreement with Osaka Gas to acquire Osaka Gas' 10% interest in the Sunrise Joint Venture, subject to satisfaction of relevant conditions precedent.
"Greater Sunrise has been an important part of Woodside's portfolio for many years, and we recognise the project has the potential to deliver long-term economic and energy security benefits for Timor-Leste and the region," Woodside CEO Liz Westcott said.
"While Sunrise remains a high-quality resource, the transaction further simplifies Woodside's portfolio and allows capital and management attention to be focused on opportunities that present the greatest shareholder value."
Completion of the transaction is subject to conditions, including relevant government, regulatory and joint venture approvals.
Key Event
Canadian pension giant takes stake in La Trobe Financial
Canadian public pension fund OMERS has taken a minority stake in La Trobe Financial, one of Australia's largest non-bank lenders, from Brookfield.
The Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System (OMERS) is one of Canada's largest defined benefit pension plans.
La Trobe did not disclose the price or the size of the stake but Brookfield said it will remain majority shareholder and OMERS will sit alongside Brookfield and Axight as an institutional investor.
Earlier in the year, Brookfield also sold a 30% stake in the non-bank lender to Abu Dhabi-based private equity firm Axight for $3 billion.
That was almost double the amount Brookfield paid to acquire it in May 2022.
The latest transaction needs customary regulatory approvals and is expected to close by January next year.

Key Event
Directors of 1 in 5 companies going into liquidation have been there before
The corporate regulator has released a review on business liquidations that gives us an insight into how often directors of one company that goes under have been there before.
ASIC's review says there were 26,664 grouped appointments — 7,023 court liquidations and 19,641 creditors' voluntary liquidation (CVLs) — for the period from July 1, 2021, to June 30, 2025.
It found that roughly one in five involved a company with at least one director who had previously been a director of another company when it entered liquidation.
Many companies in the review were small in financial and operational scale, with limited assets available by the time they entered liquidation.
The median age of a company entering liquidation was seven years, with 60.9% of appointments involving companies aged six years or more.
About half of all liquidations realised no more than $10,000 in assets, and about one-quarter realised no assets.
About 69% reported liabilities of less than $1 million and 89.6% had five or fewer employee creditors. Liabilities reported by companies entering liquidation remained relatively stable across the review period, with median liabilities ranging between $410,000 and $530,000.
Limited assets also affected the work and remuneration of liquidators. In 88.1% of finalised liquidations, no dividend was paid to ordinary unsecured creditors and either no remuneration was approved or remuneration paid to the liquidator was less than the amount approved. This indicates that unrecovered remuneration was likely common.
"Directors should closely monitor their company's financial position and seek advice early when financial difficulties arise," ASIC Commissioner Kate O'Rourke said.
"Taking action early gives a company more options to address financial difficulties. The longer action is delayed, the fewer options may remain to restructure the business, preserve value or limit further losses to creditors."
Key Event
Federal Reserve expected to leave rates on hold, but it's 'tactical'
The US Federal Reserve will meet this week to decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to tackle inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday US time.
Wolfgang Bauer, fund manager at Royal London Asset Management, says "this should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than the end of the renewed tightening cycle".
"Growth and employment remain resilient in the US, inflation is still well above target, and Fed Chair [Kevin] Warsh recently described financial conditions as difficult to characterise as restrictive," he said.
"As further inflation data will only be published after the meeting, the Fed has good reason to wait without thereby adopting a softer monetary policy stance."
He adds the key question will be whether "Warsh maintains his assessment of financial conditions and clearly keeps a December rate increase open as an option".
"In our view, the most likely scenario is therefore a rate pause with a restrictive undertone: no change this week, but equally no signal that interest rates have already reached their peak," he said.

Key Event
What are analysts saying about Anthropic?
Many Australian investors will be keen to participate in Anthropic's IPO, either directly if they are wholesale investors with access, or indirectly through ETFs.
Should they? Analysts are divided.
Some like Wall Street tech analyst Dan Ives are upbeat (although he usually is on the tech sector). He says: "You're going to see probably a strong appetite for this offering."
In his view, despite making a loss, the company is "going gangbusters".
"For investors, they're going to basically need to look past this year," he told The Business.
"Looking out to the next two, three years, what does this company look like when they have revenue?
"And I think it's very similar to SpaceX in terms of that scenario."
He says while there's risk, there's also opportunity.
"I think that's something investors are going to have to weigh because we're all going into it, whether it's here in the US, Australia, wherever we are, we're all going into this fourth industrial revolution together."
Cameron Gleeson, Head of Investment Strategy at Betashares, is less positive.
He says "despite Anthropic's size and scale, investors should be mindful of letting their portfolios become too concentrated in the AI trade".
"We've seen Australian ETF investors ease back on US equities in recent months, as sentiment has cooled somewhat [with] the AI capex build-out," he said.
"While Anthropic's IPO would be historic, investors should stick to their broader investment plans and avoid seeing these stocks as a ticket to quick riches."
Renaissance Capital senior strategist Matt Kennedy says investors should be looking at the revenue per compute spend as the company grows.
Currently, the company says it makes more than $2 in revenue for every dollar it spends on computing infrastructure.
"We know that it can grow, but can it can actually turn that money into earnings? And the biggest cost right now is the compute cost, the expense side there.
"In addition to sales and marketing, they are spending heavily with their channel partners like Google to grow fast.
"But I think investors will want to take a look at that compute spend to really see if they can get the kind of margins that you get from a software company. Is this a company that can get to 60%, 70%-plus gross margins after the compute spend?"

Cybersecurity threats rise as AI menace gathers pace
Australia is getting better at protecting itself and responding to increasing cyber attacks, according to the Australian Signals Directorate.
The agency says there were more than 37,500 hotline calls and 82,000 cybercrime reports in 2025/26, as AI models speed up incidence and security threat. Cybercrime is costing individuals in the order of $33,000.
Identity fraud remains the top reported cybercrime.
The cybersecurity agency has called for further testing of frontier AI models in collaboration with operators and Five Eyes countries as well as urging for outdated technology across all sectors to be updated.
It also recommends "digital hygiene", which includes changing passwords, updating software and disconnecting tech from the internet if it doesn't need connection to reduce risk in the emerging AI landscape.

Surge in complaints about the ATO — but is it just due to crackdown on tax debts?
The Tax Ombudsman fielded 2,376 complaints against the ATO in the six months to September, up 74% from the same period in 2025 and 180% above the same period two years ago.
Debt collection and payment-related matters each accounted for 19% of complaint investigations from April to September, the agency said.
"Our latest complaint data shows more people are struggling due to the ATO's debt collection activity or interest charges or simply need to resolve delays to payments they are due," ombudsman Ruth Owen said.
In response, an ATO spokesperson said the tax office had only received 1,358 complaints over the same period, as the ombudsman's figures included cases that were resolved without any ATO involvement or that related to the Tax Practitioners Board or state tax issues. The ombudsman only investigated 501 complaints out of 2,376 it received and found in most cases the ATO had acted appropriately.
"At a time when many Australians are facing financial distress, we are seeing increased complaints about how the ATO is collecting tax debt owed and how interest is applied to the debt, often making the amount due impossible to pay back," Owen said.
In 63% of debt collection-related complaints, the agency found the ATO acted reasonably, down 9% from the same period last year.
Complaints about penalties and interest made up 18% of grievances, up from 13% a year ago.
Amid rising inflation and interest rates, tax liabilities were adding to mounting debts owed by taxpayers and small businesses, the ombudsman said.
The ATO was owed $54.2 billion in outstanding tax debt in 2024/25, according to the Australian National Audit Office.
Debts owed by small businesses amounted to $35.9 billion, an increase of $19.4 billion from 2018/29.

Star Entertainment sweats on AUSTRAC penalty
Probably our most successful regulator is one that only pops up in a very specific field: financial crimes.
The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC) worked out long ago how to get the attention of boards, directors and executives.
Absolutely massive fines.
- Commonwealth Bank, 2018: $700 million
- Westpac, 2020: $1.3 billion. With a B
- Crown, 2024: $450 million
Which is why embattled casino operator and anti-money laundering law breacher Star Entertainment is sweating today.
The company finds out tomorrow the size of the penalty.
Its annual general meeting (AGM) will be held from 10am (AEST) today and I'll follow any developments.
In the annual report, the company noted the civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court would be pricey.
"AUSTRAC submitted that a penalty of $400 million would be appropriate while The Star submitted that a penalty of greater than $100 million, payable in the 12 months following the hearing, would be challenging based on available liquidity options, including accessing equity markets. The Star is awaiting the court’s judgment."
Disclosure: I own shares in Star Entertainment, which I bought so I could ask questions at the AGM. The share price has had a precipitous fall in the past few years of relentless scandal. Five years ago a share was worth $3. Currently one is worth 0.12c. As if you needed a reminder that this blog does not constitute financial advice.

What's next for NEXTDC?
Further to our story on the The Business last night (see the video below), NEXTDC is the story I can't get enough of at the moment. Everyone hungrily using AI, huge demand for data centres (DC), yet the big question — who wants to live near them?! And what happens when vocal residents object to the potential noise pollution, air pollution, eyesore pollution.
We've seen it in Lane Cove in Sydney and, more recently, NEXTDC's shares have plummeted after it said opposition to a key project in Melbourne would cause it huge delays and torpedo its profit forecasts.
Victoria's electricity distribution network provider delayed the upgrade due to community and stakeholder opposition.
I like some of these takes from Commonwealth Bank's John Oh:
"It points to the social licence being one of the key requirements for the data centre build‑out."
To upgrade the powerlines, the network provider Jemena needs to install taller power poles in residential areas "which may reduce visual appeal in residential areas" likely underpinning the opposition, Oh says.
"It's worth noting, although underground cabling is an alternative option, it is a costlier (i.e. 2–6 x higher in Ireland) and timelier option. With electricity network operators making the final decision on upgrades made in their network, it points to the strong alignment required between DC operators and electricity network operators."
The Australian standards for AI will be geared towards ensuring DC rollout doesn't adversely affect electricity prices, water use, and consumers and communities. It's this stakeholder management that's going to potentially be the gamechanger when it comes to whether these centres are successful or not.
That and, Oh says, the need to ensure it doesn't negatively affect the power market:
"Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) expects data centre demand to grow from 2.5% of underlying National Electricity Market (NEM) demand (i.e. total electricity demand) in 2025‑26 to 7.6% of underlying NEM demand in 2030‑31."
NEXTDC's woes mount as it confronts community anger and loss of social licence

Key Event
Anthropic's numbers 'eye-popping', says Dan Ives
Anthropic has filed to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.
Here are some of the key metrics or findings from the filing, from Dan Ives at Yorkville Ives:
In September 2025, 950 customers spent at least $100,000 a year on them. This grew to 11,900 a year later, including the US's 10 largest companies and more than half of the top 500.
The company has Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900%, which means that for every $1 of revenue on average from a customer, Anthropic is generating about $9 from them a year later. Almost 2,000 customers spend more than $1 million, and roughly 250 more than $10 million.
"Concentration is easing: no single customer exceeded 10% of revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and roughly 79% of Q3 revenue came from outside the top five, up from roughly 64% in Q1, even as each top-five account hit a record. Revenue is overwhelmingly consumption-based ($13.1 billion in 1H26) with subscriptions at $3.2 billion, up from $180 million, and remaining performance obligations were $10.8 billion," Ives says.
Let's take a look at how revenue has changed in recent years:
- $41 million in 2023
- $386 million in 2024
- $4.6 billion in 2025.
The first half of last year it made $1.2b, and increased it to $16.3b for the first half of this year.
With this said, Ives says "there are some concerning (not unexpected) risk factors" in the filing.
"Anthropic has asked its cloud partners for more compute than they were willing to provide, and those same partners build competing models and could curtail, reprice, or terminate access, all while the take-or-pay commitments above are owed regardless of actual usage and have been partly debt-funded. The filing also discloses past failed or underperforming training runs, warns that scaling laws may plateau, and flags that safety-driven release delays such as holding back Mythos through Project Glasswing could slow capability gains versus competitors and may become more frequent and costly as models advance."
The filing also flagged some potential liability of the AI agents including misuse by bad actors, models acting in unintended or autonomous ways that no user directed, and contractual protections and insurance that may prove insufficient.
Ives finishes his note as the quintessential AI bull he is:
"Overall, the numbers are showing massive, eye-popping growth from a broadening group of customers as ANT aggressively goes after the enterprise market in this AI Revolution. The near-term losses are massive but investors on the IPO will be laser-focused on the growth trajectory into 2027 and 2028 as the next phase of this AI Revolution takes hold."

With Reuters
WFH issue flares again after legal case ends with a whimper
Yesterday we brought you news that retailer Myer has told employees that when it moves to a new office just around the corner from the ABC in Melbourne, everyone will be in it.
That is, work-from-home (WFH) is essentially dead, with exceptions on a person-by-person basis for people with illness, caring responsibilities or mega-commutes.
It's another flashpoint in a long-running issue that was meant to be settled.
A key case about the Clerks Award, the broad agreement about the rights and conditions of people working in administration, was meant to provide a definitive answer about this.
It didn't.
Essentially employees can ask for WFH. Employers must answer.
But it doesn't clear up if there is a clear entitlement to the right.
Here's a note from Ryan Murphy of McInnes Wilson Lawyers about the end of the case:
"Will this give all employees a standalone 'right' to work from home? No. Will it actually change a whole lot? Potentially not."
Here's the key bit:
"So, does the new clause in the Clerks Award create a right to work from home for all? No, we don't think so.
"By saying that an 'employee may request, and an employer may agree to', the proposed new clause is softer than the flexible work right in the Act. Indeed, the proposed Award clause anticipates that an employer may not agree to an employee's work from home request.
"What the clause may do, however, is broaden the scope of those who have a right to request to work from home. That presents the possibility that employees will seek to rely on this 'right' in disputes if an employee feels they have been treated less favourably because they have made the request."
The analysis from software firm Employment Hero spells it out pretty clearly:
"Can a request be refused? Yes. Because clause 5A operates on a consensual basis, an employer can decline a request. The clause does not set a response time, a requirement to give reasons, or rules around having to have any grounds for refusal."
So no 'right' but the reality that most employers and employees will negotiate.
As ever, the best bosses are not the ones that say yes to everything but those who are open to anything.

Ukraine and Moldova have deepened bilateral ties by signing a new military cooperation agreement intended to counter Russian threats, while pledging to pursue EU membership side by side.
The deal was struck during Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan’s visit to Kyiv on Monday, Oct. 26, where he met with his Ukrainian counterpart Serhii Koretsky and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We agreed to resume the work of the Intergovernmental Commission on Trade and Economic Cooperation and the ‘Odesa Triangle’ format, which brings together Ukraine, Moldova and Romania,” Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
“We plan to hold the first meeting of the triangle at the level of prime ministers,” he continued. However, no additional information was provided on when the meeting could take place.
A single path to Brussels
The two countries’ EU ambitions cannot be pulled apart, both Ukrainian leaders said.
Koretskyi argued that each country’s accession would strengthen the other’s security, adding that moving towards the bloc together also makes economic sense.
“Moldova and Ukraine are definitely stronger when we move together in this direction. It is important that we continue to be together, because this is true,” Zelensky said, according to the Presidential Office.
Two two sides agreed that any attempt to separate Ukraine’s and Moldova’s paths to EU membership would be inacceptable.
Third Political Prisoner Dies in Russia This Month – Report
Such an attempt previously came in July, when Hungary signaled it was prepared to approve the screening results only for Moldova’s Cluster 3 while continuing to block Ukraine’s progress. Other EU member states, led by Ireland – which held the rotating Council presidency – opposed splitting the two countries’ accession tracks.
Transnistria region on the agenda as well
Regional security featured prominently in Zelensky’s talks with Tofan, with a particular focus on the situation in Transnistria, the unrecognized, Russian-backed breakaway region along Moldova’s border with Ukraine.
The leaders also discussed wider security challenges in the region and closer military cooperation, which the prime ministers formalized with Monday’s military-technical agreement.
“It is important to deliver results for our people and our countries,” Zelensky said in a statement on Telegram.
Trade routes and border crossings
Because of Russia’s full-scale war, now in its fifth year, has significantly reshaped how vital cargo moves between countries, much of the discussion centered on keeping those routes open.
Zelensky proposed restoring the Solidarity Lanes, transit routes that would speed up the export of Ukrainian goods to other European countries via railway, road and inland waterways.
Meanwhile, Koretskyi thanked Moldova for discounted rail freight rates, which the sides agreed on in response to Russian attacks in the Black Sea. Ukrainian support for Moldova’s water supply was on the agenda as well, although no further details were provided.
The two countries confirmed that they are ready to expand joint control to two more border crossing points, with an agreement due in the near future.
Energy ties deepen
Energy remains a central pillar of the relationship between the two neighbors, particularly since Ukraine halted the transit of Russian gas to Europe at the start of 2025.
Zelensky thanked Chișinău for supporting the Vertical Gas Corridor, a route that allows gas to reach Ukraine through Romania and Moldova, as well as for its decision to discount gas transit via the Trans-Balkan route.
Koretskyi also praised the transit arrangements and noted that Moldovan companies are already storing gas in Ukrainian facilities.
In a Sept. 30 analysis, the Atlantic Council proposed using Ukraine’s underground storage network to distribute US gas across European markets. Ukraine’s storage operator, Ukrtransgaz, puts the network’s total capacity at 30.95 billion cubic meters (1.09 trillion cubic feet).

Why Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Is Missing So Many Key Figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:27:15 UTC
06:27:15 KST

Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.
“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.
It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”
Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
Michael Dambra, an accounting and law professor at the University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for Anthropic’s third-quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”
Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.
As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms.
However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.
Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)
Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.
Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December 2030, while others may extend through 2045.
Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, believes investors are owed more detail.
“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”
Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it has added an additional $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.
Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.
Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.
Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”
However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.
When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says, they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.
It’s unclear what Anthropic’s opening price may end up being or how investors may be interpreting the redactions in the company’s S-1. But according to Bajarin, the whole AI industry is one form of “blank” or another when it comes to crunching the numbers based on access to chips and infrastructure right now. So, yes, it’s all a risk.
“All of this,” he says, “just shows how absurdly early we are in enterprise adoption of an AI market that will be more than $3 trillion yearly and likely growing.”

PM Modi outlines key milestones in 139th 'Mann Ki Baat' (file photo)
NEW DELHI: High fever and laboured breathing threatened the life of Oho-Tahane, a child from Jarawa tribe of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. With specialist care out of reach, health workers turned to e-Sanjeevani for remote consultation. The doctor diagnosed pneumonia, and timely expert intervention helped the child’s condition improve rapidly.Oho-Tahane, a member of one of India’s most vulnerable tribal groups, is among over 50 crore cases, many in far flung areas, facilitated by the national telemedicine service since its launch in Nov 2019.The service’s achievement was highlighted by PM Narendra Modi in his ‘Mann Ki Baat’ address Sunday, as he also cited how e-Sanjeevani enabled a doctor to guide a medical team in treating Kunhi Koya (60) in Kalpeni, Lakshadweep, and helped ensure medical assistance for pregnant Kunjang Dolma in Himalayan region of Zanskar.Developed by C-DAC Mohali under the health ministry, e-Sanjeevani facilitates 2.5-3 lakh daily consultations, offers services in 15 languages and is available across all 36 states and UTs. Women account for 57.1% of the platform’s utilisation, while people aged 46 and above account for 40.1% of consultations. Those aged 60 and above account for 16.2%. The platform has recorded a peak of 6,30,315 consultations in a single day.
Modi credited the platform’s reach to dedication of doctors, public trust and the effective use of technology. He highlighted 1.9 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, saying they were bringing healthcare closer to rural communities and evolving into wellness centres for village panchayats. Regular health check-ups were becoming more common in rural areas, he said, with e-Sanjeevani playing an important role.
The PM also highlighted advances in brain research, referring to Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT-Madras, which he inaugurated this month. The centre has developed a brain imaging technology platform to create high resolution digital 3D images of human brain. Its mission is to map and study 100 human brains in detail using Param Shakti supercomputer..Modi said the initiative could deepen understanding of the brain, particularly as conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and dementia lack a definitive cure. Data from the 100 brains will be available as an open-source resource for researchers, the PM added.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Berlin plans to buy ‘drone missiles’ from Kiev – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:21:08 UTC
06:21:08 KST

Germany planning to buy ‘drone missiles’ from Ukraine – media
Germany is preparing to buy a batch of low-cost cruise missiles from Ukraine to expand its long-range strike capabilities, according to several media outlets.
The deal could be finalized in the coming weeks, the Financial Times reported, citing officials familiar with the matter. It would initially involve a small batch of missiles for testing by the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, early next year. If the tests prove successful, Berlin could reportedly place a follow-up order for several hundred missiles.
Dubbed ‘Bars’ – meaning snow leopard in both Russian and Ukrainian – the cruise missiles, sometimes referred to as “drone missiles” in Ukraine, are jet-powered weapons with a range of up to 1,000 km and a payload of up to 105 kg.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars missiles in July 2026. Under that agreement, Berlin would finance production, with all the missiles produced being delivered to Ukraine.
The potential purchase comes amid a surge in German arms procurement as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government seeks to turn the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army, citing the threat of a potential conflict with Russia. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed such claims as “nonsense,” insisting that it has no intention of attacking any NATO member.
Armament drive
Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Berlin was planning to acquire “thousands of precision deep-strike weapons” from several European and American companies. One proposed contract with US firm Covenant for the delivery of thousands of ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles could be worth more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion), according to the report.
Berlin emerged as Kiev’s single biggest military donor after Washington drastically scaled back its aid under US President Donald Trump. Merz has prioritized military spending, including assistance to Kiev, despite acknowledging that Germany’s economy is in a “structural crisis.” His government amended the constitutional debt brake to fund the buildup and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion for defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Germany’s central bank has warned that the country is on course to record its largest budget deficit since reunification by 2028.
Cashing in on war?
Ukraine, in turn, appears to be actively seeking to cash in on weapons exports, including sales to its Western backers. In February, David Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, told Reuters that the country expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue from it this year alone.
Kiev halted all weapons exports following the escalation of the conflict in 2022, but Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reversed that decision when he announced plans to open nearly a dozen weapons export centers across Europe in early 2026.
The plans have not stopped Kiev from seeking further financial and military assistance from Western nations. Last month, Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara suggested that Western donors supply Kiev with highly sought-after US-made Patriot interceptors from their own stockpiles, which would then be replenished with 1,000 missiles it plans to purchase with EU funds at some point in the future. In October, Zelensky himself lashed out at the country’s backers over their reluctance to cover a major budget shortfall.
Trump accused Ukraine in mid-October of selling American-supplied missiles on the black market. He also claimed that Kiev had failed to account for billions of dollars in American military and financial aid.
Ukrainian arms manufacturers have been implicated in some of the nation’s numerous corruption scandals. Fire Point – a defense contractor personally promoted by Zelensky during his visits to Western nations – was reportedly effectively owned by the Ukrainian leader’s longtime former business partner, Timur Mindich, known as ‘Zelensky’s wallet’ in Kiev. The businessman fled Ukraine last year after a major corruption investigation named him as one of its primary suspects.

06:18:07 KST

JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.
JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.
JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.
"Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."
JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.
JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.
"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."
Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expected
- Revenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expected
JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.
Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.
JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.
It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed across the Occupied Palestinian Territory since Oct. 7, 2023, including at least 21,500 children and 11,000 women, Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar told the UN General Assembly.
Israeli forces continue to kill and injure civilians, including children, who approach or cross the Yellow Line in Gaza, the commission said in its latest report.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
The situation in the occupied West Bank has also deteriorated sharply, with Israeli military operations and violence by Israeli occupiers forming part of what the commission described as a coordinated attack against Palestinians.
The report identifies the expansion of settlements, annexation of Palestinian territory and displacement of residents as objectives of these actions.
Israel has committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence, the commission said.
It also found that Palestinian children had been persecuted because of their age and that gender-based violence was being used to displace, subjugate and destabilize Palestinians.
The report also said Palestinian security forces had increasingly used unnecessary or disproportionate force against Palestinians in the West Bank since Oct. 7, 2023.
The Palestinian Authority has failed to conduct effective and impartial investigations into killings or provide remedies for victims and their families.
Muralidhar called on Israel to end its occupation of Palestinian territory, evacuate settlements and remove obstacles to Palestinian self-determination.
He also urged UN member states to stop providing political, military, economic or financial assistance that helps maintain the occupation and settlements.
States must use all available means to prevent and punish genocide and support the International Criminal Court, particularly amid recent US sanctions against the court and its officials, he said.
Muralidhar delivered his statement by video conference after failing to obtain a visa to travel to New York, despite his efforts to secure one.

The Trump administration told Venezuela's interim authorities "weeks and weeks ago" that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado needs to be allowed to return to the country ahead of potential elections next year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday.
Rubio told reporters in a call that the government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez replied to the U.S. by saying that Machado was free to enter the country. Machado returned to Venezuela over the weekend.
"Weeks and weeks ago, we spoke to the interim authorities and just said, 'Look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan, she belongs in her country. That’s the country she’s from. She should be allowed to return. She should be allowed to return unperturbed,’” Rubio said.
He noted that the U.S. had not discouraged Machado from returning to Venezuela except immediately after devastating earthquakes in June. He said that was because the U.S. believed the priority should be in getting humanitarian and emergency relief into the country.
Rubio spoke after Venezuelan authorities and opposition figures agreed last week on a blueprint to reform the country’s electoral process in order for free and fair elections to take place at some point in 2027.
He said the Trump administration, which captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January military operation and brought him to the U.S. to face drug-trafficking charges, would be watching events closely and urging all sides to comply with the new process.
"Obviously, we need to use our leverage with the government for the interim authorities to ensure that the process is moving forward in a responsible way," Rubio said. "Our goal here is to have an election."
Machado had been in hiding in Venezuela for most of 2025 before making a clandestine escape that December to Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She later gave her medal to President Donald Trump.
She returned to Venezuela on Sunday, her first appearance since the U.S. deposed Maduro and replaced him with Rodriguez, who had been his vice president and has now exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election yet scheduled.
Rubio said the U.S. goal is to help put in a place a sustainable election architecture that will give all parties confidence in the vote.
To get there, Rubio said Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council, and provide an open space for political expression that will hinge on press freedom and access to all media outlets, including online platforms.

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:15:21 CET
06:15:21 KST

By Jason Lange
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week’s record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters.
(Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone, Will Dunham and Sanjeev Miglani)

Pentagon’s FORTRESS Plan Prepares US Bases to Operate 90 Days Without Outside Support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:11:09 UTC
06:11:09 KST

- Category
- World
Pentagon’s FORTRESS Plan Prepares US Bases to Operate 90 Days Without Outside Support
The Pentagon is preparing major US military bases to operate independently for at least 90 days during a major conflict that could disrupt power grids, supply chains, communications, and other critical infrastructure, Fox News reported on October 25.
The requirement is part of a broader initiative called FORTRESS , which is intended to keep US forces functioning even if the civilian systems they normally rely on are damaged or unavailable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We don’t want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can’t. It’s an intolerable risk,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News.
According to documents reviewed by Fox News, major military installations in the continental US would be expected to sustain essential operations independently for at least 90 days, including electricity, water, fuel, and communications.
FORTRESS envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage, and microgrids that could allow military bases to disconnect from civilian power networks during prolonged outages.
“Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures,” Parnell stated.
Fox News reported that the Pentagon is also preparing for major disruptions to global supply chains during a large-scale war. The initiative calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies.
For the most important defense dependencies, FORTRESS would require at least two qualified supply or production pathways, reducing the risk that the loss of one factory, supplier, or industrial capability could interrupt military operations.
The outlet also noted that the Pentagon is preparing civilian factories to shift toward defense production during a crisis through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network.
The plan calls for manufacturers to be identified in advance, with technical requirements, cybersecurity protections, contracting arrangements, and conversion procedures established before a conflict begins.
Fox News reported that FORTRESS also includes recurring industrial stress tests and mobilization exercises intended to determine whether US manufacturers could maintain production during prolonged disruption.
The initiative also includes measures to strengthen military communications, navigation, and satellite capabilities against interference.
The outlet reported that the Pentagon is preparing for operations in which GPS signals are jammed or space-based systems are disrupted, reducing dependence on vulnerable civilian and commercial infrastructure.
“The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts,” Parnell told Fox News. “When that happens, global supply chains will break.”
He described FORTRESS as an insurance policy intended to ensure US forces can continue operating during a prolonged, multi-front war even if critical infrastructure and supply networks fail.
The FORTRESS plan builds on earlier Pentagon efforts to expand the US defense industrial base beyond conventional military contractors. In April, UNITED24 Media reported that US officials were exploring whether companies including General Motors and Ford could shift civilian factories toward weapons, ammunition, and military equipment production during periods of heightened demand.

The alliance also aligns with broader efforts to strengthen ties between London and the European Union.
On May 27, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a historic Security and Defense Partnership Treaty in London, officially designating Russia as the primary threat to European stability.
The agreement was designed to elevate bilateral military cooperation to its highest level and enable rapid, direct defense responses in the event of a regional crisis without awaiting unanimous consensus from NATO’s 32 members.
Tusk underscored that while Poland remained fully committed to the transatlantic alliance, building swift, bilateral mechanisms with key allies like the UK and France was essential to counter regional aggression effectively—particularly as Washington prepared to gradually reduce its military footprint on the continent.

People with migrant backgrounds make up 5.4% of S. Korean population in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:04:55 UTC
06:04:55 KST

People with migrant backgrounds make up 5.4% of S. Korean population in 2025
The share of people with migrant backgrounds living in South Korea rose in 2025 to 5.4 percent, up from the previous year, data showed Monday, with those in their 20s leading the gains, Yonhap reported.
The total migrant population came to 2.81 million in 2025, up from 2.71 million a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. South Korea's total population stood at 51.82 million.
The data ministry defines people with a migrant background as immigrants or those with at least one parent from overseas.
The category includes foreign nationals, naturalized South Koreans and second-generation immigrants.
Foreign nationals accounted for 75.1 percent of the population with a migrant background, followed by second-generation immigrants at 14.1 percent.
Another 9.1 percent acquired South Korean citizenship through naturalization or recognition of parentage, a legal process in which a parent recognizes a child born out of wedlock as their own.
By gender, males accounted for 52.5 percent, and females made up 47.5 percent. There were 110.7 males for every 100 females.
The working-age population, comprising people aged 15 to 64, stood at 2.3 million in 2025.
By age group, people in their 30s accounted for the largest share at 23.7 percent, or 667,000, followed by those in their 20s at 21.6 percent, or 607,000. People in their 40s numbered 439,000, or 15.6 percent of the total.
The number of people in their 20s rose by 36,000 over the period, the largest increase among all age groups.
The report also showed 56 percent of people with a migrant background lived in the greater Seoul metropolitan area, with 17.1 percent residing in Seoul.
South Chungcheong Province had the highest proportion of residents with a migrant background at 8.3 percent, followed by North Chungcheong Province and Gyeonggi Province, both at 6.5 percent. The figure for Seoul stood at 5.1 percent.
The southeastern city of Daegu had the lowest proportion at 2.9 percent.
The number of people aged 24 and younger with a migrant background rose 6.6 percent from a year earlier to 790,000.
By their parents' nationality, those with Vietnamese parents accounted for 28.1 percent, followed by those with Chinese parents at 15.7 percent. Those with ethnic Korean parents of Chinese nationality accounted for a separate 11.4 percent.
Other major countries represented by their parents' nationalities included Uzbekistan, the Philippines, Cambodia, Mongolia, and Nepal.
As written earlier, South Korea is set to expand international flights in the winter season.

Part of London's iconic Oxford Street pedestrianised ‘forever’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:02:33 UTC
06:02:33 KST

Part of London’s iconic Oxford Street pedestrianised ‘forever’
LONDON – A stretch of London’s iconic Oxford Street was made traffic-free “forever” from Oct 26, as pedestrians took over the country’s most famous shopping street, absent of the capital’s red double-decker buses and black cabs.
Shoppers walking along the street told AFP this was a “good idea”, but drivers of London’s famous black taxi cabs rejected the move as “crazy”.
“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street, but also for London,” Mayor Sadiq Khan told reporters on the thoroughfare, one of the busiest shopping zones in Europe.
“I want to be supporting our shops in Oxford Street and have a kilometre worth of this street – almost half of this street – traffic-free forever,” Khan said, adding the pedestrianisation would increase the number of shoppers.
Those walking in the area on a rainy Monday said they backed the move.
“Overall, I think it’s a very good idea. It should have been done before,” said John Oxford, an 83-year-old professor of virology.
“It gives people more of a chance to actually explore the shops, explore the iconic Oxford Street,” said Madaki Kanya, a 19-year-old visiting from Manchester in north-west England.
“It’s a lot more comfortable walking around, not dodging the cars and the traffic,” agreed Paul Facer, 62, from Weymouth in the south-west, who was visiting with his wife.
‘Decades of decline’
The street brings in some £3.1 billion (S$5.3 billion) spending annually, but has faced challenges, including shops shuttering during the Covid-19 pandemic and a loss of footfall due to a shift to online shopping.
“Over the last couple of decades it’s been in decline, I’d say managed decline,” Khan told BBC Radio 4 about the street lined with luxury retailers, clothing chains, and department stores.
“I’m not willing to stand by as shops leave this street, as jobs leave this street,” he said.
But the scheme has proved controversial among residents worried about traffic jams in neighbouring areas as well as among disability rights activists.
Black cab driver Jason Harvey, 51, told AFP that “to pedestrianise any part of Oxford Street is crazy”, citing needs of people with disabilities and young children.
Another taxi driver, Brendan Cooper, said people with disabilities will “have to walk 150 yards around the back of the stores to get a taxi”, calling this “just ridiculous”.
Khan insisted there were cab ranks and bus stops near the street so people can still access the area with ease.
“For centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way,” he added, saying the move would “revitalise” the road and make the capital “greener”.
Around half the street has been pedestrianised, with plans to close off the rest to vehicles depending on the success of the first phase.
“Today marks an exciting new chapter for Oxford Street as work begins to transform one of the world’s most iconic high streets,” said Meave Wall, chief retail and digital officer at the Selfridges department store, which opened on the West End road more than a century ago. AFP

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of US midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
- Trump’s approval rose to 32%, still near a record low, as Republicans fought to keep control of Congress before the Nov 3 midterms.
- Reuters/Ipsos found Democrats ahead by 47% to 36% in the generic ballot, or 50% to 41% with undecided voters included.
- Inflation and living costs are shaping the race. Voters see Democrats as stronger on the economy, and Democrats seem more eager to vote.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from his record low a week earlier, ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Oct 26.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day poll, which was conducted nationwide, also showed that registered voters broadly favoured Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would vote for in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Oct 19.
The poll that closed on Oct 26 additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress.
While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
Steep Senate climb for Democrats
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favoured Democrats over Republicans by 9 percentage points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent petrol prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters. REUTERS
