Ukraine’s Satellite Disruption Exposes a Central Risk of Modern Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:28:45 UTC
05:28:45 KST

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed over the weekend that the Ukrainian military had “violated” the terms of service for Starlink, the company’s commercial satellite internet network, which has become central to the country’s defense against Russia. Musk said SpaceX had restricted Starlink to prevent that alleged misuse. Ukrainian officials disputed his claim. His allegation came after over a week of uncertainty about why the services had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials reported on Oct. 14 that restrictions affecting SpaceX’s satellite communications were disrupting drone operations, blocking a key line of defense amid daily Russian air attacks. Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone capabilities, and reconnaissance; the throttled connection ultimately led to the cancellation of several missions, officials said.
The restrictions also affected Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications service that uses Starlink technology but is supplied through U.S. government contracts.
Over a week after the disruption began, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that both services had been fully restored. It reported that connections remained stable even when terminals were moving at speeds above 400 km/h.
At the time, the cause for the interruption had not yet been clarified, but Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara emphasized the importance of a strong and stable connection, calling it “vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications.”
Musk maintains that the United States government controls changes to Starshield, leaving questions about who authorized its restrictions—and why.
U.S. President Donald Trump declined to identify those involved in the decision, while a Reuters report from Oct. 15 cited multiple officials who said the order came from inside the White House. The sources did not identify who authorized or implemented the restrictions, but a senior U.S. official denied that it was Trump, the report said.
Experts say that the disruptions expose a growing vulnerability in modern warfare: military reliance on a single private technology supplier.
The company that controls the technology can ultimately wield significant influence over military operations, leaving governments dependent on decisions made by executives and billionaire owners outside traditional diplomatic channels, experts warn.
Why U.S. control of Starshield matters for Ukraine
Ukraine’s access to satellite communications depends on decisions made in Washington as well as at SpaceX. That leaves Kyiv navigating both a private supplier’s restrictions and a fraught relationship with the Trump Administration.
In recent weeks, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising global fuel prices and called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop those attacks—despite the fact that experts have primarily attributed the price surge to the U.S. war with Iran.
Trump said on Oct. 15 that Zelensky was “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin and on Oct. 19 suggested that it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”
Alex Crowther, an adjunct professor at Florida International University’s Jack D. Gordon Institute for Public Policy, says the Starshield dispute goes beyond Trump’s souring relationship with Zelensky to a more basic question: Who has the authority to restrict Ukraine’s access?
“Usually when [a foreign entity] signs a contract with an American company, it says who has the capability to turn this stuff on and off, and the circumstances under which they can turn it on and off,” Crowther says, questioning who has that authority over the services Ukraine relies upon. “Is it Starlink, which is private, or is it Starshield, which is an American government contract? Is it Musk? Is it Hegseth? Is it Trump?”
“Nobody knows the rules right now,” he says.
Lance Hunter, a professor of political science at Augusta University, tells TIME that this dispute exposes the potential issues of having three different actors—the Trump Administration, SpaceX, and Ukraine—with potentially incompatible priorities.
How dependence on SpaceX limits Ukraine’s military autonomy
Hunter says that what is unfolding in Ukraine underscores warfare’s growing dependence on digital technology. Beyond traditional “tanks, bombs, planes,” he says that includes factors like artificial intelligence, drones, and navigation jamming.
Reliance on ongoing technology services creates a different relationship from a traditional arms purchase, Hunter says.
He points to traditional arms deals in which a private company sells a government a set amount of missiles or interceptors.
“Let's say you purchase a piece of weaponry or vehicle or any type of object that helps you in the conflict: You own it at that point. You have control over it,” Hunter tells TIME.
The relationship between Ukraine and SpaceX, however, is different; purchasing the technology does not guarantee operational sovereignty.
“Ukraine has a lot of transmitters which interface with Starshield and Starlink, and they're very much dependent on SpaceX as far as allowing them to use those when they need to,” Hunter continues. “There's not just a one-time dependence buying the technology; it's continual now.”
That gives the company more “influence and leverage” over conflicts than it has before, he adds.
It shifts the way that countries like Ukraine need to think about who they are willing to work with and how they weigh the potential costs.
Why Ukraine cannot easily replace Starlink and Starshield
In a perfect world, Hunter says, Ukraine would diversify its technology suppliers to decrease reliance on Starlink.
The country has already been expanding its domestic weapons production, including interceptor drones. But it remains dependent on foreign suppliers for critical air-defense weapons like the U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles.
That dependence has left it vulnerable to shortages and delays. On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve supplies of missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air-defense systems.
But replicating satellite communications networks presents a different challenge. Starlink technology is not something a government can easily reproduce domestically, Hunter says, and few providers worldwide offer comparable capabilities.
“Starlink has a monopoly on that technology to a degree, as far as the speed, the availability, the flexibility,” he says. “It's not like they can just flip a switch and diversify that technology. It takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources. It takes a lot of effort, and also in Europe we don't see that same level of technology with some of the European countries and also with some of the private companies.”
In the end, he says that Ukraine is stuck between “a rock and a hard place” as the country tries to negotiate its relationships with the Trump Administration and, separately, with Musk.
“You're reliant on the politics of those bodies all matching up,” he says of Ukraine. “All of a sudden, you kind of lose that autonomy.”
“If they really push back against the U.S. government or SpaceX, they have the potential of receiving less of the technology and being cut off to a greater extent,” he adds. “But if they don't really push at all and advocate for their interest as well, then they could be in a weaker position as far as having leverage exerted over them.”
Why Ukraine disputes Musk’s Starlink claims
In a social media post on Oct. 24, Musk said that SpaceX had restricted Starlink access deliberately because Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in one post. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.”
Musk explained that Starlink continues to be “critical to the defense of Ukraine,” but that it could not be used for offensive military operations.
Ukrainian officials promptly disputed Musk’s claims.
Defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote in a Telegram post that operational and speed restrictions are in place that make it “physically impossible” for the military to use Starlink for medium- or deep-range offensive strikes.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine,” he wrote. “Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.”

Conflict-related sexual violence more than doubles as women's share of civilian deaths rises: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:27:00 UTC
05:27:00 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Women and girls are facing increasingly deadly consequences of armed conflict, with their share of civilian deaths doubling since 2021 and verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence rising sharply, UN Women officials warned Monday.
Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda, UN Women's deputy executive director for normative support, UN system coordination and programme results, told reporters that women and girls were bearing a growing share of the human cost of wars that she described as "preventable."
More than 37,000 civilians were killed in armed conflicts in 2025, with women and girls accounting for one in four deaths, twice their share in 2021, Gumbonzvanda said.
She added that at least 25 women and girls were killed every day, while more than 750 million lived within 50 kilometers (31 miles) of an armed conflict.
"The conflicts that have disappeared from our screens, but not from the lives of women and girls enduring them. And for women and girls who survive, the burden is relentless," she said.
Gumbonzvanda also warned of a sharp increase in conflict-related sexual violence, saying the UN verified 9,788 cases in 2025, more than double the number recorded in 2024 and nearly four times the figure reported in 2022.
"Women are paying the price of war," she said.
Gumbonzvanda urged governments and the international community to end armed conflicts, protect civilians, uphold international law and hold perpetrators of abuses accountable.
She also called for women to be included as decision-makers in all peace negotiations and for greater funding for women-led organizations working to save lives and build peace.
 
Sarah Hendriks, director of the Policy, Programme and Intergovernmental Division at UN Women, warned that the growing number of conflicts worldwide was worsening conditions for women and girls.
More than 185 conflicts were recorded globally in 2025, including 65 state-based conflicts, Hendriks said.
"Wars are multiplying; the ways that wars are fought are changing, and it is women and girls who are paying the price," she added.

By Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held.
Rubio spoke to reporters by phone a day after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela for the first time since the US captured the country’s then-President Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
The US believes that talks currently underway between the interim government in Caracas and opposition politicians are expected to see a new supreme judicial tribunal in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” said Rubio, who has acted as US President Donald Trump’s point person on Venezuela. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
Maduro’s government had set up the country’s electoral infrastructure to rig elections so must be quickly changed, Rubio added.
But Rubio stopped short of giving a target date for elections. Machado has said elections should be held by mid-2027, though Trump has previously said he did not believe Venezuela was ready for a nationwide vote.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with Trump’s administration.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging Maduro for the presidency in 2024, had been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
Washington has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
Rubio said the only time he had “discouraged” Machado from going back to Venezuela was in the immediate aftermath of devastating earthquakes in the summer, because the country was grappling with a humanitarian crisis.
But Rubio said that weeks ago the US told Venezuela’s interim authorities that Machado “belongs in her country” and “should be allowed to return unperturbed,” and the government had agreed.
Asked about Machado’s criticism of an oil deal that Trump had struck with the interim rulers, Rubio insisted that the agreement was a good one for both countries but that she had a right to express her opinion on the matter.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country.
But some critics have accused Trump of a neo-colonialist approach to Venezuela aimed at exploiting its natural resources.
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.

Britain told to plan for war without Trump’s America
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:25:26 GMT
05:25:26 KST

Defence spending should go to five per cent of gross domestic product immediately, the country should be prepared for a wider European war and planning should assume Britain may have to fight without the United States, according to a security academic at the University of Leicester.
Dr Simon Bennett, director of the Civil Safety and Security Unit in the university’s School of Business and author of a 2025 book on security lessons from the war in Ukraine, set out the argument in comments issued through the university press office.
Bennett said: “Given these facts, we must prepare ourselves to fight alone. Like Keir Starmer, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is in denial about Trump. The American president is a lost cause. Better to focus finite energies and budgets first, on supporting Ukraine, and secondly, on preparing this country for a wider European war. Defence spending must be increased to 5% of Gross Domestic Product immediately and, as suggested by former Secretary of State for Defence Lord Hutton of Furness in the 17 October edition of The i Paper, the British public must be told the truth about Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign.”
On the range of threats he believes the country is exposed to, Bennett said: “The United Kingdom faces a spectrum of threats. The country has suffered two Kremlin-initiated chemical warfare attacks, in London in 2006 (Polonium) and in Salisbury in 2018 (Novichok). The Council on Strategic Risks recently highlighted the UK’s vulnerability to biological weapons. Prime Minister Burnham, it is time to focus on what really matters – giving Ukraine the weapons it needs and securing a vulnerable United Kingdom. Do not prostrate yourself before Trump, as your predecessor did. As Volodymyr Zelensky and Mark Carney have shown, the only way to deal with Trump is to stand up to him.”
Bennett is asking for far more than the government has signed up to. Ministers have committed to NATO’s target of three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent figure. Bennett is calling for core defence spending itself to reach five per cent now, a distinction ministers have had to set out repeatedly.
Lord Hutton of Furness, whose intervention Bennett cites, was Secretary of State for Defence from 2008 to 2009. His argument that the public must be told the truth about Russian hybrid warfare runs close to what ministers have themselves begun saying. Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism, and Louise Sandher-Jones confirmed in a written answer last week that “we know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe.”
Ministers have also confirmed that government messaging on defence and security will build ahead of Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW and NATO’s crisis management exercise in spring 2027, and the Cabinet Office launched its Be Ready campaign this month asking households to prepare to look after themselves for three days.
The two chemical incidents Bennett refers to are the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko with polonium-210 in London in 2006, which a public inquiry found was probably approved by the Russian president, and the Novichok attack on Sergei and Yulia Skripal in Salisbury in 2018, which killed Dawn Sturgess and which Britain attributed to the GRU. The Council on Strategic Risks is a Washington-based institute publishing on biological, climate and nuclear security.
Bennett’s case rests on his reading of the American president, whom he describes as a Russophile and, in his words and expressly as his opinion, a traitor to the West’s liberal-democratic values. He said he predicted in March 2025 that Trump would ally the United States with Russia through accords and treaties, and took criticism for saying so at the time.

UN urges Iraq, Kuwait to intensify search for 315 people missing since 1990 invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:25:11 UTC
05:25:11 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The UN on Monday urged Iraq and Kuwait to accelerate efforts to determine the fate of 315 people still missing following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, as investigators continue searching burial sites believed to contain their remains.
"More than thirty-five years after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, this humanitarian file remains unresolved," Senior UN Representative Mari Yamashita told a Security Council meeting.
Yamashita said the fate of only 290 of the original 605 missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals had been clarified over the past three decades.
Of the 315 people still missing, 308 are Kuwaiti nationals, she said, adding that the last confirmed identification took place in August 2023.
She said extensive efforts have been undertaken to locate the missing, including excavations at suspected burial sites across Iraq, particularly in the south of the country.
Yamashita said Iraqi authorities have excavated approximately 14,000 trenches at the Khamisiyah site and conducted numerous field missions to other locations of interest.
Khamisiyah remains a priority because investigators believe it may contain the remains of 150 to 180 missing Kuwaiti nationals, potentially accounting for roughly half of the unresolved cases.
In September, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and Iraqi authorities conducted a joint field mission to the site.
Yamashita expressed hope that the findings would lead to further excavation work as soon as possible.
 
Kuwaiti archives, property remain missing
The UN representative also highlighted the unresolved issue of Kuwaiti property taken during Iraq's invasion, including the country's national archives.
Although some materials have been returned, progress has been "limited," she said.
Items were transferred to the Kuwait National Library in 2019 and the country's Ministry of Information in 2022, while additional books and microfilm recordings were returned in 2025.
Yamashita called for a "clear pathway" to identify and locate the remaining property, suggesting that a proposed Joint Iraq-Kuwait Committee could provide a framework for regular dialogue and cooperation.
She also welcomed a recent meeting between Kuwait's crown prince and Iraq's prime minister on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where the two countries announced a working group to address outstanding bilateral issues.
"Such engagements remain important in sustaining the constructive environment needed to advance the humanitarian objectives of this mandate, to strengthen mutual confidence, and to support continued cooperation in the future," she said.

The offer will be made available to employees on select teams across the US, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff could be included. Around 60,000 employees are reported to be eligible.
US tech giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to employees around the globe, its chief people officer announced on Monday.
In a memo sent to staff, Amy Coleman called the "Voluntary Exit Offer" an "important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter."
The offer will be made available to employees on select teams across the US, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff could be included.
"This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources," the memo continued.
It added that eligible employees would receive an email with a link to their offers in the coming hours.
Around 60,000 staff are reported to be eligible.
In July, Microsoft announced it was eliminating around 4,800 roles, or roughly 2.1% of its global workforce at the time, as the company sought to shift its focus and cut costs as the AI era continues to take hold. Those cuts mostly affected the firm's commercial and Xbox gaming divisions.
Microsoft also offered some staff the option to retire early this year.
The company has said that more than 30% of those eligible for the early retirement scheme chose to participate and that it would "continue exploring similar approaches in the future."

05:20:44 KST

BRUSSELS, October 26. /TASS/. The EU Council has decided to mobilize 4.9 billion euro from the European Peace Facility, including 4.7 billion to partially reimburse EU countries for their arms supplies to Kiev and 230 million euro to expand the budget of the EU Military Assistance Mission in Support of Ukraine.
"The Council today adopted a set of eight decisions enabling the use of funds for Ukraine under the European Peace Facility (EPF). These decisions allow for the partial reimbursement, through the EPF, of military aid already delivered by member states (since the spring of 2023 - TASS), amounting to a total amount of €4.7 billion. They also provide additional financing for the EU Military Assistance Mission in Support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine), amounting to a total of €230 million," the Council said.
This is the first tranche of aid funding for Kiev from the European Peace Facility that was blocked by Hungary in 2023. The total amount of frozen funds is 6.6 billion euros. Hungary lifted its veto this spring, but the process has stalled due to disagreements over how EU member states will distribute these funds among themselves.
Funds from the European Peace Facility have never been transferred to Ukraine; instead, they were allocated as compensation to EU countries that supplied weapons from their own stockpiles to the Kiev regime. On average, the European Union has compensated for about 40% of the weapons’ cost under this scheme. At the same time, the technical condition of the weapons was not verified. As the Euractiv portal (now Rapporteur) reported, a number of EU countries may have significantly inflated the actual cost of their shipments, making it very profitable to receive compensation for decommissioned weapons.

Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus. There was no immediate comment from Syrian authorities. Five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of the Jordanian strikes, a health official told Syria's state news agency.
There was no immediate comment from Jordan on that account.
Hours earlier, senior government security officials said their security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that killed nine people.
"God willing, they only represent themselves," said Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah.

In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism.
"The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added.
At least 34 injured after gunmen attack funeral service
Friday's assault during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman, also wounded at least 34 people. Witnesses said gunmen opened fire for several minutes. The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three suspects were named in the press briefing.
Reuters video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate.

No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects' possession.
There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack.
Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups in the press conference.

It added that authorities are closely monitoring the situation and will provide "immediate required support and humanitarian relief.
Additionally, it said that "comprehensive investigations" have been launched to "establish the full circumstances of the targeting" and underscored the importance of joint security coordination between the two countries.
Syria also closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan and suspended passenger and commercial traffic from both sides.

'Legitimazes Jihad': Foreign Affairs Ministry slams UN report accusing Israel of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:18:43 UTC
05:18:43 KST

The Foreign Affairs Ministry on Monday called the report from a United Nations commission accusing Israel of genocide a "propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel’s right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
The UN commission released a report Monday accusing Israel of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza.
The report also mentioned wrongdoings by the Palestinian Authority, claiming that it had pushed for arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
In contrast, Hamas is named exactly twice, and neither mention accused Hamas of committing a crime or other wrongdoing.
The UN reported an increase in the number of Palestinian deaths in the West Bank, with almost 500 Palestinians killed annually in the West Bank since 2022, which were the highest numbers recorded since the UN started collecting data on the topic in 2005.
The report also claimed that Israel is continuing to commit “genocidal acts” with the “intent to destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part” in spite of a ceasefire agreement that went into effect in October 2025.
The report focused on Palestinian casualties in the West Bank due to Israeli military action and settler violence, as well as analysis of elected MKs and senior military officials.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, an Indian jurist who currently serves as the chair of the Commission of Inquiry.
Report cites increase in West Bank airstrike deaths
The Commission reported a sharp increase in Palestinian deaths caused by airstrikes in the West Bank since October 7, 2023. Six Palestinians were killed by airstrikes between 2008 and October 6, 2023, compared with 254 between October 7, 2023, and September 30, 2026, according to the commission’s findings.
It said airstrikes had become more frequent following the launch of Operation Iron Wall in January 2025, particularly in refugee camps and areas around Jenin, Tulkarm, Tubas and Nablus.
The Commission described the operation as a shift toward widespread destruction of Palestinian housing and infrastructure and the clearing of refugee camps. It cited the IDF's stated aim to “dismantle and restor[e] the operational freedom of action for IDF forces”, while reconstruction of the infrastructure is considered to be “endangering the citizens of the State of Israel and the military forces”.
Commission's analysis of statements by Israeli officials
The commission also cited statements by Israeli officials including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and IDF Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth in assessing Israeli military conduct and the intentions behind operations in the West Bank.
Smotrich referred to “two million Nazis” in the West Bank in November 2023, citing a poll on Palestinian support for the October 7 Hamas massacre. In November 2024, he said “The only way to remove the danger of a Palestinian terror state from the agenda is to apply Israeli sovereignty to Jewish settlement in the entire Judea and Samaria,” he said.
In January 2025, he wrote that Fondouk, Nablus and Jenin should “look like Jabalia,”.
The Commission also highlighted a reported May 2026 statement by Bluth that Israeli soldiers were “killing like we haven’t since 1967.”
Report alleges sexual violence against detainees
The Commission said it had verified four additional cases of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees since its March 2025 report on gender-based violence. Two victims were from the West Bank. The cases included alleged gang rape, genital violence, groping, threats of sexual violence, forced nudity, and searches conducted without an apparent security justification.
One case involved a male detainee at Megiddo Prison in 2025. He was allegedly blindfolded, forced to remove his lower garments, and repeatedly raped with objects during interrogation.
The Commission alleged that guards mocked and photographed him, threatened to mutilate his genitals and threatened sexual violence against his family and colleagues. The detainee reportedly suffered serious injuries, including rectal bleeding, without receiving medical treatment.
The Commission claimed that the cases it investigated involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence were not isolated incidents. It alleged that these acts formed part of a broader attack against the civilian population and concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed crimes against humanity involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence.
Israel has rejected previous allegations by the Commission of Inquiry that its forces systematically used sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinian detainees, describing the claims as unfounded and disputing the Commission's verification methods. In a March 2025 response, the Foreign Ministry said the IDF had rules prohibiting such misconduct and mechanisms for investigating allegations.
Commission also reports abuses by Palestinian Authority
The report also accused the Palestinian Authority of suppressing political dissent through arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
It cited reports of excessive force during West Bank protests in October 2023, when at least two men, a boy and a girl, were killed in Ramallah, Tubas and Jenin. The PA accepted responsibility for the death of the boy, who was run over by a security forces vehicle during clashes with protesters.
The Commission also investigated the December 2024 killing of a Palestinian journalism student in Jenin refugee camp who had documented alleged abuses by Palestinian security forces. Witnesses said a security force member had threatened to shoot her the previous day. She was killed by a single shot to the neck near her home.
The report said information conflicted on whether clashes were underway at the time. Palestinian security forces had a significant presence in the area, and their spokesman blamed the killing on “outlaws,” saying the case was under investigation. The Commission said key witnesses had not been asked to testify.
It also reported cases of arbitrary detention, including instances in which the PA allegedly ignored court orders for detainees' release.
The Commission concluded that the PA had violated the right to life and the right to security of person and had failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into killings or provide effective remedies to victims and their families.

Israel’s moment of truth: Knesset election pivotal to future US-Israel relationship - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:18:24 UTC
05:18:24 KST

The upcoming election in Israel will likely prove pivotal in determining whether the ongoing erosion in support for Israel in the United States devolves further into a full rupture that makes both Americans and Israelis less secure.
As Americans, we are not interested in picking winners and losers. Israelis should decide such things, but our friends there should understand the consequences of their decisions.
Our colleague Mark Dubowitz has recently warned of possible American financial warfare against Israel. Some of this risk is linked to a growing campaign of antisemitism and anti-Zionism that has exploded since the October 7 terror attacks plunged the Middle East into conflict. But some of this is also linked to senseless violence in the West Bank and other concerns.
If the next government in Israel, regardless of who leads it, fails to punish and end lawlessness and cruelty by anarchists in the West Bank, there could be painful consequences.
We firmly support Israel’s right to exist and defend itself and believe that America is safer, and US interests in the Middle East are more secure, when a strong Israel works closely with Washington. We are proud that America and Israel have fought together to defend common interests and to counter common enemies.
Enemies of US engaged in unprecedented cooperation, understand value of partnerships
America’s enemies – namely the Axis of Aggressors, consisting of China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea – are engaged in unprecedented cooperation. Our foes understand the value of partnerships.
America needs partners, too, especially capable and motivated partners like Israel. We need Israel’s muscles in the Middle East so we can focus more on deterring and defeating aggression by Beijing, Moscow, or Pyongyang. Americans also benefit from Israel’s defense-technology expertise and defense-acquisition agility, which can help ensure American warfighters wield the best weapons.
But we are witnessing a sad paradox with Israel. On one hand, Israel has demonstrated that it is the most powerful military in the Middle East, worthy of closer cooperation with the United States. Israel has battled back and gained the upper hand in a regional war that it neither started nor wanted. And yet, in the United States, Israel is more unpopular than it has been in years. This is clear in recent polls from Pew, Gallup, and the Ronald Reagan Institute.
This is a strategic liability for Israel. A steep decline in approval could lead the next Congress and US administration to adopt policies that undermine our bilateral relationship, including defense cooperation. That would materially damage the security of both the US and Israel.
Some in Israel may respond by shrugging and saying, “Fine, Israel will just become independent and self-sufficient in its defense production and arm itself.”
But that is not possible. Israel is heavily reliant on major American-made platforms and will remain so for decades.
True defense production independence doesn’t just require assembly lines in Israel. It also requires suppliers and raw materials in Israel. Many of the inputs for Israeli-produced weapons are imported, meaning a hostile administration could try to block them.
Israel’s enemies are actively working to drive a wedge between Washington and Jerusalem. The goal is to slowly but surely deprive Israel of the means to defend itself. Unfortunately, those enemies are capitalizing on some Israeli unforced errors.
It is certainly true that some of the withering criticism of Israel will continue regardless of the country’s policies. It is also true that enemies are increasingly well-organized and funded, and they are conducting information warfare against the United States and Israel.
But explaining the negative shift in opinion in America solely through those dynamics is simply unrealistic. Such efforts ignore the agency of the Israeli government and encourage a dangerous apathy in terms of undertaking necessary reforms. The rule of law and the distinction between combatant and noncombatant are a primary difference between defenders of Western civilization and the terrorists who murdered innocents on September 11, 2001, and October 7, 2023.
US-Israel security cooperation needed more than ever
As threats to Americans grow, we need US-Israel security cooperation more than ever. And Israel needs continued American diplomatic and defense cooperation. But this could prove difficult if some Israeli policies continue.
Battles against the terrorist regime in Iran and its proxies will continue, as will the fight against disinformation and blind hate that unfairly targets Israel. But that does not absolve Israel from making some crucial decisions about its own conduct. The fate of the US-Israel alliance could hang in the balance.
Bradley Bowman is senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD). Jonathan Schanzer is executive director at FDD.

Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:17:16 UTC
05:17:16 KST

French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.
“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”
More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.
High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.
Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.
The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.
Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.
The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.
The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.
Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

‘Deflections’: Abdul El-Sayed responds to Trump’s anti-Muslim attacks
The Democratic candidate for the US Senate has been the subject of Islamophobic attacks from Trump.
Detroit, Michigan – Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has dismissed United States President Donald Trump’s anti-Muslim attacks against him, saying that they are an attempt to move the attention away from the president’s own record.
At a news conference in Detroit on Monday, El-Sayed said Trump is trying to distract from issues that matter to Americans – including petrol prices and the war on Iran – by accusing the Democratic candidate of being a “jihadist”.
El-Sayed called the attacks “deflections and deceptions based on no evidence”.
“They have nothing to say about solving the problems in your life. They’re not talking about you,” the Democratic candidate said of Republicans.
“They’re not talking about your gas or your groceries … They’re not talking about clean air or clean water. They’re not talking about any of the things that the government is actually supposed to solve. Why? Because Donald Trump has created those problems.”
At a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump unleashed repeated baseless claims against El-Sayed, accusing the Democrat of wanting to impose “Sharia law” on the country.
“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said. “I want him to have a metal detector.”
El-Sayed laughed off the suggestion that he may personally be a physical threat to Congress. “He knows I got those Wolverine claws,” he said, a reference to the sports teams of his alma mater, the University of Michigan.
The progressive Democrat and former public health official is locked in a close race with former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers, a contest that could decide the Senate majority for the next two years.
Rogers has made unfounded allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah a central point of his campaign.
On Monday, El-Sayed said most Americans reject such attacks.
“There are always a few small people who want to make America small like that. You see them; they’re very loud, and they bark,” El-Sayed said.
“The vast majority of folks in this state believe in a big America. They’re open-minded. They’re big-hearted. And the story of America is those who believe in big America, overcoming the deception, the distraction, the sad attempts of the small-minded to make us small.”
He added that “Michiganders are a lot bigger than that”.
El-Sayed also addressed Trump’s statements mocking his name and misrepresenting it as “Mohamed”.
“My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas – not the reason you can’t afford your groceries, not the reason you can’t pay your rent, your mortgage, not the reason you can’t see a doctor,” he said.

Paramedics caught under fire as Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:16:41 UTC
05:16:41 KST

Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv university, medical centers, major bridge — 1 dead, 15 injured
Key developments:
- Russia attacked Kyiv overnight on Oct. 26-27, launching multiple waves of ballistic missiles at the capital.
- One person was killed and 15 injured. Nine medical personnel have been hospitalized.
- The attacks targeted Kyiv's Southern Bridge, a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
- Damage to metro infrastructure has caused temporary disruptions to public transportation in the city.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.
Kyiv, a city of three million people, has been relentlessly assaulted by Russian ballistic missiles in recent months as Moscow exploits Ukraine's air defense shortage. While its battlefield offensive has slowed, Russia has chosen a strategy of mass aerial strikes against vulnerable civilians.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people have been injured in the latest Russian attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Victims injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
Nine injured medical personnel have been hospitalized, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
The mayor later reported a strike on the city's Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Kyiv's major traffic arteries. The bridge connects the cities eastern and western sides and is crucial for the daily commutes of hundreds of thousands of residents.
The bridge and infrastructure related to its metro system were damaged overnight, Klitschko said. Train service on the bridge has been temporarily suspended.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a university campus in the city was struck by Russia alongside Kyiv's well-known Kyoto park and residential buildings.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground first reported that loud explosions rocked the city in the Podilskyi and Obolon districts at around 9:45 p.m. local time.
Just minutes earlier, Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles and other missiles were headed towards Kyiv.
Explosions were heard near a Metro station in Kyiv's Desnyanskyi district, where a car was damaged, Klitschko reported.
Two medical facilities in the Dniprovskyi district were also damaged in the attack, Klitschko said. At one of the two sites that came under fire, blast waves shattered windows in the intensive care unit. Windows were also shattered at the other site.
A three-story commercial building was also "partially destroyed" in the district where one person was found dead, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) added.
A school building in the district was also damaged in the attack, the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote.
"Buildings of a university campus, dormitories, and nearby residential buildings were damaged" in the Desnyanskyi district, DSNS said.
Hours later, another wave of ballistic missiles attacked the city in the middle of the night.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported a new round of explosions at around 3:30 a.m. local time. At least seven explosions rocked the city in the space of three minutes. The blasts came minutes after Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian ballistic missiles were bound for the capital.
Another blast shook Kyiv some 15 minutes later, without warning.
The second wave of missiles hit an administrative building in the Podilskyi district, Klitshcko said. Non-residential buildings were also targeted in two other unspecified locations.
Some metro stations elsewhere in the city were damaged during the earlier attack, but were repaired by emergency workers overnight, the mayor reported.
Russia has attacked the Southern Bridge and other key bridges multiple times in October, possibly in an attempt to disrupt logistics and daily life in Kyiv.
Earlier in the night, Zelensky condemned Russia's attack on Kyiv and renewed calls for allies to provide Ukraine with air defense.
"Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it — effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings," he said in a post to X.
"(I)t is precisely under such circumstances, when the threat is constant, when strikes can come at any moment and target cities and villages directly, that artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror," Zelensky added.
Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war.
Ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal Russian attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25.
At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22, during which cluster munitions also targeted the city.

Third Political Prisoner Dies in Russia This Month – Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:16:34 UTC
05:16:34 KST

A Russian television production designer arrested after returning from Kyiv to renew his passport has died in a Moscow hospital, the rights group First Department reported Monday, Oct. 26.
Aleksandr Kondratov, 52, was transferred from a pretrial detention center to Botkin Hospital on Oct. 23, the group said in a Telegram post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The cause of death has not been disclosed. First Department said his death was at least the 11th this year among defendants in cases it considers politically motivated.
Kondratov had lived in Kyiv since 2012 and returned to Russia to replace his passport, according to rights monitors. He was subsequently held through repeated administrative arrests before authorities opened a treason investigation.
Passport trip leads to months in detention
Kondratov was detained at Moscow’s Vnukovo airport on May 5.
Before the criminal case was opened, he spent more than 70 days under successive administrative arrests for alleged petty hooliganism, OVD-Info said. Such repeated short sentences are commonly described by Russian rights monitors as carousel arrests.
The treason case was opened Aug. 5 and investigated by the Federal Security Service’s (FSB) directorate for Moscow and the Moscow region.
Mediazona reported from a Moscow City Court hearing in September that his lawyer, Natalia Tikhonova, said the case concerned “at least six publications” online. She did not disclose their contents.
The court rejected an appeal against his detention. The publicly reported details do not establish what the posts said or how investigators argued they constituted treason.
12-Year-Old Boy Dies After Weeklong Fight for Life Following Russian Strike on Nova Vodolaha Park
Kondratov was best known for his work as production designer on “Likvidatsiya” (“Liquidation”), a 2007 crime drama set in postwar Odesa. He received Golden Eagle and TEFI awards for his work on the series. His other credits included Odesa-Mama and Return My Love.
Rights group records at least 11 deaths this year
First Department’s death count covers those among individuals prosecuted in politically motivated cases. It is a rights-monitoring assessment, rather than an official Russian category or a finding that all the deaths had the same cause.
The Moscow Times reported that Kondratov was the third such defendant whose death became known in October.
The other two were Igor Yakovenko, 52, who died in a Krasnodar detention center, and Rustam Khalikov, 49, who died in a penal colony in the Penza region. Both had been convicted on terrorism-related charges that their defense teams disputed, according to the outlet.
The newspaper said that eight of the 11 people in its tally had entered custody aged 50 or older. It described complaints about detention conditions, pressure from prison administrations, and difficulties obtaining medical treatment.
Those broader allegations do not establish the circumstances of Kondratov’s death. The reports announcing it did not identify a medical cause.
Campaigners warn prisoners may not survive their sentences
Kondratov’s death follows renewed appeals by Russian human rights campaigners for international attention to those imprisoned in politically motivated cases.
Earlier in October, Memorial estimated that more than 1,800 people in Russia were recognized as political prisoners. Its broader estimate of individuals imprisoned or facing politically motivated prosecution was approximately 5,700.
At an event in the French National Assembly on Oct. 7, Memorial co-chair Oleg Orlov urged European lawmakers to prioritize prisoners whose health and circumstances put them at particular risk.
“While there is still a chance, we must save at least some of those who will not survive imprisonment,” he said.
Orlov asked lawmakers to follow individual prisoners’ cases, speak about them publicly and maintain scrutiny of their treatment. His appeal focused on securing releases while prisoners could still benefit from them, warning that some might otherwise die before completing their sentences.

E100 flex-fuel vehicles get regulatory push ahead of launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:14:48 UTC
05:14:48 KST

Govt allows registration of flex-fuel vehicles running on 85% to 100% ethanol-blended petrol (file photo)
NEW DELHI: Paving the way for roll out of flex fuel vehicles (FFVs) that can run on up to E100 — nearly 100% pure ethanol or about 93-95% ethanol-blended with petrol — road transport ministry Monday modified changes in Central Motor Vehicles Rules.This comes barely months before some car manufacturers launch their E100 models.FFVs with an internal combustion engine can run on petrol, biofuels like ethanol or methanol, or any mixture of both stored in a single fuel tank. E100 fuels are “intended only for vehicles designed and certified to use it”.Officials said this is not applicable for other vehicles.“Vehicles that use E20 or normal fuel can’t use E85 or E100 fuel. Hence, the notification doesn’t require owners of existing vehicles to switch to these fuel categories or modify their vehicles now or in the future,” said a transport ministry official.TOI has learnt that the change in rules was essential for type approval and registration of FFVs on E100 considering that vehicle manufacturers are ready with their products.
Depending on the vehicle’s design and certification, the range of blending may extend to E85 or E100, a fuel predominantly consisting of ethanol.Flex fuel technology is used in countries such as Brazil and the US.
Ethanol has a lower fossil carbon footprint than conventional petrol and the use of higher ethanol blends can help reduce tailpipe emission of carbon monoxide (CO) and certain hydrocarbons. Greater ethanol use will also reduce dependence on import of crude oil.While govt notification will enable OEMs to manufacture FFVs, this won’t be enough to push adoption of these vehicles, experts said. This is evident as even after almost seven months of the launch of E85 cars, only 17 such vehicles have been registered.Industry players called reduction in GST on FFVs from 28% to 5% (on par with EVs) to bring down vehicle cost for buyers and compensate for mileage loss, which is about 27% while using E100 fuel.Besides, they sought a reduction in fuel cost to around Rs 75 a litre.But a bigger problem is availability of E100 given that there are only a handful of pumps, although it can run on other grades of ethanol-blended fuel.

Brazil's Bolsonaro says barred from leaving country after election loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:11:00 UTC
05:11:00 KST

Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said Monday that a Supreme Court justice had prohibited him from traveling abroad, a day after his election defeat and refusal to acknowledge the result.
"I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also banned from leaving the country," the right-wing senator said, denouncing "a clear attempt to intimidate me."
The right-wing senator received 48.2% of the vote compared to 51.8% for incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, denounced "a clear attempt to intimidate me."
The senator is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering during the financing of a biopic about his father. He denies any wrongdoing.
The 45-year-old said the decision to seize his passport stems from a statement made by his brother, U.S.-based former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, that Flavio would have to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
"I never said that," the defeated candidate insisted in the Instagram video.
Bolsonaro reiterated that he would seek to annul the election, arguing that an extension of voting hours on Sunday favored Lula, despite having also requested the measure.
He also promised to lead the resistance to Lula's government, however.
"To withstand the chaos, I'm going to organize the opposition," Bolsonaro said.
At a news conference Sunday, Bolsonaro said he planned to request an annulment of the election following a chaotic extension of voting at the request of both candidates. However, it's unclear what legal avenue he would have to do that.
Early signs from Brazil's institutions and from leaders across the region, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the results will be respected nationally and internationally.
Even with the vote extension, Lula's win was decisive. The soon-to-be 81-year-old incumbent won more than 64 million votes compared to just under 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
President of Brazil's electoral authority, Kassio Nunes, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, was among those who recognized Lula's victory Sunday.
"This is a really uphill battle for Flavio Bolsonaro. Important Brazilian power brokers are closing ranks behind Lula, sometimes begrudgingly," said Brian Winter, Brazil analyst and editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly.
"I sense that Brazilian power brokers that matter don't really want to go down the path of a truly contested election," he said.
The key to Lula's win was the additional 14.1 million voters who showed up for the second-round election, including those who voted for other candidates in the first round. Analysts say three-quarters of those votes went to Lula, handing him the victory. And notably, the first round set a record for the number of Brazilians who decided not to vote, while the second round had the least number of abstentions ever.

Serbia may halt arms exports to Ukraine - Reuters

Serbia may halt arms exports to Ukraine - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
"Student List" plans to halt arms exports to war zones and not join EU sanctions against Russia.
The political movement "Student List," which won Serbia's parliamentary elections on October 25, advocates halting arms exports to war zones, including Ukraine, and also does not plan to join the European Union's sanctions against Russia. Reuters reports this, UNN writes.
Details
As the publication notes, the "Student List" will have to navigate a complex energy and foreign-policy context in relations with Serbia's traditional ally—Russia.
In particular, party representatives said they did not intend to join the EU or impose sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government will have to rely on an exemption from U.S. sanctions to maintain oil imports while the sale of Russia's stake in the energy company NIS, which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to the Hungarian company MOL is being finalized.
The article notes that the Russian company "Gazprom" is Serbia's largest gas supplier. It delivers about 2.2 billion cubic meters per year at prices below market rates. The "Student List" party stated that this energy dependence is not a geopolitical choice but an acute economic dependence.
In addition, leading candidates from the "Student List" stated that the future government would halt all arms exports from Serbia to areas of military conflict, including sales to Western intermediaries who transfer weapons to Ukraine.

Young Kazakh padel players rank among Asia's best
Young Kazakh athletes have improved their positions in the updated rankings of the International Padel Federation (FIP), Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the Kazakhstan Padel Federation, Arnur Tursynkhan and Islam Duissengazin have risen to second place in the FIP Promises Asia Ranking for under-16 players. The Kazakh athletes have 1,785 points. They trail Qatar's Saeed Hashem Al-Mazayed by 1,285 points.
In the under-18 category, three Kazakh female athletes entered the top 10 of the FIP Promises Asia ranking for the first time. Sofiya Pak took fourth place, while Ailin Amantay and Adiya Bektemissova share eighth.
The second FIP Promises Almaty junior tournament recently concluded. Arnur Tursynkhan and Islam Duissengazin won the U16 category and also reached the U18 final.
Sofiya Pak, for her part, won titles in two age categories at once — U16 and U18. Strong performances at the tournament allowed the Kazakh athletes to significantly improve their positions in the Asian ranking.
Earlier, Kazakh juniors Arnur Tursynkhan and Islam Duissengazin won the international FIP Promises Tbilisi tournament in Georgia. The Kazakh duo claimed two championship titles — in the under-16 and under-18 age categories. It was Kazakhstan’s first victory at a competition under the auspices of the International Padel Federation (FIP).
As Qazinform reported, Elena Rybakina retained the world No. 1 ranking after defending her Ningbo title.

Gyurov Accuses Radev of Campaigning for Yotova Through Government Channels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:07:31 UTC
05:07:31 KST

Bulgaria's PM Congratulates Serbia’s Student List on Election Victory
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev congratulated Serbian citizens on their participation in the democratic process and the “Student List” on its election victory
Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov accused Prime Minister Rumen Radev of using the Council of Ministers’ official channels to promote Iliana Yotova and attack her political opponents, warning against the use of state institutions for election campaigning.
“Mr. Radev, you hold an absolute majority and bear full responsibility. Leave the choice to the citizens,” Gyurov said in response to messages disseminated through the government’s official channels in support of Yotova.
Gyurov called the incident a dangerous blurring of the boundaries between state authority and the election campaign. He said the problem was not the prime minister’s political position itself, but its promotion through an institution financed by all Bulgarian citizens.
“This is not the opinion of a commentator, nor is it a speech by a party leader in a public square. This is the official voice of the state, funded by the money of all taxpayers - including those who do not support the current government,” Gyurov said.
He noted that the Council of Ministers controls the state budget, the administration and the executive branch, arguing that this authority carries a particular obligation to prevent public resources from being used to benefit a single candidate.
“The Council of Ministers is not an election campaign headquarters. The state is not the property of a political party. And no Bulgarian citizen should be cast as an adversary simply because they vote differently,” the presidential candidate said.
Gyurov defended the right of every citizen to choose politically without being subjected to labels or division. He argued that people who back another candidate are not enemies but equal citizens entitled to the same treatment by the state.
“Yesterday, one in three voters chose us. These people are not some hysterical mob. They are teachers, doctors, entrepreneurs, pensioners, and young families. They are Bulgaria. And I will not accept anyone dividing them into 'ours' and 'yours.'” Gyurov said, adding that he would take the same position if a prime minister used official state channels to campaign for him.
He insisted that election rules must apply equally to everyone, including those in power, or they would have no meaning.
Gyurov also opposed efforts to portray the presidential election as a division between citizens deemed “the right kind” and “the wrong kind.” He said all sides wanted peace and framed the central question as whether those in government would serve the public or use state resources to influence voters.
According to Gyurov, one of the presidency’s main roles is to act as an independent check on concentrated power and defend the rules regardless of who governs.
“I want a president who stands between those in power and the citizens. Someone who upholds the rules even when it is inconvenient for the powerful. Someone who does not resort to intimidation or division, but instead demands that the institutions do their jobs. Bulgaria needs a state that its citizens can trust,” he said.
“Mr. Radev, govern. That is your responsibility. The choice of a president belongs to the Bulgarian citizens,” Gyurov concluded.

A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:07:00 UTC
05:07:00 KST

A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
October 26, 2026
Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.
"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.
Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.
"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.
Controversial ban
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.
"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."
Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.
The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."
A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Bad omen?
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?
Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.
Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.
All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers
Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.
Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.
In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.
Gender stereotypes
"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."
The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.
"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."
But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"
