Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:43:54 UTC
04:43:54 KST

Israelis head to the polls Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long rule or leave the country facing another political deadlock, with neither major bloc projected to secure a governing majority, Anadolu reports.
The vote will be Israel’s first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip, as well as military confrontations with Lebanon and Iran.
It will also be the first Israeli general election held on schedule since 1988, following decades in which successive governments collapsed before completing their four-year terms.
Around 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). Election day is a public holiday.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing for seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
Under Israel’s proportional representation system, voters choose parties rather than individual candidates. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter parliament.
No party has ever won an outright Knesset majority, making coalition negotiations decisive in determining who becomes prime minister.
Eisenkot’s party leads final polls
Final surveys published by Israel’s three main television broadcasters put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud.
Yashar is projected to win 22 to 23 seats, compared with 19 to 21 for Likud.
The B’Yachad, or Together, alliance led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid is projected to finish third with 14 or 15 seats.
Other opposition parties include the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
The three surveys project Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc winning 50 seats, while the opposition bloc is forecast to secure between 52 and 56.
Palestinian-led parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
The figures suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.
Winning the largest number of seats does not automatically determine who becomes prime minister.
President Isaac Herzog will consult the elected parties before assigning the task of forming a government to the lawmaker considered most likely to command a parliamentary majority.
READ: Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday’s parliamentary vote
Netanyahu fights for political survival
Netanyahu, 77, is seeking another term after serving as prime minister for more than 18 years across three separate periods.
His campaign has focused heavily on national security, portraying his experience and military policies as essential to confronting regional threats.
However, he faces criticism over his government’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, its handling of subsequent conflicts and its opposition to establishing an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures.
Netanyahu is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
His potential coalition partners include far-right parties led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alongside the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, rejected Palestinian statehood and encouraged Palestinians to leave Gaza.
The ultra-Orthodox parties have meanwhile faced mounting criticism over demands to preserve military-service exemptions for religious students as the Israeli military struggles with personnel shortages after years of conflict.
Eisenkot offers change in leadership, no major shift in security issues
Eisenkot, 66, served as chief of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and joined Netanyahu’s emergency government following the Oct. 7 attacks.
He later left the government after criticizing Netanyahu’s management of the Gaza offensive and the absence of a clear political strategy.
His son was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in December 2023.
Eisenkot has campaigned on government accountability, political stability and restoring public confidence in state institutions.
He supports establishing an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures and ending broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Despite positioning himself as an alternative to Netanyahu, Eisenkot maintains similar positions on several major security issues.
He opposes establishing a fully sovereign Palestinian state under current conditions and says Hamas’ military capabilities and rule in Gaza must be dismantled.
The election therefore presents voters with competing approaches to leadership, governance, judicial independence and relations with far-right parties, even as the two leading candidates share positions on key security issues.
OPINION: Israeli elections and the limits of change
Arab parties could hold balance of power
The Joint List and Ra’am, the principal parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, could play a decisive role if neither major bloc secures 61 seats.
Polls project the Joint List winning around nine seats and Ra’am securing between five and seven.
An Eisenkot-led government could require support from one or both Palestinian-led parties, either through formal coalition participation or outside parliamentary backing.
Such an arrangement would face political obstacles.
Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while other opposition figures have been reluctant to commit to such an agreement.
Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked the possibility of Palestinian-led parties influencing the next government to mobilize right-wing voters.
Coalition scenarios, possible deadlock
Several possible outcomes could emerge from Tuesday’s vote.
Netanyahu could form another government if his bloc secures enough additional seats or attracts lawmakers from outside his existing alliance.
An Eisenkot-led coalition would likely depend on an agreement involving Palestinian-led parties, defections from other camps or difficult compromises among ideologically divided opposition leaders.
A unity government involving Likud and major opposition parties is another possible arrangement, although Eisenkot and several allies have ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
If neither side assembles a majority, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister during prolonged coalition negotiations, potentially leading to another election.
The performance of smaller parties polling near the 3.25% electoral threshold could prove decisive. Parties that fail to meet the threshold win no seats, potentially weakening their political allies and shifting the balance of power between the competing blocs.
Exit polls are expected immediately after voting ends at 10 pm local time Tuesday.
Initial official results will begin emerging overnight, although counting ballots from military personnel, hospitals, prisons and other special voting arrangements could take several days.
Official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, after which coalition negotiations could continue for weeks.

A year's salary buys a bathroom: Demographic crisis grips one of Europe's youngest countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:40:23 UTC
04:40:23 KST

Slovakia is facing a deepening demographic crisis, with births falling to a historic low of just over 42,000 in 2025, while the population aged 65 and older reached 1.03 million, accounting for 19% of residents. According to Slovak news outlet Pravda, the trend is placing growing pressure on public finances and essential services, raising concerns about the country's ability to support an increasingly elderly population.
Despite the alarming figures, Slovakia remains relatively young by European standards. The average share of residents aged 65 and older across Europe is 22%, and only four European Union countries have younger populations than Slovakia. Italy leads the continent, with 24.7% of its population aged 65 or older, followed by Portugal at 24.3%, Bulgaria at 24%, Greece at 23.7% and Finland at 23.6%. Germany, Europe's largest economy, stands at 22.7%.
But projections suggest Slovakia is rapidly catching up. The number of elderly residents already exceeds the number of children under 15, and the share of people aged 65 and older could reach 30% by 2050 and stabilize at around 33% between 2060 and 2080. Meanwhile, annual births are projected to fall below 35,000 by 2060 and remain between 32,000 and 33,000 through 2080.
The financial consequences are already becoming apparent. The report cites projected annual pension spending of 13.7 billion euros, alongside a planned 3.5% increase in benefits from January. The average monthly old-age pension was estimated at 703 euros at the end of 2025. Slovakia's fiscal watchdog has warned that age-related spending could gradually increase by the equivalent of 3.8% of GDP by 2060, while domestic and European Union assessments have identified significant risks to the pension system's long-term sustainability.
A year's salary buys barely enough space for a bathroom
The demographic crisis is closely intertwined with Slovakia's increasingly unaffordable housing market. The country's average annual gross salary of 23,500 euros is enough to purchase just 8.1 square meters of residential property. In the capital, Bratislava, where average annual gross earnings reach 30,000 euros, an entire year's salary buys only 6.8 square meters, roughly the size of a bathroom. Only 16 Slovak cities offer more than 14 square meters for the equivalent of one year's salary, most of them in the Nitra and Banská Bystrica regions.
Financial pressures are also keeping older Slovaks in the workforce. According to data from Eurostat, the European Union's statistical agency, 24.7% of Slovak retirees continue working or earn supplementary income, nearly twice the EU average. Of those, 18.3% continue working without changing their schedules, while 6.4% switch to adjusted working hours.
For many, the decision is driven by financial necessity rather than personal fulfillment. Some 30.3% of working retirees describe employment as an economic necessity, while 31% say continuing to work is financially worthwhile. Relatively few cite enjoyment or social connections as their primary motivation, placing Slovakia among the EU countries where retirees report the lowest levels of work-related enjoyment.
The healthcare system faces mounting pressure as the number of elderly patients with complex medical needs grows alongside persistent staffing shortages. The problem is particularly visible in residential neighborhoods built during the housing boom of the 1970s and 1980s, where large concentrations of elderly residents now live after younger families moved to suburban areas.
Pensions, healthcare and long-term care are competing for limited public funds alongside education, defense and infrastructure. At the same time, young households struggling with housing prices are finding it increasingly difficult to save for mortgage down payments, particularly without financial assistance from relatives. Many are postponing starting families, creating a cycle in which unaffordable housing contributes to declining births, leaving fewer young workers to support an aging population.

Europe’s five leading NATO members have pledged to take greater responsibility for the continent’s security while maintaining the United States as an indispensable ally, seeking to strengthen Europe’s role within the military alliance amid uncertainty over Washington’s future military presence.
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, known as the E5 group, made the commitment after talks in Paris on Monday, stressing that Europe must shoulder a greater share of the burden while preserving close coordination with Washington and other NATO members.
“We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition,” the ministers said in a joint statement.
“The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO,” they added.
E5 seeks a stronger Europe within NATO
French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin said the five countries had agreed to pursue “a stronger Europe within an equally stronger NATO” through a coordinated plan developed in “full transparency” with Washington.
The group’s next meeting will take place in Rome in March 2027, Vautrin said.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who attended the meeting, also called for further investment in Europe’s military capabilities.
“We must continue to modernise our forces and capabilities to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” Kallas said.
Poland was represented by Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski.
Planned US troop reduction raises coordination concerns
The talks come as Washington plans to withdraw around 5,000 troops from Germany, roughly 15 percent of the approximately 36,000 US troops stationed there.
The Pentagon announced the planned reduction in May, catching European allies off guard. Washington said the withdrawal would take place over six to 12 months.
Zalewski said he was confident that any agreement on the US military presence would be coordinated with allies to avoid gaps in deterrence or military capabilities.
The E5 statement sought to balance calls for greater European responsibility with an acknowledgement that continued US engagement remains central to NATO’s collective defence.
European ministers reaffirm support for Ukraine
The five countries also reiterated their commitment to supporting Ukraine, although they announced no new financial or operational assistance following the meeting.
British minister Wes Streeting said European support would continue for as long as necessary, warning that the Russian threat was “of a kind we haven't seen since the end of the Cold War”.
At the same time, Streeting stressed that the allies were not seeking a direct confrontation with Moscow.
“None of us seek war with Russia. And we certainly have no quarrel with the Russian people,” he said.

From Iran to Gaza: What are Netanyahu, Eisenkot and Bennett’s competing visions for Israel’s security?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:38:11 UTC
04:38:11 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Israel without Netanyahu: Still a nation at war
Israel without Netanyahu: Still a nation at war
Netanyahu’s rivals promise to repair Israel after three years of war. But both of his main opponents back a hard military line, similar to that of Netanyahu
Two days before Israel’s election, Benjamin Netanyahu shared a post with an AI-generated image of a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a warning that choosing a leader incapable of confronting Iran could expose Israelis to a “second Holocaust.”
Gadi Eisenkot, his leading challenger and a former IDF chief of staff, accused him of threatening voters with mass destruction after failing to achieve his own war aims. “Netanyahu, you’re hysterical,” he wrote.
Netanyahu says only he can finish the job. His opponents say his leadership is endangering Israel. But replacing him would not necessarily bring the country’s wars to an end.
“The way Israel is being led today is dangerous,” Eisenkot told a party conference.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett offers an equally blunt promise: “The October 7 government destroyed, and the October 27 government will repair.”
Both challengers support confronting Iran and removing Hamas from power.
Their differences with Netanyahu concern what military force should achieve, how long Israeli troops should remain deployed — and which agreements could follow.
Iran: What counts as victory?
“I am personally committed to finishing the job,” Netanyahu said earlier this month. “Finishing the job means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran.”
Eisenkot argues that regime change must come from the Iranian people rather than being imposed militarily. His priorities include eliminating Iran’s nuclear weapons potential and cutting its support for Hezbollah.
That distinction affects how a war is fought, says military affairs analyst Yaakov Lappin.
“If the regime is to be toppled, resources have to be allocated to that, for example within Mossad. If the air force also has the regime as a target, it has to hold bombs in reserve for that. The objectives determine how resources are distributed.”
It also changes the finish line. Weakening Iran’s military capabilities would fall short of a declared objective to bring down its leadership.
But any government would inherit the same regional threats — and a military that has already changed its approach since October 7.
“Over the past three years, the Israeli military has formulated a new doctrine. It is still being adjusted, but the broad outlines are fairly clear, and the military will press hard for the next government to follow it,” Lappin says.
The principle is to confront threats before they become attacks, rather than simply contain them. A different prime minister would still face pressure to act.
Gaza: The Road to Removing Hamas
“From the moment I enter the Prime Minister’s office, within 18 months, Hamas will no longer rule the Gaza Strip,” Eisenkot has pledged.
He leaves open both Trump’s Gaza framework and military force. Bennett would maintain the yellow line separating Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas until Hamas disarms, while seeking a central role for Egypt — one Cairo has not agreed to assume.
Lappin, meanwhile, expects military operations to continue under any government.
“All the candidates will face the same difficulties, both militarily in removing Hamas from power and politically in finding a new leadership that can actually take over governing Gaza.”
But a change of government could affect the extent and duration of Israel’s military presence, he explains.
“It remains an open question whether a center-left government would be more inclined to withdraw the army more quickly from more areas of Gaza than a Netanyahu government. That is very possible. But who knows how access to all the intelligence would change that assessment?” Lappin says.
West Bank: Partial crackdown, but continued support
Lappin expects a different government to act more quickly and forcefully against the growing wave of attacks on Palestinians by violent settler groups. Something the international community has criticized Netanyahu's government for failing to do. But it will likely not be easy nor quick, since both Eisenkot and Bennet do not want to get into a broader confrontation with the settler community as a whole.
In addition, the existing power dynamics between the PA and Israel in the West Bank will likely not change overnight - and the major threats will not disappear. Meaning Israel’s room for maneuver is rather limited, says Lappin.
A Different Way?
But one man does promise change. Yair Golan, the former deputy military chief who leads the left-wing Democrats, proposes a more explicit diplomatic approach: a new, long-term nuclear agreement with Iran under intrusive inspections; replacing Hamas with a Palestinian technocratic administration in Gaza, backed by regional and international support; and halting annexation moves in the West Bank while strengthening security coordination with the Palestinian Authority and cracking down on violent settlers.
How much of that program he could advance would depend on negotiations with the other parties needed to form a government.
Netanyahu as a barrier
Abroad, Netanyahu’s departure could create an opening even where Israel’s security interests remain unchanged.
He has become the face of the Gaza war. A government without him and his far-right partners could give European and Arab leaders political space to rebuild ties, negotiate over Gaza’s future and pursue regional cooperation.
Some cooperation already takes place away from public diplomacy. The Jerusalem Post reported on October 22, citing a defense official, that Israel was providing intelligence through US mediation to help Saudi Arabia counter the Houthis. The arrangement shows how common threats can bring the countries together without formal diplomatic relations.
Lappin sees a change of government as a possible opening for more public ties, rather than a prerequisite for all cooperation.
“Another government could make it easier to have a more open relationship. Saudi Arabia is clearly waiting for a new government. It looks very bad to be close to Netanyahu, especially in the Arab world. But the United Arab Emirates has maintained its position and its cooperation. It depends on each country’s interests.”
Moving from discreet security cooperation to normalization would still require political decisions. Saudi Arabia’s demand for Palestinian statehood remains at odds with the leading candidates’ positions. Netanyahu’s departure could remove one barrier without resolving that disagreement.
Israel without Netanyahu would still face the same enemies. And with the faces leading the opposition, it means it would still face a similarly hard line. What could change is how far it fights, what it considers victory — and whether a different leadership can turn military gains into agreements.

Ukraine Pushes to Move Abu Dhabi Talks Earlier and Bring EU Into Negotiations
Ukraine is seeking to move up the Ukraine-US-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi by at least a week and to bring an EU representative into the negotiations, Ukrainska Pravda reported on October 26.
The round is currently scheduled to begin around November 10, after the US midterm elections. Kyiv and Washington are trying to persuade Moscow to agree to an earlier meeting, while Russia, and at times Washington, is resisting European participation at the opening round, according to sources close to the negotiating team.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The Russians, by the way, do not want Europeans at the table at the first meeting,” one source told Ukrainska Pravda. “But our people will bring them and brief them there in Abu Dhabi in real time.”
The source added that the main difficulty for the Europeans is the absence of a clearly empowered representative capable of making decisions during the talks.
Kyiv considers the timing important because negotiations are expected to extend across several rounds. A source in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s team noted that every week could become increasingly important as winter deepens and Ukrainians face potential disruptions to electricity, water, and heating.
As of the evening of October 25, Moscow had not given final confirmation that it would agree to move the meeting forward, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Ukrainian officials do not expect a breakthrough at the first round. One member of Zelenskyy’s team indicated that updated delegations may need an initial meeting to establish working relationships before more substantive negotiations begin.
“There is a feeling that the composition of the groups will change,” the source stated. “At the first meeting, the new delegations will get used to each other. At the second, substantive work will begin. And somewhere around the third, there may already be some real decisions.”
Ukraine also wants negotiations to focus first on the broader structure of a postwar settlement rather than immediately bargaining over individual villages or specific territorial lines, Ukrainska Pravda wrote.
“We need to show what this part of the world will look like after the war, how Ukraine will be protected, what cooperation with NATO will look like, or whatever else there will be,” another source explained.
Sources in Zelenskyy’s diplomatic team indicated that US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had presented the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, with the idea of discussing a new security model, which he reportedly agreed to consider.
European participation has also begun to take shape around Björn Seibert, head of cabinet and a close aide to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who has emerged as a potential EU representative in recent meetings.
Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arakhamia has also argued to US officials that any final peace arrangement must be acceptable not only at the negotiating table but to Ukrainians living in major frontline-adjacent cities such as Kharkiv and Dnipro, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
According to the source, Kyiv believes Russia still expects that pressure during the coming winter could weaken Ukraine’s negotiating position.
The talks also come as Moscow is expected to revive broader demands over Europe’s security architecture. UNITED24 Media reported that Russia may use the Abu Dhabi negotiations to press for NATO to roll back its military presence in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels, alongside demands affecting Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial concessions.

How Ukraine's annual radio dictation brings a nation together, one word at a time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:33:01 UTC
04:33:01 KST

How Ukraine's annual radio dictation brings a nation together, one word at a time
People take part in the Radio Dictation of National Unity at the Odesa Regional Universal Scientific Library named after M.S. Hrushevsky in Odesa, Ukraine, on Oct. 25, 2024. (Viacheslav Onyshchenko / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
As it turns out, dictation exercises are not just for schoolchildren. On Oct. 27, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians — from diaspora communities abroad to service members on the front lines — will take part in an annual tradition: listening, writing, and testing their mastery of the Ukrainian language.
Organized by Ukrainian Radio since 2000, the annual Radio Dictation celebrates the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language, bringing participants together to transcribe a text broadcast live across multiple platforms. Those who wish to have their work assessed can submit it to a professional review panel.
For Ukrainian author and war veteran Artur Dron, who wrote this year's dictation, the invitation to craft a text that so many people would follow word by word was "daunting." Still, he didn't hesitate to accept.
"I've taken part in (the dictation) myself several times, and I see something truly special in it," Dron said.
"The fact that, even during the full-scale war, we're holding this initiative for the fifth time — that we continue to do so even under these circumstances, and that language still brings us together — means a great deal."
Yuliia Sheludko, an executive producer at Ukrainian Radio, told the Kyiv Independent that she believes the dictation serves as "a kind of anchor" for Ukrainians during wartime.
Bringing Ukrainians together around a shared love of the Ukrainian language also carries particular weight as Russia intensifies its attacks against the country.
"We know from history that the Ukrainian language was suppressed for many years, so we must value and protect it," Sheludko said.
Under Russian imperial rule, successive restrictions curtailed Ukrainian use in publishing and education, while Soviet authorities continued to subordinate Ukrainian to Russian, despite periods of official support for Ukrainian-language culture. Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and cultural figures were also persecuted, imprisoned, and even killed for their pro-Ukrainian stances.
The 2014 EuroMaidan Revolution helped accelerate a broader societal shift back to Ukrainian, which has gained further traction since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. For many, speaking Ukrainian has become one of the most powerful expressions of their national identity.
Despite its power to unite Ukrainians through a shared love of the language, however, the Radio Dictation also tends to stir up strong opinions.
Ahead of this year's event, volunteer and civic activist Dasha Astafieva received what she described as "an avalanche of hate" for being chosen to read the dictation alongside teacher Artur Proidakov, with people criticizing everything from her past as a Playboy model to her former use of Russian in public life.
Since 2022, Astafieva has worked to promote Ukrainian culture. She launched the audiobook app UnderBooks in 2023, and wrote on Facebook that "the hysteria over the fact that the dictation will be read by someone who narrates audiobooks marks a whole new level of absurdity."
Public debate isn't limited to this year's dictation. Actress Nataliia Sumska drew criticism in 2025 for delivering the dictation at what many felt was too fast a pace, with many participants saying that it left them scrambling to piece their sentences together.
The uproar grew when a longtime participant with a track record of top marks reportedly had her microphone switched off after she criticized the pace of Sumska's dictation and called author Eugenia Kuznetsova's text "silly."
In 2024, author Oksana Zabuzhko's text was so challenging that only one person in the country wrote it without any errors.
The disputes point to a tension at the heart of the dictation's mission: how to celebrate Ukrainian as a shared national language while navigating disagreements over who represents it and what mastery of it should look like.
The organizers, however, seem to take the controversy that comes with the Radio Dictation in stride, pointing out that when an event draws this much public attention, some people will always be dissatisfied.
As for the controversy surrounding Astafieva, Sheludko encouraged those who haven't heard her narrate audiobooks to do so, describing it as "something she does with real mastery."
Ukrainian Radio can't provide the exact number of people who take part in the Radio Dictation every year, but it can estimate participation in the hundreds of thousands based on how many people post about it on social media and submit their written work to the professional committee for review.
According to Sheludko, Ukrainian Radio received more submissions in 2022 than in any previous year — and encouraged people to keep doing so not only for the commemorative prizes given to those with top marks.
For all the arguments over who reads the dictation and how difficult the text should be, its enduring appeal lies in something simpler: the chance for Ukrainians, wherever they are, to take part in a shared cultural tradition.
"I believe that this year thousands of people will enjoy the text, the act of writing, and, above all, the sense of unity around the Ukrainian language," Sheludko said.

UNICEF chief says children 'cannot wait another 30 years' for protection in war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:28:48 UTC
04:28:48 KST

Merve Aydogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
By Merve Aydogan
HAMILTON, Canada (AA) - The UN Children's Fund chief on Monday warned that children caught in today's conflicts "cannot wait another 30 years for the protection they have been promised," stressing that the reality for children living through war is becoming more dangerous.
"While the international community has built a strong framework to protect children in war, the reality for children living through conflict is increasingly dangerous," UNICEF chief Catherine Russell said at a UN Security Council briefing marking 30 years since a landmark report by Mozambican children's rights advocate Graca Machel on the impact of armed conflict on children.
"Since 2005, the United Nations has verified more than 430,000 grave violations against children in armed conflict — more than 38,000 were in 2025 alone," she said.
The highest numbers of violations last year were verified in the state of Palestine, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria, she said.
"And these are only the violations the United Nations was able to verify. The true scale is undoubtedly greater," Russell noted.
She said the UN has verified more than 44,000 incidents of denial of humanitarian access since 2005, including more than 8,000 in 2025 alone.
"At the very moment children most need protection, our ability to reach them is being undermined," she added.
Pointing to the use of explosive weapons in populated areas, she stressed: "More than 70% of verified child casualties in 2025 were caused by explosive weapons."
"These weapons do not only kill and injure children. They destroy schools, hospitals, water systems, and other infrastructure essential to children’s survival and development. The consequences can last long after the fighting has stopped," she said.
Describing it as "deeply alarming," Russel emphasized that such trends "are not inevitable."
 
Progress is possible given ‘political will’
"Three decades of experience have shown us that progress is possible when political will is matched by sustained engagement and concrete action by member states," she added.
Russel urged the Security Council to act immediately, saying that "the children caught in today’s conflicts cannot wait another 30 years for the protection they have been promised. We must act and we must act now."
Vanessa Frazier, the secretary-general’s special representative for children and armed conflict, told the council that decades of legal frameworks, advocacy, and engagement with parties to conflict had produced "concrete results."
"More than 40 action plans have been signed to date with parties to conflict, contributing to the release of over 220,000 children from armed forces and groups and their transfer to civilian child-protection actors," she said.
Noting the current violations, Frazier said: "In 2025, the UN verified 38,558 grave violations affecting 24,174 children. This is the highest number of children affected since this mandate was established."
She said government forces were responsible for the majority of verified grave violations for the first time in the mandate’s history.
"This is deeply troubling. I condemn all grave violations against children, in every situation and every conflict, irrespective of who commits them," Frazier said.
"No party is exempt from its duty to protect children or from scrutiny when violations are committed," she said.

ICC turning into an EU court – researcher (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is increasingly becoming Europeans’ “own personal court” as the US expands sanctions on the institution, an expert has told RT.
George Szamuely, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute in Budapest, pointed out that major global powers such as the US, Russia, and China do not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction, leaving European nations as its main backers.
“So essentially the ICC is becoming a European project,” he said.
Szamuely argued that the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navi Pillay underscored Europe’s support for the court.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded Pillay the prize on October 9, just hours before Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution, expanding measures that had previously targeted individual officials.
The ICC is now becoming increasingly the tool of the Europeans.
According to Szamuely, European lawmakers sought to reaffirm their backing for the court despite mounting pressure from Washington.
“The European Parliament wanted to send a message to the Trump administration… to say: ‘we thoroughly endorse the ICC. The ICC does our work’,” he said.
Szamuely noted that Washington’s “war against the ICC really intensified” during President Donald Trump’s first term, when the US sanctioned several court officials, including then-chief prosecutor Fatou Bensouda.
“Now he has imposed much harsher sanctions against the ICC,” he said, arguing that the latest measures effectively impose secondary sanctions on “anyone who actually engages in any kind of dealings with the ICC.”

The campaign ends with Iran, and the question of trust - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:26:47 UTC
04:26:47 KST

In the end, it is all about Iran.
At least narrowly. More broadly, as Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday, it is about trust.
Do they trust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who presents himself as the one leader capable of preventing an Iranian-inflicted second Holocaust?
Or do they accept the change bloc’s argument that Netanyahu can no longer be trusted, including to distinguish between what the country needs for security and what he needs for his own political survival?
Do they trust the military leadership reportedly questioning his judgment? Do they trust the media reporting those questions?
October 7 hovering over Israel's elections
And hovering over all of this is October 7, which makes each question considerably more complicated.
It seems fitting that Iran should be the campaign’s closing issue. The Iranian threat, and Netanyahu’s claim to have the experience, determination, and international standing to confront it, have framed his reelection case. As the campaign ends, that same issue is being used to argue against giving him yet another term.
For Netanyahu, Iran is the reason he must remain. For his opponents, the way he is handling Iran embodies the reason he must go.
That divide came into sharp focus on Sunday when the prime minister shared an AI-generated image of a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning suggesting that his defeat could expose Israel to a second Holocaust.
The message went well beyond the familiar argument that one party’s security policies are better than another’s. It linked the country’s very survival to the continued tenure of one man.
That is an enormous claim. It asks voters to believe that the institutions, capabilities, and alliances Israel has built over decades cannot adequately protect it without Netanyahu at the helm.
For supporters who believe Netanyahu identified the Iranian danger early and showed a willingness to act against it, the message may reinforce an existing conviction: this is not the time to change leaders.
His opponents see a prime minister turning a real national threat into a claim that he is indispensable.
Iran is dangerous. It does not automatically follow that replacing Netanyahu increases that danger. Yet his campaign is asking voters to make that leap.
Sunday night’s N12 News site report about a confrontation between Netanyahu and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir gave his rivals an opportunity to challenge that leap.
Zamir reportedly avoided Iran war-triggering action
According to the report, Zamir resisted an instruction for an undisclosed military operation that defense officials feared could trigger a confrontation with Iran. He reportedly sought further deliberations and signed documentation concerning its legal authorization.
Netanyahu denied any such confrontation or tension with the military’s top brass over Iran.
The political significance was clear. Netanyahu wants voters to ask whether they can entrust Iran policy to his rivals. The report invited them to ask whether even the military’s leadership trusts his judgment.
But before voters get to that question, they must ask another: Do they believe the report?
For some, N12’s account will be evidence that military professionals are trying to restrain a prime minister whose political considerations are shaping his security decisions.
For others, it will look like another anonymously sourced story – like the subsequently contradicted report that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel visited Israel shortly before October 7 to warn of an attack – appearing at precisely the moment it could do the most electoral damage.
Anonymous sources are essential to security reporting. They can expose disagreements the public has a legitimate interest in knowing about.
But sources can also be motivated by institutional interests, personal grievances, and political preferences. Anonymity does not make their information false. Neither does it shield their motives or the timing of their disclosures from scrutiny.
Likewise, suspecting a media agenda does not make an uncomfortable report untrue.
The details matter. Zamir’s request for written authorization does not, by itself, establish that an operation is unlawful. Nor does a disagreement between Netanyahu and the chief of staff establish that the prime minister is acting for electoral reasons.
But in a deeply polarized country, people often consider the messenger before the message. Those who distrust Netanyahu may readily credit the account. Those who distrust the broadcaster may dismiss it just as readily.
Regardless, the political significance is clear.
Then October 7 enters the picture.
The instinct to view the military’s leadership as a professional counterweight to political calculation is understandable. But assuming military judgment deserves automatic deference – which the change bloc seems to be doing in this instance – is much harder to sustain after that catastrophic day.
The military and intelligence establishments failed disastrously in their assessments and preparations, and in protecting the communities overrun by Hamas.
For voters who remember those failures, a report that military officials oppose a prime minister’s proposed action may prompt a blunt response: Why should we trust their judgment now?
That is a legitimate question. This does not mean Zamir’s judgment is wrong. It does mean that just because the military says one thing, we should automatically treat it as settled.
But the question runs both ways.
Netanyahu was prime minister on October 7 and bore ultimate political responsibility for the country’s security. If the military’s failure undermines its claim to unquestioned trust, the political leadership cannot emerge from the same disaster with its own claim intact.
October 7 damaged confidence in both the political leadership and the security establishment. That is what makes this election’s trust question so difficult: voters are being asked to choose whom to believe among leaders and institutions whose credibility has been badly shaken.
And there is no simple formula.
Military leaders can be wrong. Political leaders can correctly overrule them. Yet the decisions of elected officials – especially just days before an election – can be clouded by those electoral considerations.
The Iran controversy has brought all this into focus.
Netanyahu is asking voters to trust his experience. The change bloc is asking them to trust that different leaders can manage the same threats more responsibly. Both are making their case against the backdrop of October 7, which exposed the limits of experience and expertise.
When Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday, they will choose a party and help determine the coalition and government that will have to address many issues beyond Iran.
But the competing closing arguments about Iran sharpen the choice: whose judgment do they trust, whose warnings do they credit, and whose motives do they trust?
Netanyahu says the danger is too great to replace him. His opponents say it is too great to leave him in place.
On Tuesday, Israelis will decide which warning they believe.

Beyond the Headlines: Three small stories, one important message - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:26:43 UTC
04:26:43 KST

The following are three special messages I received this week that I’d like to share here. Each is beautiful and moving in its own right, but together they reminded me of our strength and unity, and of something we may have lost sight of amid the election campaigning.
The first message came from Sderot. A group of tenth-grade girls from the city's Be’eri Ulpana recently took a trip to Kiryat Shmona. They encountered a city coming back to life, with new families moving in, but they also saw the enormous challenges it still faces. So they decided to return this week, this time with a different purpose.
"We're heading to Kiryat Shmona, all the way from Sderot, for three days of volunteering and community service. Every donation we receive by next week will help us bring light to Kiryat Shmona."
Then they sent me a detailed document titled "Partnership Proposal." With youthful enthusiasm, but also an impressive sense of responsibility, they outlined exactly how they intend to spend the NIS 50,000 they are raising.
"Precisely because we know what it means to be resilient, to be evacuated from our homes, to miss home, and to cope with hardship, we want to come and help, from the south to the north."
Their proposal includes an itemized budget, from board games that will remain in the city's schools, to shopping at local businesses, to a project in which they will interview 20 longtime residents, hear their stories, and publish a special newsletter honoring them.
'Nice to Meet You'
The second message came from an initiative called "Nice to Meet You," a project that was first featured right here in this column.
Dr. Eliezer Be'eri, director of the Rehabilitation and Respiratory Care Department at ALYN Hospital for children, suffered a cardiac arrest while playing squash. His wife, Shira, was shocked to discover that he had been rushed to the hospital and admitted as an "unidentified patient" because no one had recognized him.
She chose a lovely photograph of her husband, wrote a short account of his life, and hung it beside his hospital bed. The first nurse who saw the poster told Shira how inspiring and motivating it was. When Dr. Be'eri recovered, thank God, the two of them began promoting the idea.
Their goal is to help medical staff in hospital departments see the patient as a whole person, rather than simply as a medical file. Volunteers create personalized posters that are displayed beside patients' beds, allowing everyone to get to know them a little better and bring a greater sense of humanity to the medical experience.
The volunteers visit hospital departments, sit with patients or their families, and get to know the person behind the diagnosis. To date, they have created some 3,000 posters.
Remembering those who fell in Kfar Aza
Then came the third message. Rabbi Moshe Shachor of the Ein Yehudit organization from Sderot sent me moving photographs from the Keshet School in the Sha'ar HaNegev Regional Council.
Another public, nonreligious school is helping to write a Torah scroll. This happens quite often, but this week there was a particularly poignant moment of coming full circle, a special connection between religious and secular Jews, and between this world and the next.
"A few years ago," Rabbi Shachor told me, "my friend Ofir Libstein, of blessed memory, from Kibbutz Kfar Aza called me and our mutual friend, Rabbi Yehuda Alon of the Sulamot organization. He wanted to commission a Torah scroll for the children of Sha'ar HaNegev. We began working on the project.
"On October 7, Ofir, who was head of the Sha'ar HaNegev Regional Council, was among the first people murdered. We remembered his request, which had now become his final wish.
"Precisely on October 7, three years later, we held a ceremony as part of the Otiot Shel Ahavah (Letters of Love) organization, which brings Torah scrolls to Jewish communities around the world. After Jews from around the world had written letters in the scroll, the schoolchildren also wrote letters in the new Sefer Torah, in memory of Ofir and all those from Kfar Aza who fell on October 7.
"The new head of the Regional Council, Uri Epstein, came to offer his blessings. Uri is Ofir's brother-in-law. Uri's son, Neta, was also killed that day, as was his mother, Bilha Epstein.
"It's hard to describe the emotion and the extraordinary intensity of that moment, as we watched the sacred letters being written into the Torah scroll that will be brought to Kibbutz Kfar Aza.
"Something shifted within all of us, especially the children, who have all been through so many challenges and upheavals. We saw the light in the eyes of the next generation. We felt that we had fulfilled the mission Ofir had entrusted to us."
Choices
These words are being written before the elections in Israel, but they will be published after the elections.
A great deal of energy has gone into deciding which ballot to place in the ballot box. That is important, of course, but let’s take the word elections, which in Hebrew also means choices, and apply it to other areas of our lives. Let’s think about the other decisions we make. Even without multimillion-shekel campaigns trying to influence our opinions, we should remember that we have the right to choose, and not only in the political sense.
This is a good time to recall the words of Maimonides: “Every person should regard himself throughout the year as though he is half meritorious and half guilty. And the entire world, too, is half meritorious and half guilty. If he commits a single sin, he tips the balance for himself and the entire world toward guilt, bringing about destruction. If he performs a single mitzvah, he tips the balance for himself and the entire world toward merit, bringing salvation and deliverance to himself and to them.”
Our freedom to choose does not end at the ballot box. It continues every moment of our lives.
In these weeks, as we read the weekly Torah portions, Avraham Avinu and Sarah Imeinu step onto the stage of history. Verse after verse, they choose goodness, faith, justice, and integrity. The Torah describes the good and righteous choices they make in their relationships with their family, their neighbors, and even their enemies.
Generation after generation, we continue to choose to follow in their footsteps.

Hebron business demolitions carried out without prior hearing, state tells High Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:26:13 UTC
04:26:13 KST

Parts of two business premises near the site of Friday’s deadly shooting terrorist attack in Hebron were demolished without a prior hearing, the state acknowledged in a response to the High Court of Justice on Sunday, saying the military commander considered the work urgently necessary.
The state also said it had not posted a demolition notice at the site because of an error. In connection with the affected site, business owners, who deny any involvement in the attack, petitioned the court to stop the demolitions, arguing they amounted to collective punishment.
The petition concerns two commercial compounds near Hebron’s northern entrance. It is separate from the broader evacuation of Palestinian residents and restrictions imposed across the city following the October 23 attack in which two IDF soldiers were killed.
In her initial decision on Friday, Justice Gila Canfy Steinitz directed the state to respond and said she expected it to refrain from changing the existing situation pending a further decision.
The state subsequently said the demolition work described in its response had taken place before the petition and the court’s decision reached the authorities, and that work stopped immediately upon their receipt.
Mustafa and Sufian Qawasmeh and the Al-Quds ceramics and sanitary ware company filed the petition through attorney Muhammad Dahleh. It concerns approximately 17 dunams of commercial property containing offices, display areas, and merchandise.
IDF soldiers operated without written order, explanation, petition claims
According to the petition, soldiers instructed the owners to remove goods ahead of demolition without providing a written order or explaining how they could challenge the decision.
The petitioners said the business was closed on Friday apart from a guard, and that the gunmen had climbed over a locked gate. They denied assisting the attackers, knowing about the attack in advance, or being connected to the ploy in any way.
The state’s response presented a different account of the grounds for demolition. It said the terrorists had used a factory at one of the premises as cover and fired from behind a corrugated fence and equipment.
According to the response, the military assessed that construction near the checkpoint posed an immediate security risk. The work included removing fencing at the premises used by the attackers and demolishing a fence and an office container at the compound opposite it.
The state also cited a demolition order issued in August 2012 for the fence and office at the second compound, but did not explain the intervening enforcement history.
Those grounds differ from the punitive-demolition allegations presented in the petition. The owners’ charge of collective punishment remains disputed.
Regarding the matter of the absence of a hearing, the state reiterated that military officials considered the demolition urgently and immediately necessary. It said officials had orally explained the intended work to the owners and allowed them an opportunity to remove merchandise.
The response added that no further demolition was immediately planned at either compound and that any subsequent enforcement against unlawful construction would follow the applicable procedures.
These proceedings come amid a wider dispute over the military’s actions in Hebron following the attack.
In a separate legal letter to the military, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) demanded that displaced residents be allowed to return, movement restrictions be lifted, and demolitions carried out as punishment be halted. It also requested the orders authorizing the measures already taken.
ACRI: Approximately 1,500 Palestinians forced from their homes
ACRI said approximately 1,500 Palestinians had been forced from their homes, citing Palestinian authorities. It argued that public statements by ministers indicated a punitive purpose, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s description of demolitions as serving as deterrence and as exacting a price for the attack.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city,” ACRI executive director Noa Sattath said.
The IDF, in information provided to reporters, described civilians’ departure differently, saying residents who wished to leave temporarily were permitted to do so through designated checkpoints.
It estimated that approximately 2,000 people lived in the area and were part of the Jaba’a clan, which the military described as associated with Hamas and as the clan from which the attackers came.
The military said forces had searched approximately 200 sites and arrested 10 suspects. It described demolition near the attack site as enforcement against unlawful construction and the removal of potential security risks.
Beyond that briefing, The Jerusalem Post repeatedly requested clarification from relevant IDF officials about how a mass evacuation could be legal absent evidence that the vast majority of the evacuees had taken illegal action and were not ideologically pro-Hamas.
Additionally, several media reports confirmed that IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir insisted on withdrawing troops from the area, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisted on them staying and maintaining the evacuation of the Palestinians – without specifically articulating a security necessity.

Netanyahu election win could spell early exit for IDF chief Zamir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:22:34 UTC
04:22:34 KST

Major disagreements between IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz during a meeting Monday at Palmachim Air Base could raise questions about Zamir's continued tenure and potentially cost him a fourth year in the post.
During the meeting, Zamir opposed a directive from the political leadership to continue IDF operations in the West Bank city of Hebron following Friday's attack, in which two soldiers were killed. Zamir argued that the operation had run its course militarily, partly because no weapons had been found. He also maintained that residents evacuated from their homes during the operation should be allowed to return on legal grounds.
In line with the chief of staff's position, the IDF halted the operation. Netanyahu and Katz ordered it resumed Monday, directing the military to maintain the cordon around Hebron as a measure of deterrence and to impose a cost for the attack.
Katz explained his position by saying the investigation had not yet been completed.
"Beyond the clear considerations of deterrence and imposing a cost, the investigation into the attack has not yet been exhausted," Katz said. "We still do not know who among the terrorists' associates knew or did not know about the attack. Therefore, it is inconceivable to end the operation just one day after it began."
The sequence of events means the military did not carry out the political leadership's initial directive to continue the operation, requiring another order Monday to resume it.
The confrontation illustrates the depth of the crisis in relations between the chief of staff and the political leadership, particularly Katz. The tensions did not emerge in recent days, but they have reached a new peak in recent weeks.
With polls set to open Tuesday, the election results could also affect Zamir's future. His relationship with Netanyahu, and especially Katz, has reached a low point. According to current assessments, if the two remain in power, they could move to end his tenure.
At the Palmachim meeting, Zamir argued that the immediate operational objectives in Hebron had already been achieved and that there was no justification for continuing a broad offensive operation in the city's densely populated neighborhoods.
He also presented intelligence suggesting that the attackers may have been directed from abroad, including by Hamas operatives in Turkey, and argued that the military should conclude the operation and redirect its forces and attention to other areas.
Zamir's position was reinforced by commanders on the ground.
Commanders in the Hebron sector said the operation had exhausted its military purpose after troops searched the area without locating weapons. They argued that keeping forces deployed in the city without additional findings would provide no operational benefit and would not advance the mission's objectives.
Their assessments supported Zamir's argument that a distinction should be made between the need for a forceful response to the attack and the continuation of military activity that was no longer producing operational results.
Beyond the operational and legal considerations, Zamir was concerned about the risks to soldiers' lives, unnecessary operational friction and the possibility that prolonging the operation would increase the danger of escalation.
The political leadership, by contrast, viewed maintaining the cordon and keeping residents out of their homes as part of the necessary response to the attack.
The disagreement escalated into a heated exchange in the presence of several senior generals. Ultimately, the decision was made to continue the operation.
Disagreements over Iran
Differences also exist between the chief of staff and the political leadership over Iran, although the dispute is not necessarily about whether Israel will need another round of fighting. Rather, it centers primarily on timing and how Israel manages its confrontation with Tehran.
As previously reported over the weekend, senior IDF officials have made clear that there is no reason to attack Iran before the elections unless intelligence indicates that Tehran is preparing to strike Israel.
The military is monitoring developments and preparing accordingly, but commanders want to avoid a situation in which heightened military alertness escalates into war because one side misreads the other's intentions.
IDF officials are also concerned about the conduct of the political leadership.
While the military seeks to maintain a high level of readiness without sliding into escalation, Netanyahu and Katz have continued making public statements about the possibility of an Israeli attack.
Zamir has warned about the potential consequences of those statements, which could heighten Iranian suspicions that Israel is preparing to strike and lead to a miscalculation.
Under such circumstances, the two sides could become trapped in a dangerous cycle of actions and reactions.
Israel might detect Iranian military preparations and raise its alert level, while Iran could interpret Israel's heightened readiness as preparation for an attack and respond accordingly.
A misunderstanding of the other side's intentions could trigger a confrontation that neither side necessarily planned.
That is the danger Zamir is seeking to avoid on the eve of the elections.
The intelligence involved is highly sensitive, making it difficult to provide a complete picture. Nevertheless, current assessments suggest Iran continues taking steps that could eventually require Israel to enter another round of fighting.
Netanyahu and Katz denied reports Monday evening that they intended to dismiss Zamir, calling the claims false.
"I recommended Zamir's appointment as IDF chief of staff," Katz said. "We are working together for the security of the State of Israel, with unprecedented historic achievements, and that is how I intend to continue working in the future."

Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

British F-35Bs flying from HMS Prince of Wales and Norwegian F-35As have escorted a United States Air Force B-52 over the High North during Exercise Global Thunder, the American nuclear readiness exercise, according to a post by Defence Operations.
The post said: “UK F-35Bs & @RoyalAirForce Voyager, with @Luftforsvaret F-35As, escorted a @usairforce B-52 on Exercise Global Thunder. Above @RoyalNavy & @Forsvaret_no vessels including @HMSPWLS. Operating together to defend @NATO’s northern flank.”
An RAF Voyager tanker supported the formation. HMS Prince of Wales is in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest, accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and operating under NATO command, a deployment this publication covered as the ship sailed.
United States Strategic Command describes Global Thunder as an annual exercise involving personnel throughout the strategic enterprise, including its own components and subordinate units, and says the purpose of Global Thunder 27 “is to enhance nuclear readiness and ensure a safe, secure, effective and credible strategic deterrent force.”
The command added: “This is an annual exercise and is not in response to actions by any nation, other actors or current world events,” and that “as in previous years, Global Thunder 27 may include an increase in bomber and other aircraft flights throughout the exercise.”
Britain’s part in the American nuclear exercise comes as the country prepares to take on a nuclear role of its own in the air again. The Defence Investment Plan confirmed the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear task to the Royal Air Force for the first time since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998. RAF Typhoons also escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike over the Mediterranean last week on Exercise Rummy, the first British participation in a French nuclear exercise.
Norway operates fifty two F-35As from Ørland and Evenes and has become one of the closest partners in British operations in the High North, hosting Royal Marines for Arctic training and working alongside the carrier group through the Firecrest deployment.
