Catholic leaders distance themselves from Trump after Oval Office prayer video

====================================================================================================

Why Catholic Bishops Are Apologizing Over 'Exploited' Trump Meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:18:02 UTC
04:18:02 KST

A video of Catholic bishops praying around President Donald Trump during a meeting at the White House last week has sparked debate, with some bishops claiming their attendance was “exploited” for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections.
The 12 clergymen joined Trump on Thursday in the Oval Office, for what Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee has said was intended to be a private meeting to discuss matters such as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, and human dignity. But in a “public apology” issued Sunday, Grob expressed deep regret over the meeting that he suggested was used as a "political photo opportunity” after White House officials shared images and footage of a moment of prayer. The video, which Grob claims was posted without the bishops’ consent, has been viewed over 1.8 million times on X alone.
Grob said he had received “many questions” over the encounter and wanted to emphasize that the meeting “was in no way an endorsement of the President, his policies, or his party.” He said his invite to the meeting had been extended by Heritage Foundation, the think tank behind the conservative policy playbook Project 2025, and that he had been informed ahead of time there may be an opportunity to pray privately with the President. “Several photos were taken and we were ushered out [after the prayer]. Unbeknownst to the group of bishops, a video was also taken. But permission for the public distribution or posting of either the video or photos was not given by the bishops,” he claimed, insisting the bishops “should never have been put in that position by the White House.”
The White House did not directly respond to questions over whether permission was obtained from the bishops prior to the video and photos being shared. Spokesperson Taylor Rogers told TIME “there has never been a greater President for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it,” citing the pardoning of “pro-life activists” as one such example.
Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines also issued a statement suggesting that the meeting had been ”exploited.” Acknowledging that “there are many things tied to this present [Trump] Administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith,” Joensen said he attended the gathering as the advance communication he had received “indicated that we were to have a conversation and that key officials would be interested in hearing our perspective.”
“None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election,” he said. “Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate.”
He added: “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes. I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.”
Archbishop James Golka of Denver, who led the prayer in the Oval Office, has also addressed the matter after people raised questions over the timing of the video.
“I understand that many people saw the video, posted by the Administration twelve days before an election, as an endorsement. That was never my intention,” Golka told Denver Catholic magazine. “The bishops of the United States teach that the Church cannot champion any candidate or party. I hold to that.”
He continued: “I’ve had a lot of people, really good friends, ask me, ‘What were you doing?’ ‘Why did you do that?’ I just answer: ‘I was being a Catholic priest. We pray for people.'”
Other clergymen in attendance included the former Archbishop of Kansas City Joseph Naumann. In a statement to TIME, his successor, Archbishop Shawn McKnight, said Naumann’s presence at the White House “was in his own individual capacity” and that “his actions and presence at that event were not on behalf of, or representative of, myself or the Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas.”
A separate statement from Archbishop Emeritus Naumann’s office said of the event: “The bishops were assured that no photographs would be made public. They came to have a discussion on important policy matters. As Catholic bishops, they pray with everyone, but do not endorse candidates or political parties.”
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB), meanwhile, has distanced itself from the gathering. A spokesperson for the group told TIME that “the meeting was not organized by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops” and emphasized it was “not affiliated” in any way.
Trump described the meeting as “really good” when speaking with reporters Friday, calling the bishops a “nice group of people” who “mostly prayed” in the Oval Office. Amid the online discourse, White House Faith Office director Jenny Korn defended the gathering, describing it as “not politics,” but “policy in action ending with meaningful prayer with, and for, the President.
The controversy comes as the Trump Administration seeks to maintain support among Catholic voters ahead of the midterms. According to data circulated by the Pew Research Center in 2025, 20% of U.S. adults describe themselves as Catholic. Trump's approval rating among Catholics has fallen to 30% as of October 2026, compared to the 47% he held when he returned to the White House in January 2025, per the D.C.-based think tank.
When asked about the drop in support from Catholic voters in an Oct. 22 interview, Vice President J.D. Vance, a Catholic convert, said that while he believes Catholics, and Americans in general, are not “displeased with the direction” of the country, he acknowledges that “a lot more work needs to happen.”
“The Catholic vote is absolutely critical in electoral politics in the United States, and particularly in the midterms,” says David Gibson, director of the Center of Religion and Culture at Fordham University. He adds that while certain religious groups may stick more with a particular political party, the “Catholic vote can shift between Republicans and Democrats much more easily than any other religious bloc.”
Trump won a majority of Catholic voters in the 2024 Presidential election, taking 55% of the Catholic vote to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 43%, according to the Pew Research Center. With Republicans attempting to retain control of both chambers of Congress amid tight races, Catholic voters could prove an important voting bloc.
Yet the Administration has also faced growing tensions with Pope Leo XIV in recent months. Trump and the first American-born Pope have repeatedly clashed over policy disagreements, particularly Leo's opposition to the Administration's immigration crackdown and the Iran war.
“The dynamics are shifting. For the past few years, the white Catholic vote was very solidly with the Republicans and with Trump, but Catholics are growing disaffected with him,” says Gibson. “Now you have an American Pope, from Chicago, the Midwest, and he is widely popular. American Catholics identify with him, and Trump has not ceased picking fights with the Pope, and American Catholics [could be] getting kind of fed up with it.”
American Catholic leaders have raised concerns over Trump's policies
In January, three Catholic Cardinals issued a “rare joint statement on the morality of U.S. foreign policy.”
Archbishop of Chicago Blase Cupich, Archbishop of Washington Robert McElroy, and Archbishop of Newark Joseph Tobin said the “events in Venezuela, Ukraine, and Greenland have raised basic questions about the use of military force and the meaning of peace.” They argued that the “building of just and sustainable peace” is being “reduced to partisan categories that encourage polarization and destructive policies.” The statement bolstered remarks Pope Leo had made earlier that month, in which he warned against a “diplomacy based on force.”
Trump’s war with Iran has prompted further warnings from American Catholic leaders.
Archbishop of Oklahoma City Paul Coakley, who serves as president of the USCCB, earlier this year joined Pope Leo in urging Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement to the war.
The Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement practices have also prompted debate. Upon returning to the White House, Trump rescinded previous government guidance that restricted immigration arrests in sensitive locations, including schools, churches, and hospitals. Immigration enforcement efforts subsequently intensified, with arrests reported outside churches, drawing backlash from religious leaders.
In November 2025, the USCCB approved a special message opposing indiscriminate mass deportations by an overwhelming vote of 216 in favor and five against. The bishops also raised concerns about detention conditions, family separation, the loss of legal status, and “the lack of access to pastoral care.”
The message was later echoed by other Catholic leaders across the country. In December 2025, the Catholic bishops of Wisconsin issued a statement that expressed “strong concern” over what they referred to as “the indiscriminate nature of the current federal immigration enforcement.”
Gibson says that although the USCCB used to have a somewhat friendly relationship with the Republican party, particularly on the pursuit to overturn Roe v. Wade, relations have grown increasingly frayed during Trump’s return to the White House. He points to the USCCB’s argument that the Administration has denied visas for priests and bishops, and the announced cuts to the resettlement of refugees for Catholic charities.
However, Catholic bishops have diverse views on politics and the Trump Administration.
Last year, Bishop Robert Barron was among those selected to serve on Trump's Religious Liberty Commission.
The 2025 National Study of Catholic Priests found that from a sample of 1,164 priests, 30% identified as somewhat to very liberal, 36% as moderate, and 34% as somewhat to very conservative.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:18:01 UTC
04:18:01 KST

The Air Force unit tasked with training Tactical Air Control Party Airmen has halted all rope training events after one of its instructors was killed Oct. 17 in a rappelling demonstration in front of thousands of spectators at a college football game.
Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, died Oct. 17 from injuries he suffered from rappelling rapidly from the 180-foot ceiling of Alamodome, failing to stop before his body crashed into the field below. Patterson was participating in a pregame event before the University of Texas-San Antonio played Navy as part of its Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night.
It’s unclear when the service will complete the investigation into the cause of Patterson’s fatal accident, a spokesperson at the Air Force Warfare Center at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., said.
Detachment 2 of the 6th CTS teaches rappelling and other skills TACPs need to embed and operate with Army and Marine units while coordinating and deconflicting all surface and air fires on the battlefield. But less than a week after Patterson’s death, the unit “paused all rappel and ropes training and demonstrations,” according to the spokesperson, who added that it’s unclear how long the pause will stay in place.
Other media outlets previously reported the unit’s pause in training.
Military units specializing in rappelling have frequently put on demonstrations at the Alamodome. In 2013, instructors from the Army’s 101st Airborne Division Air Assault School from Fort Campbell, Ky., conducted a pregame rappelling demonstration inside the stadium before the U.S. Army All-American Bowl game.
But the Alamodome’s ceiling is much higher than most service members are used to, measuring more than double the height of most military rappel towers.
Rappelling from such heights can cause increased friction to build up, radiating intense heat even through rappelling gloves. While practicing for the 2013 event, 101st instructors “complained about their hands feeling pretty warm, despite wearing gloves,” according to an Army release from the time. After their first practice rappel, the Soldiers added special inserts into their gloves to protect their hands from the heat buildup.
It’s unclear if Patterson had practiced rappelling from the stadium’s ceiling before the event. But the native of Fort Stewart, Ga., received recognition for his skill during his 15 years of service, including being named as the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to an Oct. 18 press release.

Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy sector deemed crimes against humanity by UN commission
Russia has committed crimes against humanity in carrying out its systematic attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has concluded.
Source: a statement by the commission published on 26 October
Details: The evidence gathered indicates that the strikes were part of a state policy aimed at depriving civilians of electricity and other essential services and inflicting suffering.
The commission examined the consequences of attacks since autumn 2022, paying particular attention to the winter of 2025-2026. The frequency, intensity and geographic range of the strikes have increased over time.
Last winter, when temperatures fell to -21°C, millions of people were left without heating, electricity, water and gas for extended periods. Older people and those with limited mobility were particularly affected.
According to the commission's assessment, Russian commanders were aware that the heating infrastructure was indispensable to civilians. The commission also classified the deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure as war crimes.
Background: On 26 October Ukraine's national energy company, Ukrenergo, reported further power outages following Russian attacks in six oblasts: Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, Kharkiv and Sumy.

Libya says int'l aviation restrictions removed after 11 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:16:00 UTC
04:16:00 KST

Libya's transport ministry announced on Monday that airspace restrictions issued by the U.N.'s International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) back in 2015 during the country's civil war have now been lifted.
The ministry said the decision, which was formally issued on Oct. 23, was announced by ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar at the opening of a meeting of civil aviation officials from the Middle East in Doha.
"This measure comes as a result of the notable progress made and the confidence placed in the capabilities of the Libyan civil aviation sector in recent times," the Tripoli-based Ministry of Transport said in a statement on its verified Facebook page.
The ministry, in a separate statement, said the North African country has received requests for permits to transit Libyan airspace that it characterized as "unprecedented demand from international airlines."
"The total number of permits registered for the 2026-2027 winter season has surged to 61,968 flights per month, effective from this November," the ministry said, calling it a significant jump from an average of 2,000 transit flights per month during the 2025-2026 season.
"Such an increase will generate substantial financial revenues using Libyan airspace," it added.
Libya slid into chaos after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011. Three years later, a civil war broke out between armed factions vying for power and divided the country between eastern and western administrations.
The war caused damage to up to 20 aircraft, including Airbus models, at Tripoli International Airport in 2014.
There are currently few airlines operating flights in and out of Libya, and they have long been limited to destinations such as Tunisia, Jordan, Türkiye, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Sudan.
The ICAO's decision would be circulated to all 193 member states for their implementation, the ministry added.

Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units.

Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch.
“We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said.
One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it and posted their experience on Reddit.
“I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen,” they wrote alongside an image of the phone showing an apparent display malfunction where a white strip of light ran along one half of the screen.
“As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.”
They said their local Apple store had replaced the phone immediately. The Guardian has been unable to verify the user’s claims. Another user in Australia posted that they had heard “almost a cracking noise” on their handset, which resulted in a similar screen malfunction.
A report by the Bloomberg news service also highlighted similar issues among users in the US and India.
Apple believes the affected units are showing defects quickly after use. It said the response from early users had been “incredibly positive”.
The company said demand had been “nothing short of extraordinary” for the iPhone Duo, its most high-profile product launch under the company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
The device has sold out and the next round of shipments is not expected until January, according to a report in the Economic Daily, a publication based in Taiwan, the home country of Foxconn, Apple’s main device manufacturer.
Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of data and analytics at IDC, a tech research company, said it was too early to tell whether the screen issue was significant. “This is quite common when a new product comes to market,” he said.
Citing similar problems at Samsung in 2019, he said: “What matters now is how the company responds … Samsung experienced problems with the original Galaxy Fold in 2019, but it also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category.
“Apple said that any customer with problems should ask for a replacement, which is the right first step.”
Ben Wood, the chief analyst at the research firm CCS, said he was taking a very cautious view of the Duo screen problem and that there was as yet no evidence of a more widespread issue with the device.

The US has designated the USS Colorado, a Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarine, as the first American vessel to join a rotational submarine force based in Australia beginning in late 2027, the Pentagon announced Monday.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting announced the designation ahead of a submarine maintenance period scheduled to begin later this week, the Pentagon said.
The maintenance activities are expected to demonstrate Australia's growing ability to service US and British nuclear-powered attack submarines under the three countries' AUKUS security partnership.
Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) will operate from HMAS Stirling, a Royal Australian Navy base in Western Australia.
The base is expected to host up to four US attack submarines and one British attack submarine on a rotational basis.
The initiative is part of AUKUS Pillar I, which aims to help Australia acquire conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines.
The rotational force will allow Australia to develop the technical expertise, infrastructure and regulatory capabilities needed to operate and maintain its future submarine fleet.
It will also expand regional maintenance capacity and support submarine deployments by the three partner countries.
"The selection of USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first submarine assigned to SRF-West in 2027 marks a significant milestone for AUKUS Pillar I and is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific," the Pentagon statement said.

UN calls Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:13:00 UTC
04:13:00 KST

UN calls Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure crimes against humanity
According to Ukrinform, this information is posted on the Commission’s website.
“The Russian authorities have committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts, by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure,” stated the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine in its new report to the UN General Assembly.
The Commission investigated the impact of large-scale attacks by Russian armed forces on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure on the civilian population, particularly during the difficult winter of 2025–2026, as well as the cumulative effects of these attacks since the fall of 2022. The report notes that systematic waves of Russian attacks, during which hundreds of drones and missiles were deployed simultaneously, became increasingly frequent and intense and covered an ever-wider area, causing significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
Last winter, when temperatures dropped to -21 °C, millions of people in Ukraine faced prolonged disruptions in the supply of heat, electricity, water, and gas and were forced to live in unbearable conditions.
“As winter approaches, the attacks have intensified again, raising serious concerns given the threats to the lives and health of the civilian population,” said Commission Chair Erik Møse.
The report emphasizes that prolonged exposure to the cold, lack of access to basic utilities, and the constant need to find ways to survive have significantly affected the physical and mental health of Ukraine’s civilian population.
Due to the risk of getting stuck in an elevator in the event of a sudden power outage, they were unable to go down to the shelter during an air raid alert and were forced to remain in unheated homes without electricity or water, without access to life-support equipment or basic services.
Due to the prolonged closure of schools during the acute energy crisis, children were unable to receive a full education. The lack of heating in their homes led to children falling ill and created additional hardships for their families.
The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects. The evidence gathered indicates that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure were carried out in a targeted manner, in accordance with a state policy aimed at depriving the civilian population of electricity and other vital services dependent on energy supply and causing them suffering. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts. The Commission relied on the testimony of 255 individuals who survived the winter under the conditions described above in the Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions, as well as on information provided by Ukrainian authorities, doctors, and nongovernmental organizations.
According to the Commission’s assessment, the Russian commanders who issued orders to carry out the attacks were aware that the heating facilities they targeted in large population centers were vital to the civilian population, especially in winter. Russian authorities officially stated their intention to continue the attacks and referred to plans for their implementation.
The Commission also examined attacks by the Ukrainian armed forces on energy facilities in the Russian Federation and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It is noted that the Commission was unable to investigate the consequences of these attacks in detail, as the Russian Federation did not grant it access to the relevant territories and did not respond to the Commission’s requests for information.
The Commission also concluded that Russian authorities recruited men who had been victims of human trafficking in various countries into their armed forces, which constitutes a violation of international human rights. In particular, compelling evidence was found that Russian authorities engaged in human trafficking involving individuals from 29 countries.
Human trafficking was carried out through deception and coercion in collaboration with agents and agencies operating in various countries around the world. The agents and agencies that recruited men in various countries presented themselves as legitimate companies or government-backed enterprises. They arranged visas and travel documents for groups of recruits and, in some cases, accompanied them during the trip. However, shortly after their arrival, they were forced to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation, written in Russian.
The Commission noted a high level of coordination between agents operating in various countries around the world and the Russian authorities.
As a result, the men were sent to the front lines in Ukraine and assigned dangerous tasks. Many of them were killed or went missing; others voluntarily surrendered or were captured by the Ukrainian armed forces and were granted prisoner-of-war status.
The Commission reiterates that international law prohibits attacks on the civilian population and civilian objects and calls for an end to such attacks. The Commission also calls for the release from the Russian armed forces of all individuals who have been victims of human trafficking.
As previously reported, as of April 2026, Russian troops had attacked Ukrainian power substations—which are critical to nuclear safety—a total of 155 times since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Since October 19, 2026, alone, Russian troops have carried out approximately 60
targeted strikes, damaging energy and oil and gas infrastructure in a number of regions (including Rivne, Volyn, Khmelnytskyi, and Vinnytsia), as well as the Kyiv power coal depot.
As of May 2026, 80 repeat strikes on infrastructure facilities had been recorded at the very moment when State Emergency Service rescuers and law enforcement officers were arriving at the scene.

Lula’s victory is a cry for sovereignty against imperialism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:10:23 UTC
04:10:23 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in the second round of Brazil’s presidential election safeguards the country’s path towards determining its own destiny and contributing to the construction of a less unequal international order.
For me, his victory over Flávio Bolsonaro also represents a defeat for the project of subordinating Brazilian foreign policy to the priorities of the United States and Israel. The ballot box has renewed the responsibility to translate diplomatic independence into development, solidarity and the defence of peace.
According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Lula secured 64,256,232 votes, representing 51.79 per cent of valid ballots, against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 59,826,041 votes, or 48.21 per cent — a margin of 4,430,191 votes. In the first round, Lula had trailed his opponent, receiving 45.16 per cent compared with Bolsonaro’s 47.03 per cent.
Overturning this deficit demonstrated the campaign’s ability to mobilise society once again, increasing its vote by more than ten million between the two rounds.
Lula’s victory strengthens the prospects for a foreign policy committed to the Global South, expanding economic, scientific and cultural partnerships while advocating international institutions that better represent developing countries.
Strengthening BRICS is central to this strategy. During Brazil’s presidency of the grouping in 2025, cooperation among Global South countries and reform of international governance were among its priorities. Lula’s renewed mandate provides an opportunity to deepen this agenda, expand alternative sources of development finance and promote technological cooperation.
Among Brazilian citizens voting in BRICS countries, Lula won in mainland China with 73.67 per cent and Russia with 64.52 per cent. He also secured majorities in India, Iran and Egypt, where he received 78.95 per cent. The results were not uniform across the bloc: Flávio Bolsonaro won among Brazilian voters in South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. These figures reflect the choices of Brazilian voters abroad, not the political preferences of the populations or governments of those countries.
In Palestine, the election result carried particular political significance. Lula received 1,000 votes, equivalent to 95.60 per cent, compared with just 46 for Flávio Bolsonaro. Although voting decisions are shaped by multiple factors, I see this overwhelming preference as reflecting an affinity with Lula’s defence of Palestinian rights.
In Israel, by contrast, Flávio Bolsonaro, who advocates alignment with Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, which I regard as responsible for genocide, received 699 votes (80.8 per cent), compared with Lula’s 166 votes (19.2 per cent). The figures reveal a striking contrast between the two groups of Brazilian voters.
READ: Pro-Palestine protests sweep Latin America as Brazil’s presidential race intensifies
Lula’s relationship with Palestine has deep historical roots. In 2010, his government recognised the State of Palestine within the 1967 borders. As I examine in my book, Palestine: From the Myth of the Promised Land to the Land of Resistance, recognising Palestinian self-determination means acknowledging Palestinians as a people entitled to rights and sovereignty.
Faced with the devastation of Gaza, Lula denounced the genocide of the Palestinian people, condemned the complicity of Western powers and demanded an international response. In challenging Israel’s impunity, he reaffirmed that no state stands above international law.
Lula’s new mandate must reinforce this position and translate it into more effective diplomatic, commercial and military initiatives. Solidarity must have tangible political consequences, confronting the impunity of the Zionist regime that enables the continuation of violence and upholding the Palestinian people’s right to freedom and sovereignty.
Mercosur is another indispensable pillar. Brazil will have greater negotiating power internationally if it strengthens integration with its neighbours, develops regional production chains and expands the infrastructure connecting South American countries.
This approach also enables Brazil to contribute to conflict mediation. Our diplomatic strength depends on the credibility to engage with opposing parties, put forward proposals and uphold international law. Peace requires initiatives that reduce tensions and protect populations affected by war.
Brazil’s diplomatic efforts concerning Iran’s nuclear programme illustrate this potential. On 17 May 2010, Brazil, Turkiye and Iran signed the Tehran Declaration. The proposal envisaged transferring 1,200 kilograms of Iranian low-enriched uranium to Turkiye in exchange for 120 kilograms of nuclear fuel for the Tehran Research Reactor, used for medical purposes. The agreement sought to build confidence and open the way towards a negotiated settlement.
Although the declaration did not resolve the dispute and was separate from the 2015 nuclear agreement, it demonstrated that countries of the Global South can formulate diplomatic alternatives to international deadlocks. This experience should inspire renewed efforts towards negotiation, non-proliferation and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
Lula’s victory should usher in a new phase of sovereign national assertion. It offers an opportunity to strengthen BRICS and Mercosur, expand cooperation with the Global South and transform solidarity with Palestine into concrete political action.
Solidarity with Palestine and dialogue with Iran are integral to a foreign policy that must serve Brazilian sovereignty and the pursuit of peace. Lula’s renewed mandate must turn this opportunity into action.

‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:09:51 UTC
04:09:51 KST

A future Royal Air Force will rely on “autonomy not flesh”, its chief said on Monday as he described plans in which Typhoon fighters are accompanied by four AI-enabled drones capable of patrolling hundreds of miles in the distance.
The technological shift would revolutionise warfare, limit the role of military personnel “towards the outside” and ease the pressure on recruitment, Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth said in a speech in London.
The senior military officer was setting out a strategy for the RAF, which has been told it must be ready to fight against Russia by 2030, at a time when the use of artificial intelligence by the US, Israel, Russia and Ukraine has made warfare more deadly.
“AI will enable warfare that speeds well beyond human comprehension, meaning that our role will shift towards the outside, and it will shift towards controlling the activity and setting the guardrails,” Smyth said.
The aim, he added, was to mirror the Anglo-American second world war model of “steel, not flesh” – relying on tanks and combat aircraft rather than infantry – to avoid the bloody trench warfare that had led to millions of deaths in the first world war.
“Given today’s changing character of war, I would argue strongly that the modern paradigm must now become autonomy, not flesh,” the chief of air staff said in a lecture at the Royal United Services Institute.
Few examples were given about the future use of AI by the air force, but Smyth did point to the £300m Storm Fighter programme of “loyal wingman” drones announced in July as part of the delayed defence investment plan. “Crewed platforms are no longer enough,” Smyth said.
Four armed, AI-enabled uncrewed craft would work alongside every RAF Typhoon, with the first tests to be conducted next year. The aim is for the drones to be in service by the end of the decade, in line with a Nato directive for the UK and other alliance members to be ready to fight Russia if necessary by 2030.
Over the weekend Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win”.
The drones would “provide force multiplier function and the affordable mass we so definitely require” and, Smyth added, would be “placing sensors, weapons, and united warfare capabilities well within contested airspace”.
One possibility would be to use the drones to track Russian aircraft seeking to cross the Greenland-Ireland-UK gap into the north Atlantic, controlling them from a cockpit of a Typhoon flying over Scotland, several hundred miles away.
AI has been used by the Israeli and US military to dramatically increase the pace of target selection in the wars in Gaza and Iran, allowing them to run more bombing missions.
The IDF used two databases, Lavender and Habsora (or the Gospel), to increase the pace at which it could attack people and buildings during the war in Gaza. The US’s Maven Smart System, developed in conjunction with Palantir, was used to identify and strike 1,000 targets in Iran in the first 24 hours of the war this spring.
Russia and Ukraine have begun to use AI to identify and strike targets on the ground, eliminating the need for satellite or radio communication as they descend on their bombing mission. In July, Ukrainian investigators concluded that a drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was relying on AI for its attack.
“Autonomous air systems penetrate Russia’s perceived sense of sanctuary on a routine basis,” Smyth said, describing how Ukrainian drones conduct long-range strikes against targets inside Russia, such as oil refineries.
Drones would allow the RAF to increase its ability to strike at a time when recruitment has been challenging. The RAF’s fully trained personnel numbers have fallen from 29,800 in 2020 to 27,850 today, and the total has only begun to increase over the last 18 months.

====================================================================================================

As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia | Novak Simin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:04:33 UTC
04:04:33 KST

Two years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until the canopy collapse at the newly renovated train station in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point.
This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We were vilified and attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul.
Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials began branding us fascists and traitors.
I was personally targeted for speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’s propaganda machine of money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press.
But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of the Student List. Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society.
Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wanted Serbia to be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum.
Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands.
We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.
This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants.
We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely.
- Novak Simin is a member of Serbia’s Student List movement

15 young Canadians take federal government to trial over climate policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:04:27 UTC
04:04:27 KST

Merve Aydogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
A trial began Monday in Vancouver in a lawsuit brought by 15 young Canadians who accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights through its climate policies and actions.
The case, La Rose v. His Majesty the King, was filed in 2019 and marks Canada's first federal youth-led climate trial.
The plaintiffs argue that Ottawa's conduct, including subsidies for fossil fuel industries, approval of major extraction projects and failure to meet emissions-reduction commitments, violates Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which protects the rights to life, liberty and security of the person.
They are asking the Federal Court to declare that their rights have been violated and order the government to develop a science-based Climate Recovery Plan to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and decarbonize Canada's energy system.
"I was 13 when I joined this case. I have grown up in it, and for seven years it has been part of my life, through all the ups and downs," Sadie Vipond, a plaintiff from Calgary, Alberta, said in a statement released by Our Children's Trust.
"The climate crisis is harming us now. We deserve protection. We deserve a future we can believe in. And our rights are worth standing up for," she added.
Catherine Boies Parker, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs at Arvay Finlay LLP, said the case centers on the constitutional rights of children and young people.
"The question for the Court is not what Canada's climate policy should look like, but whether the government's conduct is consistent with the Constitution," she said.
The evidentiary phase of the trial is scheduled to run through Nov. 20, with testimony from the plaintiffs and experts in climate science, children's health, renewable energy, public policy and economics.
The proceedings follow a unanimous 2023 Federal Court of Appeal decision allowing the case to move forward.

It is known that the Ukrainian Armed Forces use Serbian ER Grad 2000 122-mm rocket shells. The Ukrainian military also received a shipment of Serbian 30-mm grenades for the AGS-17 automatic grenade launcher.

French government fails to convince students to stop protests

France's Education Minister Edouard Geffray delivers a press conference at the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space in Paris on October 26, 2026. | Dimitar Dilkoff/ AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — The French government failed Monday to convince students to end their protests.
On the sidelines of meetings with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and education and university ministers Édouard Geffray and Philippe Baptiste, representatives of high school and university students made it clear they were not yet satisfied with the government’s proposals and vowed to keep protesting.
“Not all our demands have been satisfied, and we will see this through to the end,” Louis Letoublon, vice-president of the organization “Les Lycéens!” said after the meeting, calling on high school students to continue protests on Oct. 31 and Nov. 5.
Advertisement
Students have demanded up to 250,000 extra places in higher education and universities, better conditions in educational institutions, more teachers and a major overhaul of the selection process for university entry.
On Monday, the government told students it would look into reforming France’s university admissions platform, Parcoursup, which student groups consider opaque and a source of inequality, starting in 2028. It also promised more money to renovate schools, an extra 15,000 places in higher education in industry, health and technical education, and a maximum of 28 students per classroom in the first year of high school.
Those measures, widely reported by French media and confirmed by student representatives who attended the meetings, will be detailed at a press conference later this evening.
But university students are not impressed.
“Once again, the government is missing the point. If the government’s strategy is to show contempt for our demands, then we will remain mobilized in the streets and on university campuses, and we won’t back down,” university union UNEF said earlier in the afternoon, when news of the government’s proposals began to circulate.
Student demonstrations and blockades in schools and universities earlier this month were among the first expressions of broader social unrest, which later turned into protests over the cost of living and spiraled into riots two weeks ago.

Plans unveiled to tighten sunscreen testing after SPF scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:01:42 UTC
04:01:42 KST

Australian sunscreens face tough new rules in wake of SPF scandal
In short:
The medicines regulator has proposed stricter testing rules after 16 sunscreens failed to meet their SPF claims.
The possible changes also cover the way sunscreens are labelled and laboratory testing is conducted.
What's next?
Some changes could be implemented soon but others will require further consultation and possible legislative amendments.
The consumer group whose testing sparked last year's sunscreen scandal has criticised sweeping new reforms for failing to force companies to publicly release their SPF test results.
Under the proposed changes, released today by medicines regulator the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), Australian sunscreen brands would be forced to test the SPF of their products multiple times and provide the results to the TGA before going to market.
Consumer faith was battered last year when Choice testing revealed 16 out of 20 popular sunscreens failed to meet their SPF label claims.
One 50+ sunscreen that returned an SPF result of just four was later recalled, followed by 19 others that shared the same base formula.
"Our investigation has identified multiple factors that could contribute to low SPF results — not a single cause," chief medical adviser Robyn Langham said.
"Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence. These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation."
While Choice welcomed the proposed changes, consumer impact director Andy Kelly said it was not enough to force companies to do more testing on their products.
"Unfortunately, the TGA is not proposing to be routinely checking and evaluating the data that's put before them," he said.
"We really think that's something that's incredibly important that the TGA should be doing, especially because they're proposing that these test results won't be made public as well."
Mr Kelly said that meant Australians still would not be able to check the data behind a sunscreen brand's claims.
"So we're still … just a little bit in the dark if that's the proposal that goes forward."
The TGA told the ABC some of the changes could be implemented in the short term while others would require further consultation and may need legislative amendments.
Mr Kelly said while Choice appreciated regulation was complex, last year's sunscreen scandal showed it was well overdue.
"It was quite shocking for us to see the result with so many [sunscreens] failing to meet their claims. I think consumers were rightly outraged by that as well.
"As more came out about how the TGA actually regulates sunscreen and how much reliance is put on manufacturers to do the right thing … change can't come quick enough."
SPF testing will not be made public
Currently, sunscreen makers do not have to provide SPF testing data to the TGA unless it is requested, meaning there is limited transparency around the evidence underpinning a rating.
Under the proposed changes, brands would have to test the SPF of their finished product, rather than just the base formula, before listing it with the TGA.
They would also have to continue to test the sunscreen periodically over its shelf life.
Additionally, brands would be required to provide their SPF test results to the TGA on a confidential basis before their sunscreen could go to market.
"This is about making SPF claims more reliable, reinforcing suppliers' responsibility for their products and giving the TGA faster access to evidence when concerns arise," Professor Langham said.
But in a document explaining the proposals, the TGA said it would not routinely check SPF testing data before a product hit the shelves.
The TGA considered making SPF testing public. However, in its proposal it noted there were concerns about confidentiality, intellectual property and potential misinterpretation of highly technical SPF data.
The TGA has not released the results of its investigation into Choice's sunscreen testing more than a year ago, and it is unclear how the proposed reforms will affect sunscreens already on the market.
TGA to expand how sunscreens can be tested
One of the most significant proposed changes is to how sunscreens would be tested before entering the market.
Companies would be allowed to test their products using an in vitro method, which involves testing sunscreen by putting sunscreen onto a plastic plate instead of human skin.
Currently products must be tested using in vivo test methods, which involve applying sunscreen to volunteers and measuring how effective it is under simulated sunlight UV exposure.
The TGA said it made this recommendation due to significant concerns about variability in SPF testing results using the in vivo testing method.
It said in vivo would not be replaced entirely, because the in vitro method might not be suitable for some formulations or water-resistant SPF testing.
Increased oversight of laboratory testing
The TGA has also proposed improvements to oversight of laboratories performing SPF testing because it currently does not regulate or accredit them.
Under the changes, the TGA is proposing strengthened international accreditation of testing labs.
It comes after an ABC investigation revealed more than half of the sunscreens that failed to meet their SPF label claims had used an overseas lab, which had its results called into question by experts.
The TGA acknowledged the measure could make testing more expensive and harder to access.
The TGA said it was still considering changes to how SPF was labelled on sunscreen packaging.
Three options were proposed during consultation, including moving from the current number-based system to a "low", "medium", "high" and "very high" format.
Sunscreen safety advice
Read more
Two in three Australians will be diagnosed with skin cancer in their lifetime and about 2,000 Australians die from skin cancer every year.
Sunscreen is one of five important ways to reduce the risk of skin cancer. The others are wearing protective clothing, wearing sunglasses, wearing a hat and seeking shade.
It is important to apply enough sunscreen. The recommended amount for an adult is seven teaspoons for the whole body. You should cover every bit of exposed skin and reapply every two hours and after being in water.
SPF 20 filters about 95 per cent of UVB rays and SPF 50 filters about 98 per cent of UVB rays.
Source: Cancer Council
Other proposed changes to sunscreen rules include:
- Making the difference between cosmetic and therapeutic sunscreens clearer. Currently, some cosmetic products are able to claim an SPF of up to 50+ without being listed as therapeutic goods.
- Developing quality requirements for sunscreen ingredients in response to a range of views on whether the current regulations provide "sufficient assurance of the quality, safety and efficacy of sunscreen ingredients and formulations".
- Conducting a review of sunscreen good manufacturing process guidance.

Exclusive: Russia significantly expands glide-bomb production, research shows
Russia is significantly expanding its glide-bomb production, indicating that Moscow has no plans to scale back its war against Ukraine, a new report by Kyiv-based think tank Center for Defense Reforms exclusively shared with the Kyiv Independent reveals.
"Given the role of guided aerial bombs in destroying defensive positions, isolating battlefields and facilitating ground advances, this provides a basis for sustaining high-intensity offensive operations over an extended period," the report concludes.
The report reveals that in 2025, the centralized procurement entity TRV-Engineering JSC obtained nearly 278,000 servo drives, used to control the flight surfaces of glide bombs — enough to manufacture 139,000 of the deadly munitions. The report identifies the key Russian supplier of servo drives, CED Sail LLC, which is currently not subject to any Western sanctions, and suggests this entity should be a "priority target" for sanctions designation.
"Russia is building the military-industrial capacity to continue waging wars even after the war in Ukraine ends. These are not the actions of a country preparing for lasting peace," Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Center for Defense Reforms and former chief adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, told the Kyiv Independent.
The report also identifies a network of interconnected Russian companies which are responsible for importing key components and raw materials essential for the production of UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits.
Russia converts older, unguided bombs into precision-guided weapons with these guidance kits, significantly increasing their range and accuracy. The increase in range allows Russian fighter-bomber aircraft to remain within Russian territory, out of range of Ukrainian air defenses, as they deploy their deadly payloads.
As with many other Russian munitions, both UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits are heavily reliant on foreign components for their manufacture.
Ukrainian military intelligence has repeatedly identified a range of foreign components in Russian glide bombs, including parts from the U.S., Japan, China, Switzerland, and Taiwan, among others.
The report also reveals the majority of entities and individuals involved in the production of Russia's glide bombs are currently unsanctioned, despite the munitions being a key part of the Kremlin's offensive airborne arsenal.
Out of 20 corporate entities involved in the manufacture of Russian glide bombs, only eight are subject to some level of Western sanctions or export restrictions. The "uneven sanctions coverage," the report assesses, allows Russia to continue to "procure necessary components without significant restrictions."
Four Chinese companies are identified as being critical to the supply chain, with some, such as Shenzhen Fire Power Control Technology Limited, not hiding the explicitly military application of their products. Only one of the four Chinese companies is subject to U.S. export restrictions, and none are sanctioned by the U.K. or the EU.
"Despite its repeated declarations of readiness for peace, Russia continues to dramatically expand the production of offensive weapons, particularly guided aerial bombs," Danylyuk said.

Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes
Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers.
Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant.
The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said.
Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems.

Mystery money from super PACs floods US midterm election campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:00:18 UTC
04:00:18 KST

With just over a week until voting day, the records in the notoriously expensive US election system have been shattered.
An AFP news agency analysis of federal data shows just five groups known as super PACs (political action committees) accounted for nearly a third of non-party spending in this election cycle as of October 25.
Significantly funded by dark money, they have poured more than $1 billion into the US midterm election campaign.
Three of the five groups skew Republican, and about two thirds of the billion dollars spent will benefit the Republican Party (GOP), fuelled by ultra-wealthy Republican-leaning donors like Elon Musk — a key ally of President Donald Trump.
Musk alone has put almost $450 million into Republican groups, including the biggest of the super PACs, the Senate Leadership Fund.
Meanwhile, Democrats have a fundraising edge when it comes to direct donations to candidates' campaigns and to the party's national committees.
Democratic candidates in competitive Senate and House races have consistently outraised their Republican counterparts.
That suggests smaller donors in the Democratic base are highly motivated.
But tortuous US election laws impose strict caps on how much individuals can give, while there is no limit — or really any control at all — on how much super PAC groups can throw at candidates.
Unlimited contributions
The six giant spenders in this cycle are technically a mix of super PACs and hybrid PACs, entities that didn't even exist before 2010.
They grew out of a Supreme Court ruling, known as Citizens United, which held that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.
A lower court decision ruled that these organisations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors.
The result was that big donors can funnel vast sums of money to try and influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organisations.
In contrast, direct contributions to a candidate's official campaign are limited to a mere $3,500, and donations to national party committees have a cap of $44,300.
The PAC spending sprees have surged ever higher during the Trump era, with Musk's mega-million donations encapsulating the new reality of pay-to-play politics.
Across the nation, super PACs have put far more of their money into Senate contests and spent it largely on attack ads.
The Texas Senate election tops the list in terms of expenditure. Democrat James Talarico has faced more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups as he attempts to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.
Second is Ohio's special Senate election, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has also faced extensive outside spending against him — nearly $170 million — as he tries to return to the Senate.

Air Force Plans $1 Billion Campus for Testing F-47 at Nellis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:56:52 UTC
03:56:52 KST

The Air Force is taking the first steps to build a $1 billion campus including hangars, laboratories, maintenance and training facilities, and more to test the F-47 at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev.—and the service plans to finish construction by 2031 as it moves quickly to field the upcoming sixth-generation fighter.
In a presolicitation notice posted Oct. 22, the Air Force said it is looking for as many as four qualified firms that can quickly work on a project to design and build the proposed F-47 campus. The entire project, including construction, design, security, and other expenses, will ultimately cost about $1.057 billion.
The project would include a nearly 117,000-square foot facility, largely on the east side of Nellis, combining flightline operations and maintenance. It would also have a specialized laboratory for reprogramming the plane’s systems, an aircraft apron with sunshades, and a nearly 41,000-square foot simulator facility.
The notice lists several other facilities that could be built later as “potential subsequent work,” including additional hangars for fuel system maintenance, corrosion control of its stealth coating, weapons load training, maintenance training, and other maintenance needs.
The Air Force plans to issue an initial award for the F-47 campus in February 2027, which would then kick off about nine months of design and preconstruction, and then about 40 more months of more intensive construction into early March 2031.
The presolicitation notice for the campus provides the latest window on how the Air Force is preparing to bring the Boeing-made F-47 into its fleet. It follows the Air Force’s 2027 budget proposal, which requested $730 million for hangars and other support infrastructure for the F-47 and revealed its operational testing will take place at Nellis.
The Air Force in March 2025 announced it had chosen Boeing to build the F-47, which will replace the F-22 Raptor sometime in the 2030s and eventually make up 20 percent of the Air Force’s fleet. It is expected to have advanced stealth, data sharing, and electronic warfare capabilities, and it will be able to direct semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in September 2025 that the first F-47 fighter was in the process of being built and would fly in 2028. Service officials have stuck to that schedule ever since and said its first flight will take place before the end of the Trump administration.
Allvin also said in a May 2025 social media post that the F-47 will be able to fly faster than Mach 2, or more than 1,500 miles per hour, and have a combat radius of more than 1,000 nautical miles, far more than the F-22 or F-35A Joint Strike Fighter. That expanded range would give the F-47 an advantage in a potential conflict with China, where aircraft will have to fly long distances over stretches of the Pacific Ocean.

Iran holds ‘very good’ talks with Mecca pact nations on region’s security
TEHRAN – Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Oct 26 in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were “very good”.
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to “de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis”, a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.
The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.
It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defence alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.
The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they “agreed to continue discussions” according to Iranian state media.
But Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital Tehran were “very good”, according to state television.
“I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen,” said the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
He said they agreed that security in the region “should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention”, saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Prince Khalid, Pakistan’s powerful army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.
Regional tensions have risen ahead of Israel’s pivotal elections on Oct 27 and next week’s US midterms, where US President Donald Trump’s Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.
As the talks in Tehran began, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said it was “essential to stop any escalation” in the Middle East.
“The risk to have the combination of an overwhelming military attack on Iran, and an overwhelming military attack by Iran on the countries of the Gulf, needs to be avoided at all costs,” he told a press conference in Cairo.
Hesham Alghannam, a Saudi security analyst and researcher, posted on X, that “this historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control”.
‘Powerful signal’
Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, which has suffered weeks of attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, after the group claimed a new attack on the Saudi capital’s international airport on Oct 25.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen later reported intercepting three Houthi-launched drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh region.
Responding to the weeks of attacks, Egypt’s parliament approved President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s request to approve defensive military support for Saudi Arabia “if requested”.
US-Iran mediation efforts have been led by Qatar and Pakistan. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Oct 25, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.
Andreas Krieg of the London-based risk consultancy MENA analytica said Prince Khalid’s presence in Tehran was “hugely significant”, calling him the “strategic mastermind of Saudi Arabia”.
Prince Khalid, brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler, has emerged as one of Saudi Arabia’s key diplomatic interlocutors, repeatedly dispatched on sensitive regional missions.
“Riyadh is investing serious political capital in dialogue with Iran, seeking to contain escalation and create a credible diplomatic path out of the crisis,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst who is close to the government, posted on social media.
‘Don’t test us’
Recent comments have heightened speculation about renewed conflict.
US President Donald Trump said on Oct 23 that Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the US-Israeli campaign against Iran that began on Feb 28.
On Oct 25, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran may try to disrupt the Israeli elections, where he is in a neck-and-neck race to stay in power.
“We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections,” Netanyahu, who faces an election on Oct 27, said in a video released by his office.
The remarks came as Israel’s Channel 12, citing unnamed sources, reported a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the premier denied. AFP

Breakthrough moment beckons for Australia's Wheelaroos at home Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
Australian wheelchair rugby league is poised for a breakthrough moment this week, with Wollongong, south of Sydney, hosting the nation's first World Cup since 2008.
Bundled in as part of the larger Rugby League World Cup, which also includes the men's, women's and physical disability tournaments, the wheelchair competition will benefit from free-to-air coverage in prime-time slots.
It is the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of, and Australia's Wheelaroos are well aware of the gravity of the moment.
"I think it's going to bring a whole different experience for wheelchair rugby league in Australia," Australia captain Bayley McKenna told ABC Sport.
"It's gonna bring people together, it's gonna bring people in to support our sport."
The Wheelaroos are currently ranked fourth in the world and are yet to claim a world title, with their game generally taking a back seat to the likes of wheelchair basketball and wheelchair rugby at a grassroots level in Australia.
But coach Brett Clark has told ABC Sport his charges are ready to take the rough-and-tumble sport into living rooms across the country.
"We know this is a quality game for all to play and this is the opportunity for us to show it at its top level," Clark said.
A unique kind of inclusion
Wheelchair rugby league, not to be confused with Paralympic favourite wheelchair rugby, is played on a basketball-sized court and with five athletes per side.
The sport replaces tackles with tagging like in Oztag and uses AFL-style handballing instead of kicking, but otherwise, remains relatively faithful to the running game.
Played across full-length 40-minute halves, it is a game filled with exhilarating chair skills, hair-raising collisions and retains much of rugby league's trademark physicality.
For Wheelaroos captain McKenna — who played the running game for years before joining the wheelchair sport — wheelchair rugby league's physicality is one of its biggest drawcards.
"In hindsight, I've had more injuries playing wheelchair rugby league than I did in the running game," McKenna said.
"You can hit people as hard as you want as long as you're going for the tag."
At 26, McKenna is a Wheelaroos trailblazer, being both the youngest and first non-disabled national team skipper.
Wheelchair rugby league is unique among international wheelchair sports in allowing teams to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.
This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from the grassroots all the way to elite competition, allowing for both non-disabled and disabled friends and family to share the same court.
McKenna, who began playing wheelchair sports alongside his disabled father, has seen the benefits of that inclusiveness firsthand.
"Being a non-disabled athlete in this sport is one of the most unreal things you can ever be a part of," McKenna said.
"The sport's so big, it's so broad, you can travel all across the world … it's so inclusive, because for me it gave me an opportunity to play a sport underneath my dad as a coach."
Wheelaroos squad member Liam Luff, living with hereditary spastic paraplegia, told ABC Sport the policy was an "incredible benefit".
"It just opens the doors to more and more people in our sport, which is what we need to grow awareness, get more people in chairs and show how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
The importance of the moment
Beginning on Friday, the 2026 World Cup will be just the fifth edition of the wheelchair tournament, with France and England having split the first four titles evenly.
With the sport having been first designed in France in the early 2000s, the two northern hemisphere titans have benefited from close contact and regular meetings.
In England, the sport experienced an explosion in popularity after the nation hosted the 2022 World Cup, which was also held alongside the men's and women's competitions. Grassroots participation saw a sharp uptick in the year after the event, while standalone international games have attracted audiences in the thousands since.
The Wheelaroos are now optimistic the 2026 tournament will have a similar impact in Australia, and Luff believes the sport is well and truly ready for it.
"I think more people are going to stumble across the game and find out about how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
Finding a way past France and England will undoubtedly be an almighty task for the Wheelaroos, who will play three group-stage games before the knockouts.
But the team is bullish on its chances in the Illawarra, and Luff is convinced the Wheelaroos are finally ready to take a seat amongst the world's elite.
"This is our biggest opportunity to really prove where the Australian Wheelaroos are in wheelchair rugby league," Luff said.
"We are gonna make sure we can prove ourselves taking on those top dogs … I think we're gonna really send a message about where we stand."

The Council of the EU allocates €4.7 billion in compensation to member states for supporting Ukraine

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:53:40 EET
03:53:40 KST

The Council of the EU allocates €4.7 billion in compensation to member states for supporting Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Council of the EU approved €4.7 billion in compensation to states for military support to Ukraine. A further €230 million will be allocated to the EUMAM mission.
On October 26, the Council of the EU adopted a package of eight decisions enabling €4.7 billion from the European Peace Facility to be used for the EU member states providing support to Ukraine. This was reported by the press service of the Council of the EU, UNN writes.
Details
These decisions allow for partial reimbursement from the European Peace Facility for military assistance already provided by the member states, totaling €4.7 billion. They also provide additional funding for the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine, EUMAM, totaling €230 million.
These decisions are an important step toward implementing the political agreement reached by the EU member states on September 25, 2026, to mobilize €6.6 billion for Ukraine from the European Peace Facility. The agreement provided for €1 billion in new military assistance to Ukraine and further strengthening of EUMAM Ukraine in 2027
The adopted decisions increase the total volume of EU support for Ukraine under the European Peace Facility to €10.8 billion, including €9.9 billion to reimburse the cost of military assistance provided by the member states and €950 million for military training under EUMAM, the Council of the EU stated.
Background
The European Peace Facility was established in March 2021 to finance measures under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) aimed at preventing conflicts, preserving peace, and strengthening international security and stability. In particular, the European Peace Facility enables the EU to finance measures designed to strengthen the capabilities of third countries, as well as regional and international organizations, in the military and defense spheres.
