How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:59 UTC
02:55:59 KST

Ricardo Contreras’s new leg rests on a wooden countertop.
More than four months after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the 24-year-old is still recovering from his injuries.
When he was trapped beneath the rubble on the night of June 24, he waited hours to be rescued. His left leg had been pinned beneath a fallen door frame, limiting its blood circulation. It had to be amputated.
“One of the biggest achievements is that we survived,” Ricardo said, glancing towards his 16-year-old brother, Andres Contreras. “At first, when I found out Andres was well, I didn’t care about my leg too much. I would have chosen a thousand times over for Andres to be OK.”
But now Ricardo is adapting to his new reality.
He and his brother are still undergoing physiotherapy for their injuries. On a scorching afternoon, he sits in a small workshop in the hills of northwestern Caracas, waiting to do rehabilitation exercises to prepare for his new prosthetic leg.
“Now it’s about regaining a little of the independence I had before the earthquake, because that’s what limits me most," Ricardo said.
But recovery is only part of the challenge he is facing. His parents died in the collapse.
Resources and aid have also grown scarcer, particularly as global attention faded and international donations dried up.
As of September, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said it had secured only $29.5m of the $65.7m needed to continue its earthquake support in Venezuela, a shortfall of 55 percent.
Separately, that same month, the International Red Cross said its Venezuela response effort was only 39.8 percent funded.
Not only are survivors like Contreras left to grapple with loss of limbs and family members, but they now face the prospect of lifelong health costs — with dwindling support.
From rescue to recovery
More than 6,500 people have been confirmed dead as a result of the earthquakes, according to government authorities.
At least 226,696 people have received hospital treatment for injuries. The government says it has compiled a census of amputees, but no details have been made public.
At Ortoprotecnica, a Caracas workshop that makes prosthetic limbs, director Bianca Damaso is helping survivors like Ricardo through the next stages of recovery.
For those who have lost limbs, it typically takes two to three months of physiotherapy, rehabilitation and preparation to be ready for a prosthesis — sometimes longer depending on how their wounds heal and any pre-existing health conditions.
“It’s a very individual process where you have to support each person from where they are, because some are very anxious to have the prosthesis already, but their skin hasn’t even healed yet,” Damaso explained.
She said there are more than 100 types of knees to choose from, as well as more than 200 skin shades.
But the process does not end with the first fitting. Children may need five or six replacement prostheses as they grow, while adults might require ongoing adjustments and repairs.
Then there are the psychological hurdles. Many earthquake survivors wonder about practical realities like whether they will walk again, whether they will need a wheelchair or whether they will be able to urinate independently.
Many, in Damaso's experience, also question whether they will find a partner who will love them.
"Right now, the challenges for them are going to be more than just physical. They’re mental battles," Damaso said.
There is one rule she is adamant about in her workshop: “We tell them that the only thing that’s forbidden here is saying, ‘I can’t.’”
Karina Bechara, who lost both her legs in the earthquakes, is hoping to stand on her new feet by December 1. For now, she relies on a wheelchair.
“That motivates me every morning to get up and say, 'One day less to go.' It's painful, yes, but we're getting closer to the goal,” Bechara told Al Jazeera.
Before the earthquake, Bechara ran her own business and had an active life, training regularly with high-intensity CrossFit workouts. Her children saw her as an independent mother who did not depend on anyone.
“Now I am the opposite, a mum who needs their help, a dependent mum,” Bechara said.
After the earthquakes struck, Bechara was stuck in the rubble for 23 hours, immobilised by a piece of heavy furniture that crushed her legs.
She describes her recovery as an “emotional rollercoaster”. She said she allows herself to cry on the harder days but tries to keep looking ahead.
“Because if I don’t see the future for myself, no one else will.”
More than just limbs
But readjusting to routines can be difficult for those who have sustained life-altering injuries — not to mention other losses.
So far, Ricardo is optimistic about his daily activities. He has resumed work at his family's truck parts business, as well as his university studies. A new semester of classes has started, and he uses crutches to get around.
“I was really quite nervous. I was even worried about where the classes will be because we have three floors and also the distances are long,” Ricardo said.
But his concerns quickly melted away. The professors even moved his lessons to ground-floor classrooms to make the courses more accessible.
“It was actually great going back," Ricardo explained. "My classmates have always been there, helping me.”
The most difficult adjustment, however, has been grappling with the loss of loved ones.
“If my leg hurts, I take a pill, but with that, there’s nothing I can do. There’s no cure, there’s no remedy, there’s nothing,” Ricardo told Al Jazeera.
His mum and dad both died from suffocation during the earthquakes while the family was waiting to be rescued. Their building was one of dozens in the state of La Guaira to collapse.
“I fell in the bathroom hugging my mother, and Andres fell near my father. She was telling me she was fine, but I saw that her head was covered with concrete, with a wall on top, and dust,” Ricardo said.
Before the earthquakes, he remembers his mother cooking, singing and spoiling the family dog, who also died in the destruction. He credits his father with teaching him and Andres the value of work and the importance of being strong.
The brothers often look through photographs of their parents on their phones. One shows their family home, overlooking the sea. Another has them by the pool.
“As time goes on, the crying is the same, but the reason is different. Instead of crying so much from sadness, it's more like remembering the good times,” Ricardo said.
Following his parents' death, Ricardo has taken on additional responsibilities beyond school and work.
He is now Andres's legal guardian, and he is hoping the pair can soon find a home of their own through a government housing programme for earthquake victims.
His university has also offered him a full scholarship to finish his studies, to help relieve the financial burden.
Money, however, is still expected to be tight. The average salary for a private-sector worker in Venezuela is not much more than $200 a month.
“Of course, I'm worried about my financial situation,” Ricardo said, explaining the family business has slowed since the earthquakes.
“Sometimes it's hard to cover all the expenses, given everything that's happened, but we find a way. I think that's what Venezuelans do: We’re always finding a way to make things work.”
The cost of recovery
The Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation, a Venezuelan nonprofit, is among the groups helping earthquake amputees. Its founder and namesake, Dos Santos, lost his legs in a car accident in 2019.
He remembers realising the scale of June's tragedy when, at the first hospital he visited, he encountered a ward with 12 children. All of them had either lost limbs or were facing amputation.
“It's very difficult for everyone in general but especially for children, who suddenly lost so much. They lost family members, their homes, their schools, their abilities, and on top of that, they're missing a part of their body,” he told Al Jazeera.
One of his priorities was to show them what their lives could look like after amputation, telling them of his own achievements as an athlete and model.
But alongside the physical and psychological challenges, he knew they would face another obstacle: the cost of prosthetics.
“A prosthesis for a below-knee amputation, which is a transtibial prosthesis, can cost between $3,000 and $5,000," Dos Santos said. "And a prosthesis for an above-knee amputation can cost between $7,000 and $12,000."
The price tag for artificial limbs with electronic components — that react to the body's muscles — can stretch even higher, into the tens of thousands of dollars.
Even before the earthquake, the foundation had a waiting list of hundreds of people who needed a prosthetic limb but could not afford one.
After the seismic disaster, some 200 people were added to its database, Dos Santos said.
He explained that the foundation focuses on functional prostheses rather than the most expensive technology, partly because patients also need to be able to afford adjustments, repairs and replacements.
For many families, the cost is simply beyond reach.
The foundation is now planning to set up a specialist orthotics and prosthetics centre in Venezuela, which it says is essential to provide ongoing support for amputees.
Navigating the healthcare system
Medical professionals also see continued care as fundamental to recovery.
“For patients who suffered serious injuries or amputations, being saved and discharged from hospital is only the beginning. The recovery can be long, and that’s where we encounter many limitations,” Ana Rosario, the president of the Caracas Nurses Association, told Al Jazeera.
She said the earthquake compounded problems in Venezuela’s health system, which was weakened by years of economic crisis.
There are often too few nurses for the number of patients. Hospitals sometimes relied on supplies donated by citizens and organisations to help meet their needs.
“Although healthcare is technically free, patients may still have to pay for medicines, medical supplies, tests, transport and rehabilitation,” Rosario said. “And these are costs that can continue for months.”
For families who cannot afford them, the consequences can be serious.
“We see it every day: Families ask for help through social media, look for donations, go into debt, or simply have to wait,” she said. “When a test, medication or procedure is delayed, recovery can also be delayed, and new complications can arise.”
For survivors like Ricardo, private donations through organisations such as the Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation are helping pay for prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation.
“A few days ago, I saw my leg being made, and that got me really excited,” Ricardo said.
Though Ricardo is his guardian, Andres explained they help care for one another as they each recover from their injuries.
“Just getting out of the wheelchair was already a big step," Andres said of his brother. "He’s getting better every day. Honestly, it makes me so happy that he’ll be able to walk again."
The brothers attend physiotherapy sessions together, with Andres encouraging his older brother as he learns to walk again.
“My brother makes me feel like a world champion,” Ricardo said, laughing as his younger brother breaks into a smile.

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
Niger requested troops to secure shared energy interests in what would be Algeria’s first deployment abroad since 1973.
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy and economic interests shared by both countries.
The decision, announced by Algeria’s presidency on Monday, came after both chambers of parliament approved the deployment in an emergency session on Sunday.
The presidency said authorities in Niger had requested military assistance.
If carried out, it would be Algeria’s first overseas military deployment since 1973, when it sent soldiers to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.
The move marks a departure from Algeria’s longstanding reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
A 2020 constitutional reform allows the president to authorise overseas deployments with the approval of at least two-thirds of legislators in each parliamentary chamber.
Algeria sent fighter jets and support aircraft to Niger in August after what Algerian officials described as an attempt to destabilise its military government.
The presidency said the deployment decision was made under provisions of Algeria’s constitution allowing the military to operate abroad with parliamentary approval.
It has not been announced how many soldiers will be sent or when.
Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after Sunday’s parliamentary vote that the soldiers would protect economic infrastructure, particularly Algerian oil facilities in Niger.
He said Algeria was “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, describing the mission as a response to changing security conditions in the Sahel region.
Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has been working with Niger on the proposed Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline. It would carry natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria for export to European markets.
Niger and neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso have faced years of attacks by armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
All three countries are governed by military leaders who seized power in coups and subsequently formed the Alliance of Sahel States, a regional political and security bloc.
The deployment follows an improvement in relations between Algeria and Niger, which has been led by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a 2023 military coup that Algeria initially condemned.
Tensions deepened in April last year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border, prompting the three alliance members to recall their ambassadors from Algiers.

Quebec’s new separatist government wants a bigger role in EU ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:04 UTC
02:55:04 KST

BRUSSELS — Quebec’s new separatist government is treating this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal as the start of a wider diplomatic push to get the province in the room whenever Ottawa and Brussels strike deals that concern its powers.
The separatist Parti Québécois returned to power this month at the head of a minority government in the province, promising to assert greater control over Quebec’s affairs and eventually hold another referendum on independence.
“Quebec has to be at the table, and Canada understands that very well,” Hélène Drainville, the province’s delegate general to the Benelux and the EU institutions, said in an interview in Brussels.
Advertisement
Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa on Thursday and Friday for a summit the two sides have billed as a step change in relations, driven by Donald Trump’s tariffs and a shared need for new partners. Von der Leyen has even proposed to make Canada an “associate member” of the EU — an offer that goes too far even for some of the bloc’s member countries.
Early drafts of a joint summit declaration include a digital trade deal, a pact to let the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects, and a consignment of Canadian water bombers for Europe’s emergency services.
While Canada is responsible for negotiating the text, much of it lands in areas where its 10 provinces have extensive powers, such as over natural resources, education and health. Quebec is the second-largest province by population after Ontario and has a territory more than twice the size of France — with which three-quarters of its people share French as their mother tongue.
“Canada negotiates the umbrella agreement, and where we come in is when what’s negotiated touches our areas of jurisdiction,” said Drainville, who has been in post for a year. Natural resources are a provincial matter, she added, noting that Quebec has deposits of 22 of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical list.
The province is already talking to the European Investment Bank and DG GROW, the European Commission’s industry department, about the bank’s entry into Canada, she noted.
Asked whether Quebec’s interests line up with those of Ottawa, Drainville said federal and provincial officials have already set up joint working groups to implement the summit’s outcomes. “Right now, all the signals are green,” she said.
Advertisement
New arrival
The cooperation comes at an unusual moment. Quebec’s new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, won power on Oct. 5 while promising a third referendum on sovereignty, though not as long as Trump is in the White House. His cabinet includes the new position of minister for “accession to independence.”
However, support for independence in the province is the lowest it has been for three decades, around 29% in a poll from earlier this year — hardly a popular mandate for the project.
The Parti Québécois has nevertheless pledged to double Quebec’s 34 offices abroad. A party blueprint published last year would raise the number of countries with a Quebec office from 19 to 38 and, if the referendum delivers a “yes” to sovereignty, would turn those delegations into embassies and consulates.
“Quebec is going to start to exist and shine everywhere in the world,” St-Pierre Plamondon said last year, describing the representative network as a prerequisite for independence.
Drainville said the new government, which has been in office for three weeks, has not yet set its line on Europe.
“Our political leaders haven’t taken a position yet, which is normal,” she said. “But if they decide to double [the network], it’s because they believe in this partnership.” As for the associate-member label, she declined to engage: “We’re not really into semantics. That’s Canada.”
Advertisement
What Quebec does want from the EU, she said, is “win-win partnerships,” noting that the province and Ottawa complement each other and are stronger together when it comes to relations with Europe.
It hasn’t always been so amicable.
Quebec’s diplomatic ambitions date back to the 1960s, when the provincial government asserted the right to pursue international relations in areas under its constitutional jurisdiction.
Its international aspirations became politically contentious when French President Charles de Gaulle publicly embraced Quebec’s independence movement in 1967 — ending a speech in Montreal by proclaiming: Vive le Québec libre! (“Long live free Quebec!”)
The Brussels office opened in 1972, and the province now counts 10 posts in Europe, which Drainville called the most of any Canadian province.
Quebec never consented to the constitutional changes Canada enacted in 1982, and its 1995 independence referendum failed by the narrowest of margins (49.4% to 50.6%). A decade ago, Quebec lobbied Europe for a seat at the table in negotiations on the CETA EU-Canada trade deal.

Oil spill off UAE widens, satellite images show, prompting more beach closures
Satellite images show that an oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated 24 October show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is nearing the shores of northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along the coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that it was working to contain oil leaking from an offshore tanker, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill came from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
Images from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that it temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Centre, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that they would close all beaches in the emirate until further notice.
The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.

Cabinet publishes resolution on updating system for granting deferments from conscription
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:53:48 EET
02:53:48 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has published a resolution on updating the organization of deferments from conscription for those liable for military service during the period of mobilization and under martial law.
Specifically, in accordance with Resolution No. 1328 dated October 23, central executive authorities, other state bodies, public administration entities with jurisdiction covering the entire territory of Ukraine, as well as regional and Kyiv city state administrations (or military administrations, where established), are required within ten days of the resolution’s entry into force to ensure the review and harmonization of the criteria used to designate enterprises, institutions, and organizations as "critically important" for the functioning of the economy.
Following this review, an analysis must be conducted to determine whether enterprises still meet these criteria. If a criterion—on the basis of which an enterprise was originally designated as "critically important"—is removed, the decision designating that enterprise as "critically important" must be revoked.
The Government has established that decisions designating enterprises as "critically important"—in effect as of the date this resolution enters into force—shall remain valid for the duration for which they were originally issued, unless they have since been revoked.
It is noted that decisions by the Minister of Defense to increase the quotas for the deferment from military service ("reservation") of liable individual, adopted prior to the entry into force of Resolution No. 1608, shall remain in effect for the entire duration of the enterprise’s designation as "critically important," but no later than December 8, 2026. Decisions by the Ministry of Defense to increase such quotas, adopted after December 8, 2025, shall remain in effect for the duration of the enterprise’s "critically important" status, but not beyond the specific timeframe stipulated in the relevant Ministry decision.
Furthermore, the Cabinet of Ministers has established a Coordination Center for the organization of the deferment from military service for liable individuals during periods of mobilization and wartime.
Enterprises may be designated as "critically important" to the functioning of the economy and the provision of essential services to the population during special periods if they operate within the following sectors: the defense-industrial complex; the fuel and energy complex; housing and utility services; the extractive industry; the manufacturing (processing) industry; the agro-industrial sector (including the assurance of food security); retail trade; construction; transport and logistics; information technology; banking; healthcare; and communications. This also applies to entities engaged in emergency rescue and other urgent operations (emergency rescue services), as well as those operating in sectors approved by the Coordination Center, following a substantiated request from a central executive body or another state authority responsible for developing and/or implementing state policy in the relevant field. It has been established that the number of individuals liable for military service who are eligible for deferment (exemption from mobilization) may exceed 50%, subject to the recommendations and proposals of the Coordination Center.
Substantiated proposals to increase the number of deferments are to be submitted to the Coordination Center by the relevant government authority. Grounds for the Coordination Center to refuse to consider such proposals include, among other things, the documented, systematic violation of legal requirements regarding the organization and maintenance of military registration by the head of a critical institution, specifically, the occurrence of two or more such documented violations within the preceding 12 months, and/or the imposition of administrative liability upon the head for committing such violations.
Furthermore, it is established that for individuals liable for military service who hold positions within the representative offices of donor institutions or with entities implementing international technical assistance projects, the number of those eligible for deferment shall not exceed 50% of the total number of such employees directly engaged in the tasks of a single project, and in any case, shall not exceed 7 individuals.
Pursuant to a decision by the State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers, made in light of the Coordination Center’s recommendations, the number of individuals eligible for deferment may exceed 7, provided it does not exceed 50% of the total number of employees liable for military service.
For critical institutions, defined by the Ministry of Defense as critical within the defense-industrial complex, the fuel and energy sector (including their contractors), or as domestic manufacturers of transformer equipment for the energy sector, the number of employees liable for military service, who are eligible for deferment, may reach up to 95%. This applies to entities engaged in the construction, repair, restoration, manufacturing, and/or supply of equipment, the provision of services, or the execution of other engineering and technical activities aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the unified [energy/power] system.

Ukraine Hits Russian Drone Workshop and Control Post, Targeting Frontline Attack Capability
Ukrainian forces struck Russian military communications facilities, command posts, drone infrastructure, and supply depots across three regions on October 25 and overnight into October 26.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the strikes on its official Facebook page on October 26, identifying targets in the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This disrupts the enemy’s communications and command and control of its troops," the General Staff wrote, describing the strike on a Russian military communications hub near temporarily occupied Melitopol.
According to the military, Ukrainian forces targeted:
- a Russian military communications hub near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian command posts near Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region and Chervonohirka in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- a Russian UAV control post near Vyshneve and a drone workshop near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian military equipment and supply depots near Komisarivka and Katerynivka in the Luhansk region.
The General Staff explained that the strikes on command posts were intended to disrupt Russian battlefield coordination, while targeting drone infrastructure could reduce Moscow's ability to attack Ukrainian military positions and frontline communities.
The attacks on supply depots were also intended to undermine Russian logistics by destroying materiel needed to sustain military operations. The General Staff did not disclose the weapons used, the number of Russian casualties, or detailed damage assessments for the targeted facilities.
"Operations against the enemy’s key military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ends completely," the General Staff stated.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces carried out a similar wave of strikes across the same three regions on October 19 and overnight into October 20.
Targets included a command post near Fedorivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a military repair unit near Kalmiuske in the Donetsk region, and logistics depots near Kripenskyi, Rivnopil, and Lahidne.
Russian troop concentrations were also hit near Horlivka, Selydove, Svatove, and several settlements in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Russian Spy Network Exposed in Alleged Scheme to Stage Fake Pro-Nuclear Rally in Budapest

Russian Spy Network Exposed in Alleged Scheme to Stage Fake Pro-Nuclear Rally in Budapest
Russian intelligence-linked operatives allegedly attempted to stage a paid demonstration outside Hungary’s parliament in Budapest to promote a nuclear power project backed by Russia’s state-owned Rosatom, according to a new investigation based on leaked intelligence documents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The alleged operation was uncovered by InformNapalm and Ukrainian Militant, which published their findings on October 26 after examining correspondence, internal documents, and digital records obtained by the hacker group 256 Cyber Assault Division.
Investigators identified Russian Colonel Timur Sirtlanov and Lieutenant Colonel Irina Parman, both linked to military unit 33949, previously identified in open-source investigations as a structure associated with Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
A leaked email dated September 16 reportedly showed Sirtlanov asking Parman to conduct psychological profiling ahead of a postponed operation in Budapest. The correspondence referred to an “active measure,” a term used by Russian intelligence services for covert influence operations targeting foreign governments and public opinion.
The planned demonstration was intended to generate public support for Paks II, a nuclear power plant expansion project involving Russia’s Rosatom.
Organizers reportedly recruited Russian-speaking residents through Facebook advertisements and coordinated preparations in a private Telegram group called “Friendship of Peoples,” which had 106 members.
Participants were instructed to prepare banners and promotional materials supporting the nuclear project. Organizers also offered additional financial compensation, although investigators found no evidence that payments were actually made.
InformNapalm further traced promotional materials to Parman after discovering that a PDF file contained the author name “Irina Larina,” matching a surname she had previously used online.
The rally was initially scheduled for September 20 outside Hungary’s parliament before being postponed to September 26. However, organizers canceled the demonstration approximately 30 minutes before it was due to begin.
The alleged Russian influence operation emerged amid worsening relations between Moscow and Budapest. On September 8, Hungary expelled ten Russian diplomats over activities incompatible with their diplomatic status.
Meanwhile, the Paks II project has faced increasing scrutiny. Hungarian authorities launched an investigation into financial transactions associated with the project in August, following a European Union court ruling in 2025 overturning the European Commission’s approval of state aid for its construction.
Earlier, in May 2026, Hungary expelled a Russian diplomat identified as an undercover officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. According to VSquare, the diplomat had allegedly spent years cultivating contacts within Hungarian institutions and gathering intelligence on government officials and the Paks II nuclear power project.

Kremlin Spokesperson Says Oleshky Ceasefire Could Set Precedent for Other Humanitarian Pauses

Kremlin Spokesperson Says Oleshky Ceasefire Could Set Precedent for Other Humanitarian Pauses
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said a ceasefire in occupied Oleshky could set a precedent for similar humanitarian pauses in other areas where civilians need assistance, Interfax reported on October 26.
Asked whether the Oleshky arrangement could serve as a model elsewhere, Peskov indicated that Moscow considered such agreements possible when they were intended for humanitarian purposes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has temporarily occupied Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region since 2022, leaving around 2,000 civilians trapped under a worsening humanitarian blockade. Russian forces have mined roads, restricted movement, blocked regular food and aid deliveries, and targeted evacuation routes with drones, leaving residents facing severe shortages of food, water, medicine, electricity, and heating.
UNITED24 Media reported that some residents have survived on almost nothing, while Russian forces have also seized humanitarian food delivered by Ukrainian drones.
“For humanitarian purposes, absolutely, especially when we are talking about the direct, very positive coordinating involvement in this process of the American side, American negotiators, and US First Lady Melania Trump,” Peskov stated.
“We highly appreciate these efforts, and of course this can become a precedent,” he added.
Peskov also expressed hope that Ukraine would fulfill what he described as agreements reached with the direct involvement of US negotiators acting on behalf of Melania Trump.
The ceasefire in Oleshky was announced on October 23 following US-mediated talks involving Melania Trump. UNITED24 Media reported that the arrangement was intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, while Russian forces were expected to suspend operations in the area and Ukraine prepared humanitarian corridors.

You’ll Never Guess What Ukraine Uses to Keep Drones Flying at −20°C

You’ll Never Guess What Ukraine Uses to Keep Drones Flying at −20°C
Ukraine’s defense industry builds drones capable of reaching deep inside Russia and cruise missiles carrying massive warheads—but when temperatures plunge to −20°C (−4°F), one surprisingly effective engineering solution is considerably less sophisticated: salo .
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point on October 26 revealed that extreme cold can cause frost to form on drone cameras and cables while batteries discharge significantly faster, threatening the reliability of unmanned systems operating through the winter.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One workaround is a simple layer of salo used to help shield vulnerable components from freezing conditions.
It is an unusually low-tech solution from a company responsible for some of Ukraine’s most advanced long-range weapons.
Fire Point manufactures the FP-1 deep-strike UAV and FP-2 strike drone, as well as the FP-5 Flamingo ground-launched cruise missile. The company is also developing the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles, with the latter designed for strikes at ranges of up to 850 kilometers.
Its FP-1 and FP-2 drones are already used extensively for strikes deep inside Russia, while the Flamingo has become another component of Ukraine’s expanding domestic long-range arsenal.
Yet battlefield engineering is not always about finding the most technologically sophisticated answer.
At around −20°C, preventing a camera, cable, or other exposed component from freezing can matter just as much as advanced guidance software or propulsion.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine and Norway were accelerating development of the Fire Point FP-5.x FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.

Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Iran have agreed to continue talks aimed at strengthening cooperation on regional issues, including peace and security, according to a joint statement issued after a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran.
Monday’s discussions covered regional security, Israel’s activities across the region, and the latest developments in Palestine and Lebanon, reflecting the four countries’ focus on regional stability and cooperation.
The meeting brought together senior security and military officials from the four countries, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also in attendance.
Türkiye was represented by National Intelligence Organization Director Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi Arabia by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Pakistan by Chief of Army Staff Asim Munir.
Iran’s delegation was hosted by Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.
Pezeshkian calls for unity among Muslim countries
Speaking at the meeting, Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to take concrete steps to deepen regional cooperation, address differences and strengthen ties among Muslim-majority countries, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran, with firm conviction and serious determination, is ready to take steps toward deepening regional cooperation, resolving differences and drawing on the shared capabilities of Islamic countries,” Pezeshkian said.
He added that Tehran supported any understanding that would promote regional unity, cohesion, security and development.
Tehran backs shared approach to regional challenges
Pezeshkian said Muslim countries could use their collective capabilities to present the world with a model based on justice and development.
The quadrilateral meeting comes as regional issues, including the situation in Palestine and Lebanon and wider security concerns, remain central to diplomatic engagement among countries in the region.
The four countries’ agreement to continue discussions signals a commitment to maintaining dialogue on shared challenges, although the joint statement did not specify a timetable or format for future meetings.

What Israel's election could mean for the West Bank's future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:51:28 UTC
02:51:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Beyond the ballot: The West Bank's future after Israel's election
Ramallah - Driving in the occupied West Bank, motorists are confronted with a barrage of campaign billboards for the Israeli elections.
The messages are geared towards Israeli settlers in the territory, not the Palestinians barred from voting.
Many of the posters express support for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party, as he draws his core voter base from settlers.
But there are also numerous posters for Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud party, including an ominous ad along the road to Jerusalem featuring Zohran Mamdani and Ayatollah Khomeini, warning against the power of Palestinian allies.
Against this radicalised backdrop, Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday in an election that many hope will spell the end of Netanyahu’s 19-year non-consecutive rule as prime minister.
The election comes in the wake of growing domestic resentment against Netanyahu over reports of his advanced knowledge of the 7 October attacks.
Netanyahu’s Likud is seemingly facing an uphill battle against a bloc of four Jewish opposition parties that have joined forces to defeat him: the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beitenu party, and the Together alliance.
After the bloc’s establishment, the parties announced their goal was to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The elections are projected to be a near deadlock with no bloc winning an absolute majority. That outcome would trigger a period of negotiations and coalition building, where different parties must agree to come together to form a government.
But as settler violence reaches record levels in the West Bank, many Palestinians are left wondering: will any electoral outcome change the facts on the ground?
West Bank violence surges ahead of election
Approximately 750,000 Israelis live in settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem today, illegal under international law.
The settlers comprise a disproportionately powerful bloc in Israeli politics, despite accounting for around 7-8% of the total Israeli population.
Under Netanyahu’s current administration, which has brought settlers from the far-right fringes into a governing coalition, the settlers’ political influence has coincided with a rapid acceleration of settlement expansion.
But it’s unlikely that another government would slow the pace of settlement building.
“In order to ameliorate pressure from the settler lobby, the left often are tempted to expand settlements even more than the right,” Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, a political commentator and former Israeli diplomat, tells The New Arab.
“It [the opposition winning] might even lead to an increase in settlement construction in order to pay them off for concessions.”
As settlements expand, so does the pressure on Palestinians living nearby. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded an average of six settler attacks per day this year thus far.
Those numbers were released before the autumnal olive harvest commenced, when violence dramatically escalates as settlers launch coordinated attacks against Palestinian farmers in their olive groves.
And after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli checkpoint on 23 October, Ben-Gvir suggested that Palestinians should be barred from driving on the roads in the West Bank - or the land of Judea and Samaria, as he refers to it.
The Israeli army subsequently launched a collective punishment operation and began home demolitions across the neighbourhood where the shooters hailed from, displacing 400 families thus far.
Netanyahu has promised the biggest military occupation in the West Bank since 1967, though many experts say he may be bluffing to bolster support for Likud ahead of the elections.
The election will now take place against a backdrop of expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement, fuelling fears that tensions across the West Bank are near boiling point.
“There are a lot of people in the Israeli security forces who want Palestinians to have a better quality of life, just so that the West Bank doesn't explode into another Intifada,” says Ben-Ephraim.
Projected electoral outcomes
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar!, is seen as the leading centrist alternative for Prime Minister.
Eisenkot has promised to rein in settler violence while firmly opposing a two-state solution. Once the Israeli army Chief of Staff, Eisenkot was the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2006, which advocates "disproportionate force” against Israel’s perceived enemies.
“None of the Israeli governments that would come is going to give a Palestinian state to the Palestinians, but change may come, depending on how you define change,” Muhanned Qafesha, a Palestinian journalist from Hebron, tells The New Arab.
An Eisenkot government could mean greater restrictions on settler violence and a slight change in settlement policy, without fundamentally interfering with the settler project.
Alternatively, if Netanyahu secures another term or temporarily heads a caretaker government if a stalemate arises, the settlers in his administration may feel their time is limited and accelerate their existing plans for the annexation of the West Bank.
As it stands, neither major political bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
While the opposition bloc has sworn not to form a coalition with either of the Palestinian parties on the ballot - the left-leaning Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) - that pledge may not hold, as they could be a potential lifeline to forming a government.
“The two Arab parties can maybe win like 15 seats or something, and this will make a huge difference because if they can make a coalition with the opposition, they can kick out Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir,” Qafesha tells The New Arab.
“I do believe that the opposition in Israel is saying they won’t form a coalition with the Arabs because they want to get as many votes from the Jewish community as possible. But if they need the Arab parties to form a coalition to kick out Netanyahu, they might do it,” he adds.
But any coalition will also depend on parties that oppose Palestinian statehood, and thus a fundamental shift in Israel’s approach to the occupation is virtually impossible.
Even if Eisenkot eventually forms a government, his fragile coalition across the ideological spectrum would struggle to agree on significant changes towards settlement policy in the West Bank.
Will the opposition improve life in the West Bank?
The 3.4 million Palestinians living in the West Bank under military occupation cannot vote in Israeli elections, but Palestinian citizens of Israel can.
Arab voters have long boycotted Israeli elections, but there has been a recent push for their participation - with a record turnout for the group anticipated.
The vast majority of Palestinians in the West Bank want Palestinian citizens of Israel to vote in the elections to improve their daily lives, explains Qafesha, who himself cannot vote.
He believes an administration without settlers at the helm may alleviate some of the daily struggles in the West Bank.
“We live in hell. We just want to breathe,” Qafesha says.
But if Netanyahu finally goes down, some Palestinians believe Western governments may attempt to rehabilitate Israel’s image under a new administration - and lift the recent round of European sanctions against settlements that were years in the making.
“The upcoming election is between fascists and ultra-fascists. If Netanyahu loses the chance to lead the next government, his loss can be used to alleviate the pressure that is just starting to build from the international community,” Mazin Qumsiyeh, Director of Palestine’s Natural History Museum in Bethlehem, tells The New Arab.
Yet Qafesha remains adamant that the reality on the ground is more important than the views of the international community, which could promote a new government as an example of Israel’s return to democracy.
“Over the past three years, Israel has killed more than 100,000 Palestinians in Gaza. What has the world done for us? Has anything changed in our life? I don't want the view of the world to change at the expense of the blood of Palestinian children, whether it's in Gaza, West Bank, or Jerusalem,” says Qafesha.
An opposition government less reliant on far-right parties could potentially curb some of the policies driving unchecked violence and forced displacement, ameliorating a few of the numerous obstacles to a dignified life under occupation. But any improvement would likely be limited in scope.
“If the opposition wins, the intensity of the ethnic cleansing will probably somewhat lessen, but it's only temporary,” concludes Ben-Ephraim.
“I think that the Israeli public opinion has turned so far in favour of genocide and ethnic cleansing that it will just be a respite at best.”
Kate McMahon is a freelance journalist and foreign correspondent focused on the Middle East and South Asia. She reports on environmental change, human rights, and geopolitical conflicts

A jury at Winchester crown court will this week begin hearing the trial of four other men charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young.
The alleged offences carried out by the four – Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48, and Mohammed Hassan, 38 – are said to have taken place between the summer of 2016 and the winter of 2023.

He told them it would involve evidence and videos involving “graphic and sexually explicit imagery” that some people could find upsetting. “It’s not going to be an easy case to be a juror in,” the judge said.
Saini asked the panel to reflect overnight if they had any concerns and to let him know on Tuesday morning.

Sarah Jones KC is scheduled to open the case on Tuesday.

Polish city of Przemyśl suspends cooperation with Lviv over Year of UPA decision
Councillors in the Polish city of Przemyśl agreed on Monday 26 October to suspend cooperation with Lviv following a recent decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun on Facebook, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Twenty-one councillors voted in favour of the resolution to suspend the partnership with Lviv. No one voted against or abstained.
According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Przemyśl councillors said the decision adopted by the Lviv Oblast Council on 20 October "insulted" the memory of Polish victims of crimes committed by the UPA and ran counter to efforts to build relations based on historical truth and mutual respect.
The resolution requires Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun to take legal steps to terminate the 1995 cooperation agreement.
However, it also provides for cooperation between the cities to resume if the Lviv Oblast Council definitively repeals or formally withdraws the resolution and Lviv's city authorities clearly distance themselves from initiatives that "glorify structures responsible for crimes against civilians".
The mayor must inform Lviv's city authorities of this position and report to Przemyśl councillors on the measures taken and the date on which the agreement will cease to be in force.
"After a lengthy discussion on the matter, all councillors unanimously decided that we would suspend all joint activities until Lviv's authorities clearly state their position on the promotion of ideologies directed against Poland and the Polish people. I would like to thank the councillors for taking this position and demonstrating that we will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions," Bakun wrote.
Background:
- On 20 October, the Lviv Oblast Council voted to declare 2027 the "year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and Oleh Olzhych". The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk later said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear that he would not support further steps by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.
- The city council of Wrocław, Poland, unanimously condemned the decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army.
- Meanwhile, Kraków's new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has proposed suspending the city's partnership with Lviv in response to the Lviv Oblast Council's decision to declare 2027 the year of the UPA.

Algeria's Kaylia Nemour wins double gold at gymnastics worlds
Algerian gymnast Kaylia Nemour won gold on the balance beam on Sunday at the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships, a day after claiming another gold medal on the uneven bars.
The two gold medals came after a difficult start for the 19-year-old, whose poor vault performance on Friday dashed her hopes of an all-around medal in Rotterdam.
"I'm extremely happy, but I'm completely in shock. In shock at this gold medal on beam," Nemour was quoted by International Gymnast as saying. "My goal was to do a nice routine, and that's what I did, so I was already proud of myself. And with the score, I was hoping it would be enough for a medal. And now, having the gold medal is unimaginable. I think I'll need a lot of time to digest it. Maybe a month, knowing me."
Nemour was first to compete in the uneven bars final, scoring 14.566 before seven other gymnasts took their turns. China's Zhang Qingyang finished second with the same score, with Nemour taking gold on the execution-score tiebreak.
"I knew there was the Chinese gymnast, last year's world champion, who is extremely strong, with a big start value and exceptional cleanliness," she said. "And then we had the same score, so I think it was the execution score that made the difference, and it's exceptional."
Nemour's success at the championships was celebrated by Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on social media on Sunday.

Ukraine will appeal the decision by the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow and will boycott the competition if it takes place in Russia. Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi said this in a comment to UNN.
Details
"Ukraine will use all legal, political and diplomatic instruments to ensure that the decision by the International Weightlifting Federation to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow is reviewed. Our principled position is to be present on the international stage, win, raise the Ukrainian flag and not vacate the arena for Russian propaganda. We remind you

This is the first case since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in which an international federation governing an Olympic sport has entrusted Russia with hosting a World Championship of this level.
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the IWF and the IOC demanding a review of the decision to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow. Matvii Bidnyi called on partners to prevent the competition from taking place in Russia.

Tax service advises gas producers to report export volumes of gas injected into storage for royalty administration
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:47:56 EET
02:47:56 KST

The State Tax Service (STS) recommends that gas-producing companies notify it in writing of the volumes of domestically produced gas exported after being injected into underground gas storage facilities (UGS).
According to a statement on the agency's Telegram channel, the information should be submitted together with monthly acts documenting the movement of natural gas in storage facilities. This will allow tax authorities to administer subsoil-use royalty payments without making additional requests to taxpayers.
The STS recalled that certain provisions of Ukraine's Tax Code exempt companies from paying royalties on extracted gas injected into UGS facilities until it is sold. The obligation to pay royalties resumes in the reporting period in which the gas is sold, with the amount due calculated based on the actual volume sold.
The procedure for exporting domestically produced gas was approved by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1251 of October 7, 2026.

Israel's Hebron raid displaces nearly 4,000 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:47:51 UTC
02:47:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's Hebron raid displaces nearly 4,000 Palestinians as homes turned into military outposts
Israeli forces have forced nearly 4,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron since Friday, leaving hundreds of families displaced as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly rejected military advice to end the operation in the southern occupied West Bank.
The number of displaced Palestinians reached around 3,971 on Monday, according to figures reported by Palestinian news agency WAFA. This includes approximately 200 children under the age of two, at least 258 elderly people and 137 pregnant women.
Riyad Khamis, spokesperson for Hebron’s Follow-up, Support and Relief Committee, said 619 families had been affected, including 266 unable to find safe accommodation.
More than 80 Palestinians have been arrested, while hundreds of others have been detained and interrogated, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club. Israeli troops have also raided and ransacked hundreds of homes, leaving residents unsure when they will be allowed to return.
Hebron's Governor Khaled Dudin reported that Israeli authorities established 128 gates and 120 checkpoints across the southern governorate, saying that it fragments the area and severly restricts movement as well as access to healthcare and basic services.
The Israeli operation followed a shooting attack on Friday in which two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron. Israeli forces killed both gunmen.
Netanyahu subsequently ordered the evacuation of residents from the neighbourhood where the attackers lived ahead of house-to-house searches. The ensuing assault has extended to Palestinian homes, businesses and industrial facilities.
In a statement issued on Monday, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) warned that these actions "raise grave concerns about ethnic cleansing and collective punishment".
"Palestinians in Hebron are being driven from their homes and cut off from healthcare and basic supplies," Aseel Baidoun, MAP's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications, said. "This is collective punishment. People are being punished simply for being Palestinians."
A home turned into a military outpost
For Ramadan Faisal al-Hashlamoun, a 47-year-old Palestinian displaced with his family, the uncertainty centres on a house he says Israeli soldiers have turned into a military outpost.
Speaking to The New Arab, Hashlamoun said troops entered his home and took it over because it overlooks the main road. He has been unable to return since.
His household numbers 10, including children, the youngest of whom is aged 12. The family has been split apart since residents were ordered to leave the entire area, he said.
"You can only feel at ease in your own home," he told The New Arab.
Hashlamoun said neighbours had heard the sound of objects being smashed inside his house, leaving him deeply worried about the condition of his belongings, including money, gold and other personal possessions. Unable to enter, he has no way of checking what has happened to them.
He also said Israeli forces had marked four X signs on the exterior walls of the house – a mark that has since been circulating in images across social media on multiple houses whose inhabitants had been forcibly displaced.
Israeli occupation forces mark several Palestinian homes with "X" signs in the Ein Deir Bahha neighborhood of Hebron, south of the occupied West Bank, after forcibly displacing their owners. https://t.co/3lNmvZ4yO7
— Quds News Network (@QudsNen) October 24, 2026
At the time of the interview, his family had received no aid or essential supplies, although Hebron Municipality had contacted them. He told The New Arab that his immediate concerns were the separation of his family and the uncertain fate of their home.
Local relief officials said on Monday that a first batch of aid and basic supplies was being distributed to displaced and affected families. Hundreds of other residents remained trapped inside homes in neighbouring areas, according to WAFA.
Israeli forces have sealed off the neighbourhoods of Deir Baha and al-Jilda, where much of the displacement has taken place, while imposing closures at entrances to Hebron and surrounding towns and refugee camps. The restrictions have disrupted movement and access to homes, businesses and services.
A staff member at a MAP local partner in Hebron described the sudden incursion, saying it was "unexpected to see this kind of mass forced displacement" where residents including persons with disabilities, pregnant women, and children "left their homes carrying whatever they could. A lot of those who were displaced are elderly people with chronic illnesses, meaning there is a need for medicines as well."
Netanyahu reportedly rejected an end to the operation
The sudden displacement of thousands of residents comes as Israeli media reported that Netanyahu had rejected Israeli Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir's recommendation to end the operation, despite being told its objectives had been 'achieved' and there was no justification for continuing to prevent residents from returning home.
Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported on Monday that Zamir had recommended ending the operation, telling Netanyahu during a situational assessment on Sunday that its objectives had been met.
According to Kan’s reporting, Zamir said there was no operational justification for continuing the raid and no legal justification for keeping displaced Palestinians from their homes.
Netanyahu nevertheless insisted that the operation continue despite the military having wanted to announce as early as Saturday night that the operation was winding down.
The reported disagreement emerged a day before Israel’s general election, as displaced Palestinian families remained unable to return.
“Across the West Bank, we are living in high uncertainty, especially with Israeli elections this week; there is no safe place due to the situation deteriorating day by day," MAP's staff member said.
"We are wondering if this will last days, weeks, or months. People are worried about forced displacement and it's becoming a real fear, especially when looking at what happened in Jenin and Tulkarem in the past couple of years. We are losing trust in the international community."

Analysis-Now home, Venezuela opposition leader Machado walks tightrope with supporters, Trump
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:11 CET
02:47:11 KST

By Mayela Armas and Julia Symmes Cobb
CARACAS/BOGOTA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned on Sunday after nearly a year away, will walk a tightrope as she seeks the elections her supporters want without running afoul of a US-backed negotiation process between the interim government and other opposition groups.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Washington has said she has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
The talks, which have continued this month, would remake the electoral council and top court ahead of eventual elections. Both bodies are staffed by ruling party loyalists and backed ousted President Nicolas Maduro in a disputed 2024 presidential election, despite tallies published by Machado’s movement that showed her candidate had won. The US military captured Maduro in January.
Machado supporters, tens of thousands of whom swarmed her caravan between Barquisimeto and Caracas on Sunday, waving flags, chanting her name and festooning her with rosaries, are eager for elections and call her the next president. She has said a presidential vote should happen in 2027.
Machado’s team did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked whether Machado would participate in the negotiations, Rodriguez said she hopes the dialogue will lead those who called for sanctions against the country — a common ruling party critique leveled at Machado — to feel remorse. Rodriguez added that the talks offer a chance for all voices to be heard.
“I hope both the dialogue and the program for democratic coexistence and peace can provide a space where all voices can be heard, where voices seeking the good of the country can be heard,” the acting president said during a visit to a military hospital in Caracas, where she urged politicians to concentrate on serious issues and not put on a “show.”
Though Machado cultivated Trump as an ally for years, he said last month it was too soon to consider democratic elections. On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of her return plans, though a person briefed on her movements disputed that.
RISK OF SHORT CIRCUIT WITH WASHINGTON
Machado’s eagerness for a vote could “short-circuit” the relationship with the US and its three-phase stabilization, recovery and transition plan for Venezuela, said Ricardo Rios, head of Poder y Estrategia, a political risk consultancy.
“The idea (at the negotiations) is to hold a regional election before a presidential election. She will probably push for electoral guarantees and for a presidential election to be held as soon as possible,” Rios said.
But much remains to be defined before voters cast ballots.
“What guarantees does the ruling sector have to leave power (if it is defeated)?” Rios asked. “That still needs to be defined in order to make this viable, because otherwise, no matter how popular she is, it complicates matters.”
US AND EU URGE DIALOGUE
Machado’s safe return was a direct outcome of the negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a longtime champion of Machado, said on Sunday, adding he expects all political actors to support the talks.
Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held, he told reporters on Monday. He did not provide an estimated date for elections.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” Rubio said. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
The EU echoed that sentiment, saying on Monday authorities and all political actors should advance “an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue towards free and fair elections.”
The negotiations will lead to a top court being in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
“The reception (Machado) got yesterday will only reinforce the tendency to demand instant results,” said Phil Gunson, senior analyst for the Andes region at the International Crisis Group think tank. “Not only might that provoke a reaction from government hardliners, but it could — if successful — produce a political rupture instead of a peaceful transition, with inadequate post-electoral guarantees and a potentially ungovernable country.”
The opposition included in the talks, led by Dinorah Figuera, a lawmaker elected in 2015 to the last Venezuelan legislative body recognized by the US, said Machado’s return was a significant step in the US plan.
“Her role is also tied to how she interprets the signals from the United States, which has called for reconstruction and reconciliation. She has to be an ally in the negotiations,” said Oswaldo Ramirez, managing director of ORC Consultores.
“Rubio sent a clear message,” he added. “I don’t see her trying to torpedo the negotiations. She can’t stray outside the lines.”
(Reporting by Mayela Armas in Caracas and Julia Symmes Cobb in Bogota; additional reporting by Deisy Buitrago in Caracas and Simon Lewis in WashingtonEditing by Rod Nickel and Nick Zieminski)

E5 Defence Ministers' Statement: 26 October 2026
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:44:22 GMT
02:44:22 KST

E5 Defence Ministers' Statement: 26 October 2026
E5 Defence Ministers' Statement.
Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability. Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine, on the one hand, and its continued violations of Allied airspace, acts of sabotage and growing use of multi-domain hybrid attacks, on the other, do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory, through a 360-degree approach that takes into account threats from all strategic directions.
We, the Defence Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom (the Group of Five/E5), share a deep conviction: Europe must assume greater responsibility for its own security. We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition. The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO.
This greater responsibility must begin with the empowerment of European Allies within NATO.
With the aim of building a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO, we are already taking concrete measures to implement the commitments taken in The Hague, emphasized in Ankara, and to meet agreed capability targets.
We will assume greater political and military leadership within the Alliance, modernising forces and capabilities, including through closer defence-industrial cooperation based on common and standardised requirements,. We reaffirm our commitment to further strengthening NATO’s collective defence in order to rapidly adapt to current and future challenges, including with a more proactive deterrence and defence posture.
We will bolster our contributions to enhance readiness, resilience and our ability to respond to evolving threats across all domains, by promoting the development of the necessary capabilities, in line with NATO-agreed priorities and targets, including through an appropriate, tailored and effective mix of complementary capabilities to meet the full range of operational requirements.
NATO remains the cornerstone of our collective security. The Group of Five/E5 will support greater European ability to act through different frameworks and initiatives, including the European Union, complementing the sovereign responsibilities of States and intergovernmental cooperation.
We emphasise the importance of a nation-led, coordinated approach, aligned with NATO. We commend the European Union’s efforts to support nations in meeting NATO’s defence capability requirements and in strengthening European defence readiness. The EU’s regulatory and financial capacity is a valuable tool in support of our nations’ efforts and ambition. EU defence initiatives should complement NATO, avoid duplication and remain open, under certain conditions, to meaningful cooperation with non-EU NATO Allies.
We will maintain our unwavering commitment to supporting Ukraine in its fight back against Russian aggression. Ukraine’s ability to defend itself now and in the future is critically important to Euro-Atlantic collective security.
We stress the need to keep supporting Ukraine by all available means — politically, militarily and financially.
We reaffirm our determination to continue tackling the activities of Russia’s shadow fleet, in accordance with international law and in coordination with relevant partners.
We stand united with Ukraine in its determination to secure a lasting peace, underpinned by robust security guarantees. The Coalition of the Willing will contribute to robust and credible security guarantees once a cease-fire or a peace agreement is in place.

Likud files police complaint against Eisenkot campaign manager over Polymarket post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:40:00 UTC
02:40:00 KST

Likud filed a police complaint on Monday against Ronen Manelis, campaign manager for Gadi Eisenkot, accusing him of breaking Israel’s election campaigning law by sharing a post on X that gave Eisenkot strong odds of becoming prime minister after the upcoming election. Attorney Ilan Bombach filed the complaint on Likud’s behalf.
At the center of the complaint is a Polymarket post that Manelis reshared on his X account on Sunday. The post said that former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, is expected to become Israel’s next prime minister after Tuesday’s election, replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It gave Eisenkot a 52% chance of winning the post, compared with 28% for Netanyahu, and included a photo of Eisenkot in IDF uniform.
The complaint included a screenshot of Manelis’s repost, showing the original Polymarket post, the figures and a chart comparing Eisenkot’s and Netanyahu’s chances.
Likud claims Manelis shared post without clarifying context
Likud argues that the figures do not come from a public opinion poll conducted using accepted statistical methods, but from a platform that forecasts the outcomes of future events. Even so, the complaint claims, Manelis shared them without making clear that they were not a statistical survey and could not be used to draw conclusions about voting patterns or public opinion.
The figures reflect the probability of a political outcome, not a candidate’s level of support among voters. Eisenkot’s 52% chance of becoming prime minister does not mean that 52% of the public plans to vote for him.
In his letter to the police, Bombach stressed that, in Likud’s view, this is not merely a technical violation, but an attempt to influence voters through illegal means.
Post was shared 'to influence the voting public," complaint claims
The complaint claims the offense was committed “in order to influence the voting public, under aggravating circumstances and through prohibited means.” Likud views it as especially serious that the post was shared by Manelis, who runs the campaign of one of the candidates. “There is a significant and pressing public interest in investigating and bringing the offender to justice,” the complaint said, calling on police to investigate the post and pursue charges to the full extent of the law.
However, the claim that Polymarket’s figures count as an election poll under the law is Likud’s own legal interpretation, not a ruling by any authority. The question is a substantive one, since the platform presents the probability of future outcomes rather than the results of an opinion poll. Whether the law’s rules on publishing election polls apply to this kind of data may prove central to how the complaint is handled.
