Breadcrumb
'Destruction of truth': UN report finds Israel's mediacide in Gaza seeks to bury evidence of genocide
Israel is attempting to "systematically eliminate" journalists in occupied Palestine in a bid to cover up evidence of genocide and war crimes, according to a UN report.
The paper, authored by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, says that "destruction of truth" has been integral to the assault on Gaza, and describes Israel's attempts to control information as "mediacide".
Israeli forces have killed hundreds of journalists in the occupied territories since October 2023 while most of Gaza's infrastructure lies in ruins.
Albanese will present her findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday.
The report identifies three ways in which Israel and its supporters attempt to destroy or hide evidence of crimes committed in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
These include the systematic targeting of journalists and communications infrastructure, and the Israeli government's attempts to censor and manipulate information.
It also highlights the complicity of Western news organisations and technology platforms, which it accuses of promoting Israeli narratives and suppressing Palestinian voices.
"These practices have not merely accompanied genocide but have facilitated its commission and obstructed accountability," the report reads.
The UN documented the killing of almost 300 Palestinian journalists between October 2023 and February this year. Hundreds of others have been wounded or unlawfully detained by Israeli authorities.
Some were killed in indiscriminate attacks while at least 70 are known to have been deliberately targeted.
Israel has replicated its assault on Palestinian journalists in its other conflicts in Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, where dozens of other media workers have been killed in airstrikes.
The report says that the Israeli military has wiped out more than 80% of Gaza's communications infrastructure and damaged another 12%. By October 2025, Israeli forces had destroyed 125 media offices and institutions, including news agency headquarters, broadcast towers and radio stations, it says.
Blackouts caused by the damage have prevented local journalists from broadcasting events and people outside the strip from verifying information.
The destruction has gone hand-in-hand with the Israeli government's media restrictions, which have prevented foreign journalists reporting from Gaza and censored thousands of articles related to the war.
"In the ongoing genocide, the systematic elimination of media witnesses and the destruction of the means of documentation are probative of genocidal intent," the report says.
"They reveal an effort not only to destroy a protected group, but also to destroy the conditions in which that destruction can be seen, documented, remembered and ultimately adjudicated," it continues.

Milan event commemorates child victims of Gorla, Minab and Gaza
TEHRAN- Italian artists and activists have commemorated children killed in wars in the country’s Gorla district, Iran’s Minab and the Gaza Strip, marking the 82nd anniversary of the bombing of an elementary school in Milan during World War II.
The commemorations took place on October 20, the anniversary of the 1944 Gorla massacre, which claimed the lives of 184 children and 19 school staff members when an Allied air raid struck the Francesco Crispi elementary school in northern Milan.
This year’s anniversary carries additional significance following the Italian parliament’s approval of a law establishing October 20 as a national day of remembrance for the child victims of the Gorla massacre and children killed in all wars. The legislation, Law No. 85 of May 6, 2026, aims to preserve the memory of the victims and promote a culture of peace.
During the recent commemorations, participants drew parallels between the Gorla tragedy and the deaths of children in the Israeli-American attack on a school in Minab, southern Iran, as well as the killing of children in Gaza.
Media activist Zio Filippo took part in the activities, accompanying his public outreach with music videos as he moved from Piazza della Repubblica toward Piazza Venezia, according to reports on the event.
Italian artists have also released a song titled “Gorla, Minab, Gaza” to honor children killed in armed conflicts and highlight the shared tragedy of civilian victims across different historical and geographical contexts.
The song links the memory of the children killed in Milan during World War II with that of children who have lost their lives in more recent conflicts, including those in Iran and Gaza.
The Gorla massacre occurred on October 20, 1944, when American aircraft taking part in an Allied bombing operation over Milan targeted industrial facilities in the surrounding area. A bomb struck the Francesco Crispi elementary school, killing 184 children and 19 members of the school staff.
The tragedy became one of the most painful episodes in Milan’s wartime history and a lasting symbol of the devastating impact of aerial bombardment on civilians.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:24:43 UTC
02:24:43 KST

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
TEHRAN – The Persian translation of the book “Freshwater: A Comedy” written by Virginia Woolf has been released in bookstores across Iran.
Yousef Najafi Jablou is the translator of the book that has been brought out by Tagh Publication, ISNA reported.
“Freshwater: A comedy” is a play written and produced by Virginia Woolf in 1935, and the only play she wrote. Although only performed once in her lifetime, it has been translated into many languages and produced in many countries since. Alfred Lord Tennyson appears as a character in this play.
Virginia Woolf researched the life of her great-aunt, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, publishing her findings in an essay titled “Pattledom” (1925), and later in her introduction to her 1926 edition of Cameron's photographs.
The play is named after Freshwater, Isle of Wight, where Julia Margaret Cameron lived in a somewhat bohemian atmosphere at her home, Dimbola Lodge, surrounded by a number of artists and literary figures, including George Frederick Watts and Tennyson in the 1860s.
Tennyson's nearby home, Farringdon, was another artistic center. The plot revolves around the attempts by the young actress Ellen Terry to escape from her marriage to the much older Watts, partly family history, partly mocking the conventions of the Victorian times that the Bloomsbury group had fought to escape.
The Camerons are set to embark for India, while both Mrs. Cameron and Watts are intent on portraying Ellen in their respective media. Ellen, on the other hand, views a young naval lieutenant as her escape, with an offer to escape to Bloomsbury. This collapses a number of historic events into a single afternoon.
Although a slight work not intended for publication, and easily dismissed as frivolous, it has been given a larger meaning when placed in the broader context of Woolf's work and views. For beneath the comedic elements, there is an exploration of both generational change and artistic freedom. Both Cameron and Woolf fought against the class and gender dynamics of Victorianism, and the play shows links to both “To the Lighthouse” and “A Room of One's Own” that would follow.
Virginia Woolf (1882 – 1941) was an English writer and one of the most influential 20th-century modernist authors. She helped to pioneer the use of stream of consciousness narration as a literary device.
Woolf began publishing professionally in 1904 and rose to prominence during the interwar period with novels including “Mrs. Dalloway” (1925), “To the Lighthouse” (1927), and “Orlando” (1928). She also wrote the influential feminist essay “A Room of One's Own” (1929), followed by “Three Guineas” (1938), which explores the roots of fascism in society. Her work became central to 1970s feminist criticism and remains influential worldwide, having been translated into more than 50 languages.

Baran Auction to showcase Iranian calligraphy, miniatures

Baran Auction to showcase Iranian calligraphy, miniatures
TEHRAN – The fifth edition of Baran Auction, specializing in Iranian and Islamic art, will be held in Tehran on Friday, October 30, featuring works of traditional calligraphy and Persian miniature painting, including “The Third Feather” by the late Iranian master Mahmoud Farshchian.
The event will take place at 5 p.m. at the Raizan International Conference Center, IRNA reported on Monday.
A public exhibition of the selected works will be held at the same venue on October 28 and 29, offering art enthusiasts, researchers and collectors an opportunity to view the pieces before the sale, the report added.
The upcoming edition continues Baran Auction's focus on preserving and promoting Iran's calligraphic heritage while expanding its presentation of traditional visual arts. Alongside calligraphic works, this year's selection includes pieces from the country's miniature painting tradition, highlighting the historical connections between the two art forms.
Among the featured works is “The Third Feather” by Farshchian, whose paintings frequently draw on Persian literary, spiritual and mythological themes. According to the organizers, the work evokes the mysterious feather of the Simorgh, the legendary bird associated with wisdom and spiritual discovery in Persian literature. They describe it as a symbol of awareness, hope and renewal, reflecting the enduring power of Iranian cultural thought.
Calligraphy remains central to Baran Auction's identity. Previous editions have featured works associated with major figures in the history of Iranian calligraphy, including Mir Emad Hassani, Darvish Abdolmajid Taleqani and Mirza Gholamreza Esfahani, alongside works by contemporary artists.
The fourth edition of Baran Auction, held in 2019, demonstrated the market appeal of Iran's traditional arts, with five folios from a rare copy of Ferdowsi's “Shahnameh”, written in the nastaliq style during the Timurid period (1370–1507), selling for more than $2.1 million.
The auction, held at Tehran's Raizen International Conference Center, presented 94 works and generated more than $6 million in sales, although 25 lots failed to attract buyers.
Other notable sales included a miniature portrait of Princess Navab Akbari Beigom, created by an Indian artist during the Zand dynasty (1751–1794), which fetched more than $1.3 million, and a cylinder inscribed with a Persian translation of the Cyrus Cylinder by calligrapher Hossein Niktalab, which sold for approximately $930,000.
The results underscored the commercial potential of traditional Iranian and Islamic art within the country's art market.
By bringing together calligraphy and miniature painting, the fifth edition aims to present a broader view of Iran's artistic legacy while providing a platform for the appreciation and circulation of works rooted in its cultural traditions.
Founded by Mahbubeh Kazemi Dulabi in 2016, Baran Auction specializes in calligraphic paintings and works of calligraphy.

Russian attacks on Black Sea ports cut Kernel’s edible oil sales by 48%

Source: Kernel's operations update
Details: Grain exports fell by 54% in the same period to 574,000 tonnes. Kernel redirected some shipments through Danube ports and Ukraine's western land border.

Iran-Pakistan border trade serves mutual interests: ambassador
TEHRAN– Iran’s Ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri-Moghaddam, has stressed that cross-border trade is an integral part of high-level bilateral agreements and serves the mutual interests of both neighboring countries, while attributing the failure to implement the Islamabad understanding to 'US breaches of commitments.'
In remarks on Sunday, the ambassador addressed reports in Pakistani media about the status of trade across the shared border, emphasizing that disruptions to commercial exchanges under the current circumstances would serve neither country’s interests.
“There are currently no restrictions imposed by Iran on the export of Iranian goods, including liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), to Pakistan,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, adding that Iran’s borders with all its neighboring countries remain open.
He explained that difficulties affecting traders transporting goods from Iran to Pakistan stem from the implementation of an “E-Form” procedure by the Pakistani side for imports from Iran. Consultations are underway between the two sides to resolve the issue and facilitate the movement of goods.
The ambassador also acknowledged reports that several hundred LPG tankers had crossed the Gabd-Rimdan border into Pakistan but had yet to be unloaded or cleared. The situation, he said, had complicated the movement of goods and disrupted the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
Amiri-Moghaddam emphasized that Iran had consistently worked to facilitate and strengthen cross-border commerce and remained committed to cooperating with Pakistani counterparts to overcome existing obstacles and expand economic ties.
Border trade, he noted, is a vital component of economic cooperation between the two neighboring countries and benefits both nations and their peoples.
Pakistani media have meanwhile reported that the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has resumed operations, with commercial transport moving again on both sides of the border.
US breaches are behind stalled Islamabad understanding
Separately, Amiri-Moghaddam addressed speculation in Pakistani media about Tehran’s position on the future of negotiations with Washington, stressing that decisions and official announcements concerning whether talks will take place fall within the remit of Iran’s senior political authorities and Foreign Ministry.
Speaking to IRNA in Islamabad on Sunday evening, the ambassador said Iran remained committed to the Islamabad understanding, arguing that its implementation had been obstructed by the US side’s failure to honor its commitments.
He said that, during a recent meeting with think-tank figures and media representatives in Islamabad, he had reiterated Iran’s continued commitment to the understanding.
“The person who declared the Islamabad understanding over and violated it was US President Donald Trump,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, according to IRNA.
He added that Washington’s actions had created conditions in which understanding could not be implemented in practice.
The ambassador said Iran’s repeated emphasis on honoring the understanding reflected its respect for commitments and agreements undertaken within the framework of international law. He drew a parallel with Washington’s unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), arguing that Trump had similarly failed to implement the Islamabad understanding he had signed.
Amiri-Moghaddam stressed that any decision or announcement concerning the holding or cancellation of negotiations would be made by Iran’s senior political authorities and the Foreign Ministry in Tehran, with official information conveyed through the spokesperson for the Iranian negotiating team and official media outlets.
Tehran says diplomacy remains open as Iran stresses readiness to defend itself
The ambassador’s remarks come as Iranian officials have reiterated that diplomacy remains an option while emphasizing the country’s readiness to respond to any hostile action.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei, speaking to German public broadcaster ARD, said the United States continued to insist on unilateral demands in negotiations. He stressed that Iran was keeping the door to diplomacy open while remaining prepared to defend the country against any aggression and deal with every possible scenario.
Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, speaker of Iran’s Parliament and head of the Iranian negotiating team, also addressed the issue in remarks at the beginning of a parliamentary session held in person and online.
Qalibaf said Iran was prepared to deliver a response beyond its adversaries’ expectations to any act of aggression against the country’s territorial integrity. He added that threats of a wider war or assassination would not force the Iranian nation to abandon its rights and interests.
The statements underscore Tehran’s position that diplomatic engagement must be accompanied by respect for commitments and Iran’s national interests.
For Iran and Pakistan, maintaining the smooth operation of border crossings remains important to bilateral commerce and regional economic cooperation. Resolving the outstanding administrative obstacles would help restore the uninterrupted movement of goods and strengthen trade ties between the two neighboring countries.

Araghchi: Iran-Russia coop can strengthen global gas market stability
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for closer cooperation between Iran and Russia to diversify energy supply routes, strengthen global gas market stability and create new opportunities for investment and foreign-exchange earnings, warning that geopolitical tensions and military threats are disrupting international energy supplies.
In an opinion article published in Russia’s Vedomosti newspaper on Monday, Araghchi said energy security had become one of the world’s most pressing challenges, alongside food security, linking the situation to 'the coercive and arrogant actions of the United States in the region.'
Araghchi cited estimates by the International Energy Agency indicating that more than 112 billion cubic meters of liquefied natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, accounting for nearly one-fifth of global trade in the fuel.
He said the recent US-Israeli military aggression against Iran, together with continued military threats, had led to the closure of the strategic waterway and disrupted global gas supplies, particularly to Asian markets.
The disruption has also driven European gas prices sharply higher, while gas storage levels ahead of winter have fallen significantly below those recorded a year earlier, he added.
Araghchi noted that Asian markets consume around 90% of the gas transported through the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the waterway’s importance to global energy security and the economic interests of both producers and consumers.
He warned that instability in the region could have far-reaching consequences for international energy markets, calling for greater dialogue among gas-producing countries, diversification of supply routes and stronger protection for critical energy infrastructure.
The Iranian foreign minister also stressed the need to develop practical mechanisms to mitigate the impact of geopolitical shocks on energy supplies and market stability.
Iran and Russia see potential for deeper energy cooperation
Araghchi highlighted the potential for expanded energy cooperation between Tehran and Moscow, particularly in investment, technology, equipment, production, operational efficiency and energy exports.
He said closer bilateral cooperation could help diversify energy transportation routes and generate additional foreign-exchange revenue, while contributing to the stability of international gas markets.
The article also referred to the Global Gas Outlook 2055 published by the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), which projects that 86% of global gas production by 2055 will come from fields that are not currently producing.
Iran, which holds the world’s second-largest proven natural gas reserves after Russia, has significant potential to expand its role in the global gas sector, Araghchi said.
According to the outlook cited in the article, GECF member countries’ share of global gas production is projected to increase from 38% in 2024 to 44% by 2055, accounting for 65% of net growth in global production over that period.
Araghchi acknowledged that realizing the potential of Iran-Russia energy cooperation would require substantial investment, advanced technology and equipment, as well as solutions to challenges arising from unilateral coercive measures and the complexity of long-term energy contracts.
He described the GECF as an important multilateral platform for strengthening coordination among gas-producing countries and advancing cooperation in response to shared challenges. Political will and mutual trust, he said, would be essential to translating this potential into practical results.
Hormuz security central to global energy stability
Araghchi also addressed maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iran had proposed a seven-day plan to facilitate the waterway’s reopening and the resumption of normal maritime traffic, provided the necessary conditions were met and military threats were removed.
He said responsible dialogue and mutual commitments could help reduce tensions, strengthen sustainable maritime security and restore stability to global energy markets.
“Whether that path can be pursued ultimately depends on the choices made by the United States,” Araghchi wrote, concluding that cooperation and dialogue were essential to building greater stability in global gas and energy markets.

Pope Leo cleared to make his trip to South America after successful lung cancer surgery
Only two weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV has been given the medical green light to embark on an ambitious 12-day tour of South America next month.
"Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned," the Vatican said in a statement on Monday. "The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church."
The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling. The 71-year-old pontiff plans to travel to 10 cities, board 14 flights, and attend many public appearances and religious ceremonies.
The Vatican also confirmed that the trip would proceed "according to the program previously published," which means that a visit to the Peruvian city of Cuzco, Peru, situated at more than 11,000 feet above sea level, remains on the schedule. The thinner air there could pose difficulties for someone recovering from lung surgery.
Doubts about the pope's ability to undergo the South American trip surfaced again last week, when, on the advice of his doctors, Leo canceled a visit by helicopter to Assisi for an international peace gathering to take place Tuesday. Doctors said they advised him to do so preventively, because of the unpressurized air on the helicopter journey.
The upcoming journey carries particular personal significance for the first American-born pope, who spent more than two decades working as a missionary and bishop in Peru.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a statement Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy."
Leo was operated on Oct. 13, when doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.
Since leaving the hospital, Leo has gradually resumed his public duties, including his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square and meetings with visiting church leaders.

Iran says Europe has yet to offer concrete proposal for negotiations
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that Tehran had received no concrete proposal from European countries for negotiations, questioning whether recent European calls for diplomacy reflected a genuine change in policy.
Speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran, Baqaei described the statements as potentially no more than a political gesture, criticizing France, Germany and the United Kingdom for failing to explicitly condemn the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran over the past two years.
He also criticized Europe's role in efforts to reinstate UN sanctions on Iran through the snapback mechanism, urging European governments to adopt a more independent and constructive approach to developments in West Asia.
Baqaei criticized the 'selective application of human rights principles' by European governments and institutions, citing police actions against protesters in France and Belgium.
He said Iran had summoned the French ambassador and, more recently, the Italian ambassador to convey its concerns over reported human rights violations during protests in Europe. He also criticized European officials for attributing domestic unrest to foreign interference rather than addressing underlying grievances.
Regarding protests in Albania, Baqaei said public opposition to corruption and the transfer of land to foreign business interests was an internal matter. He argued that allegations of foreign interference failed to address the reasons behind the demonstrations.
Iran reaffirms position on nuclear program
Addressing US allegations about Iran's nuclear program, Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed or sought to acquire nuclear weapons.
Referring to former US President Barack Obama's remarks on diplomacy and Iran's nuclear program, he said Tehran had entered the 2015 nuclear agreement in good faith, while Washington withdrew from the deal three years later.
Baqaei argued that allegations about Iran's nuclear intentions had been used to justify military action, pointing to a 'contradiction between US assertions' that Iran's nuclear program had been destroyed and subsequent military threats and attacks.
He stressed that Iran remained prepared to defend itself against threats. Asked about potential threats to submarine communications cables and digital infrastructure, he said decisions on any response rested with the competent authorities and would not be disclosed in advance.
Regional diplomacy and security
Baqaei said a visit by a Qatari delegation to Tehran formed part of ongoing regional consultations on bilateral cooperation and Qatar's mediation role amid heightened tensions.
He also said the cancellation of a meeting in Salalah would not change Iran's position that regional countries should establish collective security arrangements based on their own capabilities. Tehran had advanced similar proposals at meetings in Baghdad and within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, he added.
On Yemen, Baqaei called for the dispute between Yemen and Saudi Arabia to be resolved through dialogue, warning that sanctions and military action harmed the Yemeni people and their rights.
Pezeshkian's Russia visit to focus on energy cooperation
Baqaei said President Masoud Pezeshkian's planned visit to Russia for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit on Tuesday would provide an opportunity for major energy suppliers to consult on shared challenges and priorities.
He highlighted longstanding energy cooperation between Iran and Russia, particularly efforts to increase investment, facilitate technology transfer and diversify natural gas export routes. Pezeshkian was also expected to hold bilateral meetings with other leaders attending the summit.
Iran questions US commitment to negotiations
Baqaei said Iran remained open to diplomacy but questioned Washington's commitment to a genuine negotiating process, citing its withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and 'its failure' to honor the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
He stressed that meaningful negotiations required reciprocal commitments rather than demands for unilateral concessions while sanctions and military threats continued.
Iran's foreign policy decisions, including those concerning possible negotiations with the United States, were guided by national interests and a broader diplomatic process, he added, rather than short-term fluctuations in global oil prices.
Iran monitoring border and security developments
On border issues with Pakistan, Baqaei said consultations were continuing over technical matters involving system upgrades and security concerns, describing the process as positive.
Regarding Iran-Iraq border issues, he said Iran's embassy in Baghdad and its consulates were pursuing a resolution, stressing the importance of protecting the interests of both countries. He also noted that US sanctions had consequences for the Iraqi people.
Baqaei added that Iranian authorities were monitoring reports concerning drone bases near Iran and Ukrainian movements in Iraq, saying the relevant institutions would take necessary measures to counter threats.

Pentagon preparing for ‘major war’ – Fox News
Major military bases in the continental US will be expected to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without external support under a new Pentagon strategy, Fox News has reported.
The autonomy target was set out in FORTRESS documents reviewed by the network, it said on Sunday. Critical military supplies would also require at least two qualified supply or production routes to guard against disruption.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the initiative last month. The US military has faced serious logistical disruption in the Middle East following Iranian strikes on American facilities and other sites used by US forces in retaliation for the US-Israeli attack on Iran.
Fox News, which is generally supportive of President Donald Trump’s agenda, wrote that the US needed to be prepared for a contingency in which military action would “cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil.”
FORTRESS stands for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply and Survivability. A founding memorandum signed by Hegseth last month identifies five pillars: energy independence, supply-chain resilience, strategic reserves, physical protection and cybersecurity, and resilience in space and the electromagnetic spectrum.
Pentagon planners aim to reduce reliance on civilian infrastructure that could be severely damaged in a major armed conflict. Proposed options include small nuclear reactors and large battery banks to support base microgrids if external electricity supplies are cut. The program also envisages preparing civilian factories to switch to defense production in an emergency, alongside other measures.
The report comes less than two weeks before midterm elections in which polls suggest the ruling Republican Party could suffer significant losses. The Iran war and the resulting surge in fuel prices are major factors bolstering opposition candidates.
Trump’s rhetoric has fueled widespread expectations that the US could escalate the war with Iran shortly after the election, or even before it. According to NBC News, Washington has withdrawn some personnel from its Middle Eastern bases ahead of a possible renewed airstrike campaign.

Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
TEHRAN – Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — the three countries that recently signed the Mecca defense pact — traveled to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with President Masoud Pezeshkian and with Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
Speaking at a joint meeting with the three visiting officials, President Pezeshkian welcomed dialogue among Islamic countries and stressed the failure of enemies to achieve their objectives against Iran.
"They imagined they could bring the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse through pressure and aggression; but the result of these actions was the strengthening of internal unity and cohesion and increased solidarity of the Iranian nation," Pezeshkian said.
"Our people, despite the imposed losses and hardships, defended their land with power and steadfastness. The notion that the Iranian nation can be forced into surrender is a false and void notion," he added.
The president said the Islamic Republic of Iran pursues its legal rights within the principles and rules of international law, and relying on those very principles, will firmly defend the legitimate rights and interests of the Iranian nation.
Call for united front against Israel
Pezeshkian expressed hope that the presence of major and influential Islamic countries could play an effective role in strengthening regional stability and unity.
"We should not allow the Zionist regime to commit terror and aggression against any individual or country whenever it wishes. I am confident that if Islamic countries stand together and adopt a coordinated position, such actions cannot be repeated," he said.
"I believe that if we manage our differences and emphasize commonalities and shared interests instead of focusing on divisive issues, we can overcome regional problems more easily and effectively," he added.
He warned against interventionist and divisive policies, saying one of the objectives pursued in the policies of the US and the Zionist regime is to weaken regional countries, create rifts among Muslim nations and gradually weaken major Islamic states.
"We must, by strengthening mutual cooperation and supporting one another, prevent the realization of such objectives and not allow regional countries to be exposed separately to pressure and threats," Pezeshkian said.
He added that Islamic countries should move to meet each other's needs through constructive engagement, economic cooperation and the use of mutual capacities. "The notion that nations can be forced into surrender through pressure and sanctions is a void notion. The deeper and broader cooperation among regional countries becomes, the greater their ability to manage problems and confront external pressures will be."
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran, relying on domestic efforts, the support of the nation and the guidance of the Leader, will successfully pass through difficulties, adding that Islamic countries must understand the interconnectedness of their security and interests. Weakening any major regional country, he said, could pave the way for increased pressure and threats against other Islamic countries as well.
From words to joint action
Emphasizing the need for consistency between words and deeds in regional relations, Pezeshkian said: "We should not say what we do not believe in or fail to uphold in practice. We must, hand in hand, provide the ground for flourishing the region's scientific, economic, cultural, political and security capacities; develop communication routes, facilitate travel, turn borders into opportunities for cooperation and link the universities, scientific centers, traders and merchants of Islamic countries to one another."
He said expanding multilateral cooperation lays the ground for sustainable security, noting: "When science, culture, trade and economy cross borders and communications among nations expand, the ground for the spread of terrorism and insecurity will disappear. Therefore, strengthening scientific, cultural and economic bonds not only helps the development and welfare of nations, but is one of the most effective ways to consolidate collective security in the region."
Pezeshkian said any understanding reached in such meetings that leads to stronger regional unity, cohesion and cooperation will enjoy Iran's serious and all-out support, adding that focus must be placed on common ground and areas of cooperation and differences must not be allowed to hinder shared interests.
Nuclear rights and double standards
In another part of his remarks, Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran's principled position on nuclear activities, saying the Islamic Republic is not seeking nuclear weapons and, as a member of the NPT, wants to continue its nuclear activities within the framework of international rights and obligations.
"Iran accordingly reserves the right to benefit from peaceful nuclear activities and expects these rights to be respected within the framework of international regulations," he said.
He criticized dual approaches toward Iran, saying: "Using the nuclear issue as a pretext for exerting pressure, threats, attacks on nuclear facilities, and claiming readiness for talks and dialogue simultaneously with attacking Iran is a contradictory and unconstructive approach that has undermined public trust and increased distrust among Iranian officials and people."
Pezeshkian said Islamic countries must, by strengthening their interactions and coordination, not allow such approaches to become a routine for dealing with regional nations. Safeguarding nations' rights, respecting countries' sovereignty, countering aggression and strengthening regional cooperation require common will and coordinated action, he added.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran is also ready, relying on religious commonalities, mutual interests and respect for nations' rights, to expand its cooperation with Islamic countries in this path," he said.
The officials of the three neighboring countries also held separate meetings with SNSC Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. At the end of the meetings, the four countries issued a joint press statement, stressing: "The participants agreed to continue talks to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, including in the field of peace and security in the region."

British PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime

“I don’t think things have worked out as people said they would,” Burnham told ITV of his country’s 2016 decision to leave the bloc, adding that he wasn’t proposing any changes during this Parliament. “I’m going to lead a discussion on how we make it better.”
Reshaping Britain’s relationship with the European Union has become one of Burnham’s key pledges since he became prime minister three months ago, as he gambles on revisiting a divisive issue that dominated UK politics over the last decade. The 56-year-old prime minister opened the door to rejoining the EU at his party’s annual conference in September, saying he would set out options for a new relationship later this year.
Burnham said he wouldn’t seek to re-run the 2016 referendum, nor break Labour’s 2024 election pledge not to join the EU’s single market or customs union.
He was speaking ahead of a UK-EU summit which is due to take place on Nov 20, when the premier has said he wants to make progress on boosting economic growth and tackling illegal immigration into the UK.
Burnham said he’s seeking a deal that aims “to support our farmers, our food manufacturers, but also to increase collaboration on immigration because we lost that and we need to get it back”, he told Sky News later on Oct 26. “I’m talking about practical steps to deal with the things that matter to people.”
He said the UK had stronger return agreements for the arrival of people in small boats when it was in the EU, and that immigrants have now become more likely to settle in the country permanently, rather than leaving after a few years.
He added that he’ll “never move ahead” of public opinion on the issue of Brexit, though it’s unclear how he intends to achieve that. Asked whether Burnham would use a referendum or a general election to gain a mandate for his new EU position, his deputy official spokeswoman Cat Simmons declined to comment.
“We’re not at that stage yet,” Simmons said to reporters at a briefing on Oct 26. “The first step here is the substance rather than the process.”
Burnham also used the ITV interview to rule out an early election, saying it’s not something he’s thinking about.
“There is no election coming any time soon,” he said. “Britain is starting to regain its momentum.” BLOOMBERG

Profound, accelerated scientific surge must build strong Iran
Unknown

Profound, accelerated scientific surge must build strong Iran
TEHRAN – A ceremony honoring dozens of scientific and sports medal-winners, titled “Medal-Avaran-e Keshvar-Doost”, was held at the martyrdom site of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei in central Tehran, where a message by the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, was read out.
On the days coinciding with the martyrdom anniversary of Lady Fatima Zahra (pbuh), Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, issued a message addressed to Iran's elites, as well as its scientific and sports medalists, on Oct. 26.
 
In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful, the Leader said that according to one of the narrations, these days coincide with the martyrdom anniversary of the Master and Lady of the women of Paradise, Lady Siddiqah Tahirah, Fatimah Zahra (pbuh). It’s remarkable that the exact time of her martyrdom remains unknown, just as the honorable resting place of that divine light is still hidden.
He described her as an exemplary figure in worship, servitude and devotion to God, as a supreme example in uniquely close companionship with the Noble Prophet (pbuh), and as a valiant defender of the Wilayah of the Commander of the Faithful. She was a paragon in acquiring and imparting knowledge, in situational astuteness and rising up for the truth, in patience, sacrifice, selflessness, and compassion for others, and as wife and mother in raising the line of the Infallible Imams (pbut). In one word, he said, she’s a role model for all believing men and women.
Iran, a manifestation of determination and hope
The Leader said that among the shining virtues of a society based on the example of Lady Fatimah (pbuh) is that it lays out a roadmap for the revolutionary, Muslim nation of Iran for undertaking great social movements, being present in the fields of struggle and jihad, participating in popular movements, and even aspiring to achieve progress in the sciences and serve others with humility without expecting anything in return.
At this point in time, our beloved Iran is a manifestation of determination and hope more than anything else, he said, stressing that the role of Iran’s elite and its talented, capable young people in fostering this hope and setting the country on the path toward a bright future is unparalleled. Excellence, he added, is not confined to science, technology and sports. Any positive distinction can be a mark of excellence, now seen in those who strive to elevate the sacred flag of their homeland.
“They are the elite in insight and jihad,” he said. “We consider figures like Rizali Khajavi and Ali Landi to be among the distinguished elite, and their names deserve to be inscribed above the entrances of cultural institutions.” Martyrs and self-sacrificing individuals who offered their lives and health, he added, have left an extraordinary mark on the fate of Islamic Iran and have received from the One God the medal of servitude to Him.
Congratulations to medal-bringers of Olympiads and sports
The Leader congratulated the nation and all those who brought honors, numerous awards, medals and scientific awards in the Olympiads in astronomy and astrophysics, mathematics, earth sciences, geography, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, artificial intelligence, and the humanities, as well as many recent achievements in sports.
He expressed admiration for the determination of those leading the caravan of honor and hope, the standard-bearers of progress, from adolescents and young people to coaches, professors and eminent scholars. The motivation and hope of elites to bring about changes, he said, is a bright flame witnessed over many years and decades, whose manifestation in repeated annual championships in Olympiads and sports is a source of honor and pride for the entire nation.
He said the outstanding results and new records of hardworking athletes attest to their effort, determination, resolve, and faith, elevating dear Iran before the eyes of all nations. He praised the female athletes who make the honorable symbol of the Iranian women’s attire shine before the world, and all medalists who bring joy to the nation and honor to the flag of Islamic Iran, each playing a vital role in realizing the vision of a strong Iran.
Elite status as divine blessing and heavier responsibility
Noting that these are days marked by cheerfulness and renewed focus on science and research in universities, hawzas and schools, the Leader addressed seekers of knowledge, elites and scholars.
“Being among the elite is a divine blessing and gift,” he said. At its core are talent and intellectual ability, a profound divine gift and immense wealth that Iranians, particularly youth, possess in abundance. Reason and servitude require gratitude in heart, words and actions, which opens the way for that blessing to reach its full potential.
Appreciation, he said, must begin with the individual and be cultivated by parents, teachers, schools, universities and the national system. An elite individual thus bears a heavier responsibility to apply talent optimally to resolve the country’s challenges. The distinguished elite, he added, aren’t people who regard themselves as set apart and think only of personal desires, but those who see themselves as effective members of society and use talent for the advancement of self and society.
From knowledge to daily life and defense power
The Leader said Iranian elites have shown knowledge can be turned into tools for real problems, from stem cell research, nanotechnology and biotechnology to aerospace, industry, mining, medicine, agriculture, nuclear energy and infrastructure.
Visible manifestations, he said, include electricity generated by Iranian turbines, knowledge-based technology in desalination plants on southern islands, agricultural drones over northern farms and rice paddies, children born to infertile couples through Royan’s advanced technologies, diagnosis and treatment with radiopharmaceuticals, monitoring of land and crops with remote-sensing satellites, and gains in productivity and food security. Furthermore, he added, many other achievements, particularly in the defense and military sectors, have repeatedly astounded the world in their time and will continue to do so in the future.
Strong Iran depends on science; enemy targets elites
“A strong Iran depends on scientific and technological power, and this core pillar is one of the most important factors for shaping Iran’s role in the emerging global equations and the new world order,” the Leader said. The key to empowerment lies in pushing boundaries of knowledge and solving scientific challenges.
He said the malice and criminal actions of enemies against Iranian scientists prove this pivotal role. The same enemy that assassinated prominent scientists and elites during the Second and Third Imposed Wars – and in academic settings years prior – cannot bear to see Iran advance. It seeks to spread hopelessness, capture minds, draw talents into neo-colonialism and turn them into cogs in Western plunder, he said. Yet every drop of blood shed from martyred elite, scientists, professors, students and schoolchildren has unleashed a storm of determination and progress.
Recalling ancient civilization and luminaries, contrasted with two centuries of stagnation in Qajar and Pahlavi eras, he said the nation recognizes the strategy of “Knowledge is Power” (Al- ‘ilm sultan) and rapid growth over three decades, largely indebted to the guidance of our illustrious martyred Leader. If before a new surge had to be urged, the experience of two recent wars has proven it must now be both profound and accelerated.
Five priorities to shift center of knowledge to Iran
To that end, the Leader said, elites alongside officials must devote themselves to building a glorious future, keeping five points in mind:
First, a serious, practical plan for basic sciences and humanities, as physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics are the foundation of all sciences. Second, sustained attention to undiscovered truths, pushing boundaries and racing to solve famous unsolved problems, particularly in mathematics. Third, creativity and innovation through scientific courage, self-confidence and attractive incentives for practical solutions. Fourth, self-reliance in solving challenges and removing bottlenecks for transnational engagement. Fifth, developing talents in experimental disciplines through industry-university cooperation from early years, knowledge-based enterprises, and linking elites, universities, companies, industries and startups with government support across the chain from knowledge to consumption, focusing on water, soil, food, energy and artificial intelligence.
Rapid advancement, he said, requires harmonizing economic incentives and commercialization with elite motivation, linking research, industry and markets, and direct participation of elites from universities and seminaries in planning and policymaking.
If pursued, he said, the center of gravity of knowledge will gradually shift from Western countries to Iran, Iran will emerge as a leading authority, and the martyred Leader’s objective of establishing Persian as one of the world’s primary scientific languages will be realized.
“God willing, by the blessing of the blood of the martyrs who were elite scholars, and through the benevolent prayers of our Master and Mawla [Imam Mahdi, may God hasten his noble reappearance], a profound, accelerated advancement in the sciences by the nation's elite and distinguished scholars, together with the comprehensive advancement of an ever-stronger Iran, will pave the way toward the realization of a New Islamic-Iranian Civilization.”

Trading halted in Brazil as stocks sink following Lula reelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:14:02 UTC
02:14:02 KST

NEW YORK/BRASILIA, Brazil/LONDON (Reuters) -- Brazil's stock exchange halted trading via a circuit breaker safety mechanism on Monday in the wake of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection, undoing bullish investor sentiment after his right-wing rival led the first round of voting earlier in the month.
The real weakened around 12% against the U.S. dollar in spot trading as trading in Brazil got underway and Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15%, while interest rate futures rose sharply. The selloff extended to Brazil's international bonds, with longer-dated debt hit hardest and the 2056 maturity down nearly 3 cents.
Trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted for 30 minutes after the benchmark Ibovespa index fell 10% from its previous close, triggering the market's circuit breaker mechanism, stock exchange operator B3 said in a statement.
The move came after B3 had initially expanded the daily trading limits for Ibovespa stock index futures, dollar futures and interest rate futures in response to heightened market volatility.
As Brazilian markets hemorrhaged, the country's Treasury cancelled its regular auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds scheduled for Oct. 27 and Oct. 29, respectively.
The collapse is a sharp reversal from the rally seen earlier this month, when markets soared on expectations of a shift to the right after Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, unexpectedly finished first in the opening round of Brazil's presidential elections.
Stocks closed on Friday almost 7% above their level before the first round, while the real was nearly 5% stronger against the U.S. dollar.
Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under Flavio Bolsonaro would allow borrowing costs to decline.
Prediction markets had pointed to a Bolsonaro win, with Kalshi pricing in a more than 75% chance of that outcome on Friday.
"We expect a sharp market reaction on Monday, with aggressive repricing, a selloff in assets and interest rate futures likely to hit their upper limit shortly after the open," said Luis Felipe Vital, head of macro strategy at Warren Investimentos.
Bolsonaro's refusal to concede and his pledge to seek an annulment added to investor uncertainty.
"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result -- or at least allows the constitution to run its course," said Chris Turner, strategist at ING in London.
Attention will now turn to Lula's choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach.
"The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," said Graham Stock at RBC BlueBay Asset Management.
Lula faces the challenge of slowing the rise in Brazil's debt while protecting social programs and investment, with investors looking for signs his gradual fiscal approach can bring borrowing costs down.
"(The) Lula administration will have no choice but to do some fiscal consolidation too, but most investors doubt it will be enough to put debt sustainability back on track," said Thierry Larose, portfolio manager at Vontobel Asset Management.
Without confidence that Lula can deliver, lenders could demand higher interest rates, adding to Brazil's debt burden and making credit more expensive for businesses and households.
"Investors want a clear and credible commitment to fiscal discipline," said Alejo Czerwonko, chief investment officer for emerging markets at UBS Global Wealth Management. "We expect the rally that followed the first round to be largely priced out, and sentiment to stay weak until a clear fiscal plan emerges."
Czerwonko said investors wanted an end to campaign-related spending and a believable path to stabilize public debt. "It also means a working relationship with an opposition-leaning Congress, because no fiscal plan passes without it," he said.
Lula's team aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3% of gross domestic product by 2030. That would leave money to cover part of the interest bill, reducing the need for fresh borrowing. But public debt already exceeds 82% of GDP, while pensions and other legally required spending limit where savings can come from.
"Lula's policies have talked about spending cuts, but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look," said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital.

Fears for Palestinians as Israel election observers allowed guns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:13:30 UTC
02:13:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Fears of intimidation of Palestinian voters as Israeli election 'observers' allowed to carry guns
Israel’s High Court of Justice on Sunday rejected a petition to ban polling station officials and party representatives from carrying weapons at voting sites during Tuesday’s general election, amid concerns from rights groups that an armed presence could intimidate Palestinian voters and undermine the electoral process.
Filed on Thursday by Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel and the Joint List, the petition argued that "an armed presence could deter voters, undermine the electoral process, and could even lead to violent confrontations that endanger human life".
Adalah attorney Ariel Remez, who led the petition, told The New Arab: "by declining to intervene, the Court has left Palestinian voters exposed to intimidation and placed responsibility for any violence on Election Day on the police and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a minister previously convicted of incitement to racism who has driven the mass arming of Israeli civilians."
The petition followed an announcement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism parties that they would deploy approximately 2,000 'observers' to polling stations in what they called "Arab population centres". Police also issued a directive allowing licensed gun owners to carry firearms at polling stations.
More than one million Palestinian citizens of Israel are eligible to vote, with their turnout potentially decisive in determining whether Netanyahu can form another government.
"Our concern is that these so-called 'observers' will take advantage of their authorization to enter multiple polling stations during the day, thus recreating the 1981 'National Ballot Security Task Force' in the [gubernatorial] elections in New Jersey," Remez said, referring to the Republican National Committee (RNC)-led initiative that deployed armed, off-duty police officers and used targeted mailing lists in minority neighbourhoods.
"We have no doubt that the Likud and its partners from the extreme right intend to copy the RNC’s playbook of voter suppression of minorities," he added.
Adalah argues that fears of intimidation of Palestinian citizens are heightened by the sharp rise in licensed firearms under Ben-Gvir, whose tenure has seen the number double from around 150,000 to 300,000.
"The danger lies in the branding of the entire Palestinian public in Israel as prone to voter fraud, amid widespread incitement against Palestinian citizens," Remez said.
"At the same time, the violent settler movement in the West Bank is increasingly active inside Israel, including, for example, an outpost established near Majd al-Krum. Against this backdrop, the threats to Arab votes are real and immediate."
Majd al-Krum is a Palestinian village in the Galillee region where settlers recently set up a West Bank-style outpost.
Adalah also pointed to a survey published by the Israel Democracy Institute in November 2025, in which 81 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel surveyed said civilians carrying weapons in public spaces made them feel less safe.
The 2,000 individuals set to be deployed have no legal authority to oversee the voting process. Police are required to enforce strict rules governing who may enter polling stations and what they are permitted to do there.
Israel’s Election Law prohibits campaigning inside polling stations and wearing clothing or symbols identifying a political party. It also bars individuals from interfering with another person’s vote.
Adalah will operate an election-day hotline, Remez told The New Arab, with legal teams working alongside Arab parties to monitor and respond to voting irregularities.
"Where necessary, we will turn to the Central Elections Committee, the police and, if needed, the courts. We will advise activists who contact us to carefully document any disruption at polling stations, so that we can assess whether the integrity of the results has been affected," he said.

An infinite regress is a series of appropriately related elements with a first member but no last member, where each element leads to or generates the next in some sense.[1] An infinite regress argument is an argument that makes appeal to an infinite regress. Usually such arguments take the form of objections to a theory, with the fact that the theory implies an infinite regress being taken to be objectionable….

Zelenskyy signed decrees extending martial law and mobilization in Ukraine

Gaza’s displaced families are struggling to keep the lights on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:09:05 UTC
02:09:05 KST

The sun is slowly setting earlier as winter approaches in Gaza. When night falls, Aseel Ayesh’s tent in the Nuseirat refugee camp goes dark. Last week, her private electricity provider cut her off after she couldn’t pay a bill of over 180 shekels (around $59).
“I need to use the light all night, so I can prepare milk and dinner for my daughter,” said Ayesh, 24, who shares the tent with her husband and their infant daughter. Her husband, Wassim Mohammed Ayesh, said he got bit by a rat that snuck into the dark tent, which resulted in an infection.
With Gaza’s power grid in ruins, private generators are now the only source of electricity for most people in the Strip, and the price has soared. Generator power costs about 30 shekels (around $9.80) per kilowatt-hour, compared to three or four shekels before the war, according to providers. Generator owners connect subscribers to their power lines, with a meter to measure energy consumption, and bills are collected every week. Anyone who doesn’t pay in time is cut off.
Gaza never had enough electricity in the past. Before October 2023, the Strip had about 212 megawatts of power, less than half of what it needed to function. Most of the electricity was supplied from Israeli power lines, with the remainder coming from Gaza’s only power plant. At best, homes got electricity in alternating eight-hour shifts. Around 350 private generators were already operating to cover the gaps.
On the night of October 7, 2023, Israel cut the power lines and stopped the fuel that ran the power plant. Since then, the bombardment has destroyed about 5,080 kilometres of power lines and 2,285 distribution transformers, according to Gaza’s government media office, which puts the sector’s losses at $1.4 billion. The generators that replaced the grid run on fuel, engine oil and spare parts, all of which Israel restricts from entering the besieged Strip.
Not far from Ayesh, Ashraf Mohammed, known as Abu Mohammed, lives with his family of nine in a hasil, a small storeroom once used as a shop or warehouse and now rented out as a home because so few houses are left standing. He lost his job in the war, and now every shekel counts.
“I lost my work because of the war, and now I need more than 2,000 shekels ($655) a month,” he said. “I sold my car during the war to provide for my family.”
Last month, the family’s weekly electricity bills added up to 582 shekels ($190). They now use power only to charge their phones, so two of his children can follow their university classes online, and to turn on a single light for a few hours at a time.
“We have to cut back on our basic expenses to pay for electricity,” said his wife, Umm Mohammed. “We don’t spend much on food, and we can’t pay the full university fees for our children.” Before the war, she explained, they had electricity for only about six hours a day, but the price was more reasonable.
The private generator economy
Abu Zayed Sons Trading and Import is one of the largest generator providers in central Gaza. Founded in 2017, the company moved into electricity when the war began, running its first lines in al-Zawayda, where it started, before expanding to ten branches across the Strip.
The private generators run about 20 hours a day, from 7:00am to 3:00am, and burn between 40 and 100 litres of fuel an hour, said general manager Aya Shaheen. “Our generators have very high capacity. They can’t be compared with competitors who own small generators.”
With fuel imports restricted, the company makes its own diesel in a private factory. It was among the first in Gaza to do so, Shaheen said, and that has allowed it to continue running. When asked about their running costs, Shaheen said that the figures change too often to provide an estimate.
The company has around 25,000 subscribers today. “The price per kilowatt is fixed at 30 shekels,” Shaheen said. “Each subscriber has an independent meter. They bring their own, and we connect it.” Bills are collected weekly so that debts don’t pile up as prices rise.
Abu Zayed doesn’t run lines to tents, because a single short circuit could start a fire and cause a catastrophe, Shaheen said. Its customers live in houses still standing and in hawasil like Abu Mohammed’s.
Mahmoud al-Baba, who owns a generator in the Central Governorate, does extend power lines to tents, including Ayesh’s. “Why, aren’t the people in the tents human beings, that I shouldn’t run lines to them?” he said.
He charges 29 shekels per kilowatt-hour and uses the same system of meters and weekly bills. “Payment is in cash or by bank transfer, and whoever doesn’t pay, we cut off the electricity.”
Opting out of electricity
Families who can’t keep up are canceling their subscriptions, choosing to live in the dark so they can cover food and rent. Some charge their phones at charging points set up across the Strip, which cost a few shekels a time but offer nothing more: no light, no heat, no way to cook.
Solar panels, which have eased electricity shortages in places like Lebanon, are too expensive and hard to find in Gaza, said economic analyst Ahmed Abu Qamar. High electricity prices have also raised production costs for small businesses by 10 to 15 percent, he said, and goods could be 15 percent cheaper if power were available at normal prices. If prices keep rising, he warned, families will drain their savings and sink into debt just to cover the basics.
They are likely to keep rising. On October 12, Gaza’s Energy and Natural Resources Authority capped the price of generator electricity at 29 shekels per kilowatt-hour. Shaheen said her company holds a permit from the authority but can’t bring its price down.
“There is a severe shortage of generator oil,” she said. “I expect the price to rise within days,”

Russia: Exiled advocate faces “extremism” charges over human rights work for Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO Memorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:09:03 UTC
02:09:03 KST

Reacting to news that a prosecutor’s office in Moscow is about to initiate criminal proceedings on “extremism” charges against prisoners’ rights advocate Anna Karetnikova, from the Memorial Human Rights Centre, who is currently living in exile, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:
“Amnesty International has long warned of the danger that Russia’s vague and overly broad anti-extremism legislation would be used to criminalize lawful human rights work. Today, those fears are being realized with the criminal case against Anna Karetnikova – the first time such charges have been used against an individual solely because of their human rights work.”
“Although Anna Karetnikova is living in exile and can only be tried in absentia, the threat of prosecution sends a chilling message that is intended to silence human defenders in Russia and abroad, stop them from documenting violations and deter them from speaking up for the victims of these abuses. Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives.
Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives
Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director
“The Russian authorities must drop these charges against Anna Karetnikova, close this case and stop abusing absurdly broad and vague ‘extremism’ legislation against their critics, whether they be human rights defenders, political opponents, LGBTI people or dissident religious groups. Russia’s repressive legislation must be brought into line with the country’s international human rights obligations.”
Background
On 26 October 2026, the Lefortovo Interdistrict Prosecutor’s Office in Moscow announced that it had gathered materials to initiate criminal proceedings against Anna Karetnikova on charges of “participation in activities of an extremist organization” (Article 282.2(2) of the Criminal Code) and “evasion of duties of a foreign agent” (Article 330.1(2)).
Although the prosecutors didn’t name the “extremist organization” in question directly, Anna Karetnikova has worked or collaborated since 2002 with Memorial Human Rights Centre, Russia’s oldest human rights group. Four years after it was awarded the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize, Memorial was arbitrarily designated as “extremist” by Russian authorities in April 2026.
Between 2008 and 2016, Karetnikova served on Moscow’s Public Monitoring Commission, an independent public body monitoring detention facilities. She later worked as a lead analyst for the Federal Penitentiary Service before being fired from her position in January 2023 and leaving Russia. In April 2025, she was arbitrarily designated as a “foreign agent” by the Ministry of Justice.

Defense Forces strikes communications hub, command posts, supply depots belonging to Russian troops – AFU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

On Sunday and into Monday night, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a communications hub, command posts, a drone control center, a UAV workshop, and warehouses containing logistical supplies belonging to Russian troops in the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions.
According to a Telegram post by the press service of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), a communications hub belonging to a Russian unit was struck near Melitopol in Zaporizhia region, and the occupiers' command posts were struck in the vicinity of Myrnohrad in Donetsk region and the village of Chervonohirka in Zaporizhia region.

As noted by the General Staff, striking a communications hub disrupts the enemy's communications and command and control, while destroying command posts complicates the coordination of its units on the battlefield. The destruction of the command post and the UAV workshop reduces the Russian troops' ability to attack the Defense Forces' positions and frontline communities with drones, while the destruction of the supply depots hinders the resupply of Russian units.

17:08:31 UTC
02:08:31 KST

9/11 cost Americans their privacy. AI could take what’s left
On October 26,2001, US President George W. Bush signed the USA PATRIOT Act into law, less than seven weeks after the September 11 attacks killed nearly 3,000 people in New York. The speed of its passage reflected the extraordinary political and social atmosphere in the United States. The tragedy had shattered the country’s sense of security, and fears of further terrorist activity continued to haunt the country in the months that followed.
In the weeks after 9/11, grief and anger were accompanied by an unprecedented surge of patriotism and national solidarity. President Bush’s approval rating reached 86 percent by late September, and public trust in the federal government rose to levels unseen in decades. A majority of Americans also expressed a willingness to sacrifice at least some civil liberties if doing so would help combat terrorism. Under intense pressure to prevent another catastrophe, Congress moved rapidly to expand federal investigative and surveillance powers.
The Patriot Act facilitated information sharing between intelligence and law enforcement agencies, broadened certain authorities to obtain records, and expanded investigative tools available in terrorism cases. Supporters argued that these measures were necessary to confront a transnational threat with legal instruments suited to a new security environment.
Yet national unity did not eliminate concerns about civil rights. Arab and Muslim Americans, as well as people perceived to belong to these communities, faced increased discrimination and violence. As the immediate shock of 9/11 receded, questions grew over how far the governments’ new powers should extend and what safeguards were needed to prevent abuse.
These tensions would shape the law’s legacy for decades. The debate intensified after Edward Snowden’s 2013 disclosures exposed the scale of certain US surveillance programs, helping spur the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which curtailed the government’s bulk collection of domestic telephone records. The controversy revealed that the challenge was not simply how to protect Americans from terrorism, but how to preserve privacy and civil liberties while doing so.
The Patriots Act’s legacy in the age of AI
The surveillance debate that follows 9/11 has evolved alongside technology. Today, governments can analyze enormous volumes of digital information, from communications metadata to online activity, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish targeted intelligence gathering from the broader collection of personal data.
However, not all modern US surveillance powers originate in the Patriot Act. One important distinction is between Section 215 of the Patriot Act, which became associated with the NSA’s bulk collection of domestic telephone records, and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), enacted in 2008.
Section 702 allows US intelligence agencies to target non-US persons reasonably believed to be outside the country for foreign intelligence purposes. Yet communications involving Americans may also be collected when they interact with foreign targets. A separate framework. Executive Order 12333 governs much of the intelligence community’s overseas surveillance activity.
These authorities raise questions that extend beyond the original post-9/11 debate. Artificial intelligence is adding a new dimension to the problem. Machine-learning systems can process vast quantities of communications, financial records, location data and other digital information, identifying patterns that human investigators might overlook. Such capabilities could help intelligence agencies detect terrorist networks and anticipate emerging threats. Yet they also raise the possibility of increasingly comprehensive surveillance, in which individuals can be assessed through their digital associations, behavior and inferred characteristics rather than through evidence of specific wrongdoings.
The risks are not limited to the amount of information collected. AI systems can produce false positives, reproduce biases present in their training data and generate conclusions that are difficult to explain or independently verify. If such assessments inform investigations or security decisions, errors may have serious consequences for individuals. The challenge for governments is therefore not simply to regulate access to data, but also to establish accountability for how algorithms analyze it, how their conclusions are used and whether affected individuals have meaningful avenues for redress.
Twenty-five years later: Has America found the balance?
Twenty-five years after the Patriot Act became law, the United States has neither abandoned its expanded national security apparatus nor settled the debate over its proper limits. The government’s ability to collect and analyze information remains an important instrument in counterterrorism and foreign intelligence. At the same time, experience has shown that powers introduced in response to an emergency can endure long after the circumstances that justified them have changed.
The law’s defenders argue that intelligence agencies need effective tools to identify threats before they result in violence. Critics counter that broad surveillance authorities, secret legal interpretations and insufficient oversight can undermine privacy and weaken public trust. Both concerns are fundamental to a democratic society: security is essential to protecting freedom, but security measures can also threaten it when they operate without adequate safeguards.
The central lesson of the Patriot Act is therefore not that national security and civil liberties are necessarily incompatible. It is that the balance between them cannot be established once and left untouched. It requires clear legal limits, meaningful judicial and congressional oversight, transparency wherever possible, and public debate about how surveillance powers are used.
Artificial intelligence makes this balance even harder to maintain. Surveillance systems are increasingly capable of drawing connections across datasets and generating assessments at a speed and scale that traditional oversight mechanisms were not designed to handle. Decisions may depend partly on algorithmic outputs that are difficult for the public, and sometimes even for officials, to scrutinize. Democratic oversight must therefore evolve alongside technology, requiring clear rules on the use of AI, independent testing, safeguards against discriminatory outcomes and human accountability for consequential decisions.
The digital age makes this task more urgent. As governments acquire increasingly sophisticated tools to monitor communications and analyze personal information, lawmakers must ensure that technological capabilities do not automatically translate into unlimited authority.
The question raised in October 2001 remains relevant today: how can a democracy protect its citizens without compromising the freedoms that give its political system legitimacy? Twenty-five years later, the United States continues to grapple with the answer.

Zelenskyy calls out monthlong wait for Hegseth to sign off on Patriot missiles
