Kyiv has repeatedly pressed the need for more interceptors to be delivered to its forces as Ukraine continues to defend against deadly Russian missile attacks and jet-powered drone strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on much coveted Patriot interceptor missiles.
In an update on weapons supplies shared on social media, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been awaiting approval to receive missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
"We are working on several tracks – with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles," he wrote.
"In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS," Zelenskyy continued, adding that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington once again.
"Conversations with other countries are also ongoing," he said.
Kyiv has repeatedly pressed the need for more interceptors to be delivered to its forces as Ukraine continues to defend against deadly Russian missile attacks and jet-powered drone strikes.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had fired 48 missiles - including ballistic missiles - at Ukraine over the past week, as well as around 1,600 guided aerial bombs and close to 2,300 attack drones.
"Unfortunately, almost every day, these brutal strikes leave people killed and injured," he wrote on X. "We need to unblock the deliveries of Patriot interceptors already approved by European countries."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriot missiles through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.
Munitions stockpiles under strain
Global munitions stocks have come under significant pressure in recent months amid the US' war in Iran.
A report from the US Department of Defence's inspector general, published in September, said American forces had fired $22.3 billion worth of munitions from the start of Operation Epic Fury in late February to the end of June.
Yurii Ihnat, a colonel in the Ukrainian military, said in an interview published on Monday that the number of Patriot missiles used in the Middle East could have supported several years of combat operations in Ukraine.
It is unclear how many of the missiles Ukraine is waiting for Hegseth to sign off on, although Ukrainian media reports suggest that it is a sizeable figure.

In a report submitted to the UN General Assembly, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concluded that Russian forces intentionally targeted civilian facilities, causing widespread suffering, particularly during the winter of 2025-2026.

The commission called for an immediate end to attacks on civilian infrastructure and the discharge of all trafficked recruits from Russian forces.

Autogas is rapidly becoming more expensive, while diesel has crossed the UAH 100 mark: what is happening to fuel prices
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:02:32 EET
02:02:32 KST

Autogas is rapidly becoming more expensive, while diesel has crossed the UAH 100 mark: what is happening to fuel prices
Kyiv • UNN
The average price of diesel reached UAH 103.40, while autogas cost UAH 54.45 per liter. In October, gas rose in price by 21%, while petrol increased by only 77 kopecks.
At the beginning of the new working week, diesel and autogas prices surged. The average cost of diesel fuel at Ukrainian filling stations currently stands at UAH 103.40 per liter, A-95 petrol at UAH 90.93, and autogas at UAH 54.45. At the same time, the difference between the cheapest and most expensive offers from individual networks reaches several hryvnias per liter.
Why the most noticeable trend in October has been the rapid rise in autogas and diesel prices against the backdrop of relatively restrained petrol price dynamics, and where drivers can currently buy fuel at a favorable price, was determined by UNN.
How much does A-95 petrol cost at Ukrainian filling stations?
At the beginning of the week, the average price of the popular A-95 petrol is UAH 90.93 per liter. Among the networks listed, Avantage 7 offers the lowest price — UAH 86.95 per liter. At Market, petrol costs UAH 87.59, at KLO — UAH 87.90, and at BRSM-Nafta — UAH 87.99 per liter. At MANGO filling stations, a liter of A-95 costs UAH 88.60, while at AMIC it costs UAH 88.90. UPG, BVS, and Marshal have set the same price of UAH 89.90 per liter. Considerably more expensive fuel of this grade is sold by OKKO and WOG — UAH 92.90 per liter. The highest price in the sample was recorded at SOCAR — UAH 94.90 per liter.
The difference between the minimum and maximum price of A-95 currently stands at UAH 7.95 per liter. For a car with a 50-liter tank, this means a difference of nearly UAH 398 for one full refueling.
Premium petrol: where prices are highest at filling stations in the capital
The average price of A-95+ is UAH 94.90 per liter, nearly UAH 4 more than regular A-95. AMIC sells the most affordable premium petrol in the sample — UAH 91.90 per liter. At BVS, Marshal, and UPG, the price is the same — UAH 92.90 per liter.
At KLO, A-95+ costs UAH 95.60, while at OKKO and WOG it costs UAH 95.90 per liter. The most expensive offer is at SOCAR — UAH 97.90 per liter. Thus, the price gap in this segment reaches UAH 6 per liter, or UAH 300 when filling a 50-liter tank.
Diesel fuel: prices approach UAH 107
Diesel remains the most expensive among the main types of fuel for which an average price is provided: UAH 103.40 per liter. The lowest offer was recorded at MANGO — UAH 99.90 per liter. At BRSM-Nafta, diesel costs UAH 100.99, at Avantage 7 — UAH 101, and at UPG and Marshal — UAH 102.90 per liter. AMIC sells diesel fuel for UAH 103.90, Market for UAH 104, and KLO for UAH 104.40 per liter. At OKKO, the price is UAH 105.90, while BVS and SOCAR offer it for UAH 106. The highest figure among the networks listed is at WOG: UAH 106.90 per liter.
The difference between the extreme offers is UAH 7 per liter. For 50 liters of diesel, one would have to pay UAH 4,995 at the cheapest of the specified filling stations and UAH 5,345 at the most expensive.
Experts are already warning that the rise in diesel prices will affect far more than just car owners. This fuel is used by freight transport, agricultural enterprises, and generators, so a prolonged increase in its cost could raise expenses for logistics, production, and backup power supply.
Autogas: the price gap exceeds five hryvnias
As of October 26, the average price of liquefied automotive gas is UAH 54.45 per liter. Among the operators listed, BVS sells it most cheaply — UAH 51.90. Gas at Avantage 7 costs nearly the same — UAH 51.95. At BRSM-Nafta, the price is UAH 52.49, and at Marshal — UAH 52.90. The KLO, UPG, MANGO, and AMIC filling station networks offer autogas for UAH 54.90 per liter. At OKKO and SOCAR, a liter costs UAH 56.50, while at WOG it costs UAH 56.90. The highest price in the list is at the Market network, where drivers are offered gas for UAH 57 per liter.
The difference between the extreme values is UAH 5.10 per liter. Filling 40 liters of autogas will cost UAH 2,076 at the lowest price and UAH 2,280 at the highest. At the same time, an average liter of autogas costs about 60% of the price of a liter of A-95, although the actual savings during operation also depend on the vehicle’s fuel consumption.
What happened to fuel prices in Ukraine during October
The month’s dynamics show that autogas became more expensive considerably faster than gasoline. According to statistics from the Consulting Group "A-95," from October 1 to 23, the average price of autogas rose from UAH 43.93 to UAH 53.35 per liter. This is an increase of UAH 9.42, or approximately 21%, in less than a month.
Over the same period, diesel rose in price from UAH 98.44 to UAH 103.45 per liter, an increase of UAH 5.01. Meanwhile, the average price of A-95 gasoline increased from UAH 89.27 to UAH 90.04 per liter, or by just 77 kopecks. These figures are provided to compare trends within the same historical series; they may differ from the average values in the current snapshot because of the methodology and the time when the data were updated.
The reasons for the pressure on the market vary. In particular, energy expert Hennadiy Riabtsev believes that the price of autogas is affected by dependence on imports and the seasonal increase in demand for liquefied gas with the onset of cold weather.
And Serhii Kuyun, director of the Consulting Group "A-95," explained the rise in diesel prices by the tense supply situation and high wholesale prices. At the same time, he assessed the situation with gasoline as more balanced.
Fuel prices are rising in Ukraine: what drivers should expect in the near future
At the beginning of the last week of October, diesel and autogas remain the main areas of price risk. If purchase costs and supply difficulties persist, pressure on retail prices may continue. In this situation, energy experts offer Ukrainian drivers several pieces of advice.
First, do not buy large quantities of fuel "for future use." Artificial shortages here will only create favorable conditions for another sharp price spike. Second, it makes sense to develop a new habit: every morning, before buying gasoline or diesel, compare the prices for the same type of fuel at nearby gas stations. Practice shows that they can often differ. By choosing the most advantageous option, over the course of a month you can save not a particularly large amount, but still some money.

Earlier, we wrote that on October 23, autogas and diesel became more expensive at some gas stations in Kyiv.

‘You are set up to fail’: homeless people say system in England is broken and they need help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:02:20 UTC
02:02:20 KST

Martin Fletcher had been homeless for more than 20 years after being made redundant before he finally got accommodation in Sunderland in 2024.
What was the one thing that finally ended his rough sleeping and sofa surfing? “My mindset, mainly,” the 61-year-old said. “The realisation that I was getting old and I couldn’t live like this for ever. And also help from a charity who didn’t judge, who didn’t bombard me with forms – they made me a cup of tea and built up a picture of what I needed and helped me get back on track.”
That charity was Basis Sunderland’s drop-in service for housing support, which closed its doors in July for lack of funding.
Fletcher found this devastating: “How are they going to end rough sleeping when services like this are closing? You’ve got to remember, unless people want to come in off the streets, it won’t happen. They said they did it during Covid but they didn’t – I was still on the streets. And not all homelessness is visible. So these local services are vital.”
Andy Burnham, who had announced plans in July to end rough sleeping and offer everyone in need a bed by Christmas, hosted a summit on the issue on Monday.
The prime minister told the Downing Street event this commitment would be backed by a further £432m to sustain the support into next year. A number of charities had raised concerns that people would simply end up back on the streets after Christmas. Burnham said he was “bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts”.
Those who work in the homelessness sector have warned there is no easy solution. The Guardian has spoken to several formerly homeless people to find out what helped them back into housing, sometimes after decades of sleeping on the streets.
Amy Bell, 37, was street homeless and struggling with heroin addiction for seven years between 2013 and 2020. She said she hit “rock bottom” when her council said it could offer her only a voucher for a two-man tent, which she “cried herself to sleep in at night”.
The next morning, workers employed by the same council put her tent and all her belongings in the bin because it was classed as litter. Borrowing a phone from a Citizens Advice centre, she secured a place at a hostel for a few weeks, which enabled her to reconnect with a local drug treatment service, get a phone with a sim card and start to rebuild.
She said being offered a bed in a hostel, even though she was still taking drugs, was the key to getting her off the streets. “The hostel system is broken. You are basically set up to fail,” she added.
“They don’t accommodate people with addiction problems, and that’s who it should be for. Eventually you will do something that shows you are still using and they ban you. It doesn’t take long to get kicked out of all of them. And then you’re left with nothing.”
Bell said for Burnham to succeed in abolishing rough sleeping he must get rid of the “ridiculous bureaucracy” that stops people from accessing support.
“Everything is done by app now. When you’re homeless, you don’t have that – believe me, if you get a decent phone, you sell it,” she said. “The days of being able to walk into the Citizens Advice bureau or the jobcentre don’t exist any more. Homeless people need a real-life person to help them.”
Others the Guardian spoke to said they moved from England to Scotland because it was easier to get help there after it abolished the priority needs test in 2012. According to Crisis, Scotland has some of the most progressive homelessness rights in the world.
Tony* became homeless after being released from prison in 2024. He told his probation officer he had nowhere to go but was simply advised to contact a council homelessness team the day of his release.
No housing was available and he ended up sleeping in a tent in the woods. “I was a prison leaver, I hadn’t made myself intentionally homeless, but there was nothing. The support was nonexistent,” he said. “I was telling my probation officer where I’m sleeping at our weekly meetings but they didn’t help.”
A chance meeting led him to the Salvation Army, where he has been living in supported accommodation for the past two years. With evidence suggesting the amount of people being released from prison into homelessness is on the rise, Tony said the government must deal with this issue if it wanted to end rough sleeping.
“I was in for three years, and they only started talking to me about accommodation 10 days before I was released,” he said. “If I’d been set up with a bedsit or something like that, the government would have paid less in the long run. I would have begrudgingly gone to a hostel but that wasn’t even offered. Something has to change.”
* Some names have been changed to protect anonymity

Türkiye hosts clean industry event ahead of UN climate summit

Mert Davut and Emir Yildirim
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Turkish capital Ankara hosted the Build Clean Now Türkiye Workshop on Monday to accelerate the country's clean industrial transition.
The workshop gathered officials, financial leaders and industrial project developers in a meeting organized by the Industrial Transformation Accelerator and the Boston Consulting Group in collaboration with Türkiye's Industry and Technology Ministry.
The discussions focused on the steel, cement, fertilizer and aluminum sectors.
The workshop aimed to advance final investment decisions for clean industry projects.
A summary report from the program will compile findings from the cross-sector discussions for publication ahead of the UN's COP31 climate summit in November.

She noted that global momentum is growing, with 19 final investment decisions reached for commercial-scale clean industry projects in the first half of the year, double last year's figure.
Delasalle added that Türkiye's manufacturing infrastructure within what she called "the new industrial sunbelt" and its deep commercial ties with Europe are major strengths.
The main goal in the coming years should be scaling up deep decarbonization projects in heavy industry, she said.

Did you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of math
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:00:47 UTC
02:00:47 KST

Earlier today, I set a puzzle by UCLA professor Terry Tao, who is widely regarded as one of the world’s top mathematicians.
Here it is again with solutions.
The magic money plant
In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant:
- a regular plant produces a single coin per day
- a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.)
At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each.
Suppose that I begin on Day 1 with a mother plants, b regular plants and c coins.
1. How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3?
2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X.
3. At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What are a, b and c?
Solution
1. Day 2: 4a + 2b + c. Day 3: 9a + 3b + c
Workings: At the end of day 1 the number of coins is is a + b + c. Each mother plant has also produced 2 seeds, but these have not yet grown into regular plants. On day 2, these plants produce a coin each, so there are 2a of these, added to another a from the mother plant and the a from day 1, makng 4a. The regular plants produce another coin each, making b in total to add to the b from day 1. This gets us 4a + 2b + c for day 2, and the same reasoning gets us the above expression for day 3.
2. aX2 + bX + c
We calculated for X = 1, 2 and 3. You hopefully saw the pattern emerge. The number of coins produced by the mother plant and her descendants is the square of the day.
3. a = 4, b = 2, c= 7.
When X = 10, there are 427 coins. Thus
100a + 10b + c = 427. So a, b and c must be 4, 2 and 7. The answer was in the question!
Tao said he suggested this puzzle because he likes the way it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve a problem.
“It turns out that the number of coins at day X is given by a polynomial, aX2 + bX + c. In modern algebra, we have realized that polynomials are very similar to numbers in many ways: for instance, one can add and multiply two polynomials together much as one can add and multiply numbers. For this problem, it is more than an analogy: on day 10 (X=10), the value of the polynomial aX2 + bX + c is just the three-digit number abc (assuming that a,b, and c are at most nine). So one can now read off the desired unknowns a, b, c just by inspecting the digits 4, 2, and 7 of the given coin value 427.”
The idea that polynomials behave like numbers is one of the themes of Tao’s first book for a general audience, Six Maths Essentials.
I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.
Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at the Guardian Bookshop.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

'Maxxing' crowned 2026 Word of the Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:00:21 UTC
02:00:21 KST

Dictionary.com named “maxxing” its 2026 Word of the Year, highlighting a growing internet-driven culture focused on optimising different aspects of life, the Guardian has reported.
“Maxxing,” sometimes written as “-maxxing,” is short for “maximising” and refers to doing something to the fullest or optimising it as much as possible, according to the online dictionary on Monday.
The term gained popularity among Gen Z and Gen Alpha and has evolved into a flexible slang expression that can function as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Examples include “gymmaxxing” for optimising workout routines, “healthmaxxing” for maximising health and wellness practices, “sleepmaxxing” for optimising sleep and “tokenmaxxing” for deliberately maximising the use of artificial intelligence tools.
“Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains,” Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, which operates Dictionary.com, told CBS News.
The term has also appeared in political messaging, including the use of “homelandmaxxing,” while “cozymaxxing” has been used to describe efforts to optimise leisure and comfort.
Dictionary.com said its selection was based on an analysis of search data, social media trends and news coverage, as well as the word's cultural significance.
Johnson said the dictionary's lexicographers maintain a list of words to monitor throughout the year, examining their frequency and how they reflect broader cultural developments.
The choice marks a contrast with Dictionary.com's 2025 Word of the Year, “67,” a viral expression whose meaning often remained unclear to users.
Other 2026 finalists
Dictionary.com selected finalists from internet culture, politics, technology and wider media trends.
They included “affordability,” reflecting concerns over housing, groceries, childcare and other rising costs; “data centre,” amid the expansion of infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence; “unc,” a Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang term for an older person perceived as uncool or out of touch; and “odyssey,” referring to a long and eventful journey that gained renewed cultural attention following Christopher Nolan's 2026 film adaptation of Homer's epic.

Protesters kill longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in Congo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:11 CET
02:00:11 KST

KINSHASA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Angry youths armed with machetes attacked two community health workers raising awareness about the Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo, killing one and wounding the other, according to officials and a memo seen by Reuters on Monday, in the latest in a series of attacks fueled by misinformation.
The worker who was killed was an experienced nurse who had worked at the general hospital in the town of Bafwasende in Tshopo province, and was recently tasked with helping to raise awareness about the deadly virus in the local community, where he was a well-known figure, a local official and the memo said.
“We are shocked at how the population turned against this nurse. It is impossible to believe that he was mistaken for a stranger,” a local health official told Reuters.
The attack took place on Friday afternoon, when the nurse and a colleague, a teacher also working on community outreach, stopped to check on a lot of land. A group of people building a home next door began to accuse them of spreading the disease by contaminating water.
“Here are the people that are spreading the Ebola virus through people’s toilets and rivers!” they shouted, according to the memo shared by a health official.
The angry group was joined by youths wielding machetes and batons, who attacked the pair. The nurse died on the spot before the hospital’s emergency services could reach them, the memo said, while the teacher survived.
MISINFORMATION FUELING ATTACK
Tshopo is among eight provinces in Congo that are battling a fast-spreading outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus. Congo’s public health institute on Friday reported 9,964 total confirmed cases with around a 48.6% fatality rate since the outbreak was declared in May.
Attacks on health workers have targeted hospitals, vehicles and staff involved in the Ebola response, underscoring the challenge of building trust among the population.
The local official said health workers in Bafwasende, where the latest attack took place, are sheltering at the general hospital under police guard, too afraid to go home, while the army also briefly deployed to the area.
“None of the nurses have slept at their homes because they fear for their security,” the official added.
Only days earlier, an angry mob attacked another community worker raising awareness about Ebola, and set his house on fire, the memo said.
Reuters previously reported on how the rapid spread of health misinformation posed a threat to healthcare workers in eastern Congo even before Ebola began to spread, with multiple health workers killed in Tshopo after they were accused of spreading an imaginary disease that caused male genitals to atrophy.
“The killing of a nurse yesterday in Bafwasende is a loss to the Ebola response and an even greater loss to patients,” Julien Harneis, the senior United Nations Ebola coordinator, said in a post on X on Sunday.
(Reporting by Congo newsroom and Jessica Donati; Writing by Jessica Donati; Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet, Aidan Lewis and Bill Berkrot)

Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:09 CET
02:00:09 KST

By Edward McAllister and Aleksandar Vasovic
BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing - something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.
The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
WINNERS, BUT CAN THEY STICK TOGETHER?
The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024 and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support, before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.
It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.
Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.”
REFORMING PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS
Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.
“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.
(Writing by Edward McAllister; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

Finland proposes cuts to child benefits, pensions and education to reduce debt
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:00:03 EET
02:00:03 KST

Finland's Ministry of Finance has presented around 400 options for cutting public spending and raising taxes, including abolishing child benefits, reducing pensions and restricting healthcare services, as the country prepares for fiscal adjustments of up to €11 billion after next April's parliamentary elections.
The proposals cover social security, education, healthcare, public administration and taxation. They will inform negotiations to form the next government.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The ministry stressed that the measures are alternatives for political parties to consider, not an official programme of recommended cuts.
Finland faces an estimated adjustment requirement of €8–11 billion during the next parliamentary term. Government expenditure has exceeded revenue as a share of GDP every year since 2009, according to the ministry.
"Public finances are in a weak state," said Mika Niemelä, Director General of the ministry's Budget Department, calling for changes to public spending.
Abolishing child benefits would improve public finances by approximately €1.17 billion annually by 2031, although demand for other welfare payments would increase.
Other options include removing supplements for single parents and families with several children, ending child maintenance support and abolishing the guarantee pension for people with the lowest retirement incomes.
The ministry also examined replacing student grants with loans, potentially saving €537 million annually, and freezing inflation-linked increases to pensions, benefits and public funding. A broad freeze would generate estimated annual savings of €2.1 billion by 2031.
Healthcare measures include reducing the number of wellbeing services counties, restricting emergency care and ending publicly funded dental treatment for adults. The latter would reduce expenditure by an estimated €250 million annually, subject to corresponding reductions in operating costs.
Public sector employees also face possible changes to employment conditions. Options include halving holiday bonuses, shortening annual leave, extending working hours and reducing salaries.
Education measures include reversing the extension of compulsory schooling to age 18 and reducing vocational education funding.
The ministry also examined cancelling planned increases in research and development funding. Returning expenditure to 2023 levels would save approximately €1.84 billion annually by 2031 compared with current plans.
Tax measures include raising reduced VAT rates to the standard 25.5%, generating an estimated €3.9 billion annually. Increasing VAT on food and restaurant services from 13.5% to 18% would raise approximately €1.2 billion.
Other options include higher income and property taxes, changes to dividend taxation and new taxes on air and ferry tickets.
The proposals drew criticism from trade unions and opposition politicians.
Tom-Henrik Sirviö, an economist at trade union confederation STTK, accused the ministry of prioritising reductions in public services over maintaining their funding.
He argued that higher progressive taxation and changes to corporate dividend taxation deserved greater attention.
Left Alliance MP Pia Lohikoski criticised the potential cuts to education, research and family benefits, warning that they would increase inequality.
The ministry maintained that its surveys were intended to show the available options and their estimated financial effects. It also cautioned that some measures overlap, meaning their projected savings cannot simply be added together.

German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision

German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
October 26, 2026
German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.
The collision caused damage estimated to be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.
Why are police investigating the captain?
A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.
Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.
How did the collision happen?
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.
The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.
The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.
All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.
Could more cruises be canceled?
Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.
The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.
It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.
The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

Among them were the desire for a spiral staircase inside the house, the presence of a tree integrated into the interior environment, the ability to see the slope of the roof from the inside, and the creation of a double-height space. In addition, there were general programmatic requirements: four suites, an office, spacious social areas prepared to host around forty people, strong integration with nature, and, at the same time, privacy from the gated community.

2026-10-26

01:58:19 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Monday called on those seeking to exclude Türkiye from the Eastern Mediterranean to respect the "joint will" of his country and Libya.
"I would like to remind once again those who seek to exclude Türkiye from the Eastern Mediterranean that we expect them to respect the joint will of our country and Libya," Erdogan said following a Cabinet meeting at the Presidential Complex in the capital Ankara.
Erdogan said Ankara is not seeking to outmaneuver anyone in the Eastern Mediterranean, but is focused on protecting its maritime jurisdiction rights and interests.
"We are not, so to speak, trying to score against anyone in the Eastern Mediterranean. We are only concerned with protecting our rights and interests regarding maritime jurisdiction areas," he said.
His remarks came days after Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives approved the 2019 maritime jurisdiction agreement between Türkiye and Libya.
He said Türkiye supports resolving disputes peacefully through dialogue with all coastal states and expects all parties, particularly the European Union, to demonstrate the same constructive approach.
Erdogan stressed that aggressive rhetoric detached from reality serves no one's interests, adding that Türkiye does not shape its policies in response to such statements.
Erdogan also stressed Ankara's desire to see Libya overcome its internal divisions.
"Türkiye no longer wants to see division or discord in Libya or any other Muslim country. God willing, we will see this aspiration become a reality in Libya," he said.
He said Türkiye stood firmly by the Libyan people during their most difficult times, seeking to fulfill its obligations under their brotherly ties.
Beyond the unanimous Libyan parliamentary vote, what is particularly commendable is that the agreement embodies the principle of "One Libya, One State," which Türkiye has consistently advocated since the outset, he added.
Another important aspect of the decision is that “our Libyan brothers and sisters” have acted collectively on matters of national interest despite their political differences, Erdogan said.
Erdogan also said global developments showed that preserving an environment of peace and stability at home would become increasingly important for Türkiye in the days and years ahead.
"Our sole compass in both politics and foreign policy is Türkiye's interests," Erdogan said.
 
Türkiye's 103rd birthday
Erdogan said Türkiye is committed to defending the rights of its kin, compatriots, and friends wherever they are, from the Balkans to the Turkic republics.
He added that Ankara is working to build friendly, mutually respectful relations with countries around the world, starting with its neighbors, while seeking to establish new partnerships with countries with which it had maintained limited ties for years.
Erdogan told how over the weekend, Türkiye hosted the 9th Istanbul Mediation Conference and the R4 and R4+E4 foreign ministers' meetings, adding that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is set to visit Ankara on Wednesday.
He said Türkiye would celebrate the 103rd birthday of the republic this Thursday, Oct. 29, with great enthusiasm alongside distinguished guests from the Turkic world.
"We will never hesitate to do what is right and beneficial for Türkiye and the Turkish nation, even if it comes at a cost," he added.
Turning to the upcoming 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States, Erdogan stressed the importance of unity among Turkic countries.
"As the Turkic world, I believe we will once again stand together in unity and solidarity against those who seek to undermine our unshakable brotherhood," he said.
Addressing conflicts in the wider region, he said Türkiye is working to help end violence and bloodshed.
“Türkiye is sincerely striving, with all the means at our disposal, to extinguish this fire, alleviate suffering, and stop the bloodshed, opposing those who fuel the fire in our region with expansionist ambitions," he said.
 
Türkiye aims to boost bilateral trade with Canada to $10 billion
Erdogan said since the previous Cabinet meeting, Türkiye has witnessed developments expanding its international influence.
He highlighted visits by Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet on Oct. 16 and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, calling the latter a milestone in the two countries’ 83 years of diplomatic ties.
Türkiye and Cambodia discussed cooperation in trade, investment, energy, education, and defense, while signing a military framework agreement. Türkiye and Canada signed three agreements covering defense, air transportation, and energy, and agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year.
Erdogan said Türkiye aims to increase bilateral trade with Canada from around $3 billion to $5 billion initially, and eventually to $10 billion.

Russia’s Freight Train Erupts in Flames as 39 Railcars Derail and Seven Fuel Tankers Catch Fire
A freight train derailed near Yekaterinburg in Russia’s Sverdlovsk region on October 26, sending 39 railcars off the tracks and setting seven fuel tankers ablaze. The incident triggered a large fire, with residents reporting explosions and thick black smoke rising above the railway.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russia’s Ministry of Emergency Situations (EMERCOM) on October 26, the derailment occurred at approximately 2:21 a.m. local time along the Reshety–Sedelnikovo railway section, west of Yekaterinburg.
The fire spread across approximately 1,500 square meters, prompting a large-scale emergency response involving more than 300 firefighters and rescue personnel, supported by dozens of specialized vehicles.
By 4:47 a.m., emergency crews had disconnected the burning railcars, while a recovery train moved another 54 unaffected cars to a safe distance.
Russian emergency authorities reported that the fire was fully extinguished at 12:44 p.m. local time, more than ten hours after the incident began. According to the Russian Telegram channel Astra, several of the derailed tank cars were carrying fuel and caught fire following the accident.
Witnesses reported hearing a powerful explosion before seeing flames and thick black smoke rising into the sky. One resident said the blast illuminated the surrounding area so brightly that it appeared to be daytime.
Russian authorities have not established the cause of the accident, and official emergency reports did not provide information about possible casualties.
In November 2025, Ukrainian military intelligence reported sabotaging Russia’s Trans-Siberian Railway near Sosnovka in Khabarovsk Krai, derailing a freight train and damaging the tracks. The operation reportedly disrupted a key supply route used to transport Russian military equipment and ammunition, including shipments from North Korea.

Lithuania has deployed military personnel to patrol its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region amid concerns that Russian deserters could attempt to cross illegally if Moscow launches another wave of mobilization, LRT reported, citing BNS on October 26.
Around 100 Lithuanian troops have been assigned to patrols near the town of Vištytis, with the deployment expected to continue through mid-November as a preventive measure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Authorities have increased monitoring across the entire border area, including land routes, waterways, and airspace. The additional military presence has nearly doubled patrol density along Lithuania’s roughly 300-kilometer border with Kaliningrad.
Near Vištytis, part of the border runs through a lake, where the boundary is marked by special buoys. Lithuanian authorities monitor the area using surveillance systems and patrol boats.
Border guards are preparing for possible attempts to enter Lithuania illegally from Russia. Earlier this year, two Russian citizens crossed into the country over the frozen lake.
Personnel from Lithuania’s National Defence Volunteer Forces are taking part in the mission, rotating through four border posts every four to five days.
The deployment also gives Lithuanian troops practical experience operating along the frontier and preparing defensive positions in case of a wider security escalation.
Lithuanian authorities said the increased military presence does not restrict daily life in the border community, while enhanced checks are being conducted under existing border-security procedures.

Nearly 30,000 excess cancer cases linked to inequalities across EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:56:55 UTC
01:56:55 KST

A study has estimated nearly 30,000 excess lung and cervical cancer cases in EU countries with above-average incidence rates in 2024, revealing wide disparities across the bloc.
Italian epidemiologist Diego Serraino presented the findings at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid on Monday, the ANSA news agency reported.
Based on European Cancer Information System estimates, researchers identified 29,412 excess cases in countries where incidence rates exceeded the EU average.
For lung cancer among men, rates ranged from 38 cases per 100,000 in Sweden to 130 in Hungary. Researchers estimated 11,105 excess cases across 12 countries.
Among women, Denmark recorded an estimated 83 lung cancer cases per 100,000, compared with 20 in Lithuania, with 13,441 excess cases across 11 countries.
Cervical cancer disparities
Cervical cancer rates were more than seven times higher in Romania than in Malta, at an estimated 36 cases per 100,000 women compared with five.
Researchers identified 4,866 excess cervical cancer cases across 10 countries, with Romania accounting for 2,475, more than half the total.
The researchers called for stronger anti-smoking measures to reduce lung cancer risks, alongside human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and regular screening to prevent cervical cancer and detect precancerous lesions early.

EXPLAINED: Can Oleshky Be Evacuated, Razed to Eliminate Russian Strategic Lookout?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:56:25 UTC
01:56:25 KST

A ceasefire is due to take effect along the front line near Oleshky, a city close to Kherson, on Oct. 27 to allow a humanitarian evacuation operation.
It will involve delivering humanitarian aid to the city and evacuating civilians who wish to leave.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, the idea has not been welcomed by everyone, despite support from Pope Leo XIV and US First Lady Melania Trump.
The idea that partial ceasefires and humanitarian initiatives can gradually de-escalate the Russian-Ukrainian war is not new. But in Ukraine, it is met with skepticism, particularly by people living in Kherson, a major regional center located directly across the river from Oleshky.
Why?
Key staging ground for attacks
Oleshky is a district-level city in southern Ukraine, on the left bank of the Dnipro River — Ukraine’s equivalent of the Mississippi — directly opposite Kherson, a regional capital with a population of 300,000 on the right bank. Before 2022, Oleshky had a population of more than 20,000.
During the fighting in 2022, both Oleshky and Kherson were occupied by Russian forces. The Russians were driven out of Kherson in the fall of 2022. However, Ukrainian forces were unable to cross the major water obstacle and dislodge Russian troops from Oleshky. Since then, the city has remained under Russian occupation, with the Dnipro serving as a de facto line of separation. Both Oleshky and Kherson found themselves on the front line.
Trump to Nominate Viktor Orbán as UN Secretary General
                                                                                                                                                                         Kherson and Oleshky on the Deepstate OSINT map. Green-colored – zone of Ukrainian military control; Red-colored – Russian occupied and controlled territory (Screenshot from Deepstate map)                             
Over time, Oleshky became a staging ground from which Russian artillerists, drone technicians and operators launched attacks on Kherson.
“They are simply very close. A drone just has to cross the Dnipro — and that matters for fiber-optic drones. The shorter the distance, the better. And then there is Kherson,” a military service member who spent a long time fighting on the Kherson front told Kyiv Post.
As a result, the Ukrainian forces began actively targeting Oleshky, disrupting Russian logistics.
Civilians became hostages to the fighting. Oleshky’s population has fallen to one tenth its peak during the war.
According to local Proposal, the city’s current population does not exceed approximately 2,000.
Residents face shortages of food and fresh, potable drinking water — a problem that became recurring afte the Russian military blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant in the summer of 2023, flooding large areas with contaminated reservoir water.
Fresh produce was last delivered to the city several months ago. Sometimes, the Ukrainian Armed Forces help locals by delivering food by drones, but its impossible to deliver enough food for thousands.
“It would be wrong to say that only ‘waiters’ — that is, pro-Russian people — remain in Oleshky.
Often, these are simply people who have nowhere to go and no money to leave: poor people, pensioners without relatives, and so on.
Russia uses them as cover, setting up positions directly inside their residential buildings, including private homes,” said Serhiy Nikitenko, a journalist from Kherson.
According to one service member, Ukrainian artillery crews and drone operators already know “every house in Oleshky where Russians are stationed, but they do not attack because there are civilians there.”
This is the first reason for the skepticism. Few people believe the Russians will allow civilians to evacuate from a key staging ground for attacks on Kherson.
“Once civilians leave Oleshky and the Russians no longer have a human shield in this open, steppe city, the Ukrainian military will tear them apart,” a volunteer from Kherson told Kyiv Post.
Several hundred people are expected to leave the city. However, it is unlikely that the Russians will allow everyone to evacuate.
Weapons instead of food and water
The second reason for concern is that previous attempts to establish “humanitarian corridors” to deliver supplies to various locations have generally ended with the Russian side blatantly violating the agreements and delivering … additional weapons and ammunition to the settlements instead of food and water.
“People in Kherson expect things to get even worse because, in previous cases, the Russians brought in new drone operators to replace those eliminated by Ukrainian drone crews, fuel for generators powering military equipment, ammunition, and other supplies. Everyone expects that after this ‘delivery,’ Kherson will be hit by everything that can fly, and the destruction will be even greater,” said Oleksandr Vlasov, a Kherson businessman and lifelong resident of the city.
Serhiy Nikitenko shares this view. He notes that Russian drone attacks on Kherson have become somewhat less frequent over the past month, thanks to Ukrainian drone operators who have prevented reinforcements and additional equipment from reaching Oleshky.
Meanwhile, residents are actively discussing in Kherson social media groups whether anyone will be able to monitor what exactly — and how much — the Russians bring into Oleshky through the humanitarian corridor. Their conclusion is bleak: no one will.
“The saddest thing is that the only ones who will benefit from this kind of ‘humanitarian initiative’ are the Russian military and perhaps a few dozen people who want to evacuate. For the most part, nothing will improve for Oleshky’s residents, while things will only get worse for people in Kherson,” an administrator of a Kherson social media group told Kyiv Post.
And what about the people of Kherson?
For now, sources in the city say there are no visible signs of preparations for tomorrow’s operation in Kherson itself.
However, that does not necessarily mean nothing is happening behind the scenes.
“Many Kherson residents plan to rush to their houses or apartments in the dangerous zone near the Dnipro if the ceasefire takes effect, hoping to retrieve valuables. Normally, they simply cannot access homes closer to the river,” Vlasov said.
A local activist also said he had hired a car so that, if the ceasefire comes into effect, he could “take out the household appliances” from his apartment. He has not visited it for more than two years because of the risk of drone strikes: it is too close to the Dnipro, and going outside in the area is dangerous.
However, according to locals, there are still no visible signs in Kherson of tomorrow’s operation.
Several days ago, a Russian drone struck a passenger bus in the city, killing and injuring people.
Meanwhile, residents of neighborhoods farther from the river continue to move around while constantly scanning the sky.

These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate in Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:54:22 UTC
01:54:22 KST

Israel's election is wide open. Here's what could decide Netanyahu's political fate.
Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis have started casting ballots in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents.
Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent.
Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over.
"It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute.
This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis are heading to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third.
Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes.
The Netanyahu camp
Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.
He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts.
Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.
President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.
Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat.
Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb."
Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel.
Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader.
"Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him."
"He's the king of Israel," Abraham added.
The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc"
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.
The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.
Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.
Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv."
"This time, it won't work for him," he said.
Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas — something Netanyahu has thus far blocked.
Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu.
"Eisenkot is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said.
The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft
There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side.
One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side.
Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population.
"The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute.
More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News.
"The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future."
There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales — in either direction — toward a new coalition government.
Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service.
It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners.
Not all election outcomes are neat and tidy
In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.
One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.
Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.
Plesner told CBS News that, if all the politicians running effectively stick to their campaign promises and refuse to swap sides in the event of a stalemate "we will roll into another election."
"I'm sure that most politicians are not interested in that," he added.

What the claw arcade game tells us about the cost of living crisis | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:54:18 UTC
01:54:18 KST

About a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so I was spending a lot more time in arcades. There’s a particular game involving a metal claw – it goes by the name of claw-game. You put in a pound, and try to manipulate the claw to grab a toy that is worth nothing like a pound. You would take that as the price of a bit of family fun, except the claw never grabbed a toy.
The frustration for a six-year-old was immense, every lost pound making the probably flammable stuffed hamster more urgently desirable. But it was way worse for me, because I was clinging on to some residual 80s idea of arcade-honour. Surely, after pound #7, the machine would just give you a sodding toy? That would represent an astronomical return, lessen the possibility of an adult kicking the machine to death and assure a returning market of maybe 10% of the dumbest or most spineless parents. But no, nada. No toys, ever.
So it wasn’t a good game, but it was starting to feel like a really good metaphor for the economy. This was in the twilight period between 2015 and Brexit, after which politics stopped troubling itself with day-to-day liveability. Previously, if you studied hard you got a job, then if you worked hard, you could afford to live; and in the fullness of time, if you met another person who worked hard, you could have a family and afford to feed them – this was basically the honour-code of capitalism. But it was breaking down and nobody wanted to admit it.
Trade unions noticed: the TUC crunched the numbers in 2014 and found that only one in 40 new jobs were full time. The geographer Danny Dorling noticed that a fifth of people needed a cash benefit to make rent, and average house prices were nearly nine times average salaries in England and Wales. The NHS noticed, in the same year, inasmuch as the number of children with vitamin D deficiency and rickets had tripled since 2009. A lot of people privately thought, “This whole thing is rigged,” though, as far as I know, I alone noticed the irresistible likeness to the Ramsgate arcade.
Scroll forward a decade and people are much more public about their noticing – but expectations have changed and with them, the language. We talk about a cost of living crisis, but we don’t cast ourselves as agents in the economy, whose wages aren’t keeping pace with prices. Rather, we’re a bunch of luckless dopes to whom bad things keep happening. The New Economics Foundation thinktank, with Best for Britain, has dropped into these new times an “attainability index”. It takes the wage data from the past 20 years and calculates how many hours you would have to work to attain a set of things: a holiday, a night out, an outfit, a car.
The figures aren’t at all surprising. Low-paid workers have their wages mostly eaten up by essentials. Social participation is sporadic, holidays out of reach. A secondary school teacher looks as though they are doing OK, because they would only have to work 23 hours to afford a ticket to a festival. But that would assume they are not going to do any other discretionary spending whatsoever.
Just about the only things that have gone down in price in real terms, over the past 20 years, are gym memberships, budget clothes and meal deals, which makes sense. In all the crazy supermarket moments of this decade, the remarkable value of a prawn mayo sandwich, as long as you get some crisps and a Red Bull at the same time, has often felt like the only thing standing between us and revolution.
The important thing isn’t the numbers (no offence, researchers, your data is beautiful) but the fact that everyone is experiencing the same degradation. The pilot of 2026 is as far removed in his or her housing prospects from the pilot of 2006, as is the chef or the accountant from theirs. So much political rhetoric goes into the creation of rivalrous silos – the woke v the anti-woke, the liberal elite v the left-behind – all of it constructed to mask the fact that everybody’s expectations have been thwarted for two decades straight. Realising this might shunt the discourse out of phase “get mad” into phase “get even”.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist
On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan.

Anthropic’s IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:53:51 UTC
01:53:51 KST

Anthropic’s IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs
The filing sets up the company for a wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing SpaceX’s IPO.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has filed papers for what could be the biggest ever initial public offering (IPO) of stock, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
The filing on Monday sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86bn.
The filing comes weeks after chief executive and cofounder Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as does its final valuation and offering price. But even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and cofounder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.
The prospectus highlights the AI company’s rapid growth over the past year, fuelled by Big Tech’s breakneck spending that has driven a rally in AI stocks, while raising concerns about lofty valuations and rising debt.
The company also flagged growing risks from AI technology, underscoring concerns over its potential to cause harm, which had led Amodei to call for a slowdown in development of advanced models.
Anthropic’s net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $80.7bn, largely due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into the company’s shares. Revenue in the period was about $16.3bn.
The company’s revenue grew a staggering 1,368 percent in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but warned in the prospectus that the revenue growth rate could decline over time and fluctuate occasionally.
The IPO, which is anticipated to be before Thanksgiving in the US, late next month, is expected to establish Anthropic, the AI lab behind the viral Claude models, as a benchmark for how Wall Street values leading AI companies, including rival OpenAI.
The IPO push comes despite a once-busy autumn listing calendar thinning out as choppy markets prompt companies to delay their offerings. Analysts said that would give Anthropic access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions.
Growing investor unease with the debt-fuelled AI investment boom has led to a global selloff in AI and tech stocks, as they start to doubt whether the trillions spent on data centres, chips and computing capacity will generate fast returns to support lofty valuations. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have added to their caution.
However, tech companies are still hungry for cash. Meta is aiming to raise up to $95bn in its largest-ever equity fundraising, while SpaceX has inked a $40bn deal with Apollo to lease AI chips and server hardware.
Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a recent investor event, Reuters reported.
The prospectus also details the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI, from potential misuse and security threats to concerns that advanced systems could produce outputs that “could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative”.
“Anthropic’s IPO will establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure build-out,” IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
“Its success would not necessarily benefit every AI business equally,” he added.
Balancing AI’s promises and perils
Anthropic said that more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 percent of Global 2000 firms were customers generating at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30.
The IPO comes as Anthropic’s own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviours including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation.
The findings have fuelled concerns about how companies can keep powerful AI systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially.
The prospectus also highlighted risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including behaviour “resembling blackmail”.
“Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate and implement corresponding safety, alignment and security measures,” it said.
The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud service providers, such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical parts of its infrastructure. These relationships can create “dependencies and potential vulnerabilities”, it said.
Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq after the IPO closes under the ticker symbol “ANT”.
The filing did not reveal the terms of its offering, including the number of shares it plans to sell and the proposed price range.
Red-hot growth
Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers, was valued at $965bn in May in a funding round that drew some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
Amazon and Google were among Anthropic’s early strategic partners, investing billions of dollars in the startup while providing the cloud infrastructure needed to train and deploy Claude models.
“We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialisation, electricity, semiconductors and the internet,” the prospectus said.
The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were named as the lead banks for the IPO alongside 20 others as underwriters. Morgan Stanley will act as a stabilisation agent, overseeing the stock’s early trading.
The roles mark another major win for Goldman and Morgan Stanley as they also led SpaceX’s IPO.

EU country turns to AI to slash government workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:53:36 UTC
01:53:36 KST

EU country turns to AI to slash government workforce
The Netherlands has unveiled plans to cut around 25,000 full-time government positions by 2035, turning to artificial intelligence and sweeping administrative reforms to reduce costs and bureaucracy.
Announced on Monday, the overhaul aims to save €900 million ($1 billion) by next year, with annual savings projected to reach €3.5 billion by 2035. The job cuts will be phased in over several years, with police and security services exempt.
Planned measures include simplifying regulations, reducing advisory bodies, standardizing IT systems, and expanding digital services.
The plan follows years of rapid growth in the Dutch civil service. The central government workforce reached a record 160,000 positions in 2025, an increase of more than 40% since 2018, according to official figures.
State Secretary Eric van der Burg said excessive rules, exceptions, and procedures had made it increasingly difficult for the government to address problems, while mounting costs demanded action.
“We cannot continue to do what we did,” he said, calling for a government that is “simpler, smarter and smaller.”
Other European countries are also embracing AI to streamline public administration.
Denmark announced plans last year to free up 50 million working hours annually by 2035 through AI, equivalent to roughly 30,000 full-time positions, without committing to corresponding job cuts.
Albania went a step further in September 2025, appointing an AI-generated virtual minister to help combat corruption in public procurement. However, the country’s AI procurement system had yet to be rolled out as of October.
The push comes as rapid advances in AI fuel concerns about widespread disruption to employment.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in July that the transition would be “a bumpy road,” predicting that AI would eventually outperform humans in any job.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also warned of major upheaval in the labor market, while arguing that certain professions, including caregiving, should remain “human reserved” even if AI becomes capable of performing them.
