Vučić Out, Students In: Still, No Sanctions Against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:52:31 UTC
01:52:31 KST

Serbia’s Student List won the Oct. 25 parliamentary election, ending 14 years of what many described as Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić’s dictatorship.
Tens of thousands of people in Serbia and abroad rallied behind the list, made up of students, professors and doctors, hoping to free the country from corruption and political pressure on its institutions. The country secured a historic win in its highest turnout of 70%, the biggest Serbia has seen in nearly three decades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Yet even as the result brings Serbia a step closer to the European, the list has said it will not impose sanctions on Russia, despite Vučić’s claims that it would do so within months.
Speaking to RT Balkan, a Serbian-language broadcaster run by the Russian state-owned network RT (formerly Russia Today), Professor Jovo Bakić of the Student List claimed that Belgrade respects Russia, “both as a great power and as our historically important partner, and in many cases even our protector,” adding that “there will be no changes.”
He claimed that sanctions from such a small country would essentially change nothing for Moscow, since even the entire EU had failed to harm it.
However, the move would damage bilateral relations, he said, adding that Serbia knows what “kind of misery that [sanctions] is,” having lived through UN sanctions during the 1990s.
“I said this during the election campaign, and I’m saying it after the elections,” Bakić said, echoing the Student List’s earlier position.
Putin Just Lost His Key Ally in Europe. Here’s What Happens Next
“The Republic of Serbia will retain its principled stance on not introducing restrictive measures toward the Russian Federation,” the list previously said in a statement on Sept. 30.
With the list holding an absolute majority of nearly 140 seats, the next step is a presidential election, which Serbia’s constitution requires by Dec. 26. Until then, Ana Brnabić of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), closely linked to Vučić, is serving as acting president.
Vučić concedes, but vows to fight back
Vučić conceded defeat, saying his coalition, United Serbia, won 105 seats.
The name of his coalition closely echoes United Russia, which won the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections, held in Russia and occupied territories of Ukraine, without the main election-monitoring body of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).
The same Duma elections that the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) deemed illegitimate earlier this month.
Vučić’s concession quickly proved to be anything but a surrender. He claimed that “you will see, in six months, no one will be happy and joyful anymore,” adding that “from tonight, we start preparing. We are going to defeat them.”
He also blamed foreign forces for his defeat, echoing Russia’s similar rhetoric towards the West.
“What brought us down is this verified revolution, which they carried out with direct support from various European countries, and the deep American state, the one against [US] President [Donald] Trump,” Vučić said.
“I congratulate them, even though they are just executors of work. Executors of dirty work, which someone else designed to bring down a sovereign country. For a moment you have succeeded. For how long, we shall see,” he continued, as if years of intense public frustration with corruption had not been enough to produce such a result.
From a collapsed canopy to a new regime
The Student List grew out of the Nov. 1, 2024, collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, north of Belgrade, which killed 16 people.
Four children were killed as well, with the youngest victim aged 5.
The tragedy sparked mass protests across Serbia, which escalated over Vučić’s refusal to accept responsibility and the use of a sound cannon against the students, a high-frequency weapon that causes disorientation, nausea and panic.
The movement eventually formed its own list, led by Novi Sad cardiologist Ilija Srdanović.
Its program, the “Student Plan,” has 11 points in three sections, aiming not just to change the people that hold power, but to dismantle decades of systemic corruption.
“Serbia or the Mafia” pledges an independent anti-corruption police unit, a purge of Interior Ministry officers tied to organized crime or the protest crackdowns, confiscation of illegally acquired assets, audits of opaque state projects and an end to political control over the media regulator and public broadcaster RTS.
“Knowledge Is Power” promises merit-based public hiring, free textbooks for all primary and secondary students and support for startups, entrepreneurs and farmers to move Serbia beyond a cheap-labor economy.
“Serbia Grows With Us” would cap fixed-term employment at 12 months instead of 24, curb the import lobby’s grip on food prices, offer affordable housing to young families and essential workers, lower medicine prices and reopen rural clinics.
Vučić informed Putin about his resignation
Vučić, first elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022, signed his resignation live on television on Sept. 26, cutting his final term short by eight months.
Following months of what could be described as world’s biggest anti-government protests, he stepped down to campaign “as an ordinary citizen,” planning to become prime minister if SNS won.
On the same day of his resignation, Vučić held a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which he emphasized Serbia’s energy partnership with Moscow, while also boasting their 14 year long friendship.
In a video address posted on social media, Vučić said that he secured a “good and low gas price” of €318 (roughly $361) per 1,000 cubic meters (264.172 gallons), far below the market rate of €868 ($987) at the time.
Currently, Serbia remains one of the few European countries that have not joined EU sanctions on Russia, and it continues to import discounted Russian gas and oil.
Vučić has long insisted no sanctions would be introduced while he was in power. On election night, he claimed the students would impose them by March or April, something the list had ruled out a month earlier.
A fresh choice ahead
Around the same time of Vučić’s resignation, Russian-state-owned media TASS reported that while analysts expected no major foreign policy shift, a student win could move Serbia closer to Western positions.
Polina Sokolova, a research fellow at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, said a Serbian turn against Russia under Western pressure “cannot be excluded.”
According to TASS, this is because European countries, “which have been Ukraine’s main sponsors, do not demonstrate any intention to enter substantive negotiations.” However, EU leaders consistently urge Russia to agree to a ceasefire; it is the Kremlin that has rebuffed every such proposal so far.
The argument mirrors Vučić’s own claim about “dirty work” designed abroad.
However, despite Vučić’s decades-long ties to Moscow, Serbia has backed Ukraine on several main issues, including territorial integrity on Crimea and Donbas. Belgrade has also provided Kyiv with non-military assistance throughout the war, which has drawn sharp criticism from Russia.
Similarly, Vučić showed support to Kyiv by attending the Carpathian Eight (C8) initiative, launched by President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 18 in Bukovel, western Ukraine.
“We have much to offer - from railway lines and roads to more open borders,” Vučić said, signaling openness to future cooperation with Ukraine across several sectors.
Results welcomed by European leaders
Several European leaders welcomed the result.
“This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine is ready to continue expanding cooperation with Belgrade.
In a telephone call with the Student List, Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar compared Serbia’s elections to its own, held earlier in the year. “I assured them of Hungary’s support,” he said. “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
Meanwhile, President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said that Europe stands “ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos reiterated that Europe is ready to support the new government in progressing on its EU path, citing “their [Serbia’s] demands for the rule of law, the fight against corruption and free media.”
While cheap gas could keep Serbia close for now, should the EU membership ever demand a choice, the country may have to take a stronger stance towards Russia.
The question now is how the students, who campaigned for democracy and freedom, will steer Serbia toward European standards while still nurturing its friendship with Moscow and avoiding sanctions.
The Kremlin urged Serbia’s incoming leaders to maintain ties with Russia, claiming that cooperation “is in Serbia’s interests.”

Established Long-Term Relationship status for service personnel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:52:26 GMT
01:52:26 KST

Established Long-Term Relationship status for service personnel
The process for recording and approving a defence-recognised Established Long-Term Relationship (LTR(E)).
Established Long-Term Relationship (LTR(E))
An LTR(E) is a relationship between two people that has continued for a long time and has the intent of permanence, but does not have the legal recognition of marriage or civil partnership.
Having accurate data on LTR(E) relationships enables defence understand and meet the couple’s needs.
Benefits of LTR(E) status
Service personnel may seek LTR(E) status for:
- eligibility for service housing
- transfer of leave (for dual-serving LTR(E) couples)
- joint career management discussions (for dual-serving LTR(E) couples)
How to apply for LTR(E) status
Application form
Service personnel must complete the application form available from their HR admin team, or at Annex A within the and provide supporting evidence.
Only one service person within a dual-serving couple needs to apply for LTR(E) status. If approved, Joint Personnel Administration (JPA) will be updated for both partners.
The form must be signed by both the serving person and their partner, whether or not the couple is dual-serving.
Evidence requirements
To support an LTR(E) application, applicants must provide:
- one piece of evidence from Section A, or
- 3 pieces of evidence: two from Section B and one from Section C
Section A
Proof of shared children (e.g. joint birth certificates, adoption papers).
Section B (evidence must be more than 365 days old)
Evidence of long-term commitments, such as joint financial, domestic, legal, or child-related responsibilities.
Examples include but are not limited to:
- joint tenancy/mortgage agreements
- shared utility bills or financial accounts
- named beneficiary on life insurance or Armed Forces Pension Scheme
- having Recorded Long Term Relationship (LTR(R)) status - this is achieved when a service person’s partner is added to the ‘emergency contacts’ section on JPA for more than 365 days
Section C (evidence must be less than 90 days old)
Evidence that demonstrates ongoing commitment, such as utility bills or bank statements.
Exceptional circumstances
Where a service person cannot satisfy the qualifying criteria for LTR(E) they may submit casework to the Armed Forces Families and Safeguarding (AFFS) team via: People-AFFS-LTR-Casework@mod.gov.uk.
Submissions must include the application form, alternative supporting evidence and justification for the alternative evidence.
A service person may not meet the criteria if:
- HR cannot verify the provided evidence
- the evidence specified is unavailable
Contact
For queries or casework submissions, email: People-AFFS-LTR-Casework@mod.gov.uk

Pope says happy to return to South America after trip confirmed
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:52:12 CET
01:52:12 KST

Pope Leo XIV said Monday he was happy
to be able to return to the continent where he lived after his
November 6-17 trip to South America was confirmed after his
recent lung-cancer surgery including Peru, where he worked as a
missionary for many years before becoming a bishop there and
whose citizenship he holds along with his US one.
                                    
"I am happy to be able to return to the continent where I
experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a communiqué
from the Holy See Press Office, which confirmed that the Pope's
trip to South America will proceed as scheduled.
                                    
"May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one
another, to strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters,
and to renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy!
"The Pope," the statement reads, "is following medical
recommendations with scrupulous care and attention, while
remaining deeply determined to continue serving the Church.
                                    
"The Holy Father looks forward to this journey with great joy
and enthusiasm; it will offer an opportunity to strengthen the
bonds of communion with local Churches, encourage the faithful
in their mission, bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to
the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encounter their
faith, and share the hope and peace that Christ brings to our
world."
Leo's apostolic journey to South America his sixth international
trip.
                                    
He will be in Uruguay November 6-8, visiting Montevideo,
Paysandú and Florida, then travel to Argentina, where he will go
to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján November 8-11, and
subsequently stay in Peru until November 17.
                                    
The American pontiff spent large chunks of his life in Peru
after first going there as a missionary in the 1980s and served
as the bishop of Chiclayo between 2015 and 2023.
                                    
He also acquired Peruvian citizenship.
                                    
Chiclayo and the capital Lima are among the Peruvian cities he
will travel to.
                                    
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis never returned to his homeland of
Argentina during his 12-year pontificate.
                                    
Confirming the trip, the Holy See Press Office said: "Dr. Luigi
Carbone confirms that the Holy Father's post-operative recovery
continues to progress, and the latest medical examinations
confirm his good health.
                                    
"Given the current clinical picture and the results of the
diagnostic tests and laboratory analyses performed, there are no
contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking the
upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned.
                                    
"Accordingly, the Holy See Press Office confirms that the
Apostolic Journey of Pope Leo XIV to Uruguay, Argentina, and
Peru—scheduled for November 6-17, 2026—will take place according
to the previously published itinerary."

The Diesel Diversion: Trump’s Faulty Attempt to Blame Inflation on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:50:55 UTC
01:50:55 KST

The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States since 2022 is expected to arrive in New York within the next few weeks, but its 40,000-ton cargo amounts to less than two hours of American consumption. The shipment will barely register at the pump—and it answers the wrong question, since what drove American diesel past $6 a gallon was never a shortage of Russian supply, but historic bottlenecks from the war in the Middle East.
Recall what happened between May and July of this year, when Ukraine launched one of the most destructive phases of its energy war against Moscow, sending waves of drones attacking massive Russian refineries at Kirishi, Ryazan, Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, and Omsk one after another. If Russian refining capacity governed American fuel costs, prices at U.S. truck stops should have exploded. Instead, American diesel fell by $1.06 a gallon.
With the midterms days away and September’s consumer price index showing fuel oil up a staggering 74% on the year, President Donald Trump has cast Kyiv as the architect of American inflation. “What’s happened in Russia with Ukraine has been really the biggest problem for diesel,” he said in the Oval Office on September 30 before naming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the culprit, telling reporters that Zelenskyy “wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The charge is politically convenient but economically backward. Until this month’s waiver, Russian fuel had been barred from American ports since 2022, meaning Ukrainian strikes have reached U.S. pumps only through the gradual tightening of global supply. The real shockwave runs through the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran can choke off a fifth of the world’s seaborne crude overnight. Diesel was $3.48 a gallon in January and still under $4 the week American and Israeli bombs fell on Iran. When Tehran closed the Strait, the price jumped 96 cents in a single week.
From that moment, the U.S. price line has moved in lockstep with the Iran war—cresting at the April ceasefire, dipping only after the June truce, climbing after the pause in hostilities collapsed in July. By September, the tanker war had driven diesel to a record $6.53.
Ukraine’s unceasing drone campaign has at most modestly nudged up the global floor, while the Iran war has steered every spike and plunge.
By authorizing the sale of Russian diesel, Washington provided Moscow the relief that sanctions are meant to withhold. And when Zelenskyy refused to halt strikes on Russian refineries, Americans throttled the Starlink defenses only they can supply.
Now, Ukraine and its European backers are left with a narrowing set of options. Pulled with discipline, however, the levers they hold can still keep Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on a tightening clock.
A cure that feeds the disease
After an Oct. 9 phone call with Putin, President Trump directed the Treasury to reopen American ports to Russian diesel through April 2027. On paper, the deal promises 4.8 million tons of fuel. In reality, the promise amounts to roughly 10 days of U.S. demand, and analysts doubt that Moscow can ship even that much after months of Ukrainian strikes on the refineries that would fill the tankers.
Carnegie’s Sergey Vakulenko calls the arrangement “largely for show,” yet for a Kremlin watching its September oil and gas tax revenues plunge 22% year-over-year, the spectacle is the prize. What former U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul condemned as “absolutely deplorable,” and Zelenskyy called “a gift to Putin,” was followed a week later by a concession of far greater strategic weight. Two days before the Russia provisions of the Graham sanctions act were scheduled to bite, an executive order waived them. In a single stroke, the White House neutralized both the 100 and 500% tariffs and stripped out the clause locking existing sanctions in place.
While Moscow collected waivers, Kyiv got the vise. Washington announced an “energy ceasefire” the Kremlin never bothered to acknowledge. After Zelenskyy held his fire for three days, Russia pounded Ukrainian energy infrastructure 76 times in the week that followed. By the Ukrainian president’s account—one Secretary of State Marco Rubio denies—the American satellite alerts that warn Ukraine when a Russian missile is in the air went dark for a period of time. Procurement contracts required for the transfer of an allied-funded batch of Patriot interceptors reportedly sat unsigned on the desk of U.S. Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth.
Meanwhile, the speed of Starshield datalinks, the military-grade Starlink network that Ukraine’s drone units rely on, was throttled. Starshield datalinks need to operate at speeds up to 550 km/h (342 mph) to effectively intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed and Geran drones.
The 160 km/h (100 mph) cap was apparently instituted—simply insufficient to protect Ukrainian civilians from Russian ballistic missiles.
Trump and Elon Musk finger-pointed at each other for the restriction. Trump has reportedly since called Musk to lift the cap. U.S. officials say service is running more normally. Kyiv says the limit remained in place into this weekend, with President Zelenskyy tweeting on October 24 that service has now been restored.
The Trump Administration should also allow Ukraine to use the system in Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers. Take out the archer, not the arrows.
What Ukraine can still do
Washington’s squeeze rests on the premise that Kyiv is losing and must be forced to settle, but the front-line situation does not support that notion. Russian forces have made virtually no net territorial gains in 2026 despite suffering more than 40,000 casualties a month since July. At this year’s rate of advance, we estimate that Moscow would need 60 years to capture the rest of Donetsk Oblast.
In fact, the momentum has tilted the other way, with Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as the exceptionally innovative Operation Vivaldi. For months, Kyiv’s forces have killed or seriously wounded more Russian soldiers than the Kremlin can recruit. Closing that gap would require a mass mobilization Putin has been afraid to order, wary of unrest in a country reeling from the fuel shortages created by Ukraine’s refinery strikes. The myth of an inevitable Russian victory amounts to a Kremlin sales pitch aimed at Washington, and the very energy campaign the White House wants to shut down is what keeps Putin boxed in.
Nor can the White House physically switch that campaign off. For all the damage the administration’s freeze inflicted on Ukraine’s air shield, enough Ukrainian drones and missiles were able to reach their targets. Washington’s leverage is entirely defensive, whereas Ukraine’s offensive reach is built at home and in Europe. The 1,000-strong armada that struck St. Petersburg in mid-October was built around FP-1 drones, 90% of which are Ukrainian-made, flying into Russian airspace where Starlink does not function, and Starshield caps do not apply. The E.U.’s Kaja Kallas has rightly defended Ukraine’s actions as legitimate self-defense.
By Putin’s estimate, the wider Ukrainian campaign has cost Russia about 1% of GDP, more than a year of Russian growth, as the central bank’s fight against punishing inflation pushed interest rates to their highest level since the early 2000s. The true toll is almost certainly worse. As we have previously argued, even after Moscow blacked out mandatory economic data, the IMF continues to recycle unverified Kremlin figures to dub Russia the world’s fourth-largest economy at peak output, despite ranking just 51st in GDP per capita.
In 2022, hundreds of billions of dollars abandoned the Russian economy after our team helped spur the withdrawal of more than 1,000 major corporations following the invasion. Firms that curtailed operations outperformed those that did not, in terms of market performance.
Even where Kyiv chooses to look beyond oil, its domestic weapons require no American permission and offend no American farmer. Homegrown Long Neptune missiles have already crippled four of the Black Sea Fleet’s Kalibr missile carriers and recently destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, proving that Ukraine can systematically hunt the launchers, airfields, and factories that fire on its cities. The same freedom of action applies to striking Russian data centers, an asymmetric campaign that an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute judges lopsidedly in Kyiv’s favor because Ukraine’s critical data is already safely hosted abroad.
Holding an offensive campaign that Washington wants to stop but cannot physically block changes the terms of diplomacy. Toward the White House, Kyiv should act as a customer rather than a supplicant. Any pause in energy strikes should be treated strictly as an opportunity to make a deal—offered only in exchange for verified Russian reciprocity and binding, written guarantees from Washington on Patriot interceptors, satellite-based missile launch warnings, and uncapped Starshield access, a bargain of the kind legislators like Senator Roger Wicker and organizations like the Foundation for Defense of Democracies have urged.
What Europe must now do
Kyiv’s balancing act rests on a hard truth in Brussels. Europe can replace most of America’s financial support and much of its weaponry within two years, but it cannot replace Patriot-class interceptors, space-based ballistic-missile warning, or Starlink-scale connectivity this winter. The vulnerability is partly of Europe’s own making after three decades of over-reliance on American dominance, and it now collides with an American arsenal running dry.
The on-again, off-again war with Iran that drove U.S. diesel to $6.53 is also the conflict that emptied the Pentagon’s magazines. According to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the Gulf conflict consumed roughly two-thirds of America’s Patriot inventory and more than a third of its THAAD interceptors, leaving a rebuild measured in years at the exact moment Ukraine’s Patriot stockpiles are reportedly exhausted. Europe’s scramble to build sovereign air defenses—four SAMP/T NG batteries currently on order, a 10-nation FREYJA program aiming for a first intercept in mid-2027, and the diplomatic courtship of Japan, the sole non-American producer of PAC-3 interceptors—is real and necessary, but slow. Every euro spent on European interceptors is one less dollar earned in Washington, and one fewer armament President Trump can delay.
A similar bottleneck applies to space. While Europe’s radar and optical satellites could potentially replace American targeting imagery within weeks, OneWeb and the E.U.’s GovSatcom offer only a partial hedge against a Starlink slowdown. And a European satellite constellation capable of warning of a ballistic launch probably will not exist before the 2030s.
Because Europe cannot buy its way out of those technical bottlenecks overnight, it must lean aggressively into the financial and maritime levers it controls today. The E.U.’s €90 billion loan covers 2026 and much of 2027, and when the remaining €70 billion gap comes to a head at the December European Council, moving the €202 billion in frozen Russian assets out of Belgium offers the clearest route around Belgium’s objections. Better still, a full ban on shipping services for Russian crude, along with expanding the shadow-fleet boardings that European navies have already begun, could squeeze Moscow’s war chest at almost no cost to European taxpayers.
Ukraine’s most decisive advantage, though, is found on the factory floor. Domestic drone production has surged 370% this year, and the Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missile costs just under $600,000, less than a fifth of an American Tomahawk’s $3.5 million price tag. By guaranteeing a loan to the Flamingo’s manufacturer, Denmark has laid out a blueprint for surviving an erratic Washington: European capital behind Ukrainian weapons.
The lesson of the lever
A bitter paradox governs the current battlefield. The offensive campaign squeezing Moscow is the one Washington objects to, while the defenses faltering over Ukrainian cities are the ones only the U.S. can supply. By blaming Kyiv for an energy shock originating in the Persian Gulf, the White House has struck a bargain that lowers no prices at home, replenishes the aggressor’s coffers abroad, and teaches the Kremlin that American sanctions expire if Putin simply waits them out. Such a posture delivers neither peace nor strength.
Ukraine is akin to the Biblical hero David, who, through cunning, triumphed over the lumbering giant Goliath. Moscow's “card hand” is neither the colossus Trump believes it to be nor the colossus its propaganda advertises. Russia is not remotely an economic superpower. Beneath its vast map lies a concentrated population—over 80% of the population lives in the 20% not plagued by extreme cold, permafrost, and poor soil—and a brittle economy dependent on raw materials the world can increasingly buy elsewhere, backed by a military with a long history of failing to subdue smaller, more determined foes, from Japan in 1905 and Poland in 1920 to Finland in 1940 and the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s. Sheer land mass has never guaranteed victory when the smaller side is fighting for its existence.
The silver lining is that Washington’s attempted coercion is forging the European autonomy it assumed would never materialize. If European leaders withstand Russian pressure over the next 18 months and resist the political disarray stoked by Kremlin disinformation, the continent will emerge a far more formidable power—proving the quip circulating in allied capitals that Europe has found no better unifier since Charlemagne than Donald Trump. Europe, Ukraine, and the world now know what an American guarantee is worth when the guarantor changes its mind, and Washington is about to learn that leverage, like interceptors, is a stock that depletes with every use.
As Mark Twain advised, “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight; it’s the size of the fight in the dog.”

Worried about what your phone 
is doing to your brain? 
This new fad will make it worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:29 UTC
01:49:29 KST

Seven or eight years ago, a new kind of televisual entertainment was born in China. Microdramas: Over-the-top, soap opera-type series with splashy, schlocky premises such as infidelity, arranged marriage and secret billionairehood, in which each episode is a mere 60 to 90 seconds long, took off there among an audience of the phone-addicted.
And now, as with many cultural phenomena that start in China, microdramas have made it over to the UK. The form is forecast to take in US$1.5 billion in revenue in the US by the end of this year. Channel 4 announced recently that it was launching its first microdrama, and the UK is already leading Europe in terms of microdrama-watching, with 8.2 million of us tuning in to these things every month.
Numbers such as this give me a queasy, vertiginous feeling about the vast difference in possible human experiences existing alongside each other at the same time. What do you mean, millions and millions of people are watching this stuff that seems, to me, catastrophically brainless and objectively bad? Who? What do they eat for breakfast? What do they dream of at night?
Illustration: Mountain People
Before I read those numbers, I had only seen tiny snippets of microdramas embedded into news pieces about the phenomenon. I wanted to know what it was like to actually watch one. I downloaded ReelShort, one of the apps that hosts microdramas exclusively, and flicked through the homepage. Recommended for me were Trapped in the Boss’s Embrace, I Had a Baby Without You and Carrying His Triplets, Becoming His Wifey. I went to the “HOT” tab and selected the one with the most convoluted title, Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, although Let Me Taste Your Husband also appealed.
In Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, it is legible right from the get-go who the bad guy is (the ex) and who the good guy is (the protagonist) and what is going to happen, not least because it is right there in the title. The question of “what is going to happen?” that is supposed to drive you into the next episode, the question that has driven all narrative since time immemorial, is rendered oddly moot.
There is no setup, no world-building, no padding whatsoever, just rapidly cut dramatic denouements over and over again: someone being cheated on, someone slapping someone else, a car window getting smashed, a new love interest being introduced, a sex scene. All of this happens in the first three minutes of the series. Helpless women swoon over geometrically jawed hunks on sets lit like a morgue and say exactly what they are thinking in voiceover, so that there is no room at all for nuance to creep in and engage your brain while you watch.
You can watch the first few episodes of any given series for free, and then you hit a paywall, which you can get around by watching ads for another form of phone brain rot: colour-matching mobile games. I have been told by loved ones before now that I couldn’t be a newsreader or a jury member because I can’t keep my emotions off my face. This is true. I caught sight of myself in my phone screen reflection while watching microdramas and saw there a person who looked as if they’d just spotted a pile of dog sick on the carpet.
I’m not incapable of enjoying bad television. I do not come here having descended from a lofty perch of only watching heritage BBC adaptations of classic novels or whatever. My appetite for dreck is hearty enough. But, my God — and can there be such an entity in a universe producing microdramas? — this stuff is awful. Flagrantly so, though, to the degree that I start to feel there is something wrong with me for desiring quality in this format.
Or I sense that I’ve done something wrong by intentionally going to watch one. In a piece for the New York Times Magazine, writer Daniel Kolitz described these shows as happening to people “like a food-borne illness,” rather than something that people elect to get into. They appear on your phone screen, and there you are, watching them in a half-conscious malaise while you wait for the day to end.
I would love for this kind of thing to go the way of non-fungible tokens: something we all had to hear about for a short time and that are now patently doomed to the scrapheap of short-lived modern Internet detritus.
Maybe this is partly because my own feelings about Internet detritus have changed lately. Whereas in the past I had a known, but not felt, understanding that the allure of apps and games and scrolling on my phone was bad for me, nowadays I am regularly experiencing real, bodily panic that my brain is being atrophied. I am scared of my phone, and my sick want for it. So the emergence of an all-new, even more terrible way of being on your phone does provoke the reactionary in me. “Just let people enjoy things!” a better person might think. Not this time.
Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist.

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has dominated the campaign narrative over the past month, but has also galvanized opposition supporters to mobilize quietly, a Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmaker said.
“Ocean Wave (洋流)” — a play on the last character of Shen’s name, which means “ocean” (洋), emerged last month as Shen campaigned, quickly becoming a dominant theme, KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said.
KMT and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) supporters did not disappear, but went quiet and were working behind the scenes, Lee said.
Photo: I-hwa Cheng, AFP
Shen’s Ocean Wave has heightened opposition supporters’ sense of urgency, she said, adding that the relative silence of KMT and TPP supporters was also reflected in Taipei mayoral election polls.
KMT Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) supporters are calling friends and relatives to solicit votes and sharing messages in online groups to urge people to vote, a marked departure from their previously more passive attitude, she said.
The greatest impact of the Ocean Wave was in Taipei, with its influence diminishing as it spread to other administrative regions, she said.
DPP candidates in other administrative regions naturally wanted to capitalize on its popularity, but were also concerned about a possible backlash, she said.
Elections are similar to marathons, with the first candidate to cross the finish line on Nov. 28 emerging as the winner, Lee said.
With a month remaining before voting day, the greatest advantages of Chiang were his personal qualities, charisma and record in office, she said, adding that she believed Taipei voters would make the smartest choice.
The rapid rise of the Ocean Wave is a case study in campaign strategy, said Chang Yuan-hsiang (張元祥), an adjunct assistant professor in Soochow University’s Department of Political Science.
Despite the unfavorable political landscape for his party in Taipei, Shen has had the momentum, combining scrutiny of municipal governance with digital media and large public gatherings, Chang said.
The movement had also disrupted Chiang’s re-election campaign, he added.
Although the Ocean Wave has downplayed Shen’s previous emphasis on resisting China and defending Taiwan, his personal stance and public image remained clear, Chang said.
Beyond criticism of municipal governance, the movement’s core driving force is the momentum generated during last year’s mass recall campaign, he said.
The Ocean Wave has made a major impact on online discussions, news coverage and opinion polls in a short period, prompting KMT supporters facing unfavorable political conditions to conceal or suppress their views in what is known as the “spiral of silence,” Chang said.
The Ocean Wave resembles the “bandwagon effect” in elections, he said, adding that the outcome on Nov. 28 would depend on whether the wave’s momentum translated into actual voting behavior.
Hostility among supporters of the DPP and the KMT-TPP alliance remained high, meaning their willingness to vote would likely be strong, Chang said.
However, centrist voters are increasingly weary of political turmoil and therefore less inclined to vote, he added.
Next month’s local elections would still largely be a contest between the parties’ established support bases, Chang said.

Beijing is boosting ‘Ocean Wave’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:26 UTC
01:49:26 KST

Since last month, the most eye-catching phenomenon in Taipei’s politics has been the “Ocean Wave” (洋流) — officially called “Taipei Current” — stirred up by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and his supporters. However, if we only attribute this political wave to innovative campaign tactics or social media mobilization, we might overlook another key variable that is secretly fueling the situation behind the scenes — the “Chinese factor.”
Shen’s rise in politics has always been intertwined with the “Chinese factor.” Even before he announced his mayoral bid, Beijing listed him as a “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist” and imposed sanctions against him in 2024.
Fundamentally, the reason Beijing dreads and loathes Shen is not because he has proposed a highly systematic “Taiwan independence” doctrine, but because his research on prevention and coping with “gray zone” conflicts in the past few years has struck at the weakness of China’s infiltration and information manipulation efforts.
Traditional political criticism often remains stuck in a war of words, but Shen’s defense theory directly addresses social resilience and the construction of civil defense systems. His attempt to institutionalize and popularize the concept of defense naturally is seen by Beijing as a difficult institutional obstacle.
Beijing’s crackdown on Shen includes its Taiwan Affairs Office issuing the sanctions, the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau filing a case for his “crime of secession,” as well as the extension of the sanctions to his family and affiliated enterprises. A case filed by the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office further confirms that some Hong Kongers hired a detective agency to secretly monitor Shen’s Taipei residence. Shen was also tracked by China when traveling overseas.
More recently, Taiwanese entertainer Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) was boycotted by Chinese Internet users after he attended the opening of Shen’s campaign office. Tsai’s deals with Chinese brands were cut.
This series of maneuvers of “transnational repression” and a “chilling effect” by Beijing have a clear intention.
Despite this deterrence logic being part of authoritarian rule, when it fell into the democratic soil of Taiwan, it generated a huge counterforce.
Strong external threats often fail to achieve internal deterrence due to the “rally round the flag effect” and negative participation theory, according to political science. Instead, they might quickly transform into the political defense legitimacy of the oppressed. When an external power oppresses a Taiwanese politician, voters are likely to develop a defensive group mentality.
When the Chinese side condemned Shen harshly and filed a criminal case, its actions not only failed to isolate him, but also pasted an “anti-China, pro-Taiwan” label on him. This has laid an irreplaceable symbolic position in the eyes of the pro-independence camp and even the center-green voters. In other words, Beijing’s overwhelming oppression has become the best catalyst for the “Ocean Wave” to flood out of the green camp’s bubbles.
If Beijing continues to fail to understand the true logic of voter psychology and power operation under a democratic system, and further intensifies its criticism of Shen during the critical campaign period, it might allow the “Chinese factor” to boost the wave and repeat its mistakes.
John Lim is a distinguished research fellow at the University of Tokyo’s Institute for Advanced Studies on Asia.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Critical PHP flaw forces Web sites worldwide offline, sparks cyberattack fears PHP爆重大資安漏洞　全球網站緊急下線防駭客攻擊
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:23 UTC
01:49:23 KST

Web sites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the World Wide Web.
Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70 percent of Web sites.
The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday last week, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of Web sites will need to be fixed. One Internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organized criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
WordPress, one of the most common Web site systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and — at least historically — much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday last week as a precautionary measure until they could be patched.
The organization behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday last week after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organizations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database.”
Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.
Photo: EPA 照片：歐新社
AI was powering a “race to exploit,” said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the Internet.”
OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public.
Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on Aug. 1 and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.
Photo: AFP 照片：法新社
The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said.
Michal Wozniak, an Internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.
He also said large crime organizations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks.
The issue highlighted the poor state of Internet infrastructure, Wozniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old.
“This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”(The Guardian)
由於廣泛用於架設全球資訊網的程式語言發現嚴重安全漏洞，全球多地網站紛紛暫時關閉。
比利時、荷蘭、芬蘭、法國及德國等國的部分網站，都因政府緊急修補PHP程式語言的重大安全漏洞而暫時下線。PHP是全球近七成網站使用的程式語言。
PHP程式語言的漏洞上週二曝光後，美國華府與英國倫敦的國家安全機構紛紛發出警示，意味全球數百萬個網站都必須進行修補。一名網路基礎設施專家表示，俄羅斯國家級駭客或組織犯罪集團可能會利用這個漏洞發動網路攻擊。
全球最普遍使用的網站建置系統之一WordPress採用PHP，維基百科（Wikipedia）、通訊軟體Slack，以及Facebook過去的大部分系統，也都使用PHP語言。維基媒體基金會（Wikimedia Foundation）表示，已於上週三預防性關閉數個系統，直到完成漏洞修補為止。
研究人員在測試網路防禦系統時發現這個漏洞後，PHP開發團隊於上週三發布修補程式。美國國家安全局（NSA）呼籲所有使用PHP的機構，若無法立即修補漏洞，就應將相關系統暫時下線。NSA指出，這項漏洞可能「讓攻擊者直接存取伺服器的檔案系統或資料庫」。
由於修補程式已經公開，加上人工智慧（AI）工具能夠輕易逆向分析漏洞，專家表示，正準備因應可能接踵而來的大規模入侵行動，因為駭客正爭相在系統更新完成前發動攻擊。
網路安全研究與事件應變公司TLP:Black共同創辦人科斯汀．拉尤表示，AI正在推動一場「漏洞利用競賽」。他說，接下來可能出現的情況，是「網際網路上所有存在漏洞的網頁伺服器遭到大規模入侵」。
OpenAI表示，由該公司領導的研究團隊聯盟發現了這項漏洞，並聲稱「前沿AI」（FrontierAI）對於漏洞的發現扮演了關鍵角色。不過，實際發現漏洞的研究人員表示，他們使用的是一般大眾也能取得的AI模型。
網路安全公司Calif在部落格文章中表示，該公司8月1日在大型語言模型的協助下發現這些漏洞，接著便持續投入修補工作。Alphabet旗下的網路安全公司Wiz也在部落格文章中表示，該公司同樣發現了這些漏洞，所使用的是旗下自主式AI漏洞研究工具Wiz Atlas，以及Google的Gemini 4 Argon和OpenAI的GPT-5.6 Sol。
Wiz指出，這些漏洞隱藏在PHP程式碼中超過10年，人類駭客若要利用它來攻擊，技術難度將極高。
網路基礎設施專家米哈烏．沃茲尼亞克表示：「這項漏洞將引發大量自動化攻擊」。他指出，此漏洞可能讓加密貨幣挖礦業者利用有安全弱點的伺服器，在未經授權的情況下使用他人的運算資源進行挖礦。
他也表示，大型犯罪組織及俄羅斯國家級駭客可能利用這些有漏洞的網站作為跳板，發動分散式阻斷服務攻擊（DDoS）及其他網路攻擊。
沃茲尼亞克指出，這起事件凸顯網際網路基礎設施長久以來狀況很差。隨著AI模型能力不斷提升，這些問題逐漸浮上檯面，但實際上早已存在多年。研究人員發現的底層安全漏洞，甚至已有數十年歷史。
他說：「這是整個產業環境的問題，因為業界有強烈誘因追求快速開發與修改」。「企業有誘因迅速部署系統，之後卻再也不更新，也不考慮維護問題」。

Group proposes AI system to predict, prevent roadkill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:22 UTC
01:49:22 KST

The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network (TaiRON) has proposed using artificial intelligence (AI) to simulate and predict road sections at high risk of wildlife-vehicle collisions, along with an early warning network to help prevent roadkill and other traffic accidents.
Over the past eight years, an average of 3,000 traffic incidents per year involving animals have been reported, TaiRON said, citing government statistics.
Motorcycles accounted for 95 percent of the cases, while the accidents caused a total of 25,345 injuries over the period, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network’s Web site
Authorities estimated that the incidents have resulted in NT$800 million to NT$6.4 billion (US$24.61 million to US$196.9 million) in economic losses per year, it added.
The actual number of traffic accidents involving animals is likely much higher, as available data cover only major cases, TaiRON said.
It estimated that 500,000 to 1 million collisions involving medium-to-large mammals occur annually.
The AI proposal aims to identify high-risk road sections to create warning systems rather than waiting to put up signs after an animal has been killed, the group said.
To do so, TaiRON proposed integrating existing datasets, including its own records of animal deaths, wildlife activity data from the Taiwan Biodiversity Network, reports of injured or dead wild animals made through hotlines and Ministry of Transportation and Communications data on traffic accidents involving animals.
These data would be cross-referenced with road maps, speed limit and traffic volume information, gridded microclimate data from the Central Weather Administration and Google Street View images to identify conditions associated with frequent roadkill.
AI would then be used to simulate and predict high-risk areas, according to the proposal.
TaiRON also proposed installing a network of electronic signs linked to a real-time warning system equipped with heat and light sensors to alert drivers to animals crossing or approaching roads.
The prediction system would initially focus on pangolins as a pilot species, with plans to expand it to other wildlife such as leopard cats, endangered land crabs and frogs.
The group has also developed a low-cost, solar-powered warning device that works in low light and uses infrared sensors to detect passing warm-blooded animals and light sensors to detect vehicles.
The device would be tested on roads managed by the New Taipei City Government before potentially being deployed nationwide, TaiRON said.
The proposal was submitted to the Presidential Hackathon and is among 20 proposals advancing to the final round next month.
Winners would receive government support to implement their proposals, the Ministry of Digital Affairs said.
TaiRON is a citizen science initiative launched by the Ministry of Agriculture’s Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute in 2011 to document wildlife deaths associated with roads, with the aim of reducing threats to wildlife, improving road safety and preventing collisions.
More than 36,000 people have contributed over 330,000 records of animal deaths involving more than 600 terrestrial vertebrate species to the network, its official Web site says.

ETF gains split as stock picks face fresh test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:22 UTC
01:49:22 KST

Taiwan’s fast-growing actively managed exchange-traded fund (ETF) market is facing a test of managers’ stock-picking skills as volatility and closer scrutiny of artificial intelligence (AI) investments widen performance gaps across the sector.
The 20 Taiwan-focused active ETFs in the latest performance rankings posted an average return of just 0.60 percent over the past three months, with fewer than half generating gains.
The gap between the best and worst performers reached 17.61 percentage points, according to the Securities Investment Trust and Consulting Association. Cathay Taiwan High Dividend Momentum Active ETF (00400A) topped the rankings with a 7.91 percent return, outperforming the category average by 7.31 percentage points, the association’s data showed.
Photo: EPA/Ritchie B. Tongo
The divergence comes as investors increasingly demand evidence that heavy spending on AI infrastructure can translate into sustainable revenue and earnings growth. Even within the same supply chain, differences in order quality, profit margins and earnings prospects can lead to sharply divergent share-price performance.
Taiwan’s active ETF market has expanded rapidly, with 40 funds managing a combined NT$988.6 billion (US$30.41 billion) at the end of last month, nearing the NT$1 trillion milestone. Together, the funds had more than 4.25 million beneficiary accounts, association data showed.
Despite overlapping portfolio holdings, active ETFs have delivered widely differing returns, as performance depends not only on which stocks managers select, but also on when they buy, how much they invest and when they adjust their positions.
Cathay fund manager Liang En-yi (梁恩溢) said recent volatility reflected investors’ reassessment of corporate prospects as the AI investment theme entered a phase in which earnings must justify expectations.
Although AI-related stocks have propelled Taiwan’s equity market to new highs this year, investors are looking beyond the hype to determine which companies can turn AI demand into sustainable profits, he said.
The supply chain spans semiconductors, servers, cooling systems and power infrastructure, with demand and earnings growth varying across segments, he added.
Rapid shifts in investor preferences make it increasingly critical for fund managers to adjust their portfolios as industry conditions change, Liang said.
A market correction does not necessarily mean growth opportunities have disappeared, but it can expose differences in companies’ earnings prospects and valuations, he said.
For active managers, the challenge is to identify companies whose earnings can justify their valuations while managing the risks of concentrated positions in a volatile market, Liang said.

Flu season came early; your vaccination is overdue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:18 UTC
01:49:18 KST

This fall, like every other, I tried to game the flu season. My goal, always, is to get my vaccine at just the right moment: before the first cases pop up, yet late enough so that its protective effects last beyond the holidays and well into January or February, when infections tend to peak. That typically means scheduling my appointment for sometime in mid-to-late October.
This year, the virus snuck up on me. Earlier this month, I started hearing from friends with sick kids — weeks before my own teen and I had gotten vaccinated. Drat.
The US is experiencing an unusually early flu season, one that, in another twist, started to pick up steam on the West Coast rather than following its more typical path from southern states north. Not only is that leaving many people unprepared, but early indications suggest it could be another year when our vaccines are not an ideal match against the circulating virus.
It has been a humbling reminder that the flu has a way of thwarting even the best-laid plans.
Infectious disease experts like to say, “You’ve seen one flu season, you’ve seen one season,” says Melissa Stockwell, professor of pediatrics and of population and family health at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. Because it is so hard to predict when it’ll hit, she recommends skipping my game-the-system strategy and trying to get vaccinated by the end of September or early October.
What is behind this early takeoff for the flu? Nobody can say for sure, but the virus’s infuriating ability to stay one step ahead of humans could take some of the blame. Influenza is constantly undergoing tiny genetic changes (and in very rare instances, abrupt, major ones) to the pieces of the virus targeted by vaccines. Global health authorities and infectious disease experts closely track those shifts with the goal of choosing the most protective composition for annual vaccines.
It is hard to get that recipe exactly right. The WHO’s flu team typically picks the strains in February so that vaccine manufacturers can have the shots ready for the fall — a long enough lag for the flu to surprise us. The world was reminded of the challenge last year, when a new strain called subclade K, a mutant of H3N2, was able to circumvent both the flu shot and our preexisting immunity (protection acquired from past infections and vaccinations).
This year, preliminary evidence suggests the culprit behind the West Coast’s unexpectedly early flu cases is a mutation in H1N1 called G155E, says Alex Greninger, a virologist who leads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. About 80 percent of the patient samples sequenced by Greninger’s lab in August and September carried the mutation, which he says was also prevalent in cases during flu season in the Southern Hemisphere and Southeast Asia.
To be clear, existing vaccines, while not a perfect match, are still worthwhile. Last year’s shots offer a good case for that: though subclade K rendered them less effective than in prior years, they still lowered the risk of doctors’ visits and hospitalizations for the flu. And they seemed to work best at protecting kids, who in recent years have been hit hard by the virus.
So even though the G155E mutation is not present in this fall’s flu shots, lab studies suggest the vaccines should still offer some level of protection. Moreover, anyone who did not get the flu last year will want the updated shot, as it protects against subclade K, which is still hanging around, as well as against influenza B, a strain that tends to circulate later in the season.
Another piece of good news: We are moving closer to a world where flu shots can be better matched to the circulating virus. In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s flu vaccine for older adults, making it the first mRNA-based shot against the virus to reach the market. Studies suggest the technology can elicit a broader and longer-lasting antibody response than conventional shots, and it takes far less time to manufacture. That in theory suggests a future where the vaccine composition could be chosen much closer to the actual flu season.
For now, though, anyone feeling behind on the crucial task of getting their flu vaccine should take some comfort in the fact that there are more options out there than ever before — whether that is conventional shots, Moderna’s mRNA-based product, or even an intranasal spray that this year can be mailed directly to the majority of Americans.
And remember that there are no bad choices — so long as you follow through and get vaccinated.
Lisa Jarvis is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering biotech, health care and the pharmaceutical industry. Previously, she was executive editor of Chemical & Engineering News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

New Taipei City has fined a Web site operator for posting QR codes that link to a parking payment service beneath public parking signs in Tamsui District (淡水), a practice that could expose users’ personal data.
Residents reportedly found suspicious parking payment signs at several locations in Tamsui, where an additional QR code had been hung beneath official public parking signs.
The signs could mislead people into thinking the QR code payments were part of an official government service. People reported it to the borough warden, who reported it to police.
Photo: Hsu Sheng-lun, Taipei Times
An investigation by police and the city’s Transportation Department found that the QR code linked to a legitimate Web site for paying parking fees.
However, as private companies are prohibited from placing advertisements on public signs, the operator was fined for contravening the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), police said on Saturday.
Under Article 27 of the act, posting advertisements without approval carries a fine of N$1,200 to NT$100,000, the department said.
People should not trust unfamiliar QR code links posted on public signs, as criminals could exploit them to steal money or personal information, police said.
People should verify links with government agencies or call 110 for assistance, they said.
Parking meters are public facilities and not places for private advertising, the transportation department said, adding that it would step up enforcement in collaboration with police and the Taipei Department of Environmental Protection.
The only platforms offering self-service roadside parking payment options are the Parking Loudspeaker (停車大聲公) and Space4Car (易停網) apps, the transportation department said.
People should follow the information on their parking tickets and pay through legitimate channels, such as the city’s roadside parking fee Web site or convenience stores, it said.

Democracy makes its own waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

A simple orange ribbon has become one of Taiwan’s most unexpected political fashion statements. Supporters of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) have transformed “The Taipei Current” campaign ribbons into roses, stars, accessories and imaginative designs. What began as a campaign symbol has taken on a creative life of its own in Shen’s “Ocean Wave” (洋流).
Who knew an election campaign could inspire a fashion movement?
The phenomenon is more interesting than a passing campaign trend. Citizens are not merely consuming political messages; they are producing and reshaping them. In communication theory, this reflects participatory culture, in which audiences become creators rather than passive recipients.
Taiwan’s politicians are also showing their less conventional sides. Shen plays the clarinet, while the DPP’s New Taipei City mayoral candidate, Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), has demonstrated her piano skills. These performances say little about administrative competence, but they narrow the symbolic distance between politicians and members of the public.
Imagine China’s top leaders inviting similar public playfulness — including jokes at their own expense.
The contrast reveals an important distinction between democratic and authoritarian political aesthetics.
Beijing has devoted considerable resources to cultivating emotional identification with China among Taiwanese audiences. Its cross-strait cultural initiatives increasingly employ documentaries, animation, artificial intelligence-generated films and exhibitions to portray family reunions, shared ancestry and historical belonging.
That approach can be understood as the aestheticization of peace: translating political objectives into visually attractive and emotionally reassuring narratives.
Three mechanisms are particularly revealing. Emotional domestication transforms political separation into stories of family longing. Aesthetic normalization presents closer cross-strait relations through appealing images of everyday life. Cultural depoliticization embeds political messages within apparently nonpolitical artistic and cultural experiences.
Productions such as the documentary Letters Across the Strait (兩岸家書) and the animated short The Reunion Journey (團圓令) illustrate these approaches. Despite their different artistic forms, their institutional presentation repeatedly returns to familiar themes of separation, shared identity and reunion.
The problem is not the authenticity of emotions or the creativity of Chinese artists. It is the predetermined political framework surrounding these narratives. When the preferred conclusion is established before the story begins, even sophisticated imagery risks becoming predictable.
However, cultural appreciation should not be confused with political consent. Taiwanese audiences can enjoy Chinese artistic traditions without accepting Beijing’s political claims.
The limits of this approach become particularly apparent when humor challenges political authority.
Taiwanese comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), known for satirizing Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), was last month injured in a vehicle collision. Taiwanese prosecutors have indicted five suspects, alleging that a China-based suspect financed a staged collision to prevent his performance.
The case highlights the tension between cultural attraction and political intimidation. Soft power depends on credibility and voluntary identification; coercion can undermine both.
An authoritarian political system restricting independent expression faces a structural dilemma: It seeks the emotional appeal of cultural creativity while limiting the freedom from which much of that appeal emerges.
Taiwan’s democracy is noisy, polarized and far from perfect. Nor does a fashionable ribbon make a good mayor. Yet its political culture allows Taiwanese to improvise, parody, disagree and transform public symbols in ways that no campaign headquarters can fully control.
That is a form of democratic soft power rarely captured by official publicity campaigns.
The beauty of The Taipei Current is not that everyone follows the same direction. It is that, in Taiwan, everyone is free to make their own waves.
Bonnie Yushih Liao is an assistant professor in Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations.

Japanese firms to pay out after wave of cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted Internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.
GMO Internet Group Inc, a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorized access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive ￥5,000 (US$32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday.
“The Internet itself is now starting to break down,” said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes Internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading.
Photo: Reuters
Japan said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI) to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organizations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the Internet.
More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks with experts saying AI is helping automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.
“The Internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people,” Kumagai said.
Government and company Web sites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts.
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply cyberdefense measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefense system this month.
The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralize threats.
“Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan,” Kumagai wrote.
GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply.
GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws.
The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses.
White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote.
Meanwhile, Park24, which operates the Times car-sharing service, said on Friday it would make ￥3,000 payments to customers following a personal data breach last month.
The company said it would no longer retain identity document images after completing registration verification and expects to book an extraordinary loss of ￥5.5 billion due to responses to the attack and compensation payments.

Cheng Li-wun hits ground in Changhua
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:13 UTC
01:49:13 KST

With fewer than 50 days to go before election day, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) has finally appointed a director-general of the campaign headquarters for Changhua County commissioner candidate Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政). KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) on Oct. 12 announced that she would be taking on the role.
The KMT’s incumbent Changhua County Commissioner Wang Hui-mei (王惠美) has enjoyed strong support in the county, but has distanced herself from Cheng’s handpicked successor candidate, Wei. The party had originally hoped that Wang herself would chair Wei’s campaign, but to no avail. The waiting dragged on so long that it became hard to watch, and Changhua voters have long grown weary of Wei. Wang is ostensibly worried about being scapegoated if the KMT were to lose the race.
After Wang’s refusals and Cheng’s announcement that she would lead the campaign, pan-blue newspapers jumped on Wang for being a turncoat and for biting the hand that feeds. One editorial resorted to old-fashioned emotional blackmail, emphasizing how Wang had been nurtured by the KMT throughout her 30-year political career from councilor to township chief, legislator and county commissioner, but now, because of a nomination dispute over her successor, she is willing to let power fall into the opposition’s hands rather than work with Cheng. It denounced Wang’s “unprecedentedly hardline stance.” With such impassioned criticism, the editorial made the KMT resemble a scorned lover: If it could not have Wang for itself, it must destroy her.
Since becoming KMT chairwoman, Cheng’s parachuting of Wei into the Changhua race has been one of the few major nominations she has directed. With Wei’s campaign showing unmistakable signs of weakness and his chances of winning appearing slim, Cheng is the obvious first target for blame. Plenty of eyes are watching to see her stumble. Remaining tied to Wei might be more of a political liability than an asset, but allowing the standoff to continue would expose the party to ridicule. With few alternatives, Cheng chose to wade in personally to clean up the mess.
It is notable that her role as party chairwoman has become increasingly marginal to this year’s election campaigns.
Candidates in other administrative regions have repeatedly asked her to stay away; Changhua has become one of the few stages on which she can still appear. Her frequent visits only underscore how unwelcome she has become at the local level.
Cheng’s opening move was to assemble a group of former KMT technocrats to act as policy advisers to Wei’s campaign. Convenor for agricultural economics Lin Hsiang-nung (林享能), a former Council of Agriculture chairman, is a nonagenarian. Convener for transport George Chen (陳世圯), a former acting transport minister, is 88. Convenor for science, technology and economics Hsueh Hsiang-chuan (薛香川), a former secretary-general of the Executive Yuan, is a comparatively sprightly 81. All three held public offices two or three decades ago and have long since fallen out of step with rapidly changing policy developments; none are particularly familiar with Changhua. Cheng has brought the advisory team to lend Wei their support, but at best has achieved a half-day excursion for retired officials whose ability to rally voters remains negligible.
By taking over as director-general of Wei’s campaign headquarters, Cheng has further cemented the impression that a vote for Wei is a vote for herself. As for whether Cheng proves to be a burden or an asset at the ballot box, that is up to Changhua voters to decide.
Cheng Yung-chang is a freelance writer.

Retiring workers set to outnumber youth 2-to-1: NDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:09 UTC
01:49:09 KST

An average of 618 Taiwanese are expected to age out of the workforce each day, more than double the number of young people entering the workforce, the National Development Council’s (NDC) latest 20-year projections showed.
The council’s research, which used data compiled up to this year, showed that the population of Taiwanese aged 15 to 64 would decrease by 4,509,000 people in the next two decades.
The figure, which represents an increase of 3,000 people over the previous year’s model — the equivalent of 60 additional retirees a day — resulted from an accelerated decline in the nation’s demographics, the study said.
Photo: CNA
This means that Taiwan would lose two workers to retirement for each young person entering the workforce, if the legal retirement age or birth rates stay the same, it said.
The model also showed that the share of middle-aged and elderly people in the workforce is set to rise to more than 50 percent, up from the 46.3 percent originally estimated, the study said.
This year, Taiwanese aged 45 to 64 numbered 7,292,000, accounting for 46.3 percent of the working-age population, it said.
This demographic would age out of the workplace by 2046, with only 3,095,000 young people taking their place, the study said.
A council spokesperson said the widening gap in the labor replacement rate is an alarming sign for the fiscal health of Taiwan’s social welfare programs.
Soaring expenditures and contracting tax revenues would make it increasingly difficult for labor pensions, civil servant retirement funds and National Health Insurance to balance the books, they said.
The nation must increase the retirement age, the workforce participation and retention rates for women and elderly people, and immigration to prevent a collapse of the welfare system, they said.

Saudi Arabian Minister of Defense Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, were to meet with Iran’s top security official negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.
Photo: EPA

Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find “ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability.”
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the U.S., as part of ongoing efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the talks.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. However, the deal unraveled quickly, as both sides renewed attacks.

Asked whether Iran was planning attacks, Baghaei yesterday only said that “the Israeli regime is highly skilled at carrying out false-flag operations.”
However, he underscored that “we are in a state of war” and that Iran would defend itself.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The fifth plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee, which opened behind closed doors in Beijing yesterday, is aimed at clearing the way for the CCP’s 21st National Congress to extend Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) rule, a Taiwanese official familiar with cross-strait affairs said yesterday.
Beijing-controlled China Central Television (CCTV) said the primary agenda of the fifth plenum is for the Political Bureau of the CCP Central Committee to report on its work to the Central Committee, and to study “several major issues concerning the unswerving promotion of the full and rigorous party self-governance.”
Outside observers are watching closely if the multiple Chinese officials brought down by corruption charges would face disciplinary action during the meeting, said the Taiwanese official, who declined to be named.
Photo: Reuters
Previous fifth plenums were usually focused on economic issues, while this one is focused on “strictly governing the party,” and that as China’s 15th Five-Year Plan was approved by the fourth plenary session last year, the focus of the fifth plenary session has shifted to “party building,” the official said.
Regarding party building, requirements for discipline would be enhanced, and a resolution would likely be passed on how to strengthen party discipline and reinforce party leadership, they said.
The official said as the 21st CCP National Congress is coming up next year, which would be a pivotal event regarding Xi’s bid to extend his tenure, he might step up the CCP’s anti-corruption efforts by using the fifth plenum to further weed out unfit members, meaning political purges and cleanups are likely to continue.
In this year’s anti-corruption efforts, the number of cadres directly managed by the CCP’s Central Committee that were targeted and disciplined reached a record high, they said.
A total of 416 central-managed cadres — CCP officials at or above the vice-ministerial level — had been purged from 2013 to last year, they said, adding that there were 57 officials targeted last year and more than 70 so far this year, making this year a record high.
“Xi Jinping will definitely extend his tenure at the 21st National Congress,” the official said, adding that “Xi is simply going to keep playing the emperor, and there is no doubt that his term will extend.”
There is no need to waste time discussing who his successor might be, they said, adding that the sole purpose of this fifth plenary session is to clear obstacles for the 21st CCP National Congress.
Among the CCP’s senior members, there is no one who can oppose Xi, as he has established complete absolute authority, they added.
The “Chinese economy has been turned into a complete mess, unemployment is extremely high, and the ordinary people of China are all living through tough times,” the official said, adding that despite Xi’s poor performance, the Chinese public does not dare to openly challenge him.
There are signs of deep public dissatisfaction with the CCP, and the party has responded by tightening social controls, intensifying its campaign to enforce party discipline and imposing stricter restrictions on Chinese people’s overseas travel, the official said.
These measures can all be seen as part of Xi’s efforts to stay in power, they said.
