“The motivation and hope of our elites to bring about changes in the country is a bright flame I have witnessed, both from near and afar, over the course of many years and decades.”
The Leader specifically praised the hardworking athletes for showcasing to the world Iran’s vitality and strength, highlighting the role of female athletes who “make the honorable symbol of the Iranian women’s attire shine before the world.”
‘Engine of national strength’
Defining the true nature of an elite, the Leader said, “The distinguished elite aren’t people who, merely by virtue of possessing a notable amount of talent and intelligence, regard themselves as somehow set apart from others and who only think of their own fleeting, personal desires.”
“An elite is someone who is deeply concerned with developing their abilities, sees themselves as an effective member of society, and uses their talent and potential for the advancement of themselves and their society alike.”
Ayatollah Khamenei pointed to the tangible impact of Iranian elites in solving real-world problems. “The Iranian elites have demonstrated that knowledge and talent can be turned into tools for addressing the real problems facing the people and the country.”
“From stem cell research, nanotechnology, and biotechnology to advanced aerospace technologies and technologies in industry, mining, medicine, agriculture, nuclear energy, and infrastructure, they have consistently sought to put their knowledge, scientific expertise, and abilities to practical use.”
“We’re all seeing the tangible effects and manifestations of this progressive movement in our daily lives.”
The Leader cited electricity generated by Iranian turbines, knowledge-based desalination plants, agricultural drones, advanced technologies at the Royan Institute, as well as radiopharmaceuticals, remote-sensing satellites, and groundbreaking advancements in the defense and military sectors.
Condemning ‘neo-colonial’ plots
“A strong Iran depends on scientific and technological power, and this core pillar is one of the most important factors for shaping Iran’s role in the emerging global equations and the new world order.”
The Leader pointed to the hostility of Iran’s enemies, noting that their crimes are a testament to the pivotal role the elites play in maintaining Iran’s power.
“The same enemy that has assassinated our society’s prominent scientists and the influential elite during the Second and Third Imposed Wars – and of course, in academic settings and in their everyday lives years prior to that – cannot bear to see Iran advance and grow stronger.”

Pumpkin carver brings artistry to Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:07 UTC
01:49:07 KST

When fall arrives and leaves start changing color, Mike Valladao, a systems engineer at a cybersecurity company, slips into his alter ego, “Farmer Mike,” also known as the “Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers.”
Farmer Mike has been chiseling whimsical faces and comical creatures into big pumpkins for more than four decades. Wearing his trademark orange overalls and farmer hat, he has sculpted hundreds of gourds into ghoulish faces, seaside landscapes, witches, dragons and pop culture figures, such as Yoda and Charlie Brown.
Valladao does not have any formal artistic training, but he is always looking for inspiration.
Photo: AP
He gets ideas from looking at art in a museum or just walking down the street.
“Sometimes I’ll look at somebody and I’ll think, oh, I like the teeth or I like ears or the way the nostrils flare,” Valladao said.
This year, “Farmer Mike” celebrated 40 years of Halloween artistry at the Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival, which is held in mid-October and is best known for its giant pumpkin weigh-off.
At the two-day festival on the coast south of San Francisco, Valladao works on stage so people can watch.
Valladao stumbled into his artistic hobby after he began growing big pumpkins at his San Jose home in the mid-1980s. He did not know what to do with the massive gourds, so he pulled out a knife and started slicing faces into them.
“I’m an engineer by trade and I tend to look at it as building something the same way I would build a piece of hardware, one layer at a time,” he said.
In 1986, festival organizers saw a picture of Valladao’s pumpkins and invited him to showcase his carving skills in Half Moon Bay, where his family opened the town’s first feed and seed store in the 19th century. He grew a 363kg pumpkin once, but it was a lot of work, so he does not participate in the giant pumpkin contest.
His art has since taken him to different parts of the country, including an appearance on The Tonight Show.
He has gotten requests to carve pumpkins at venues such as the San Diego Zoo, the California Academy of Sciences and the State Fair of Texas.
He uses Atlantic pumpkins that weigh from 45kg to 454kg. They have thick skins that allow him to cut protruding facial features shallow or deep.
“It’s really about the illusion of depth,” Valladao said. “I can make it so that it’s three-dimensional, such that the eyes are inset and the nose sticks out. So it’s a little bit of carving, but it’s just adding a little more magic to it.”
Valladao said he does not name his creations because he recognizes the ephemeral nature of his art, which only lasts a few days.
“It never really bothers me when a pumpkin starts to age, because in some cases they’ll build character,” he said.
And there is always more pumpkins to be carved.
After 40 years at Half Moon Bay, Valladao does not have any plans to hang up his carving knives.
“It’s fun, it’s enjoyable and, quite frankly, it’s a piece of me,” he said.

Endangered salmon thrive in restored creek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:07 UTC
01:49:07 KST

Taiwan’s endangered Formosan landlocked salmon has returned to Atayal ancestral lands, with wild spawning expected next month, the Shei-Pa National Park Headquarters said yesterday.
The landlocked salmon has re-established itself in the upper reaches of Sihjielan Creek (司界蘭溪) in central Taiwan, with a survey recording 117 adult fish after an aerial release last year, the headquarters said in a statement.
The survey found a visible survival rate of 48.75 percent and documented courtship and pairing behavior, indicating the fish are likely to spawn naturally in the wild as early as next month, it said.
Photo courtesy of Shei-Pa National Park Headquarters
The fish, now nearly two years old, have matured into healthy adults, with males and females displaying distinct secondary sexual characteristics.
According to Atayal oral history, Sihjielan Creek once supported a thriving wild population of Formosan landlocked salmon, but the fish eventually disappeared due to environmental changes and human development, the park headquarters said.
The headquarters described the creek as the final piece of the puzzle in restoring the species across its historic habitat in the Dajia River (大甲溪) basin.
The salmon has already been restored in Cijiawan Creek (七家灣溪), Hehuan Creek (合歡溪), Nanhu Creek (南湖溪) and Luoyewei Creek (羅葉尾溪), while several earlier reintroduction campaigns in Sihjielan Creek failed due to habitat degradation.
The creek’s habitat began to recover about a decade ago when floodwaters destroyed a downstream check dam. Natural erosion of the riverbed then recreated the deep pools and gravel beds the salmon need.
In September last year, the headquarters used a helicopter for the first time to airlift 240 salmon, then about 10 months old, to the upper reaches of Sihjielan Creek for release.
To assess the outcome, a research team set out from the Atayal village Sqoyaw (Huanshan, 環山部落) earlier this month, trekking 3.1km along the Jhihjayangshan (志佳陽大山) trail before descending into the river valley and wading 5.5km upstream for an overnight survey.
The team then snorkeled along a 600m section around the release site to record data on the fish, the headquarters said.
Because the fish were also seen beyond both ends of the surveyed section, suggesting some had dispersed farther upstream and downstream, the actual survival rate could exceed 50 percent, it said.
The headquarters said it would continue to monitor the emergence of juvenile salmon and the population’s resilience to flooding, with full annual survey results expected at the end of the year.

Reverse mortgage growth defies lull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

Taiwan’s reverse mortgage business continued to expand in the first nine months of this year, as older homeowners increasingly used their properties to supplement retirement income, although new lending slowed in the third quarter, Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) data showed.
Banks had approved a cumulative total of 11,285 reverse mortgage loans worth NT$67.8 billion (US$2.09 billion) as of Sept. 30, with their combined value up 16.3 percent from a year earlier, the data showed.
However, banks approved only 274 new loans worth NT$2.187 billion in the third quarter, with the number of cases falling below 300 for the first time in about two years, according to the commission.
Photo courtesy of First Commercial Bank
Property consultancy Colliers International Taiwan (高力國際) attributed the slowdown partly to higher market interest rates and a cooling housing market, saying lenders had become more cautious about property valuations and the long-term risks of reverse mortgages.
Although the central bank has kept its policy rates unchanged, rising market borrowing costs have pushed up reverse mortgage lending rates, reducing the monthly payments available to borrowers and making the product less attractive to some older homeowners, Colliers Taiwan said.
Reverse mortgages allow homeowners to receive regular payments against the value of their properties while continuing to live in their homes.
The loans provide an additional source of retirement income for older people who own property but have limited cash savings, allowing them to remain financially independent without selling their homes or relying entirely on support from their children.
Unlike conventional mortgages, reverse mortgages require lenders to assess how property values and resale prospects might change over an extended period. With loan terms averaging more than 22 years, the long-term value and marketability of a property are key considerations.
Banks have increasingly favored homes in established urban districts, where properties are generally easier to resell, while taking a more conservative approach to lower-priced homes in less central locations and properties bought primarily for investment.
The Greater Taipei area accounted for the largest share of approved loans, reflecting the concentration of property wealth in the region. Women accounted for nearly 58 percent of approved loans, FSC data showed.
Taiwan Cooperative Bank (合作金庫銀行) led in the number of approved loans, followed by Land Bank of Taiwan (土地銀行), Hua Nan Commercial Bank (華南銀行) and First Commercial Bank (第一銀行).
Each of these four government-backed banks had approved more than 1,000 loans cumulatively as of Sept. 30, the data showed.
In the first nine months, the average amount approved per loan rose 8 percent from a year earlier to NT$7.77 million, while the third-quarter average stood at NT$7.98 million, little changed from NT$8.03 million in the second quarter, indicating that the slowdown in new approvals did not translate into a comparable decline in average loan size.

Former prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, known for trying to build stable ties with China, has died at the age of 90, a ruling Liberal Democratic Party official said yesterday. Fukuda passed away on Oct. 22, the official said. He led Japan for a year from September 2007 after replacing the late prime minister Shinzo Abe, whose first term ended after just 12 months. During his stint in power, he sought to improve relations with China and invited then-Chinese president Hu Jintao (胡錦濤) to visit Japan. Hu’s trip in May 2008 made him the first Chinese head of state to visit the country in a decade. The two leaders issued a joint statement committing to a “mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests.” Fukuda resigned in September 2008 as his approval ratings dropped. He retired as a politician in 2012.

EDITORIAL: AI is a double-edged sword
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:01 UTC
01:49:01 KST

Last week, cybersecurity researchers disclosed two serious vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source, server-side programming language used by about 70 percent of the world’s Web sites, prompting its developers to release urgent patches for the bugs, and forcing governments and companies worldwide to fix their systems immediately.
Normally, cybersecurity flaws are kept secret until a patch is ready, but the situation this time caught many people off guard as hackers launched millions of attacks to exploit the bugs within hours of them being identified. In Taiwan, the Administration for Cybersecurity was among those working hastily to patch systems.
The two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, involve memory management issues and allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely, leading to risks such as data theft, file tampering or service disruption. They were each ranked 9.2 out of 10 in severity by cybersecurity researchers, indicating a considerable risk. Interestingly, the flaws had existed undetected in PHP for more than a decade, but were discovered by researchers using artificial intelligence (AI), media reports said.
In light of the cybersecurity threat, Web site owners should check whether their PHP-based portals are affected and, if so, apply the latest patches or go offline temporarily to reduce the risk of being hacked. About 28,000 public-facing Web sites in Taiwan are built on PHP and about 200 are government portals, data released by the Administration for Cybersecurity showed. The administration said it had received no reports of attacks on Web sites in Taiwan as of Thursday. However, experts said that cyberattacks could be hard to detect in the short term, and that Web sites might still appear normal even though they could already have been compromised.
For Web site operators who cannot complete system reviews in time or find it difficult to install security updates immediately, the window before patching could become a cybersecurity vulnerability. That is especially true for smaller organizations with limited security resources, as well as for legacy platforms running on outdated code that is incompatible with the latest PHP versions. As hackers are likely to make more attempts to exploit PHP flaws in the coming weeks, affected Web sites might be better off taking their systems offline until the vulnerabilities are patched.
However, for Taiwan’s small and medium-sized enterprises that rely on Internet portals to run their core business, quickly completing a comprehensive systems review and patching vulnerabilities is no easy task, while temporarily taking their Web sites offline means losing business. Against this backdrop, experts have encouraged firms to deploy Web application firewalls at the front end of Web sites as an alternative precaution. Such applications can act as the first line of defense to intercept malicious requests before they reach Web servers and prevent known PHP bugs such as PHP2Shell during the critical window ahead of patching.
Nonetheless, the PHP incident highlights how AI is a double-edged sword for cybersecurity. Based on media reports, researchers used frontier AI agents to discover PHP flaws that humans alone might never have found, and experts attributed the strength of AI agents to their ability to operate continuously, test thousands of pathways simultaneously and identify vulnerabilities at a speed humans struggle to match. By the same token, AI could also enable threat actors to enhance their attack capabilities. That is because advances in AI agents allow faster, more automated and more persistent attacks, while cutting the time organizations have to patch bugs. It is scary to find out that AI can uncover deeply rooted software vulnerabilities with minimal human input, but at the same time it can also scale up attacks larger and faster than ever. What is scarier is that the gap between uncovering software flaws and their exploitation is narrowing.
Moreover, reports about data breaches at companies in South Korea and Japan which link the attacks to the Chinese AI cybersecurity tool ARTEX have made global headlines and raised concerns about the misuse of AI tools. When ARTEX or other open-source, autonomous AI agents — whose parameters are publicly available for downloading and fine-tuning — fall into the wrong hands, and once their cyberattack capabilities catch up and become available to the public, it would create an irreversible risk of larger-scale misuse. While AI-assisted security tools could slowly enhance defenses and machine-speed cyberresilience would become increasingly necessary for all companies, those with weak cyberdefense capabilities would likely face greater risk of attack by misused AI agents.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

A chorus of boos echoed through Rogers Arena as Quinn Hughes stepped on the ice for warm-ups on Sunday night. They never stopped.
The former Vancouver captain was back for the first time since being traded to Minnesota in December last year. He made it memorable, scoring a goal to reach 500 NHL points and adding an assist in the Wild’s 4-2 victory.
“The passion with the fan base is what makes it special to play here,” Hughes said.
Photo: Bob Frid-Imagn Images
Hughes scored off a rebound on a power player midway through the second period to make it 3-0, and set up Kirill Kaprizov’s NHL-leading 13th goal early in the third for a 4-0 advantage. In 13 games this season, Hughes has three goals and 13 assists.
“He was pretty dominant again tonight, especially the second half of the game,” Canucks defenseman Luke Schenn said. “So, obviously they’re booing him, but at the end of the day I think everyone is proud that he was once a Canuck.”
Hundreds of people — many clad in Canucks jerseys emblazoned with Hughes’ name and No. 43 — stood around the glass ahead of warm-ups, hoping to get a glimpse of the star American defenseman.
One held a sign reading: “And I thought I had commitment issues.”
More boos rained down when Hughes’ name was mentioned on the big screen ahead of puck drop, and again as a tribute to the blue liner began on the big screen during the first TV time-out.
However, the boos transformed into a mixed review, with whistles and clapping, and some in the crowd standing in ovation.
“He definitely deserved the cheers,” Schenn said. “I don’t know if there’s really much reason to be negative as far as what he’s done for the organization.”
As the video ended, Hughes skated out from the bench and raised his stick in salute as both his current and former teammates tapped their sticks on the boards.
“I was just proud,” Hughes said. “And obviously I was here for six-and-a-half-year; I tried my best. And got some cheers there. That was cool for me.”

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan’s defense buildup needs more than shiny new toys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:58 UTC
01:48:58 KST

On Oct. 2, after years of delays, Taiwan’s air force took delivery of the first two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County. In a sign of how eagerly anticipated this arrival was, speculation and rumors had been flying as to why they had been sitting for weeks in Hawaii en route to Taiwan.
These are part of a total of 66 F-16V Block 70s on order. There are hopes the rest will arrive by the end of next year, but no one will be surprised if that extends into 2029 or even later. Worse, in the two that have already arrived, according to an Air Force briefing of the legislature on Oct. 12, the Viper Shield electronic warfare suite is only partly installed and its software is still in development
On Sept. 24, AIDC delivered the final two aircraft in the 66-aircraft Brave Eagle trainer program. One aircraft had previously been lost in a crash. In July, the last AT-3 jet training mission ended, and the F-5E/F jets are being phased out.
Photo: Peter Lo, Taipei Times
Taiwan’s armed forces — the Army, Navy, Air Force and Military Police — and Coast Guard are in the midst of a boom in (typically delayed) arrivals of shiny new weapons systems and kit. Far more is on order or planned. According to Taiwan Security Monitor’s September estimate, there is a US$29.72 billion (NT$968 billion) backlog in orders from the US.
Alongside the increased annual defense budget, lawmakers approved a special procurement framework authorizing up to NT$780 billion in US arms purchases over 2026–2033, subject to subsequent appropriations. Separately, the government is investing NT$44.2 billion over 2025–2030 in developing Taiwan’s drone industry.
In April, the Army received the final batch of the controversial 28 M1A2T Abrams tanks purchased from the US, bringing the total to 108. The Army is also planning to procure 178 domestically developed Cheetah armored vehicles between next year and 2033.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
According to a Taipei Times report last month citing a military expert, Taiwan’s first domestically built submarine, the Hai Kun (Narwhal, 海鯤), could be delivered to the Navy as early as this month. This is the first of eight planned submarines.
Both the Navy and Coast Guard have been taking delivery of various types of ships in recent years. On Oct. 2, the keel-laying ceremony was held to launch construction on the Coast Guard’s second 5000-tonnes high-latitude oceanic patrol vessel, out of a planned six total by 2031.
These examples highlight some of the flashier headline-grabbing additions currently flooding into system to defend Taiwan, but there are many, many more. There are smaller ships growing the Navy and Coast Guard fleets, mine-layers and missile systems for the Army and Air Force and hardly a day passes without some missile, unmanned vehicle or drone program being announced.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
Surely that is all good news, right? Maybe.
PEOPLE NEEDED
To illustrate the problem, imagine if you received a top-of-the-line Formula 1 racing car. No doubt for many fans, that would sound like a dream come true. But what would you do with it?
A first thought would be: how do I drive this thing? These are not for amateurs; you had better get some training.
On reflection, the challenge gets harder. They require pit crews, supply chains of highly specialized and very expensive parts, and specialists to keep them in top running condition. There are legal and insurance issues, never mind finding a place to simply park it.
The challenges would be enormous, but nothing compared to what is required to fly and maintain those two new F-16V fighters and the 64 more that are expected to arrive soon. They will join 139 older-version F-16s, 52 aging French Mirage 2000s, 129 indigenously developed F-CK-1 Ching-kuo fighters and the aforementioned Brave Eagles.
Despite the Hollywood glamor and prestige of flying a fighter jet, the Air Force is struggling to maintain enough pilots for its existing fleet. They may struggle to have enough pilots for the new jets as they arrive, or be required to ground existing ones.
It takes years of flight, simulator and operational training to prepare a fighter pilot. In a report to the legislature, the Ministry of National Defense proposed scrapping the maximum length of service for air force pilots amid a shortage of experienced pilots, many of whom leave the military to fly for civilian airlines. Reportedly, civilian pilots make about NT$100,000 to NT$200,000 more a month.
Under current law, pilots holding the rank of lieutenant colonel can serve a maximum of 26 years and colonels a maximum of 30 years, so pilots at these ranks must generally leave military service at about 48 and 52 years of age, respectively. The new proposal would extend their service to around age 58.
If the Cabinet approves the proposal and it takes effect, the ministry aims to retain 72 pilots ranked lieutenant colonel or colonel in service longer. Hopefully, the proposal is accepted and all those pilots are retained; they will be needed.
The problem is that may not be enough. Gray zone incursions by Chinese forces are in part designed to wear down the personnel and the jets themselves. Exhaustion may make those higher-paid civilian jobs, with their regular schedules, look even more appealing.
Now spare a thought for the equally critical, highly skilled crews needed to keep those planes flying. They face all the exhaustion and stress without the sexy job title of fighter jet pilot. Does the Air Force have enough of them?
‘GOOD AS DEAD’
Recently, gray zone incursions have increasingly been at sea. The brunt of handling those falls on the Coast Guard, and there the situation is dire.
A report by the National Audit Office found that at the end of June last year, of 108 vessels in service, only four had a full complement of sailors. That means that 96 percent were sailing without full crews. The same report found that the problem is getting worse, just as the Coast Guard is rapidly adding new vessels.
A report in Storm Media paints a grim picture. Because gray zone incursions can happen at any time, sailors can be forced to respond, regardless of holidays or personal plans. The Chinese can use their far larger navy and fishing boat militia to probe endlessly.
That report describes how in calmer times, a three-day tour meant exactly that. Now, sailors on vacation can be called to active duty for up to 15 days, put in dangerous standoffs with Chinese vessels and often called to duty sleep-deprived. With spotty cell phone service, one insider quoted in the report told Storm that some spouses complain that their husbands are “as good as dead.”
Unsurprisingly, despite offers of high salaries right out of police colleges, the Coast Guard is struggling to recruit sailors willing to take on this challenging, unglamorous and exhausting job that offers little personal freedom or control over their lives.
The government is acutely aware of all of this, and has actively been working to boost pay and benefits to make these jobs more appealing. They have also restored the one-year mandatory conscription, up from four months, which may help with some of the more mundane tasks.
Already struggling with personnel issues in both the military and Coast Guard, and with automation filling the gaps years away, the ability of the military to handle the influx of new platforms is a significant concern.
Though they disagree on how to go about it, both the administration and opposition parties agree that making these careers more attractive is a priority.
Faced with a demographic meltdown, they have their work cut out for them.

Nature cannot wait for calmer times to return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:58 UTC
01:48:58 KST

In times of war, geopolitical turmoil, and fiscal tightening, it is tempting to view the defense of nature as a desirable but non-urgent goal — an objective that can be pursued when calmer times return. But we embrace this view at our peril.
As world leaders gather for the UN biodiversity and climate-change conferences this fall, they must remember that over half of global GDP depends on nature and the services it provides. Healthy soils underpin a US$9.5 trillion global food industry, while forests support 1.5 billion livelihoods around the world. Healthy rivers help absorb floodwaters and sustain vital transportation networks. Nature is the backbone of the global economy, and protecting it must be a top national and international priority.
Nature-related crises will not wait until the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are over. This summer’s sweltering drought in Europe caused US$2 billion to US$3 billion in crop losses, a double blow for farmers after the war-induced closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused fertilizer prices to surge by 71 percent. The combined effects of conflict and extreme weather have helped push global food prices to their highest levels since 2022.
All told, scientists predict that a partial collapse of ecosystems could cost the global economy US$2.7 trillion annually. Despite intense geopolitical instability, we cannot afford to undermine the natural systems on which our economies depend. The global goal to protect and conserve at least 30 percent of the world’s land and ocean by 2030, known as 30x30, is more important than ever.
Protecting nature is an investment in resilience and solidarity. Resilience strengthens food and water security, and the capacity to weather climate shocks. It sustains livelihoods, public health, and long-term economic stability. The 30x30 goal, adopted by governments in 2022 under the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, recognizes that protecting nature is fundamental to providing these and other public goods.
For example, kelp beds, mangroves, and marshes absorb carbon dioxide, while coral reefs help protect against storms and provide natural habitats for some of the world’s most diverse ecosystems. On land, forests regulate rainfall and support the livelihoods of local communities, and healthy soils retain water and nutrients that are vital to global food security and flood protection.
Four years on, the world has made significant strides toward the 30x30 goal. New analysis from Campaign for Nature shows that 20 percent of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and that fully delivering on existing commitments could increase this share to approximately 27 percent by 2030, closing much of the remaining gap.
Progress at sea, however, has been much slower. Only 10 percent of the ocean is formally designated for conservation, and existing commitments would increase this to a mere 12 percent by 2030. Worse, Together for the Ocean’s latest Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that only 3.5 percent of the ocean is assessed as effectively protected, with harmful activities continuing in many areas that are supposed to be off limits.
With just four years remaining, the world still has a chance to achieve 30x30, which is one of the defining global commitments of this decade. But what will it take to make up for lost time?
For starters, governments must dramatically increase financing for nature. Delivering 30x30 will require approximately US$100 billion to US$180 billion annually, compared with current annual spending of US$24 billion. But, again, this spending represents an investment, not just a cost. Achieving 30x30 could add up to US$450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050 and support an estimated 4 million to 7 million jobs.
Policymakers at all levels urgently must move from talking about solutions to implementing them. As of May this year, 116 countries had submitted commitments to protect up to 27 percent of land and inland water areas. But many have yet to follow up with mapped, costed, and financed plans. Commitments alone will not protect nature.
Protecting more of the planet is only part of the challenge. Governments also must ensure that protected and conserved areas are well managed, deliver real benefits, and meaningfully preserve biodiversity. That requires long-term funding arrangements that can endure through changing economic and political cycles.
There is no denying that the global outlook is uncertain. The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth. But it would be a mistake to put nature on the back burner. Protecting natural systems is not just for the bees. Investing in their future is an investment in our own.
Mary Robinson is a former president of Ireland and a former UN secretary-general’s special envoy for climate change.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

01:48:57 KST

Agricultural losses caused by Typhoon Champi had reached NT$221.63 million (US$6.82 million) as of 11am yesterday, with garlic crops sustaining the heaviest damage, the Ministry of Agriculture said.
Crop losses accounted for NT$210.73 million, while livestock losses, primarily pigs, stood at NT$90,000, data compiled from local government reports by the ministry’s Agriculture and Food Agency and Department of Animal Industry showed.
Damage to private facilities reached NT$10.8 million, which included NT$8.57 million in livestock and poultry facilities and NT$2.23 million in agricultural infrastructure, such as horizontal trellises and plastic greenhouses, the ministry said.
Photo: Huang Shu-li, Taipei Times
Among crops, garlic sustained the most severe damage, with losses totaling NT$63.59 million.
Other heavily affected crops included peanuts (NT$15.91 million), onions (NT$11.65 million), tangerines (NT$11.51 million) and corn (NT$9.99 million).
By region, Yunlin County reported the heaviest agricultural losses at NT$137.07 million.
It was followed by Miaoli County (NT$24.83 million), Taichung (NT$20.42 million), New Taipei City (NT$16.18 million) and Yilan County (NT$9.38 million).
To mitigate the financial impact, the ministry announced cash relief and low-interest loans for nine municipalities: New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Taichung, as well as Changhua, Nantou, Yunlin, Yilan and Taitung counties.
The subsidies cover crops, forestry, fisheries and livestock, the ministry said, adding that all agricultural products in Yilan County are eligible for the relief program.
The relief package also includes items that did not strictly meet weather parameter thresholds, but were confirmed to have sustained severe damage during on-site inspections, it said.

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) yesterday proposed revitalizing the capital’s waterways before attending a Halloween event where parents expressed support for his childcare policies.
At a news conference at his campaign headquarters in Taipei’s Zhongzheng District (中正), Shen outlined a plan to revitalize the city’s waterways, drawing inspiration from Singapore’s approach to urban water management.
The plan focuses on five priorities -- Active, Beautiful, Clean, Detention and Ecosystem -- collectively known as "ABCDE," Shen said.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
Specific measures include improving waterfront facilities along the Tamsui and Keelung rivers to make them more accessible to the public, using wetlands and vegetation to improve water quality, and developing small-scale floodwater retention facilities in schools and parks to strengthen the city’s flood control capacity.
"We use water every day, but we are actually very far removed from the water in our city," Shen said, arguing that urban water management should incorporate education, culture and environmental protection rather than focus solely on engineering.
Shen said many of Taipei’s streams and irrigation channels had been covered, filled in or incorporated into underground drainage systems during urban development, distancing residents from the city’s waterways.
He said the initiative aimed to reconnect residents with these waterways and make water a central consideration in urban planning.
Later yesterday, Shen, dressed as a ship captain and wearing an Afro wig, handed out candy to children and other attendees at a Halloween event outside the Tianmu Baseball Stadium.
Among those at the event was Taipei resident surnamed Wu (吳), a 35-year-old designer who came with his wife and 2-year- old daughter.
Wu said he was not a staunch DPP supporter and had previously supported former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), but welcomed Shen’s childcare proposals.
One proposal that particularly appealed to him was Shen’s plan to provide up to four hours of free drop-in childcare per week for preschool children.
Taipei currently offers drop-in childcare at designated facilities, most of which charge NT$200 (US$6.13) per hour, according to the city government.
Wu said the proposed free childcare could provide much- needed relief, as he and his wife both work and their daughter spends around 12 hours a day with a nanny on weekdays.
"I think it would give parents some breathing room," he said, adding that the service could allow them to rest on weekends or deal with emergencies.
Shen is challenging incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) in the elections.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva was re-elected against all expectations on Sunday, but his conservative rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to have the vote annulled.
Lula’s dramatic comeback meant Brazil had not followed Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Peru, all backed by US President Donald Trump, in swinging to the right.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed Lula’s re-election as a triumph for “democracy and multilateralism,” joining a slew of world leaders who welcomed the leftist figurehead’s return for an unprecedented fourth term.
Photo: AFP
Lula, who turns 81 today, defied projections to defeat Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, and win an unprecedented fourth term.
He won 51.8 percent of the votes to 48.2 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling about 4.4 million more votes, official results showed.
Lula was warmly congratulated by the leaders of left-wing governments across Central America, including Mexico, Cuba and Venezuela.
“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on X.
Right-wing governments in Chile, Ecuador and Peru said they wanted to work toward common goals with the region’s economic powerhouse.
China echoed that sentiment, while Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi also offered his friend Lula his “heartiest congratulations.”
Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.
“People went to vote, because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country,” Lula said in his first comments after the win.
Sunday’s vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, because some polling stations had already closed.
The move came at the request of Lula, who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as “unacceptable” and a “dirty trick.”
“It is impossible to recognize the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections,” he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia.
Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country’s last election in 2022.
No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the military dictatorship.

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) yesterday began a four-day meeting of its highest-ranking members, targeting concrete measures for “full and rigorous party self-governance,” as Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) seeks to reinforce his authority and enforce ideological uniformity.

The implementation of major decisions and plans of the Central Committee, the largest of its top decisionmaking bodies, must not be empty rhetoric, the commentary wrote.
Photo: EPA
“It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation,” it said.
The Central Committee is hlding closed-door meetings until Thursday — the fifth since the current cohort was formed in 2022 and therefore known as the fifth plenum.
Analysts say this could be the last major party gathering before its leadership reshuffle next year, when Xi is expected to hold on to the top job for a fourth term.
“The plenum will present Xi as in control, and able to continue his command,” said Kerry Brown, director of King’s College London’s Lau China Institute. “It is likely everything will be centered on him, to dispel any rumors or doubts about his physical fitness and ability to continue in his role.”
With substantive policy issues already largely set in previous gatherings, “this will be a plenum where appearances will matter as much, if not more, than substance,” Brown added.
Xi has overseen a vast anti-corruption campaign in recent years, which has led to the purge of hundreds of senior officials and top generals, even his one-time allies.
While critics argue the purges — particularly those targeting the highest ranks of the armed forces — are destabilizing and undermine combat readiness, the party has portrayed the campaign as both necessary and regenerative, saying the military must undergo a phoenix-like rebirth and “bathe in flames and be forged anew.”
The Xinhua commentary propped up the anti-corruption drive as a demonstration of “sustained and systemic” self-governance to “ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption.”
“For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability,” it said, adding that China was creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation as merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery.

Kimi Antonelli said his mindset will not change as he heads to next week’s race in Mexico seeking the two points he needs to become Formula One’s youngest world champion.
The 20-year-old Italian on Sunday delivered a well-executed and dominant drive to claim his ninth victory this year for Mercedes in the US Grand Prix and move within reach of the title.
Antonelli is on the brink of smashing the previous record for youngest champion, held by Sebastian Vettel who was 23 years and 133 days old when he won his first title in 2010
Photo: Reuters
He is also set to become the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
“The best way, the perfect way, would be to finish off in style and then just enjoy the rest of the season,” he said. “I’m very aware that it’s very close but the mindset doesn’t change. I want to finish the season on a high in order to then go with high hopes into 2027, but we’ll first focus and worry about finishing this well, and then we’ll see.”
After Sunday’s triumph at the Circuit of the Americas he leads with 365 points ahead of nearest rival and teammate George Russell on 242 and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari on 241. He will be champion if he finishes in the top nine or, if he does not score, Russell or Hamilton fail to win.
However, on current form, after winning again for the first time in four races, he looks certain to take the title in his own happy, generous and infectious style.
“That was the perfect way to end the weekend,” he said. “It was an incredible team effort, especially from strategy, to believe in me and go for one stop because I wasn’t sure whether one or two stop was the quickest.”
Antonelli’s ability on the track and infectious attitude off it have landed him numerous admirers around the paddock, including 1996 world champion Damon Hill.
“The team love him, he’s enjoying everything he’s got in F1 and he’s very grateful for all the breaks they’ve given him at Mercedes,” Hill said on the BBC. “But he delivers. He’s such a nice kid. It’s incredible. Twenty years old and he’s on the verge of winning his first championship, which I’m sure will be the first of many.”
Russell needed to finish in the top eight to remain notionally in the title race and he did indeed finish eighth after taking an early five-second penalty.
“My pace was just rubbish today. That’s the long and short of it,” he said.
“Of course, the five seconds didn’t help things and probably cost me two or three positions, but nevertheless, the pace was not good enough when it needed to be,” he added.
Hamilton is the only other driver who still has a mathematical chance of catching Antonelli, but the seven-time champion was left to rue missed opportunities in Sunday’s race.
“I felt the race was lost in my first two stints,” said Hamilton. “I lost so much time. I couldn’t turn the car in the lower speed corners particularly.”
“I was adjusting my settings and by the last stint I was closer to the right balance,” he said. “I think I’ve lost a lot of points in the last five races or so and I think it’s really come from set-up or just not perfecting the set-up. It’s something I’ve really got to get on top of.”

Taipei’s school lunch program has run into trouble yet again. This time, Shilin District’s (士林) Shihtung Elementary School (士東國小) was exposed by parents on social media for serving rotten, blackened pears. The incident once again sparked criticism about food safety in Taipei schools and the quality of the city’s free lunch policy.
Free school lunches for all elementary and junior-high schools is a flagship policy announced by Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) in January, but at the time it attracted criticism from other administrative regions. Since the policy’s official implementation last month, the city — which has the largest budget of any local government in the nation — has been plagued by controversies. There have been multiple reports of food poisoning, and an incident in which students received just three blueberries as their serving of fruit. The education commissioner’s response that the “blueberries were larger” sparked outrage.
In contrast, other administrative regions have not experienced the same issues. In Tainan, which is governed by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), schoolchildren enjoy tasty, filling and safe meals.
With just over one month remaining before election day, the rotten-pear incident is bound to impact Chiang’s electoral prospects. Chiang still lacks a grasp of municipal affairs. He has also become a laughingstock for repeatedly giving answers that miss the point of the questions. The member of the “Chiang family,” as the argument goes, truly embodies the Taiwanese saying, “a rotten pear pretending to be an apple.”
John Yu is a civil servant in Taipei.

China beats Japan in Europe car sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:46 UTC
01:48:46 KST

Chinese automakers outsold Japanese rivals in Europe for the first time over a full quarter, underscoring how quickly brands like BYD Co (比亞迪) and Chery Automobile Co (奇瑞汽車) are gaining ground in the region.
Registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled from a year earlier in the three months through September to make up 12.7 percent of total sales across the region, led by hybrids, according to market researcher Dataforce. That has put them ahead of Japanese manufacturers, including Toyota Motor Corp, at 11.9 percent.
The advance accelerated at the end of the quarter. Chinese brands’ European share jumped to a record 14.5 percent last month, according to Dataforce, almost three percentage points higher than in August.
Photo: Reuters
While European manufacturers like Volkswagen AG or Renault SA still dominate the region, the speed of China’s surge has been a surprise. Five years ago, Chinese brands accounted for barely 1 percent of European sales. Japanese automakers, by contrast, have spent decades building their position in Europe.
Toyota has sold cars in the region since 1963 and now operates factories across the continent, while Nissan Motor Co has produced vehicles at its Sunderland plant in the UK since 1986. China’s offering is especially successful in the UK, where Chery’s Jaecoo 7 SUV was the country’s best-selling model in March and last month.
Earlier this month, Chery, BYD and Geely Holding Group Co’s (吉利控股集團) Zeekr Intelligent Technology Co (極氪智能) showed off a range of new models at the Paris car show, offering well-priced cars like the BYD Dolphin G DM-i, a compact plug-in hybrid specifically developed for Europe. Bringing their electric vehicle lineups to Europe also positions them to benefit from a jump in demand as fuel prices hit record highs.
The EU is trying to temper an expansion that is partly fueled by state-backed subsidies. After adding extra tariffs on China-made battery-electric vehicles, the bloc this month agreed in principle to curb fast-growing imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU is also considering new rules that would favor locally made cars when granting subsidies and other incentives.
Chinese manufacturers have been preparing to produce locally already. Chery is preparing production in Barcelona and BYD is nearing the completion of a manufacturing site in Hungary. Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co (零跑科技) has started making its B10 SUV at Stellantis NV’s plant in Zaragoza, Spain, as part of the companies’ joint venture.
Luxury powerhouses including Hermes and Cartier are suffering steeper slumps in China, in a sign that a spending pullback by the country’s wealthy consumers is hitting even the most resilient brands. Sales at the brands in mainland China fell as much as double-digits in August and last month compared to the same period a year ago, two research firms surveyed by Bloomberg that track industry data said. The drop is significant as Hermes International SCA and Cie Financiere Richemont SA’s Cartier had been relatively unaffected in the country as a broader slowdown in luxury consumption took hold in June, the firms’

Chip capacity an asset for Taiwan, researcher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:43 UTC
01:48:43 KST

Countries seeking to advance their artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities are increasingly partnering with leading AI powers to access advanced models, with Taiwan holding a potential advantage because of its chipmaking capabilities, a US researcher said.
He described Taiwan’s position as potentially “the strongest card in the world.”
Most countries recognize that they might be unable to develop their own advanced models from scratch and must explore ways to cooperate with AI powers such as the US and China, said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Countries developing AI are considering which parts of the AI technology they can control and how to use those advantages to secure benefits from nations developing the most advanced AI models, said Mehta, a former Google employee who worked on AI policy.
“In Taiwan’s case, they have maybe the strongest card in the world to play,” he said. “They’re home to the foundries that build and manufacture the most advanced chips in the world.”
That gives Taiwan significant leverage in negotiations with the US and other countries, he said.
“This is an enormous leverage point that can allow Taiwan to really engage in aggressive negotiations with a place like the US,” he said.
For example, Taiwan could seek priority access to the most advanced AI models developed by US companies or preferential consideration when applying for computing resources, he said.
Taiwan produces 90 percent of the world’s AI servers and advanced AI chips. Asked whether Taiwan’s advantage could be affected as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) and other Taiwanese companies expand their investments in the US, Mehta said global demand for computing power was growing rapidly.
Existing foundries, particularly those with mature manufacturing processes and high yields, would continue to play an important role, he said.
“All the existing foundries, especially the ones that have very mature manufacturing processes with high yield, they’re going to continue to be really important,” he said.
New foundries under construction would take several years to reach full production capacity, meaning much of the world’s chip manufacturing would continue to rely on existing facilities in the short term.
“Certainly in the near term, Taiwan’s going to continue to be important,” he said.
Taiwan would remain important in the longer term, Mehta said, adding that it could use the scale of investments by companies such as TSMC in the US, as well as its alignment with Washington on export controls and access to AI technology, as geopolitical advantages in negotiations with Washington.
As technological competition between the US and China intensifies, Taiwan is preparing to tighten export controls on AI chips to bring its measures further into line with those of the US, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) told Bloomberg.
The move would put Taiwan alongside US President Donald Trump’s administration in efforts to combat the smuggling of advanced semiconductors to China.
Taiwan is already deeply connected to the US in many respects, including technology, broader geopolitical and economic interests, and military and security matters, Mehta said.
To some extent, Taiwan has already chosen a side, he said, adding that further aligning its export controls and technology-access policies with Washington would not necessarily further damage relations with China.
Instead, such alignment could improve and enhance Taiwan’s relationship with the US, he said.

Paris game festive despite protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:43 UTC
01:48:43 KST

The Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday defeated the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the first NFL regular-season game in Paris, in a calm and festive atmosphere, a day after fresh demonstrations drew more than 100,000 people into the French capital.
Forty-two-year-old quarterback Aaron Rodgers left the pocket on third-and-six and picked up eight yards before being tackled just before the two-minute warning to help Pittsburgh seal the victory.
“Sometimes you’ve got to suck it up and make a play for your guys,” Rodgers said. “I think because I am so much less athletic than I used to be, it actually fires up the guys even more.”
Photo: AFP
Rodgers threw a touchdown pass — the 540th of his career, moving past Peyton Manning for third in NFL history — and Chris Boswell kicked three field goals at Stade de France.
Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards on 18 carries and Rodgers completed 19 of 30 passes for 212 yards as the Steelers (5-2) won their third consecutive game.
The nationwide protests largely overshadowed the buildup to the game, with some fan and NFL events canceled over the weekend, mainly due to their location in central Paris.
Photo: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images
As Saturday’s rain gave way to sunshine, the mood was peaceful before kickoff in Saint-Denis in front of a sold-out crowd of 78,488 people.
James Brown, a 51-year-old Saints fan who traveled to Paris especially for the game, said the atmosphere around the stadium was “wonderful, really good.”
The police presence appeared neither heavy nor unusual at the Stade de France, which hosted rugby sevens and athletics during the 2024 Paris Olympics and regularly serves as the home ground for the French national rugby and soccer teams.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
“We didn’t notice much yesterday,” 38-year-old Steelers fan Lukas Baldridge said. “We came in, went to a bar, got some drinks, got dinner, went home, didn’t see any protesting.”

OAC and university developing maritime AI drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:42 UTC
01:48:42 KST

The Ocean Affairs Council (OAC) yesterday said it is funding a National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) team to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered system to coordinate different types of drones to enable wide-area maritime surveillance and sustained monitoring.
Developing a multilayered coast guard surveillance network and enhancing maritime domain awareness are core strategies to address maritime law enforcement needs and various forms of “gray zone” harassment from China, the council said.
Regional conflicts in the past few years have shown that drone technology has evolved from single-aircraft operations to coordinated missions involving multiple types of drones and fleets operating in swarms, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Affairs Council
The AI-powered drone swarm system being developed by the research team achieved a breakthrough by coordinating different drone fleets, providing wide coverage and continuous monitoring over territorial waters, the council said.
“This system would bolster Taiwan’s maritime defense, rescue capabilities and whole-of-society defense resilience,” it said. “It has laid a solid technical foundation to build a smart and multilayered coast guard patrol system and demonstrated Taiwan’s research and development capacity in marine technology and smart aerospace sectors.”
The team, led by the university’s aeronautics and astronautics associate professor Chueh Chih-che (闕志哲), built an intelligent multiple drone operating system by integrating AI, vertical takeoff and landing fixed-wing drones, flight dynamics, and swarm coordination and control technology.
The team explored the strengths and control models of three types of drones used in the project — Jump 20, V-Bat and Flexroter — through 3D shape modeling, aerodynamic parameter analysis and “six degrees of freedom” flight simulation, the council said.
The team further used AI multi-agent reinforcement learning technology to enable multiple drones to autonomously assign missions, plan flight paths and coordinate with one another, flying in formation like a flock of geese.
To improve formation flexibility and flight safety, the research team incorporated “leader-follower formation control” and “intelligent dynamic obstacle avoidance,” enabling the drone swarm to adjust its flight path according to mission requirements and autonomously respond in real time to sudden environmental changes or obstacles, the council said.
The team has completed simultaneous flight simulations of two drone fleets, comprising a total of 20 drones, it said.
To avoid drone swarm collisions, the team has incorporated into its control algorithm the 3D separation distance and a minimum vertical separation of 30.5m, the council said.
The team would further test the reliability and feasibility of drone fleets under different marine environments by conducting hardware-in-the-loop and prototype integration tests, as well as real-world flight tests over open water, it said.

2026 Elections: China trying to isolate Puma Shen: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:38 UTC
01:48:38 KST

China is attempting to isolate Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) by pressuring people and businesses associated with him, a source familiar with national security cases said after a celebrity’s statement denying support for Taiwanese independence.
Television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) faced a backlash from Chinese authorities and Internet users after on Oct. 4 attending an event marking the opening of Shen’s campaign headquarters. Tsai on Sunday night in a post on Chinese social media apologized, saying that he had never supported Taiwanese independence.
Beijing cannot easily use the Chinese market to pressure Shen directly, so it is targeting Taiwanese entertainers and companies that attend his events or appear alongside him, the source said yesterday.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
By threatening their commercial interests, Beijing hopes to deter others from participating in Shen’s campaign and limit his ability to secure resources and support, they said.
Tsai had attended Shen’s event to familiarize himself with Shen ahead of a potential interview with the candidate, Tsai’s manager said.
However, business partners in China continued to distance themselves from Tsai.
The pressure could lead businesses and people to avoid even routine professional interactions with political figures, as the risk lies not only in what a person says but also in which events they attend and who they appear alongside, the source said.
If potential supporters become reluctant to meet a candidate, accept invitations or publicly collaborate with them because of their business interests in China, the candidate loses not only potential campaign surrogates, but also opportunities to explain their positions and attract new supporters, they said.
Beijing has said that it would target people and businesses associated with political figures, they said, citing the Chinese government’s investigation and penalties against Taiwan’s Far Eastern Group in 2021.
At the time, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said businesses would not be allowed to make money in China while funding people it described as advocates of Taiwanese independence. It also identified affiliated companies and financial backers as targets for punishment.
Shen yesterday said the timing of Tsai’s post denying support for Taiwanese independence appeared to have been determined by outside forces, adding that it showed signs of Chinese interference in Taiwanese people’s ability to make their own decisions.
He was referring to the statement issued a day before his opponent — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is seeking re-election — was slated to launch his campaign headquarters.
Tsai, who previously said he would attend the event, showed up yesterday.
Shen said that Tsai was the top trending topic on Chinese social media yesterday, adding that topics in the top three positions on the platform’s trending list were generally determined by Chinese authorities.
Regardless of whether Tsai had been directed to issue the statement, the incident showed signs of Chinese intervention, Shen said.
The interference was not necessarily in the election itself, but in Taiwanese people’s ability to make their own decisions, he added.
Chiang yesterday said he respected Tsai’s post and political position, adding that he would not accept threats against people because of their political views.
In local media, Tsai’s post was widely compared to a 2016 incident in which Taiwanese K-pop star Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜), more commonly known as Tzuyu, issued a video apologizing for holding a Republic of China (Taiwan) flag on television.
Chiang was asked about the comparison and whether the controversy could affect his election campaign.
Chiang said he welcomed Tsai’s attendance at the opening of his campaign headquarters, adding that regardless of whether Tsai or any other citizen supports him, he respects their opinions and is committed to serving them as mayor.
Chiang also criticized the tendency to attack, boycott or ostracize people because of their differing political views.
“I absolutely will not permit or accept such anti-democratic intimidation,” he said.

Taiwanese gymnast wins gold at world championships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:37 UTC
01:48:37 KST

Taiwanese gymnast Tang Chia-hung (唐嘉鴻) on Sunday won gold in the men’s horizontal bar final at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
Tang scored 14.966 in the final. He had advanced to the final in second place with a score of 14.566 points in qualifying, with a difficulty score of 6.000 and an execution score of 8.566.
In the final, he raised his difficulty score to 6.600, the highest among the eight finalists. Although he did not fully steady himself on landing, his score was still enough to claim the gold medal.
Photo: Iris van den Broek, EPA
Taiwan had previously won two silver medals and one bronze at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships. Chang Feng-chih (張峰治) took silver in the men’s vault in 1993, while Lee Chih-kai (李智凱) won silver in the men’s pommel horse in 2019 and bronze in the same event in 2018.
With his gold medal, Tang became the first Taiwanese gymnast to win a title at the world championships.
Tang said he had found a way to reset his mindset after finishing fifth and missing out on a medal in the horizontal bar final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan.
Photo: Patrick Post, AP
He said he had reviewed his performance with coach Huang Bo-rui (黃柏瑞) and a sports psychologist after the Asian Games.
He decided to treat the world championships final as a practice session and compete without pressure, which helped him stay calm and in control without overthinking.
This approach seemed to work quite well, he said with a laugh, adding that he now felt more confident about qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics at next year’s world championships.
Tang said he was unsure how he had performed after his unsteady landing and kept wondering how he had made such a mistake.
He said he was most grateful to everyone who had supported him, including his coaches, teammates and athletic trainers.
“We won this gold medal together, helping take Taiwan’s gymnastics another step further on the world stage,” he said.
Tang said he struggled with his preparations during the first week of training under the pressure of back-to-back major competitions. His wife, Tseng Jo-yu (曾若語), arrived in Rotterdam a day before the event and gave him a much-needed boost.
“I was physically and mentally exhausted during the training camp and didn’t feel I was in my best form, but after my wife arrived, simply having a meal and chatting with her made me feel recharged,” he said.
Tang, who has been married for two years, said his wife is his “invisible coach.”
She understood how he was feeling, kept him grounded when he got overly excited and encouraged him when he was feeling down, he said.
Huang said he had been sleeping poorly in the days leading up to the world championships because of the high level of competition, but Tang continued to train as usual after qualifying, without making any special adjustments.
Tang’s routine had the highest difficulty score in the field, so he would be hard to beat as long as he completed it, Huang said, adding that he had urged Tang to stay calm and avoid putting too much pressure on himself.
This year’s Artistic Gymnastics World Championships were held from Oct. 17 to Sunday.

Taiwan’s 14th urgent care center to open on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:36 UTC
01:48:36 KST

The nation’s 14th urgent care center (UCC) is to open in Tainan on Sunday, while Taipei aims to open a new center at Huashan Market, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said yesterday.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare in November last year launched a pilot program with 13 UCCs in the six special municipalities to provide emergency treatment for mild illness and injuries on weekends and on holidays to relieve pressure on crowded emergency rooms.
With schools and work suspended nearly nationwide due to Typhoon Champi on Friday, the long holiday weekend became a four-day weekend for many people.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
About 75 percent of clinics were open yesterday and some hospitals also resumed outpatient services, which helped relieve overcrowding at emergency departments, Shih said.
In addition, a new UCC would open at Tainan’s Da-an Women and Children Hospital on Sunday, he said.
As there was an average of more than 100 patients at the UCC at Tainan’s Yongchuan Hospital, the city’s public health bureau proposed opening another one, he said.
Before the Double Ten National Day three-day weekend, the ministry had announced that during long weekends through the end of this year, a 50-percent surcharge would be added to consultation fees, nursing fees and pharmacist service fees at primary care clinics and hospitals’ outpatient and emergency departments, Shih said.
Eighty percent of the surcharge must be distributed to on-duty staff, he said.
To alleviate overcrowding at National Taiwan University Hospital’s emergency department, the Taipei Department of Health is planning to set up a UCC near the hospital at the Huashan Market, Shih said.
Preparations for the center are under way, and the department hopes to open it before the Lunar New Year holiday next year, he said.
Between July and Oct. 18, the most common reasons for visiting the nation’s 13 UCCs were for fever and respiratory infections (46 percent), followed by minor wounds (13 percent) and gastrointestinal discomfort (9 percent), National Health Insurance Administration data showed.

輕鬆華語GO: EASY CHINESE GO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:35 UTC
01:48:35 KST

對話 Dialogue
華華：最近天氣終於涼快一點了，我想找一天去騎腳踏車。
Huáhua: Zuìjìn tiānqì zhōngyú liángkuai yìdiǎn le, wǒ xiǎng zhǎo yì tiān qù qí jiǎotàchē.
Photo: Unsplash / 照片：Unsplash
清清：我也想去！秋天最適合騎車了，不會像夏天那麼熱。
Qīngqīng: Wǒ yě xiǎng qù! Qiūtiān zuì shìhé qí chē le, bú huì xiàng xiàtiān nàme rè.
華華：你平常都去哪裡騎？
Huáhua: Nǐ píngcháng dōu qù nǎlǐ qí?
清清：我很喜歡去河濱自行車道，一邊騎車一邊看風景，很舒服。
Qīngqīng: Wǒ hěn xǐhuān qù hébīn zìxíngchēdào, yìbiān qí chē yìbiān kàn fēngjǐng, hěn shūfu.
華華：聽起來不錯，不過我很久沒騎了，可能騎一下就累了。
Huáhua: Tīng qǐlái búcuò, búguò wǒ hěn jiǔ méi qí le, kěnéng qí yíxià jiù lèi le.
清清：沒關係，我們可以慢慢騎，累了就停下來休息。
Qīngqīng: Méiguānxi, wǒmen kěyǐ mànmàn qí, lèi le jiù tíng xiàlái xiūxi.
華華：那我們這週六早上六點出發吧！騎完車再去附近吃早餐。
Huáhua: Nà wǒmen zhè zhōuliù zǎoshang liù diǎn chūfā ba! Qí wán chē zài qù fùjìn chī zǎocān.
清清：蛤？六點也太早了吧！我可能爬不起來，我們晚一點出發吧！
Qīngqīng: Há? Liù diǎn yě tài zǎo le ba! Wǒ kěnéng pá bù qǐlái, wǒmen wǎn yìdiǎn chūfā ba!
翻譯 Translation
Huahua: The weather has finally gotten a little cooler lately. I’d like to go cycling soon.
Qingqing: Me too. Autumn is the perfect time for cycling. It’s not as hot as summer.
Huahua: Where do you usually go cycling?
Qingqing: I really like cycling along riverside bike paths. It’s relaxing to ride while enjoying the scenery.
Huahua: That sounds nice, but I haven’t ridden a bike in a long time. I might get tired pretty quickly.
Qingqing: That’s OK. We can take it slow and stop for a break when we get tired.
Huahua: Then let’s head out at six this Saturday morning. After our ride, we can get breakfast somewhere nearby.
Qingqing: What? Six is way too early. I might not be able to get out of bed. Let’s leave a little later.
生詞 Vocabulary
1. 終於 (zhōngyú) finally; at last
2. 涼快 (liángkuai) cool; pleasantly cool
3. 河濱 (hébīn) riverside; riverbank
4. 自行車道 (zìxíngchēdào) bike path; bicycle path
5. 週六 (zhōuliù) Saturday
6. 蛤 (há) Huh?; What?
7. 爬不起來 (pá bu qǐlái) can’t get out of bed;
can’t get up
8. 出發 (chūfā) set out/off; depart; leave
教材音檔 Audio Files
國立清華大學華語中心提供
By National Tsing Hua University Chinese Language Center:
After Taiwan and India signed a memorandum of understanding in 2024, Taiwan’s Ministry of Labor announced that roughly 1,000 Indian migrant workers could arrive as early as the end of this year. The policy immediately sparked fierce online debate, with supporters calling it a remedy for labor shortages while opponents launched petitions urging suspension. Who is the Hebrew-speaking ‘fox applying for the henhouse guard job?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:47:39 UTC
01:47:39 KST

Who is the Hebrew-speaking ‘fox applying for the henhouse guard job?’
Lana Nusseibeh’s close alignment with Israel shadows her bid to lead the UN
TEHRAN — Having spent years whitewashing Abu Dhabi’s submission to Israeli interests, Lana Nusseibeh is now being promoted by her handlers to run the United Nations.
Nominated on Oct. 21, the 48-year-old minister of state is the newest and most contested entrant in the race to succeed António Guterres, and the objections started within hours.
Nusseibeh was born in 1978 into a family in al-Quds (Jerusalem). Her grandfather Anwar sat in Jordanian governments, her father Zaki advises the UAE’s rulers, and her uncle Sari is a philosophy professor.
She read history at Cambridge, then took a master’s in “Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies” in London, where her teacher Colin Shindler later called her “instrumental” in the 2020 normalization deal. She is fluent in Hebrew.
In 2013, she became the UAE’s first female ambassador to the UN and stayed eleven years, twice presiding over the Security Council.
‘The fox applying for the henhouse guard job’
Weeks before the Abraham Accords were signed, she told the Emirati outlet The National that the “empty chair policy” toward Israel “had produced no peace.” She went on to host Israel’s then-UN envoy, Gilad Erdan, at the Emirati mission.
In March, she rushed to condemn Iran’s defensive counterstrikes against U.S. bases across the region, while ignoring the underlying U.S.-Israeli campaign of aggression that precipitated them. She uttered not a word regarding the loss of Iranian civilian lives, including the devastating American attack on an elementary school in Minab that killed 155 civilians, over 120 of them children.
Her defenders point to her September 2025 warning against Israel annexing the West Bank as proof of her independence. But a closer look shows she was actually protecting the anti-Palestine Abraham Accords, which formal annexation would have destroyed.
The UAE has kept and even upgraded its ties with Israel through every month of the ongoing genocidal war on Gaza, whose toll now exceeds 74,000.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reacted to her nomination in an X post. He called the bid a runway-clearing exercise for the “Greater Israel” project and a way to whitewash genocide, then added that “the fox is updating the LinkedIn profile to apply for the henhouse guard job.”
He attached excerpts of an interview in which she defends normalization with the genocidal Israeli regime.
The field and the arithmetic
Behind the sudden push lies Security Council arithmetic. In the Oct. 16 straw poll, front-runner Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica, who leads UNCTAD, secured nine “encourage” votes but faced “discourage” votes from two permanent members.
With IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and Guyana’s diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett capturing only two votes apiece, the Security Council vote ground to a halt, opening the door for Abu Dhabi’s push.
Into that deadlock stepped a candidate whom some observers now call the front-runner. Nusseibeh has quickly drawn support from a broad pro-Western coalition.
Key Washington voices, including Brett McGurk, as well as Israeli outlets such as Ynet and The Times of Israel, along with members of Tel Aviv’s foreign policy establishment, have welcomed her bid. Perversely and tragically, she is also backed by the Arab-led Persian Gulf Cooperation Council and the Palestinian Authority’s UN delegation.
Proxy networks and the independence question
Sudan poses a steep hurdle for Nusseibeh’s candidacy, casting a direct spotlight on Abu Dhabi’s aggressive regional posture.
A UN fact-finding mission reported in September reasonable grounds to believe UAE-linked entities armed and trained the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), fueling a devastating civil war and enabling genocidal massacres.
This policy forms part of a broader imperial strategy: across North Africa and the Horn, Abu Dhabi has cultivated proxy networks and armed non-state actors, from Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya to the Southern Transitional Council in Yemen and separatist movements in Somalia, fragmenting sovereign states to secure ports, gold-smuggling routes, and strategic influence.
In Sudan, this patronage network translated into direct logistical support for the RSF, causing deep friction across the Global South and making the UAE complicit in severe war crimes.
Justin Lynch, managing director of the Conflict Insights Group, told the AP that Nusseibeh operated as Abu Dhabi’s primary point person on Sudan, routinely offering assurances that the UAE was not aiding the RSF even while Washington and other Western capitals privately knew otherwise.
Lynch noted that the Secretary-General’s core duty is protecting civilians from atrocities such as the El Fasher siege, warning that “handing the job over to the diplomat who ran cover for it would be an insult to the survivors.”
Similarly, Nathaniel Raymond, executive director of Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab, cited an insurmountable “dual loyalty” and conflict of interest.
Pointing out that the RSF’s assault on El Fasher was made possible by UAE-supplied drones, mortars, and logistics, Raymond argued that the UN should not mark the anniversary of the El Fasher massacre by appointing an official from the very state credibly accused of enabling the carnage.
