Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:37 UTC
01:24:37 KST

A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.
Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.
The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.
Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."
Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.
Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.
James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out.
James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.
Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation."
"Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.
Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.
The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.
Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service."
"The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim.
"That is because the argument borders on frivolous."
The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews.
"Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.
The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on her
performance," Furman noted.
In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'"
"Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.
Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
"This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.
The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."
That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case.
The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds.
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to a post by the DOJ's Rapid Response account on X, which said, "The Department disagrees with this decision, which obstructs President Trump's constitutional authority to fire individuals who wield executive power on his behalf. We intend to appeal the decision in due course.
Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain."
"Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:24 UTC
01:24:24 KST

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Israeli demolitions and road closures have devastated businesses in Hebron, leaving owners facing millions in losses.
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Sufyan al-Qawasmi stood near the rubble of his factories in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron, lamenting the business he watched vanish beneath the debris.
Israeli bulldozers demolished the factories on Friday without any prior warning or notice, following a shooting attack carried out by two Palestinians that morning near Hebron’s western entrance. The attack killed two Israeli soldiers, as well as the two Palestinian gunmen, and prompted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to announce a large-scale military operation across Hebron and order preparations for a wider closure of the illegally occupied West Bank.
Demolitions are regularly used by Israel to punish Palestinians, typically the family members of attackers, but in al-Qawasmi’s case, for the misfortune of being close to the site of an attack. Human rights groups decry the practice, which is regarded as collective punishment.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich justified the demolitions as “establishing deterrence and exacting a price”.
The Israeli bulldozers destroyed a business that al-Qawasmi’s family had built up for his whole life, and provided a livelihood for more than 70 people. The first factory, which produced ceramics, is the same age as he is – it was established 50 years ago. Fifteen years later, the family opened a marble factory.
Their business flourished, becoming one of the most significant industrial operations in the West Bank, with goods exported to Israel.
In the space of a few hours on Friday, the ceramic factory and marble factory were gone, as well as several neighbouring buildings, including a three-storey house and various commercial facilities. Simultaneously, the city faced an Israeli military incursion that included the closure of all entrances, raids, arrests, and the forced evacuation of more than 3,000 Palestinians from their homes, severely disrupting the lives of residents and the city’s commercial activity.
The message was clear: the whole city would be punished for the actions of the attackers.
A devastating loss
Al-Qawasmi says he was given no chance to retrieve goods from the family businesses’ warehouses and factories before the demolitions began, leaving the stock buried under the rubble, where it remains.
“We managed to retrieve some marble slabs and store them in facilities belonging to friends nearby, but most of the stock was destroyed,” he told Al Jazeera.
Al-Qawasmi says that 1,300 square metres of their business’ property was destroyed, including the family’s offices. He estimates the losses at no less than 60 million shekels ($19m).
Those losses are devastating for al-Qawasmi’s family, but also for the wider economy in Hebron and the Palestinian economy as a whole.
According to the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Hebron serves as a primary pillar of the Palestinian economy, contributing approximately 42 percent of the Palestinian gross domestic product (GDP). It is home to more than 23,000 economic establishments, including more than 5,000 industrial and artisanal facilities that employ approximately 40,000 workers.
Hebron’s economy is notably diverse, encompassing sectors such as stone and marble, plastics, metals, food production, leather and footwear, and glass, alongside robust commercial and agricultural activity.
Adnan al-Natsha, vice president of the Hebron Chamber of Commerce, told Al Jazeera that there are no precise figures yet regarding the total losses resulting from the Israeli military operation so far. He noted that work is currently under way to compile statistics on the damage inflicted on businesses and homes, losses estimated to be in the millions of dollars.
Al-Natsha explained that the extensive Israeli measures, including closing off areas of the city, displacing residents from their homes, demolishing buildings and shutting down commercial shops, have exacerbated the already difficult economic situation in Hebron – which already has an illegal Israeli settlement in its commercial centre that severely disrupts Palestinian movement and trade there.
“Business owners have been unable to operate their facilities because workers couldn’t reach their workplaces, and employees have been unable to get to their jobs. The impact of these measures is not limited to Hebron; it extends to the Palestinian economy as a whole,” he stated, adding that work was ongoing to assess the losses and damages of the ongoing Israeli operation so far.
Paralysed commerce
The Israeli military continues to lock down Hebron, including the installation of checkpoints, earthen berms, and concrete blocks across the city, as it conducts raids. As a consequence, economic activity has been severely disrupted.
Ibrahim Ahmaro, who owns a vegetable shop in the al-Jalada neighbourhood, one of the areas targeted by the Israeli operation, told Al Jazeera that he had been arranging his stock on Friday, preparing for Saturday, which is typically the busiest day for commerce due to the arrival of buses carrying Palestinian citizens of Israel shopping for cheaper produce.
Military vehicles suddenly stormed the area, and soldiers forced Ahmaro to leave his shop immediately. He says that he wasn’t given an opportunity to turn on the refrigeration units, which would have kept his goods from spoiling, nor allowed to retrieve his vehicle, which remained parked in front of the shop.
“My brother, the staff and I all left, thinking it would only be for a few hours. Instead, we were met with a total lockdown of the area, and we were unable to reach our shops, meaning everything inside was lost after being left unattended for days,” he added.
On Sunday morning, Ahmaro was able to return to check on his stock, despite the heavy military presence in the area. As soon as he entered, he said soldiers attacked him inside the shop and forced him out. He pleaded with them to let him remove at least a few crates; they granted him a few minutes to do so.
“I placed the crates 400 metres away from the shops so that local residents, facing the lockdown, could take whatever they needed. My losses on these goods alone exceed 50,000 shekels [$16,200],” he said with a sigh.
Economic expert Ali Oweiwi said that the Israeli military’s restrictions and lockdowns imposed on Hebron have created significant challenges for commercial and industrial establishments, which rely on road access to transport production supplies and distribute their products.
He explained that the impact of the closure is not limited to retail shops but extends to companies, factories, suppliers, and the transport and logistics sector, not to mention the workers who are forced to take alternative routes to reach their workplaces, all of which ultimately affect consumers.
Oweiwi said that if the Israeli operation concludes within a day or two, the economy might recover relatively quickly. However, if it persists for more than 10 days, it could lead to significant problems, including the accumulation of goods, disruptions to transport and a decline in productivity due to the difficulty of moving both workers and merchandise.
Israel – which will vote for a new parliament in pivotal elections on Tuesday – has not announced an end date for the lockdown in Hebron.
“The destruction of facilities specialising in vehicle dismantling, spare parts, and tile shops has resulted in losses estimated at 70 to 80 million shekels ($22.7m to $26m), in addition to the seizure of dozens or perhaps hundreds of vehicles belonging to the owners of these establishments,” Oweiwi said.

Italy flotilla torture case against IDF officials even broader than ICC war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:23:43 UTC
01:23:43 KST

Italy’s criminal probe of flotilla activists’ torture claims against Israel impacts far more IDF officials than even the pending file before the International Criminal Court (ICC), multiple Israeli officials with knowledge of the case have confirmed to The Jerusalem Post.
Since 2007, flotilla activists have periodically sought to block Israel’s blockade to prevent weapons smuggling to Hamas in Gaza.
Although the activists claim they are seeking to bring Gazans humanitarian aid, Gazans have been receiving over 600 trucks of aid per day since the October 2025 ceasefire – almost triple what they were receiving pre-war.
Gazans’ overall situation is still far worse because the Strip is years away from being rebuilt, but there is no actual food shortage.
ICC seeks to arrest Netanyahu, Gallant, may target other Israeli officials
Currently, the ICC is confirmed to be seeking to arrest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, with reports that it is also seeking to arrest minister Betzalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, and possibly also Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, and former IDF chief Herzi Halevi.
That is still a short list, and most of the officials are government officials because Israel has not probed its government officials.
In contrast, the Italian criminal probe relating to Israel’s treatment of arrested activists from the September-October 2025 and April-May 2026 flotillas not only includes many of the same ministers, but it also implicates a long list of IDF and prison service officials, of around a dozen.
In fact, the IDF officials being targeted are even more noteworthy than the prison service officials, given that there is some cloud of impropriety hanging over the prison service since it has been managed in recent years by Ben-Gvir.
Ben-Gvir himself was condemned by the entire Israeli government for various actions he undertook and statements he made relating to the flotilla activists.
But the IDF officials include completely apolitical and generally highly regarded officials, such as: former navy chief David Saar Salame, current Navy Chief Eyal Harel, each of their top advisers Tal Politis and Guy Levy, Ashdod Naval Base Chief Eitan Paz, and the Shayetet 13 Naval Commander.
While none of the activists’ claims against Israeli officials have been proven, there have been Israeli officials concerned that police and prison guard officials, who are under Ben-Gvir’s command, may have roughed up some of the activists.
Put differently, even if some of the most sensational charges might be untrue or exaggerated, some officials recognize that some of the lesser claims against officials under Ben-Gvir may be true.
Yet, there are no Israeli officials who believe that the navy’s conduct was anything other than highly professional, leaving many mystified as to what prosecutors from Italy – a country which has been one of Israel’s stronger allies even after October 7- could really be trying to get after going after IDF and naval officials.
The Post understands from officials with knowledge of the case that the prosecution is being run by a local Italian prosecutor, who is not coordinating with the Italian federal government.
Italian prosecutor rogue prosecutor, Israeli officials tell 'Post'
In other words, Israeli officials speaking to the Post portrayed the prosecutor as a rogue prosecutor who is using an Italian law for universal jurisdiction that the government would not have intended or expected to use against an ally like Israel, as much as it may have been passed to go after a traveling warlord from a more broken non-democratic country.
Further, the case has been a major domestic politics issue within Italy, such that some officials may see it as advantageous internally to make noise about such a case, without necessarily moving it forward to the end, something which could take many years in any event.
Around the time of the flotillas, Italy suspended certain defense cooperation arrangements with Israel, and the sides have sparred publicly over the treatment of some activists who were recently detained in the West Bank while assisting Palestinians with the olive harvest.
However, Israeli officials still view this criminal proceeding as being in conflict with overall Italian government policy, which has not sought to inflame relations.
Rather, multiple sources with knowledge of the case said that the long list of IDF officials who are considered highly professional simply indicated how politicized and disjointed the specific prosecutor likely was.
Moreover, they indicated that once a criminal probe is opened, it is always easier to add other suspects into the probe, even if they have less of a true connection to the heart of the issue.
The Israeli minister, IDF officials, police, and prison officials were all put under official investigation in Italy on October 16.
The move expanded an investigation that was previously focused on Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns alleged torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors’ office said in a statement.
Probe opened after activists launched complaints
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Notably, being insulted and being accused of terrorism might be problematic or fully justified, but would usually not be criminally probed.
Activists involved in the second mission alleged even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of rubber bullets, and tasers, a statement said.
Once again, some of these actions would clearly be criminal, but using a non-lethal taser to subdue a person resisting arrest is standard even in the West.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
Questioned about their response, multiple Israeli authorities declined to address the issue, signaling that Israel may view the request as invalid if it is not endorsed by the Italian federal government or may choose to deal with it through diplomatic channels as opposed to strictly technical channels.
An interesting question would be whether Israel might comply more if the requests were more limited to Ben-Gvir and some of his officials, who took videos of themselves at minimum verbally harassing detainees.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Moldovan PM: Country’s airspace violated over 100 times since war began
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan made the statement while speaking to the media alongside Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi in Kyiv, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Speaking from the Ukrainian capital, Tofan addressed the citizens of his country, stressing that Ukraine, by defending itself against Russian aggression, is contributing to peace and security across Europe.

“Our duty is to protect the peace and security of our citizens,” Tofan stressed.

According to Tofan, this would help attract investment and create jobs in the country.
“That is why supporting Ukraine is a choice in favor of the security, peace and prosperity of the Republic of Moldova,” the prime minister stressed.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan hold rare Iran talks as Houthis strike again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:20:55 UTC
01:20:55 KST

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday in an unusual diplomatic effort to ease tensions across the Middle East, even as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved military assistance to help defend the kingdom. Reuters reported that the meeting marked the first high-level talks between Iran and the three countries since the regional war expanded to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit, initiated by Pakistan, was intended to prevent further escalation. Saudi Arabia was represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, the younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, also attended. Reuters reported Sunday that Qatari mediators had arrived in Tehran as part of the broader diplomatic effort.
The meeting brought together Iran and the three members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. Iran has previously been mentioned as a possible future participant in the pact, but the arrangement is facing a significant test as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue despite the mutual defense commitments.
Iran rules out nuclear talks as threat of US strikes grows
An Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran's nuclear program was not discussed at the meeting and would remain off the agenda until Iran's conditions for ending the war were met. Those demands include lifting the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and removing sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iranian reports said the discussions instead focused on regional security and assistance to people in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon.
Pezeshkian expressed support for greater cooperation among Muslim-majority countries, saying Iran was prepared to deepen regional ties, resolve disagreements and strengthen collective security. He urged countries in the region to stand together against common threats and accused Israel, with U.S. support, of committing atrocities while accusing others of terrorism. According to Iranian reports, participants agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation among the four countries, particularly on regional peace and security.
The diplomatic initiative comes amid renewed threats of military confrontation between Washington and Tehran. Reuters reported that Iran had prepared detailed plans to attack undersea cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel launched another offensive. CNN, meanwhile, reported that U.S. forces already deployed in the Middle East could begin major military operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei during the Tehran talks, where Iran's nuclear program was reportedly not discussed
According to two U.S. officials cited by CNN, sufficient forces are positioned in the region to carry out an operation potentially broader than previous limited strikes against Iranian radar systems, missile launchers and other military assets that could be quickly rebuilt. Trump has not issued an order to launch such an operation.
Egypt approves military assistance as Houthis target Saudi oil lifeline
Meanwhile, Egypt's parliament approved defensive military assistance for Saudi Arabia in a closed-door session Monday, following an earlier postponement of the vote. The authorization allows President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to help Riyadh defend its territory and sovereignty against external aggression. The parliament did not disclose a detailed breakdown of the vote or specify the scope of the assistance.
A regional official familiar with the plans said Egypt would deploy air defense systems to help intercept missiles and drones launched toward Saudi Arabia. The official emphasized that Cairo's involvement would be strictly defensive and would not include ground forces. "Egypt will not send ground troops," the official said.
At the same time, the Houthis claimed to have launched new attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline and on Riyadh's airport, where two terminals had resumed operations only a day earlier after previous attacks forced their closure. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the latest Houthi claims.
The East-West pipeline has become a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, allowing Saudi Arabia to transport oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea port of Yanbu without relying on the strategic waterway. A pumping station strike disrupted the route about a month ago, highlighting its vulnerability to further attacks.
According to an earlier report by The Guardian, the pipeline played a critical role in protecting Saudi oil exports during the war with Iran, when shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was severely disrupted. Saudi Arabia used the route to divert approximately 4 million barrels of oil per day, equivalent to roughly 4% of global supply, to Yanbu. The renewed attacks threaten an energy lifeline that has helped the kingdom withstand one of the most serious disruptions to Gulf oil exports in recent years.

Pope Leo's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru to go ahead, Vatican says

Pope fit enough to make Latin America trip next month, Vatican says
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru will go ahead, the Vatican said on Oct 26, indicating that his recovery from lung cancer surgery was on track and that he was fit enough to make the Nov 6-17 journey.
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering from an Oct 13 surgery in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
“The Holy Father’s recovery after the surgery continues, and the latest medical examinations attest to his good health and favorable clinical condition,” the Vatican said in a statement, citing the Pope’s personal physician Luigi Carbone.
“Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey,” the statement said.
Pope returning to familiar region
The Pope’s South America tour is set to be one of the most intense foreign trips taken by a Catholic leader in decades. He is scheduled to travel some 31,000km over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said the trip would proceed with no changes to the previously published agenda.
The Pope had spent decades as a missionary in Peru before his predecessor Francis called him back to Rome in 2023 and promoted him to Vatican positions, so the trip will mark a homecoming of sorts for the first US pontiff.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” he said in the Vatican message.
“May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy,” Leo said.
In its statement, the Vatican said the Pope was “adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfil the responsibilities of his ministry”.
On Oct 25, the Pope addressed the faithful in St Peter’s Square, but on doctors’ advice he cancelled a day visit to the central Italian town of Assisi, which had been scheduled for Oct 27. REUTERS

IDF and Shin Bet kill Hamas military intelligence commander and engineering commander in Gaza strikes
The IDF and Shin Bet killed Mohammed Halawa, a commander in the military intelligence apparatus of Hamas’s military wing, in a strike in the Gaza City area on Saturday, according to a joint statement.
In a separate strike last week on Thursday, the IDF killed Ahmed Zahir Fuad Abu-Odeh, an engineering commander in Hamas’s military wing.
The IDF said the terrorists had advanced terror plots against troops and Israeli civilians throughout the war and especially recently, and worked to rebuild Hamas’s capabilities in systematic violation of the ceasefire.
It said both were killed from the air to remove the threat they posed, and that security forces remain deployed in the area in accordance with the agreement and will continue to act to remove any threat.
Netanyahu pushed for new Iran strikes, but the US asked him to wait for joint operations - report
PM Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing for new attacks on Iran, but US officials asked him to delay until the Trump administration is ready to conduct joint operations, according to two US officials and an Israeli security source who spoke with CNN.
“Netanyahu really wanted and tried to convince Trump for a joint attack in Iran before the elections, and Trump did not give a green light,” the Israeli security source said.
One source claimed Israel had been preparing for additional strikes over the last week or so and lobbying US officials to support them, but senior US officials, including President Donald Trump, told Israel to hold off and signaled the two countries would launch joint operations soon.
Separately, recent US intelligence assessments indicate Iran and the Houthis are taking the possibility of renewed US and potentially Israeli attacks very seriously. However, they are unlikely to carry out preemptive escalatory attacks on American personnel or Israel at this point.

Defense Minister Israel Katz said on X that reports of rifts between the political echelon and the IDF concerning Iran are “completely baseless and false.”
“Since I assumed the role of Defense Minister, the coordination between the Prime Minister, myself, and the IDF regarding Iran has been absolute, yielding unprecedented, historic achievements for the security of the State of Israel,” Katz wrote.
“I state unequivocally that Israel had no intention of initiating an attack on Iran prior to the elections in Israel. We made it clear that should Iran attack Israel, we would respond with great force; any reports to the contrary are entirely false.”
He also accused opposition figures of exploiting the reports to attack PM Benjamin Netanyahu and himself, calling it “shameful and irresponsible.”

Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot said in a post on X that Israel’s elections would begin in 24 hours, calling them “the fateful elections in the history of the state,” concerning “its future, identity, and security.”

In response to US President Donald Trump’s second endorsement of Netanyahu, Eisenkot wrote, “Donald Trump is a true friend of Israel. I appreciate his actions and commitment to Israel’s security, and I am convinced that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people.”

Top officials from the Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss regional coordination, two people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the Turkish head of intelligence will also join, one of the people said.

Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected Sunday, with Brazil’s electoral court announcing that he won 51.8% of the vote, a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, with 100% counted.

The electoral court’s president said the extension did not affect the results, and a law professor said there is little legal basis to annul the vote. Lula, who will begin a fourth non-consecutive term on Jan. 5, 2027, told supporters: “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard.”

If Netanyahu loses, who will Democrats blame next? - analysis

If Netanyahu loses, who will Democrats blame next? - analysis
As Israel heads to the polls, a potential change of government could test whether Democrats' criticism is directed at Netanyahu or at Israeli policies that may outlast him.
It’s coming.
For the last couple of years especially, an increasing number of Israel critics have couched their denunciations with the phrase “the Netanyahu government,” inferring their condemnations apply specifically to the current administration in Jerusalem, and not to the Jewish state as a whole.
We may be about to find out whether “the Netanyahu government” will join “anti-Zionism” as short-lived code words for antisemitism, as a potential change of government in Israel will bring about a masks-off moment back in the United States.
Sen. Bernie Sanders has long railed against “the Netanyahu government” in calling for weapons boycotts against Israel.
Wannabe heirs to the progressive throne, like Sens. Chris Murphy and Chris Van Hollen, have since joined in the refrain, making “the Netanyahu government” a key part of their vernacular.
But what happens if Gadi Eisenkot or another challenger emerges from this week’s election as the new prime minister?
Well, we are already starting to catch a glimpse.
Jon Finer, who served as principal deputy national security adviser in the Biden administration, believes his year as a reporter in Israel and his time John Kerry’s Iran-fanboy State Department gives him better insight into Israel’s security than Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff.
“Rather than offering a new Israeli government the benefit of the doubt, Democrats should learn from the past and make it choose between the abundant and irreplaceable benefits of the US relationship and the indefensible policies that are driving a wedge between our societies,” Finer wrote last week in the New York Times, noting Israelis largely agree with Eisenkot, Netanyahu and every conceivable near-term leader, that a Palestinian state would endanger Israel’s security.
There is little doubt that many old-school Democrats, looking to keep the base from swallowing them whole, have used “the Netanyahu government” refrain, together with recriminations of various Israeli government ministers, in order to give cover, which they feel they need, for votes in support of Israel.
The thinking, it goes, is that they can say to their constituencies that they aren’t going to throw the US-Israel relationship down the drain when governments come and go.
But the Murphys and Van Hollens of the world appear to want to do exactly that: throw away the relationship.
Murphy recently plugged his Middle East tour, ostensibly to challenge the Trump administration on the Iran war.
https://www.facebook.com/reel/2641013736318799

He curiously touted the notion that while he and Saudi Arabian leadership disagree on issues – some of which he’s vocal about – there are opportunities to work together.
Similarly, Qatar, that bastion of American values, does “so many things” to “protect US interests,” Murphy said.
“They were key to getting the hostages out of Gaza,” Murphy added, in a masterclass of gaslighting.
Of course, he challenged them on his “deep concerns about the transfer of the luxury plane” to the Trump administration.
This is key to understanding where we are heading: To the new-age Democrats who have succumbed to the progressive base, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and their ilk don’t need to be beaten over the head. They can be partners. They can even “protect US interests.”
But, Murphy said this summer that while “I support Israel. I cannot support this government’s actions. They are not aligned with US national security objectives.”
Van Hollen has made similar remarks.
Yes, you can talk with Saudi Arabia, and you can tout Qatar’s protection of America, but the Israelis? Not so much, if you’re Murphy, because apparently America’s primary national security interest in the Middle East is a post-Oct. 7 Palestinian state.
This is key to understanding what is coming. Some have made it starkly clear that Israel has no place in the Middle East for any reason. But those that are vying for leadership of the Democratic party, especially on matters of foreign affairs, are soon going to have to make a choice as to what to do if “the Netanyahu government” is no longer around the blame.
While the Eisenkots of the world may take a more conciliatory approach to bipartisanship, and may be able to deliver a different message on behalf of Israel, the bottom line is that most of the policies Israel detractors abhor will remain in place, because they are necessary for Israel’s security.
Ironically, the Bernie Sanders of the world may give a new government some space to breathe and potentially shape new or varying approaches to policy. But it’s already clear that others, like Murphy, Van Hollen, et. al, who have ridden Sanders’ coattails, have long had their minds made up.
It’s not about US security at all. It’s about the base, and their own desires to move up the party ladder. As a result, “the Eisenkot government” would simply become the new refrain.

Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky has said competitions for civil service positions will resume in stages, with competitions for Category A positions announced from the date the relevant law takes effect.
"We are resuming competitions for civil service and local government positions. Competitions will resume in stages: for Category A positions, they will be announced from the date the law takes effect, for Category B positions one month later, and for Category C positions and local government positions two months later. We are also updating the procedure. All vacancies will be listed in Diia. War veterans will have priority in appointments," Koretsky wrote on Telegram.
The prime minister recalled that resuming competitions is one of Ukraine's commitments under the Ukraine Facility programme, and that fulfilment of this commitment is linked to the disbursement of EUR 137 million in support.
According to Koretsky, the government is currently preparing the necessary decisions to introduce the new procedure as soon as possible.
As reported, on Oct 26 the Verkhovna Rada reinstated competitions for civil service positions. The law provides for the resumption of competitions for civil service and local government positions, and changes to the procedures for entering, serving in and leaving the civil service. It also grants priority in civil service appointments to people with war veteran status.
The law also allows civil servants appointed without competition during martial law to continue serving, provided they receive a positive annual performance assessment, and introduces integrity criteria. At the same time, it allows appointments without competitive selection to civil service positions in local government bodies located in areas where hostilities are taking place.

Indian and Russian forces deploy drones and robotic systems in simulated combat
Indian and Russian troops have finished up the INDRA-2026 military exercises in Chelyabinsk Region. During simulated combat, they worked with drones, artillery, tanks, and robotic systems, making use of real-world battlefield experience.
The ground phase of the exercise ended on Friday after ten days at a Russian Central Military District training ground, Russia’s Defense Ministry said.
The final operation simulated the enemy occupying a settlement and establishing defensive positions. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground-based robotic systems carried out reconnaissance before artillery units and strike drones targeted mock command posts, weapons positions, and supply depots, clearing the way for a joint assault.
The joint contingents then advanced under cover from tanks, air defense systems, mobile fire teams, and first-person-view (FPV) drone interceptors. The forces practiced securing the settlement and pursuing the retreating enemy, completing the ground exercise.
The October 14-23 drills focused on joint command and control and coordinating operations against armed groups. The Russian contingent consisted primarily of personnel from the Central Military District’s 90th Guards Tank Division.

Joint statement by the members of the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and…

Joint statement by the members of the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan - First Anniversary of the October 26th, 2025 atrocity in El Fasher Sudan Human rights Joint statement On : October 23rd 2026 One year ago, on 26 October 2025, the violence in and around El Fasher reached a devastating peak following months of siege and escalating attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Civilians were subjected to horrific atrocities including mass killings, ethnically motivated killings, summary executions, torture, disappearances, forced recruitment, arbitrary detentions, and widespread sexual and gender-based violence. Entire communities were forcibly displaced, and humanitarian access was obstructed, exacerbating hunger, insecurity, human suffering and deprivation. Today, the Coalition for Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan stands together to remember and recognise the suffering of victims and survivors, and reaffirm our shared determination to prevent further atrocities and pursue accountability. The findings of the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan have laid bare the scale and severity of violations of international humanitarian law and violations and abuses of international human rights law committed in and around El Fasher. The Coalition supports the UN Fact-Finding Mission and its work, and welcomes the recent renewal of its mandate. We also welcome the work of the African Union’s Fact-Finding Mission, and its collaboration with the UN. One year on, many civilians continue to bear the consequences of these atrocities. Across Sudan, civilians continue to be victims of violence, including systemic and widespread use of sexual violence, displacement, attacks on civilian infrastructure and restrictions on humanitarian assistance. The growing use of drones in attacks affecting civilians, and civilian infrastructure is deepening humanitarian needs and protection risks. Taken together, this demonstrates that the risk of further large-scale atrocities in Sudan remains acute. Restrictions on humanitarian access and repeated attacks on humanitarian actors, local and frontline responders are unacceptable, and are compounding the suffering of millions of Sudanese civilians. This anniversary is a reminder that we must act collectively to prevent their repetition. Justice and accountability are vital to achieving sustainable peace in Sudan. Victims and survivors deserve justice and accountability for the heinous crimes perpetrated during this conflict. Those responsible for serious violations and abuses must be investigated and held to account. The Coalition will continue working with Sudanese and international partners to support credible accountability processes, including the work of the International Criminal Court concerning Darfur, and meaningful transitional justice for the people of Sudan. Sudanese human rights defenders and civil society organisations play a crucial role in supporting victims and survivors, documenting abuses, and ensuring that Sudanese perspectives help shape future accountability and justice efforts. Often working at great personal risk, they are indispensable partners in the pursuit of peace, justice and accountability. Victims of conflict related sexual violence must have safe and confidential access to medical, psychosocial and legal support. There is no military solution to this conflict. The war must end. The Coalition calls on all parties to comply fully with international humanitarian law, including by protecting civilians and facilitating safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. We also call on all states to comply with international law, and use their influence to protect civilians, prevent further atrocities and help bring this devastating conflict to an end, including by ceasing to arm, finance and otherwise enable the war in Sudan, and by fully respecting UN sanctions including the arms embargo on Darfur. One year after El Fasher, our message is clear: the victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.

Europe is living in a new ‘era of darkness,’ Finland’s Stubb warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:16:52 UTC
01:16:52 KST

Alexander Stubb after a meeting with the President of the French Republic at the Élysée Palace in Paris. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Europe is living through an “era of darkness” as multiple wars and competition between the U.S. and China trample the rules-based global order, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Monday.
Speaking at the College of Europe in Bruges, Stubb said the post-Cold War age has ended and the world now faces a pivotal moment, like those at the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of communism in 1989.
While he tends towards optimism, there are now “unfortunately, plenty of reasons to be pessimistic,” he told an audience of students at the institution, which Stubb himself attended in the 1990s.
Advertisement
“In a sense, I began my studies during an era of light and you begin your studies in an era of darkness,” he said. “We used to be able to say that the three biggest killers of mankind, disease, famine and wars, have been defeated. That is not true anymore. The light has given way to darkness.”
Stubb, who has studied and written extensively on geopolitical upheaval, has been intimately involved in European efforts to navigate U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term — particularly when it comes to the question of a peace deal for Ukraine.
He told his audience they would graduate into “a dog-eat-dog world” in which there are, by some estimates, 65 conflicts or wars playing out — “more than at any time after the Second World War.”
Global security will “depend on what the big powers — namely the U.S. and China — end up doing. Will they choose co-operation or confrontation?” he said.
“The key question for all of us is to create a European security structure which makes sure that Russia does not attack its neighbors again,” he said. NATO will remain a vital security alliance but new processes should also be developed, he said, including “confidence building” measures between Russia and Europe to build “trust.”
Stubb urged the audience of future diplomats, politicians and officials not to be pessimistic, but to be ambitious for a new “era of light,” despite the challenges. He said that in 30 years’ time, the European Union could grow to 40 member countries from the current 27 — including the U.K. rejoining the bloc alongside Norway, Moldova and Ukraine.

electronic fibers weave touchscreen into sleeve that survives machine washing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:15:44 UTC
01:15:44 KST

electronic fibers weave touchscreen into sleeve that survives machine washing
the technology can display images and video, respond to finger presses, and connect wirelessly to digital devices, while retaining the breathability and flexibility of everyday fabric.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
electronic fibers turn fabric into a touchscreen
Researchers at the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed a touchscreen integrated directly into a garment using electronic fibers that combine light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and touch sensors. Led by Assistant Professor Tural Khudiyev, the team integrates 54 of these fibers into a sleeve to create a flexible display that shows images and video, responds to finger presses, and connects wirelessly to digital devices. The research introduces a textile interface that retains the breathability and flexibility of everyday clothing while withstanding machine washing.
Unlike conventional wearable technology, which typically attaches a screen or electronic device to the body, the NUS team’s approach builds display and touch functionality into the fibers themselves. Each thread contains interconnected microelectronic components within a structure just one millimeter thick, allowing the fabric to function as an interactive screen without a rigid display panel. The prototype measures 168 by 105 millimeters, refreshes at 30 frames per second, and retains nearly unchanged display and touch performance after 50 machine-washing cycles. The technology could eventually allow clothing to function as an interface for digital information, environmental sensing, and health monitoring.
how to turn a thread into a screen
Conventional electronic circuits are designed on flat surfaces, where components can be arranged and connected across two dimensions. A thread, by contrast, is narrow and cylindrical, leaving little room for the complex wiring needed to operate a display. In order to overcome this limitation, the researchers developed an interconnection architecture that allows thousands of microelectronic devices to be connected along a single fiber. The process begins with tiny, insulated wires. A laser exposes specific points along their surfaces, while controlled wetting directs molten solder to the designated locations, creating electrical connections without joining unintended areas. Using this method, the team integrated more than 5,000 chips through over 20,000 electrical connections.
The interconnected digital LEDs are then incorporated into a multilayer fiber using a thermal drawing process. The resulting thread measures approximately one millimeter in diameter and 10 meters in length, with separate layers responsible for displaying images and detecting touch. A touch-sensitive layer sits beneath the LEDs. When someone presses the fiber, the contact completes an electrical circuit, allowing the system to identify the location of the touch and illuminate the nearest pixel. Display and interaction therefore happen within the same thread, rather than through separate components attached to the fabric.
a device that behaves like fabric
For the prototype, the team threaded 54 pixel-bearing fibers into the forearm of a sleeve. Each fiber carries 96 LEDs, combining to form a 96-by-54-pixel display measuring 168 by 105 millimeters. The screen refreshes at 30 frames per second and supports 8-bit color depth. The display is still modest in resolution compared with a smartphone, but its capabilities extend beyond showing static images. It can play video, display photographs, run a calculator, and function as a compass. Users can also receive images over Bluetooth, interact through voice commands, and rotate the display or adjust its brightness automatically. The sleeve incorporates additional fibers that carry a microphone, a speaker, and sensors for movement, temperature, magnetic orientation, and ambient light. A temperature-sensing fiber positioned under the arm, for example, can measure body temperature and display the reading on the sleeve itself. Each pixel fiber also has its own control channel, meaning a fault in one line does not necessarily interrupt the others. The system can register multiple touches simultaneously, bringing it closer to the interactive behavior of a conventional touchscreen.
According to the researchers, the prototype retained nearly unchanged light output and touch response after 50 machine-washing cycles with detergent and 1,000 bends around a radius of five millimeters. The integrated display is also reported to be as breathable as cotton, polyester, and denim, while remaining within established skin-contact safety limits.
toward clothing that senses and responds
Healthcare is one potential application identified by the team. Fibers equipped with physiological sensors could collect information continuously and present it directly on a garment, allowing wearers to access measurements without consulting a separate device. Combined with artificial intelligence, the researchers suggest, such systems could eventually support personalized monitoring and feedback. That possibility remains a future direction rather than a demonstrated capability of the current prototype. The team’s next steps include improving resolution, integrating more sensing functions, and exploring on-device AI. The broader implication is a shift in how digital interfaces are designed. Smartphones and computers have accustomed us to accessing information through dedicated screens, while wearable technology has largely miniaturized existing devices or attached them to the body. The NUS research proposes a different relationship between electronics and everyday objects, one in which information can be displayed on the material already in contact with the wearer.
project info:
 research team: Tural Khudiyev, Heng Fu, Ziang Li, and Swetika Chaturvedi
institution:College of Design and Engineering, National University of Singapore (NUS)
lead researcher: Asst Prof. Tural Khudiyev, Department of Materials Science and Engineering

However, the war is taking place right on our borders," Tofan said during a joint briefing with Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He noted that the people of Moldova are also well aware of the threats to energy security.
The Prime Minister stated that since the beginning of the full-scale war, Moldova’s airspace has been violated more than 100 times, with drones and debris from projectiles falling onto its territory. Specifically, there were five such incidents this past Saturday alone.
"Supporting Ukraine is a choice in favor of the security, peace, and prosperity of the Republic of Moldova," Tofan emphasized.
As previously reported, on October 26, Ukraine and Moldova signed an agreement on military-technical cooperation, which paves the way for an exchange of expertise.

Volunteer urges residents to leave Oleshky in evacuation, as town may face greater destruction
The Russian-occupied town of Oleshky may face even greater destruction after civilians leave as part of a recent U.S.-negotiated ceasefire, evacuation volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 26.
"When television channels around the world show that dozens of buses full of people have left Oleshky, when it is reported that the evacuation has taken place and the town is practically deserted, we are very much afraid that, after that, Oleshky will simply be wiped off the face of the earth," Arkhipova said.
"Those who remain may find themselves in even more dreadful conditions," she added.
Her warning comes after U.S. first lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid. The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 3:00 a.m. on October 27th, Kyiv time, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a local ceasefire during the evacuation, but the exact evacuation routes remain unclear, and the sides are still working on the arrangements.
Arkhipova urged local residents remaining in the town to consider evacuation. She acknowledged that leaving home is a difficult decision for residents who have spent their entire lives there, but staying could expose them to escalating danger, intensifying hostilities, and lacking access to help.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, it has faced a deepening humanitarian crisis, with residents struggling to access food, medicine, electricity, and other basic necessities.
Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank, including Oleshky, to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Amid possible Russian escalation in the area, Arkhipova highlighted the risk that residents who remain in the town could be overlooked if reports of mass evacuations make it seem as if no civilians remain behind.
"The worst thing would be if the whole world came to believe that everyone had been evacuated from Oleshky, whilst (people) were still there. And (they) would simply be forgotten."
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. But in recent months, dangers posed by drone attacks, artillery fire, and mined roads have made evacuation by road almost impossible.
Russian forces have also prevented Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had previously verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.

Ukrainian military rescues two wounded soldiers using aerial evacuation drone – video
Fighters from Ukraine's 475th Separate Assault Regiment (also known as CODE 9.2) have rescued two wounded soldiers from the battlefield within a week using the StarGate drone designed for aerial medical evacuations.
Source: 475th Separate Assault Regiment; SkyFall, the drone's manufacturer, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The drone was used to evacuate two soldiers: 25-year-old Yevhen, alias Izium, and 24-year-old Artem, alias Kolobok.
"Both sustained severe limb injuries and were in the grey zone, approximately 5 km from the Russian border. Due to the difficult terrain, water obstacles and the threat posed by enemy FPV drones, ground evacuation was impossible. Aerial evacuation was the only available way to save them," the unit said.
The military spent a week preparing the complex evacuation missions in coordination with representatives of SkyFall, the company behind the casualty evacuation drone. The operations required fire support and coordination with other units of the Ukrainian defence forces. Heavy Vampire attack drones were used to suppress Russian positions.
"During one of the missions, StarGate travelled almost 30 km to reach a serviceman's position and approximately the same distance back, this time with the soldier on board. In the operational area, the enemy actively deployed electronic warfare systems in an attempt to completely suppress satellite navigation signals," CODE 9.2 explained.
The StarGate drone's flight was controlled using an AI-based navigation system, enabling the evacuation mission to be completed successfully despite the loss of satellite navigation.
The experience gained from using drones for aerial evacuation is expected to help the regiment establish a dedicated medical aviation unit, said Oleksandr "Flint" Nastenko, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment.
"It will specialise specifically in evacuating wounded soldiers from the battlefield by air," the commander explained.
SkyFall was previously reported to have developed the StarGate drone for the aerial evacuation of wounded personnel and handed it over to the military for frontline testing.
StarGate has a range of up to 30 km and can carry a payload of up to 150 kg. For casualty evacuation, it is fitted with a dedicated medical capsule equipped with a stretcher.
The SkyFall drone has a maximum speed of 105 km/h and is remotely operated. Its AI-powered systems allow it to function without GPS and in the face of electronic warfare interference.
On 19 October, a unique operation was also reported, in which the military evacuated a wounded soldier using an aerial drone for the first time. The operation was carried out using a drone manufactured by the Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence.

Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru to go ahead, Vatican says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:11:14 CET
01:11:14 KST

By Alvise Armellini
VATICAN CITY, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru will go ahead, the Vatican said on Monday, indicating that Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery was on track and that he was fit enough to make the November 6-17 journey.
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering from an October 13 surgery in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
“The Holy Father’s recovery after the surgery continues, and the latest medical examinations attest to his good health and favorable clinical condition,” the Vatican said in a statement, citing Leo’s personal physician Luigi Carbone.
“Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey,” the statement said.
POPE RETURNING TO FAMILIAR REGION
Leo’s South America tour is set to be one of the most intense foreign trips taken by a Catholic leader in decades. The pope is scheduled to travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said the trip would proceed with no changes to the previously published agenda.
Leo had spent decades as a missionary in Peru before his predecessor Francis called him back to Rome in 2023 and promoted him to Vatican positions, so the trip will mark a homecoming of sorts for the first US pontiff.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” he said in the Vatican message.
“May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy,” Leo said.
In its statement, the Vatican said Leo was “adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritize his recovery while continuing to fulfil the responsibilities of his ministry.”
On Sunday, the pope addressed the faithful in St Peter’s Square, but on doctors’ advice he cancelled a day visit to the central Italian town of Assisi, which had been scheduled for Tuesday.
(Reporting by Alvise Armellini, editing by Gavin Jones and Tomasz Janowski)

EU facing trillion-euro debt hole while seeking more cash for Kiev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:09:57 UTC
01:09:57 KST

EU facing trillion-euro debt hole while seeking more cash for Kiev
The EU faces a growing budget squeeze after borrowing hundreds of billions for pandemic recovery and Ukraine. Rising repayment costs threaten future spending and rushed payouts raise fraud risks, its chief auditor has warned. Brussels is nevertheless seeking billions more for Kiev.
Speaking to Rapporteur, Tony Murphy, president of the European Court of Auditors, described the budget situation as a “pressure cooker,” with EU debt potentially reaching €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion) by the end of 2027.The bloc’s debt stood at €739 billion in 2025, up from €601 billion a year earlier.
“You have to pay it back at some time. It’s not free money,” Murphy said. He emphasized that “it’s real money that has to be paid back.”
However, concerns have repeatedly been raised about the EU getting back any of the billions it has spent on Ukraine, including its recent €90 billion ($100 billion) loan, which Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico recently slammed as “gifts” that Ukraine will “never pay back.”
Kiev is required to repay the loan only after receiving Russian reparations – something Moscow has vehemently ruled out. Ukraine’s own former Prime Minister Nikolay Azarov has also acknowledged that such scenarios are “just fairy tales” and that Brussels will never get its money back, which is being actively embezzled by Kiev.
The EU, however, must still repay the money it borrowed. According to Murphy, servicing pandemic debt alone would consume 8% of the bloc’s proposed 2028–2034 budget and governments have yet to agree on new revenue to cover the repayments, leaving Brussels with less money for other priorities.
The squeeze comes as households and businesses continue to face high energy costs following Europe’s break with Russian supplies, compounded by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Murphy also warned about how quickly money is being spent. He called the requirement to process €90 billion in remaining pandemic recovery payments by December “crazy,” describing the impending payouts as a “tsunami.”
Pressure to meet deadlines could also encourage weaker checks and more abuse, he said, as European prosecutors are already investigating hundreds of suspected fraud cases involving recovery funds.
Despite the crisis, Brussels is again looking for more money for Kiev after Vladimir Zelensky requested another €70 billion ($78 billion) for 2027, beyond existing commitments. European Council President Antonio Costa said Friday that the EU expects to cover roughly two-thirds, with a decision potentially coming in November.

Italian father, son recall abuse by Israeli forces in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:09:39 UTC
01:09:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Italian father and son recount Israeli abuse in occupied West Bank
Israeli violations in the occupied West Bank are increasingly targeting foreign activists as well as Palestinians, with Italian NGO researcher and campaigner Manuel Tartarotti telling The New Arab how he and his father, Alberto, were arrested by Israeli police near Masafer Yatta in the southern occupied West Bank on 20 October.
The two men were blindfolded, transported in a military jeep to a base in Hebron, beaten and detained for 24 hours on suspicion of "terrorism" before being deported to Italy, according to Tartarotti.
Manuel Tartarotti, 35, is a doctoral researcher in NGO management at the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano in Italy, while his father, Alberto, is 67.
The Tartarotti family's West Bank experience
"They didn't tell us where they were taking us, and they beat me in the back of the vehicle. I didn't know what was going to happen. I was scared," Tartarotti said.
The father and son arrived in the West Bank on 18 October to deliver funds raised in Italy to Youth of Sumud, a Palestinian grassroots organisation that received the Alexander Langer International Award in 2024 in recognition of its peaceful resistance in the southern Hebron Hills.
Tartarotti said he had travelled with Palestinian members of the group and three Al Jazeera journalists to monitor and document demolitions in Palestinian villages after his friend Sami Huraini, a Palestinian activist and one of the group's founders, informed him that further demolitions were taking place.
Around half an hour later, Israeli police arrived and checked their IDs before taking the two Italians away.
They were interrogated, fingerprinted and had DNA samples taken, Tartarotti said. They remained handcuffed until the evening.
Israeli authorities subsequently informed them that they would be deported over suspected links to terrorism because they had entered an area declared off-limits and were associated with Youth of Sumud, which Israel designates as a terrorist organisation.
According to Tartarotti, they were told that their presence with the group, which does not advocate violence, meant they were linked to a terrorist organisation.
Israeli police, however, said the two men were suspected of illegally entering a military zone and having links to Al-Haq, a Palestinian human rights organisation that Israel also designates as a terrorist group.
Police also said the pair had participated in olive harvesting without a permit near the village of At-Tuwani and had fled with Palestinian farmers into a military training zone when officers arrived.
Tartarotti said their phones and social media posts were searched, after which they were both given a 10-year ban from entering Israel.
He expressed regret that he would no longer be able to return to the area and feared that the consequences of being accused of terrorism could last a lifetime.
He believes the deportations are intended to deter international solidarity activists from travelling to the West Bank to support Palestinians during the olive harvest season.
Tartarotti said Israeli authorities had provided no concrete evidence of any crime. During questioning, officers showed them social media posts published by the two men, which he said expressed support for Palestine and opposition to the Israeli occupation rather than advocating terrorism.
The authorities then handed them documents revoking their visas and imposing the 10-year entry ban. He and his father were not considering appealing the decision, he added.
However, Tartarotti remains in contact with Luisa Morgantini, president of Assopace Palestina, an organisation promoting solidarity with the Palestinian people, peace and human rights.
Morgantini, who has previously been expelled from the region, hopes to organise a collective return trip for people who have received deportation orders, he added.
Palestinian activists face greater risks
Tartarotti said Palestinian activists faced the greatest dangers, risking their lives daily to document violations by Israeli soldiers and settlers.
"All my friends have been arrested and tortured simply for documenting violations by settlers and the army," he said.
He remains in touch with members of Youth of Sumud, who, he said, continue to face repeated attacks by settlers and the military.
Tartarotti also referred to the detention of Italian women activists in the al-Buweib area of Hebron on 22 October while they were accompanying Palestinian farmers.
He said he had met the women at a guesthouse run by Youth of Sumud but did not know them personally. He added that they, too, were due to be deported.
"What happened to the women was the same as what happened to us: people are on the ground accompanying Palestinians and witnessing what is happening, only to be detained and expelled," he said.
No contact with Italian authorities
Tartarotti said neither he nor his father had contacted an Italian diplomatic mission in Israel following their arrest, and they had received no assistance from Italy's foreign ministry or government.
Upon their return, Italian authorities briefly listened to their account before returning their passports, he said.
He believes such incidents are specifically intended to discourage international volunteers and observers from travelling to the West Bank and documenting abuses by settlers and the Israeli military.
European governments, beginning with Italy, should acknowledge what he described as Israeli violations of international law, he said, arguing that Israel systematically treats the West Bank as a colony under military rule.
Tartarotti, who has visited the West Bank for several years, said conditions had steadily deteriorated, particularly since 7 October 2023.
"Palestinians live in terrible conditions. They are constantly afraid of demolitions, arbitrary arrests without trial, and the confiscation of land, livestock and equipment," he said.
"Settlers have become more violent. People are killed daily by settlers and the army, yet very little is said about it."
He added that the presence of international volunteers had previously provided a degree of protection for Palestinian activists, as Israeli soldiers were more cautious about committing abuses in front of foreign observers.
That protection has significantly weakened, he said, with international activists now also facing detention, arrest and deportation.
Their expulsion, he warned, further restricts the ability to document events in the West Bank and communicate them to the outside world.
