If no candidate is elected, a new vote is held within seven days, with the two candidates who received the most votes taking part.
The results of the presidential and vice-presidential election show the following distribution:
Ilana Iotova/Kiril Valchev - 34.76%
Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev - 31.95%
Kostadin Kostadinov/Petar Volgin - 12.54%
Radostin Vasilev/Krasimir Manov - 4.61%
Ivelin Mihaylov/Yuliana Mateeva - 3.79%
Ivan Hristanov/Stoyanka Cherkezova - 2.39%
The “I do not support any candidate” option was chosen by 4.43% of voters.
A total of 6,637,238 voters were eligible to take part in Sunday's election, in which 27 presidential and vice-presidential tickets competed. Some 46,001 people were eligible to vote for the first time.
As previously reported, Bulgarian citizens were voting Sunday to elect the country's seventh president.

====================================================================================================

How will growing US-Ukraine tensions shape the course of the war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:07 UTC
23:16:07 KST

Growing tensions between Washington and Kiev are exposing differences that extend beyond the personal rivalry between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the White House pursues closer ties with Moscow.
The latest signs of a US-Russia rapprochement emerged last week when US mediator Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg, with both sides issuing positive statements about renewing peace talks and ending the war in Ukraine.
Yet just hours after the statements, Russia and Ukraine exchanged a deadly barrage of attacks, underscoring the challenges facing efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict.
The growing US-Russia rapprochement, marked by Washington brokering a diesel deal with the Kremlin and lifting most US sanctions on Moscow, has frustrated Zelenskyy, who has recently publicly opposed Washington's softer approach toward Moscow.
Trump has also demanded that Zelenskyy stop targeting Russian refineries.
The disagreements mark a further deterioration in relations that have remained strained since a heated White House meeting in March, when Trump and Zelenskyy engaged in a public shouting match.
Although Zelenskyy subsequently sought common ground with Trump through European mediation, their latest exchanges suggest that the divisions between Washington and Kiev run deeper than disagreements over how to end the war, reflecting increasingly divergent geopolitical priorities and international alignments.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US president said in a speech last week, underscoring his affinity for the Russian leader, who recently proposed a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to address the war in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has shown less hesitation in confronting the US administration, which has long provided Ukraine with weapons, funding and essential intelligence in its war against Russia.
“How can Trump be friends with him? I think that it’s a mistake. It’s his choice again and again,” Zelenskyy said in a recent Financial Times interview, referring to the political rapprochement between Russia and the US.
Rapprochement disrupts Ukrainian resistance
Growing differences between Washington and Kiev, coupled with Trump's rapprochement with Putin, could strengthen Moscow's position both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table, according to experts.
The deepening tensions between the US and Ukraine are “exerting a disruptive influence on the dynamics of the war in Ukraine, affecting both military operations on the ground and the parameters of a potential peace settlement,” Ozgur Korpe, an academic at National Defence University, tells TRT World.
“On the battlefield, uncertainty regarding US aid—compounded by political conditionality—is compelling Ukraine to adopt a more defensive, resource-conserving strategy, while simultaneously granting Russia greater latitude to maintain its offensive tempo and intensify pressure,” he says.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced disruptions to US intelligence sharing and Starlink satellite connections, which Kiev believes contributed to its vulnerability during recent deadly Russian missile attacks on the capital.
Shortages of missile interceptors, compounded by delays in US supplies, have further strained Ukraine's air defences.
According to Korpe, Ukraine's predicament reflects a well-documented phenomenon in international relations: when a weaker partner depends heavily on a stronger ally for security, declining support or growing uncertainty over assistance can undermine its willingness and ability to continue fighting.
Since the war began, Kiev has relied heavily on American political, economic, military and intelligence assistance.
Under the Trump administration, however, that support has declined, while the US president has increasingly portrayed Zelenskyy as an obstacle to a potential peace settlement.
Ukraine has sought to offset shortages of American weapons and disruptions to intelligence sharing with support from Europe.
But questions remain over whether countries such as France, the UK and Germany have the military capabilities to replace US assistance.
Domestic priorities
Trump and Zelenskyy have different pledges to their respective national audiences, making compromise increasingly difficult.
While Trump has long pledged to Americans to bring immediate peace to the Russia-Ukraine war, Zelenskyy aims to minimise any territorial concessions to Moscow to keep national support for his presidency strong.
The tensions between Washington and Kiev are “largely a product of US domestic political factors, with the Trump administration facing pressure due to rising energy costs amid prolonged wars in both the Middle East and the Russia/Ukraine conflict,” says Eugene Chausovsky, senior director of analytical development and training at the New Lines Institute.
With the US midterm elections approaching, Trump is seeking ways to ease economic pressures, particularly rising diesel prices and their wider impact on inflation.
“This frames the US agreement with Russia on allowing diesel shipments, as well as Trump’s frustration with Zelensky for Ukraine continuing to target Russian energy and refinery infrastructure at a politically sensitive time,” Chausovsky tells TRT World.
However, experts warn that the diesel deal is unlikely to immediately affect US fuel prices, as European countries continue to enforce their own sanctions on Russia.
Trump’s declaration of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia also failed, as both sides said they did not sign the agreement.
“Trump frames Ukraine not so much as a front line for the defence of liberal democratic norms, but rather as a costly foreign burden in the context of US domestic politics and a bargaining chip to be used at the negotiating table when striking a ‘grand deal’ with Russia,” Korpe says.
By contrast, Zelenskyy views Ukraine's struggle as existential and closely tied to the country's aspirations to join Western political and military institutions, according to Korpe.
Will Ukraine and the US break up?
Ukraine has long sought closer integration with Western political and military institutions, including NATO and the EU. But deteriorating relations with Washington have raised questions about whether Kiev can keep relying on American support.
Oleg Ignatov, a senior analyst on Russia at the International Crisis Group, says the Trump administration has recently changed its approach to negotiations aimed at ending the war.
“Previously, Washington tried to reach an understanding with Moscow first, then took its proposals to Ukraine and its allies, who rejected them.
“Now the United States is trying to secure support from Ukraine and its European allies first and find out what they are prepared to accept. It would then take those proposals to Putin,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
Last week, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo before Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg for further talks with Putin.
“This approach requires Zelenskyy to be clearer about the compromises Ukraine might accept. That is likely to cause friction between Kiev and Washington because their approaches still differ,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
If the US continues to push Zelenskyy to make further concessions to Russia, this approach could “lead to further friction or even conflict between Kiev and Washington,” Ignatov says.
Zelenskyy has insisted that any potential ceasefire must be backed by Western security guarantees without territorial concessions to Russia.
In a recent CNN interview, Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine “will survive” and “will stay strong” despite tensions with Washington, while rejecting territorial concessions to Russia.
Although some analysts attribute the tensions partly to personal animosity between Trump and Zelenskyy, Korpe argues that the differences run deeper.
“The rift between the two leaders is not merely personal; rather, it is rooted in deeper disagreements regarding the objectives of the war and the vision for a final settlement.”
Korpe says institutions such as the US Congress and the Pentagon, alongside NATO, have helped prevent American support for Ukraine from collapsing entirely.
Nevertheless, “it is fair to say that the crisis of trust between the two leaders is moving distinctly toward a complete ‘break’,” he adds.
Chausovsky, however, offers a different assessment.
While Zelenskyy and the Trump administration remain at odds, he says, “these tensions should not be seen as a sign of a breakup” between Washington and Kiev.
Instead, Chausovsky describes the current friction as “rather a down period in the ebb and flow of their ties amid the protracted conflict with Russia.”
“Greater diplomatic activity can be expected as a result, though any sustainable ceasefire or peace agreement is unlikely to materialise in the short term,” he tells TRT World.

Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:04 UTC
23:16:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Syrian authorities have arrested several senior officers from Bashar al-Assad's former regime, including his cousin, as part of an ongoing crackdown on suspects accused of atrocities during the country's 14-year-long civil war.
Syrian Interior Ministry spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba announced the arrests on Monday, saying those detained included senior military and intelligence officials, former air force pilots and individuals suspected of involvement in massacres and attacks on civilians.
Among those arrested was Yahya al-Assad, a cousin of ousted president Bashar al-Assad who held the rank of colonel in Branch 105, a unit of the former regime's security apparatus.
Al-Baba said the detainees also included a major general who had commanded the 24th Division and the Air Defence Directorate, as well as senior officials from the Air Force Intelligence Directorate.
Another suspect was allegedly involved in the Tadamon massacre, one of the most notorious atrocities committed by Assad's forces during the Syrian uprising.
The arrests also included a fighter pilot accused of bombing Syrian cities, a brigadier general from the Political Security Directorate, the head of investigations at Air Force Intelligence and a judge who served in the former regime's Counterterrorism Court.
Other detainees included two brigadier generals from the Republican Guard, a senior officer at Tishreen Military Hospital, a military doctor, a helicopter pilot and another fighter pilot accused of taking part in attacks on civilian areas.
The arrests are part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to pursue former military and security officials suspected of committing abuses during the uprising against Assad, including aerial bombardments, arbitrary detention, torture and massacres.
Former regime pilots targeted
Syrian authorities have stepped up arrests of former air force personnel in recent weeks, targeting officers suspected of involvement in bombing campaigns against opposition-held areas.
In September, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of nine former regime pilots in Latakia province.
According to the ministry, preliminary investigations indicated that the pilots had participated in combat missions and airstrikes targeting several areas, including Eastern Ghouta, Aleppo and its countryside, Deir ez-Zor and rural Hama.
On 18 September, authorities detained five former air force officers and commanders in Tartous province, including pilots and officials who had held operational and field responsibilities.
Two days later, security forces arrested Brigadier General Zakaria Mohammed Sannoun, who served as head of operations in the 22nd Division between 2012 and 2020.
Authorities accused Sannoun of overseeing operations at the Hama, Tiyas (T4) and Shayrat military airbases during the conflict.
On 28 September, internal security forces arrested Colonel Khaldoun Hussein Mubarak in the Jableh countryside of Latakia province.
He was accused of participating in combat sorties against Syrian areas during the uprising.
The Interior Ministry has described the arrests as part of continuing investigations into former officers and military personnel suspected of war crimes and other violations, with judicial proceedings expected to follow.
Suspect in 2013 massacres arrested
The latest arrests come less than two weeks after Syrian authorities announced the detention of Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural and nicknamed the "Butcher of Baniyas".
Kayali was arrested on 15 October over his alleged role in the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al-Bayda, in the Tartous countryside.
Syrian authorities accuse him of responsibility for the killings, which took place during the early years of the uprising against Assad.
The successive arrests mark a widening effort to track down former regime figures accused of involvement in atrocities committed during the conflict.
Authorities have said investigations will continue and that suspects will face further judicial proceedings over their alleged roles in abuses against Syrians.

This Tuesday, millions of Israelis will enter the voting booth with mixed emotions – feelings of trauma and pride.
Trauma from the invasion and a sense of pride in the military actions that followed. During an ongoing existential war on seven fronts, Israel needs proven, clear, and decisive leadership.
That’s why in that quiet, sacred cubicle – I will be voting for victory.
Yes, I am still living through the trauma of October 7, which needs to be thoroughly investigated through a cross-party inquiry that will question current and former IDF chiefs of staff, prime ministers, and defense ministers on both sides of the aisle – but that doesn’t change the current challenges on the horizon.
In the past three years, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rewritten our national defense doctrine and delivered some of the greatest military feats in the history of warfare.
Every step of the way, he faced immense pressure from home and abroad, including from those who seek to replace him in this election.
Had he capitulated and ended the war when Gadi Eisenkot had suggested, we would have never entered Rafah. We would have potentially left countless hostages in the hands of Hamas. Not to mention the beeper attacks on Hezbollah and actions against the Houthis and Iran.
Instead, we now control over 60% of Gaza.
All the hostages were returned to Israel.
Hezbollah is crushed.
And the Islamic Republic of Iran is on its last legs.
The current government has many naysayers, but nobody can deny that what they have achieved on the battlefield thus far is historic; however, much of the progress could unravel if the missions are not completed.
Voting for victory
Voters need to ask themselves who is more likely to bring down the Iranian Regime, end the nuclear threat, and usher in a new era of regional peace and stability.
Those with a proven track record in war and peace who have committed to Iranian regime change or a newly formed amalgamation of parties who agree on few things beyond their disdain for Netanyahu.
There is no path for Eisenkot to reach a Knesset majority without joining forces with the far-left, Arab and Islamist parties, which would render his government impotent.
Imagine we are on the eve of a joint American Israeli attack against the remnants of the Iranian nuclear program, and the Pentagon is waiting to hear if Israel is on board, pending a decision from the Islamist Ra’am movement’s Shura Council of elders.
This isn’t a joke; it’s a dangerous possibility.
In contrast, Netanyahu has a much clearer path to a majority and has already stated that once he joins with his natural allies, he will reach out to others to bolster the national consensus.
This comes alongside an unprecedented endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who clearly wants to keep the winning team together to finish the job.
Now is not the time to throw the dice on Israel’s security.
That’s why I solemnly believe that a vote for Netanyahu is a vote for victory.
The writer is a seasoned public relations professional, political strategist, and former Israeli government spokesman who is currently heading English-language outreach for the Likud party in the upcoming election.

Israel continues to commit genocide in Gaza despite a cease-fire agreement, independent U.N.-commissioned experts said in a report Monday, also accusing Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the occupied West Bank.
The Associated Press could not independently corroborate multiple graphic accounts described in the report of sexual assaults by prison guards and soldiers on Palestinian detainees since October 2023. In one, female guards strip-searched a pregnant Palestinian, touching inside her anus and vagina. In another, guards beat a detainee and hurled sexist slurs while denying her access to the toilet and sanitary pads. She bled onto her clothes and interrogation chair.
The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.
The report Monday said Israel was "continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Much of the harm has come from Israel’s occupation deeper into Gaza during the cease-fire period, the report says. Since October 2025, when the cease-fire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53% of Gaza to at least 60%, the commission said.
In that time, Israeli fire across the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians - including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
The report also accused Israeli soldiers and prison guards of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.
In one case, it says guards raped a Palestinian detainee with a stick, then forced him to put the stick in his mouth until he vomited. It also recalled another episode in which guards instructed a Palestinian man to urinate as they tied a plastic cord around his genitals.
The cease-fire scaled down a devastating war started by the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Israel responded with a genocidal campaign that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Government extends 15% compensation for Ukrainian-made industrial equipment
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:13:19 EET
23:13:19 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has extended the partial compensation scheme for the cost of Ukrainian-made industrial machinery and equipment for another two years, until September 30, 2028.
The relevant resolution extends the experimental project developed by the Ministry of Economy as part of the Made in Ukraine state policy, the ministry said.
The program provides compensation of 15% of the purchase price of Ukrainian-made industrial machinery and equipment, excluding value-added tax (VAT).
"The 15% compensation program for machinery and equipment has already demonstrated its effectiveness, so it is important to ensure its continued operation. It allows businesses to reduce the cost of modernizing production, while Ukrainian machinery manufacturers receive new orders, increase production and invest in their own development," Deputy Economy Minister Vitaliy Kindrativ was quoted as saying.
The program has operated since September 2024 and covers equipment manufactured in Ukraine with a localization level of at least 40%.
As of May 2026, buyers had purchased 476 units of Ukrainian machinery and equipment worth nearly UAH 1.2 billion under the program. Total partial compensation amounted to UAH 148.8 million, according to the ministry.
A total of 29 Ukrainian banks participate in the program.
The Federation of Employers of Ukraine previously named the continuation of existing support programs under the Made in Ukraine platform among the key industrial policy challenges requiring urgent attention from the new prime minister and government.

The Italian Embassy in Bratislava presents the sixth edition of the “Raccontare in Italiano” contest, open to students of Italian in schools and undergraduate programs in Slovakia.
The initiative, promoted as part of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, is organized in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Bratislava and Eduitalia, an association of over one hundred schools, academies, and universities.
Participants must submit a short story of no more than 350 words, choosing from two themes: “Even if you don’t know it, you recognize it,” on the presence of Italian in unexpected contexts, and “Italian, the Language of Genius,” on the fields in which the Italian language excels, drawing on personal experiences or readings.

Israel heads to the polls: Netanyahu seeks to survive another election
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end the nearly four-year rule of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition, following years of war, political scandals, mass protests, and deepening divisions within Israeli society.
The vote is widely viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership, with the opposition blaming him for security failures surrounding the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and accusing his government of undermining democratic institutions.
The Hamas attack killed around 1,200 people and saw some 250 taken hostage. Israel responded with a military campaign in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to the local Health Ministry.
Despite their fierce political rivalry, the main Israeli election contenders differ less considerably over the country’s military policies and its approach to the Palestinians.
Netanyahu’s fight for political survival
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who heads the centrist Yashar party, has emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger.
Speaking at a mass rally in Tel Aviv on Sunday, Eisenkot urged traditional voters for Netanyahu’s Likud party to abandon the prime minister, claiming that Israel cannot survive another four years under his leadership.
“Anyone who thinks our Israel can survive another four years like these is living under a dangerous misconception,” Eisenkot said, according to the Times of Israel.
Netanyahu is also facing accusations of attempting to provoke a new war with Iran to postpone the election. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman has demanded a criminal investigation into the prime minister on suspicion of treason after Channel 12 reported a clash between Netanyahu and Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir over a proposed military operation.
“The man has gone off the rails,” Liberman said on Monday, accusing Netanyahu of putting his political survival ahead of national security. The prime minister denied the reported confrontation, and no criminal wrongdoing has been established.
Netanyahu also failed to persuade US President Donald Trump to launch strikes on Iran before the Israeli election, CNN reported, citing American and Israeli sources. The operation has reportedly been postponed, potentially until after the November 3 US midterm elections. Netanyahu’s office rejected the report.
The confrontation is not simply between the left and the right. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid are also seeking to oust Netanyahu, but the opposition remains divided over domestic policy, coalition alliances, and who should lead the next government.
Four years of war and political turmoil
Netanyahu’s latest term has been marked by a series of crises, from mass protests over his judicial overhaul to the October 7 Hamas attack, which exposed major failures in Israel’s security apparatus and triggered years of warfare.
The attack remains a central election issue, with Netanyahu’s opponents accusing him of evading responsibility and blocking an independent state commission of inquiry. While the opposition demands a full investigation into the political and military failures, the prime minister has backed a government-appointed panel with more limited powers.
Israel’s subsequent military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran have come at a heavy human, economic, and diplomatic cost. The Gaza offensive has devastated the Palestinian enclave, killing tens of thousands and displacing much of its population.
In September 2025, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Netanyahu is also subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Israel rejects the genocide allegations and denies committing war crimes.
Another major dividing line concerns Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul, which triggered nationwide protests in 2023. His opponents have pledged to reverse measures they say undermine judicial independence. The prime minister is also standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud, and breach of trust, which he denies.
Another contentious issue is the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service. Despite a 2024 Supreme Court ruling against blanket exemptions, Netanyahu’s coalition has continued to resist compulsory conscription for religious students, fueling resentment among Israelis repeatedly called up for military duty.
The economic toll has added to public anger. Rising defense spending, higher living costs, and a VAT increase to 18% in 2025 have put further pressure on households.
Yet the wars themselves have attracted relatively little debate among the main contenders, many of whom support Israel’s military campaigns. The deeper political battle is over Netanyahu’s leadership, accountability, and the direction of the Israeli state.
Election arithmetic: Can anyone secure a majority?
Recent surveys indicate a tight race, with Eisenkot’s Yashar holding a narrow advantage over Netanyahu’s Likud in several polls.
An October 21 Jerusalem Post analysis of four major surveys put Yashar at an average of 22.5 seats, compared with 19.75 for Likud. But neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition appear assured of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.
Under Israel’s proportional representation system, parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament. Votes for parties that fail to cross the threshold do not translate into seats, meaning even small shifts could tip the balance between rival camps.
The real battle may therefore begin after the ballots are counted. Smaller parties, particularly ultra-Orthodox factions, could determine who governs, with military conscription exemptions and religious education funding among their key demands.
According to a Jerusalem Post report published Monday, possible scenarios include opposition cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, reliance on Arab parties’ parliamentary support, or even another election if coalition talks fail.
Would a defeat for Netanyahu change Israel’s course?
A new prime minister would not necessarily mean a new direction for Israel’s military and foreign policies.
Despite their fierce opposition to Netanyahu, leading opposition figures broadly support maintaining Israel’s military superiority, confronting Iran, and retaining extensive security control over Palestinian territories. None of the principal contenders has made the establishment of a Palestinian state a central campaign commitment.
The election also comes amid renewed tensions in the occupied West Bank. Israeli authorities have imposed sweeping restrictions following a shooting near Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen, including curbs on Palestinians entering Jewish settlements for work.
Meanwhile, thousands of Israelis have demonstrated against the government and violence toward Palestinians, even as younger voters increasingly identify with the political right.
Reporting from Tel Aviv, RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij described Israel as “a nation dramatically shifting towards the right,” with many young people citing the October 7 attack as a turning point in their political views.
The election could therefore remove Netanyahu from power without reversing the security policies that have defined his latest term.
What happens after October 27?
The vote could leave Netanyahu in power, hand the opposition a chance to form a government, or produce another parliamentary deadlock.
Under Israel’s parliamentary system, the president consults party leaders before choosing a lawmaker to form a government. Coalition talks can drag on for weeks, with smaller parties demanding concessions in exchange for their support. If no candidate can secure a majority, Israel could face another election.
The final result may therefore be decided not at the ballot box, but behind closed doors, as rival parties bargain over who will govern Israel next.
Yet even if Netanyahu loses power, the election may change Israel’s leadership without fundamentally altering its approach to the Palestinians or the regional conflicts that have defined his latest term.

Temu falls into line as EU backs its action plan after €200m fine

2026-10-26
14:11:03 UTC
23:11:03 KST

The Chinese-owned online retailer has promised stronger action to address several violations of the EU’s Digital Services Act, the European Commission said on Monday, following a €200 million fine in May.
The European Commission has said it has accepted Temu's action plan to address several violations of the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA).
Temu has promised to carry out a risk analysis, to keep a close eye on measures to prevent the sale of illegal products on its platform and to step up its efforts if needed.
The Chinese retailer will also review how its recommender systems "may amplify the spread of illegal goods", the Commission said.
In May this year, Temu was fined €200 million by the EU for allowing the sale of illegal products like dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on its platform.
The fine came after a formal investigation launched in October 2024 into whether Temu was meeting its obligations as a designated Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act.
Commission investigators said the platform failed to properly identify and address the risks posed by illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers.
Today, Temu welcomed the approval of its action plan by European regulators. “We appreciate the Commission's constructive engagement with us throughout the process,“ the company said in a statement.
The plan "stands as a clear testament to Temu's commitment to investing in robust compliance infrastructure to ensure a safe, trustworthy shopping environment for all EU users”, it added.
The Chinese retail giant has 130 million users in the 27-nation EU, nearly a third of the bloc's population, making it one of the biggest online retailers in Europe.
Temu is one of several ecommerce platforms dealing with the EU’s new €3 fees on low-value packages since July, while those worth less €150 had entered the bloc duty free beforehand.
The new packaging rules have seen imports, especially from China, slump by 30% to 40% since coming into force.

Russian oil tycoons' bitter feud spills into Dubai courts

Breadcrumb
Russian oil tycoons' bitter feud spills into Dubai courts
A bitter feud between Russian oil traders has spilled into courts in Dubai and Brazil, with lawsuits worth hundreds of millions of dollars and allegations of stolen trade secrets and death threats.
The dispute involves Igor Soglayev, a former Deutsche Bank executive, and traders linked to the sanctioned Coral oil network, according to an investigation published by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday.
The fallout began when a tanker carrying Russian diesel worth tens of millions of dollars failed to deliver its cargo in Brazil.
The dispute has since led to claims exceeding $500 million, a $42 million arbitration award and a Dubai court order freezing assets worth up to $704 million.
Soglayev, who previously advised Igor Sechin, the head of Russian oil giant Rosneft, partnered with traders associated with Coral in early 2024.
He established Dubai-based DIA33 to trade Russian diesel and export it to Brazil, but the partnership collapsed following the failed shipment.
Coral-linked traders accused Soglayev of failing to pay for the fuel and secured a Dubai arbitration ruling ordering him to pay approximately $42 million.
Soglayev then filed lawsuits in Dubai and Brazil, accusing his former partners of undermining his business and misusing confidential commercial information.
He is seeking more than $500 million in damages and claims to have received death threats.
In June, a Dubai judge ordered the freezing of up to $704 million in assets belonging to the defendants and associated companies.
The order remains in place while appeals continue, although questions over the court's jurisdiction have complicated proceedings. No final ruling has settled the competing allegations.
The WSJ reported that the UAE court handling the main case has not made the proceedings public.
Accusations of stolen clients
The dispute has also reached Brazil, where DIA33 accused Coral of recruiting senior employees and using its customer base, offices and infrastructure to establish a rival business.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that a commercial court in Sao Paulo had identified indications of unfair competition.
Representatives of the defendants denied wrongdoing, arguing that the dispute stemmed from a business partnership that had never been fully formalised.
Coral has separately accused DIA33 of misappropriating a diesel shipment.
A sanctioned oil network
Coral Energy, renamed 2Rivers in 2024, has been a major player in Russian oil trading, with commercial roots in Azerbaijan and offices in Dubai and Singapore.
Western officials accuse traders associated with the network of helping Moscow maintain oil exports and finance its war in Ukraine despite sanctions.
Britain sanctioned the group in December 2024 and added five executives to its sanctions list in May 2025.
The European Union has also sanctioned associated entities, accusing them of facilitating Russian oil exports, disguising the origin of shipments and using vessels linked to Moscow's so-called shadow fleet.
The network has denied breaching sanctions and announced plans to wind down operations in August 2025, citing Western pressure.
Dubai has become an important hub for Russian oil trading since Moscow redirected exports away from Europe following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday highlighted the potential of artificial intelligence to modernize the EU executive's administration, improve working methods, and make services less burdensome for businesses and citizens.
Speaking at a news conference in Brussels alongside European Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud and Public Administration Piotr Serafin and Catherine Day, chair of the High-Level Group on the Future of the Commission's Civil Service, von der Leyen said technological advances offer new opportunities to improve administrative processes and make the EU more efficient.
"Artificial intelligence offers new ways to work, new ways to improve processes, and find less burdensome ways to make the European Union work for business and citizens," she said.

"We must give our colleagues the skills and tools to best use it, and we must develop talent, simplify services, and make better use of technologies," von der Leyen said.
Stressing the need for the commission to act "effectively and quickly," she said simplifying procedures, clarifying structures, and improving cooperation across departments would allow staff to focus their efforts on areas where they could make the greatest difference.
She identified making "every euro count" as the commission's second priority, emphasizing the need to ensure that public spending delivers added value and tangible results, particularly as Europeans continue to face cost-of-living pressures.
"Our ambition remains clear: to deliver the best possible public service for our European citizens," she said.

The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.
Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.
The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.
Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.
“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”
Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.
The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”
Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”
Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay.
Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers.
Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version.
This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.”
While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.”
According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.”
Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.”
Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.”
The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March.
Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it.

Israel’s half a million first-time voters: The algorithm-bred ‘generation right’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:08:52 UTC
23:08:52 KST

As Israel goes to the polls on Tuesday, more than 550,000 first-time voters will be eligible to vote in the country’s first elections since October 7, 2023.
Together, this bloc can command up to 17 of the 120 seats in Israel's Knesset.
It’s significant enough to fundamentally alter the balance of power in an election in which neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud nor any other party has support for an outright 61-seat majority.
Half a million new votes in Israel might change the captain of the ship but not alter its course: around three-quarters of first-time voters identify as hard-right or centre-right, according to polls.
Dubbed ‘Generation Right,’ Israel’s youth stand in sharp contrast to those participating in sweeping protests across the European continent and parts of Southeast Asia.
Millions of young people worldwide, including in France, Spain, Italy, Albania, Serbia, India, Indonesia, and more, have risen in the past year, aligning themselves with ‘left-wing’ or even ‘hard-left’ ideologies.
Israel’s arguably most progressive party, the Democrats, the only one even entertaining a two-state solution, stands at around 5 percent support among Israeli youth.
The overwhelming majority, more than 60 percent, support Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition.
This features parties led by his hard-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who campaign on illegal settler expansion and capital punishment for Palestinian prisoners.
In fact, if only youth aged 18-22 voted, their hard-right parties could control an unprecedented 29 seats, nearly a fourth of the Knesset, a poll reported by Israeli news outlet Ynet finds.
The same two parties only totalled 14 seats in 2022.
Around 30 percent of Israeli youth express support for opposition parties that emphasise economic stability and the restoration of trust in public institutions, including Yashar and B’Yachad.
While these more centrist parties criticise Netanyahu’s wartime manoeuvres, they are mostly led by army-vetted, conservative politicians who remain hawkish on national security and committed to a Zionist state.
Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot is a former Israeli army Chief of Staff who resigned from Netanyahu’s war cabinet over strategic disagreements.
B’Yachad’s Naftali Bennett is a former illegal settlement leader who has campaigned harder than Netanyahu for occupied West Bank annexation.
No real-world civic engagement, high screen time
Israel’s right-leaning young voters emerge alongside a conundrum that calls into question the source of their fervent ideology.
The Israel Democracy Institute reports that a staggering 80 percent of surveyed youth say they are likely to cast their first ballot.
Yet around 65 percent also say they have never taken part in any real-life political activism, such as protests or petitions.
These figures reveal a highly opinionated yet practically disengaged group of young voters.
Although young voters may not engage in physical political activity, they remain fully immersed in the fear-driven, hyper-saturated digital climate following October 7.
The Israel Democracy Institute survey notes that social media platforms, combined with WhatsApp and Telegram channels, are the dominant source of political information for Jewish youth.
Importantly, though, most participants say they do not actively seek political content online, suggesting they are passively and routinely exposed to algorithmically driven political framing.
The Israeli hard-right has exploited this passive intake model through propagating military aesthetics online and algorithmic campaigning.
IDI’s Democracy in the Digital Age program director Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler calls Israeli political parties ‘data factories.’
They go beyond tracking basic demographic data like age or location, and instead use AI-assisted software that parses search histories and social media engagement.
Altshuler warns that political parties can build ‘opaque inference systems’ about voters' identities or vulnerabilities.
They can do this by creating sensationalist content tailored to provoke shock, anxiety, rage, and, most importantly, clicks from segmented voters, which the algorithm rewards. And they have…
Political Parties or ‘Data Factories’?
In August, Otzma Yehudit party head Ben-Gvir published an AI-generated video showcasing Palestinian prisoners on an industrial processing line.
This video, posted on X, depicted Palestinians in brown uniforms, visibly craving food, marching on a conveyor belt being transported to a fenced compound.
It garnered more than 4 million views before being forcibly removed from Ben-Gvir’s account.
It has been widely documented, though, and continues to circulate online, generating hundreds of thousands of additional impressions.
It’s by far the first time Ben-Gvir has utilised AI in his online campaigns, which regularly record some of the highest engagement figures of any politician in Israel. There may be room for doubt, though.
The Israeli watchdog FakeReporter has flagged Ben-Gvir's TikTok account for ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’.
The organisation uncovered more than a hundred fake accounts using AI-generated profile images to artificially boost engagement with Ben-Gvir’s content.
TikTok itself conducted a major crackdown on the platform ahead of Israel’s elections, permanently banning 306 more bots pushing partisan ideology in the country.
TikTok also removed nearly 1,500 accounts for impersonating political candidates or elected officials; most ran smear campaigns or deepfakes using generative AI.
In fact, a study by the Open University of Israel found that 76 percent of all AI political content in the country consists of video, a high-stimulation format that social media algorithms favour to maximise watch time.
TikTok has scrubbed 45,000 videos posted in Israel due to misinformation or violations of election integrity and hate speech laws.
This aligns with research from Ashkelon Academic College that ‘emotionally charged and unfiltered content’ on social media can exacerbate distress during a crisis.
A 2025 study by the college examined Israeli citizens’ digital media use during the ongoing Israeli genocidal war on Gaza.
It concluded that reliance on social media for news purposes was correlated with increased anxiety and lower perceptions of national resilience among Israelis.
As citizens consume algorithmically boosted, war-related content, their sense of security begins to deteriorate.
So it's less surprising, but perhaps even more alarming, that polls estimate a third of support for Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit comes from voters under 23.
More than a decade of youth growing up under Netanyahu’s government might have fundamentally shifted Israeli society to the right.
Or Netanyahu might have brought these ideologies into the mainstream through opportunistic coalitions with hard-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
Regardless, as young Israelis spend their formative years consuming algorithmically boosted triggers of existential fear, this trend will pay political dividends long after the current government.

Satyam Panday, chief US economist at S&P Global, disagreed and instead forecast an immediate 25-basis-point hike in October, while expecting an additional 50 basis points of tightening in the current cycle amid sticky core inflation.
Panday noted that despite the upcoming US midterm elections, the Fed will operate independently under a strict inflation-targeting mandate and will not hesitate to hike rates near an election if the data demands it.
ING economists James Knightley, Padhraic Garvey and Chris Turner recently published an article predicting that any Fed decision to hold rates will likely face internal opposition, as officials who previously favored tightening, such as Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan, may dissent.

====================================================================================================

Lizard's secret of defense preserved in 100-million-year-old amber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:05:13 UTC
23:05:13 KST

Almost 100 million years ago, a lizard in what is now Myanmar was in mortal danger.
We know this because the presumably terrified reptile did exactly what lizards do today in similar situations: It "voluntarily" shed its tail and the rest of it scuttled off.
The tail would have remained on the ground wriggling madly, which the lizard would have hoped would distract the hunter. How this scenario panned out and whether the lizard survived, we do not know.
But we do know that the tail did exactly what it shouldn't have: It survived – the decay process at least – and became embedded in tree resin. Over millions of years, the resin fossilized into amber and now, according to researchers at Tel Aviv University, we have the earliest known proof of the reptilian defensive mechanism known as autotomy – voluntarily shedding one's tail.
Theoretically it's possible that the lizard wasn't being hunted but some creature stepped on its tail, which it promptly shed. But close analysis of the tissue shows the hallmarks of voluntary discard, which is important, because it's no great defensive trick for the tail to simply get stomped.
The wonder is that now we know that the real defensive trick existed in lizards at least 100 million years ago, explain doctoral candidate Dolev Fabrikant and his supervisor, Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, of Tel Aviv University's School of Zoology and its Steinhardt Museum of Natural History. They worked in collaboration with researchers from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and Israel's Volcani Institute, publishing in Palaeontologia Electronica.
Until now, we could only speculate that ancient lizards living with dinosaurs had this defensive ability, Davranoglou notes. Now we know they did because the paleontological team observed a clean ring of tissue resembling the structure seen in tails shed by living lizards – absent trauma damage.
In fact, the small piece of cloudy amber had been found years ago but only now did Fabrikant examine it, using micro-CT scanning, and realize that what looked like a twig or insect fragment was covered in scales.
"Micro-CT… allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open," says Ahmed Nasser, head of the Volcani Institute's Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.
Which lizard it was, we do not know because this amber contained only its tail, not its head. Could have been almost anything.
"Possible affinities include the groups containing today's wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards," says Apostolos Christopoulos, a student at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
Note that snakes aren't lizards, they're snakes, and almost none in travail shed tail. They can't regenerate it. But likely, the ability goes back an insanely long way – tuataras can defensively shed their tail, and they split from other reptiles a quarter billion years ago, in the Jurassic.
There is one other option beside being stepped on or attacked. The lizard may have been climbing a seeping tree, its tail got stuck in the sticky resin and it shed it and moved on. If that's so, the little reptile may have regrown its tail. That's a nice thought.

====================================================================================================

The architectural heritage of Greece's Kea island: Vibrant colours, stone houses and watermills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:03:18 UTC
23:03:18 KST

Kea has around 2,500 permanent residents, and despite the growth of tourism, the island has managed to retain its traditional character.
Every summer, Greece's Cyclades islands attract countless visitors from all over the world.
In recent years, the Cyclades have become increasingly popular with tourists looking for more than just the sun and the sea, with many also choosing to make the trip in autumn or spring to go hiking and take in the local archaeological sites and architecture.
Kea, also known as Tzia, is an island in the western Cyclades known for its history and natural beauty.
It is described as the "gateway to the Cyclades" due to its proximity to Athens. It is just 16 nautical miles from the port of Lavrio.
Ioulida is the island's capital and one of its four historic towns. It is the only one situated inland, having once been the commercial centre of Kea. The architecture of Ioulida differs from typical Cycladic styles, as it incorporates elements of urban and neoclassical construction.
"We see the narrow streets, the arches and the stone buildings, and we also see colour on the walls. In fact, Tzia has always been a colourful place. During the Metaxas regime (1936–1940), white and blue were imposed, with white mainly for reasons of hygiene," Rena Velissaropoulou, the mayor of Kea since 2019, said.
"But Tzia has colour, and we see this every time we come across an old building where we can see the plasterwork. There, we almost always find colour," Velissaropoulou added.
Kea has around 2,500 permanent residents, and despite the growth of tourism, the island has managed to retain its traditional character.
Ioulida is built in an amphitheatre-like layout on the slopes of two hills (Kastro and Mylos). In 1978, it was granted the status of a protected traditional settlement.
Its distinctive architectural identity is also due to a distinctive type of rock found on the island.
"There was also miltos, a type of stone that was quarried in the cave-like pits of an exceptional cave in the Otzia area. This colour is a shade of greyish red, like the colour we see at Knossos, and in the past this stone was exported to Athens,” Velissaropoulou said.
As you leave Ioulida and drive up the island’s hills, you will also come across a number of traditional stone buildings. Most of them are uninhabited. Some have undergone minor alterations, whilst others have been converted into tourist accommodation.
Preserving them is vital for safeguarding Kea’s cultural heritage and history.
"The farmstead is the home, the base of the island’s farmers and livestock breeders, which used to be situated in the countryside. Because their main home was in Ioulida. All farmers who owned farmhouses also had a home in the capital. Usually, the home was the wife’s dowry, and the farmhouse belonged to the husband,” livestock farmer Dinos Vrettos told Euronews.
As a rule, farmers did not build on hilltops so as to avoid the strong northerly winds. However, they did not build low down in the ravines either, so as not to suffer from the summer heat.
For 25 years, Vrettos he worked as a stonemason, whilst for five years he was part of the excavation team at the ancient theatre of Karthia.
With his help, we were introduced to one of the traditional houses which, although no longer in use, retains all the characteristic features of the "Tziotiki dwelling."
"They used stones from ancient structures to build the houses. Over the years, the craft passed from one generation to the next, so I learnt it too. Unfortunately, the house in this condition has changed hands; it has been sold. Usually, the houses are bought by foreigners, not Greeks – mainly foreigners who, however, try to preserve them as they found them,” Dinos Vrettos told Euronews.
In the Mylopotamos area, along the stream and near the Flea spring, there were also once 11 watermills. Of these, one is now used as a residence, whilst another operates solely for visitors to the island.
The watermills likely date back to the period of Ottoman rule. They remained in operation until the Second World War and were gradually abandoned by the 1980s. Savvas Michael, a retired aviation worker, feels he has a duty to keep the island’s history alive.
"Technology has advanced enormously. Young people and children being born today have no idea what life was like in the past. So we’re trying to bring young people closer to tradition so that they know what we’ve inherited. Even if we don’t use them anymore, it’s important to keep at least one of them ‘alive’,” Michael said.
White and blue dominate most of the Cyclades islands. On Ioulida, however, one encounters vibrant colours, such as yellow and, of course, the red miltos of Kea, a mineral-based red dye that was highly prized in antiquity.
When you visit the island, look out for the "kathikies," the traditional stone houses that have stood the test of time.

High-level delegation in Iran in push to avert flare-up of conflict with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:03:06 UTC
23:03:06 KST

The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.
Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.
He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.
Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.
Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.
Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.
He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.
“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”
He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.
He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”
Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.
Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”
The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.
No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.
The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.
A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.
