Challenges to political beliefs might engage brain networks tied to self-reflection, new study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

People with strongly held left-wing views barely budged when confronted with arguments against their political beliefs, but they were more willing to revise factual beliefs, according to a brain imaging study conducted in Poland. Challenges to political beliefs were accompanied by greater activity in brain networks linked to self-reflection, which the researchers interpret as a sign that political convictions are tied to personal identity. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, largely replicate an earlier American study.
When people encounter facts or arguments that contradict their existing views, they rarely evaluate the new information like impartial judges. Instead, they tend to engage in a psychological process known as motivated reasoning, which involves filtering, reinterpreting, or dismissing evidence to protect their prior conclusions. This resistance to changing one’s mind is especially pronounced for political beliefs, which are normative statements about how society should work rather than simple matters of testable fact. For many individuals, political stances on issues like abortion or immigration are deeply woven into their sense of self and social belonging.
Modern neuroscience has begun to map how these psychological defenses play out physically inside the brain. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that reading belief-confirming political messages activates the brain’s reward centers, whereas encountering contradictory messages triggers regions associated with detecting errors. Similarly, research covered by PsyPost in 2020 indicated that liberal and conservative viewers exhibit distinct patterns of brain activity in the prefrontal cortex when watching the exact same political videos, and that alignment with a group’s brain activity predicts adopting that group’s stance.
The direct blueprint for the new research comes from a 2016 neuroimaging study that compared how American liberals responded to counterarguments targeting their political and non-political views. That earlier experiment showed that challenging a person’s political beliefs increased activity in the default mode network, a collection of connected brain structures along the midline and sides of the brain that becomes active when people look inward and think about who they are. The 2016 study also observed that people who were less willing to change their minds showed higher activity in the amygdala and the insula, two deep brain structures involved in processing fear, disgust, and emotional arousal.
Because that earlier experiment took place in the United States, which features a rigid two-party system and a distinct history of partisanship, it remained uncertain whether those brain patterns represent a universal human trait or a product of American politics. The new research, led by Małgorzata Kossowska, a professor at the Institute of Psychology at Jagiellonian University in Kraków and head of the Behavior in Crisis Lab, tested whether the same neural responses emerge in a European country shaped by a post-communist transformation, different cultural values, and a multi-party political landscape.
By examining both everyday factual beliefs and deeply held political convictions, the researchers sought to determine if identity-protective brain activity crosses cultural borders. The study was preregistered, meaning the researchers publicly recorded their plans before collecting data.
“One of the most intriguing questions in psychology is why people hold on to their beliefs even when confronted with information that challenges them,” Kossowska told PsyPost. “This is particularly important in the political domain, where presenting facts or counterarguments often does little to change people’s minds. We were interested in understanding why political beliefs are so resistant to change and whether this resistance reflects something fundamental about how our brains process information.”
To investigate this question, the researchers recruited 46 politically engaged Polish adults through social media, though a technical error left a final behavioral sample of 43 participants. The participants had an average age of about 25 years, ranging from 18 to 62, and included 34 women, 8 men, and 1 nonbinary individual. All participants were right-handed, had no history of neurological or psychiatric conditions, and identified as strongly left-wing on a screening questionnaire. Focusing on a single, strongly committed ideological group allowed the team to match the design of the 2016 American study and control for baseline differences in political interest and personal investment.
Before visiting the laboratory, participants rated their agreement with various claims to verify that they strongly endorsed eight political statements and eight non-political statements adapted for the Polish cultural context. Rather than asking about American topics like gun control, the political statements addressed locally relevant social issues, such as “Abortion should be legal,” “Poland should agree to accept refugees,” and “Sex education should be mandatory for every student.” The non-political statements consisted of factual or widely held empirical claims, such as “A college education generally improves a person’s economic prospects,” “Thomas Edison invented the light bulb,” and “Reading ability in early childhood is a sign of intelligence.”
During the laboratory session, participants lay inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner, a machine that indirectly measures neural activity by tracking changes in blood oxygen. Across four scanning runs lasting about seven minutes each, participants viewed each of the 16 statements they had previously endorsed for 10 seconds at a time.
Each statement was immediately followed by five separate counterarguments or pieces of opposing evidence, with each challenge displayed on the screen for 10 seconds. For political items, these challenges consisted of opposing social or moral arguments drawn from public discourse in Poland, whereas non-political items were paired with contradictory factual evidence.
After reading all five counterarguments for a given statement, the original claim reappeared, and participants had 12 seconds to rate how strongly they still believed it on a scale from 1 (strongly disbelieve) to 7 (strongly believe). When analyzing the brain scans, the scientists statistically controlled for six head-motion parameters so that physical movement inside the scanner would not distort the neural data. After the session, participants were told that not all of the counterarguments they had read were accurate. Roughly one week after the scanning session, 32 of the participants completed an online follow-up survey in which they rated their belief in the exact same 16 statements once again.
The behavioral ratings showed a sharp contrast in how participants responded to factual versus political pushback. When confronted with contrary evidence for non-political statements, participants’ average belief ratings dropped from 6.13 out of 7 before the challenges to 5.37 afterward. When presented with counterarguments against their political beliefs, their ratings held nearly steady, shifting from 5.72 to 5.68, a tiny change that was not statistically significant. That drop for non-political beliefs corresponded to a large effect (a Cohen’s d of 1.13, where values of 0.8 or higher are considered large), compared with a negligible one for political beliefs (0.06).
This gap between factual openness and political rigidity persisted one week later among the 32 participants who completed the follow-up survey. Their average belief rating for non-political statements remained lower at 5.65 compared to their initial baseline of 6.07, while their political belief ratings showed no meaningful change, sitting at 5.83 compared to a baseline of 5.79.
Inside the scanner, participants also took less time to evaluate political statements after reading the counterarguments, submitting their ratings in an average of 5.16 seconds compared to 5.70 seconds for non-political statements. The authors suggest this half-second difference may reflect quicker, less deliberate judgments about political statements, though other explanations are possible.
The brain imaging data showed different patterns for the two kinds of challenges. When participants read counterarguments targeting their political beliefs, they showed heightened activity in the default mode network compared to when they read non-political challenges. Specifically, political challenges triggered greater activation in the medial prefrontal cortex at the front midline of the brain, the posterior cingulate cortex near the back midline, and the right supramarginal gyrus above the ear. The authors interpret this activation as a sign that participants processed political counterarguments as challenges to their personal identity, since these areas are often active during introspection and thinking about the self.
On the other hand, reading counterarguments against non-political statements sparked greater activity in brain networks responsible for external attention and flexible thinking. These regions included the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the orbitofrontal cortex, which sit behind the forehead and above the eyes and are thought to help people weigh new evidence and revise their expectations.
When the researchers examined how strongly the group clung to specific statements across both categories, they found that greater belief resistance corresponded with higher activity in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, an upper-front brain area involved in thinking about oneself and others, which the authors link to protecting one’s identity. Meanwhile, greater willingness to change one’s mind on a specific item was linked to stronger activity in the right inferior temporal gyrus and the left temporal pole, areas positioned along the sides of the brain that assist in processing meaning and conceptual knowledge.
“The main takeaway is that changing someone’s political beliefs is not simply a matter of presenting better arguments or more information,” Kossowska said. “Our findings suggest that political beliefs are often closely connected to our sense of who we are.”
“This suggests that political disagreement is not always just about facts,” she continued. “It can also involve identity, values, and the need to maintain a coherent understanding of ourselves. The practical implication is that if we want to encourage openness to different perspectives, we need to consider not only what information we communicate, but also how that information relates to people’s identities and values.”
To see whether emotion-related brain activity tracked belief change, as it had in the 2016 American study, the researchers closely examined the amygdala and three subregions of the insular cortex. In contrast to the earlier American findings, the Polish study found no statistically significant correlation between activity in any of these emotion-related brain structures and the degree to which individual participants changed their non-political beliefs. Additional statistical tests provided moderate evidence that activity in the amygdala and insula was unrelated to belief updating in this group. The authors suggest that holding onto existing views may be driven primarily by cognitive, identity-focused processes rather than emotional arousal.
“One particularly interesting finding concerned the role of emotion,” Kossowska explained. “We did not replicate these associations. Instead, our results pointed more strongly toward brain systems involved in self-referential processing and maintaining a coherent sense of identity. This suggests that resistance to changing one’s mind may not necessarily be driven by strong emotional reactions.”
The faster reaction times for political items also stood out to the research team. “One might expect politically sensitive issues to require more deliberation, but our findings suggest that strongly held political convictions may sometimes lead people to reach conclusions relatively quickly, perhaps because their positions are already well established,” Kossowska noted. “These findings reinforce the idea that resistance to belief change is not necessarily a matter of intense emotional reactions or extensive deliberation. Sometimes, people may simply rely on deeply established convictions without seriously reconsidering them.”
Taken together, the Polish results reproduced the American study’s main behavioral pattern and its default mode network findings, but not its link between emotion-related brain regions and belief change.
“By reproducing several key findings of an earlier American study in Poland, we provide additional evidence that these patterns are not restricted to a single national political context,” Kossowska said. “At the same time, the differences we observed, particularly concerning emotion-related brain regions, remind us that replication is also an opportunity to refine existing theories.”
There are several methodological caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these results, and one independent researcher views the neuroimaging evidence with skepticism.
“This paper provides unsurprising evidence that political beliefs are hard to change,” Paul J. Zak, a professor of economic sciences, psychology, and management at Claremont Graduate University and director of its Center for Neuroeconomics Studies who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “The functional imaging results are thin and over-generous in their interpretations. Just observing human beings shows that political beliefs, especially among strongly committed individuals, are unlikely to change.”
A primary consideration is that the political statements in the experiment were value-based claims about what society “should” do, whereas the non-political statements were factual claims that can be tested against objective evidence. This distinction aligns with a 2015 neuroimaging study of 14 adults, which found that evaluating testable factual claims engages different brain regions than evaluating untestable propositions.
As a result, the differences in default mode network activity could reflect how the brain processes value judgments versus verifiable facts in general, rather than politics alone. The authors acknowledge this difference but argue it is meaningful rather than incidental, since political beliefs are bound up with values and identity in a way that factual beliefs typically are not.
Zak’s broader objection concerns how the brain activity was interpreted. Inferring a specific mental state from activity in a brain area, such as reading activity in the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) of the default mode network (DMN) as a sign of self-reflection, is a practice neuroscientists call reverse inference, which Zak referred to as reverse causation.
“The authors, like in many neuroimaging studies, misinterpret their findings using reverse causation,” Zak said. “That is, region or network X was more active in one task and then claim this means psychological process Y has occurred. Such a 1:1 mapping in the brain simply does not occur for higher-level cognitive functions. For example, greater political-condition activity in medial PFC/PCC is described as DMN activity reflecting ‘self-referential processing,’ which becomes evidence for the ‘identity-protective function’ of political beliefs.”
Kossowska also pointed out that neuroimaging data must be interpreted with caution. “Brain activation does not provide direct evidence of a specific psychological process,” she noted. “Our interpretation in terms of identity protection is consistent with the observed neural patterns and previous research, but it is not the only possible explanation.”
The study also relied on a narrow slice of the public, consisting exclusively of strongly left-wing individuals, nearly 80 percent of whom were women. Although recruiting a uniform group helped the researchers isolate specific brain signals, it leaves open the question of whether conservatives or political moderates exhibit the exact same neural responses.
In fact, a 2026 behavioral study of more than 1,000 Polish adults by several of the same authors indicated that political moderates revise their beliefs more readily than people on either the far left or the far right, suggesting that resistance is tied more closely to ideological extremity than to political direction. Future neuroimaging studies will need to recruit gender-balanced samples across the entire political spectrum to test whether these brain mechanisms operate symmetrically on the right and the left.
“First, our findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that left-wing individuals are particularly resistant to changing their political beliefs,” Kossowska emphasized. “We deliberately recruited participants with strong left-wing convictions to replicate an earlier American study using a comparable sample. We did not compare left-wing and right-wing participants, so our results cannot establish whether one ideological group is more resistant to belief change than another.”
“Second, our findings do not mean that political beliefs are impossible to change or that people’s responses are neurologically predetermined,” she added. “We examined how participants reacted to particular counterarguments in a controlled experimental setting. Different forms of communication, social contexts, or experiences might produce different outcomes.”
Additionally, although Poland has a very different history and party structure than the United States, it shares many institutional and media features with other Western democracies, pointing to the need for future research in non-Western societies. The experiment also measured short-term belief ratings on a 1-to-7 scale inside a laboratory scanner rather than tracking real-world political behaviors such as voting, donating, or activism. Finally, the link between brain activity and belief change for specific statements was based on just 16 statements, with each statement’s results averaged across participants.
“This line of analysis needs a better experimental design to compare strongly vs. weakly held political beliefs and see if they can be changed using observable actions, e.g. donating to a political party,” Zak added. “Beliefs are most effectively changed not with facts, but with stories and social proof, that is more interesting and useful research program.”
The Polish study also did not measure individual personality traits, such as a person’s need for mental closure, which could help explain why some people are more flexible than others when facing counterarguments. The authors argue that when beliefs are tied to personal identity, simply presenting counterarguments or evidence may not be enough to change their minds.
“We are also interested in understanding why some individuals are more willing than others to reconsider their convictions,” Kossowska said. “Factors such as the need for certainty, cognitive rigidity, and the personal importance of political identities may play an important role. Ultimately, we would like to move beyond identifying the mechanisms of belief resistance toward understanding the conditions under which people become more open to alternative perspectives without experiencing those perspectives as threats to their identity. This has implications not only for theories of belief formation and change, but also for political communication, misinformation, and efforts to reduce polarization.”
“I think the broader message of this research is that our beliefs are not simply collections of propositions that we evaluate independently of who we are,” she concluded. “They are often embedded in our identities, values, and broader understanding of the social world. This is especially true of political beliefs. When people defend a political position, they may be defending something much more personally meaningful than a particular opinion.”
The study, “Neural correlates of belief change in political and non-political domains among left-wing individuals confronted with counterarguments,” was authored by Małgorzata Kossowska, Paulina Szwed, Gabriela Czarnek, Sofiia Honcharowa, Aleksandra Domagalik, and Łucja Doradzińska.

Olive trees irrigated with treated wastewater, a pilot project to combat drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:00:19 UTC
23:00:19 KST

Olive trees irrigated with treated wastewater: in Puglia, southern Italy, a pilot project thus combats drought and emerging pollutants. The molecule is generated by combining hydrogen peroxide and ultraviolet rays. The results of this experience will be known in two years.
Farmland, especially in southern Europe, is thirsty. Every drop of water counts in the Adriatic basin.
In Puglia, in southern Italy, water shortage has been accentuated by climate change and, in addition, a bacterium, Xylella fastidiosa, has decimated the olive groves.
The European project ECO FLOW brings together Greek and Italian experts. It proposes reusing Gallipoli's treated wastewater for irrigation, which would otherwise go to the sea. They are focusing on the so-called emerging contaminants. These chemical, material or biological substances, created by humans, come from industrial activities and are present in urban and hospital wastewater.
The experiment is carried out in a field adjacent to the Gallipoli water treatment station. There are three rows of bacteria-resistant olive trees and three forms of irrigation: the traditional one, with the water from the well, the water treated in the purification station and the water subjected to a particular treatment, with which it is intended to reduce the amount of polluting substances.
Rocco Protopapa, of the Regional Agency for Irrigation and Forestry Activities (ARIF), a public body in the Puglia region, explains that ECO FLOW's objectives also include "comparing the plants irrigated with the water from the well with those that have received the treated water and those that have received the water treated with hydrogen peroxide. We want to see how much fruit they produce and how they produce it. And that way we avoid wasting water that would otherwise end up in the sea," he said.
At the Gallipoli purification station, the treated water destined for ECO FLOW is purified even more than that of the station's tanks, using the patented technology of a mini station, conceived in another European project, RE-WATER.
How does this process of additional water disinfection work?
Fabrizio Dell'Anna, in charge of the technical coordination and development of the project from the Aquedotto Pugliese – the organisation in charge of the management of the comprehensive water cycle in Puglia and Campania - comments that the technique "is based on the use of hydrogen peroxide combined with ultraviolet radiation generated by a lamp. This combination enables the formation of an extremely reactive molecule, capable of degrading pollutants. The challenge was important because the equipment used did not exist on the market." The reactor where the water subjected to this treatment is located is "thermally insulated to avoid temperature variations that could disturb the operation of the hydrogen peroxide". They realised that the number of reactive molecules available to attack the contaminants increased if the water circulated and they completed the system to do so.
ECO FLOW has a budget of more than one and a half million euros, of which 75% have been financed by European cohesion policy and the remaining 25% by funds from Greece and Italy, the two countries participating in the project. In Greece, researchers worked on a physical membrane to better treat and filter wastewater, while in Italy, they concentrated on the chemical solution. Both solutions are complementary, insisted the experts who share this know-how in the framework of the ECOFLOW pilot.
The laboratory of the Polytechnic University of Bari provides technical and scientific support to Acquedotto Pugliese, the project's main partner in the experiments carried out at ECO FLOW.
Danilo Spasiano, professor and researcher at the Polytechnic University of Bari explains that the monitoring of ECO FLOW has recently started. They study water and plant development, but also soil characteristics and the accumulation of contingent substances in the soil where the two varieties of olives irrigated in this experiment grow: Favolosa and Lecciana, both resistant to Xylella.
This pilot project will run for two years.
The Francesca Stajano farm produces more than sixty tons of olives per year. Its owner, Antonio Astuto, irrigates part of the production with water from his well and another younger olive grove with treated water at the Gallipoli purification station and sees the difference.
"We didn't expect four-year-old trees to start producing now. Therefore, we were very happy to see that the plants grew faster, probably thanks to the type of water used," he said.
In his facilities, the olive trees are irrigated with a drip system to "achieve a good result, avoiding the use of as little water as possible" so that it is not wasted, he concludes.

Sybiha reacts ironically to idea of nominating Orbán for UN Secretary-General
Ukrinform
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has reacted with irony to the idea of nominating former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán for the post of UN Secretary-General.
The minister posted his comment on X, Ukrinform reports.
“I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions,” the minister wrote.
He added that Ukraine could share with the rest of the world its “great experience of taking him out for coffee at the right moment.”
As reported by Ukrinform, the U.S. administration is promoting former Hungarian Prime Minister Orbán for the post of UN Secretary-General, counting on support from Russia and China.

Wing Commander Neal Henley: So I think there is now a, a growing recognition of the dependency upon space. It's no longer optional. I would argue it hasn't been for a number of years, but people are now recognizing that, and therefore we understand, better understand our vulnerabilities. And therefore that which needs protecting and assuring to ensure that we have access to those services that we need for the war fighter, but also for society who is increasingly dependent and increasingly aware of that dependency on space.
Squadron Leader Amy: We hear the phrase space power increasingly often. So what does that actually mean in practical terms for the Royal Air Force and indeed defence?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: So in the same way that we talk about air power as a combination of the capabilities and the roles and the missions that the RAF deliver and the air domain deliver, space power can be thought of in the same way. So it is about the products, the services, and the effects that we deliver for the joint and the integrated force.
It's about the capabilities and the people, most importantly, that enable the flow of those products and services. So it's awareness of the dependencies that we have, things like GPS, space weather forecasting and warning, and its impacts on both the society and also the military capabilities, particularly on the electromagnetic spectrum.
It's about things like missile warning, space-based earth observation or intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance. Space also enables secure and assured communications, which underpin command and control, especially for an expeditionary or a deployed force. But also within the homeland provides a diversity and resilience of communications paths through using space-based satellite communications, as well as terrestrial communications paths.
That earth observation and intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance underpins the capability to detect, track, and target threats. And more and more relevant now is the reliance upon space for autonomous and uncrewed systems. The combination of communications and precision navigation and timing are key for those systems to actually function effectively
Squadron Leader Amy: One of the strongest messages from the conference was that space is becoming increasingly contested. So what are we actually defending against?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: The space domain comprises of a number of segments. There is the satellites on orbit. There's the space segment, as it's sometimes referred to. There is the link segment, which is those radio frequency and electromagnetic links that connect our ground segment to the space segment.
And then within the ground segment, there is both control and user elements, so like the terminals or the GPS receivers. There are a number of threats to those. We're heavily dependent on those radio and electromagnetic links, so they are vulnerable to both jamming, so disruption, or spoofing, which can change the nature of the signals we're receiving or transmitting.
But also, there is a huge cyber dependency, which is a vulnerability. And equally, the ground systems themselves are vulnerable to f- kinetic or non-kinetic attack to deny their capabilities, which in turn could render a satellite system unusable or un- useful. There are a number of potential adversary satellites on orbit, and one of our key tasks is to detect them, to track them, and to characterize them. A lot of the threat mechanisms that are present on the Earth could also be exported into space, and therefore understanding what the nature of those threat satellites is will help us understand and react to those threats should they materialize.
Squadron Leader Amy: And there was a significant RAF announcement at the conference, No 3 Space Effects Squadron. So what is it, and why does it matter?

Squadron Leader Amy: Control of space sounds quite confrontational.
Does this mean that we are preparing for war in space?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: No. Control of space is underpinned by space domain awareness. We need to understand the domain first. But equally, if we wish to deter hostile acts or unwelcome activity in space, we need to be able to detect it, characterize it, attribute it, and if necessary, respond in an appropriate manner.
And therefore, control of space is both about assuring our capabilities, but also potentially denying an adversary those same capabilities.
Squadron Leader Amy: So why should somebody who isn't in defence care about any of this?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: Space is a hidden enabler of day-to-day activity. Most of what we rely upon for modern society has a dependency on space in some fashion. Typically, people will be familiar with satellite navigation, so usually derived from GPS. But the European Galileo system is similar, and there are other systems operated by different nations, both friendly and less friendly. But also, that timing signal that comes from GPS is particularly important for things like the distribution of power, management of water, and things like that.
So it's there in the background. Space is always assumed that it will be there. It's much like electricity. You turn on the light switch and you expect the light to work without necessarily thinking about how it works, and it's the same for space. Similarly, just, things like weather forecasting. A lot of that is derived from space-based systems that provide that the data to enable the accurate forecasting that we now come to expect on a daily basis.
Squadron Leader Amy: I suppose most people would be horrified to think of somebody just turning their internet off. Like you can't even imagine it, right? So the day-to-day functions of everything that we do would be affected.
Wing Commander Neal Henley: Absolutely, yeah. And as I say, a lot of that is down to that GPS timing signal which allows you to synchronize your networks, be they computer networks, traffic management networks, all that sort of thing.
Squadron Leader Amy: What capabilities are actually being developed rather than simply talked about?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: At the moment, we have the Skynet 6 program, which is going to deliver a replacement for the current Skynet 5. Skynet 1 actually launched in 1969, so it's a longstanding name and a satellite communications constellation that has a real provenance. My capability development colleagues are also working on a Project ISTARI, which is our space-based intelligence surveillance reconnaissance, or earth observation.
We are looking at the deep space advanced radar capability, which will give us a radar tracking and detection capability out to the geostationary belt, which is at 36,000 kilometres, and that's where things like our Skynet satellite communication satellites live. So it's important to be able to, again, detect and track the objects that are up there, both from a hazard point of view, so potential collisions, as well as from a threat point of view.
We're improving our space domain awareness through the delivery of the NOCTIS sensors and also through the use of the Borealis mission system, which takes the data from NOCTIS and other sensors and other partners' sensors, and then integrates it to provide us with the domain awareness that we need to make decisions
Squadron Leader Amy: Another major theme was partnership. So why can't the UK simply build sovereign capability and do this itself?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: I would say that we are building and developing sovereign capability, which is important both for industry, for the economy, but also for our freedom of action. But that won't be enough. It won't give us the capacity, and certainly globally it won't necessarily give us the coverage that we need for sensors. And in the same way for other allies and partners, they can do a certain amount themselves at a sovereign level, but they need partners as well to access the rest of the globe. So space is very much a team sport. We work with our partners in Operation Olympic Defender and also in the Combined Space Operations Initiative, and we share data and information, we share perspective, but also we share concerns, and therefore we will frequently communicate with each other and to others about our concerns about activities in space or potentially unwelcome activities that could hazard not just our access to space, but also everybody else's access as well.
Squadron Leader Amy: Now, throughout the conference, we also heard a lot about one space. I know you've just lent into it a little bit there. What does that really mean in real terms?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: So one space is His Majesty's government operating in the most efficient and effective manner, sharing what we do as a department with other departments, and similarly them sharing with us so that we know that we are not paying multiple times for the same product, that if we are acquiring a capability, it's complimentary, or where we are duplicating, it's done deliberately and consciously for good reason rather than accidentally and therefore inefficiently.
Squadron Leader Amy: So pulling all the strands together to be agile, but in space.
Wing Commander Neal Henley: Yeah, to be agile, but also just to be mindful of what is the best value for money approach to get to a, a comprehensive solution that serves everybody's purpose but without wasting resource or time.
Squadron Leader Amy: And I suppose that there is very little of both of those things.

Wing Commander Neal Henley: It can be very expensive, but some of the things is just about reusing either information or systems we already have, so it doesn't all have to come with a big price tag, although the more exquisite the capabilities are tends to be the more expensive they are, but it's not always the way.
Squadron Leader Amy: So industry and investment featured heavily as well. Why is that important to military space power?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: Just as in any of the other operational or war fighting domains, we need to be able to develop the capabilities we need, but we also need to sustain them. And therefore, having an industry that can not just develop and deliver, but to maintain and improve those capabilities is really important as we continue to move into what is not just a contested environment, and increasingly contested at that, but also congested.
The amount of objects in space is only trending upwards, and therefore the risk of a hazard rather than a threat is becoming more and more prevalent, and we need those capabilities to be able to be survivable against whatever risks they face not just against deliberate risks from a potential adversary.
Squadron Leader Amy: You deal in this environment every single day when you're looking at how congested it is in our orbit. There is so much space junk up there. But also, it's about national legislation a- around the globe ensuring that satellites, when they reach the end of their life, are adequately disposed of so that they don't remain as clutter, and therefore a risk to other orbital objects.
Squadron Leader Amy: If there was a military lesson from the conference, what would it be?
Wing Commander Neal Henley: For me, it's the positive is the growing understanding of the significance of space and the space capabilities. But at the same time, it's the need to fully understand your own dependencies which could become vulnerabilities, and therefore understanding why we need to invest in the space domain to ensure that those services people depend upon will be there when they're actually needed.

Egypt in daily contact with Iran, US to prevent new escalation, top diplomat says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:59:13 UTC
22:59:13 KST

CAIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Egypt negotiates with Iran and the United States as well as regional partners on a daily basis to avoid another escalation of tensions, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Abdelatty said.
"Every day, we talk with the Iranians, the Americans and our regional partners to prevent a transition to a new bout of military escalation," Egypt’s top diplomat said at a joint news conference with US Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in the Arab republic’s new capital, as broadcast by the Al-Qahera Al-Ekhbariya television channel. "Military methods would not guarantee a long-lasting result of stability," Abdelatty emphasized as he called on both sides to return to the negotiating table.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
On October 24, US President Donald Trump hinted that he might decide to launch new strikes against Iran if Washington and Tehran fail to reach a deal. On the next day, however, he ruled out immediate military action against the Islamic Republic for the time being.

Belgium postpones terrace smoking ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:59:06 UTC
22:59:06 KST

Belgium introduced a slate of new anti-smoking laws last year, including curbs on smoking in airport rooms and a ban on flavored vapes, aiming to achieve a “smoke-free generation” by 2040. | Cristina Quicler/AFP via Getty Images
People in Belgium will be able to smoke at restaurant terraces for a little while longer after the government announced it would be delaying its outdoor ban planned for early 2027.
The federal government planned to prohibit smoking outside cafés and eateries as a public health measure from Jan. 1 , spearheaded by social democrat Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke.
But Belgium’s Council of State, its supreme administrative court, "has asked us to adjust some measures, and we are working on this," a statement from Vandenbroucke’s cabinet, shared with local media outlet VRT, said.
Advertisement
The minister’s move initially prompted backlash from the Belgian hospitality sector; the statement added the postponement would allow enough time for venues to adjust to the new rules.
Several other EU countries are moving forward with similar bans — albeit with different success rates. France recently introduced a smoking ban on beaches, gardens and near schools.
Spain, meanwhile, approved a draft bill in July that would extend the ban to outdoor terraces and other public spaces, including restrictions on e-cigarettes — but which faces pushback from restaurant owners.
Belgium introduced a slate of new anti-smoking laws last year, including curbs on smoking in airport rooms and a ban on flavored vapes, aiming to achieve a “smoke-free generation” by 2040. Outdoor smoking bans are one of many measures advocated by the World Health Organization (WHO).
According to the Belgian Cancer Foundation, nearly a quarter of Belgians smoke and 19% do so daily.
It is unclear how long Belgium will postpone its outdoor smoking ban. Once published, the country's national parliament still has to approve the Council of State's amendments.

Meanwhile, PostNL recorded a significant increase in parcel deliveries within Europe, with volumes rising by more than 40% compared with the same period last year.
However, the company said this growth was insufficient to offset the sharp decline in deliveries originating from Asia.

The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:57:55 EET
22:57:55 KST

The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian businesses are gradually developing practices for employing and adapting veterans — from preparing teams and retraining to creating specialized positions.
Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and reintegrating veterans. Businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, creating adaptation and retraining programs, while some companies are introducing dedicated positions to support veterans. At the same time, it is still too early to speak of mass employment. Tetiana Karelska, head of the HR and CSR division of the European Business Association, said this in a comment to UNN.
We are observing a moderate increase in engagement. We have not measured separate, precise statistics that would representatively demonstrate the dynamics of veterans’ employment in recent years—and objectively, such statistics do not currently exist because of the dynamics of the hostilities. However, we are tracking an increase in preparatory work within companies
According to her, among the Association’s member companies there are both businesses that already have systematic practices for engaging and adapting veterans and those that are only beginning to develop their own programs.
Tetiana Karelska noted that the Association is recording growing demand for team training, including specialized training—from basic communication etiquette and psychological literacy to the specifics of interacting with people who have combat experience, injuries, or experience of captivity. In addition, the EBA is recording positive dynamics in the creation of internal adaptation and retraining pathways.
Introducing a veterans’ affairs officer position—companies that have the necessary resources are creating dedicated positions (veterans’ affairs officer/CVO) responsible directly for veterans’ reintegration. On our side, we have a vision for creating a specialized training program for such professionals
Adapting workplaces and teams
Veterans’ adaptation involves both arranging a physical workplace in accordance with the employee’s individual needs and preparing the team for their return.
The first aspect—adapting the physical workplace—is always about additional funding. Not every employer is able to independently arrange a workplace according to the individual needs of an employee with a disability. The state provides substantial assistance here, in particular through compensation programs, but this sometimes remains a complicated process that requires time and knowledge
At the same time, team adaptation and psychological support depend on the company’s willingness to invest in employee training, engage external specialists, or develop its own educational programs. According to the EBA’s assessment, this does not always require substantial budgets, since free training programs developed as far back as 2014 are available publicly.
What obstacles remain
One of the key challenges for employers is the so-called "military-to-civilian translation."
Recruiters and HR professionals still find it difficult to properly assess candidates’ military experience and match it with civilian vacancies. This requires systematic cooperation with support services and directly with veterans
Other obstacles include insufficient staff preparedness, a lack of communication and management skills, as well as stereotypes about people with combat experience, experience of captivity, or disabilities.
We continue to work on stereotypes concerning interaction with people who have combat experience, experience of captivity, or a disability. This is a lengthy process, and it is not solely the responsibility of the employer or a matter of training within the company. It is a global task for the state and society to develop a culture of respect and gratitude toward every citizen, regardless of their experience
As noted by the EBA, more effective integration of veterans requires companies to have not only their own programs, but also coordinated state policy and access to the necessary support tools.
Businesses are currently creating numerous initiatives and programs at their own expense. The main expectation businesses have of the state is synergy instead of duplication, along with a reduction in the number of fragmented working groups. Instead, there is a demand for the creation of a single specialized structure (or coordination center) that would bring together all process participants and provide convenient access to analytics, methodological materials, grant programs, and state compensation in one place, so that employers would not have to collect information separately
Let us remind you
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is also working to support veterans. According to the words of FPU Chairman Serhii Byzov, the Federation’s sanatoriums provide medical rehabilitation services to military personnel, while the organization itself, together with specialized ministries and the National Health Service of Ukraine, is developing programs to support, socially adapt, and employ veterans. According to the FPU, more than 32,800 military personnel have undergone medical rehabilitation at its sanatoriums.

Consultant doctors in England will stage a two-day strike on Nov. 25 and 26 over pay and working conditions, the British Medical Association (BMA) announced Monday.
Consultants will provide emergency cover during the walkout, with staffing similar to Christmas Day and significant disruption expected to routine appointments and planned procedures.
In a joint statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr. Helen Neary and Dr. Shanu Datta said they had attempted to negotiate with the government in “good faith,” but that “time-and-time again ministers have kicked the can down the road.”
“Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes,” they said.
Consultants received a 3.5% pay increase this year. However, the BMA argues that their pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years when adjusted for inflation.
The union is also seeking a reduction in the standard working week from 40 to 35 hours, higher pay for out-of-hours work and changes to pension arrangements, including greater flexibility over when pensions can be taken.
The union said 76% of consultants who participated in the strike ballot voted in favor of industrial action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.
The government said this amounted to around one in five consultants employed by the National Health Service (NHS) in England, noting that nearly half of consultants are not BMA members.
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper described the strike announcement as “disappointing,” saying the government had been engaged in “constructive discussions” with the union. She called the planned action “irresponsible” and warned it would place the health service under greater pressure.

Gyurov Files Complaint Accusing Radev of Using Government Resources to Campaign for Yotova
The Gyurov-Kandev Initiative Committee has filed a complaint with Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission (CEC), alleging that Prime Minister Rumen Radev used official government communication channels to campaign for presidential candidate Iliana Yotova, while We Continue the Change leader Asen Vassilev accused Radev of delaying the state budget and failing to take a consistent position on national security.
The initiative committee is seeking an urgent CEC ruling over two alleged violations of the Electoral Code involving campaign messages distributed through the Council of Ministers’ official channels.
According to the committee, the government has effectively become a press office for Yotova. In a statement on October 26, Radev appealed directly to voters, saying, “Let us vote for Iliana Yotova,” while also making accusations against Andrey Gyurov. The same content was then published through the Government Information Service, the official gov.bg website and the Council of Ministers’ Facebook page.
The committee alleges that the actions breached Article 182, Paragraph 1 of the Electoral Code, which prohibits election campaigning through state institutions, and Article 168, Paragraph 3, which prohibits the free use of public administrative resources for campaign purposes. It argues that government communication channels, civil servants and taxpayer funds were used to benefit one candidate.
The complaint sets out six requests to the CEC: establish whether the violations occurred; order the immediate removal of the posts and stop campaign activity through official government channels; document the published content; identify the officials who drafted, approved and published the messages, as well as who instructed them to do so; take steps to issue administrative violation citations against Radev and any officials found responsible; and refer the materials to the National Audit Office for assessment within its jurisdiction.
“We are referring this matter to the CEC: the posts must be taken down immediately, and those responsible must be held accountable,” Gyurov said.
The initiative committee has called for the complaint to be considered urgently, within the prescribed 24-hour period.
Separately, Vassilev accused the government of postponing the presentation of the state budget, preventing citizens from examining its financial parameters before the elections. He said that if the National Council for Tripartite Cooperation does not meet this week, the Public Finance Act will be violated and the budget will not reach Parliament before October 31.
“I have just learned that there will be no tripartite meeting this week; this means the Public Finance Act will be violated, and the budget will not be submitted to Parliament before October 31. What are you hiding, Mr. Radev? What is in this budget that you do not want to show the Bulgarian citizens before the elections this coming Sunday?” Vassilev said.
He argued that the main budget parameters were already known and indicated that incomes would deteriorate in real terms.
“For the first time, you have officially included in a budget the fact that Bulgarian citizens will become poorer. Their incomes will grow at a slower rate than inflation. But what else have you hidden in this budget, and on what else are you spending money—to the point where, even with this impoverishment, you still cannot manage to stay within a 3% deficit?” the PP leader asked.
Vassilev urged voters to back Gyurov, arguing that he could scrutinize executive decisions and veto measures that harmed citizens or violated the Constitution. He said Yotova would not be able to perform that role.
The PP leader also sharply criticized Radev and Yotova over national security, accusing Radev of taking inconsistent positions on Russia, Ukraine and Bulgaria’s European allies.
“Let him, once and for all, take a firm, sensible stance - instead of saying one thing here and something else in Brussels, spinning around like a top wherever the wind blows,” Vassilev said.
He argued that protecting Bulgaria’s maritime and air borders required a clear position toward its allies and readiness to respond to violations. Effective defenses against drones and maritime threats, he added, required cooperation with Romania and other allies.
Vassilev also questioned the country’s defense preparedness, noting that Radev had served as president and commander-in-chief for nine years. He asked why Bulgaria still lacked a sufficiently developed system for countering drones and modern radar capabilities.
“I have done my job as Minister of Finance. I provided the funding, securing it within the 3% deficit limit, without taking anything away from pensioners or cutting salaries. What have they done since then?” Vassilev said.
He also challenged political allegations concerning “dependencies” and backroom deals, disputing Radev’s claims about links between political and economic circles. Vassilev said the president should be chosen by voters rather than through arrangements negotiated in party headquarters.
“The country’s President must be elected by the Bulgarian citizens,” he said.

A Movement’s Promise: The Making of Contemporary Palestinian Theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

When Palestinian negotiators returned from the Madrid peace talks in the early 1990s, they briefed the press at a theatre in East Jerusalem. It seems an odd setting for news of talks that held the world’s attention, until you discover the role theatre had played in Palestinian life since the Nakba.
A burned-out cinema until 1984, the Palestinian National Theatre was where the negotiator Hanan Ashrawi and the Jerusalem leader Faisal Al-Husseini accused Israel of ignoring its commitments. It also hosted a festival for local schools and a literary festival marking twenty years since Ghassan Kanafani’s assassination. In Al-Saber’s words, the theatre “stepped into the role of an acting ministry of culture”.
That a theatre could take on such a role says a great deal about what it had come to mean for Palestinians. The mass displacement of 1948 scattered the artists, troupes and audiences of pre-war Palestine. In the years that followed, Palestinian culture survived inside Israel under military rule, which lasted until 1966, and in the West Bank under Jordanian rule.
After the 1967 war and Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza, a generation of young people in Jerusalem and Ramallah turned to the stage.
Writing from exile in Lebanon, the Jerusalem writer Mahmoud Shqair observed that the theatre movement “became the most conspicuous artistic phenomenon on our occupied land. None of the other arts matched it in drawing and influencing the audiences.”
Al-Saber explains why. Under an occupation that restricted Palestinian assembly, attending a play was a social activity and a political act at once. In his words, theatre had become “a site for free thought and a battleground that did not require forbidden arms”.
Read: Theatre community slams Israel lobby attack on touring Palestinian play
A Movement’s Promise tells how that movement, known to its members as Al-Haraka Al-Masrahiyya (the theatre movement), came into being and grew into the theatre industry Palestinians have today.
Al-Saber assembled this history from scattered records and the recollections of the people who made it. “Due to the absence of a Palestinian state,” he writes, “Palestinian theater history has not been collected into a centralized archive.” During fieldwork between 2009 and 2023, he interviewed theatre artists and gathered material from their personal collections: reviews and interviews cut from period newspapers, posters, photographs, brochures and actors’ copies of scripts.
Further material came from the archive of El-Hakawati (The Storyteller), the Jerusalem company founded in 1977 whose theatre later became the Palestinian National Theatre, and from the papers of its founder, François Abu Salem. Records of the Israeli censorship board, held in the Israel State Archive, show how companies dealt with the censors.
El-Hakawati’s satire Mahjoub Mahjoub (1980), about a hapless Palestinian everyman under occupation, shows how artists slipped their plays past Israeli censors, and how censorship backfired.
To obtain a performance permit, El-Hakawati’s co-founder Jackie Lubeck sent the censors an English summary that made the play sound harmless. In one scene, Mahjoub is interrogated for wearing clothes in the colours of the Palestinian flag, which was then illegal. In Lubeck’s summary, this became simply: “Mahjoub is questioned about the outfit he wears to work one day.” The censors saw nothing political, and the play was approved in December 1980.
The following month, the authorities stopped a performance in Nazareth, claiming El-Hakawati had departed from the approved text. The audience turned the evening into a protest, and the actors improvised a new scene, sitting on stage tied to their chairs with their mouths taped. The novelist Emile Habibi condemned the ban, and the play went on to tour Europe.
Episodes like this lead Al-Saber to argue that Israel “inadvertently and unknowingly promoted Palestinian theater” through its efforts to suppress it. Censorship taught artists to say things indirectly, and every ban or arrest only drew more attention to their work.
Al-Saber concentrates on East Jerusalem and its close ties with Ramallah, from 1967 to the Oslo Accords. The two cities worked as a single cultural centre, linked by family, social and professional bonds, and most of the pioneering artists lived and worked in one or both.
Al-Saber wants readers to understand Palestinian theatre through the people who made it. Occupation shaped their working lives, but so did artistic ambition, friendships, rivalries and the effort to build an audience. As he explains, accounts centred on the “conflict” too often leave Palestine’s story existing only in relation to Israel. His approach stresses “the right of Palestinian theater makers to exist on their own merits, without being subsumed by crisis narratives or orientalist motifs”.
Balalin (The Balloons), the first independent Palestinian theatre company formed in the West Bank after the 1967 occupation, showed how theatre could rally an audience without saying a single forbidden word. In its best-known production, Al-‘atma (The Darkness, 1972), a young troupe sets out to perform a play, but the lights fail and the actors ask the audience to help repair them.
Many spectators believed the blackout was real, and electricians sometimes climbed onto the stage to offer help. As Al-Saber explains, “the struggle to end the darkness and perform the play represents the Palestinian struggle to fix its internal conflicts and end the occupation.” When the eager carpenter Adel dies at the lighting board, the cast carries him out on their shoulders as Palestinians carry their martyrs. “It was truly a call for an uprising, but using symbols,” recalls Emile Ashrawi, a founding member of the company.
Obliterated: Theatregoers’ dreams of seeing Palestinian play in London
Fifteen years later, El-Hakawati turned to the memory of the Nakba. By then it had become, in Al-Saber’s words, “a de facto representative of the Palestinian theater” in the international media. The Story of Kufur Shamma (1987) follows Walid, a young man who returns from studying abroad to find his village deserted. Kufur Shamma is fictional, but it stands in for the hundreds of Palestinian villages destroyed in 1948. With the village fool, Walid sets out to bring its scattered people home, tracking them across the diaspora, only to return and find the village erased.
Telling the story of 1948 met resistance well beyond the occupied territories. At a festival in Acre in 1987, a mixed Palestinian and Jewish city inside Israel, supporters of the Jewish extremist group Kahane Chai stood up in the front row, raised an Israeli flag and chanted “Death to Arabs”.
Two years later, Joseph Papp, one of America’s leading theatre producers, cancelled the play’s booking at New York’s Public Theater for fear of offending his audience, many of them Jewish and, in his words, “very sympathetic to Israel”. Each time, El-Hakawati performed anyway: the actors in Acre returned to the stage to applause, and weeks after Papp’s decision the play opened at another New York theatre to warm reviews.
The movement’s divisions run through the book as strongly as its achievements. Factional loyalties split ensembles, and the row over who controlled El-Hakawati’s theatre ended with its founders leaving the building they had rebuilt. Yet Al-Saber sees this constant breaking and re-forming as the movement’s strength: a “self-sacrificial” process that kept making way for new companies and artists.
After Oslo came new pressures. Foreign donor money professionalised the theatres but turned a collective movement into separate organisations competing for grants. At the same time, the Separation Wall, military checkpoints and expanding settlements cut East Jerusalem off from the West Bank.
Within a few years, most West Bank Palestinians could no longer enter Jerusalem without a permit. The Palestinian National Theatre lost its largest audience, and Jerusalem was separated from Ramallah, the city whose family, artistic and professional ties had given birth to the movement. Theatre-makers now had to tour to audiences trapped in their own cities, and artists with West Bank identity cards could rarely work across the new lines.
Al-Saber closes by asking whether the movement still exists. He believes it does, carried in the stories that two generations of theatre-makers still tell one another. “Even during war, genocide, and uncertainty,” he writes, “the movement is alive in its lore and lineage, promising and delivering a richly diverse theater industry.” If at times it seems dormant, “its history has shown that it may simply be under the radar”.

Von der Leyen’s big Commission shake-up moves a step closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:29 UTC
22:56:29 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen’s push for a sweeping overhaul of the European Commission moved closer to fruition on Monday, as a group of external advisers handed over a report that will help shape the institution’s biggest administrative shake-up in two decades.
The report, drawn up by a high-level group led by former Commission Secretary-General Catherine Day, marks a new stage in the so-called large-scale review — an exercise intended to make the Commission more efficient, streamline its sprawling bureaucracy and turn it into a more attractive employer.
“Now we’re reaching the second phase,” von der Leyen said at the handover, referring to the conclusion of an initial phase that involved 15 internal workstreams and contributions from thousands of Commission staff.
Advertisement
“We need to be able to act effectively and to act quickly,” she said about the needed changes in the EU Executive’s machinery. “That means simpler procedures, clearer structures, better cooperation across departments so that our colleagues can focus their efforts where it makes the greatest difference.”
The external group, consisting of Day and eight other experts with experience in national administrations and international organizations including the OECD and OSCE, put forward nine interrelated recommendations aimed at making the Commission more agile and better equipped to adapt to future challenges.
Among its main proposals is a shift away from working in siloed departments toward greater collaboration across directorates-general, including through cross-DG portfolios.
This part of the exercise is politically sensitive. Behind the push to modernize the Commission lies the prospect of a far-reaching reorganization of its departments, potentially redrawing the responsibilities of powerful directorates-general that oversee billions of euros in EU spending.
As POLITICO first reported, several major Commission departments face an uncertain future under plans to overhaul how the bloc manages and distributes EU funds, raising the prospect of mergers or other structural changes.
Among the departments potentially affected is the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO), which oversees cohesion policy funding, accounting for almost a third of EU spending. Other departments facing uncertainty include the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI), responsible for Common Agricultural Policy money; DG EMPL, which oversees employment and social funding; DG MARE, which handles fisheries funding; and DG RTD, responsible for research and innovation.
Advertisement
The group also called for a stronger Secretariat-General to act as a strategic center driving results, and for a human-centered approach to artificial intelligence to simplify administrative processes and modernize the institution’s operations.
But the release of the report on Monday does not mean that any restructuring decisions have been taken. Day’s report will feed into a wider review overseen by Budget and Public Administration Commissioner Piotr Serafin, who is tasked with presenting final recommendations to von der Leyen by the end of 2026.
Catherine Day, Chair of the High-Level Group on the Future of the Commission’s Civil Service gives a press statement in Brussels on October 26, 2026. | Dati Bendo/European Commission Audiovisual Service
Serafin said at the handover that the external assessment, combined with feedback from Commission staff, provided a “mandate to go for far reaching changes.”
Day, for her part, said the Commission had already demonstrated a willingness to reform, pointing to the wealth of ideas emerging from within the institution.
“The work done on the large scale review has shown that there is a broad coalition for change right across the Commission,” she added.
A separate internal process produced an initial set of recommendations in July, drawn up by Commission officials. Those proposals were intended to kick-start a broader discussion within the institution rather than serve as final decisions.
Advertisement
Any major reshuffling of the Commission’s structure, however, is likely to take considerably longer.
Speaking in July to a small group of journalists, including POLITICO, Serafin acknowledged that structural reforms would be closely tied to negotiations on the EU’s next long-term budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, which will determine how EU spending is organized from 2028 to 2034.
He indicated at the time that he did not expect decisions on major structural changes before those budget negotiations are concluded.
For now, Day’s findings will provide another input into Serafin’s final proposals, bringing von der Leyen one step closer to deciding how far she wants to go in reshaping the institution she leads.

Geneva to offer free home delivery of groceries to elderly
Following a trial phase, the Swiss city of Geneva is making its free home grocery delivery service a permanent feature for people aged 65 and over. This service will now also be available to recipients of a care allowance.
These people can enjoy free delivery of their shopping once a week. Launched in the summer of 2025, the pilot scheme for free home delivery of groceries has been a resounding success, with an average of 260 deliveries made each month, the Department for Social Cohesion and Solidarity (DCSS) said on Monday.
The beneficiaries, currently numbering 300, have an average age of 79.
Building on this positive outcome, the DCSS has decided to make this initiative a permanent service, whilst expanding the group of beneficiaries. The aim remains the same: to promote independence, mobility and social connections, while making everyday shopping easier.

France: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
October 26, 2026
The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.
France braces for 'lively' Halloween
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.
"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."
Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.
He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.
Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'
The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."
He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."
While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.
"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."
The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.
"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands
Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."
He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.
"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.
"But to answer them, there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."
Edited by: Alex Berry

Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:51:21 UTC
22:51:21 KST

Israelis will elect a new parliament next Tuesday. The main issues in the campaign are foreign and security policy, mistakes regarding the 2023 Hamas attack, military service for ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews, and high inflation. The right-wing religious bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the more moderate forces led by former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces Gadi Eisenkot are neck-and-neck in the polls.
Opposition overtakes PM on the right
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Many of Netanyahu’s opponents share his worldview, political scientist Sergei Medvedev explains on Facebook (Russia) :
“The opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot has a slight lead in the polls. ... Nevertheless, the election is taking place on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s terms. The key leaders of the opposition bloc have adopted Netanyahu’s worldview on a number of key issues and have even shifted further to the right than he has. ... The majority of Israeli Jews now see the world as Netanyahu has long viewed it. This is Netanyahu’s great victory. But it is matched by his great defeat: much of the world now sees Israel as the residents of the Gaza Strip do.”
No healing without facing the past
To move forward, Israel must first come to terms with the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, La Libre Belgique (Belgium) argues:
“It is precisely in view of these painful wounds that Israeli voters will have to make their choice on Tuesday. Not in the hope of healing this or that wound by any means necessary, but in order to set their country on the path to genuine recovery. ... Three years on, Netanyahu is still refusing to allow a state commission to be set up to clarify political responsibility for the events of 7 October. ... Yet every Israeli has the right to know what led to that fateful day in October. No society can look calmly toward the future if it turns a blind eye to its past.”
Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
Display of direct access to Washington
According to military expert Alexandru Grumaz writing in Adevărul (Romania), Monday’s surprise visit by US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was aimed at helping Netanyahu score points with his voters:
“The fact that the US secretary of defence came to hold talks with him at a military base – eight days before the election – reinforces the image of a prime minister who has direct access to the decision-makers in Washington. For voters, the message is easy to understand: a change of government would also mean replacing the very person who maintains those relationships just when the country is in a dangerous phase. This is a powerful election argument, even if the partnership between two states should not depend on who is leading them.”
Even small changes are important
TVNet (Latvia) explains why a change of government does not necessarily mean a change of course:
“Overall, it’s clear that Netanyahu’s departure would not automatically mean that Israel is prepared to end the wars or support the Palestinians’ right to their own state. Many voters want a more responsible government but are still in favour of military operations. A victory for the opposition cannot therefore be interpreted as a clear demand for a change of course in relations with the Palestinians and other neighbours. Nevertheless, even small changes would be important for both sides.”
Last stop before the abyss
The Israelis must use their votes to stop Netanyahu, urges Le Temps (Switzerland):
“In recent years, Israel has undergone a fundamental transformation: it is a country governed by a prime minister who is under investigation by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity, and which finds itself in a state of open war with multiple neighbours in the region. ... Tens of thousands of Israelis have already fled the country. ... Netanyahu’s potential departure would certainly not be enough to change the country from the bottom up, however urgent that may be. But at the very least it could allow Israelis to halt their rapid descent into the abyss.”
Bellicose slogans poisoning the campaign
The situation may well deteriorate futher, El Periódico (Spain) de Catalunya fears:
“Israel’s founding Father David Ben-Gurion is said to have remarked: ‘The Land of Israel is our homeland, and we shall defend it with all our might.’ ... This bellicose mindset still prevails today – the idea that the first defeat will drive the Israelis into the sea, and it is poisoning the campaign slogans – against a backdrop of an exhausted Palestinian society, an uncontrolled energy crisis and uncertainty hanging over the entire region, from Egypt to Iran. ... This already toxic atmosphere could deteriorate further if the election result prolongs the formation of a government amid a sea of irreconcilable parties. Things are liable to get worse.”
Outcry of the ultra-Orthodox
According to the Kronen Zeitung (Austria), the compulsory conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews is making waves:
“With just under a week to go before the elections a campaign bombshell has exploded, stirring up emotions like hardly any other issue: the privileges enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox (known as Haredim), particularly when it comes to compulsory military service. Israel is at war and there is a shortage of soldiers. Now the army has made an example of them. It intercepted a flight bringing young Haredim returning home from New York at Tel Aviv airport. Two coaches were waiting outside: the one on the right to take them to collect their uniforms, the one on the left to take them to a military prison. An outcry from the Haredim ensued. For years their parties – as sought-after coalition partners – have been extorting precious privileges. ... The Haredim have become a test of faith in the truest sense of the word.”
