The Russia-Africa summit 2026: What you need to know about building a multipolar world without the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:28:11 UTC
22:28:11 KST

The Russia-Africa Summit 2026: What you need to know about building a multipolar world without the West
Trade, sovereignty and peace are on the table as African leaders gather in Moscow this week for the third Russia-Africa Summit.
Their participation comes despite what Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has described as Western pressure on African governments to stay away. This prodding prompted Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama to retort that partnerships should deliver investment and fair returns rather than be determined by competition among outside powers.
The October 28-29 meeting will set cooperation priorities for the next three years, alongside an Economic and Humanitarian Forum bringing together officials, businesses and experts. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current African Union (AU) chairman, will co-chair the leaders’ plenary session on the second day.
The gathering follows summits in Sochi in 2019 and St. Petersburg in 2023.
Who is coming to Moscow?
Russia has invited all African heads of state and the leaders of regional organizations. Most African delegations have confirmed their participation, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa arrived in Moscow on Sunday. Writing on X, he said Zimbabwe’s participation would focus on “driving economic diversification, boosting industrial trade, and creating sustainable jobs for our youth,” alongside cooperation in energy, food security and technology.
The presidents of Mali and Mozambique as well as the Senegalese prime minister have also arrived. Delegations from Ghana and Uganda are in Moscow, according to Ruptly footage showing their motorcades in the city center on Monday.
Republic of Congo President Denis Sassou Nguesso left Brazzaville for Moscow on Sunday, according to a Facebook post made by his office.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama arrived in Moscow on Monday after confirming his participation at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London last week. At that event, he defended Ghana’s nonaligned foreign policy, citing friendly relations with Russia, China, the US, and the EU.
Mahama also said he would “try to convince President Putin to have a ceasefire if I can,” referring to the Ukraine conflict. His appeal follows earlier African peace efforts, including a seven-country mission led by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to Ukraine and Russia in June 2023.
Kenyan President William Ruto and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni are expected to attend, their ambassadors in Moscow confirmed in June. Kenya’s envoy, Peter Mathuki, said he anticipated “very fruitful talks.”
Burkina Faso President Ibrahim Traore and Niger’s President Abdourahamane Tchiani will also participate, according to Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Alimov.
South Sudanese President Salva Kiir confirmed his attendance in a letter to Putin delivered through diplomatic channels in July, according to Russia’s embassy in Juba. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has also announced the participation of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional leader, Horta N’Tam.
Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah will attend, her office confirmed, announcing her scheduled departure on Monday. It said Namibia would seek partnerships supporting mineral processing, job creation, technology transfer, and economic diversification.
Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed al-Menfi is also expected to participate, Sputnik reported, citing a source in the council. Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan will attend, Russian Ambassador to Sudan Andrey Chernovol told RIA Novosti.
Nigerian Vice President Kashim Shettima will lead his country’s delegation, Nigeria’s ambassador to Russia, Joseph Olusola Iji, told TASS.
Ramaphosa will not attend. During talks with Putin in September, he cited local election campaigning, saying he would be “in the middle of a very vigorous campaign.” South Africa’s embassy subsequently confirmed that its delegation would be led by Zane Dangor, director-general of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation.
What is on the agenda?
The topic of sovereignty is central to the forum, which features sessions on development financing, food security, and technological independence.
Discussions will cover infrastructure, transport corridors, industrial cooperation, and payment mechanisms that reduce reliance on the dollar and euro. Participants will also assess closer links with BRICS and the Eurasian Economic Union, including barriers that continue to restrict trade.
Interdependence regarding agriculture is a foundational sector for Russia-Africa relations, and the forum is expected to address fertilizer supplies, farm machinery, local production, and the financial and logistical obstacles facing food trade.
Peaceful nuclear energy is another priority. Rosatom is building four reactors at Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant and has signed roadmaps to advance planned nuclear power projects in Ethiopia and Rwanda. Its cooperation with Rwanda also includes a proposed nuclear science and technology center for research, specialist training, and applications in medicine, agriculture, and industry.
Digital infrastructure discussions come as Africa’s online economy expands. GSMA’s 2025 assessment put the continent’s mobile internet users at 416 million, projected to reach 576 million by 2030. African companies also bring established financial technology expertise: Kenya’s Safaricom said its M-PESA mobile money service reached 40 million customers in March 2026.Other sessions cover artificial intelligence, healthcare and training African specialists.
Why is the summit important?
African priorities include processing more resources at home, building energy and technological capacity, and diversifying partnerships on their own terms.
Disputes with Western governments have reinforced the emphasis on sovereignty. In September, South Africa’s Foreign Ministry challenged US visa restrictions linked to Washington’s criticism of its domestic policies, declaring: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice.”
The summit builds on sustained diplomatic engagement. Since 2022, Lavrov has visited countries across the continent, including repeated trips to Egypt, Ethiopia and South Africa. His July 2026 tour included Ethiopia, Niger, Mozambique, and Burundi.
The summit framework has also developed into regular ministerial consultations. Sochi hosted the first ministerial conference of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum in November 2024, followed by a second in Cairo in December 2025.
The gathering for Russia “is a momentous event – hardly ever before have so many leaders gathered together in the Kremlin,” Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT on Monday. He described relations as undergoing a slow but sustained strengthening, supported by an expanding network of intergovernmental commissions, business councils, and other institutions.
Trade between Russia and Africa rose from $16.8 billion in 2019 to $27.1 billion in 2025, according to Nikolay Golovko, a leading expert at HSE’s Center for African Studies. The balance remains heavily tilted toward Russian exports, which accounted for $22.7 billion, compared with $4.4 billion in imports from Africa.
Has the threat of Western sanctions reached Russia-Africa relations?
There still might be concerns about secondary sanctions; however, “they are being removed from the first plan,” Maslov said. A new group of partners has emerged, ready to develop new logistics networks and payment mechanisms. “Sanctions have gone from being a problem to a cost of doing business,” he noted.
Economic cooperation already includes major projects. Russia is building Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant, while Rosatom’s subsidiary Mantra Tanzania opened a pilot uranium processing facility at the Mkuju River project in July 2025.
Russia and the AU also reiterated support in July for greater African representation in the UN Security Council, reflecting their push to reform global institutions.
What was the central theme of Summit 1.0?
The inaugural summit took place in Sochi on October 23-24, 2019, co-chaired by Putin and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, then the AU chair.
Held under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development,” it established a framework for cooperation across politics, security, trade, science, education, and culture.
The event provided a foundation for 92 agreements, contracts and signed memorandums of understanding between participants, with publicly disclosed values totaling more than 1 trillion rubles, approximately $12.5 billion at the time. These were signed commitments rather than a measure of completed investment.
What did the second summit deliver?
The second gathering, held in St. Petersburg on July 27-28, 2023, expanded the format to include a humanitarian forum. Official delegations from 48 African countries attended.
Participants adopted a joint declaration and a cooperation action plan for 2023–2026. Separate declarations addressed counterterrorism, international information security and preventing an arms race in outer space. Organizers recorded 161 publicly disclosed agreements, many covering education, science, and other humanitarian cooperation.
Food security was a prominent issue and remains a pressing concern. An estimated 309 million people in Africa faced hunger in 2025, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s latest report.
At the 2023 summit, Putin pledged free grain for six African countries. Russia completed the 200,000-metric-ton delivery program in February 2024, according to its Agriculture Ministry. Somalia and the Central African Republic received 50,000 tons each; Burkina Faso, Eritrea, Mali, and Zimbabwe received 25,000 tons each.
In August 2026, Russia delivered nearly 556 metric tons of split peas and sunflower oil to Burkina Faso through the UN World Food Program, according to Russian Ambassador Igor Martynov.
What can we expect for Summit 3.0?
A central expected outcome is a new Russia-Africa action plan for 2027-2029, replacing the framework adopted in St. Petersburg. Lavrov has said it will be approved at the Moscow gathering.
Zakharova has also said a substantial package of intergovernmental agreements and commercial contracts is expected. Putin will hold bilateral meetings, while Lavrov will host a working breakfast for African foreign ministers on October 28.
The gathering will also provide an opportunity to review implementation of the 2023-2026 action plan, Golovko writes. Its 181 points cover areas ranging from politics and security to agriculture, energy, transport, education, and investment.
What other events are taking place?
The Russia-Africa Media Forum opened in Moscow on Monday, bringing together more than 200 participants from 46 African countries. Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the four-day event focuses on media cooperation and journalism’s role in shaping Africa’s image abroad.
Sebastian Maganga, head of content at Tanzania’s Clouds Media Group, highlighted the value of exchanging stories.
“If you have forums similar to this, that’s when you get the opportunity to share our stories and get stories from Russia and other places respectively and package them,” he said on the sidelines of the event.
The media forum’s published program identifies “strengthening the media sovereignty of African countries” as a priority. Sessions will examine how African newsrooms can develop their own sources, expand the international reach of their reporting and cooperate with Russian outlets through content production, resource sharing, and journalist exchanges.
Moscow will also host the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit on October 27. The gathering will address global market developments, energy security, and investment opportunities.
The GECF’s members account for 70% of proven global natural gas reserves and 42% of gas exports, according to the organization. Its African members are Algeria, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, and Nigeria, while Angola, Mauritania, Mozambique, and Senegal hold observer status.
Africa exported 39.77 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas in 2025, up 1.8 million tons from the previous year, according to the International Gas Union. Mauritania and Senegal joined the LNG export market that year through their shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project.
Russian companies already have investments in African gas production. Rosneft acquired a 30% stake in the concession containing Egypt’s giant Zohr gas field in 2017 for $1.125 billion, excluding reimbursement for past project costs.

Serbia has sought to balance its EU membership ambitions with longstanding ties to Moscow. Russia supplies Serbia with energy and backs Belgrade’s position on Kosovo, whose independence Serbia does not recognize.
Belgrade has also supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity and provided humanitarian and financial assistance to Kyiv, while avoiding sanctions against Moscow.

Arab parliament launches international initiative to support Palestinian rights and pursue accountability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:26:59 UTC
22:26:59 KST

The Arab Parliament has launched an international parliamentary initiative aimed at mobilizing legislative bodies worldwide to increase pressure to end the Israeli occupation and hold those responsible for violations against Palestinians accountable.
The initiative was announced by Arab Parliament Speaker and Chairman of its Palestine Committee, Saad bin Salib Al-Otaibi, during the committee’s first meeting of the third session of the fourth legislative term.
Al-Otaibi called for moving beyond expressions of political solidarity with Palestinians toward coordinated international parliamentary action capable of translating political positions into concrete measures.
He emphasized that the Palestinian issue would remain a central priority for the Arab world, stressing the need to transform parliamentary resolutions and declarations into practical steps that could be monitored and evaluated.
The initiative includes efforts to strengthen accountability through the International Criminal Court, improve documentation of violations against Palestinians and mobilize international parliaments and organizations to address the conditions of Palestinian prisoners.
It also seeks to increase pressure to halt attacks against prisoners and oppose legislation that could threaten their lives.
Other priorities include protecting Al-Aqsa Mosque and Islamic and Christian holy sites in occupied Jerusalem, as well as ensuring that the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) can continue carrying out its humanitarian responsibilities.
Addressing the situation in the Gaza Strip, Al-Otaibi urged the international community to take immediate action to stop the killing of civilians, destruction, starvation, blockade and forced displacement.
He also called for unrestricted humanitarian access and the reconstruction of Gaza under Palestinian responsibility, rejecting proposals to displace Palestinians or separate the Gaza Strip from the West Bank and Jerusalem.
Regarding the occupied West Bank, Al-Otaibi warned against escalating settler attacks, settlement expansion and the seizure of Palestinian land.
He said these practices threatened the Palestinian presence in the territory and undermined prospects for achieving a just and lasting peace.
The initiative seeks to establish a broader framework for coordinated parliamentary engagement, combining diplomatic pressure, legal accountability and international advocacy in support of Palestinian rights.

Exclusive: Russia significantly expands glide-bomb production, research shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:26:17 UTC
22:26:17 KST

Russia is significantly expanding its glide-bomb production, indicating that Moscow has no plans to scale back its war against Ukraine, a new report by Kyiv-based think tank Center for Defense Reforms exclusively shared with the Kyiv Independent reveals.
"Given the role of guided aerial bombs in destroying defensive positions, isolating battlefields and facilitating ground advances, this provides a basis for sustaining high-intensity offensive operations over an extended period," the report concludes.
The report reveals that in 2025, the centralized procurement entity TRV-Engineering JSC obtained nearly 278,000 servo drives, used to control the flight surfaces of glide bombs — enough to manufacture 139,000 of the deadly munitions. The report identifies the key Russian supplier of servo drives, CED Sail LLC, which is currently not subject to any Western sanctions, and suggests this entity should be a "priority target" for sanctions designation.
"Russia is building the military-industrial capacity to continue waging wars even after the war in Ukraine ends. These are not the actions of a country preparing for lasting peace," Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Center for Defense Reforms and former chief adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, told the Kyiv Independent.
The report also identifies a network of interconnected Russian companies which are responsible for importing key components and raw materials essential for the production of UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits.
Russia converts older, unguided bombs into precision-guided weapons with these guidance kits, significantly increasing their range and accuracy. The increase in range allows Russian fighter-bomber aircraft to remain within Russian territory, out of range of Ukrainian air defenses, as they deploy their deadly payloads.
As with many other Russian munitions, both UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits are heavily reliant on foreign components for their manufacture.
Ukrainian military intelligence has repeatedly identified a range of foreign components in Russian glide bombs, including parts from the U.S., Japan, China, Switzerland, and Taiwan, among others.
The report also reveals the majority of entities and individuals involved in the production of Russia's glide bombs are currently unsanctioned, despite the munitions being a key part of the Kremlin's offensive airborne arsenal.
Out of 20 corporate entities involved in the manufacture of Russian glide bombs, only eight are subject to some level of Western sanctions or export restrictions. The "uneven sanctions coverage," the report assesses, allows Russia to continue to "procure necessary components without significant restrictions."
Four Chinese companies are identified as being critical to the supply chain, with some, such as Shenzhen Fire Power Control Technology Limited, not hiding the explicitly military application of their products. Only one of the four Chinese companies is subject to U.S. export restrictions, and none are sanctioned by the U.K. or the EU.
"Despite its repeated declarations of readiness for peace, Russia continues to dramatically expand the production of offensive weapons, particularly guided aerial bombs," Danylyuk said.
Russia has heavily relied on glide bombs to support its slow advance in the east of Ukraine, targeting Ukrainian fighting positions, fortifications, and buildings. Russian forces have also increasingly used the munitions to target Ukrainian cities that have come within range of the bombs.
Earlier this month, five Russian glide bombs struck the city of Zaporizhzhia, killing 20 people, including three children, and injuring 32 others.
Ukraine has attempted to counter Russia's glide bombs using electronic warfare to disrupt their guidance systems, as well as targeting the Su-34 fighter-bomber aircraft used to deploy them. Earlier in October, Ukraine struck six Russian Sukhoi Su-34M fighter-bombers in a "Neptune" cruise missile strike on a Russian airfield in Borisoglebsk, Voronezh Oblast, destroying at least four and likely heavily damaging two more.

Healey is expected to shield low-income pensioners from income tax – but how will it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:25:03 UTC
22:25:03 KST

A scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard allowance. Photograph: Geoff Smith/Alamy
A scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard allowance. Photograph: Geoff Smith/Alamy
Healey is expected to shield low-income pensioners from income tax – but how will it work?
Retirees will get a personal allowance aligned with the new state pension, but experts say it could get complicated
Retirees in the UK on low incomes are expected to be given a new personal allowance so that they do not have to hand any of their state pension to HMRC.
The full details are due to be revealed by the chancellor, John Healey, in Wednesday’s budget, but here is what we know so far.
New state pension is set to overtake personal allowance
The state pension rises each April. There are two different pensions, the basic state pension which is received by older retirees and the new state pension which is received by anyone who has retired since 6 April 2016.
How much the new state pension goes up by is determined by the triple lock, which promises that it will be the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%.
This year, the highest of the three has been wage growth, which for the relevant month was 3.9%. As a result, from April 2027 the full state pension will be worth £13,036 a year. Thanks to a freeze in the personal allowance that applies to everyone, the amount anyone can earn before paying tax has remained at £12,570 since 2021.
This year, the full new state pension was just under that figure, at £12,547.
Lots of pensioners have money from private and workplace pensions which already puts them over the personal allowance, and 9.6 million are already taxpayers.
As the prospect of the state pension overtaking the allowance loomed last year, the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, promised that anyone deriving all of their income from the state pension would not be taxed. This was confirmed this year.
It had been suggested that this could be done by writing off tax bills below £100, as next year’s numbers would mean people owing about £90 each if they were on only the state pension. However, it is reported that instead pensioners will have a higher personal allowance.
New allowance for some
A report in the Times suggests Healey will set a personal allowance for low-income pensioners that is exactly aligned with the full new state pension. This means that in the 2027-28 tax year it will be £13,036, and it will rise in subsequent years in line with the pension increases.
With the regular personal allowance frozen until 2030-31 and the triple lock in place until 2030, that means this special allowance is expected to pull away from the one that most taxpayers will have.
It could get very complicated
The former pensions minister Steve Webb says that this way of lifting the pension out of tax could prove “messy and increasingly expensive”.
We do not know the details, but a scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard £12,570 allowance.
Trying to solve this could mean introducing complicated tapering.
Webb says: “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off. But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow.
“And if the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff-edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing.”
To make things more complicated, it is not clear how pensioners on the old state pension will be given the same protection. Their pension consists of two elements and in some cases people who get only the state pension are already being paid a figure above the personal allowance.
Pensioners’ higher allowance has been scrapped before
Up until the 2013-14 tax year, people aged 65 or older could claim one of two age-related additions to the personal allowance. The year before this was introduced, the personal allowance was £8,105 for under-65s, £10,500 for those aged 65-75, and £10,660 for those aged over 75. The allowance was tapered so pensioners with incomes of just over £30,000 did not get the extra relief.
The larger allowance was supposed to help older people retain money to meet higher heating costs and other expenses associated with ageing.
The change was made by the then chancellor, George Osborne, to make the system simpler: lots of pensioners did not realise they had to claim it, and the tapering was complicated. He froze the existing allowance for pensioners.
He said at the time: “This will protect the existing level of allowance pensioners have while introducing a new single personal allowance for all. It is a major simplification, it saves money, and no pensioner will lose in cash terms.”
The change will benefit only pensioners
Another thing that might make the policy unpopular is that it will give pensioners a benefit that is not shared by low-income workers. Some may argue that it would be fairer to increase the personal allowance for everyone. That would, of course, be much more expensive for the government.

No oil pollution found along Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast after vessel incidents
Monday 26 October 2026 15:00
Monday, 26 October 2026, 15:00
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Water analyses in three areas along the Bulgarian Black Sea coast have detected no petroleum products following vessel-related incidents, according to the results of regular tests conducted along the entire coastline by the Black Sea Basin Directorate. No oil slicks were observed during the inspections, and the water appeared visually clean and clear.
Elevated levels of ammonium nitrogen were detected in the Sozopol area. All other parameters tested at the three sampling sites were within the applicable limits and quality standards.
The Black Sea Basin Directorate said the elevated levels could not be attributed to the vessel-related incidents in the Black Sea. However, water sampling and testing will continue.

An election marked by disillusionment sends a warning to Bulgaria's government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:24:49 UTC
22:24:49 KST

Author
Vesela Krasteva
An election marked by disillusionment sends a warning to Bulgaria's government
Monday 26 October 2026 14:26
Monday, 26 October 2026, 14:26
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
The first round of Bulgaria's presidential election saw record-low voter turnout, both at home and among Bulgarians abroad, surprising even pollsters. Neither of the leading presidential tickets secured an outright victory, setting up a run-off between Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev and Andrey Gyurov/Georgi Kandev on Sunday, 1 November. To win in the first round, a candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes, with turnout exceeding 50%.
With 99.95% of polling station returns counted, Iotova and Valchev had won 34.76% of the vote, against 31.95% for Gyurov and Kandev – a gap of less than three percentage points. But behind these closely matched results lie two very different groups of voters. Iotova and Valchev drew stronger support from older voters, people with lower levels of education and residents of smaller towns and villages. Gyurov and Kandev appealed more strongly to younger, university-educated voters, people living in major cities and Bulgarians abroad.
"Yes, there has been an overall decline in interest and willingness to vote, but that decline has not been evenly spread among supporters of the different political parties," Boryana Dimitrova of Alpha Research told Radio Bulgaria. Alpha Research is one of the two polling agencies working with Bulgarian National Radio on its election coverage.
Boryana Dimitrova
PHOTO BGNES
"After the parliamentary elections in April this year, when we saw strong mobilisation and high turnout, people are now staying away from the polls. And we need to make one thing absolutely clear: the biggest drop in participation has been among voters who supported Progressive Bulgaria," Dimitrova said, referring to the party that won the spring parliamentary elections. "Progressive Bulgaria's candidate, Ms Iotova, received nearly 900,000 fewer votes than the party won in April's parliamentary elections. That is an exceptionally serious drop." 
Some analysts see the result as a personal setback for incumbent President Iliana Iotova. Dimitrova, however, sees it as a warning to those in power.
"A great deal of disappointment has built up over recent months – over finances, the economy, national security and people's personal safety. There have been many developments that have left Bulgarians feeling increasingly insecure, while the expectations raised by Progressive Bulgaria's election victory have not been met."
PHOTO BGNES
"We could see this process unfolding, but its scale turned out to be much greater than expected. Of course, we still have to see what happens in the second round, when different social groups may be mobilised to vote. But whatever happens, the first-round result is a very strong warning to the government that there are serious shortcomings it needs to address."
Bulgarians living abroad could vote at 613 polling stations in 60 countries, but interest was subdued there too.
"About 88,000 votes were cast abroad in the presidential election, down from around 189,000 in April. Even so, turnout abroad was slightly higher than in Bulgaria, where it was disastrously low," Dimitrova said.
"Two things stand out. There was stronger mobilisation in Western Europe and the United States. But this election was different from previous ones, when we often talked about high turnout in Türkiye. This time, only about 7,000 votes were cast there, compared with 27,000–28,000 in previous elections, and sometimes as many as 50,000."
PHOTO BGNES
"In other words, voting patterns in Türkiye mirror what we saw in Bulgaria: the Movement for Rights and Freedoms has effectively boycotted the election. Its voters simply did not turn out.
"It will be extremely interesting to see what happens in the second round. We already know that Gyurov and Kandev won a decisive victory among Bulgarians abroad, taking around 45% of the vote, compared with 22% for Iotova and Valchev – roughly twice as many votes. Kostadinov and Volgin came third, as they did in Bulgaria.
"So, to sum it up in three points: turnout fell, although it remained higher than in Bulgaria; Gyurov and Kandev won a clear victory abroad; and voting among Bulgarians in Türkiye was exceptionally low."
Historical voting patterns suggest that between a third and half of those who backed candidates eliminated in the first round do not return to the polls. That makes it difficult to predict whether turnout will rise in the run-off.
Dimitrova believes a public debate between the two remaining candidates could influence voters' decisions.
"A debate would give people a chance to see what positions the two presidential tickets stand for, what kind of Bulgaria they envisage and what future they are offering the country.
Iliana Iotova and Andrey Gyurov.
PHOTO BGNES
"Despite the low turnout, both tickets have substantial support. They are almost neck and neck. Both have their own views and arguments to put forward, and it's up to voters to decide," Dimitrova said.
"And we should not forget that these are elections about individual candidates, but they are also political elections. A great deal will depend on whether GERB and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms change their positions, because both parties have substantial, disciplined electorates.
"The difference between the two leading candidates is around 37,000 to 40,000 votes. We will see what the final figures show, but that is a very narrow margin. Mobilising voters behind either ticket could increase turnout and, more importantly, determine the final result."
Editor: Elena Karkalanova
This publication was created by: Elizabeth Radkova

“Strasbourg Calling" Why is data on data centres' environmental impact missing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:24:09 UTC
22:24:09 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
“Strasbourg Calling" Why is data on data centres' environmental impact missing?
A conversation between Irina Nedeva and Nico Schmidt, a finalist for the European Parliament’s Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize with Investigate Europe
Interview with Nico Schmidt
Monday 26 October 2026 14:21
Monday, 26 October 2026, 14:21
Nico Schmidt
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
An investigative report has revealed how major technology companies have helped write secrecy into European Union legislation to conceal the environmental impact of data centres. German investigative journalist Nico Schmidt of Investigate Europe spent months examining the “black box” behind Europe’s technology boom and the so-called cloud services industry. The report was among the ten finalists for the 2026 Daphne Caruana Prize for Journalism awarded by the European Parliament.
“We wanted to find out why the European Union is hiding the environmental footprint of data centres because they collect them in a database", Nico Schmidt said in an interview for the BNR. "We then looked into the law that actually makes all of that information secret. We looked at the final text and looked at the first proposal and we found out that in the first proposal the secrecy was missing. So we asked ourselves a simple question - where did that come from?
So we looked at all the submissions that the Commission received from various people, companies, associations and we found that they got a letter from Microsoft and Digital Europe, a lobby organization representing Amazon, Google and other tech companies. We read the letter carefully and the final law carefully and we saw that the same law was proposed by these two actors, saying that all of the information submitted by data center operations should be secret. Our conclusion is that the European Commission must have almost copy-pased this information into the final law.
When we put both texts side by side, on the one side the text by Microsoft and Digital Europe and on the other one - the final law, and we found that they were the same almost word for word. Of course, coincidences do happen in life, but then the question woud be - what are the chances?
We spoke with people from the European Commission off the record. They said that they feared that the big tech companies would not submit any data on the environmental impact of data centeres if this was not inaccessible for the public. The question is - should the European Commission be powerful enough to force these companies to submit this information, even if afterwards normal people or journalists can see the environmental impact of data centers.”
There is a lack of precise data on the environmental impact of these facilities, Schmidt said in BNR's special programme "Strasbourg Calling":
“We don't know how much water is actually being consumed by data centers, we don't know how much electricty they are actually consuming and how much greenhouse gas emissions are connected to this. Another important question is at what capacity are these data centers actually running, are all these data centres really running at 100% capacity? If they are not, this would put into question all the plans to build new data centers. For example, we have information about some data centres in France showing that they actually consume less electricity than they could at full capacity. There are indications that data centers are not running at full capacity but we don't have ultimate proof yet.”
Bulgaria has already expressed its intention to attract investment in data centers. Schmidt advised the country to look at Ireland, where the environmental consequences of data centres are particularly visible:
“Bulgaria is not alone in pursuing these plans. Many countries now are interested in attracting investment connected to data centres as a sign of progress and innovation. The consequences are most apparent today in Ireland. It has the largest number of data centres currently existing compared to other consumers of electricity. This is partly for historical reasons, as many of the major technology companies have their European headquarters there. What happens in Ireland to power their data centres, data center operators now are also using natural gas as a fuel, which runs counter to the European Union’s goal of a climate-neutral Europe.”
Nico Schmidt and Irina Nedea at the Radio Studio at the European Parliament in Strasbourg (21 October 2026)
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
The investigation by the Investigate Europe consortium prompted a response, but the journalist is not optimistic about the eventual outcome:
“After the publication of our investigation, 35 Members of the European Parliament sent a letter to the European Commission calling for the confidentiality clause to be removed. The director of the European Environment Agency also stated that the clause was unacceptable. But it has not been removed.
The issue is not just the influence of major technology companies. It is also about the response of the US government, because whenever the European Union has tried to introduce laws that in some way restrict the tech giants, the United States has intervened with tariffs and retaliatory measures. So, at the moment, I am not very hopeful that real change will happen."
Is “green AI” possible when the EU wants both to lead in artificial intelligence and to be a global leader in sustainability?
“On the one hand, there is the position of the major US technology companies, which insist on keeping this data confidential. On the other hand, European data centre operators want the opposite: they want information about their environmental footprint to be publicly available because they believe they are competitive and could operate more sustainably. But could we have entirely green data centres, or make them greener than they are today? Yes, I believe that is possible", says Nico Schmidt.
A broad consortium of respected European media organisations conducted the investigation, and the story was published on the same day by all media partners including Die Zeit, El País, EU Observer, the Guardian, the Journal, Le Monde, Publico and Tech Policy Press, the journalist explained:
“It required a great deal of coordination and organisation, but for all of us this is an extremely important issue that needs urgent attention. The first step is to expose the secrecy surrounding this data. The second is to continue investigating and producing new reports.”
Read the full report How Big Tech wrote secrecy into EU law to hide data centres’ environmental toll.
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with Nico Schmidt was aired on BNR's Horizon channel and can be heard HERE.

The IDF announced on Monday that it had discovered a concealed underground shaft near the home of one of the Hamas terrorists who killed two IDF soldiers in an attack on Friday.
According to the IDF, the shaft was approximately 15 meters deep and relatively narrow. It was found near the terrorist’s home in the Hebron area of the West Bank.
While the discovery was not unprecedented, underground shafts are extremely rare in the West Bank. Underground warfare has been more commonly associated with Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, where tunnels have played a significant role in military operations, than with Hamas in the West Bank, where the IDF maintains greater control and surveillance.
The discovery came after the IDF searched approximately 500 Palestinian homes and other locations throughout the West Bank, particularly in the Hebron area, as part of its efforts following Friday’s attack.
The IDF also said it had found an unidentified electronic device inside the shaft. The device was transferred to investigators for examination.
Two troops killed after terrorists with machine gun open fire in West Bank
Staff Sergeant Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, from Ashkelon, and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, from Hod Hasharon, were named on Friday as the two soldiers killed in the attack.
Roytman was a squad commander, while Svilem was a combat soldier in the Ari Battalion (775) of the Search and Rescue Brigade, according to the IDF.
Both soldiers were killed in combat at the Judea Junction when two terrorists traveling in a car, armed with an M4 machine gun and a pistol, opened fire on soldiers at the scene.

Hundreds of Hebron families displaced by IDF operations, uncertain when they can return - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:23:11 UTC
22:23:11 KST

The IDF did not give families ample time to pack before they were made to evacuate their homes and has not offered any assurances on whether and when they will be allowed to return, Riyad Khamis, the spokesperson for Hebron’s official Support and Relief Committee, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
The IDF has established new checkpoints and evacuated parts of Hebron following a terrorist attack carried out on Friday by Ahmed and Hamouda al-Jabar, two Palestinians from the Ein Deir Bahha neighborhood, which killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded several others.
Sharing data collected on Monday from Ein Deir Bahha, Al-Jilda, Khillet Al-Magharbeh, Farsh al-Hawa, and surrounding areas, Khamis said 407 households, comprising 2,649 people, were affected by the military action.
The figure included 1,109 people under the age of 18, of whom 180 were under the age of two; 218 elderly people; 115 pregnant or postpartum women; 28 people with disabilities; and 162 living with chronic illnesses.
Milena Ansari, the director of the Occupied Palestinian Territory Department at Physicians for Human Rights Israel, told the Post on Sunday that the disruption of routine for the chronically sick and/or disabled might create an emergency.
“People with chronic conditions like diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, or cancer depend on regular treatment and medication. These arbitrary closures interrupt that care. Displacement also separates people from their medications, doctors, and medical records,” Ansari warned.
“A condition that could be managed with routine care can quickly become an emergency, which then runs into the same blocked roads, closures, and restrictions on movement. Of course, winter makes every one of these risks even worse,” she added.
Majority of displaced Palestinians have found alternative accommodation
Though the large majority of the displaced Palestinians have found alternative accommodation, with relatives or by renting other homes, Khamis said that 168 households had no available housing options.
“Some families found themselves without safe accommodation or a suitable alternative, and some were forced to spend the night outdoors,” he said.
“When we say that 185 families have no safe place to stay, we are describing a difficult humanitarian reality. These families have no alternative accommodation beyond staying with relatives, resulting in overcrowded and unsuitable living conditions. Some are also struggling to obtain the most basic necessities of life.”
Asserting the need for humanitarian intervention, he told the Post that, based on data collected from the displaced so far, 231 households needed food supplies, 129 needed medicines, 107 needed baby formula and diapers, and 126 needed shelter.
Others have reportedly requested aid with clothing, mattresses, blankets, and psychological support.
Displaced families given inadequate time to prepare for their evacuation
Khamis said that the displaced families said they were not given enough time by the IDF to prepare to leave their homes and that the evacuations “took place under difficult, high-pressure conditions … without sufficient clarity about how long the evacuation would last or when families would be allowed to return to their homes.”
“There was no direct communication with the military, except through notices and demands to leave. These did not provide clear and sufficient information about the duration of the operation, the nature of the measures being taken, or the guarantees concerning residents’ return to their homes,” he said.
Adding to this, Khamis said that they had received no information to suggest Israeli authorities established any arrangements to help facilitate the evacuation of elderly, disabled, or sick Palestinians, which “presented a significant humanitarian challenge, particularly because some families include people who require medical care and ongoing assistance.”
In a statement to The Post, the IDF said that the operation, which came in response to Friday’s terror attack, has seen a cordon imposed where the military is operating and that civilians were allowed to voluntarily leave the area as a way to mitigate potential harm.
“Their departure was facilitated through designated, safe corridors that had been established in advance and communicated to the civilian population,” the military insisted. “Consequently, residents were unable to return to the area while the operation was underway.
“Once military activity in the area concludes, and in accordance with the law, residents will be permitted to return to their homes immediately.”
The military also emphasized that the area of operations is affiliated with Hamas and has a “direct link” to the terrorists responsible for the murder of two soldiers on Friday.

Duchess Meghan confronted dad over child sexual abuse allegations with 2025 letter delivered to hospital bed
London — Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, confronted her estranged father last year about child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, about six years after she was first made aware of the claims, according to new information from CBS News' British partner BBC News.
Last week, police in the Philippines confirmed they were investigating Thomas Markle Sr. over his alleged possession of a large stash of child sexual abuse photos and videos, which were handed in to authorities by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Meghan, who is married to Britain's Prince Harry, said in a statement last week that she was "deeply distressed" by word of the investigation into her father, and that she had first learned of allegations against him in 2018, when London's Metropolitan Police shared a letter with her laying out related claims. She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.
Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025. According to the BBC, in that letter the duchess wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet Meghan and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Thomas Markle Sr., 82, was quoted by the Mail in a Sunday article as saying he didn't remember what was written in the letter from his daughter, but "if Meghan says that's what she wrote, then she's probably right."
The Mail quoted her father on Friday as saying he had "never downloaded anything like that in my life," and dismissing the allegations against him as "sick lies." On Sunday, the tabloid ran a new article quoting him as saying he had paid for sex in the Philippines, but reiterating his denial of possessing child sexual abuse materials and insisting he never had sex with anyone under the age of 18.
He vowed to cooperate with authorities, according to the Daily Mail.
Another British tabloid, The Sun, reported over the weekend that the Metropolitan Police were made aware in 2019 of a number of claims against Markle, including alleged sexual abuse of a child, and that they had passed them on to the Duchess of Sussex's office at that time.
In a statement last week, the duchess said it was because of these allegations that she had kept her family distanced from her father.
"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said in her Friday statement.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.
"We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018," a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said last week. "We are undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."
It is understood that the London police are not currently investigating Thomas Markle.
It is unclear what allegations were in the letter about her father that Meghan says police shared with her in 2018, or what allegations she was referring to when she wrote to him last year.
CBS News contributor Roya Nikkhah, royal editor for the Sunday Times newspaper, told CBS News on Monday that the revelations of the last week were very likely to garner new public sympathy for the duchess.
"I don't think the wider public can not have sympathy for Meghan going through this," she said. "It's an ordeal, an extraordinary thing to learn about your own father."
"I think a lot of the feeling by the British public around what has happened the last few years has been more about the way Harry and Meghan left the royal family and what we have heard from them since, which is completely separate to this — their grievances against the royal family, their feelings of not feeling comfortable here," said Nikkhah. "But they are now back, and they are back, we understand, for a considerable period of time. I'm sure the British public and wider public will have sympathy for what's happened regarding her father. I don't know whether this will change people's views about what's been said and done the last six or seven years since they've left."

Five things to know about Israel’s election and what it means for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:20:01 UTC
22:20:01 KST

Israelis head to the polls on October 27 in the country’s first general election since October 7, 2023.
The vote comes after nearly three years of Israel launching a genocidal war on Gaza, mounting international condemnation and growing domestic anger over security failures under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership.
Here are five things to know about the election and what the result could mean for Palestinians.
What do the polls show?
Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies are fighting to retain power, but polls suggest they could struggle to secure a parliamentary majority.
A poll published by Israel’s public broadcaster KAN projected 52 seats for the opposition bloc and 50 for Netanyahu’s allies in the 120-seat Knesset. Neither bloc would reach the 61 seats needed to form a government independently.
The prime minister’s standing has suffered since the October 7 attacks, which exposed major security failures under his government.
Netanyahu is now fighting for political survival while facing an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
But a poor showing for Likud would not automatically end Netanyahu’s premiership. If his rivals cannot assemble a governing majority, he could remain in power.
Who are Netanyahu’s main rivals?
The main challengers include Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the centrist Yashar party, and former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who heads the Together alliance with former premier Yair Lapid.
Former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, are also key opposition figures.
Eisenkot has sought to position himself as a security-focused alternative to Netanyahu, despite his own hard-line record and role in the government’s war cabinet during Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Bennett, a former settler leader and right-wing nationalist, previously served as Netanyahu’s aide and has opposed Palestinian statehood while supporting Israel’s illegal settlement enterprise in the occupied West Bank.
Neither offers a break with the policies underpinning Israel’s oppression of Palestinians.
How do Israeli elections work?
Israel uses a proportional representation system. Voters choose a political party rather than directly electing a prime minister, and seats are allocated broadly in proportion to each party’s share of the national vote.
A party must win at least 3.25 percent of the vote to enter parliament.
The leader who can assemble a governing majority then has the opportunity to become prime minister.
This gives smaller parties considerable influence. A party with only a handful of seats can determine who governs and what policies the government pursues.
Why do coalitions matter?
No single party has ever won a majority in Israel’s parliament.
Governments therefore depend on alliances between parties with different political, religious and economic priorities.
Netanyahu’s bloc relies on far-right parties led by Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, along with the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism.
Both Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expelling Palestinians from Gaza and resettling the territory with Israelis.
Smotrich has also spearheaded the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and openly opposed Palestinian statehood.
Although neither is currently leading a rival bid for prime minister, both could retain considerable influence in a future government, including one led by another right-wing politician.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Palestinian-led Ra’am party, could also prove pivotal. Abbas has signalled he would consider joining an opposition-led government, as his party did under Bennett in 2021.
However, most opposition leaders have ruled out a coalition with Arab-led parties.
What could the result mean for Palestinians?
For Palestinians, the election offers little prospect of a break with Israel’s occupation, illegal settlement expansion and denial of their right to self-determination.
Netanyahu’s government has overseen the destruction of Gaza and the mass killing of Palestinians, while far-right ministers have openly called for their expulsion.
Yet his main rivals have also opposed Palestinian statehood, backed illegal settlements and supported policies that threaten Palestinians with further displacement and ethnic cleansing.
Palestinians in Gaza and those living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, cannot vote in an election that will help determine their future.

The return of student politics: Why campus leaders still matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:19:30 UTC
22:19:30 KST

NEW DELHI: From protests over examination irregularities and electoral rolls to debates over caste, education and government policies, students have returned to the streets, raising questions that extend far beyond university campuses. The recent demonstrations in Delhi have once again put student organisations and their leaders in the national spotlight.In October, student activists joined demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The protests brought together student groups, political activists and Opposition leaders, turning a dispute over electoral processes into a wider political confrontation.Among those who gained attention was Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students' Association (AISA). Images of Bora being pursued by police in Connaught Place and her subsequent appearance alongside Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during the October 12 march towards the Supreme Court showed how quickly campus activists could move into the national political conversation.But Bora is only one example of a much older phenomenon. Across political ideologies, student organisations have helped mobilise protests, shaped political debates and produced leaders who later entered Parliament and state assemblies.
The question is whether today's student movements can have a similar impact, and how effectively they can represent students while navigating national party politics.
When student protests became political movements
Student politics in India has a history stretching back to the freedom struggle. Established in 1936, the All India Students' Federation (AISF) was among the earliest nationwide student organisations. After Independence, campuses remained important spaces for political mobilisation.One of the most significant examples came during the Bihar student movement of the 1970s. Protests against corruption, inflation and misgovernance expanded under Jayaprakash Narayan into a mass political movement challenging the Congress government.The movement and the Emergency of 1975 shaped a generation of political leaders. Lalu Prasad Yadav, Nitish Kumar, Sushil Kumar Modi and Ravi Shankar Prasad were among those whose early political careers were influenced by the student activism of that period.Student politics also opened doors for leaders from different political backgrounds. Former Union minister Arun Jaitley and Congress leader Ajay Maken served as Delhi University Students' Union (DUSU) presidents. Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta began her political journey through the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP).Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), meanwhile, produced Left leaders such as Sitaram Yechury and Prakash Karat. Kanhaiya Kumar, who gained national attention during the 2016 JNU controversy, later joined the Congress.These examples show that student politics has not been limited to one party or ideology. For many leaders, campuses provided their first experience of elections, public speaking, organisation and political debate.
DUSU and JNU: Where political careers begin
Delhi University and JNU remain important centres of student politics, although their political cultures differ.At Delhi University, elections are largely contested between the RSS-affiliated ABVP and the Congress-backed National Students' Union of India (NSUI).In the 2026 DUSU elections, ABVP won three of the four central panel posts, with Yash Dabas elected president, Riya Chhawdi secretary and Lakshya Raj Singh joint secretary. Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen, a former NSUI member, won the vice-president's post.The results reflected the continuing influence of national political organisations in campus elections, as well as the ability of independent candidates to challenge them.JNU has traditionally been a stronghold of Left student groups, including AISA and the Students' Federation of India (SFI), although ABVP has also made electoral gains.In 2025, ABVP won the JNUSU joint secretary post and secured 24 of 46 councillor positions in one election. Later that year, the Left Unity alliance swept the central panel, with Aditi Mishra becoming president.Such elections give students experience in political mobilisation, but they also raise questions about whether national party rivalries overshadow concerns about fees, hostels, scholarships and campus infrastructure.
From Mandal to Assam: When campuses shaped policy
Some student movements have influenced debates well beyond university politics.The implementation of the Mandal Commission's recommendation for 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in central government jobs triggered widespread protests in 1990. The anti-Mandal movement exposed deep divisions over reservation, merit and social justice.In 2016, the death of University of Hyderabad research scholar Rohith Vemula led to nationwide protests over caste discrimination and institutional accountability.Student organisations also played important roles in regional movements.In Assam, the All Assam Students' Union (AASU) led the six-year agitation against alleged illegal immigration that ended with the Assam Accord in 1985. Former AASU leader Prafulla Kumar Mahanta subsequently became chief minister.In Tamil Nadu, student participation in the anti-Hindi agitations of the 1960s helped strengthen the movement against the Congress establishment and brought language politics to the centre of the state's political debate.Students at Osmania University were also active during the movement for a separate Telangana, particularly between 2009 and 2014.More recently, students from Jamia Millia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University participated in protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act in 2019. At Jadavpur University, the Hokkolorob movement of 2014-15, which followed protests over an alleged molestation case and police action, ended with the resignation of vice-chancellor Abhijit Chakrabarti.The issues and outcomes differed, but these movements demonstrated how student mobilisation could influence public debate, government decisions and political leadership.
What should student politics actually achieve?
Despite its connections with national politics, the primary purpose of student unions remains representation within educational institutions.Dr Ashok Sharma, a former JNU student leader, says universities have a responsibility beyond academic learning."Universities are not merely centres of academic learning; they are also spaces where young people develop political awareness, leadership qualities, democratic values and a sense of social responsibility," he says.According to Sharma, elected student representatives must also focus on the everyday concerns of students."Elected representatives have a mandate to raise issues involving academic policies, fees, scholarships, accommodation, campus infrastructure and administrative decisions," he says.However, the close links between student organisations and national political parties can complicate their responsibilities."Many student groups have ideological or organisational affiliations with national political parties, which is not necessarily undesirable because political engagement is part of democratic life. However, problems arise when the priorities of parent political parties overshadow students' academic, administrative and welfare concerns," Sharma says.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to produce future politicians but to ensure that campus politics continues to serve students.
The limits of campus politics
Concerns over money, violence and political interference have also shaped how student elections are conducted.The Lyngdoh Committee, appointed in 2005, recommended reforms including eligibility requirements and campaign spending limits. Its recommendations, accepted by the Supreme Court in 2006, set a spending ceiling of Rs 5,000 per candidate.Implementation has differed across universities. Allahabad University, for example, moved from direct student union elections to a student council system in 2019. Supporters argue that such arrangements can reduce disruptions, while critics say they weaken direct student representation.Sharma cautions that student politics should not interfere with education."Excessive politicisation, intimidation, vandalism and prolonged disruptions can undermine academic activities and damage institutional credibility," he says.There is also the question of whether visibility on protest platforms translates into sustained political influence. Many student leaders enter mainstream politics, but not all succeed in building careers beyond their campuses.
What recent movements tell us about student power
The growing visibility of student leaders in India's recent protests comes at a time when student activism is also influencing politics elsewhere.In Serbia, protests began after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024 killed 16 people. Students demanded accountability and organised demonstrations that developed into a broader movement against the government.On October 25, 2026, the student-backed Student List won the country's parliamentary election, with preliminary official results giving it over 52% of the vote. The outcome followed nearly two years of demonstrations and showed how sustained student mobilisation could develop into electoral political power.
Serbia's experience is not directly comparable with India's, where student organisations have long-standing links with established political parties. But it shows that movements beginning with specific grievances can develop into wider campaigns.In India, the latest protests have once again brought student leaders into the national conversation. Whether they eventually enter electoral politics or remain activists, their immediate test lies in representing the concerns that brought students together in the first place.Student politics has produced chief ministers, MPs and national leaders. Its larger significance, however, lies in giving young people a platform to question decisions, demand accountability and participate in public life, while ensuring that their educational concerns do not get lost in party politics.
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

Turkish seismic exploration vessel Oruç Reis is in the eastern Mediterranean on July 23, 2020.
Libya’s ratification of a 2019 maritime agreement with Türkiye has sparked a domestic political rift in Greece, with lawmakers from the ruling New Democracy party describing the development as a foreign policy failure and drawing criticism from Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ office, Greek newspaper Kathimerini reported.
Libya’s House of Representatives unanimously approved the maritime boundary agreement with Türkiye on Oct. 20, reversing its previous rejection of the deal and a decision to sever political ties with Ankara, according to a statement from the Libyan parliament.
The agreement has long been a source of regional tensions, with Greece, Egypt and Greek Cyprus opposing it on the grounds that it conflicts with their maritime claims in the eastern Mediterranean, where competing territorial claims are closely linked to energy exploration rights.
Ruling New Democracy lawmakers Dimitris Kalogeropoulos said Greece had “swallowed the bitter pill,” while another MP Dimitris Keridis described the development as a “political defeat.”
The newspaper argued that Keridis’ remarks had caused greater concern at the prime minister’s office than Kalogeropoulos’ comments.
“Keridis’ statements caused concern not only because he is a professor of international relations, but also because he serves as New Democracy’s parliamentary spokesperson. The prime minister’s office would have preferred him to be more cautious in his remarks,” the report said.
The Greek opposition also described the development as a failure of the government’s foreign policy, adding to domestic political criticism over the agreement’s approval.
Greece and Egypt have agreed in principle to launch negotiations on extending their exclusive economic zone (EEZ) agreement eastward.
