Italy's Matera uses art, culture to bridge Mediterranean divides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:16:38 UTC
22:16:38 KST

Italy's Matera uses art, culture to bridge Mediterranean divides
As Mediterranean Capital of Culture and Dialogue 2026, Italy’s southern city of Matera uses exhibitions, music and artistic residencies to foster dialogue across region marked by conflict and division
Giada Zampano
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
MATERA, Italy
Artists from several Mediterranean countries explore shared histories, migration and cultural identities through creative projects
Organizers say cultural diplomacy can help overcome differences, challenge preconceptions and build understanding where conventional diplomacy struggles
There is no sea in sight from Matera’s ancient cave dwellings. From the Sassi, the southern Italian city looks out over a landscape of pale rock, scrub and ravines, far from the Mediterranean coast.
Yet the sea is everywhere in Matera this year, evoked through art, music, ancient languages and centuries of migration as the city serves as Mediterranean Capital of Culture and Dialogue 2026.
Behind the exhibitions, concerts and artistic residencies lies an ambitious proposition: that culture can open channels of communication across a Mediterranean increasingly associated with war, migration and political division.
A ‘vast liquid continent’
“The Mediterranean is, as I like to call it, a vast liquid continent that carries with it millennia of history and culture,” said Rita Orlando, general director of the Matera Basilicata 2019 Foundation.
For Orlando, the initiative is an exercise in cultural diplomacy, grounded in the belief that encounters among artists, musicians and communities can foster understanding where conventional diplomacy struggles.
“Cultural diplomacy that brings people together can truly be the system, the tool, to facilitate understanding between peoples and thus contribute to a world of peace,” she said.
The idea runs through the year’s cultural program.
In Michelangelo Pistoletto’s “Love Difference,” installed in Matera’s rock-hewn Complesso Rupestre Madonna delle Virtu e San Nicola dei Greci, a mirrored table takes the shape of the Mediterranean.
Chairs representing the cultures surrounding the sea are arranged around it, transforming a familiar geopolitical map into a shared space for encounter.
A language of encounter
The idea of finding a common space while preserving differences also emerges through language.
Musician and composer Stefano Saletti’s residency revisits Sabir, the lingua franca once spoken in Mediterranean ports, drawing on elements of Italian, French, Spanish, Arabic and regional dialects.
“It was the language of possible encounter within the Mediterranean,” Saletti said, describing a project that combines music with a dramaturgical text about Matera and its history.
The work has brought together local artists, actors and other residents, assembling what Saletti called “the various ingredients of the Mediterranean.”
Another project traces how migration carried those ingredients into southern Italy centuries ago.
Driant Zeneli, an Albanian visual artist and film director working in Matera, has been researching traditional songs preserved by the Arbereshe communities of Basilicata, whose ancestors arrived from across the Adriatic centuries ago.
One polyphonic song from San Costantino Albanese centers on women, wheat and the changing seasons.
It is being reinterpreted through a video installation that explores how migration carries memory and culture across generations, connecting communities on opposite shores long after the original journey.
Imagining a shared Mediterranean
The interplay of place, memory and history also shapes “The Sea Is Closer Than You See,” a citywide exhibition that opened on Oct. 3 and runs through Dec. 8 across four venues in Matera.
Its premise suits a Mediterranean capital far from the coast: proximity to the sea is not a prerequisite for belonging to its cultural world.
Rather than presenting the region as a single, uniform culture, the exhibition explores connections forged through movement, memory and shared practices.
At MUSMA, Matera’s Museum of Contemporary Sculpture, Studio Azzurro’s “Il Colore dei gesti. Sinfonia Mediterraneo” draws on the gestures of fishermen, potters, luthiers, weavers and other artisans to evoke a vocabulary of work and knowledge that crosses cultural boundaries.
Another work, TEMET, emerged from research in Algeria’s Tassili n’Ajjer.
Combining photography and technology with the knowledge of Tuareg communities, it explores prehistoric rock art and histories of migration, trade and cultural exchange. The Mediterranean imagined in Matera thus extends beyond the shoreline toward the Sahara.
The same vision informs Mimmo Jodice’s “Mediterraneo,” an exhibition bringing together photographs from Italy, Greece, Türkiye, Tunisia and Jordan.
Rather than presenting the sea as a geopolitical boundary between nations, Jodice depicts it as a shared cultural space.
Images from different shores form what the exhibition describes as a “cartography of memory,” in which distinct places become part of a common Mediterranean civilization.
Music across the sea
Music offers another meeting point.
At the “Suoni Mediterranei” concert on Oct. 2, musicians from Italy and Morocco brought Italian strings together with Arab-Andalusian musical traditions. The performance formed part of a collaboration between Matera and Tetouan, Morocco, its partner Mediterranean capital this year.
Yet the Mediterranean portrayed in Matera is not an idealized sea stripped of contemporary crises.
Lebanese artist and illustrator Karen Keyrouz, who is in Matera for an artistic residency, said the Mediterranean repeatedly surfaces in her work through images of water and the marine environment, often in connection with cities facing catastrophe.
“The Mediterranean is always in my work,” Keyrouz said.
Culture amid conflict
Orlando said cultural diplomacy does not mean being naive about the conflicts surrounding the Mediterranean, a region often viewed primarily through the lenses of war, desperation, illicit trafficking and migration.
“Rather than viewing differences as barriers, it means stripping away preconceptions, listening, being willing to understand those differences,” she said.
Centuries ago, Mediterranean communities found a practical way to navigate linguistic differences in Sabir, borrowing words from different languages to communicate across boundaries.
Matera’s experiment in 2026 explores whether culture can offer a language of encounter in a region where conflict and division so often dominate the conversation.

====================================================================================================

Israel's West Bank closures are about revenge and expulsion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:15:15 UTC
22:15:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's 942 barriers are reshaping Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank
Before leaving home for work or travelling to a university in another town, Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are now used to checking their phones for road updates.
Telegram groups dedicated to traffic throughout the occupied West Bank have become part of daily life, with Palestinian residents sharing information about open and closed checkpoints, where traffic congestion and what alternative routes exist.
The status of a single checkpoint can change several times within minutes, as Israeli closures increasingly sever roads between West Bank cities and villages—a trend which has escalated since Israel launched its war on Gaza on 7 October 2023.
The Israeli military's announcement that it would seal off all land crossings into the occupied West Bank on Tuesday 27 October, the day of Israel's elections, has once again drawn attention to Israel's restrictions over Palestinian movement.
Israel has long imposed such measures during religious holidays, special occasions and elections. While these used to focus more on closing crossings between the occupied West Bank and Israel within its 1967 borders, closures within the occupied West Bank itself have expanded significantly since October 2023.
Linking West Bank settlements
Statistics released by the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission on 25 September reveal the scale of the shutdown. There are now 942 checkpoints, closure points, and physical barriers across the occupied West Bank—comprising 824 permanent checkpoints and closure points, alongside 118 linear obstacles (such as earth mounds, trenches, and road blocks) that span approximately 107.7 km.
Hebron governorate tops the list with 221 permanent checkpoints and roadblocks, followed by Ramallah and al-Bireh with 160, Nablus with 120, Bethlehem with 78 and occupied Jerusalem with 62.
The commission also documented the installation of 13 additional gates and fixed checkpoints in the two months preceding its report, including 10 iron gates in Jenin governorate.
These installations enable the Israeli army to control movement between Palestinian communities, as closing a single gate can block access to a town or village, forcing residents to take alternative routes that considerably lengthen their journeys.
The commission also documented settlers installing iron gates on Palestinian roads, including two near Kafr Ni'ma and Umm Safa in Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.
Dr. Ibrahim Rabaia, a political science professor at Birzeit University, told The New Arab that Israel has spent decades developing a complex, multilayered system to control Palestinian movement. This extended from closing the crossings linking the West Bank to the territories occupied in 1948, affecting people and goods, to restricting travel between cities and towns within the occupied territories.
Israel tightens these measures during elections, holidays and other occasions, or on security grounds, Rabaia said, adding that the restrictions also served settlement projects which themselves required limiting Palestinian movement.
He described the measures accompanying the current Israeli elections as neither new nor exceptional. However, they coincide with an Israeli military campaign in Hebron and other parts of the West Bank, alongside escalating settler attacks.
Israel has made significant progress in fragmenting the occupied West Bank into separate Palestinian enclaves through complex geographical, security and administrative arrangements, while consolidating the territorial continuity and communication networks between Israeli settlements, Rabaia said.
He argued that Israel was exploiting international, regional and domestic circumstances to advance this project.
The priority given to settler movement has been reflected in statements by Israeli officials. In August 2023, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said his right, and that of his wife and children, to travel on West Bank roads was more important than Palestinians' freedom of movement, citing security concerns.
Following the outbreak of the Gaza war, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for buffer zones around settlements and roads used by settlers, barring Palestinians from entering them even to harvest olives.
The closures also carry mounting economic costs. A March 2025 study by the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute (MAS), examining the northern and central West Bank, estimated that delays at checkpoints cost Palestinians approximately 191,000 working hours daily.
The resulting losses amounted to around $764,600 a day, or $16.8 million a month, in addition to approximately $6 million annually in extra fuel costs.
These losses coincide with rising unemployment. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics recorded a West Bank unemployment rate of 27.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 284,000 people unemployed amid shrinking employment opportunities, declining economic activity and the repercussions of the war.
From restricted movement to displacement
Some Israeli closures are linked to colonial policies intended to tighten control over Palestinian movement, often justified as measures to prevent attacks on Israelis. However, these security arguments alone do not explain the nature of the restrictions, according to Adel Shadid, a specialist in Israeli affairs.
He told The New Arab that the measures are also part of a policy of collective punishment and revenge pursued by far-right settler forces within the Israeli government, including Smotrich, Ben-Gvir, and lawmakers Orit Strock and Avi Maoz.
Shadid pointed to Smotrich's public celebration of the demolition of Palestinian buildings and confiscation of land, as well as Ben-Gvir's statements about punitive measures against Palestinian prisoners.
He argued that the political dimension was paramount, adding that the Israeli government sought to subdue Palestinians into accepting a long-term reality of restrictions and control in line with the ideological project of religious Zionism and Smotrich's "Decisive Plan" for annexing the West Bank, proposed in 2017.
The closures also aim to intensify economic and social pressures, pushing Palestinians to reconsider their political choices and fuelling internal disputes over responsibility for deteriorating living conditions, Shadid added.
Israeli affairs specialist Muawiya Musa, meanwhile, told The New Arab that in his eyes there was no direct link between the closures and the elections. Instead their origins could be traced to a policy that began taking shape during the second intifada in 2000.
Musa distinguished between what he called "Israel 1", representing the traditional Israeli political current, and "Israel 2", represented by the settler right and religious Zionism.
He argued that the former sought to turn closures into de facto borders confining Palestinians to Areas A and B under the Oslo Accords, while the latter openly advocated complete separation and the expulsion of Palestinians from the West Bank altogether.
The two interpretations share the view that Israeli closures extend beyond immediate security concerns, even if analysts differ over their precise objectives. Geographical fragmentation and economic and social pressure, they argue, operate together to consolidate control over Palestinians and restrict their ability to move, work and maintain stable lives.
The policy takes on added significance amid increasingly explicit Israeli calls for displacement. In February, Smotrich announced plans to "encourage migration" from the West Bank and Gaza, linking this to the cancellation of the Oslo Accords and the imposition of Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank.
The strangulation of the occupied West Bank, therefore, is not the result of a temporary security situation or an election season. Rather, it reflects an accumulation of restrictions and settlement policies that have accelerated since the war on Gaza, gradually turning the territory into an increasingly unliveable spaces for Palestinians.
By narrowing the geographical space available to Palestinians and undermining the foundations of their economic and social lives, the expanding network of checkpoints, gates and road restrictions is intensifying pressures on residents' ability to remain in their communities, as the displacement of Palestinians becomes an increasingly explicit component of the Israeli right's political agenda.

ICAO lifts 13-year warning on Syrian airspace, opening door to more flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:14:43 UTC
22:14:43 KST

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has withdrawn a safety warning concerning Syrian airspace that had been in place since 2013, marking a significant step in Syria’s efforts to restore international air connectivity, the country’s civil aviation authority said.
Omar al-Hosari, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, said on Monday that ICAO had confirmed that the earlier warning would no longer serve as a basis for operational decisions concerning Syrian airspace, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
Instead, assessments will rely on updated international aviation safety and security standards, allowing countries, regulators and airlines to reconsider decisions on flights crossing Syrian airspace and services to and from Syrian airports, al-Hosari said.
Airlines can reassess routes, but restrictions remain
The withdrawal could encourage more airlines to consider resuming services to Syria and increase the number of international flights passing through its airspace, al-Hosari said.
However, he cautioned that ICAO’s decision does not automatically remove restrictions imposed by individual countries or aviation regulators.
Syrian authorities will continue technical and diplomatic coordination with ICAO and other international aviation bodies to address those restrictions through internationally recognised safety and security assessments, he added.
The original warning, dated March 22, 2013, concerned the safety of civilian aircraft operating within the Damascus Flight Information Region.
European safety guidance remains in force
Despite ICAO’s move, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) continues to maintain a conflict-zone information bulletin covering Syrian airspace. The bulletin was revised on October 1 and remains valid until November 30, 2026.
The distinction means that airlines and national regulators must still consider applicable guidance and their own risk assessments before changing routes or resuming operations.
Syria reopened its air corridors and resumed operations at Damascus International Airport in April following temporary closures linked to regional tensions.
Damascus seeks wider international connectivity
Al-Hosari said restoring Syria’s role in international air navigation remains a strategic priority, with greater air traffic expected to support economic activity and attract investment in the country’s civil aviation sector.
The withdrawal of ICAO’s longstanding warning provides an opportunity for Syria to pursue closer integration with regional and international aviation networks, although any broader recovery will depend on airlines’ assessments and the removal of remaining operational barriers.

Migros aims for efficiency gains with merger of cooperatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:14:34 UTC
22:14:34 KST

Migros aims for efficiency gains with merger of cooperatives
Migros is set to undergo a major reorganisation. The ten regional cooperatives and the Migros Cooperative Federation (MGB) are to merge to form a single group cooperative. In doing so, the retail group aims to simplify its complex management structures.
The boards of all ten regional cooperatives and the MGB have unanimously approved the proposal, Migros announced on Monday. The 2.3 million cooperative members are due to make a final decision on the matter in a ballot in mid-2027. A two-thirds majority is required in each of the ten regional co-operatives for this to go ahead.
The new group cooperative is to act as the umbrella organisation for the seven business units, which will continue to operate independently. In addition to Migros Supermarket, these include discount food retailer Denner, online retailer Digitec Galaxus and Migros Bank, among others. In future, the supermarket business is to be managed from a single source across Switzerland.
Six regional councils planned
The existing regional management structures are to be largely phased out. Instead, six regional councils are planned, which will represent the regions’ interests and elect delegates to the national delegates’ assembly. According to Migros, the regional roots and the cooperative right to have a say are to be preserved.
More
The history of the Swiss retail giant Migros in pictures
According to a report in the SonntagsZeitung newspaper, the reorganisation could result in the loss of around 3,000 jobs. The potential annual savings are estimated at CHF300-400 million ($363-484 million). In its statement, Migros did not specify any concrete savings targets or the number of jobs affected.
Instead, it promises that there will be no redundancies due to organisational changes in the regional co-operatives until at least mid-2028. The changes will primarily affect administration and management. Where possible, alternative roles within the group will be found for affected staff.
CEOs to step down
The planned merger will also bring about a change in leadership. Migros CEO Mario Irminger and Peter Diethelm, CEO of Migros Supermarkt AG, intend to step down from their roles by the time of the ballot in mid-2027. Both will then be 62 years old.
+ Head of Swiss retail giant Migros says immigration key to industry’s future
Migros stated that they had championed the new structure with complete conviction. Their successors are expected to be able to lead the new organisation from the outset, as it takes several years to establish. The search for their replacements has already begun.
Second major restructuring
Migros has been undergoing a far-reaching restructuring since 2024. Irminger has overseen the largest restructuring in the company’s history to date. Loss-making businesses or those no longer aligned with the core business have been divested.
+ Swiss retailer Migros starts restructuring with 150 job losses
With the sale of specialist retail chains and other businesses such as Melectronics, SportX, Micasa, Hotelplan and Mibelle, Migros will in future focus on the retail, financial services and healthcare sectors. The restructuring resulted in the loss of around 1,500 jobs out of a total of approximately 100,000 jobs.
For decades, the complex cooperative structure has been seen as an obstacle to faster decision-making. As early as the 1990s, an attempt to reduce the number of regional cooperatives – then 12 in all – to three failed. Its competitor, Coop, merged its regional cooperatives as far back as 2001.

The introduction of e-Excise has been postponed again in Ukraine — what is the reason
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:14:18 EET
22:14:18 KST

The introduction of e-Excise has been postponed again in Ukraine — what is the reason
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy signed a law postponing the launch of e-Excise. Electronic traceability of alcohol and tobacco will become mandatory from July 1, 2027.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a law postponing the full launch of the eExcise system. It was officially published in the Holos Ukrainy newspaper, so the mandatory introduction of electronic traceability for alcohol and tobacco products is postponed until 1 July 2027, UNN reports.
Details
On 13 October, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Draft Law No. 15532 "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine and Certain Other Legislative Acts of Ukraine Regarding the Postponement of the Deadlines for Introducing Electronic Traceability of the Circulation of Alcoholic Beverages, Tobacco Products and Liquids Used in Electronic Cigarettes," which provides for postponing the full launch of the eExcise system until 1 July 2027.
On 23 October, the document was signed by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and on Monday, 26 October, the draft law was published in the parliamentary newspaper Holos Ukrainy.
What is the reason
Explaining the postponement of the system's launch until 1 July 2027, the Ministry of Digital Transformation stated that businesses had been given additional time to prepare for the launch of eExcise. "This is a balanced technical decision, given the security challenges of martial law," the Ministry of Digital Transformation emphasized.
The State Tax Service also noted that postponing the deadlines gives producers and importers of excise goods additional time to prepare IT systems, configure cash-register and accounting equipment, and integrate with the state electronic system.
What comes next
The Ministry of Digital Transformation promises to develop, "together with businesses," a "step-by-step plan for implementing the system with clear deadlines for each stage."
As noted by the Ministry of Digital Transformation, registration of economic operators will run from 1 January to 1 April 2027. "But there is no need to wait until 2027—the technical preparations are already underway. The Sandbox is open to companies—a special testing environment where they can connect their own accounting programs in advance, configure points of sale, and test processes without any legal or financial risks," the ministry stated.
The tax authorities listed what is important for businesses:
-  until 1 July 2027, a transitional period will be in effect to complete technical and organizational preparations; 
-  until that date, excise goods will be marked with paper excise tax stamps under the current rules; 
-  until 30 June 2027, the electronic system will operate in test mode; 
-  business entities are required to register in the electronic system as economic operators: by 1 April 2027—those that, as of 1 January 2027, hold licenses for the production and circulation of alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and liquids used in electronic cigarettes; no later than 1 April 2027—those that obtained the relevant licenses between 1 January and 20 March 2027; before commencing this type of activity—those that obtained such licenses from 21 March 2027; 
-  The State Tax Service will continue its awareness-raising efforts, testing of electronic services, and provision of consultations for taxpayers. 
Additional information
In October 2024, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted documents for the operation of the eExcise system, which is intended to help combat the shadow market for alcohol and tobacco. The system will make it possible to verify the legality of products through "Diia" and simplify the process of obtaining excise stamps for businesses.
In December 2025, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine extended the testing period for the eExcise system until 12 October 2026; the system was expected to launch on 1 November.

Anthropic files for US stock market listing valued at more than $1.5tn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:12:59 UTC
22:12:59 KST

Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.
Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.
“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.
A leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEO Dario Amodei founded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.
Anthropic’s audited filings will offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of a potential AI bubble swirl.
The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic has focused on businesses as its primary paying customers, unlike OpenAI, which has courted everyday consumers for ChatGPT. As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.
“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.
The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”
Investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of its business.
The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and spends billions yearly on computing power provided by third parties, according to the filing.
The misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”
Amodei has called for a slowdown of AI’s development, citing existential risk. Anthropic’s stock market listing may elicit a rush of investment in the company and the AI sector more broadly, which could speed up the pace of the industry further.
The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyber-attack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.
Donald Trump’s administration may also be a risk to the company. Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.

Israel expands expulsions in occupied West Bank to cement control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:11:08 UTC
22:11:08 KST

Israel expands expulsions in occupied West Bank to cement control
Israel escalates forced expulsions and infrastructure destruction with the goal of imposing a ‘new reality’, analysts say.
More than 3,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron as the Israeli army escalates a sweeping military operation that human rights experts describe as a calculated effort to permanently displace the Palestinian population.
Israel has imposed a lockdown across the city and detained at least 71 people over the past four days, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.
Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said on Monday a total of 488 families comprising 3,171 people had been displaced across the wider governorate, while Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera that 3,043 of those forced from their homes are from within Hebron city limits alone.
Separately, the Israeli military continues a demolition campaign that has resulted in the destruction of residential buildings, factories and roads, while also blocking roads, raiding homes and assaulting Palestinians.
The crackdown has been in place since Friday, when two soldiers were killed in a shooting near the city. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has justified it by pledging an operation “unseen” since the 1967 war.
It comes amid increased tensions across the occupied West Bank as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before Israel’s general election on Tuesday, in which Netanyahu is seeking re-election.
Forced mass expulsions
According to municipal authorities in Hebron, the majority of the forcibly displaced Palestinians are women, children and elderly individuals.
Israeli soldiers, meanwhile, have systematically converted dozens of homes of the uprooted Palestinian families into military barracks and field interrogation centres.
“The measures taken in the city of Hebron are not of a single type, but rather have surpassed any idea of temporary evacuation or deportation,” said Noman Amr, a professor of contemporary history at al-Quds Open University, Dura branch in Hebron, as he explained the multifaceted nature of the displacement. “Evacuating homes falls into three categories: evacuation for demolition, evacuation for revenge and collective punishment, and evacuation for military uses, where they have turned some homes into military barracks.”
Amr also highlighted the psychological warfare at play. “This aggressive, collective punitive, terrorist, racist behaviour aims to create a state of panic, fear and instability for the Palestinian society,” he said, quoting displaced residents who said they heard soldiers make comments such as, “You will return to your homes on Judgement Day”.
The ultimate goal, Amr added, is “to impose a new reality” that can be summarised “in one sentence: ‘more land, fewer Arabs'”.
The Jenin model
Israeli officials explicitly linked the Hebron operation to previous campaigns in the occupied West Bank. Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced their intention to apply the “Jenin camp model” to Hebron, which involves forced evacuation of residents, inspecting homes, confiscating weapons and bulldozing roads.
Rights groups have compared the current attack on Hebron with the tactics used during the “Iron Wall” operation in early 2025 in the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps, which killed at least 102 people, displaced more than 33,000 and destroyed over half of their residential buildings.
Katz previously said the aggressive tactics in Jenin represented “the first lesson from the method of repeated raids in Gaza”, where Israel’s genocidal three-year war has killed more than 74,000 people and left the vast majority of the territory in ruins.
The resulting destruction left the Jenin camp “nearly uninhabitable”, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
Last month, a UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR) report warned that the Israeli military’s actions at the three camps “appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing”. Displaced Palestinians reported being told by Israeli officers that there would be no more refugee camps and that they should “all go to Jordan”.
Israeli forces killed at least 21 children during the operation, including a 10-year-old boy who was shot while waiting for his father and a two-year-old girl killed while having dinner with her family.
Demolishing infrastructure
Analysts also pointed to the systematic destruction of vital infrastructure during the Hebron operation with the goal of making displacement permanent.
“Targeting the main infrastructure by the occupation army forces is a targeting of the life and stability of the Palestinian human being,” said Amr. He specified that targeting water wells “exceeds their direct material value, but rather relates to existence, stability and continuity”.
Amr also outlined the deep collaboration between the Israeli army and armed settler groups. “Settlers today in Hebron and other places have a militia consisting of more than 150,000 people heavily armed with modern automatic weapons and four-wheel drive vehicles, and they sometimes wear the occupation army uniform,” he said.
“The army closes the place, empties homes, demolishes them, and closes roads … while settlers continue their repeated attacks on the residents, released prisoners, and commercial interests.”
This ground-level violence is paired with administrative land grabs. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC) said on Sunday the Israeli military had established 220 barriers across Hebron, severing Palestinian communities from their lands while maintaining connectivity for illegal settlements. The CRRC noted this is part of a broader network of new outposts designed to expand control over the spaces separating settlements and to besiege Palestinian expansions.
Also on Sunday, the Israeli army said in a statement that it would bar Palestinian workers from entering most areas of the West Bank through Monday and enforce a full closure of crossings into and out of the territory on Tuesday, the day of Israel’s parliamentary election.
Mayor al-Jabari accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the military operation to secure settler votes.
Amr echoed this sentiment. “The Palestinian pays this price as electoral propaganda for the right wing,” he said.
“They do not want Palestinians to remain in their places, but rather they propose a more advanced step, which is that they want to correct the history that allowed Palestinians to stay after the 1967 setback or even after the 1948 Nakba,” he added, using the Arabic word for “catastrophe” to refer to the ethnic cleansing of Palestine nearly 80 years ago.

New business projects decline despite rising foreign investment, UN says at World Investment Forum in Doha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:10:13 UTC
22:10:13 KST

Foreign investment is rising, but fewer new projects are being announced and funding remains concentrated in a few economies. At the World Investment Forum in Doha, officials and investors are discussing how more countries can benefit and create jobs.
Foreign investment is rising even as the number of new projects falls, according to a UN report released during the World Investment Forum in Doha.
The ninth edition of the forum, organised by UN Trade and Development, known as UNCTAD, and hosted by Qatar, runs from 25 to 27 October. Governments, businesses and financial institutions are meeting to discuss how more countries can attract investment and turn it into jobs.
Published on Sunday, UNCTAD’s Global Investment Trends Monitor found that larger transactions were helping push up investment totals, even as the number of new projects and cross-border deals fell.
In developing countries, announcements of new projects linked to sustainable development were more than 25% below 2025 levels. These are preliminary estimates, using data from the first six to nine months of 2026 to estimate a full-year total.
Investment also remains concentrated in relatively few countries.
More than 80% of global foreign direct investment went to just 20 economies last year, according to UNCTAD’s World Investment Report 2026.
What investors look for
Speaking to Euronews at the forum, UNCTAD spokesperson Marcelo Risi said infrastructure, skills and reliable institutions helped explain why some countries attracted more investment than others.
"Investments are not a short-term endeavour [...] so you need to know which rules are there, who’s your partner, really the rules of the game," Risi explained.
Tax incentives were only one part of the calculation, he said. Countries also need the infrastructure and trained workforce to support businesses once they invested.
Mahmoud Mohieldin, the UN special envoy on financing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, said promoting a country’s opportunities was not enough to persuade investors.
"I know that governments in particular are expecting a lot from the rest of the world, but a great deal of work at home is required," Mohieldin told Euronews.
He pointed to obstacles in entering and leaving markets, unpredictable regulations and the need to prepare projects that investors could finance.
The opportunities also differ by country.
Mohieldin cited shipping and logistics in small island states, alongside Africa’s young population and natural resources, as advantages that could help attract investment.
"The business environment is key. It’s not enough to have the potential," he said.
In countries investors consider particularly risky, public institutions can help by sharing some of the potential losses.
Rwodah Al Naimi, director of investment at the Qatar Fund for Development, said the fund uses guarantees to encourage private investment, while setting limits on its commitments to protect its own funds.
It also shares the financing with other institutions, working mainly through international development banks.
"We don’t go alone. It has to be co-financed as well with other entities," Al Naimi told Euronews.
Job creation is one of the fund’s main measures of whether its investments were benefiting people.
"So any type of investment that we deploy, we always make sure that there is a job creation element," she explained.

Algeria approves troop deployment to Niger: what is their mission?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:09:23 UTC
22:09:23 KST

This rare move comes amid strengthened security ties between Algeria and Niamey following the thwarting of an attempted coup in Niger in August.
Algeria has approved sending troops to neighbouring Niger to "protect energy installations", in particular oil projects operated by the state-owned company Sonatrach, marking what will be the country's first foreign deployment of military forces since the 1970s.
The rare measure comes as both countries strengthen security ties months after a thwarted mutiny in Niger, which has seen Algeria gift four military helicopters to Niamey.
The move was approved in a closed extraordinary session of the parliament on Sunday, where 148 of the 174 lawmakers were present in the upper house and voted in favour of the deployment.
The parliament's lower house said it also voted "by an absolute majority" to deploy the military unit in Niger, though it did not provide numbers.
Article 91 of the Algerian constitution stipulates that any deployment of troops abroad must be endorsed by two-thirds of the members of each chamber.
The overseas deployment will be a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
So far, the authorities have not announced the size of the force to be sent or the start date of its mission, while stressing that the deployment will be limited and focused on protecting Algerian investments.
Growing military cooperation
Sunday's vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and the country's army chief Saïd Chengriha.
According to Algerian reports, a military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides during the visit.
Tebboune had paved the way for this step on 3 October, declaring in a televised address that his country was ready to defend Niger. He said, "We will protect Niger whatever it takes," accusing unnamed states of plotting against it.
After providing the helicopters in August, Algeria dispatched four Su-30 fighter jets accompanied by an in-flight refuelling aircraft, to support Nigerien authorities when a coup attempt was foiled in the same month.
Oil and gas projects
Economic interests are a central driver of Algeria’s move, particularly as Sonatrach expands its investments in Niger through its international subsidiary SIPEX, which manages projects in the Kafra oil field in the north of the country, around 85 kilometres from the Algerian border.
The company began drilling one of its wells in the area on 13 August, as part of a project whose oil resources are estimated, according to figures reported by Anadolu Agency, to exceed 2.5 billion barrels, making it one of Sonatrach’s key investments outside Algeria.
Algeria’s interests go beyond the direct oil sector, as Niger forms a strategic corridor for the Trans-Saharan gas pipeline, which will stretch for more than 4,000 kilometres to carry Nigerian gas to Europe via Niger and Algeria.
Algeria started work in June on the section of the pipeline that crosses its territory, and inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant to supply Niamey and surrounding areas with electricity.
Tebboune has linked the military moves to economic interests, referring to agreements signed with Niger in the oil and mining sectors and other fields, and warning of actors seeking to undermine these projects.
A historic shift in Algerian policy
Observers argue that the military support goes beyond protecting oil installations and reflects a broader shift in Algeria’s approach to regional crises, after decades in which the country relied on diplomacy and dialogue and remained wary of military action beyond its borders.
Relations between Algeria and Niger had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali. The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre desert border, have, however, in recent months committed to enhanced economic and security cooperation that includes combatting jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
Since July 2023, Niger has been ruled by a military junta led by General Abdourahamane Tiani, who deposed elected president Mohamed Bazoum, held in custody ever since, while the country continues to grapple with security turmoil and ongoing armed attacks.

Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

Steinmeier in China: A state visit in uncertain times
October 26, 2026
Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.
His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.
The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.
A diplomatic balancing act
The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.
Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.
Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.
Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.
"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.
Chancellor and president both in Asia
Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.
The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.
"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.
Little room for human rights
While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.
In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them:
. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.
Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.
China should assume international responsibility
On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.
Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.
"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.
To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.
The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – Germany's most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.
This article was originally published in German.

Iranian taekwondo athlete Sayna Karimi undergoes ACL surgery

She ultimately lost the third round 15-6, bringing her campaign at the Asian Games to a premature end.
The injury represents a significant setback for the Iranian international, who will now face an extended rehabilitation period before returning to competitive taekwondo.

As Syrian families struggle with missing loved ones, Assad's government figures reemerge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:03:16 UTC
22:03:16 KST

For nearly 15 years, Hussein al-Tawil and his family have waited to learn what happened to Ali Ahmad al-Tawil, a 29-year-old civilian from Jabal al-Zawiya in the Idlib countryside who disappeared in Damascus in late 2011.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Year after year, the family received no answers. They did not know whether Ali was alive or dead. According to his brother Hussein, Ali disappeared at the hands of militias loyal to former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.
When Assad's government collapsed, the family hoped Ali might be among the detainees released from prisons or that newly accessible detention facilities and records might finally reveal his fate. But they found no trace of him. They received neither a death certificate nor any official document explaining what had happened.
Now, as Hussein continues waiting for news of his brother, he watches figures who once supported Assad reappear in public life, with some seeking proximity to Syria's new authorities.
For Hussein, Assad's fall did not end his family's ordeal. Instead, it raised another question: How can Syria pursue national reconciliation while so many families still do not know what happened to their loved ones?
"We had hoped for transitional justice that would hold criminals accountable, and for moral justice that would remove from public life those who supported Assad through the media, arts, politics, and sports," al-Tawil told The Media Line.
He said the renewed public prominence of former government supporters has deepened the anguish of victims' families, particularly those still waiting for information about missing relatives.
His concerns extend beyond the absence of accountability. He fears that networks of influence established under Assad could survive by shifting their allegiance to the new leadership.
In his view, some figures who supported the former government may now be prepared to offer their loyalty to the new authorities in exchange for preserving their economic interests and influence. Without meaningful institutional change, he warned, the same practices that enabled authoritarian rule could reemerge under different leadership.
Al-Tawil's experience reflects a broader debate in Syria over the return of individuals associated with Assad's government to economic, political, and public life, even as victims' families continue demanding information about the disappeared and accountability for past abuses.
Syrian political activist and former opposition figure Jubair al-Sukkari believes Assad's removal has not yet produced the deeper changes many Syrians expected.
Speaking to The Media Line, al-Sukkari criticized the appearance of figures associated with the former government in institutions established during Syria's transition, particularly those involved in transitional justice and preserving the memory of victims.
He cited what he described as the appointment of Futah Saqr, whom he characterized as having a Baathist background and family ties to figures associated with the former government, to a role at the National Commission for Transitional Justice involving the preservation of historical memory and archives.
Al-Sukkari questioned the criteria used to select individuals entrusted with documenting the Syrian uprising and preserving the experiences of its victims, arguing that such responsibilities require the confidence of survivors and their families.
The Media Line has not independently verified Saqr's alleged position, the nature of her responsibilities, or the background al-Sukkari described. His statements are allegations, not established findings.
Al-Sukkari also raised concerns about Fadi Saqr, a figure formerly associated with the pro-Assad National Defense Forces, questioning the public reemergence of individuals linked to armed formations from the previous era without adequate scrutiny of their past roles.
He referred to allegations of abuses involving pro-government armed groups in Damascus and other parts of Syria and called for investigations into those suspected of participating in violations.
Such allegations alone do not establish individual criminal responsibility, which must be determined through evidence and appropriate legal proceedings.
Fall of regime only first objective of revolution, political activist says
For al-Sukkari, the renewed visibility of former Assad supporters sends a painful message to those who opposed the previous government and lost relatives during the conflict.
"As families of victims and relatives of martyrs, we have so far achieved only the first objective of our revolution, which was the fall of the regime," he said.
He also criticized what he described as the marginalization of some military officers who defected from Assad's forces, arguing that individuals who opposed the former government have not always been given the roles they expected in the new state.
Nevertheless, al-Sukkari emphasized that backing Assad did not necessarily mean someone had committed crimes.
"There is a difference between a supporter and a criminal," he said.
He argued that Syrians who supported Assad politically or worked in civilian state institutions should not automatically be treated in the same way as individuals found responsible for abuses against civilians.
Financial settlements involving businessmen associated with Assad's government have become another major source of controversy.
One prominent example is the settlement involving businessman Mohammed Hamsho, who was closely tied to the economic circles around the former president.
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa defended such settlements during a September meeting with members of the Syrian diaspora in New York.
Al-Sharaa said authorities had confiscated about 80% of Hamsho's assets while allowing him to keep the portion they determined was not acquired unlawfully.
He argued that companies associated with Hamsho provided employment for approximately 40,000 people and that confiscating all their assets could jeopardize those jobs and harm Syria's economy.
The president also stressed that a financial settlement would not protect Hamsho from criminal prosecution if he were found responsible for other offenses.
His remarks outlined the government's argument for separating asset recovery and economic continuity from criminal accountability.
Critics, however, question whether such a distinction can be maintained in practice, particularly when individuals with substantial financial resources and established networks may retain influence over public institutions or investigations.
Businessmen associated with Assad retained wealth after government change
Bishr al-Hawi, a member of Syria's People's Assembly, told The Media Line that it is important to distinguish between the political return of former government figures and the continued economic activity of businessmen previously associated with Assad.
According to al-Hawi, former political figures have not returned to their previous positions of influence, while some businessmen have negotiated financial settlements with the new authorities and retained portions of their wealth.
He acknowledged that traders and business figures associated with the former government have resumed economic activities but said they are less prominent than under Assad.
Al-Hawi argued that these individuals have not necessarily regained their former economic standing or political influence, adding that Syria needs the resources some of them possess.
At the same time, he acknowledged delays in implementing transitional justice.
"The transitional justice file has not received the momentum we had hoped for," al-Hawi said.
He said the People's Assembly seeks to accelerate the process in cooperation with the relevant executive institutions.
In a significant acknowledgment, al-Hawi said the assembly had not yet received a draft transitional justice law from the National Commission for Transitional Justice.
He explained that the commission was expected to submit a legislative proposal for parliamentary consideration and eventual approval, but it had not yet done so.
The People's Assembly is awaiting the proposal before beginning its legislative review, he said.
His comments highlight a central tension in Syria's transition: Economic settlements involving figures associated with the former government are moving forward while, according to a member of the legislature, the proposed legal framework for transitional justice has yet to reach parliament.
Reintegration of former Syrian government officials must abide by legal standards
Al-Moutassim al-Kilani, a researcher specializing in international criminal law, said the reintegration of individuals associated with the former government must be governed by clear legal standards that protect victims' rights and prevent financial or political influence from replacing accountability.
Speaking to The Media Line, al-Kilani stressed that support for Assad alone does not establish criminal responsibility.
Criminal accountability, he explained, must be based on specific conduct and evidence rather than former political affiliations.
He warned, however, that financial settlements could produce impunity in practice if money, personal connections, or political influence obstruct investigations or shield individuals from prosecution, even without any formal grant of immunity.
He argued that recovering public assets does not extinguish criminal liability or eliminate victims' rights to truth, justice, and reparations.
"Recovering the money is a duty, but it does not pay the price of torture, killing, or enforced disappearance," al-Kilani said.
He maintained that genuine national reconciliation requires establishing the truth, acknowledging abuses, compensating victims, and reforming the institutions that allowed violations to occur.
He also rejected collective punishment, emphasizing that former political affiliation or employment in state institutions should not be treated as proof of criminal wrongdoing.
For al-Kilani, one of the greatest risks is that old networks of influence could preserve their ability to shape political decisions, security institutions, the judiciary, and the economy simply by transferring their loyalty to the new leadership.
"Changing loyalties does not dismantle a corruption network, and changing faces is not enough if the same mechanisms of control remain in place," he said.
He argued that preventing a recurrence of past abuses requires an independent judiciary, accountable security institutions, transparent economic agreements, and effective protections for victims seeking justice.
Economic settlements are not pardons for violations in Syria
The National Commission for Transitional Justice has previously stated that economic settlements do not constitute pardons for serious violations and do not grant immunity from criminal prosecution.
Questions remain, however, about how that principle will be enforced, whether independent mechanisms exist to examine the records of individuals entering settlements, and what safeguards will protect victims' claims from political or economic interference.
The Media Line contacted the head of the National Commission for Transitional Justice for comment on criticism of the transitional justice process and settlements involving figures associated with Assad's government.
The commission's chairman referred the request to its media office.
After several hours of follow-up, the media office said it would respond later but did not specify when. The Media Line had not received responses to its questions by the time this report was prepared.
The debate reaches beyond whether former Assad supporters should be allowed to participate in Syria's public life.
While the authorities defend certain settlements as a way to recover assets, preserve jobs, and support a fragile economy, some former opposition activists and victims' families fear that reintegrating influential figures without sufficient scrutiny could undermine confidence in the country's new institutions.
Legal experts emphasize that transitional justice should neither criminalize everyone who supported the former government nor let economic arrangements replace investigations and accountability.
With a member of the People's Assembly acknowledging delays in the legislative process, the question of how Syria will balance economic stability, reconciliation, and victims' rights remains unresolved.
Individuals remain lost after Syria government collapses
For Hussein al-Tawil, however, the debate is not primarily about financial settlements or political appointments.
It is about one missing person.
Nearly 15 years after his brother Ali Ahmad al-Tawil disappeared in Damascus, Hussein and his family still do not know what happened to him.
The government Hussein holds responsible for his brother's disappearance has fallen, but its collapse has not brought the family the answer it has awaited for so long.
And as figures from Syria's past return to public life, Ali remains missing, leaving his family to ask what political change can mean for those who are still waiting for the truth.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan test new defense pact with high-stakes Iran talks - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:03:01 UTC
22:03:01 KST

On Monday, Saudi Arabia’s Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman arrived in Tehran. He will partake in talks between the countries that signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement (Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan) and Iran. These talks are significant and will test the new agreement.
The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement is a defense agreement, partially modeled on NATO. Some have questioned how the agreement will function, however. The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia led to questions about whether Turkey and Pakistan would help Riyadh.
Tehran presents a new test for the agreement: can its member countries produce results? Skeptics have argued that the three countries aren’t giving the agreement the bite to match its bark. Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish Intelligence Chief Ibrahim Kalin will also be in Iran. Notably, these men are some of the region’s heavy hitters.
Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iran’s hosting of senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey is a key development toward establishing regional diplomacy. He added that this could help with lasting stability and security in the Middle East.
Baghaei then argued that such stability could be achieved only if the region’s countries worked together. This suggests the region needs to handle its own problems without the US.
It’s unclear if the US and Israel will sign on. The two have openly said that the war with Iran will continue.
Most Israelis see the US-Israel relationship as larger than just one person
US President Donald Trump has twice endorsed Israel’s prime minister to remain in power. He has, in essence, argued that the US cannot work with anyone else in Israel when it comes to war with Iran. This is surprising to many Israelis because most see the US-Israel relationship as larger than just one person. In fact, most Israelis agree on the need to confront Iran.
Iran, for its part, knows that Israel has ordered the toppling of its regime. After all, it can read the news like anyone else. Iran also knows of reports that say the IDF was reluctant to carry out strikes right before Israel’s elections. The presence of high-level Turkish, Pakistani, and Saudi delegations in Tehran implies that they think the war can be postponed for a few more days.
The upcoming talks may show that the Makkah Defense Agreement is more about shared interests and diplomacy instead of tanks and warplanes.
Many commentators asked whether the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement would be like NATO. NATO, however, has shown that it historically isn't about waging war; it’s more about bringing together Western democracies, with militaries training together and sharing operations and culture. NATO hasn’t engaged in many wars in its 77 years since its founding in 1949. The demand from some that the Mekkah pact will immediately rush into war largely misunderstands the pact and the countries involved.
Saudi Arabia is a cautious and conservative state. Monarchies tend to be cautious and conservative; otherwise, they put themselves at risk. Turkey, by contrast, was more militarily active in 2016-2022 and has since become more cautious. Pakistan, despite recent clashes with India and Afghanistan, is also a conservative and cautious state in contrast to how it was decades ago.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan established a new trilateral security alliance in August
The background of the Makkah pact is worth examining. Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement on August 7, 2026, establishing a new trilateral security alliance. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement in Makkah.
The agreement includes a collective defense clause under which an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three. It also calls for expanded military cooperation, joint exercises, intelligence sharing, defense technology development, and cooperation between defense industries.
The alliance brings together three significant military powers, including nuclear-armed Pakistan and NATO member Turkey. It could have important implications for the regional balance of power and emerging security arrangements in the Middle East. The agreement also establishes a Strategic Political and Defense Committee to coordinate cooperation. Turkey published the full text in October as it moved toward parliamentary ratification.
Meanwhile, in Riyadh, Arab News said that “the Kingdom’s Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman is leading a delegation to Tehran for talks between countries party to the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement and Iran, to help ease regional tensions, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy said on Monday.”
The report added that “the meeting will be held with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and the Secretary-General of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.” This is important because Riyadh views it as part of ongoing efforts by the Makkah pact states to de-escalate the current situation and encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, Arab News added, based on a post by Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly.

How did Lula beat Bolsonaro after losing Brazil’s first-round election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:02:22 UTC
22:02:22 KST

How did Lula beat Bolsonaro after losing Brazil’s first-round election?
Brazil’s president secured a historic fourth term after overturning a first-round defeat, but faces a conservative Congress and a legal challenge from his defeated rival.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has achieved a stunning election victory, defeating far-right rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, despite trailing him by more than two million votes in the first round held earlier in October.
The 80-year-old leftist secured an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, becoming the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round.
“I just had to tell you that I love you. Tomorrow, the fight continues,” Lula told cheering fans at a victory parade in Sao Paulo. “No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone.”
Lula’s victory is a significant setback for the right-wing political movement that has gained ground across Latin America, often with the backing of United States President Donald Trump.
So how did Lula turn things around in just three weeks, and what challenges does he face?
What was the result?
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, secured 51.79 percent of valid votes, or 64.26 million ballots, compared with Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, or 59.83 million votes, according to the final tally.
The result marked a dramatic reversal from the October 4 first round, when Bolsonaro won 47.03 percent against Lula’s 45.16 percent, a lead of approximately 2.2 million votes.
Turnout on Sunday was 80.8 percent, nearly 2 percent higher than the previous round, when 78.92 percent of the electorate cast their votes.
Bolsonaro refused to concede and called for the run-off result to be annulled after Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered voting to be extended by two hours. Both candidates had requested extensions, citing transport disruptions and severe weather.
The controversy echoes the aftermath of the 2022 election, when Flavio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept his defeat. He was subsequently convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison, which he is serving under house arrest.
However, experts say Flavio faces significant obstacles in overturning the result.
Vinicius G. Rodrigues Vieira, an economics and international relations professor at the Armando Alvares Penteado Foundation, told Al Jazeera that Bolsonaro’s legal arguments were weak, particularly because his own campaign had requested an extension.
“I don’t think that will resonate in the courts, but certainly will help Bolsonarismo, the far-right movement here in Brazil, to remain politically strong on the streets,” he said.
How did Lula turn things around?
Lula’s comeback was driven by a revitalised grassroots campaign, youth mobilisation and a shift towards digital campaigning, analysts said.
Al Jazeera correspondent Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Sao Paulo, said young Brazilians spontaneously organised online after Bolsonaro’s first-round victory, creating what became known as “Lula’s army”.
“It was this army that went to the streets, millions of people across Brazil, and young people just mobilised themselves, energised the campaign, which frankly was not very energised at all before the first round,” she said.
Editor-in-chief of The Brazilian Report, Gustavo Ribeiro, told Al Jazeera that Lula’s campaign had initially appeared complacent.
“Lula’s campaign also got its act together after a first round in which it acted as if this election was in the bag and essentially running an anachronistic, mostly offline campaign,” he said.
“The campaign really pivoted towards a digital mentality and a grassroots effort,” Ribeiro said, adding that Lula had used “the power of incumbency very cleverly in his favour”.
“I would say this is more the merit of Lula, even if Bolsonaro just worked to run off the clock.”
Other experts agreed, saying Bolsonaro’s own mistakes were likely to have contributed to his defeat. Academic Vieira argued that the senator had become overconfident after winning the first round.
“In the first week, he was already behaving as if he were already the president-elect. He was appointing ministers,” the economics professor pointed out.
“If there is something Brazilian people don’t like [it’s] arrogance, so Mr. Flavio is paying a very high price for this,” he added.
The Brazilian Report’s Ribeiro also questioned Bolsonaro’s political appeal.
“He does not have his father’s charisma. He was essentially running on his father’s last name,” he said.
Higher turnout was another important factor.
An estimated 33.4 million Brazilians abstained in the first round, representing about 21 percent of the electorate. Abstention fell to approximately 19 percent in the run-off.
Fernando Brancoli, an international relations professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said previously absent voters appeared to have participated in the second round.
“We already know that a large number of people who didn’t vote [in] the first round, they now showed up,” he told Al Jazeera.
Brancoli also suggested some first-round Bolsonaro voters may have switched to Lula, although detailed voting patterns remain unclear.
According to Vieira, the election was arguably one of the most consequential in Brazil’s history.
After the 21-year dictatorship ended in 1985, he said Brazil built a “constitutional setting” which provided social rights to the population more than at any time in the South American nation’s history.
“That’s so important for the Brazilian people because we still have high levels of inequality,” he said, noting that it was crucial to “keep a very high degree of political participation”.
In contrast, the far-right Bolsonarismo movement had tried to “curtail voting rights” by employing “voting suppression tactics”, Vieira said.
What challenges does Lula face?
Despite his victory, Lula faces a conservative-dominated Congress that could severely restrict his legislative agenda.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies could control more than 280 seats out of 513 in the lower house, and up to 50 out of a total of 81 Senate seats, potentially giving the opposition majorities in both chambers.
Brancoli warned that Lula would have limited room to manoeuvre.
“We can definitely expect Lula’s government [is] not going to be able to push for a broad agenda. You’ll get small wins, and you’ll have to negotiate with those groups,” he said.
Economic pressures pose another considerable challenge. Brazil’s public debt has exceeded 82 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the World Bank, while the government forecasts growth of just 2.3 percent next year.
Moreover, Brancoli asserted that Lula would also need to address security and household debt, two issues that helped make the election competitive.
The president’s age raises further questions about the future of his Workers’ Party (PT), and who would replace the longtime leader, Brancoli noted.
“There’s no one that could substitute him, and he’s older,” he said.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage showed Brown hitting Diaw on the head with a glass bottle.

Russia May Seek NATO Rollback to 1997 in Ukraine Talks

The former prime minister will host guest lectures and masterclasses and will engage in mentoring, but the university said it was not a full-time teaching role.
“I’m delighted to be joining the University of Sydney,” Ardern said. “I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges.”
