“Dame Jacinda led New Zealand through events of profound consequence and her leadership demonstrated that empathy and resolve do not compete with one another; each can strengthen the other,” he said.
“For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service.”
In an ABC Conversations interview in July, Ardern said she believed people were seeking empathetic leadership despite many world leaders embodying a “dominant style” of leadership.
“You see people voting for parties [that] are often on the fringes of the mainstream. When you dive into the research, the majority of those who are doing that are often not voting for the ideology – they’re just voting against the status quo because they don’t think it serves them any more.
“So I think all the signs actually point to people wanting something different than what they’re getting now.”
Ardern retired from politics in January 2023, after more than five years as prime minister and the leader of the Labour party. She led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari volcanic eruption and the Covid pandemic.
In 2017, aged 37, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, later becoming the second world leader to give birth while in office.
Ardern has since held fellowships at Harvard University focused on public leadership and technology governance, and published her memoir, A Different Kind of Power, in 2025.
Ardern, her husband, Clarke Gayford, and daughter, Neve, moved to Sydney earlier this year, buying a property in Sydney’s northern beaches for $5.3m.

Has Pakistan reopened its border with Iran for trade?
Traders say some exports are crossing border after a weeklong halt, but Tehran says its cargo is not getting through.
Islamabad, Pakistan – On a normal day, hundreds of freight trucks and vehicles pass through Pakistan-Iran border crossings, carrying goods and people. On October 17, Islamabad suspended cargo traffic through the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings in Balochistan province, citing security risks.
On Monday, some goods started to move again.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Al Jazeera that trade “partially resumed this weekend”.
Border officials also cleared consignments that were dated from October 16 or earlier, goods truck association officials said.
Haji Noor Muhammad Shahwani, central president of the Balochistan Goods Truck Owners Association, told Al Jazeera from Quetta that Pakistani exports such as rice and bananas were crossing the border.
Trucks loaded in Iran before the closure, including those carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), were also entering Pakistan, he confirmed to Al Jazeera. “Those that were already loaded are clearing and coming out now. They are coming slowly.”
The halt of Iranian LPG to Pakistan created severe shortages and price spikes in Pakistan, which imports the bulk of its energy from the Middle East. Pakistan’s economy has already been impacted by shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by Iran and its response to the United States-Israel war.
Rizwan Ahmed, a customs clearing agent based near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing said customs had told agents to file declarations for the stranded trucks, which would then be released.
“Customs has given us the go-ahead, saying, ‘Bring in as much cargo as you can,’” Ahmed told Al Jazeera. He did not say whether this applied to goods loaded after October 16.
Ahmed said his own consignment of exports had just left. “We have rice, retail goods, potatoes, bananas,” he told Al Jazeera.
Cargo held up at the crossing
But Iran said changes to import paperwork introduced by Islamabad are holding up its cargo at the crossings.
On Sunday, Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said on X that Iran had placed no restrictions on exports to Pakistan, including LPG, and its borders remained open.
“Changes in the implementation of Pakistan’s E-Form procedure for imports from Iran have created a situation in which traders are effectively and literally unable to dispatch cargo from Iran to Pakistan,” he wrote.
The halt in trade between the two neighbours triggered speculation that the Pakistani step might have been taken under US pressure as part of Washington’s efforts to suffocate Iran economically. Pakistan insisted it was done amid a deteriorating security situation in Balochistan province on the border with Iran.
Gunmen attacked trucks waiting near the Gabd crossing on the Pakistani side of the border on Thursday. The military said 10 attackers were killed in operations around Gabd and Gwadar city, and one civilian died.
The attack came in a province that has faced a separatist rebellion for decades.
Balochistan accounted for 131 of the 225 armed attacks recorded nationwide in September, the highest monthly national total in 12 years, according to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs was asked about the border at its weekly news briefing on Friday.
“Pakistan, as a responsible member of the international community, adheres to and shall continue to adhere to all applicable sanctions regimes in accordance with international and domestic laws,” spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said.
He said he did not have direct knowledge of the situation on the ground. He did not say whether the border was open or whether the US had pressured Pakistan over the closure.
The Ministry of Commerce did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The paperwork dispute
A Commerce Ministry memorandum from October 16, seen by Al Jazeera, withdrew its October 3 memorandum extending a waiver on the E-Form, also called the EIF, for imports from Iran. It took effect immediately.
The purpose of the E-Form is to record imports and their payment through banks.
Moghadam, the Iranian envoy, said consultations with Pakistan were under way. Citing reports, he added that several hundred LPG trucks had crossed into Gabd but were yet to be unloaded or cleared.
Shahwani, from the Balochistan Goods Truck Owners Association, said the unloading problem had not been resolved.
“It is probably some problem with the banks, something to do with international trade,” he said.
Bakhtiar Ismail, the deputy commissioner of Chagai in Balochistan, wrote on X on October 18 that the closure was a temporary measure to improve border management and support counterterrorism efforts.
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei cited technical issues, according to the IRNA news agency.
Sanctions in the background
Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28. The US has since imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports, impacting Iranian exports. The US has also imposed wide-ranging economic sanctions to “asphyxiate” the Iranian government and cut off its revenue streams.
Imtiaz Baloch, a security analyst who focuses on Balochistan, told Al Jazeera that the US policy of maximum pressure on Iran had a direct or indirect influence.
That could be done directly, by forcing Pakistan’s government to close the border, or indirectly, through companies in the LPG trade or international banking channels, he said. But he added that no concrete or visible statement had linked the closure to US economic policy.
“My assessment is that security is part of it, procedures or technical glitches are part of it and the banking system is also involved,” Baloch said.

Coordinating the Philosophy Profession’s Response to the Use of AI in Research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

We have discussed in many posts here how artificial intelligence (AI) is affecting—and could affect—different aspects of academic philosophy’s research ecosystem.
We have seen AI-written articles published in peer-reviewed journals and AI-written referee reports. As journals attempt to craft policies about AI use, some have been flooded with AI-generated submissions. More and more of philosophy’s institutions are organizing and encouraging research on AI. There are efforts underway to test and measure the capacity of AIs to produce philosophical research. And there is speculation about how the technology will change philosophical research, lead to new research tools, alter our institutions, and affect how credit and evaluation in the profession works. Meanwhile, some PhD students in philosophy are starting to use AI to write dissertations. A lot has happened in the six years since the first Daily Nous post about LLMs six years ago.
How should the profession respond to these and related developments? Is an effective coordinated response desirable? Is it possible?
To help facilitate our taking up of these and related questions, the Marc Sanders Foundation is organizing a conference on them that will bring together journal and academic press editors, scholars, and representatives from some of philosophy’s institutions.
Barry Lam (UC Riverside), associate director of the Sanders Foundation, shared the following information about it:
The Sanders Foundation is hoping the field of academic philosophy will develop a coordinated response to the presence and use of AI-tools in the publication and review of philosophical research. To that end, we are funding a conference at NYU on April 3rd and 4th 2027, bringing together editors of philosophy journals, editors of academic presses that publish a significant amount of philosophy, and philosophers who have developed views about the proper coordinated response to AI. Confirmed attendees include representatives from the APA, editors-in-chief of Journal of Philosophy, Philosophical Review, Mind, Nous, Ergo, Philosophy Compass, Analytic Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy and Public Affairs, and from university presses, Oxford, Harvard, MIT, and Routledge. There will also be legal scholars who are up-to-date about AI and the laws of copyright. If you are a philosopher who has original data or research that speaks to these questions, and are interested in participating, please fill out the form at the URL. We do not plan to have many talks at the conference, but rather panel discussions and audience Q & As. All invitees will have all expenses paid.
You can find out more about the conference here.

Playing video games with trusted friends may reduce addiction risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

Video game developers constantly look for ways to keep players returning to their games without fostering unhealthy behavioral dependencies. Recent research published in Computers in Human Behavior reveals that playing video games with a trusted, familiar group of people can build player loyalty while simultaneously reducing the risk of video game addiction. These findings suggest that the social environment within a digital game plays a powerful role in determining whether a gaming habit remains a healthy pastime or becomes a psychological burden.
The video game industry faces a persistent tension between business goals and social responsibility. Companies rely on player loyalty, which describes a gamer’s intention to keep playing and recommending a specific game to others. At the same time, the industry faces scrutiny over video game addiction, a clinical syndrome characterized by a loss of control over gaming habits despite negative consequences in daily life.
Past studies have identified factors that contribute to addiction, such as social isolation, and factors that boost loyalty, like customized digital avatars. Few researchers have investigated how specific social dynamics inside a game might influence both outcomes at the same time. A team of researchers led by Shih-I Tai, a management scholar at Chang Gung University in Taiwan, wanted to find out if specific types of group interactions could help secure a player’s devotion to a game without pushing them toward maladaptive behavior.
To understand how the social environment alters a player’s mental state, the researchers looked at two established psychological frameworks. The first is the pleasure-arousal theory, which separates emotions into two dimensions. One dimension tracks how pleasant an experience feels, while the other tracks how much it stimulates or arouses the person.
The second framework is brain reward circuitry theory. This theory suggests that pleasure and arousal activate entirely different neural pathways in the human brain. According to these frameworks, feelings of comfort, harmony, and contentment increase pleasure but lower physical and emotional arousal.
In contrast, surprises and intense excitement boost both pleasure and arousal at the same time. The research team hypothesized that high pleasure encourages players to return to a game, building long-term loyalty. High arousal provides the intense neurological reinforcement that can lead to addiction.
To test these ideas, the researchers conducted an online survey of 884 video game players in Taiwan. The participants answered detailed questions about their gaming habits over the previous month. The respondents nominated a game they had played recently, which frequently included games where massive numbers of players assume fictional roles and interact in a shared digital world.
The research team ensured the reliability of their data by excluding responses from participants under the age of 18 or people who reported impossible play times. The survey measured four distinct aspects of the gaming experience. The researchers asked players about the size of their usual gaming group and how many of those group members they knew in the real world.
They also asked participants to rate their level of trust in their fellow group members. Finally, the survey assessed game escapism, which measures the extent to which players use the game to actively avoid stress from their everyday lives.
The researchers then compared these four factors against self-reported measures of game loyalty and game addiction. They analyzed the data using structural equation modeling, a statistical technique that helps identify relationships among multiple variables. The results showed that different social elements influenced players in entirely distinct ways.
When looking at the size of a player’s gaming group, the data showed a positive link to game loyalty. Players who routinely gamed with larger groups were more likely to report intentions to keep playing and recommending the game to others. However, group size was not statistically significant in relation to game addiction.
The researchers suspect that larger groups provide more social connections that make the game enjoyable, satisfying the pleasure dimension. At the same time, massive groups often introduce repetitive interactions or toxic behavior that dampen the intense overall excitement needed to form a dependency.
The findings regarding real-world familiarity showed a different pattern. Knowing fellow players in the real world was not statistically significant when predicting a player’s loyalty to a game. It did correspond with lower levels of game addiction.
The researchers propose that when gamers play with real-world acquaintances, those friends might occasionally remind them of outside responsibilities. This social grounding breaks the immersive spell of the game and lowers the intense emotional arousal that drives compulsive play.
Trust among group members proved to be the most beneficial social factor. High levels of trust within a gaming group corresponded with both increased game loyalty and decreased game addiction. Engaging with honest and reliable peers likely provides a comforting, highly pleasant experience that makes players want to return.
This same comfort and harmony create a relaxed state of mind. Trusting one’s peers reduces the high-stakes anxiety and arousal typically associated with addictive behavior. If a player trusts their group to act in their best interest, they receive social support that helps maintain a healthy balance between gaming and life.
In contrast to the protective social factors, game escapism had a dual effect. Using games to flee real-world stress strongly predicted higher game loyalty, as the temporary relief provided a rewarding experience. Yet escapism also strongly predicted higher levels of game addiction. Fleeing reality into a digital space immerses the player intensely, heightening the emotional arousal that stimulates the brain’s reward centers in a maladaptive way.
While the data offer insights into player behavior, the study relies on survey responses rather than direct observations. The researchers measured self-reported habits and feelings at a single point in time, meaning the results highlight associations rather than a strict cause-and-effect relationship. It is possible that players who are already less prone to addiction are simply more inclined to build trusting relationships with their peers.
The researchers used psychological theories regarding brain activity to interpret their findings, but they did not conduct medical brain scans or directly measure the participants’ physiological arousal and pleasure. Future studies could incorporate clinical monitoring tools, such as electroencephalograms, to verify exactly how these social interactions alter brain activity in real time.
Additionally, the survey was conducted entirely in Taiwan, which means the findings might be influenced by local cultural norms regarding socializing and technology use. Expanding this research to include gamers in different countries could reveal whether the protective effects of trust and real-world familiarity remain consistent across diverse cultural backgrounds.
The study, “The ties that (healthily) bind: Playing in groups increases game loyalty but decrease addiction,” was authored by Shih-I Tai, Thi Tuan Linh Pham, Tzu-Ling Huang, Alexander S. Dennis, Chun-Hao Liu, Gen-Yih Liao, and Ching-I Teng.

UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers.
Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.
The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand.
If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.
The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job.
Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off.
However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.
Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known as bidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets.
The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could mean an additional 147m tonnes of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by 2050.
Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, a thinktank tracking the transition to electric cars, said: “Vehicle to grid is exciting technology that could help balance the grid and cut bills, but carmakers should only be rewarded if it’s actually used, not just for fitting it.
“Under these proposals, one or even two extra credits worth around £4,000 each would hand manufacturers thousands per car for kit that costs a few hundred pounds, even though few drivers own the expensive charger needed to use it. Ministers should make sure the people who benefit from V2G are drivers and billpayers, not carmakers’ shareholders.”
Some people already sell their electricity back to the grid through companies such as Octopus Energy in the UK, Renault in France, and BMW in Germany. Octopus Energy has claimed that drivers could save £620 a year with the service.
Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Association England, which represents drivers, said: “We have millions of EV drivers in the UK, but only a fraction are using vehicle to grid or storage technologies. These technologies have enormous potential but consumers are still getting to grips with more immediate questions around the cost of their car, the cost of charging, and whether an EV meets their day to day needs.
“It is far too early to be giving manufacturers a credit that effectively allows them to sell fewer EVs, for a technology that has not even been tried and tested, at scale, by drivers in the real world.”
Once the technology takes off, electricity supplied by V2G cars could add up to the equivalent of a power station by 2030, able to provide 1.2 gigawatts of power on demand, according to the National Energy System Operator, which balances Great Britain’s grid. That could grow to as much as 41 GW by 2050, Neso forecasts, enough to meet more than a quarter of peak energy demand.

On the campaign trail in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed rides a wave of support for Medicare for All
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate, starts this day on the campaign trail in Escanaba, Michigan, where nearby Wisconsin dairy country spills into dense forests and the sandy shores of Green Bay.
This is the upper peninsula – the “UP” – a rural slash of land north of Michigan’s mitt. Electorally, it’s crimson. Donald Trump won some districts near Escanaba by more than 41%. But at the county fairgrounds, past sheds labeled “Beef” and “Swine”, hundreds of locals on the political left have gathered in the hangar-size 4H Club meeting hall to hear El-Sayed speak.
“We built this campaign on three simple things. Y’all remember what they are?” El-Sayed stokes the audience, leading them to a call-and-response.
“Money out of … ”
“Politics!”
“Money in your … ”
“Pocket!”
“Medicare for … ”
“All!”
As Americans prepare for historic cuts enacted in the Republican-led “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, which is expected to push 17 million people from their health insurance plans, El-Sayed appears to have caught a rising tide of interest in Medicare for All.
This election season, Troy Jackson, the Democratic US Senate candidate from Maine, who’s in a dead heat with Republican Susan Collins, said Medicare for All would be “great coverage”. Angie Nixon, Florida’s Democratic US Senate candidate, has made it a part of her “working families guarantee”. Chris Van Hollen, current US senator for Maryland, added Medicare for All to his platform last December after “listening to his constituents”.
El-Sayed’s supporting act in this series of stops is influential Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a longtime Medicare for All proponent and the subject of whispers about a 2028 presidential run. And, according to an October poll by the health policy thinktank the Kaiser Family Foundation, two-thirds of Americans support the idea.
Technically, Medicare for All is an insurance reform. Proposals currently before Congress would make the federal government into the nation’s health insurer, a “single-payer” system more closely aligned with health systems in peer-developed democracies, such as Canada.
Sounds simple. However, in the US, one in every five dollars goes to healthcare. The existing health insurance patchwork fuels profits of world-leading, resource-unlimited corporations and powerful local monopolies. Democrats also worry that replacing private insurance, as Medicare for All advocates call for, would provide fodder for Republicans, who have made stoking popular resentment against government into an electoral strategy.
Those enormous barriers have repeatedly relegated Medicare for All to the political hinterlands. Centrist Democrats worry that, in a nation where me-but-not-thee politics has reigned for many years, Medicare for All is nothing more than a decades-old tried-and-failed idea.
Then again, in a nation where healthcare prices are the highest in the world and climbing, when even the insured find themselves in medical debt, and where the broad-daylight assassination of an insurance executive elicits catharsis and not mourning – the yearning for change is personal and visceral.
“Not enough doctors, not enough healthcare,” says El-Sayed, who ran both the Detroit and Wayne county health departments, and received a medical degree from Columbia University.
A shout from the crowd: “Not enough psychiatrists!”
“Not enough mental healthcare,” El-Sayed answers, tossing out a campaign slogan: “It shouldn’t be this hard.”
Later, a shout from the same corner: “What about our teeth!”
El-Sayed’s campaign comes as the Trump administration enacts the largest federal healthcare cut in the nation’s history – extracting $1tn from the system primarily by through severe cuts to Medicaid, the federal-state health insurance program for low-income and disabled people. Medicaid cuts are expected to close hospitals, particularly those in rural outposts like Escanaba, and the urban core.
At the same time, some of the most popular health policies of recent years – such as reining in medical debt collections – spring directly from the policy work of Medicare for All advocates. Add to this a counterintuitive reality: almost half of all healthcare today is already paid for by federal, state or local government, according to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
“I’ve been at this for a while, and we have dips and peaks in the single-payer movement,” said Dr Stephanie Woolhandler, a professor of public health at the City University of New York, and a decades-long advocate for Medicare for All. Support “always comes back”, she said.
“And the reason it always comes back is because the healthcare system has not been fixed – and it may not be fixable at all without single-payer,” said Woolhandler.
To understand this system, and Republican enmity toward it, it pays to go back a century when the idea of tying health insurance to employment was born of entrepreneurial innovation and historical accident. In 1929, Baylor University hospital offered insurance to cover hospital bills for $6 per year to a group of 1,500 schoolteachers in Dallas. The idea caught on across the country and Blue Cross came to life.
This arrangement was institutionalized during the second world war. Amid government price controls, health insurance was one of the few ways businesses could compete for workers. The federal government made the benefit tax-exempt, as it still is today, according to the foremost history on the subject by author Paul Starr.
Since then, Democrats have pushed for reform and expansion – with their failures to reach universal coverage shaping the contours of the patchwork system that exists today.
In 1965, Democrat Lyndon Johnson passed Medicare, for people older than 65, and its sister program Medicaid, together providing insurance for more than a third of Americans today. While the reform was a momentous triumph over segregationist opposition – Medicare desegregated hospitals – it came up short against its architects’ vision.
“We expected Medicare to be a first step toward universal national health insurance,” said Robert Ball, a top official in the Kennedy and Johnson administrations, according to an article in Health Affairs.
It also created important knock-on effects: it pushed the hospital industry to commercialize in the 1980s, according to Dr Luke Messac, an emergency room doctor at Mass General Brigham, and author of Your Money or Your Life, a history of medical debt. Hospitals, the majority of which are non-profit in the US, argued they could drop the explicit charitable missions many were founded with because Medicare paid patients’ bills. As a result, the hospital industry pushed the IRS to loosen its definition of community benefit, at the same time keeping their nonprofit status and scaling up billing.
This yielded “a lot of middlemen in our system that do not provide a benefit to the public”, said Messac. “One of the things Medicare for All is intended to do is take some of the power back from those actors.”
“That poses a huge threat, so the fact that there would be opposition is like the most predictable thing in the world,” he adds. “It doesn’t mean it’s a bad idea – it may mean it’s a good idea.”
Since Johnson’s Medicare bill, the only law to rival it in scope is the Affordable Care Act (ACA), passed in 2010. Better known as Obamacare, a version of the market-based reform was first proposed by scholars at the conservative Heritage Foundation. Democrats sought to reach across the aisle; to do so, they developed a bill to subsidize insurance for individuals. But that plan for bipartisan support didn’t work out.
Obamacare was passed on a party-line vote – one of the first signposts of the new era of polarization. Republicans incessantly targeted it for more than a decade. Today, it is etched it into the minds of conservative voters as the source of all that ills healthcare.
Just ask the pro-Trump protesters outside El-Sayed’s rally in Escanaba.
“We should almost go back to square one and start analyzing what caused this,” says Bonnie, a 70-year-old Republican in Delta county, who declines to give her last name. “When the socialistic ideas started coming in, like Obamacare, that’s what threw everything in a tailspin.”
“I want everything privatized,” says Lisa Pieczyski, a woman in her 60s from near Escanaba, who carries a homemade anti-green-energy sign. “We’ve mandated too many things under insurance that have made the premiums outrageous.” She adds that she can’t trust the government because “Obamacare did all this”.
“I’m middle class, I’ve always been middle class, and what I have done to ensure I have medical insurance is give up something else like a fucking Cadillac and pay for it, all right? OK?” said Delta county’s Republican spokesperson, Michael Glass, 77, who gets insurance through a privatized version of Medicare called Medicare Advantage.
“It is the individual who should take responsibility for their own healthcare, period.”
As El-Sayed stumps through the UP, his supporters repeat a set of ideas they believe run parallel to Medicare for All: kindness, respect and shared responsibility. In Iron Mountain, he greets an overflow crowd at the local ski lodge – one of the few public meeting places in this rural town. One “lifelong Democrat” says there hasn’t been this much excitement since Bernie Sanders came to town a few years back.
After El-Sayed’s speech – his condemnations of US support for Israel’s war in Gaza, his calls for cheaper gas, groceries and healthcare, criticisms of Islamophobia – a woman asks about how to bring people around to Medicare for All.
“I was a registered nurse for 40 years,” she says. “Can you make a video or some kind of something explaining – some easy way for people to understand how great and easy it’s going to be?” El-Sayed answers – but it’s Ocasio-Cortez that captures the room.
“Raise your hand if you have waited or delayed getting a treatment or seeing a doctor because you felt you couldn’t afford it,” says Ocasio-Cortez.
Every single person raises a hand.
“Right now, we are waiting weeks, months, years – to wait until we can afford to see a doctor one day. Healthcare has become a luxury,” says Ocasio-Cortez. “Medicare exists – we provide a healthcare system for every American above the age of 65.”
Finally, she adds: “There is this idea that I don’t want to pay for someone else’s thing. First of all, does that mean you don’t want someone else to pay for your care? Does that mean we shouldn’t have Medicare today? Because I’m a young person and I gladly pay, because I want to live in a society where seniors” – then, she is drowned out by the cheers of people excited to share the cost.
At the end of the one-day, 131-mile trail, El-Sayed is in the gymnasium of Northern Michigan University with enormous pictures of athletes looking out at the audience. A physician assistant who is running for state representative opens the rally and – all of a sudden – public health is on the offense.
“All it took was the closure of my little Planned Parenthood clinic about 18 months ago,” says Anna Aho Rink, a Democratic candidate for Michigan’s 109th US House district, “and me being completely fed up with the system that is not working well for any of us to get me up here today and running for office.”
The rally is at a college, but students are a minority in the audience; there are elderly residents and middle-aged parents with children in tow on a school night.
“You don’t need a medical degree to recognize the symptoms of a broken economy,” says Ocasio-Cortez as she warms up the crowd. “Michigan, corruption is making this country sick.”
El-Sayed ticks off his public health victories: he got 16,000 kids free reading glasses; used vending machines to distribute Narcan, the overdose reversal medication; tested daycares and preschools for lead in the water, and then remediated dozens.
“You deserve to have a long, healthy life in the United States of America,” El-Sayed calls.
For many, this politics is in perfect relief to the worldview of the Trump administration – one where there is not enough to go around, where someone needs to lose, the government must be gutted, loyalty ranks much higher than fact.
The loudest chants of the day fill the gymnasium:
“Money out of … ”
“Politics!”
“Money in your … ”
“Pocket!”
“Medicare for … ”
“All!”

Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for crab and spring onion fried rice | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

This gently seasoned rice has become such a comfort blanket that I now make it at least once a week at home. That’s quite surprising, really, given that I’m guilty of drowning most of my food in chilli crisp oil, but this rice is so delicate yet flavourful that it’s just the gentle hug I need. The key is to cook the aromatics slowly and quietly in the oil, to soften and infuse, but not colour too quickly. Cook the jasmine rice in advance, if you like – it fries better once it has been cooked and cooled. Alternatively, packs of pre-cooked microwave rice work brilliantly.
Crab and spring onion fried rice
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 15 min
 
Serves 4
4 tbsp neutral oil
  
4 garlic cloves, peeled and finely sliced
 
30g ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
 
1 bunch spring onions, trimmed and cut into 1cm slices
 
500g cooked jasmine rice
  
¼ tsp white pepper
  
2 tbsp fish sauce
  
1½ tbsp soy sauce
  
Sea salt
  
2 large eggs, whisked
 
150g white crab meat
Put the oil in a wok or large frying pan and add the garlic, ginger and spring onions. Pop on to a low heat and leave for eight to 10 minutes – you want to infuse the oil slowly, so the spring onions turn tender and the garlic and ginger are lightly golden. Turn up the heat to medium-high, add the cooked rice and fry for a minute. Stir in the white pepper, fish sauce and soy sauce, and fry for two minutes, so it’s all combined and the rice is piping hot.
Season the whisked eggs and pour over the top of the rice. Give them a minute to start setting, then drag the eggs through the rice – you don’t want clumps of egg, rather a ripple of it throughout the dish. Fork through the crab meat, cook for a further minute, then take off the heat. Check the seasoning, and add more salt, soy or fish sauce as you wish. Serve straight away.

Claude helped plan risky bird flu research. What did the AI add?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Claude helped plan risky bird flu research. What did the AI add?
Anthropic’s Claude helped plan work with bird flu, but it’s unclear if harm was intended
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot helped a scientist plan potentially risky bird flu experiments.
The researcher relied on Claude to plan studies, analyze data and choose experiments involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, the company reported September 10 in a threat intelligence report. The work sought to identify and introduce mutations that could help bird flu viruses adapt to mammals and transmit more easily between them. Anthropic says that, to its knowledge, no private company had previously publicly shared evidence of potential misuse of its platform for biological weapons development. But the company did not provide enough detail to determine whether Claude simply sped up work the researcher could already do or gave the researcher a new capability, experts say.
Learning how avian influenza viruses might pose a pandemic risk “is absolutely a normal part of virology research,” says influenza researcher Thomas Friedrich of the University of Wisconsin–Madison School of Veterinary Medicine. Such research can help scientists assess whether emerging bird flu viruses pose a greater risk to humans.
But experiments that deliberately aim to boost pathogen traits such as transmissibility or disease severity draw scrutiny, Friedrich says, because of concerns about accidents or misuse.
Though the report comes amid broader debates about the security of AI models, arguments over this “gain-of-function” research predate generative AI. In 2012, studies involving H5N1 bird flu and airborne transmission in ferrets prompted an international debate over whether the scientific benefits outweighed the risks. Some H5N1 transmission experiments were put on hold for a year while researchers and officials worked out how to handle the risks.
In Anthropic’s case, discovered in May 2026, the bird flu researcher accessed Claude from a region where the service was not supported or available. Anthropic says the researcher used workarounds to access Claude anyway. Material shared with Claude suggested the group probably had physical access to relevant virus samples. Anthropic banned the researcher’s account in May for evading restrictions on access.
Anthropic says it could not tell whether the researcher intended harm because legitimate and dangerous biological research can look similar. The company did not respond to questions from Science News about why it considered the case significant, how it assessed Claude’s role in the research or whether any proposed experiments had actually been performed.
Anthropic released too little information to determine the purpose of the work, says biodefense researcher Gregory Koblentz. “There is no evidence that any of this research was connected to the development of biological weapons,” says Koblentz of George Mason University in Fairfax, Va.
The same kind of biological research can serve very different purposes, from civilian science to military defense. Even work done at a military-affiliated institution does not, on its own, show that researchers are developing a biological weapon, Koblentz says.
Anthropic also did not provide enough detail to show exactly how much Claude helped, Friedrich says. The company’s own account suggests the AI model “did not meaningfully add scientific capability,” he says. In other words, it may simply have sped up the researcher’s work, rather than enabling something they could not have done otherwise.
Even if Claude’s role was only to speed up the work, that can make a big difference in a scientist’s workflow, says virologist David O’Connor of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Systems such as Claude can help researchers find papers, synthesize results and parse data more quickly, he says. “Work or analyses that would have taken me months can now be done in an afternoon.”
As a result, existing scientific information, including about avian flu viruses, may become easier to find and use, O’Connor says. O’Connor says frontier AI models could let scientists tackle questions they might not have attempted before. “The frontier models will change the ambition of research questions that are asked,” he says.
The bird flu research was one of five instances in Anthropic’s report involving uses of Claude that the company says could support biological weapons development. None of the five look technically sophisticated or particularly concerning to biologist Kevin Esvelt of the MIT Media Lab. Esvelt is more suspicious of the researchers’ motives; he says the five cases showed signs of ill intent. But none “represented a competent attempt at weaponization.”
The poor quality of these particular attempts does not show what a more capable user might be able to do with AI-assisted biology, Esvelt says. AI can help with research and analysis, but turning an idea into a biological threat takes additional work, Koblentz says. “Even if AI is used to design a potentially dangerous pathogen, it is not a threat until the organism can be modified in a lab or synthesized.”
That requires facilities, measures for keeping viruses contained, funding, trained personnel and hands-on experience. Those barriers vary depending on who is doing the work, O’Connor says. They would be a major obstacle for an inexperienced person working alone, but less so for scientists with specialized training and access to a well-equipped laboratory.
Regardless, the remaining laboratory steps are substantial, Friedrich writes in an email. “There is a big gap between identifying mutations that could potentially adapt an avian influenza virus to humans and a ‘harmful biological outcome’.”

Some iPhone Duo Models Are Breaking. iFixit’s Teardown Might Explain Why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The first batch of Apple’s first folding phone may already have some screen issues.
The iPhone Duo is a strong first foldable from the company, but multiple Reddit reports say the phone’s inner screen cracks when customers open the device. Some apparently happen very soon, like during device setup. (Others might be from influencers trying to break the thing, like YouTuber JerryRigEverything.) People are already calling this “crackgate.”
The issue affects a small number of units—most iPhone Duo models aren't affected. If there is a problem, it crops up quite quickly after usage, not days after unboxing. (WIRED’s review unit hasn’t had any issues after more than two weeks of daily use.)
“The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor,” an Apple spokesperson tells WIRED. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.”
This is familiar territory for foldable phones. A hinge means strain on the screen and the components inside. It’s also a place for dust to seep in and break the phone, as with Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold in 2019, forcing the company to pause sales and fix the issue. Some devices handle it better than others, and as the product category has grown, those issues have largely diminished. But fewer problems don’t mean easier fixes.
On Sunday, repair company iFixit released its teardown of the iPhone Duo, including a video detailing the specific parts inside and what to look out for if people need to fix their $1,999 phone one day—maybe sooner than they think.
The culprit behind the screen breaking hasn’t been officially verified yet, but iFixit has a theory. Along the hinge, a display cable passes across the center of the hinge. In iFixit’s stress test simulation, the center support bar along the hinge fails to get out of the way as the screen folds, making a stress point right in the middle of the screen that could be leading to those cracks.
The phone got a provisional repairability rating of 5/10, though that score may be updated to factor in how Apple supplies replacement parts. A 5/10 doesn’t sound great, but it’s actually the highest repair rating iFixit has given any foldable phone.
“The state of foldables today is one of the hardest engineering challenges across a number of disciplines out there in the market today,” iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens said at an event the day before Apple announced its folding phone in September. “It is the pinnacle of material engineering and materials science. It is ludicrously difficult to accomplish this.”
The iPhone Duo earned good marks on some repair fronts. The battery and back panels are straightforward to remove and replace. The outer trim comes off in one piece. The 5.4-inch front screen comes off easily enough. Disassembling the pieces and putting everything back together is doable too, since almost everything is secured with brackets and screws you can remove and reuse.
The tricky part, according to iFixit, is the inner display. A thin matte nano-texture finish sits on top of the OLED screen, and if you’re not careful, you could easily peel the layer off. (Apple strictly tells users not to remove this finish on a support page.)
Removing the full inner screen requires melting the adhesive with a heat gun and some real elbow grease to pull the screen away. Users have reported breaking this part of the screen, and it seems it is the most fragile component and the hardest to replace. (Apple has an inner screen repair service, but it costs $999.) The Duo also collects dust in typical places like the USB-C port, outer edges, and speaker, but it accumulates along the inner hinge, causing it to sound “crunchy” like other folding devices when dust gets inside.
Apple long resisted letting users repair their own devices. When it finally started offering real repair options in 2021, its programs got off to a rough start and were less helpful than they could have been. Slowly but surely, thanks to various legislation in the US and the European Union, Apple has been introducing efforts to let people fix their own things. The iPhone Duo had a widely accessible repair manual on launch day, which hasn’t always been the case for how the company shares that kind of information.
The iPhone Duo may not be perfectly repairable—folding phones might never get there. But when a device starts having problems like cracked screens, it’ll be nice to know how to fix the thing.
Updated at 2:35 pm ET on October 26: We've added a statement from Apple.
Additional reporting by Julian Chokkattu.

'I'll kill you' — Finnish schools increasingly report threatening behaviour to police
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:59:17 EET
21:59:17 KST

Last year, police received close to 7,000 crime reports from schools, universities and research institutions, according to the National Police Board.
But the numbers do not reveal much about where exactly these incidents are happening, since they lump together daycares, comprehensive schools, upper secondary schools, universities and other research institutions.
Regional differences are also large, which may be partly explained by the varying number of educational institutions in different areas.
The most common suspected offense in these cases was assault.
In Rovaniemi, principal Petri Mäkelä said even younger pupils are threatening each other with serious violence.
"Lines like 'I'll kill you' and 'I'll shoot you' are already familiar among first-graders. The language has become harsher, but kids that age obviously don't understand what they're saying. It's a way of expressing emotional strain," Mäkelä told Yle.
Teachers threatened
Nationwide, school staff get their share of threats too. According to the teacher union OAJ, teachers are reporting such incidents more than ever before.
A recent education sector survey found that 14 percent of respondents had been the target of violence or threats of violence at work over the past year.
"This year we've had around 200 people contact us about this. Five years ago, we got only a few dozen of these kinds of crime-related contacts a year," explained Ulla Walli, OAJ's director of legal affairs.
Teachers have been threatened with murder or assault, for example. The threat can come from a pupil, a former pupil or a guardian.
Over the past two years, violence or the threat of it has increased most in primary education.
Cases in which a teacher is the victim often involve a pupil hitting, kicking or scratching an adult. According to OAJ, typical situations in which a teacher is suspected of a crime involve maintaining classroom order.

Ukraine changes tactics for using Patriot systems, Ihnat says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:58:00 UTC
21:58:00 KST

Ukraine changes tactics for using Patriot systems, Ihnat says
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command, made this statement on the RBC-Ukraine podcast, according to Ukrinform.
Ihnat explained that during the full-scale war, the Ukrainian military has changed its approach to using the American systems. In particular, they have learned to use the Patriot in various tactical situations and to use the expensive interceptor missiles more efficiently.
One example is the ability to deploy the system not only from fixed positions but also for ambushes followed by a change of location.
“For example, you can use the Patriot not as a stationary system—the way the Americans keep it at airfields or bases—but make it, so to speak, ‘mobile’: set up an ambush, shoot down five aircraft, and return unscathed,” explained the Air Force spokesperson.
Another difference concerns ammunition consumption. According to Ihnat, Ukrainian crews have learned to use one missile against a single target, whereas in the Middle East, in some cases, up to eight interceptors could be launched simultaneously.
He explained that the Patriot has three operating modes: automatic, semi-automatic, and manual. In automatic mode, the system can launch a significant number of interceptors, and in the absence of relevant combat experience, the entire salvo of missiles could be fired from the launcher at a single target.
“Due to a lack of such experience, they could have fired the entire salvo of interceptors from a single launcher at a single Shahed or a single ballistic missile,” Ihnat noted.
According to his estimate, the number of missiles used in the Middle East would have been enough for Ukraine to operate these systems for several years.
“That is why we now find ourselves in the crisis we are in—because what was spent in the Middle East would have been enough for us to operate the Patriot systems for several more years,” Ihnat concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, Volodymyr Zelensky stated that progress is being made on the issue of providing Ukraine with missiles for the Patriot systems, but the process is moving very slowly.

“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” he said, acknowledging that final results were not yet available. A parliamentary majority requires 126 seats.
The defeat marks a major setback for one of Moscow’s closest political partners in Europe. Under Vucic, Serbia maintained ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while continuing to pursue EU membership.
Vucic predicts sanctions, but winners pledged otherwise
Vucic accused his opponents of implementing an agenda devised abroad and alleged that unnamed European countries and an “American deep state” opposed to President Donald Trump had supported their victory.
“By March or April, you will have sanctions imposed on the Russian Federation,” he said, according to RFE/RL. However, his prediction conflicts with the Student List’s stated pre-election position.

Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
The election outcome therefore does not establish that Belgrade will change its sanctions policy. Vucic’s remarks were a forecast about his opponents’ intentions, rather than an announcement by the projected winners.
Student protests become an electoral challenge
The opposition movement emerged from protests following the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Demonstrators demanded accountability over suspected corruption and construction failures. The protests developed into a nationwide challenge to Vucic’s political dominance, with students organizing a parliamentary slate drawn from outside the established governing parties.
Supporters celebrated in Belgrade, Novi Sad, and other cities after Vucic conceded. The movement’s leading candidate, cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, said its next task would be building a state governed by the rule of law.
Vucic had resigned as president on Sept. 27 to contest the parliamentary election, hoping to return as prime minister. He previously held that position before becoming president in 2017.
His resignation left parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić serving as acting president pending a separate presidential election. Sunday’s vote concerned control of parliament and the formation of the next government.
Serbia’s balancing act between Moscow and Kyiv
Serbia’s relationship with Russia extends beyond sanctions. Belgrade has relied on Russian energy supplies and Moscow’s diplomatic support over Kosovo, whose independence Serbia does not recognize.
At the same time, Serbia has supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity, received Ukrainian refugees, and provided humanitarian and financial assistance. President Volodymyr Zelensky visited Belgrade in August for talks on bilateral cooperation and European integration.
Serbia had provided roughly €60 million ($69 million) in nonmilitary assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, according to earlier reporting.
The EU remains central to Serbia’s economic interests, accounting for nearly 60% of its foreign trade. But maintaining Russian ties while seeking deeper European integration has complicated Belgrade’s foreign policy. The next government will inherit that balancing act alongside the student movement’s central domestic promises to tackle corruption and restore public institutions.

‘Enough for Years’: Ihnat Says Patriot Missiles Used in Middle East Could Have Protected Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:52:50 UTC
21:52:50 KST

Ukraine could have had enough Patriot air defense missiles to sustain its systems for several years if a significant portion of the interceptors had not been expended in the Middle East, Yuriy Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said.
Speaking on the RBC-Ukraine podcast Tse Baza (“This Is the Basics”), Ihnat said Ukrainian forces had adapted their tactics for using the US-made Patriot systems throughout Russia’s full-scale war, learning to employ them in different combat scenarios while conserving expensive interceptor missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s approach differs significantly from that of other countries, Ihnat said. Ukrainian crews can deploy Patriot systems for ambushes rather than keeping them at fixed positions, such as airfields or military bases, and then relocate after engaging targets.
“For instance, rather than using the Patriot as a stationary asset – the way the Americans typically deploy it at airfields or bases – it can be used, in a sense, as a ‘roving’ system: set up an ambush, shoot down five aircraft, and then withdraw safely,” he said.
Ihnat also pointed to an incident in Russia’s Bryansk region as an example of the capabilities Ukrainian forces have demonstrated with the system.
Another key difference, he said, is ammunition use. Ukrainian crews have learned to use a single interceptor against a single target, while air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at one target.
‘Interceptors Still Not Coming’ – Zelensky Says US Has Yet to Authorize Patriot Deliveries
The Patriot system has three operating modes: automatic, semi-automatic and manual. Ihnat said that in automatic mode, the system can launch multiple interceptors at once.
Without sufficient combat experience, crews could end up firing an entire salvo from one launcher at a single target, including a relatively inexpensive Shahed drone.
“Because of this lack of experience, they might have fired an entire salvo of interceptors from a launcher at a single Shahed drone or a single ballistic missile,” Ihnat said.
He estimated that the number of interceptors expended in the Middle East could have kept Ukraine’s Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years.
“That is why we now find ourselves in the current crisis; the ammunition expended in the Middle East would have been enough to keep our Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years,” Ihnat said.
Notably, in March, a senior Ukrainian Air Force officer speaking to The Times criticized Gulf forces for using excessive numbers of expensive interceptor missiles against relatively cheap Iranian Shahed drones, saying Ukrainian crews typically use one or two missiles even against more complex targets.
Ukrainian officers said their battlefield experience has not been fully incorporated despite sharing operational data with allies.
They also described the March 1 incident in which Kuwaiti air defenses shot down three US F-15E fighter jets as “clear negligence,” arguing that better coordination could have prevented the friendly-fire incident.
During the first four days of the Iran war, the US and its allies reportedly fired more than 800 Patriot missiles – more than Ukraine received over three years of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has received just 24 Patriot air defense missiles from the US over the past 90 days, despite needing around 350 interceptors per month to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with ABC News.
Zelensky contrasted the limited deliveries to Ukraine with the roughly 2,000 partner-supplied interceptors fired during the first 84 hours of fighting in the Middle East.
Ukrainian officials have warned that the allocation of US-made Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles to the region is affecting supplies available to defend Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
On Oct. 16, Zelensky asked European leaders to provide 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter, warning that deliveries of just two to four missiles every few months were insufficient to counter Russian attacks.
He proposed that European countries with existing Patriot stocks help bridge the gap until new procurement arrangements and defense projects become operational.
However, efforts to secure missiles from European stockpiles have faced resistance. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Athens would not transfer PAC-2 missiles if doing so compromised Greece’s own defense capabilities in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:52:39 UTC
21:52:39 KST

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.
Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.
Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.
NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.
While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”
Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.
After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

A Jordanian court on Sunday sentenced seven leaders and members of the banned Muslim Brotherhood, including the group’s General Supervisor Murad Al-Adayleh, to prison terms ranging from six months to three years in a case involving illegal fundraising and money laundering.
According to Jordanian media reports, the verdicts are subject to appeal within one month.
Al-Adayleh and fellow Brotherhood leader Tariq Al-Raqab were each sentenced to six months in prison after being convicted of the misdemeanour of illegal fundraising.
Al-Adayleh was acquitted of charges related to violations of Jordan’s Anti-Money Laundering Law.
Five other Brotherhood leaders and activists received three-year prison sentences, including Ahmed Al-Zarqan, who was responsible for overseeing the organization’s financial affairs.
Al-Zarqan was convicted of violating the Anti-Money Laundering Law and engaging in illegal fundraising.
Four other defendants—Aref Hamdan, Ibrahim Hijazi, Mohammed Alayan and Omar Yassin—were also sentenced to three years in prison in connection with the same case.
During the proceedings, prosecutors alleged that funds collected by the defendants were not intended to support Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, despite claims associated with the fundraising activities.
The prosecution also alleged that some of the donations had been deposited into bank accounts through non-transparent financial arrangements, raising concerns about compliance with anti-money laundering regulations and the potential misuse of collected funds.
The verdicts come after Jordanian authorities banned the Muslim Brotherhood in April 2025.
All seven defendants retain the right to appeal their sentences within the legally prescribed period.

Russian-installed governor and two school staff members suspected of illegally transferring children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea
Volodymyr Saldo, the Russian-installed "governor of Kherson Oblast", and two staff members of the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum (specialised secondary school) have been served with a notice of suspicion over the illegal transfer of three children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea under the pretext of "recuperation".
Source: Office of the Prosecutor General; Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: The teenagers have since been brought back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
In October 2022, Saldo ordered the occupation administration's so-called "Ministry of Education" to arrange the transfer of children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea under the pretext of "recuperation".
The "ministry" issued an order for school holidays, and heads of educational institutions were instructed to arrange "recuperation" for students.
On 7 October 2022, three minors from the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum were taken to Crimea. The school's director prepared the documents, while a vocational training instructor accompanied the children. Their parents had not consented to the "recuperation".
The children were placed at the Druzhba children's camp in Yevpatoriia. They were later transferred to another camp. After the "holidays", they did not return home. Instead, in January 2023, they were enrolled at the Kerch Maritime Technical College without their parents' consent.
"The teenagers were involved in military-patriotic activities, exposed to Russian propaganda and had a Russian identity imposed on them," the Prosecutor's Office said.
One of the children had a severe form of diabetes and was admitted to intensive care in Yevpatoriia because of an insulin shortage. He spent about three weeks in hospital.
All three children have now been brought back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Saldo, the deputy director and the vocational training instructor at the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum have been served with a notice of suspicion of violating the laws and customs of war, committed by a group of people acting in prior collusion (Articles 28.2 and 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). They face up to 12 years in prison.
Background: Five children and young people were recently brought back from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.

Iran seeks to ease economic pressure from US sanctions through inflation control, food subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:51:56 UTC
21:51:56 KST

Sahin Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Iran is seeking to ease economic pressure from US and Western sanctions by slowing inflation and increasing food voucher allowances for households, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Monday.
Speaking to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency, Mohajerani said inflation was rooted in broader macroeconomic conditions and could not be addressed through short-term measures.
“We are trying to counter the economic pressure imposed on us by the West and the US by controlling the pace of inflation on the one hand and taking measures to improve people’s livelihoods, including increasing food voucher allowances, on the other,” she said.
The government is seeking to expand its electronic food voucher program, known as Kalabarg, which provides eligible households with subsidies to purchase essential food items.
Iran’s economy has faced mounting pressure from US sanctions, currency depreciation and rising consumer prices.
Washington launched a new economic pressure campaign, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, in August, targeting Iran’s oil exports, financial transactions and access to international markets.
The US also restored its naval blockade against vessels traveling to and from Iranian ports in July, further restricting Tehran’s oil trade.
Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in August that the country’s oil exports had fallen to zero amid the conflict and sanctions.
The International Monetary Fund projected in August that Iran’s economy would contract by 6.1% in 2026, with average annual inflation reaching 68.9%.
The economic difficulties have been compounded by the military conflict between Iran and the US, which began in February, and continuing disagreements over sanctions relief and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brazil’s Lula hangs on, but his final term promises to be toughest yet
- Lula won a record fourth term with 51.8% of votes, but analysts say his final term will be hard because Brazil has a more conservative Congress and weak economic growth.
- Fiscal policy is his biggest challenge. High debt, high interest rates and rising spending could block welfare promises, wage rises and tax changes.
- Congress may slow key appointments and reforms. Bolsonaro’s allies may also fight Lula and the courts, raising political tension and even impeachment risk.
AI generated
BRASILIA – Brazil’s octogenarian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva faces an uphill battle from day one of his final term, analysts say, with his plans hemmed in by economic headwinds and a right-wing Congress.
Already the country’s oldest president, Lula overcame a first-round loss to pull off a surprise run-off victory against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Oct 25, securing 51.8% of votes and a record fourth term just two days before his 81st birthday.
He will take office on Jan 5, 2027 after winning what he has said was his last election, hanging on to power in a country that has swung dramatically to the right since his first electoral victory in 2002.
Fiscal policy ‘his biggest challenge’
“Lula has shown that he still is the dominant political figure of his era, but he is weaker,” said Michael Ahn Paarlberg of the Center for International Policy think tank.
Brazil’s incoming Congress is its most conservative since the country’s return to democracy in the 1980s, with Bolsonaro’s party and its allies enjoying majorities in both chambers.
“He’s likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, an international relations professor at Sao Paulo’s Getulio Vargas Foundation, who predicted Lula would struggle to build a coalition to pass much of his agenda.
As of the morning of Oct 26, Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, had yet to concede, and Lula faced the prospect of adversaries in Congress who do not recognise his win, analysts said.
In addition, Congress has amassed significant power over government spending in the past decade, which could frustrate Lula’s promises to maintain his signature welfare programmes.
His government forecasts meagre 2.3% economic growth in 2027, adding to fiscal challenges worsened by high interest rates and public debt that has grown past 82% of gross domestic product, the highest since the Covid-19 pandemic.
“On the broad macroeconomic outlook, things are not looking great,” said Monica de Bolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
A hostile Congress “will make it very hard to push any reform through Congress and even try to manage the budget”, she said.
Lula’s promises to ensure minimum wage increases remain above inflation are among those that clash with growing pressure to get debt under control.
Lula’s aides have signalled that he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.
“Fiscal policy remains Lula’s biggest economic challenge,” said Andres Abadia, chief Latin American economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, as growing mandatory spending and high interest costs leave little room to cut deficits.
Analysts said an economic crisis could even spur Lula’s impeachment, with some drawing comparisons to Brazil’s 2014-2016 crisis, which preceded the impeachment of Lula’s ally Dilma Rousseff.
“I think the campaign for Lula’s impeachment begins now,” said Paulo Kramer, a political scientist who worked on former president Bolsonaro’s first campaign and has spoken to people close to his son.
Investors reacted nervously on the morning of Oct 26, sending Brazilian assets sharply lower as markets reassessed the country’s fiscal outlook under Lula.
Senate stumbling block
Congress is likely to block or slow Lula’s appointments to key roles in institutions such as the Supreme Court and the central bank, analysts say.
For the first time since Brazil returned to democracy, the executive branch will be clearly at odds with the Senate, said Lucas de Aragao, a partner at Brasilia-based consultancy Arko Advice.
“Lula will have some room to negotiate in the lower house by giving centrist parties more space, but in the Senate, he will have to bargain issue by issue and adjust his legislative agenda to fit what the opposition wants,” Aragao added.
Bolsonaro’s allies in the incoming Senate have also vowed to impeach Justice Alexandre de Moraes, escalating their long-running fight with a powerful judiciary that has often aligned with Lula, blocking key right-wing legislation and shaping policy on everything from Indigenous rights to the internet. Germany Moves to Buy Ukrainian-Made Bars Missiles for Bundeswehr in Historic First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:50:25 UTC

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Germany Moves to Buy Ukrainian-Made Bars Missiles for Bundeswehr in Historic First
Germany is preparing to purchase Ukrainian-developed Bars cruise missiles for its armed forces, potentially marking the first time the Bundeswehr has acquired an offensive weapon designed in Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 26, citing people familiar with the plans, Berlin could finalize an agreement for an initial batch within weeks. The missiles would undergo technical testing in early 2027, with successful trials potentially leading to an order of several hundred units.
The Bars is a jet-powered cruise missile capable of striking targets up to 1,000 kilometers away and carrying a warhead of up to 105 kilograms, depending on the variant. Ukrainian officials sometimes classify it as a drone-missile, while Germany considers it a low-cost cruise missile.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously identified Bars among the weapons used to strike Russian military bases and energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that Bars missiles are already being manufactured in Germany through a Ukrainian-German joint venture established under the Build with Ukraine initiative. The first German-funded batch was delivered to Ukraine in October 2026.
The planned Bundeswehr purchase would expand the venture’s production beyond supplying Ukraine, reflecting growing European interest in Ukrainian defense technologies developed and tested during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Germany is also seeking more affordable alternatives to American Tomahawk cruise missiles, which cost approximately $4 million to $6 million each and are unlikely to arrive before the 2030s because of production constraints.
According to the Financial Times, Bars missiles cost even less than the US-developed Anthem cruise missile, which is priced at roughly one-tenth of a Tomahawk. Berlin plans to test both systems, while a potential purchase of Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missile has been postponed.
The procurement plans form part of Germany’s broader €780 billion rearmament effort over five years, aimed at expanding military capabilities and strengthening European deterrence against Russia.
Earlier, in September, a European joint venture began producing Ukraine’s Bars jet-powered drones, with initial deliveries scheduled for October. The system can reach speeds exceeding 700 km/h and strike targets up to 1,000 kilometers away. Its modular design allows developers to adjust payload capacity and range depending on operational requirements.

Putin’s Valdai Residence Now Has 50+ Air Defense Positions—Half as Many as All of Moscow
Russia has built another 16 air-defense towers around Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing the number of identified air-defense positions in the surrounding area to more than 50, according to a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) investigation published October 25.
The new sites were identified through satellite imagery analyzed jointly with OSINT researcher jembob.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators found that the 16 towers were constructed in October within roughly 50 kilometers south of the residence—the direction facing Ukraine.
The new structures appear to form an additional outer air-defense ring and are expected to host Pantsir gun-and-missile systems, Tor surface-to-air missile systems, or similar equipment.
No corresponding new positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the outer ring, although investigators said additional construction could follow.
The new defensive belt passes through Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
Khotilovo is used for Putin’s travel, and a dedicated railway line connects the airfield area with his Valdai residence. One air-defense tower at the base had already been constructed by March 2026.
Several additional positions have appeared around the reservoir, including near Lisiy Island. Russian forces have built a laboratory complex there that, according to an earlier RFE/RL investigation, may be connected to Russia’s biological weapons research program.
Construction of two air-defense towers near that facility began in early September, roughly when the investigation into the laboratory became public.
The latest expansion pushes the number of known air-defense positions around Valdai above 50.
That figure is particularly striking when compared with Moscow. Russia has built roughly twice as many air-defense positions to protect Moscow and the surrounding region since the beginning of the full-scale invasion—but Moscow and its suburbs are home to more than 20 million people.
Fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, the surrounding district, and nearby territory within roughly 50 kilometers.
Previously, Russian leader Vladimir Putin signed an order to expand the core personnel of the Federal Protective Service, marking the fourth increase since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
