26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
More than half of research participants in Switzerland consider disinformation a "major" social problem, expressing concern over misinformation, according to a study released Monday.  
The findings were published in the University of Zurich's Research Centre for the Public Sphere and Society 2026 Quality of the Media Yearbook, Swissinfo reported.
Some 56.5% of the participants view "fake news as a major social problem," the report noted. 
The latest percentage represents a "significant" increase compared with five years ago, it added.
The study found that more than half of respondents regularly encounter misleading information, particularly through social media, video-sharing platforms, and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Some 42% were classified as "news-deprived," referring to people who rarely follow current affairs or rely on fragmented information from social media, making them more vulnerable to conspiracy theories.
Researchers found that relying exclusively on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram offered no greater protection against conspiracy theories than avoiding news altogether.
While overall news quality remained stable in 2025, media diversity declined, with 44.7% of national political coverage appearing across multiple German-language publications.
The study also found that 57.7% of respondents considered public broadcasting important or very important.
Meanwhile, technology platforms captured up to 2.5 billion Swiss francs ($3 billion) in annual advertising revenue, while domestic media revenues fell to 1.94 billion francs ($2.3 billion).
The researchers called for countermeasures, such as media vouchers for young adults.

Hamas on Sunday condemned Israeli airstrikes on the campus of the Islamic University in Gaza City, describing the attack as a war crime and urging mediators and guarantor states of the ceasefire agreement to intervene immediately.
In a statement, the movement said the strikes occurred while students were present on campus, killing three university staff members and injuring several others.
Hamas described the attack as a “clear-cut war crime” and accused Israel of continuing its military operations against civilian institutions despite the ceasefire agreement.
The movement said the bombing was part of what it described as an ongoing campaign of destruction and attacks against Palestinians in Gaza.
Hamas also accused the Israeli government of repeatedly violating the ceasefire through continued airstrikes, killings and military raids targeting residential neighbourhoods, displacement camps and civilian facilities.
The movement further said that Israeli forces were expanding the territory under their control by shifting the ceasefire’s designated “yellow line” westward.
It also accused Israel of obstructing the entry of essential food supplies into Gaza, arguing that the restrictions violated its obligations under the ceasefire agreement and undermined the efforts of mediators and guarantor countries.
Hamas called on the parties overseeing the agreement to take immediate action to prevent further attacks on civilians and ensure compliance with the ceasefire.
The movement urged mediators to exert pressure on Israel to halt military operations, lift restrictions on humanitarian assistance and provide relief to more than two million Palestinians facing severe humanitarian conditions in Gaza.
The reported casualties and circumstances of the university strike were presented in Hamas’s statement and were not independently verified in the report.

French student representatives hail govt's ‘concrete measures’, call for protests to continue
Representatives from French high school student groups on Monday hailed the government’s first measures to calm the crisis over ongoing unrest linked to their protest movement, including a gradual replacement of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup, but called for “continued mobilisation” after their meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Read about the day’s events as they unfolded on our liveblog.
This page is no longer being updated. For more of our coverage, click here.
'The success of our young people must not depend on their social background,' PM Lecornu says
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu posted on X, "The success of our young people must not depend on their social background, their high school, or the area in which they grow up."
He added, "In recent weeks, high school students and college students have expressed strong expectations. The national consultation of high school students... has brought their concerns and proposals to light."
New government measures proposed to quell high school student unrest
- Reform of the Parcoursup admissions system in 2027, ahead of its full replacement in 2028
- Creation of 15,000 additional higher education places
- A cap of 28 students per class in the "seconde" (first year of high school)
- A €5 billion low-interest loan for the renovation of educational infrastructure (€4 billion towards secondary schools, €1 billion for universities)
- 500 additional teaching positions
- Adjustment to student grants, bringing them in line with inflation
No 'empty promises', education minister says
France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray stated on Monday that "none of the decisions" made in response to the crisis involving high school students "are empty".
"Everything we say will be done and will be honoured within specific timeframes and with clear, quantifiable targets," he declared during a press conference, following a meeting held on Monday – alongside Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu – with high school and student organisations.
French student union leaders call for 'continued mobilisation' after meeting PM
The French government met student representatives on Monday following weeks of unrest. Students who had been demanding a meeting for weeks hail progress. Nonetheless they are now calling for fresh demonstrations next Saturday (October 31) to press for further measures.
Details by FRANCE 24’s French Politics Editor Marc Perelman.
Major evolution to Parcoursup admissions platform proposed
French Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste has announced that there will be a "major evolution" of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup in 2027, followed by its "replacement in 2028".
The system that has faced significant criticism from high school students since the onset of the crisis.
During a press conference, Baptiste explained the need for a "two-stage" transition by noting that Parcoursup "is anchored in law".
He stated, "Consequently, certain parametres of Parcoursup can only be altered if the law itself is changed."
Consultations with school, student groups to commence, education minister says
"Starting tomorrow, we will launch a consultation process with high school students and staff trade unions to examine the role of continuous assessment in high schools and for the baccalaureate." – Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray
Classroom cap
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray says tenth-grade classroom sizes will be capped at 28 pupils within two years.
Funds for renovation of education facilities
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray pledges a €4 billion budget to be made available for catchment areas to continue, scale up, and complete building renovation projects.
Issues raised by students
Among the main issues raised by high school students are:
- imbalanced school scheduling
- ill-suited school facilities
- subsitution issues when replacing absent teachers
- overcrowded classrooms
- challenges related to classroom atmosphere and mental health
- pressure surrounding academic orientation and the Parcoursup admissions system
- high school voices not being sufficiently heard
Education ministers to hold press conference at 7pm
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray and Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste plan to hold a press conference at 7pm to provide details of various measures to assuage the demands of protesting high schoolers.
The ministers spent the afternoon meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, as well as high school and university organisations.
Louis Létoublon, vice-president of prominent French high school union Les Lycéens! called for seeing things "through to the end", urging further mobilisation next Saturday and on November 5 – a date designated by trade unions for a general strike.
"The government is afraid; it has clearly shown that it is disoriented by everything that has been happening. This fear gives us an opening – a breach we can exploit to secure as much as possible in defence of high school students' rights."
Macron promises 'concrete measures' in response to French students' demands
French President Emmanuel Macron said the government would announce “concrete measures" on Monday to address school students’ demands after weeks of unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was scheduled to meet with students later Monday. FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago reports from the ground.
High school student representatives welcome 'concrete announcements' but call for 'continued mobilisation'
Speaking to FRANCE 24, Clément Vieillot, co-founder of the “Cachan 94” collective, said that the measures announced by the government are “not enough”.
“The announcements from the Lecornu government are woefully inadequate. The government is offering a €4 billion loan to the regions; not only is this insufficient for infrastructure, but it also means the regions will have to repay it.”
Furthermore, “we were asking for 250,000 additional spots in higher education, yet we’re only getting 4,000. This is completely absurd,” he continued, calling for “the movement to continue until our demands are heard and implemented”.
National Assembly debate on Parcoursup to be held at 5pm
The French government will hold a non-binding National Assembly debate at 5pm on the future of high-school orientation and the placement of students in higher education, following President Emmanuel Macron’s pledge to overhaul admissions portal Parcoursup.
The debate will be held under Article 50-1 of the Constitution, meaning politicians will be allowed to present proposals without involving any voting. The government plans a two-phase replacement of Parcoursup this academic year and next, amid the ongoing student protest crisis.
Amnesty International calls on French government to 'abandon' 'Make Rioters Pay' bill
Human rights organisation Amnesty International is urging the French government to "abandon" its plans to introduce a "make rioters pay" bill, which it claims could potentially "violate France's obligations under international human rights law".
"The government must abandon this new, rights-infringing bill, which poses a serious threat to the right to protests, by exposing all demonstrators to the risk of financial penalties," wrote Nathalie Godard, Director of Action at Amnesty International France in a press release.
Deemed "absolutely essential" by French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, the legislation will be debated in the Senate starting Tuesday just over a week after looting and violence marred peaceful demonstrations across France on October 17.
Higher education admissions platform Parcoursup could be replaced by end of next academic year
The government plans to replace admissions platform Parcoursup in two phases over the course of this academic year and the next, according to the education-focussed social media influencers who met with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday at midday, ahead of his meetings with youth organisations.
The higher education admissions platform has faced heavy criticism from high school students since the start of the current protest movement.
Minister of Education Edouard Geffray and Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste are set to unveil "concrete" plans at 5.30pm during a press conference.
More than 400,000 protest across France Saturday
Saturday’s demonstrations across France were largely peaceful, easing fears of a repeat of the violence seen the prior weekend.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets to demand action on the rising cost of living and more funding for public services, with students, workers and retirees marching side by side.
Many say their anger shows no sign of fading. The government put turnout at 410,000 nationwide, while the CGT union – organisers of the authorised demonstrations – estimated the figure was almost twice as high.
FRANCE 24's Jack Pownall shares more 📺.
Shopkeepers fear ongoing impact to trade
"There’s no such thing as a business without customers; the clientele needs to return."
Between precautionary shop closures and a drop in footfall, shopkeepers grow increasingly concerned about the impact that Saturday social protests are having on their sales – against an already gloomy economic backdrop.
The year's final quarter is typically a crucial period for businesses in the run-up to the holiday season.
And while Saturday’s day of protest was calmer than expected – despite some clashes and isolated incidents of looting in several cities – "the fact remains that we didn't do any business this weekend," laments Virginie Grimault, General Delegate of the Federation of Grocery and Local Convenience Stores (FECP), in an interview with AFP.
October 24 protests: 267 police officers and 150 protesters injured, including three seriously
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while the activity on October 24 in general was kept under control, "we observed a very high level of violence directed at internal security forces," with "267" police officers and gendarmes injured, he told network RMC/BFMTV.
"An estimated 150" protesters were injured" – three of them "quite seriously" in Toulouse, Reims, and Clermont-Ferrand – the minister announced, noting that the injuries occurred "during police operations, given the context of extreme violence."
He added that "investigations by the IGPN" – the national police oversight body – "are underway, as is the case every time".
🗣️ 'Not normal' for France to be in turmoil so close to election, says Macron
Macron says it is "not normal for France to be in such "turmoil" six months from the election – according to reports by AFP.
He called for the type of unrest seen on October 17 to "never" happen again.
"We will continue to hold the line," Macron told security forces on a visit to Marseille. "If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

A 51-year-old worker was crushed to
death by machinery in Brindisi on Monday in the latest in a long
spate of accidental workplace deaths in Italy.
                                    
The man died at an agricultural business in the Puglia city
after being crushed by a piece of machinery he was transporting.
                                    
The Brindisi local police and SPESAL (the occupational health
and safety service) are currently on-site investigating to
clarify the exact circumstances of the accident.
                                    
Attempts by 118 emergency medical personnel to resuscitate the
man proved unsuccessful.
                                    
Workplace deaths are a big problem in Italy.
                                    
Workplace accident insurance agency INAIL said in its annual
report recently that Italy registered 1,189 work-related deaths
in 2025.
                                    
Although this was 37 fewer than in 2024, a drop of 3.02%, it
still means that Italy is averaging over three work-related
deaths every day.

Beyond the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia’s Strategic Footprint in PNG Grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

Last week Australia’s foreign and defense ministers, Penny Wong and Richard Marles, travelled to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea (PNG) to lead Australia’s delegation to the 32nd Australia-Papua New Guinea Ministerial Forum. The meeting was the first since the Pukpuk Treaty, which established PNG’s first formal defense alliance with another country, entered into force in July. The forum focused on turning the treaty’s commitments into practical initiatives for defense cooperation, infrastructure, recruitment, and new technologies.
The headline agreement was a new rotation of Australian defense personnel to PNG. A new combat group of 130 Australian Defense Force (ADF) personnel will be based in PNG on three month rotations. The deployment, known as the Magani Rotation, is intended to deepen military cooperation and increase familiarity between the two forces.
A rotation offers greater advantages over occasional military exercises. It allows personnel to develop more consistent working relationships, become familiar with how each defense force works, and be able to coordinate activities over longer periods. For PNG, it provides greater access to Australian military expertise, while for Australia, it strengthens its ability to operate alongside a neighbor whose geography makes it important to the defense of Australia’s northern approaches.
Alongside this, the two governments also announced a $77 million infrastructure investment fund for the PNG Defense Force. This funding is intended to upgrade PNG’s military facilities to be better able to house, train, and sustain additional personnel.
While the Magani Rotation may be a significant step in advancing the integration of the two defense forces, the more radical idea is the opening up of Australian military recruitment to eligible Papua New Guineans. Applications for the first intake will open on November 16, with an initial pilot program starting in 2027. The first two cohorts will comprise roughly 50 recruits each, with candidates initially sought from the University of Papua New Guinea, Pacific Adventist University, and the University of Technology in Lae. The program is intended to expand over time, although the initial recruitment numbers are modest.
In order to address recruitment shortages, Australia has already expanded ADF recruitment to Australian permanent residents from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada who are on the pathway to citizenship. However, the new PNG recruitment is different – it has been established under the Pukpuk Treaty and will allow eligible PNG citizens living in PNG to apply directly.
The initial rationale is similar – to overcome persistent personnel shortages – but it comes with a broader strategic goal. These recruits will train and serve alongside Australians, creating personal, cultural and institutional links as part of a longer-term alliance-building objective. Australia citizenship will be an eventual requirement, but this will come via the conventional permanent residency and citizenship application processes.
At the ministerial forum, Australia and PNG also formalized a partnership covering digital governance, network security, and emerging technologies. The agreement builds on a Telecommunications Blueprint designed to improve PNG’s connectivity and digital infrastructure. For Australia, the partnership has strategic as well as economic significance: secure telecommunications networks are essential to military coordination, government resilience, and the protection of critical infrastructure. It also gives Canberra a greater role in shaping the systems connecting PNG to the outside world, while helping the country strengthen its own digital capabilities.
Australia’s alliance with PNG builds on an existing security program. Since 2023, Canberra has committed AU$200 million under the bilateral security agreement to support PNG’s police and justice institutions, including upgraded training facilities, police helicopters, and a National Forensic Science Center. A second phase of support is planned after the current program ends in 2027. Though separate from the Pukpuk Treaty, this work strengthens PNG’s capacity to maintain internal security and exercise authority across its territory.
The challenge for both Australia and PNG is to turn these commitments into lasting capabilities. Australia is investing serious capital in PNG – including across issues like health and other social infrastructure – and hopes to gain a return for its investment. This return for Australia is PNG’s ability to develop its defense, economic, and social capabilities, and to be better equipped to contribute to its own security and regional stability. This also comes with the caveat that it keeps PNG within Australia’s orbit of influence. For Port Moresby, the objective will be whether its alliance with Australia actually increases PNG sovereign capabilities and improves its development objectives, rather than simply accommodating Australia’s strategic priorities.

Jordan says three family members behind Karak church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:44:22 UTC
21:44:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Jordan says three members of one family behind Karak church attack
Jordanian authorities on Monday identified three suspects arrested at dawn over last week's deadly church attack as members of the same family.
"The perpetrators of the attack on the church were two brothers and the third was their relative by marriage," Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said at a press conference. He named the three as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.
The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, in Karak governorate, killed nine people and wounded 34 others during a funeral service.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya and Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani, the security chief described the suspects as extremists who had adopted an extremist ideology.
He said the three men lived near Hamoud village and had acted without prior planning.
According to the security chief, the suspects were following the funeral procession when they decided to carry out the attack, a decision he attributed to their extremist beliefs.
He said the three men had developed the idea together while following the procession, rather than preparing the assault in advance.
Following the shooting, the suspects fled the scene in a single vehicle, which was later recovered by investigators.
Security forces also seized firearms and a large quantity of ammunition following their arrest.
Suspects arrested after shootout
Jordanian authorities announced early on Monday that they had arrested all three suspects following an armed confrontation at an abandoned house in the village of Al-Jadida, approximately five kilometres from Hamoud.
The Public Security Director said security teams had spent three days searching designated areas before narrowing their operation to a number of abandoned buildings.
Shortly after midnight on Sunday night, officers divided part of Al-Jadida into sectors and identified several abandoned houses for inspection.
The operation led security forces to the building where the suspects were hiding.
According to the Public Security Directorate, the men refused to surrender and opened fire on officers, prompting an exchange of gunfire.
All three suspects were wounded before being taken into custody and transferred to hospital. No members of the security forces were injured during the operation.
The security chief said investigators had pursued two lines of inquiry immediately after the attack.
The first focused on criminal investigations, intelligence gathering and collecting evidence from the scene.
The second involved emergency response measures, surveillance operations and tracking the suspects' movements and escape routes.
No evidence of links to wider groups
Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said investigators had found no indications that the suspects were connected to other extremist cells or organisations.
He stressed, however, that the investigation remained ongoing and that authorities would pursue anyone found to have helped plan, encourage or facilitate the attack.
Al-Faraya described the killings as the product of an extremist ideology that was alien to Jordanian values and traditions.
He said tackling terrorism required more than arresting those responsible, calling for efforts to address the roots of extremism, hate speech and incitement.
The minister also referred to King Abdullah II's visit to survivors in hospital, during which the monarch pledged a firm response against those responsible for the killings.
Al-Faraya said the successful arrest operation demonstrated the authorities' commitment to protecting citizens and ensuring accountability.
Jordan warns against sectarian divisions
Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani urged Jordanians not to allow the attack to fuel religious hatred or divisions within society.
He described the killings as a turning point in the country's efforts to confront extremist and takfiri ideology, announcing that the government would continue working to combat radicalisation across different sectors.
Al-Momani said royal directives had called for a review of policies aimed at countering extremist thought and addressing its underlying causes through a systematic national strategy.
He stressed that confronting extremism was a shared responsibility involving government institutions, religious authorities, schools, the media and wider society.
Protecting the public, he argued, required challenging not only acts of violence but also the ideas and rhetoric used to justify them.
The minister also warned against misinformation and rumours, saying misleading information could spread fear, undermine public confidence and encourage incitement during times of crisis.
He urged the public to avoid discussions that could deepen religious or social divisions, stressing that the actions of extremists should not be used to blame entire communities.
"We must not allow terrorism to achieve through words what it failed to achieve through crime," Al-Momani said.
He added that Jordanian citizenship was not determined by religious or social identity and that no citizen should have to prove their belonging to the country.
The government would not allow extremist ideology to redefine relations between Jordanians or undermine the shared national identity that united them under the rule of law, he said.
Al-Momani also praised the solidarity shown by Jordanians towards the families of those killed, describing it as a demonstration of the country's rejection of hatred and division.
"This solidarity embodies our belief that the suffering of any Jordanian is the suffering of us all, and that our national unity is firmly rooted and cannot be undermined by terrorism," he said.
The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud took place during a funeral service, leaving nine people dead and 34 others injured.
Authorities have pledged to continue investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings and bring anyone involved to justice.

New free email service against phishing: “Protecting people with less digital literacy”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:42:42 UTC
21:42:42 KST

A suspicious email sent to his mother gave Jany Ertveldt an idea. The Fleming developed a free service that analyses suspicious emails within minutes and explains whether they are safe. The aim is to better protect people with less digital literacy, in particular against online scammers.
New free email service against phishing: “Protecting people with less digital literacy”
The idea came about a few weeks ago when Ertveldt’s mother received an email purporting to be from a parcel delivery service. She was asked to pay €1.99 to receive her parcel and wasn’t sure whether the message was genuine.
“As it happened, my mum had just ordered something online,” says Ertveldt. “She asked if I could have a look to see if the email was genuine. Because of my work, I could tell straight away that it was a typical phishing email. But not everyone recognises it that quickly.”
According to Jany Ertveldt, such messages are sent to hundreds or even thousands of people. “Some of them fall for it, and that’s how scammers make money.”
Simply forward a suspicious email
With info@checkmijnmail.be Ertveldt aims to make the process as simple as possible. Users do not need to install any app or software. They simply forward a suspicious email and receive an analysis back within a few minutes.
“You can see straight away what’s suspicious about the email,” he says. “If it concerns a perfectly normal advertising email. Even then, the system explains exactly what’s going on.”
The system checks the sender, the domain behind the email address, links in the message and even QR codes. It also checks how long a website has been in existence.
“Fraudsters often use domains that have only recently been created,” explains Ertveldt. “That can be an important warning sign.”
Database containing hundreds of suspicious websites
The email service compares emails against a database of more than 600 domains. This database is updated every week with new reports and warnings.
“We’re expanding the system every week,” says Ertveldt. “We monitor reports of online fraud and add new information. This makes the system increasingly smarter.”
Since its launch, he has noticed that more and more people are using the service. “At the moment, dozens of users have already had an email checked. We’re seeing growing interest.”
Privacy must continue to be guaranteed
According to Ertveldt, privacy has been a key priority from the outset. That is why the service does not store forwarded emails.
“As soon as someone has received the analysis, the email is deleted,” he says. “At the end of the day, we also delete all log files. We do not keep any records of the user.”
Dream of collaborating with the government
The service is free, and Ertveldt wants to keep it that way. His ambition is to reach even more people and further expand the system.
“I want it to remain as simple as possible,” he says. “Ideally, in the future we could collaborate with the government or with cyber safety agency Safeonweb. That way, we can help even more people recognise phishing for free.”

‘More they do it, stronger PDA gets’: Akhilesh Yadav alleges 'misinformation campaign' against SP-Congress alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:42:05 UTC
21:42:05 KST

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Monday alleged that efforts were being made to spread misinformation about the party’s seat-sharing negotiations with the Congress but maintained that such attempts would only strengthen the alliance’s support base among the “PDA” communities.The term “PDA”, coined by Akhilesh Yadav, stands for “Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak”, referring to Other Backward Classes, Dalits and minorities. These groups form a key focus of the SP’s political outreach.
Addressing a press conference at the SP headquarters in Lucknow, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister questioned who was putting up the posters and "funding" the campaign. He was referring to a recently installed hoarding in the state capital featuring Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, with the message: “200 seats are our right; UP trusts Rahul Gandhi.”“These objectionable posters have not appeared for the first time. Who is putting them up? Who is spending money on them? Who is running this racket?” Akhilesh Yadav asked.He added that such campaigns would only strengthen the PDA, saying, “The more they put up such posters, spread misinformation and insult others, the stronger the PDA will become.”The Congress has reportedly shared with the SP a list of 175-200 seats it wants to contest in the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections scheduled for February-March 2027.
Responding to questions about the SP’s alliance with the Congress, Akhilesh Yadav stated that his party's leaders have experience in bringing political parties together and managing alliances.“Samajwadi Party and all our leaders know how to bring people together. We all have experience in managing alliances. We will strengthen our alliance ahead of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections,” he remarked.
The SP and Congress contested the 2017 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections in alliance but suffered a setback, with the Akhilesh Yadav-led party winning just 47 of the 403 seats as it was voted out after a single term. The Congress fared worse with only seven seats, while the BJP came to power with a sweeping victory, winning 312 constituencies.In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP won 255 seats, while the SP secured 111. The Congress managed only two seats, with the SP and Congress contesting separately.However, the two parties reunited for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning a combined 43 of Uttar Pradesh’s 80 seats. The SP won 37 constituencies and the Congress six, while the BJP’s tally fell to 33, down from 71 seats in 2014 and 62 in 2019.(With PTI inputs)

Russia discredits the humanitarian truce in Oleshky — analysis
Kyiv • UNN
Russian outlets are presenting the truce in the occupied city of Oleshky, Kherson region, as a trap for Russian troops, without providing any evidence. In fact, the agreement provides for evacuation and assistance.
Russian propaganda portrays the ceasefire in the occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region as a trap for Russian troops, claiming that Ukraine plans to bring in boats and prepare to cross the Dnipro, but these accusations are not supported by evidence. This was reported by the Center for Strategic Communications in a report dated October 26, UNN reports.
Details
"Between October 23 and 25, the Center for Strategic Communications recorded 1,173 publications disseminating the corresponding narrative," the statement said.
The Pravda network claimed that Ukraine had allegedly initiated the ceasefire in order to bring in boats and prepare to cross the Dnipro. However, these accusations are not supported by evidence: propaganda groundlessly presents the humanitarian agreement as cover for a military operation.
"Russian resources are turning the agreement on evacuation and the delivery of aid into evidence of Ukraine's alleged \"military madness.\" At the same time, Russia is portrayed as the side that conscientiously fulfills its obligations and seeks peace. The aim of the information interventions is to discredit the humanitarian initiative, prepare in advance justifications for possible violations of the ceasefire regime by Russia, and reinforce Moscow's image as a peacemaker," the Center for Strategic Communications noted.
The Center emphasized that the information trigger was the agreement on a local ceasefire in Oleshky, announced on October 23 with the mediation of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump. Russian Ombudswoman Lantратova and Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets agreed to a ceasefire to evacuate people and deliver humanitarian aid.

The United States announced an agreement between Russia and Ukraine on a local ceasefire in the occupied city of Oleshky.
Later, the head of the parliamentary faction of the political party "Servant of the People" in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, David Arakhamia, confirmed that an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky in the Kherson region and its outskirts would begin in the near future.

U.S. Air Force trains with heavy drone hunter with net gun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:35:16 UTC
21:35:16 KST

- The U.S. Air Force trained with Zone 5 Technologies’ Paladin counter-drone multirotor at MacDill Air Force Base on Oct. 8.
- The drone carried a Gen12 launcher that fires net rounds to entangle and bring down hostile drones.
The U.S. Air Force has put the Paladin, a heavy counter-drone multirotor built by California-based Zone 5 Technologies, through training with Joint Interagency Task Force 401 at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida on Oct. 8, with the drone carrying a Gen12 counter-drone launcher that fires net rounds to entangle and bring down hostile drones, according to photos and captions released by the base.
Photos from the training show the compact, magazine-fed launcher mounted on a stabilized gimbal beneath the six-rotor drone, with net rounds and a deployed net laid out beside the aircraft. The base said the system uses a net round to bring down drones, giving MacDill an additional option for protecting personnel and infrastructure as part of a layered defense, but the Air Force did not say how many systems took part, whether any live intercepts were carried out, or whether the base plans to buy the Paladin.
Net rounds work by throwing a net into the path of a target drone so that it wraps around the rotors and stops the aircraft from flying, an approach that suits bases and other sensitive sites because it avoids sending bullets or explosive fragments into the area below. MacDill hosts the 6th Air Refueling Wing as well as the headquarters of U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command.
The Paladin is a multi-mission drone that Zone 5 describes as a fully autonomous wingman integrated with the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK) mapping and command software used across the U.S. military. It uses a quick-swap payload system, so operators can change it in the field between the counter-drone launcher, a munitions drop, a 7.62 mm (.308-caliber) rifle, and a loudspeaker and spotlight.
Zone 5 markets the counter-drone version as a Low Collateral Effects Interceptor, and the Paladin was the first drone of its kind added to the Department of War’s Blue UAS Cleared List, which approves drones for use across the U.S. military. The company also selected Echodyne’s EchoFlight radar to give the interceptor its own real-time picture of the airspace and the ability to track target drones autonomously.
The training at MacDill also featured the Bumblebee V2, a separate counter-drone system that intercepts hostile drones by ramming them, which the 6th Security Forces Squadron received as a low-cost option for its layered defense.
Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which Secretary of War Pete Hegseth established in August 2025, is the Department of War’s lead organization for countering small drones and has been testing and fielding systems at U.S. installations to protect them from drone incursions, which have been reported over military bases at home and abroad.
Zone 5 Technologies, founded in 2011 and based in San Luis Obispo, California, also develops the White Spike low-cost interceptor missile for counter-drone and precision strike missions, and the Air Force has not said whether the Paladin will be fielded at MacDill or other bases after the training.

Israeli elections: Will Trump’s endorsement help or hurt Netanyahu?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:35:09 UTC
21:35:09 KST

US President Donald Trump's endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could prove a double-edged sword ahead of Tuesday's election, with analysts saying it may help the embattled leader consolidate support but is unlikely to sway many voters and could even backfire.
Trump publicly backed Netanyahu on Sunday for the second time in a week, urging Israelis to re-elect the prime minister and linking his leadership to Washington's campaign against Iran.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump reiterated his support for Netanyahu, whom he had described a week earlier as a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a key partner in confronting Tehran.
The endorsement came as polls suggested Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc could struggle to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said Trump's intervention was unlikely to significantly influence the outcome.
"Trump's pledge will have little impact on the Israeli voters; it was more of a desperate attempt by Netanyahu, who begged Trump to give him an endorsement, to get some support from his friend, at a time when in Israel the opposition parties seem, at least according to recent polls, to do quite well."
Axios reported Sunday, citing US and Israeli sources, that Netanyahu had personally pressed Trump for additional public support last week, even suggesting specific language for the endorsement.
Netanyahu's Likud party denied the report, although Trump had told Newsmax earlier this month that people in Israel had asked him to intervene on Netanyahu's behalf.
Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King's College London, warned that the intervention could backfire among Israelis who resent foreign involvement in domestic politics.
"Trump's endorsement might even cause damage to Netanyahu, as many Israeli voters, including from Likud, hate this external intervention in domestic Israeli politics," he said.
Israelis head to the polls Tuesday to elect all 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in a pivotal election that will decide the country’s political direction amid the Gaza genocide and the war with Iran.
Netanyahu's bloc faces a challenge from opposition parties, including one led by Gadi Eisenkot, as both sides seek a path to forming the next government.
A recent Channel 12 poll suggested Trump's endorsement had done little to boost Netanyahu's prospects. Some 64% of respondents said it would not influence their vote, while 17% said it made them less likely to support Netanyahu.
Only 12% said the endorsement strengthened their support for his Likud party.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the RANE Network, said the endorsement could matter even if it fails to change many voters' minds.
"I don't think it'll change too many minds that are already made up, but Israel is such a fractious political environment, you don't need to change that many minds for it to necessarily be a decisive outcome."
Bohl suggested Trump's backing could discourage some traditional Likud voters from switching to rival right-wing parties, including those associated with opposition figures such as Avigdor Lieberman.
For center-right voters increasingly dissatisfied with Netanyahu, the endorsement could reinforce the argument that he is best placed to manage relations with Washington.
"I think for the center-right kind of national conservative voters that are traditionally go with Likud, who are getting sick of Netanyahu, I think this is a reminder to them that Netanyahu is, at least for the near term, at least for this presidency, indispensable."
Bohl said the endorsement could also strengthen Netanyahu's position in post-election coalition negotiations, particularly if neither bloc secures a clear majority.
Netanyahu could use his relationship with Trump to attract smaller parties or individual lawmakers during coalition negotiations, arguing that his ties with Washington give him an advantage on issues including Iran and the occupied West Bank.
Trump's endorsement marks an unusual intervention in Israeli politics, departing from the longstanding practice of US presidents avoiding explicit support for candidates in Israeli elections.
"I think it's unusual because American presidents don't usually endorse," Bohl said, describing the move as "very Trumpian."
He said the intervention comes as some Israelis question whether their country's close relationship with Washington can be sustained in the long term.
Netanyahu, however, could use his close relationship with Trump to argue that he is best placed to maintain strong ties with Washington, Bohl said.
But an endorsement from Trump does not guarantee electoral success.
Bregman pointed to Trump's backing of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who lost his country's parliamentary election in April.
“An endorsement from this guy in the White House is not necessarily a recipe for electoral success,” Bregman said.
He also questioned whether Trump's backing came without expectations in return.
Bregman raised similar questions about what Netanyahu might have offered in exchange for the endorsement.
“You don’t get a free meal from Trump,” he said. "What exactly did Netanyahu promise in return? I'm not sure. Perhaps Netanyahu pledged not to attack Iran before the Israeli elections and the American midterm elections."
The endorsement comes amid growing debate in the US over support for Israel following the wars in Gaza and Iran.
Bohl said declining support for Israel among some Americans could create political challenges for politicians closely associated with the Israeli government.
“Israel is becoming more and more unpopular in the United States,” Bohl said.
He pointed to changes in the political environment surrounding the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), including shifts in campaign spending and the use of new political action committees.
Bohl also contrasted Trump's intervention with US Vice President JD Vance's decision not to endorse Netanyahu.
He argued that Vance was mindful of growing criticism of Israel among both left-wing voters and younger conservatives, a constituency that could matter if he seeks the Republican presidential nomination in 2028.
The distinction was particularly striking given Vance's decision to campaign for Hungary's Viktor Orban ahead of April's election.
"He knows Israel is a liability for both his party and for the United States writ large, and he's trying to keep himself distant from it," Bohl said.
Beyond its potential electoral impact, Trump's endorsement could also have implications for Israeli policy toward Iran and the Palestinians if Netanyahu remains in office.
Bohl said Netanyahu's close relationship with Trump could give him greater freedom to pursue a hard-line regional agenda, although domestic and regional constraints would still limit Israel's ability to escalate conflicts on several fronts simultaneously.
He argued that Netanyahu has demonstrated an ability to persuade the Trump administration to support Israeli military action despite the political costs in the US.
Bohl said reports of possible further Israeli strikes on Iran illustrated how the relationship could shape future decisions, although the timing and likelihood of another attack remain uncertain.
A new Netanyahu government could also have implications for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, where movement restrictions and threats against Palestinian communities have raised concerns.
Bohl said Trump's backing could give Netanyahu greater room to pursue policies Washington might otherwise resist, provided they did not directly embarrass the US president.
"If Netanyahu is able to get through as the next prime minister, he will have a close enough relationship with this White House" to pursue policies including further military action against Iran and expanded Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon, he said.

German climber dies on Nepal’s Ama Dablam mountain
Italy

By Gopal Sharma
KATHMANDU, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A German climber died after a fall while descending from the summit of a Himalayan peak in northeast Nepal, a hiking company official said on Monday.
The climber, who had topped the 6,814 metre (22,256 ft) Ama Dablam peak on Sunday, fell some 1,500 metres (4,920 feet) on his way back down from the summit and died on Monday, Gokul Thapa, head of the Real Himalaya Pvt Ltd company, which provided local logistics to him, said.
“His body was recovered by a search team today itself,” Thapa told Reuters from Lukla, gateway to the mountainous region.
Ama Dablam is a popular mountain among climbers in Solukhumbu district, home to the world’s tallest peak, Mount Everest.
Last week, two Japanese climbers died on another peak in west Nepal.
Thapa said the body of the German climber had been picked up from the mountain and would be carried by a helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu for a post mortem examination.
More than 300 mountaineers have received permits to climb Ama Dablam during the current September-November Autumn climbing season.
Earlier this year, 10 climbers including a noted Nepali-British climber died on a mountain in Pakistan.

By Andrew Osborn and Dmitry Antonov
MOSCOW, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Aleksandar Vucic’s crushing election defeat by a student-backed protest movement has cast gloom over Moscow, which has lost another important partner in Europe just six months after ally Viktor Orban was ousted in an election in Hungary.
Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow who had been prime minister or president since 2014, suffered a defeat on Sunday that prompted nationwide celebrations, although few had any idea of how the Balkan country’s new student-backed leaders would govern.
Russia saw Vucic’s Serbia as a crucial ally in Europe, and as a bulwark against what Moscow has cast as the European Union’s aggressive attempts to contain and punish it over its war in Ukraine.
Serbia buys large quantities of gas from Russian energy giant Gazprom, and although it has aspirations to join the European Union, it has not signed up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Instead, under Vucic — who enjoyed close ties to President Vladimir Putin — it continued to develop close economic, political and military links to Moscow.
The Kremlin put a brave face on Vucic’s defeat, saying it had taken note of the result and that Vucic — whose contribution to bilateral ties it warmly praised — was moving into opposition.
“As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
“For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango.”
GEOPOLITICAL SETBACK
Russia can still count EU member Slovakia, under Prime Minister Robert Fico, as a friendly country. It has also been closely watching unrest in France, where far-right politician Marine Le Pen has said she would cut financial aid to Ukraine if she won next year’s presidential election.
Recent regional electoral successes for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have been welcomed in Russia, where Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has begun to speak about the possibility of one day reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia which were blown up in 2022.
But for now at least, the potential loss of Serbia as a close ally — after setbacks to Russia’s geopolitical influence in the South Caucasus region and parts of Central Asia — is being seen as a serious blow in Moscow by Kremlin-aligned politicians, media and analysts.
Before Sunday’s election, the Student List party said it would not introduce sanctions on Russia over Ukraine, that it would retain Serbia’s military neutrality, and that it would not seek to join NATO.
Vucic has cast doubts on those pledges, suggesting the party would renege on them and impose sanctions on Moscow as soon as March or April.
Jovo Bakic, a representative for Student List and university lecturer, on Monday denied his party would U-turn.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector. There will be no changes there (in the country’s foreign policy),” Bakic told Russia’s RT Balkan TV outlet.
Members of Russia’s political elite fear Serbia’s EU aspirations could see it put under serious pressure to align itself more closely with EU foreign policy however and that Moscow could find itself betrayed by a traditional ally in the process.
“Brussels, for its part, is keen to see Belgrade align itself more closely with the common European position on Russia. The main indicator of Serbia’s actual course will not be Vucic’s statements or his opponents’ electoral pledges, but rather the first decisions taken by the new cabinet,” said the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper.
Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of the influential Russia in Global Affairs journal, said it was clear that a new political era was under way in Serbia that could sharply reorient the country towards the EU, in the same way that Orban’s loss of power in Hungary saw Budapest and Brussels become much closer.
“In this sense, the Hungarian case is quite telling,” said Lukyanov. “And Russia has nothing good to look forward to.”
(Reporting by Reuters in MoscowAdditional reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic in Belgrade Writing by Andrew Osborn Editing by Keith Weir and Sanjeev Miglani)

Can GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate who's bucked Trump, keep his Pennsylvania swing seat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:33:16 UTC
21:33:16 KST

Over nearly 10 years in Congress, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has cultivated an image as a middle-of-the-road GOP lawmaker who operates above the partisan fray and is willing to buck President Donald Trump.
It's a formula that has allowed Fitzpatrick, who is among the most moderate lawmakers on Capitol Hill according to his hometown newspaper, to win swing voters and consistently outperform his party in a highly competitive district that opted for Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. But in a year when Republican candidates across the country are being weighed down by Trump, Fitzpatrick is facing a stiff challenge from Democrat Bob Harvie in Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, and testing whether his personal brand can carry him in a difficult national political environment.
"Brian Fitzpatrick is Brian Fitzpatrick. I'm not Donald Trump. I'm not anybody else. And that's the way voters should approach this," Fitzpatrick told CNBC. "I'm not happy with [Trump]. I'm not happy with his tone. I don't think he's done a sufficient job. I think leaders are supposed to unite our country, unify people. He has not done that."
The battle between Fitzpatrick and Harvie comes as Trump's approval rating craters, the Iran war drags on and consumer prices rise. The contest is one of the approximately four dozen House seats considered in play in the Nov. 3 election that will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's term. Pennsylvania voters are often an indicator of how the country will swing overall, and because the state is on the East Coast, Fitzpatrick's district is one to watch as returns come in.
Democrats are on offense and spending money in districts previously thought out of reach — including Fitzpatrick's, in a race that could signal Democratic success outside of just the most vulnerable seats.
But Harvie, a former high school social studies teacher and county commissioner, is still a long shot to win. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted the race in Democrats' direction, from "Likely R" to "Lean R," earlier this month. Erin Covey, who leads coverage of House races at the Cook Report, called Fitzpatrick Democrats' "white whale."
As part of Democrats' final push to unseat Fitzpatrick, Harvie was joined earlier this month by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for a rally in Bucks County.
"This is an incredibly important state," Jeffries told reporters after the rally. "The commonwealth is a big swing state, and Bucks County is a big swing county. And so this is a critically important race."
Fitzpatrick grew up in Bucks County, which makes up much of the district, and is a former FBI agent who succeeded his brother, Michael, in 2017. He's a co-chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus and, according to a recent Philadelphia Inquirer analysis of his voting record, has voted against the White House and his party this Congress more than any other House Republican. The paper endorsed Harvie earlier this month.
Fitzpatrick is also part of a bipartisan group that's been outspoken as the White House has taken a more conciliatory tone toward Russia in recent weeks. He led a bill last week that would undo Trump's recent authorization of the U.S. purchase of Russian diesel. And he signed a bipartisan letter urging the Department of Defense to restore Ukraine's access to satellite communications that are critical to the country's defenses, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the services were downgraded. Fitzpatrick threatened to pursue the firing of U.S. officials responsible for the slowdown, The New York Times reported.
Fitzpatrick is seeking his sixth House term and for much of his career has easily warded off Democratic challenges. Christopher Nicholas, a Republican consultant based in Pennsylvania, said Fitzpatrick "has been the most moderate member of the House."
"If they are able to beat him this cycle, it is definitely going to be a great night for Democrats," Covey said.
Harvie casts Fitzpatrick as a rubber stamp for Trump and questions the claims of bipartisanship. While Fitzpatrick was one of only two Republicans to vote against the final version of Republicans' 2025 signature tax and spending package, he voted in favor of an earlier iteration in the House that sent the measure to the Senate and set it on a path to passage. Fitzpatrick has said he supported the initial draft of the bill, but opposed cuts to Medicaid that were added in the Senate.
Harvie also called out Fitzpatrick's mixed record on tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted to overturn Trump's tariffs on Canada, but has also sided with most Republicans on procedural votes to limit Congress' ability to challenge some of the president's tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted in favor of a controversial, Trump-backed election bill, dubbed the SAVE America Act, which would require identification to cast a ballot and proof of citizenship to register to vote. And he backed a controversial GOP immigration proposal and Trump's bid to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America."
"When it comes to our economics in this country, people are suffering," Harvie, a Bucks County native, told CNBC. "The government is one that is totally detached from the people it's supposed to serve. Internationally, we've never been weaker and more isolated … and all of that is because of Donald Trump and because of people like Brian Fitzpatrick, who are just letting him run amok."
Fitzpatrick is still favored to win. But Brit Crampsie, a Democratic strategist based in Pennsylvania, said Democrats have a stronger candidate in Harvie than they have in past cycles.
"Bob Harvie, from his time as a school teacher to a local official, has deep ties to this community, and he's very representative of this community," Crampsie said. "He understands Bucks County and has high name ID."
In addition to Trump's low favorability and voters' economic concerns, Fitzpatrick and other Pennsylvania Republicans must also contend with one of the most popular governors in the country at the top of the ticket. Shapiro is expected to win reelection easily, according to recent polling. In Fitzpatrick's district, Shapiro is predicted to coast to victory by double digits, Covey said.
Pennsylvania also has three other neck-and-neck races that together could decide control of the House. Two Republican incumbents, Reps. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District and Scott Perry in the 10th, are seeking reelection in races labeled "Lean D." Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, in Pennsylvania's 8th District, is in a "toss up" race, according to the Cook Report.
Fitzpatrick, however, noted he won nearly 55% of voters in his district in 2022, even as Shapiro won 59% of the vote in the district, evidence to him that his constituents are more than willing to split their tickets.
Independent public polling on the race for the district is sparse, though a recent internal survey conducted by Global Strategy Group for the Harvie campaign showed him and Fitzpatrick tied. A September poll conducted by Public Opinion Strategies for the National Republican Congressional Committee and Fitzpatrick's campaign had the incumbent up by 9 percentage points. A poll released Sunday by The New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University found Harvie with a narrow 48% to 46% lead over Fitzpatrick — within the poll's margin of error.
Recent outside spending paints a competitive picture.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has committed more than $1.5 million to TV ads in the district since the start of October, while House Democrats' main super PAC has pitched in more than $7.5 million, according to AdImpact data. Before this election, neither group had bought TV ads in the district since 2020.
Republicans are also shelling out to shore up Fitzpatrick. The House GOP's main super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, and the NRCC have committed just under $5 million and just over $1 million, respectively, to ads in the district, according to AdImpact. And Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., recently purchased $100,000 in ads in the district opposing Harvie, according to an Oct. 12 Federal Election Commission filing.
"Here's how you know where his loyalties lie," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale told CNBC. "Donald Trump and MAGA Inc. coming in to spend $100,000 to bail him out because they know when push comes to shove, he'll be loyal to them."
Fitzpatrick has a significant cash advantage, with more than $709,000 in his war chest as of Oct. 14 according to FEC filings, compared with Harvie's just over $409,000 in cash on hand.
Reilly Richardson, a spokesperson for the NRCC, pointed to this fundraising disparity, saying Harvie had "a stagnant campaign" and "a significant cash disadvantage."

Swiss court finds Belarusian man guilty over disappearance of Lukashenko opponent
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:33:13 CET
21:33:13 KST

By Marleen Kaesebier
ST GALLEN, Switzerland, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A Swiss court on Monday found a former Belarusian security officer guilty over the abduction of businessman Anatoly Krasovsky, an opponent of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko.
Yuri Harauski, who has admitted involvement in the abductions more than two decades ago of three of Lukashenko’s opponents who were later killed, was however acquitted over the kidnapping of former Belarusian Interior Minister Yuri Zakharenko.
Harauski now faces two years on probation in Switzerland, a sentence that was reduced because of his cooperation and comprehensive confession, the court said.
Rights groups say the ruling is the first conviction anywhere of a member of Belarus’ security forces. It came after the daughters of two of the victims appealed his 2023 acquittal.
Harauski had originally confessed in a Deutsche Welle interview in 2019 that while he was working in a special police unit called SOBR in Belarus in 1999, he had been involved in the abductions of three people.
A Swiss court had ruled three years ago that Harauski’s alleged role had not been legally proven because he had made contradictory statements over time.
The court said on Monday that Harauski’s confessions were credible and in the case of Krasovsky, his intent and knowledge of the violent abduction and subsequent killing were clear. In the case of Zakharenko this intent could not be established, it said.
FIRST SUCH CONVICTION
“Even if it’s a partial victory, it’s the first conviction anywhere in the world of a member of the Belarusian security forces,” said Philip Grant, founder of rights group Trial International, which had supported the daughters of Krasovsky and Zakharenko.
The case is the first in which the Swiss courts, applying the principle of universal jurisdiction, have tried charges of enforced disappearance or alleged crimes committed in Belarus.
Lukashenko’s government has rejected criticism of its human rights record from the UN and rights groups, and denies holding political prisoners.
“An accountability gap has been closed,” said Severin Walz, lawyer for the daughters of Zakharenko and Krasovsky. ”My clients feel very relieved.”
There was no comment on Monday from Harauski’s lawyer.
The verdict could be appealed one more time, which would take the case to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court.
(Reporting by Marleen Kaesebier, editing by Linda Pasquini and Keith Weir)

Explainer-Serbia’s new leaders face host of tough challenges
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:32:53 CET
21:32:53 KST

BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Serbia’s student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday’s parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.
Here are a few of them:
KOSOVO
The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students’ candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue.
Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo’s Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency.
FRAYED EU RELATIONS
With Serbia’s European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues.
Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc.
The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc stood ready to support reforms including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU.
COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM
The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the sale of Russia’s stake in energy company NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL.
Russia’s Gazprom is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency.
The Student List’s top candidates have said a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
CORRUPTION
The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests.
They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget.
Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students’ anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds.
Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
ECONOMY
Serbia’s economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows.
The IMF has forecast Serbia’s economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August’s 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024.
The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights.
Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups.
The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work.
Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication.
(Reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

Taiwan turns to AI to identify wildlife collision hotspots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:32:18 UTC
21:32:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — An AI system will be tested in Taiwan to identify roads where wildlife collisions are most likely, as about 3,000 animal-related traffic accidents are reported annually, CNA reported Monday.
The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network’s AI model will draw on existing records of roadkill, wildlife sightings, and traffic accidents to identify areas where collisions are likely to occur. It will also factor in road conditions, surrounding land use, and weather to detect risks in areas not previously identified as hotspots.
The Formosan pangolin will be the first species covered in the pilot program. The network plans to expand the system to include leopard cats, land crabs, and reptiles.
Many animal-related collisions go unreported, the network said, making the actual annual toll difficult to determine. It estimates that collisions involving medium-sized and large mammals alone number 500,000 to 1 million annually.
Police data show that 25,345 people were injured in animal-related traffic accidents over the past eight years, with 95% of accidents involving motorcyclists. The network estimates annual related economic losses at NT$800 million (US$24.5 million) to NT$6.4 billion.
Since 2019, the network has worked with providers of in-vehicle warning systems and navigation services to issue voice alerts as drivers approach known accident hotspots. It has also developed a solar-powered LED warning device that detects nearby wildlife, with initial testing planned on roads managed by the New Taipei City Government.
The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network was launched in August 2011 by the Ministry of Agriculture's Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute. The citizen science project documents wildlife deaths caused by transportation infrastructure and related facilities to help reduce collisions.

General Staff confirms strike on Yelets plant producing batteries for aerial bombs and Iskander-M missiles

General Staff confirms strike on Yelets plant producing batteries for aerial bombs and Iskander-M missiles
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
Specifically, the strike targeted a production facility for power sources used in enemy weapons at the “Energia” plant in Yelets, Lipetsk Oblast, Russian Federation.
“A fire broke out on the plant’s premises. The strike complicates the Russian Armed Forces’ production of power sources for missiles, guided aerial bombs, and other weapons,” the statement reads.
As noted by the General Staff, “Energia” is the sole manufacturer of batteries for air bomb guidance and correction modules, and also produces batteries for the “Iskander-M” operational-tactical missile systems and sea-based cruise missiles.
Additionally, based on the results of previous strikes, the destruction of the main microchip production workshop has been confirmed, and the building and servers of the “Proton-Elektrotex” enterprise in the city of Orel, Oryol Region, Russia, have been damaged. The strike took place on October 23.
“This complicates the enemy’s production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles, which it uses to strike Ukrainian cities,” the General Staff commented.
On October 23, a storage, preparation, and launch site for attack UAVs in the Donetsk area was struck. Three buildings used for preparing and equipping attack UAVs and one launch rail were damaged.
The General Staff noted that this reduces the Russians’ ability to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure with various types of drones.
On October 24, the “Tolyattikauchuk” plant in the city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, Russian Federation, was struck. A process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units, and one rectification unit were damaged.
“This disrupts the production chain for solid rocket fuel used in tactical and ballistic missiles,” the General Staff emphasized.
The General Staff stressed that the Ukrainian Defense Forces are striking enemy military targets within the framework of the right to self-defense guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter.
“Operations against key enemy military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ceases completely,” the General Staff added.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian authorities confirmed fires at several industrial facilities in the Voronezh region following a nighttime drone attack.

Kremlin briefs media on Alyoshki agreements, decision on trilateral talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:30:55 UTC
21:30:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Agreements on a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, a decision on the resumption of trilateral talks on Ukraine, and the outcome of the parliamentary elections in Serbia were among the key topics of Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov’s Monday briefing.
TASS has summarized the Kremlin spokesman’s key statements.
On the president’s schedule
Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a meeting with Gazprombank Board Chairman Andrey Akimov on Monday.
The president continues his preparations for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit and the third Russia-Africa summit, both of which will take place this week.
The Russian leader is scheduled to hold a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of these forums.
On Ukrainian settlement
The decision on resuming trilateral talks "does not imply any restrictions on combat operations."
Russian forces continue delivering massive strikes on Ukraine’s defense sector: "Our armed forces are continuing the special military operation, delivering massive and sustained strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial complex, as well as military and military-related targets."
The territorial issue may, in one way or another, become a subject of discussion during efforts to reach a peace settlement on Ukraine: "All these issues may, in one way or another, become a subject of discussion during efforts to reach a peace settlement."
A serious discussion covering every little detail is needed to settle the conflict in Ukraine: "A very serious discussion lies ahead, one that involves a vast number of details."
Russia will not publicly discuss details of Ukraine settlement talks as it may get in the way of the potential peace process: "We would prefer not to discuss these details in public, as we believe it would undermine a potential future peace process."
On agreement on humanitarian operation in Alyoshki
Agreements on a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki could serve as a precedent for missions in other areas: "For humanitarian purposes, absolutely. Especially when it comes to a direct, very positive, and coordinated involvement of the American side, American negotiators, and US First Lady Melania Trump in the process. We highly appreciate these efforts, and, of course, this could set a precedent."
Russia hopes that Kiev will fulfill all agreements regarding the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki: "We would like to hope that the Ukrainian side will fulfill all the agreements that were reached with the direct participation of American negotiators representing Melania Trump."
On results of the presidential election in Brazil
Moscow welcomes Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s presidential election: "We welcome Mr. Lula’s victory."
Lula da Silva is doing a great deal to develop cooperation with Russia, both bilaterally and on the international stage more broadly: "He is doing a great deal not only to develop bilateral relations, but also to advance processes within BRICS and other organizations, as well as cooperation with Russia on the international stage."
Moscow hopes these processes will continue: "We hope all these processes will continue in the future."
On results of the parliamentary elections in Serbia
Moscow highly values the contribution that former Serbian President and Serbian Progressive Party leader Aleksandar Vucic has made to the development of bilateral relations between Russia and Serbia: "We acknowledge the results of the elections held in Serbia. We highly value the contribution that Vucic has made to the development of our bilateral relations."
Moscow hopes that Vucic will continue playing a role in the development of bilateral relations with Russia, even in opposition: "We know that Mr. Vucic will remain active in politics and we hope that, even in opposition, he will continue to contribute to the development of bilateral relations [between Serbia and Russia]."
Russia will continue doing everything it can to foster the development of relations with Serbia: "For our part, we intend to continue to do everything possible to promote the development of our relations with Belgrade, but, as you know, it takes two to tango."
Russia hopes that the new political force coming to power in Serbia will understand that cooperation with Moscow is beneficial for Belgrade: "When it comes to the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections [in Serbia], we would like to express the hope that its actions will also be constructively aimed at further developing relations [with Russia]. And that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia's interest because it brings benefits to Serbia. It is, first and foremost, advantageous for Serbia."
On the IWF decision
Russia welcomes the International Weightlifting Federation’s (IWF) decision to hold the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships in Moscow, viewing it as an important step toward depoliticizing sports: "Of course, we welcome such decisions. This is a very important step toward depoliticizing sports."
"Russia must return to the global sporting community as a full-fledged member, because this community cannot function fully without Russia’s participation."
The question of bidding to host the Olympics in Russia again is not currently on the agenda: "One must weigh all the pros and cons when making such decisions, of course. For now, this issue is not on the agenda."
