"An accountability gap has been closed," said Severin Walz, lawyer for the daughters of Zakharenko and Krasovsky. "My clients feel very relieved."
There was no comment on Monday from Harauski's lawyer.
The verdict could be appealed one more time, which would take the case to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court. REUTERS

Explainer-Oleshky: the occupied Ukrainian town for which Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:30:41 UTC
21:30:41 KST

Explainer-Oleshky: the occupied Ukrainian town for which Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire
Oct 26 - Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a localised ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, an arrangement that will enable aid deliveries and allow evacuations from a frontline town suffering acute shortages of food and medicine.
The agreement was announced on October 23 and brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo, as Washington seeks to revive broader peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
WHY ARE RESIDENTS OF OLESHKY AT RISK?
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since.
Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023.
The United States has said only a few thousand people remain in Oleshky, from a prewar population of 24,000. Residents and officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies.
WHAT DOES THE CEASEFIRE INVOLVE?
According to Ukrainian and Russian officials, the arrangement provides for a local halt in fighting, the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the evacuation of civilians who wish to leave the town.
The two sides said humanitarian corridors would be established to allow aid deliveries and the movement of residents.
WHO BROKERED THE DEAL?
The White House said Melania Trump helped secure the agreement after becoming involved in discussions on the humanitarian situation in Oleshky. The White House said the first lady and a representative worked with Russian and Ukrainian officials to agree the terms of the ceasefire.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets publicly thanked Melania Trump and her team for helping coordinate the talks. Russian officials also confirmed the agreement.
Pope Leo also played a role. He held a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the Vatican said, and urged Ukraine and Russia to cooperate to let aid and food in.
WHAT MIGHT HAPPEN NEXT?
The ceasefire is limited in scope and does not address the wider conflict, now in its fifth year. But it is a rare example of direct cooperation between the two sides since the start of the invasion.
The Kremlin said on Monday that the truce might serve as a precedent for similar localised ceasefires in the future. REUTERS

‘It killed us’: Fake US election polls infiltrate major media and damage campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:30:30 UTC
21:30:30 KST

A company that presented itself as a legitimate political polling firm has admitted fabricating election surveys that were published by major American news organizations and incorporated into influential polling averages, triggering a scandal just over a week before the November 3 midterm elections. One former Democratic Senate candidate says the false numbers helped destroy her campaign.
Wedgewood Polls, a relatively new firm that began publishing surveys earlier this year, acknowledged on October 20 that it had fabricated most of its results. The company insisted that the deception was part of an experiment designed to expose how easily unverified polling data could gain credibility with journalists, political analysts and election forecasters.
But the consequences may have extended far beyond embarrassing the media. The fabricated surveys reached major polling trackers, influenced political narratives and, according to candidates and campaign officials, contributed to decisions about donations, campaign strategy and whether to remain in electoral races.
More than a dozen Wedgewood surveys were included in polling databases maintained by leading organizations, including The New York Times and election analysis website FiftyPlusOne. The company also solicited donations to finance what it presented as legitimate polling operations.
The New York Times subsequently removed 15 Wedgewood surveys from its tracking project, while Decision Desk HQ removed 17 polls from its race-level lists and averages.
The admission came only after researchers at FiftyPlusOne began questioning the authenticity of Wedgewood's data and approached the company for an explanation.
In a statement posted on social media, which has since been deleted, Wedgewood described itself as an experimental project intended to demonstrate the weaknesses and lack of oversight in the modern political polling industry.
The company maintained that it had never intended to influence an election or permanently mislead the public.
Its social media account has since disappeared, and the polling operation appears to have shut down.
‘It killed us’: The Michigan candidate who says fake polling ended her campaign
One of the most prominent figures affected by the scandal is Mallory McMorrow, a Democratic state senator who competed for her party's U.S. Senate nomination in Michigan.
McMorrow had entered the race hoping to secure the nomination against two major rivals, former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens.
On June 29, Wedgewood published a survey showing McMorrow's support collapsing to just 9%, compared with 46% for El-Sayed and 39% for Stevens.
The findings appeared to suggest that McMorrow had little chance of winning the nomination. Six days later, on July 5, she suspended her campaign, a month before Michigan's Democratic primary.
After Wedgewood admitted fabricating its results, McMorrow publicly described the damage she believes the survey caused.
"It killed us," she said, explaining that the numbers contributed to an impression that her campaign was no longer viable.
In a post on X, McMorrow said donations dried up, volunteers became deeply discouraged and reporters repeatedly contacted her to ask whether she would withdraw.
She described the period as among the worst days of her campaign, particularly for her staff, whose morale suffered as the damaging polling figures spread.
Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic strategist who ran a political action committee supporting McMorrow, said several donors used the Wedgewood survey to justify withdrawing financial support.
According to Holdsworth, the funding losses were particularly damaging because McMorrow's campaign was already being outspent by approximately $80 million.
The significance of the alleged damage is difficult to establish conclusively. Other polling organizations also showed McMorrow trailing her rivals, and analysts caution that it is impossible to determine precisely how much one fabricated survey contributed to her decision to withdraw.
Nevertheless, McMorrow argues that the episode demonstrates how polling figures can become self-fulfilling political narratives, particularly when donors and campaign supporters begin making financial decisions based on them.
She has also called for greater transparency and reforms to the American campaign finance system.
The Mississippi poll that exposed the deception
The fabricated data did not appear only in Michigan. Wedgewood also published surveys involving other competitive races across the United States, including the Senate contest in Mississippi.
There, the firm released a poll showing Democratic candidate Scott Colom trailing Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just four percentage points, 48% to 52%.
The numbers suggested that a race in a traditionally Republican state could be considerably closer than previously expected. Colom pointed to the polling as evidence of growing momentum behind his campaign.
Democratic organizations were also increasing their attention to Mississippi, although there is no established evidence that Wedgewood's survey was responsible for their spending decisions.
The Mississippi poll ultimately became the key to exposing the company's operation.
Researchers at FiftyPlusOne were already suspicious of several newly established polling organizations that appeared to be publishing results without an established public track record.
G. Elliott Morris, a journalist and polling analyst at FiftyPlusOne, told TIME that the appearance of numerous unfamiliar polling companies had raised concerns among his colleagues.
After receiving a tip suggesting that Wedgewood's data might be fabricated, the researchers requested the underlying responses from its Mississippi survey.
Wedgewood supplied what it claimed was raw polling data collected through an online survey platform called Pollfish.
However, investigators noticed irregularities. The sample appeared unusually representative of Mississippi's electorate for a survey conducted through that method.
To investigate further, FiftyPlusOne commissioned its own Mississippi poll using the same platform and questionnaire.
The comparison exposed discrepancies in the technical identifiers associated with survey respondents and the timestamps recording when their responses were submitted.
The data provided by Wedgewood did not display the same patterns as the genuine responses collected through the platform, raising serious doubts about its authenticity.
On October 19, FiftyPlusOne contacted Wedgewood about the discrepancies. The following day, the company publicly acknowledged that its polling had been fabricated.
Rather than accepting responsibility for the political consequences, Wedgewood argued that the episode demonstrated how easily a fictional polling operation could win recognition from established media organizations.
How fake polls reached major news organizations
The scandal has also forced questions about the standards used by news outlets and polling aggregators when deciding which surveys deserve credibility.
Wedgewood argued that its experiment exposed a failure by major organizations to verify the identity, methodology and legitimacy of new polling companies.
However, both The New York Times and FiftyPlusOne rejected the suggestion that they had accepted its data without conducting any checks.
FiftyPlusOne said it had asked Wedgewood to identify its staff and explain its polling methods before including its results.
The company supplied the names of two purported polling professionals, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater, and provided methodological explanations that appeared consistent with industry standards.
Researchers also independently confirmed that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry.
The New York Times similarly said it had questioned the company about its staff, sampling methods and sources of funding before accepting its surveys.
The problem, according to the investigators, was that Wedgewood had presented convincing answers and supplied data that appeared credible until subjected to more detailed examination.
The episode illustrates how even organizations that attempt to verify polling firms can be vulnerable when those firms deliberately misrepresent their operations.
Another fake polling scandal just two months earlier
Wedgewood was not the first company to admit manufacturing political polling data during the 2026 election cycle.
In August, another organization, Median Strategies, acknowledged publishing fabricated surveys involving races in Wisconsin, Nevada and California.
Among the misleading results associated with that earlier operation was a survey suggesting that democratic socialist Francesca Hong was leading the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin. Hong ultimately lost the contest.
Median Strategies also described its activities as an experiment intended to test whether journalists and polling organizations would accept unsupported data.
Unlike Wedgewood, however, its surveys were largely rejected by major polling aggregators.
The Wedgewood affair proved more consequential because the fabricated numbers entered established polling databases and became part of the information available to journalists, candidates, donors and voters.
The revelations have intensified concerns about the ease with which fraudulent information can enter political reporting, particularly as technological tools make it increasingly simple to generate convincing datasets and supporting documents.
With Americans preparing to vote on November 3, the scandal raises questions not only about the reliability of individual polls but also about the political consequences of publishing figures that have never been independently verified.
For McMorrow, the damage cannot simply be reversed by deleting the surveys or shutting down the company.
The fabricated numbers may have been presented as an experiment, but the campaign she believes they helped derail was real.

Opinion
Europe can still shape the rules of AI
As Washington and Beijing race to supply AI systems, the EU can use its regulatory weight to influence how they are tested and deployed
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Hao Nan is a Susan Strange Associate Fellow with the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society, and a Nuclear Futures Fellow with Ploughshares Fund & Horizon 2045. 
In October, two technology executives offered Europe similar advice. In Turin, Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai urged European companies to use open-source models and their proprietary industrial data to build AI capabilities. In Berlin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang pressed German manufacturers to apply AI to factories, robotics and other physical industries. Both see opportunity in Europe’s engineering strengths, while their companies stand to benefit from supplying the technology.
Recent safety incidents and evaluations expose another dimension of the AI race: the difficulty of keeping increasingly capable AI agents under human control. During internal cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI agents bypassed isolation controls and accessed external systems beyond their intended scope.
In September, Reuters reported on documented cases of Chinese-model agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot displaying deception or evading constraints in controlled tests. In October, Tencent Holding acknowledged unintended browsing behaviour by agents evaluating third-party models. These cases range from controlled experiments to real security lapses. They underscore the need for better evaluation before wider deployment.

Resuming trilateral Ukraine talks does not restrict military operations: Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:29:50 UTC
21:29:50 KST

Elena Teslova
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that the decision to resume US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks on the Moscow-Kyiv conflict does not imply any restrictions on military operations.
Speaking at a news briefing in Moscow, Peskov said the territorial issue could be a topic of discussion during efforts to reach a peaceful settlement, along with other matters.
"The decision to resume trilateral negotiations does not imply any restrictions on military actions. You know that our armed forces continue the special military operation and continue to deliver massive and consistent strikes on Ukraine’s military complex, on military and quasi-military targets," he said.
"There will be a very serious conversation consisting of a huge number of details. We would not like to discuss these details publicly, because we believe it would harm the potential future peace process," Peskov added.
Asked about humanitarian efforts, the spokesman said they could set a precedent, citing the "very positive, coordinating involvement" of US negotiators and first lady Melania Trump.
"We highly appreciate these efforts," he said, adding that Moscow hopes Ukraine will fulfill all the agreements reached with the direct participation of negotiators.  
Kremlin's views on Serbian, Brazilian elections
Commenting on Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, the spokesman said Moscow highly values the contribution of Aleksandar Vucic to bilateral relations and expects him to remain on the political stage.
"Even in opposition, he will still contribute to the development of bilateral relations," he said.
He expressed hope that the new political force coming to power would act constructively and understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interest.
"We, for our part, intend to continue to promote the development of relations with Belgrade in every way, but, as you know, it takes two to tango," he added.
Serbia held an early election to the National Assembly on Sunday. With 96.47% of ballots counted, the Republican Electoral Commission said the “United Serbia” list of Vucic trailed the opposition “Student List,” with 39.27% against 52.57% of the vote.
Peskov also welcomed the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential election.
“We welcome the victory of Mr. Lula,” he said. Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier sent congratulations to Lula. 
Russia to host 2030 weightlifting championships
Peskov also welcomed the decision of the International Weightlifting Federation to hold the 2030 championships in the Russian capital, calling it an important step toward depoliticizing sport.
"Russia must return to the world sports family with full rights, because this family cannot live fully without Russia’s participation," he said.
On the Olympics, he said it was too early to talk about it.
"At the moment, not a very large number of countries are interested in hosting the Olympics. All the pros and cons must be weighed, of course. For now, this issue is not on the agenda," he said.

Macron vows ‘concrete’ measures to address student demands after unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

21:25:21 KST

French students vow to continue protests despite concessions from Macron govt
French student leaders on Monday called for more protests despite President Emmanuel Macron's pledge of "concrete and strong" measures to address their demands after weeks of nationwide unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu met with high school representatives alongside education ministers to announce follow-up action ranging from a total overhaul of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup to a cap on class sizes.
French student leaders vowed to go on protesting Monday despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, stokes unrest and deepens the economic damage.
Read moreFrench student representatives hail govt's ‘concrete measures’, call for protests to continue
The new measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes; €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans for renovating schools; and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system students see as socially unfair.
"Not all our demands were met. We'll go on for as long as it takes," Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said as he and fellow student leaders emerged from a meeting with government officials in Paris.
The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and yellow-vest activists, known for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Macron's minority government.
The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120 percent of GDP, while the turmoil is boosting support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen ahead of next year's presidential election.
The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
"It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday's protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.
Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year's presidential election, has benefitted from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
Read moreFrench far-right leader Le Pen seeks to leverage unrest in presidential campaign kick-off
An opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32 to 33.5 percent, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon on 17 percent. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Mélenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Far-right gangs confront far-left activists
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
"We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Smoking ban on outdoor terraces delayed: Council of State raises objections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:23:55 UTC
21:23:55 KST

The introduction of the smoking ban on outdoor terraces in the hospitality industry is being postponed, the office of Belgian Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke (Flemish socialist Vooruit) has confirmed. The Council of State, which vets Belgian laws before they come into force, has raised several issues. As a result, the planned start date of 1 January 2027 will not be met.
“The Council of State has asked us to amend certain measures, and we are currently working on this,” the statement from the health minister’s office reads. According to Vandenbroucke’s office, the government also wishes to give the hospitality sector sufficient time afterwards to prepare for the new rules, including the putting up of the necessary signage.
Consequently, the planned start date is being postponed. It is not yet clear when the long-awaited smoking ban will actually come into force. This depends on how quickly the amended measures are passed by parliament.
Stricter anti-tobacco policy
In September 2025, the federal government announced that smoking and vaping on and around hospitality terraces would be banned from 1 January 2027. The measure forms part of a broader tightening of Belgium’s anti-tobacco policy.
There will also be a ban on public smoking rooms, including those in hospitality venues and airports. These measures are intended to help achieve a smoke-free generation by 2040.
When presenting the plans, Minister Vandenbroucke stated that the number of smokers is falling, but that tobacco use still has a significant impact on health. According to recent figures, 12.8 per cent of Belgians smoke every day.
Hospitality federation Horeca Vlaanderen is not happy with the forthcoming ban. The federation fears it will have a negative impact on the sector.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is set to attend five international summits by the end of the year, including meetings in Türkiye, South Korea and Libya, as Ankara seeks to strengthen diplomatic and economic ties across Asia, Africa and the wider international community.
Erdoğan’s schedule includes an Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit, a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the U.N. climate conference COP31, the Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit and the Group of 20 leaders summit, according to Turkish media reports.

Talks there are expected to focus on strengthening the countries’ strategic partnership, trade, investment, defense industry cooperation and regional developments.
In November, Erdoğan is expected to attend COP31, which Türkiye will host in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya. The climate conference is scheduled to begin Nov. 9, with the Turkish president expected to participate on Nov. 11-12.
Climate action, the green transition, energy policy and climate finance are expected to feature prominently at the summit, which is projected to draw world leaders, ministers and thousands of delegates.
Erdoğan is then expected to travel to Tripoli on Dec. 8-9 for the fourth Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit. The meeting aims to deepen strategic cooperation between Türkiye and African countries, with defense, energy, agriculture and transport links among the expected areas of discussion.
The president’s final summit of the year is scheduled to be the G20 leaders’ meeting in Miami on Dec. 14-15. Leaders of the world’s major economies are expected to discuss global economic challenges and reforms at the gathering.

Orban lost power in Hungary's parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar's Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of rule with an absolute majority.
His hard-right, strongly anti-migration and euroskeptic policies, alongside Hungary's democratic backsliding on the rule of law, strained ties with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. However, Orban maintained close relationships with US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Since the election, Hungarian authorities have opened fraud and corruption investigations involving several members of Orban's former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary's National Bank have been arrested, and investigators could also examine whether Orban was involved in the cases.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the proposal remains undecided. A US State Department official acknowledged that the idea might initially sound crazy but said previous discussions with Washington indicated that Russia and China also supported it. The objective would be to put forward Orban as a candidate backed by all three countries.
“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper.
The current secretary-general, António Guterres, is due to complete his second five-year term on December 31.
The White House, Moscow and Beijing have not confirmed the report.
Euronews has requested comment from Orban's spokesperson but has not received a response. The spokesperson previously rejected media reports suggesting Orban might seek the position of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.
In May, the investigative newsletter VSquare reported that a UN post could appeal to the former prime minister because the position carries diplomatic immunity.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Orban would only enter the race if his election were guaranteed, a prospect that currently appears unlikely. A candidate needs the support of at least nine of the 15 members of the UN Security Council, while any of its five permanent members can veto a nomination. The permanent members are the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.

US holding up air defense missiles for Ukraine for nearly a month, Zelensky says
Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 26.
The delay, first reported by the Kyiv Independent, affects missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for. Ukraine relies on Patriot systems to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to stop, making timely deliveries critical to the country's air defenses.
"I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again," Zelensky said.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States, a senior Ukrainian military official said.
Zelensky has said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that the batch awaiting Hegseth's approval was "significant."
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Kyiv has also had problems with military-grade Starlink service, Starshield, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the use of interceptor drones to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as another example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.

Finding a Resting Place
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

In September this year, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) proposed an unprecedented initiative: the issuing of “certificates of Ukrainian identity” to young Ukrainians living abroad, encouraging them to acknowledge and maintain their Ukrainian identity.
A child could be awarded the certificate if they fulfilled at least one of three conditions: speaking Ukrainian in their daily life, attending a Ukrainian school, or participating in the activities of Ukrainian communities or cultural centers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It is no secret that some Ukrainian refugees strive to assimilate into their host countries as quickly as possible. Many have no plans to return to Ukraine, especially if their homes have been destroyed or remain in occupied territory. These expat Ukrainians have started life with a clean slate and intend to turn their current, temporary place of residence into a permanent home if at all possible.
These refugees may still identify as “Ukrainian” and empathize with friends and family who remain in the country, but “Ukrainianess” is not at the forefront of their lives.
Then there are members of ethnic minorities: e.g., Greeks or Armenians and also “local” minority ethnic groups – Hungarian, Bulgarian, Moldovan, or Romanian. Members of these minorities feel a deep, visceral connection to their local “homelands,” but they may not feel such a bond with the Ukrainian state itself.
Serbia’s Vucic Loses Vote, Predicts Sanctions on Russia
It appears that such discussions surrounding the “Certificate of Ukrainian Identity” initiative have prompted officials to pause for thought. For now, the project has been suspended.
Meanwhile, two recent stories have highlighted the fact that even some staunch enemies of Ukraine wish to be buried here. One sparked bewilderment, the other outrage – though, in many respects, the two cases are quite similar.
In October, Anatoly Kashpirovsky – a well-known Soviet and post-Soviet psychologist and television hypnotist – passed away in Moscow at an advanced age. He had once “cured” tens of thousands of people of hundreds of different ailments, both through television broadcasts and at large-scale stadium events. At one point, he even ventured into politics, serving in the Russian State Duma as a member of the party led by Vladimir Zhirinovsky – a man who frequently threatened to bomb London and Brussels.
Kashpirovsky, who was born in Ukraine, remained a staunch supporter of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Following his death, it emerged that he had requested to be buried at the Central Cemetery in the west-central Ukrainian city of Vinnytsia, alongside the graves of his parents and his daughter, Elena, whom he had laid to rest there in 2018 – well after the annexation of Crimea.
Remarkably, the last request of this Kremlin stooge was fulfilled, though it remains unclear who authorized the burial and the details of the event are shrouded in mystery.
In the village of Domotkan, in Dnipropetrovsk region, another funeral took place in broad daylight. The man laid to rest was Oleksandr Olenchenko, a citizen of the Russian Federation born in 1991.
According to the announcement by the family, Olenchenko had been working in Moscow as a rescue worker for the Ministry of Emergency Situations and died during a rescue operation. However, it later emerged that he had actually been serving in the Russian army and had likely been killed in Donetsk during a Ukrainian strike on a Russian military command post. All of this of course needs to be confirmed officially.
Olenchenko was cremated in Donetsk, and his ashes were brought to Domotkan – via Belarus and Poland – by his father, who lives in the village.
Controversy over the burial soon erupted, and Olenchenko’s mother contacted the police to report harassment on social media. The family installed a video camera at the gravesite to protect her son’s resting place from vandalism.
The camera is pointed toward the path leading to the grave. It is not aimed at the sky – the direction from which the greatest threat to everything on the ground originates, and from which drones and missiles fall, sometimes even onto cemeteries.
In a democratic country fighting for its existence, the thorny topic of personal rights springs up at every turn.
River crossing to Moldova
On October 15, Moldovan police arrested two Ukrainian border guards who had crossed to the Moldovan side of the Dniester River in a boat. The Ukrainian guards had been pursuing a man – a resident of Kyiv – who was attempting to cross the border illegally by swimming across the river.
Eyewitnesses captured footage showing the border guards striking the man with an oar as he swam toward the Moldovan bank of the river. This footage led some observers to suggest that the guards intended to drown him.
Some Moldovan border guards got involved to rescue the swimmer, who was taken to hospital while a criminal case was opened against the border guards, who were later allowed to return to the Ukrainian side of the river.
The man pulled from the water turned out to be Oleksiy Koval, a well-known psychologist and blogger who specializes in treating panic disorders, post-traumatic stress, and other mental health conditions. His wife and children had left Ukraine following the start of the full-scale invasion.
According to Koval, he was crossing the river to reunite with his family.
Will his children qualify for a certificate of Ukrainian identity if/when it becomes available? And, supposing he lives a long life outside Ukraine, do you think Koval will, in his twilight years, instruct his children to make sure his remains are buried in Ukraine?

What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:17:58 UTC
21:17:58 KST

A screen in Tel Aviv shows Benjamin Netanyahu, left, and his main rival, the opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the Israeli election on Tuesday. Photograph: David Goldman/AP View image in fullscreen A screen in Tel Aviv shows Benjamin Netanyahu, left, and his main rival, the opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the Israeli election on Tuesday. Photograph: David Goldman/AP Explainer What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking a new mandate in Israel’s first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks Israel election – live updates On Tuesday Israel holds its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians. Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank. Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history. Who are the main players? The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has led Israel for 19 out of the last 30 years, most recently at the head of a far-right coalition. He is seeking a new mandate with the endorsement of the US president, Donald Trump, and the fight is personal as well as political. He is on trial for corruption; losing power may mean a greater risk of jail time. His main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military and relative political newcomer, the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to the heart of Israel’s establishment from humble beginnings. His son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza in 2024. He lacks Netanyahu’s charisma, but has embraced that as part of a campaign positioning him as the opposite of Israel’s current leader, down to the name of his new party – Yashar, or “Honesty”. What are the key issues for voters? Israel’s security is at the heart of the election, overshadowing even the soaring cost of living. Opponents of the current government point to the catastrophe of the 7 October attacks, the erosion of democratic institutions, rise of religious extremism and the cost of open-ended, multi-front wars. They have promised a state commission of inquiry into 7 October, and most have pledged to end draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men, a source of deep resentment among families whose loved ones are serving or have been killed. They are also concerned about international isolation, amid broadening sanctions over settlement expansion, and an accelerating brain drain among the elite. Netanyahu has tried to shift blame for 7 October on to Israel’s security establishment, and despite presiding over the deadliest day in Israel’s history, he claims to be the only leader with the experience and international contacts to keep the country safe. He recently posted an AI image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv on social media, with the claim “anyone who cares about their physical existence” should pause before voting for the opposition. His far-right allies have called for the ethnic cleansing of Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and expansion of settlements. His ultra-Orthodox partners want to preserve a decades-old exemption from conscription and subsidies for religious study. What are the polls saying? Most polls show Netanyahu’s Likud and his current coalition parters losing their majority. That fall in voter support has been fairly consistent for more than two years. They also show a clear anti-Netanyahu majority. However, those opposition seats are divided between the bloc of Jewish Israeli parties, led by Eisenkot’s Yashar, and parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. The Jewish Israeli parties are unlikely to have a majority on their own, but have mostly ruled out going into coalition with Palestinians. Palestinian politicians have indicated they might support a minority government of the Jewish Israeli parties in order to unseat Netanyahu’s far-right coalition. How does the system work and when might we get results/a new government? The Knesset has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. When the results are in, the president invites the party with the largest number of seats to try to agree a governing coalition. Exit polls are released at 10pm Israeli time (8pm GMT), and the first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning. Getting full results could take much longer, with the outcome potentially hanging on the electoral fortunes of two small parties, which need to win 3.25% of the overall vote to take up seats in the Knesset. Polling puts both around this threshold. If they cross it, they each get four seats, which would have a significant impact on coalition building options. The far-right Amcha Yisrael is led by the former general Ofer Winter, who has pledged to back Netanyahu for prime minister if he gets into the Knesset. The Reservists is a rightwing Zionist party focused on ensuring universal conscription whose leaders sit between the two blocs. They have ruled out joining any government supported by either the ultra-Orthodox – key Netanyahu allies – or Palestinian parties whose backing Eisenkot is likely to need. If it goes down to the wire, counting could take more than a day. How democratic is the vote – and who is being disenfranchised? About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights. In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote. In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote. Two million Palestinians in Gaza, who live under Israeli military occupation, according to the international court of justice, also have no vote. Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing said Israeli quadcopter drones set the camp ablaze at about 8pm, with fires consuming tents and belongings for several hours, continuing past midnight.
The ministry condemned the incident and called for urgent international aid to provide the displaced families with shelter and essential supplies.
As of Monday, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,555 people and injured 175,727. Medical sources said the number of people killed since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” on October 11 last year has risen to 1,559, and the number of injured to 5,608, while a large number of victims remain trapped under the rubble and on the streets, with ambulance and rescue crews unable to reach them.

It highlighted the particularly severe consequences for women, children, older people and persons with disabilities, who face heightened risks as a result of displacement and restrictions on movement.
The commission characterized the measures as collective punishment and forced displacement, arguing that they constitute serious violations of international humanitarian law requiring immediate intervention.
It further linked the developments in Hebron to what it described as a broader Israeli policy of expanding displacement and destruction operations across the occupied West Bank.

According to the commission, those tactics include the evacuation of residents and the destruction of infrastructure.

Explainer-Serbia's new leaders face host of tough challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:15:43 UTC
21:15:43 KST

Serbia's new leaders face host of tough challenges
BELGRADE, Oct 26 - Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday's parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.
Here are a few of them:
KOSOVO
The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students' candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue.
Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo's Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency.
FRAYED EU RELATIONS
With Serbia's European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues.
Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc.
The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc stood ready to support reforms including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU.
COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM
The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the sale of Russia's stake in energy company NIS, which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL.
Russia's Gazprom is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency.
The Student List's top candidates had not said whether a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
CORRUPTION
The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests.
They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget.
Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students' anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds.
Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
ECONOMY
Serbia's economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows.
The IMF has forecast Serbia's economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August's 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024.
The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights.
Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups.
The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work.
Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication. ‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:15:41 UTC
21:15:41 KST

Maxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory.
But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “lethalitymaxxing”.
The explosion in the word’s use has made it Dictionary.com’s word of the year for 2026.
To choose each year’s word, Dictionary.com staffers investigate search trends, social media and the news, “and then we ask ourselves what’s telling the most compelling story of the year”, says Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI during the workday, cozymaxxing on a Friday night.”
While “maxxing” has been around in various forms for decades, it’s the phenomenon of “looksmaxxing” – putting your physical appearance above all other concerns, and going to extreme lengths to improve it – that has fueled the recent rise in the word’s use. The message board 4chan is responsible for a vast amount of current slang, according to the linguist Adam Aleksic, and looksmaxxing has roots in online “incel” communities that use it.
But the suffix has emerged from the shadow of 4chan. As associate editor of Among the New Words, which tracks emerging terms in a quarterly journal, the linguist Kelly Wright and her colleagues have documented examples of the term’s use since 1990, when it appeared in a D&D context, through looksmaxxing-related 4chan posts in the 2010s to YouTube discussions of “vibemaxxing” (“adding to my energy”) and Substack posts on “vocabularymaxxing” (“because there are some thoughts you’ll only have if you have the words for them”) in 2025.
Wright sees the word as particularly creative – it can “apply to anything”. Dictionary.com data bears this out: by August 2026, it was being used 19 times as often in digital media as its monthly average in 2025.
And these days, it says far more about our social media-driven compulsion to optimize than it does about inceldom. “If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed,” writes Jennifer Donnelly, a researcher at RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences, at the Conversation.
That comes with risks, she writes, as it suggests there is some kind of endpoint to the improvement process. “But health, wellbeing, social relationships and lifestyle habits aren’t really something we complete,” and maxxing can fuel “constant self-surveillance, self-criticism and the pursuit of an idealised ‘optimal’ self”.
In fact, that obsession is emerging on both ends of the words we use: terms recently added to the dictionary include “prefixes that mean ‘much more’ – things like ‘hyper’, things like ‘ultra’, ‘super’”, Johnson says.
The suffix benefits from being “infinitely customizable but instantly recognizable”, Daria Bahtina, a continuing lecturer in the UCLA department of linguistics, writes in an email. “You can attach the pattern to practically anything while still sounding like you are participating in a particular linguistic and cultural moment.” Saying you’re “proteinmaxxing” feels much cooler than just saying you’re eating more protein.
Its popularity could also be, in part, simply related to its sound. “The sound structure of a word tells us a lot,” Wright says, “and maximalism is trending.” A similar string of sounds – “maxx” – “was maybe a little primed to get picked up”.
Bahtina and Johnson agree that it’s unlikely most people using “maxxing” are thinking about any incel connections. Still, Bahtina wonders if its constant usage could help elevate its origins into the mainstream. “Someone encounters pheromone-maxxing or some other allegedly annoying but innocent version,” she writes, “and suddenly there is a linguistic breadcrumb trail into a much broader ideological ecosystem.”
So can we expect “maxxing” to stick around as a suffix – will it have the staying power of “-gate”, which has denoted scandal ever since Watergate, or will it go the way of “-licious”, which stretched from Bubblicious bubble gum to Destiny’s Child’s Bootylicious, but, as Johnson notes, has largely disappeared?
It’s difficult to predict, the linguists say. Once a slang term gets a mainstream platform, it often loses its cachet. But “I don’t think it’s going to fizzle out,” says Wright. It’s not just young optimizers who’ve embraced it: “Middle-aged people really love this word. Corporate brands love this word. So it’s going to have some staying power.”

Businesses can challenge the new reservation restrictions: a lawyer explained what to do
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:15:09 EET
21:15:09 KST

Businesses can challenge the new reservation restrictions: a lawyer explained what to do
Kyiv • UNN
Companies can challenge the new reservation rules in court, but filing a lawsuit does not suspend their effect. Businesses can also submit collective appeals to the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and Parliament.
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted a resolution introducing new rules for reserving military-liable employees of critically important enterprises. However, the business community’s reservations were only partially taken into account. Companies have the right to challenge the relevant decision in court. At the same time, the mere fact that entrepreneurs disagree with the government’s decision will not be sufficient grounds for its annulment. Danylo Honcharenko, senior military lawyer at Prykhodko & Partners Law Firm, told UNN what legal defense mechanisms businesses will have and whether it is possible to seek a review of the restrictions.
Business opposed the reduction in reservations: what the new rules threaten
The Cabinet of Ministers’ initiative to review the rules for reserving military-liable employees triggered a broad wave of criticism from the business community, industry associations, employers, and representatives of strategically important enterprises.
The government proposed reducing reservation quotas for defense-industrial and energy enterprises from 100% to 85%, and for municipal services from 75% to 60%. At the same time, amendments to the procedure for calculating the number of employees eligible for reservation were discussed. In addition, government officials wanted to establish a Coordination Center that would decide whether enterprises qualified as critical.
The National Agency on Corruption Prevention noted that the government initiative contained a number of corruption risks, including those related to the creation of a new body.
Representatives of the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs, the Ukrainian Business Council, the Federation of Employers of Ukraine, the Ukrainian Air Transport Association, the Aerospace Association of Ukraine, defense enterprises, trade unions, and other industry associations opposed the proposed restrictions.
The business community’s main argument is that reducing the number of reserved employees does not take into account the actual needs of production. Losing even a small number of specialized professionals could lead to the shutdown of individual production processes, the disruption of contracts and state orders, and a reduction in output.
This issue is particularly acute for defense enterprises carrying out state orders, energy companies ensuring the stability of critical infrastructure, and enterprises in related industries. The latter may not directly produce weapons or electricity, but they provide strategic production facilities with the necessary materials, equipment, logistics, and services.
Business representatives also emphasized the unpredictability of government policy and noted that there had been no dialogue with the government regarding this initiative. The constant review of reservation rules complicates long-term planning, creates investment risks, and threatens the fulfillment of contracts that have already been concluded.
The government promised to hold consultations with businesses before making a final decision. However, it is obvious that no dialogue took place after all, since none of the associations reported this publicly.
What the new reservation rules provide for
On October 23, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced that the Cabinet had finalized the resolution.
According to him, an enterprise’s critical status is separated from its economic performance. The sectors that actually contribute to defense and the economy should be considered critical: the defense industry, energy, communications, logistics, housing and communal services, and others. Nothing will change for them. At the same time, industry and regional criteria for critical status will be updated and checked for abuse.
In addition, the maximum level of reservations, in particular for the energy sector and the defense industry, will no longer be 100%. According to the Prime Minister, unconditional full reservation is unfair to those who serve and creates room for abuse.
He promises that the work of those who produce weapons or maintain critical infrastructure will not be weakened. If uninterrupted operations require reserving more employees, the enterprise will be able to submit a substantiated request to the Coordination Center.
It is planned that the Ministry of Defense will strengthen liability for evading service. "The rules must be the same for everyone," Koretskyi stressed.
According to him, the government is also preparing a mechanism for 100% reservation, provided that the mobilization obligation is fulfilled.
"An enterprise will be able to reserve all of its employees if it regularly and voluntarily involves some of them in military service. It is crucial that a person knows where they are going and for how long. Their job and salary will be retained. The conditions will be worked out by the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Economy together with businesses," the head of government added.
The mechanism is planned to be approved by December 1.
Can businesses challenge a Cabinet of Ministers resolution?
According to Danylo Honcharenko, a senior military lawyer at Prykhodko & Partners Law Firm, Ukrainian legislation provides for the possibility of judicially challenging regulatory legal acts of the Cabinet of Ministers if they violate the rights of enterprises or contradict the law.
Pursuant to Article 264 of the Code of Administrative Procedure of Ukraine, regulatory legal acts may be challenged not only by persons to whom they have already been applied, but also by those who are participants in legal relations in which the relevant provisions will be applied. Legal grounds for challenging them may include the Cabinet of Ministers exceeding its powers, the resolution contradicting the laws of Ukraine, violation of the mandatory procedure for its adoption, or failure to comply with the principle of proportionality
Enterprises do not necessarily have to wait until their employees actually lose their reservation or production is halted. If a company belongs to the group of entities to which the new requirements will apply, it may already apply to an administrative court.
Honcharenko pointed out that special rules for preparing government decisions apply during martial law. In particular, the Cabinet of Ministers' Rules of Procedure provide for exceptions under which public consultations on issues related to ensuring the state's defense capability are not held.
Therefore, the mere absence of discussions of the new reservation rules with entrepreneurs will not necessarily indicate a violation of the law. The prospects of a challenge will depend primarily on the content of the specific provisions and their compliance with the laws of Ukraine
Can the new restrictions be suspended for the duration of the court proceedings?
Enterprises may challenge either the Cabinet of Ministers resolution in its entirety or individual provisions thereof. For example, the subject of a claim may include specific reservation limits, new criticality criteria, or requirements for confirming the status of a critically important enterprise.
However, simply filing a court action will not mean that the new rules are automatically suspended.
Clause 1 of Part Three of Article 151 of the Code of Administrative Procedure of Ukraine expressly prohibits suspending the effect of acts of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine as an interim measure
This means that the challenged restrictions will continue to apply during the court proceedings unless the government independently changes the relevant provisions. Consequently, enterprises may face the need to comply with the new requirements even before the court finally assesses the legality of the resolution.
At the same time, the lawyer noted that companies may separately challenge individual decisions by state authorities, including a refusal to reserve employees or an enterprise losing its status as critically important. In such cases, the issue of interim relief will be considered separately.
What evidence will help businesses protect their rights?
One of the main issues in a potential court dispute will be proving that the new restrictions not only create economic difficulties but also violate the rights of enterprises or establish unjustified requirements.
Businesses must first substantiate which specific provisions of the resolution violate their rights and legitimate interests, contradict the law, or impose disproportionate restrictions
According to Honcharenko, mere references to possible financial losses, staff shortages, or the risk of production being halted will not be sufficient. To prepare a relevant lawsuit, enterprises should collect financial statements, staffing schedules, documents concerning reserved employees, criticality decisions, customer contracts, and confirmations of the fulfillment of government or defense contracts.
Particularly important will be evidence that the mobilization of specific specialists could lead to a production shutdown, failure to fulfill a government contract, or disruption of the functioning of critical infrastructure.
For example, if an enterprise proves that the loss of several engineers, technologists, or operators would make it impossible to fulfill a defense contract, this could become a strong argument when assessing the proportionality of the restrictions imposed.
Not only the courts: how businesses can seek a review of the resolution
Court appeals are not the only mechanism for protecting business interests. Even after the new rules are adopted, business associations and individual companies may initiate their review through the Cabinet of Ministers, relevant ministries, parliamentary committees, and members of parliament.
In his opinion, collective appeals by enterprises and industry associations containing specific facts could become an effective tool for influencing state policy.
By the way, on October 16, 63 members of parliament registered draft resolution No. 16160 in the Verkhovna Rada, which provides for the cancellation of the Cabinet's decision on employee reservations dated October 13. It was this resolution that the government revised after a wave of criticism.
Thus, even after the new reservation rules are adopted, businesses have legal mechanisms to seek their review. At the same time, court appeals may take months, while the negative consequences for enterprises may emerge much sooner. Therefore, the key issue remains the government's readiness for constructive dialogue with business and for further consideration of the risks that could jeopardize the operation of strategic industries. After all, in wartime, the state must not only meet mobilization needs but also preserve the economic and industrial potential on which its defense capability directly depends.

EKRE wants to reduce election deposit for candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

EKRE wants to reduce election deposit for candidates
EKRE's parliamentary group wants to reduce the deposit political parties pay to participate in elections from €946 to €220 per candidate and from €118,250 to €27,500 for a full candidate list.
EKRE believes the current amount is too high and has put forward a proposal to change the law.
"Under the current rules, the deposit per candidate is equal to the monthly minimum wage in the year the elections are announced, which as of October 2026 is €946. Since a party may field up to 125 candidates, submitting a full candidate list requires a payment of €118,250. Such an amount is an excessive obstacle for new and small political forces that lack state funding and accumulated financial reserves. This effectively restricts opportunities to participate in elections and reduces political competition," the proposal states.
The bill submitted by EKRE seeks to decouple the deposit from the monthly minimum wage and links it to the subsistence threshold for a person living alone or the first member of a family, as agreed in the State Budget Act under the Social Welfare Act.
"The monthly minimum wage is determined by labor market and wage policy considerations, and its increase is not linked to the conditions for participating in elections, meaning that the deposit also increases without a deliberate decision by the legislator," the party believes.
"The subsistence threshold is significantly lower and more stable: since January 1, 2026, it has been €220 per month. As a result of the amendment, the deposit would decrease from €946 to €220 per candidate and from €118,250 to €27,500 for a full candidate list, or by approximately 77 percent. This would preserve the deposit's deterrent effect against clearly unjustified candidate lists while ensuring that new political forces are not placed at a disadvantage."
However, while still in office as Chancellor of Justice, Ülle Madise said there was no reason to consider the election deposit disproportionate.
She explained that the fee's main purpose is to avoid a situation where too many voters are left without representation because they voted for a list or candidate who does not pass the election threshold and cannot enter the Riigikogu.

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky has called on the business community to prepare in advance for the most critical scenarios regarding enemy attacks and economic challenges.
"When we talk to founders and top management, I've sensed a certain attitude that 'it will somehow blow over.' Perhaps I won't be targeted by missiles or drones, perhaps my sector won't be touched. Therefore, first: I would strongly ask and recommend thinking according to the most critical scenario of events. According to the Prime Minister, enemy strikes have already caused over $7.7 billion in losses, with more than 1 million square meters of various types of real estate, both state and private, destroyed or damaged. Significant destruction has hit energy, metallurgy, logistics, processing enterprises, retail, and other sectors.
"Considering these losses, considering the strikes, we already see that by the end of the year the state budget will underfulfill its plans and forecasts by about $1.5 billion. That is the baseline forecast we have today," he stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that despite all this, the country's economy continues to function.
"If we think in terms of PnL (Profit and Loss statement), allocating a lot of funds to support business is impossible. There is no such PnL, because we can only cover one-third of the budget. Even realizing, clearly realizing this, we live even on a cash flow principle and in a certain way go all-in, allocating certain funds to support programs, to various subsidies, to grant programs. Because we realize that without this support, business – small, medium, and large in particular – cannot be sufficiently resilient to counter enemy attacks. And this is the conscious logic and tactics of the government," Koretsky said.
The Prime Minister stressed that the government will continue programs that have proven their effectiveness, notably the "Affordable Loans 5-7-9%" program. He noted that since the program's inception, UAH 580 billion has been issued, with the current loan portfolio principal standing at around UAH 200 billion. He recalled the recent decision allowing large businesses to receive about UAH 1 billion "in one hand per group of companies" at a preferential interest rate of around 10%.
"The 2026 budget allocated UAH 18 billion. We are expanding this program and see that by the end of the year it will be UAH 22 billion. We currently have a certain deficit on four billion, but one way or another we will cover it, because we consider this to be one of the fundamentally important, correct programs that genuinely supports business," the Prime Minister said.
He also pointed out the necessity of establishing a war risk insurance and damage compensation system. Koretsky recalled the proposal to create a special fund in the budget with an initial state contribution of $1 billion, which partners would double or triple.
"How will this work further? A simplified procedure. Compensation within 30 days after processing. And the tariff for this insurance risk must be very basic, symbolic, we are aiming at approximately 2%. And the maximum damage compensation will be about $5 million in one hand," the Prime Minister detailed.
Koretsky also stated that there is currently no consensus or support for increasing the Value Added Tax (VAT) from 20% to 21% to fund this special fund.
"There is no consensus among big and medium business, there is no support in parliament yet. We are looking for other mechanisms. We will see how the budgetary process proceeds in parliament and build from that. But we have no other path, we must find the instrument. Together we will see what we can contribute," Koretsky said.

‘Still Just a Child’: The Russian Teenagers Fighting and Dying in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:12:54 UTC
21:12:54 KST

“Why?! A young soldier who’d never seen combat … Still just a child,” Svetlana Serezhkina, a resident of the Moscow region, wrote on social media after news emerged of the death of Alisher Svirin, the first publicly identified Russian soldier born in 2008 to be killed in the war in Ukraine.
“It’s such a shame they let him sign a [military] contract,” wrote another commenter, Andrei. Dozens of similar comments written by residents of Svirin’s hometown of Pavlovsky Posad appeared under the same post.
According to his obituary, Svirin had served as a machine gunner in a motorized rifle brigade. He was just 14 when President Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
More than 200 Russian soldiers aged 18 have been killed in the war, according to a count by the BBC’s Russian service and the exiled news outlet Mediazona.
The real number may be higher, as the tally excludes soldiers listed as missing and fighters from the Russian-backed separatist territories in Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Turning 18, then heading to war
The pro-war Orthodox Christian VKontakte group Synodik, which has about 50,000 followers, carries dozens of obituaries for soldiers who were teenagers when the invasion began.
In Orthodox Christianity, a synodik is a list of names of the living or the dead who are remembered in prayers and church services. Likewise, Synodik’s members pray for Russian soldiers like they would in a real church. The comments, mostly posted by women, are filled with Orthodox prayers, animated images of icons and cross emojis.
One recent post commemorates Kirill Tretyakov, who was born Feb. 7, 2007, near the end of Putin’s second presidential term. He had just turned 15 when the full-scale war began.
Tretyakov grew up in Kamensk, a settlement of about 6,300 people roughly 100 kilometers (62 miles) from Ulan-Ude, the capital of Russia’s republic of Buryatia. After completing ninth grade at a local school, he enrolled in a vocational college to study construction. He enjoyed kettlebell lifting and football in his free time.
Tretyakov signed a contract with the Defense Ministry six days after his 18th birthday, according to his obituary.
“From an early age, Kirill strove to be a worthy citizen of his country. On Feb. 13, 2025, Kirill made the courageous decision to defend the Fatherland and signed a contract with the Defense Ministry,” the group’s administrators wrote.
The Moscow Times found identical obituaries in a VKontakte group about Ulan-Ude and on the website of Buryatia’s Kabansky district. Tretyakov served as a combat engineer in an obstacle-laying company of the 656th Separate Guards Engineer-Sapper Battalion. He was killed on Sept. 22 of this year.
“Kirill strove to learn everything a real man should know. He was a brave, determined and fearless warrior who always put the common cause above his own,” his obituary reads.
A psychologist in Russia who works with adolescents said that many young people struggle to grasp the reality of going to war.
“The risk of being killed is very high, but young people don’t think about that,” the psychologist told The Moscow Times, speaking on condition of anonymity for safety reasons.
“When you’re young, you feel like life will last forever, like you’re invincible. Teenagers lack the social circle, the word-of-mouth networks, that could help them think critically about the war.”
That illusion of invulnerability is compounded by a broader devaluation of life in Russia, the psychologist said, referencing television propagandist Vladimir Solovyov’s comment on air that “life is greatly overrated.”
‘They are joining the Lord’s army’
The number of “newly departed warriors,” as the Synodik group calls them, rises almost every day. The group also publishes obituaries for soldiers from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Nikolai was a simple guy. He finished school in our village and was open, cheerful and kind,” the head of the Voikovsky rural settlement in annexed Crimea, said of Nikolai Ruzov, 19. Ruzov was six when Russia annexed the peninsula in 2014 and 14 when the full-scale war began.
Like all draft-age men without a deferment, Ruzov completed a year of compulsory military service before signing a contract with the Defense Ministry and going to fight in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. He was killed on Aug. 18, 2026, less than three months after his 19th birthday.
A Crimean news outlet illustrated his obituary with an apparently AI-generated image presented as a portrait of Ruzov that was later reposted by other outlets. The soldier in the image wears a U.S. flag patch on his shoulder. The Moscow Times analyzed the image using Hive’s AI-detection software, which returned a 100% confidence score that it was AI-generated.
Ruzov had been the commander of an assault squad, state media reported.
“Can someone explain how a 19-year-old boy ended up commanding an assault squad?!” one commenter, Maxim Borisov, asked.
Among those offering condolences online were mothers whose own sons had been killed in the war.
“May Nikolai enter the Kingdom of Heaven, and may you find the strength to learn to live with this irreplaceable loss. Our children don’t die … they are joining the Lord’s army. My boy has been there for four years,” Tamara Romanova wrote on the social network Odnoklassniki.
Ruzov was posthumously awarded Russia’s Order of Courage.
Another 19-year-old soldier, David Fedorov, died on Oct. 20 after being sent on an assault mission, according to his mother.
Police stopped Fedorov on the street in Cheboksary, the capital of the Volga republic of Chuvashia, in May and forced him to sign a contract with the Defense Ministry, his mother told the independent news outlet Astra. He was officially assigned to serve as a driver despite having no driver’s license, she added.
The deaths of young soldiers also feature in state efforts to promote the war in schools.
On Sept. 21, materials for “Important Conversations,” a series of state-mandated patriotic lessons, highlighted two soldiers killed in the invasion at ages 20 to 25. One was Nurmagomed Gadzhimagomedov, a soldier from Dagestan who died in the first month of the full-scale war.
“When I see examples of heroism like this young man ... I want to say: ‘I am a Lak, I am a Dagestani, I am a Chechen, Ingush, Russian, Tatar, Jew, Mordvin, Ossetian’,” Putin said after Gadzhimagomedov’s death in March 2022.
Footage of Putin’s remarks was included in a seven-minute video shown to schoolchildren, while pupils were also offered an interactive lesson about Gadzhimagomedov’s life.
Military personnel in their early 20s also visit schools to deliver patriotic lessons. The children’s psychologist said in-person meetings with returning soldiers could have an even stronger influence on teenagers.
“Soldiers are surrounded by an aura of heroism,” the psychologist said. “The person who comes to speak to you is alive. He fought for three years and came back. Now he’s addressing an audience and has a stable position in society.”
“Young people have little to lose,” the psychologist continued. “They don’t yet have families of their own or things they would find painful to give up, so war can seem appealing.”
