German firm develops low-cost interceptor to stop mass drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:12:36 UTC
21:12:36 KST

- Helsing unveiled Contra, an AI-controlled air defense system, with two new interceptors: the jet-powered AD-1 Inferno and the Mach 2.5 AD-2 Ambush.
- The company said it will mass-produce the interceptors at prices well below existing missiles but did not disclose customers, costs or timelines.
German defense AI company Helsing on Oct. 26 unveiled Contra, an autonomous, AI-controlled air defense system designed to protect countries against large-scale drone and missile attacks, along with two new interceptor missiles, the jet-powered AD-1 Inferno and the rocket-powered AD-2 Ambush, the company announced.
Helsing said Contra fuses data from sensors and weapons into a single air picture so it can detect and engage hundreds or even thousands of incoming drones and missiles at the same time, while operators keep control over decisions and target priorities through the company’s Altra command-and-control software. The company did not name any customers, say when the system could enter service, or disclose whether the interceptors have been flight-tested.
The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor that can loiter in the air, operate in swarms and re-engage targets if it misses on the first pass, which Helsing said makes it suited to fast jet-powered drones. The AD-2 Ambush uses a solid rocket motor for quick intercepts, reaching Mach 2.5 with a range of more than 20 km (12 miles), and is intended for higher-flying threats.
Both missiles are launched from containers, receive course updates in flight from Contra’s ground radar stations, and carry their own radar seeker to find the target in the final phase of flight, which allows them to work at night and in bad weather. Helsing said the system can also take in third-party weapons such as other interceptors, counter-drone lasers, guns and net-based systems within days, and that it is already demonstrating several such integrations to military customers.
The company said it will mass-produce the interceptors at its Resilience Factories at prices significantly lower than existing interceptor missiles, though it did not give a unit cost.
“Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high – affordable and at industrial scale,” said Niklas Köhler, Helsing’s co-founder and president.
Helsing tied the launch to Russia’s growing production of jet-powered attack drones and cruise missiles, citing recent intelligence reports that output of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones alone has reached 4,000 units a month and that Russia is building additional launch sites that put parts of the European Union within range.
Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Munich, Helsing began as a software company and has since moved into hardware, including the HX-2 strike drone and the CA-1 Europa uncrewed combat aircraft. In July, it raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation and selected West Virginia for its first U.S. Resilience Factory, and on Oct. 20 it announced a commercial partnership with Swiss-Dutch drone and missile maker Destinus.

Yeast or famine: Australian convicted murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:11:31 UTC
21:11:31 KST

A convicted murderer has lost a legal bid to overturn a ban on Vegemite in Victoria's prisons, despite his claims that the ban was unlawful because it denied him his human right to enjoy Australian culture.
What constitutes a human right in prison? Not Vegemite, apparently.
An Australian convicted murderer has lost his appeal to bring Vegemite back to prison in Victoria. Andre McKechnie, 54, who is serving a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s, argued that the ban of Vegemite has denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
“Without being able to consume Vegemite, I feel deprived of being able to practise my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community,” he told the state’s Supreme Court.
For those who haven't yet had the (dubious?) pleasure, Vegemite is a strong-flavoured yeast-based food spread that is typically eaten on toast, biscuits, and in sandwiches. It's similar to Marmite in its malty, umami flavour, and because it pairs beautifully with hard cheeses - even if Marmite is less dense in texture compared to its Australian cousin. (Thereby making it superior.)
The polarising salty condiment was first developed in Melbourne in 1919, following the disruption of British Marmite imports after World War I. It was first sold in 1923.
Vegemite has been banned in prisons since 2006, with Corrections Victoria arguing that the strong smell can distract sniffer dogs doing drug searches.
Some prisons have ruled Vegemite as contraband over rumours that it was being used to brew alcoholic drinks. This has been debunked by many as an urban legend, as the yeast used to make the spread is not alive and therefore cannot be used in the fermenting process.
However, McKechnie's petition was still met with rejection by a Supreme Court judge and a response by authorities in Victoria, who stated that the thick paste could be used to disguise contraband substances.
Justice Harris said McKechnie failed to show that the Vegemite ban breached the state's Corrections Act, which requires prisons to provide food to maintain the health and wellbeing of inmates. She said it was "difficult to accept" McKechnie's sadness and isolation was caused by a lack of Vegemite and that the laws did "not extend to an obligation to provide to prisoners foods of cultural significance to enhance their wellbeing".
Justice Harris added there were other ways for prisoners to enjoy Australian culture, including by listening to local music, reading books written by Australian authors, and eating food that was not prohibited.
The Department of Justice and Community Safety welcomed the court decision. A spokesperson said: "Ensuring the safety of staff and prisoners is our top priority. We will continue to manage approved and prohibited items in accordance with operational and security requirements."

Iraq's government struggling amid threats of rebellion, protests, rising Iran tensions - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:10:39 UTC
21:10:39 KST

Iraq’s government is facing a growing challenge in the country’s Maysan province along its Iranian border, where local officials have threatened civil disobedience over the closure of a key border crossing. The dispute comes amid tensions between Baghdad and Tehran and renewed protests in the Iraqi capital marking the anniversary of the 2019 Tishreen movement.
The developments are pushing Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to make key decisions as he also has to deal with looming rumors of renewed war with Iran. Iran has turned Iraq into a frontline and has carried out around 1,600 attacks with drones, missiles, and local militias. Most attacks targeted US diplomatic facilities and Kurdish Iranian opposition groups. Nevertheless, Iran also wants the borders open.
According to Rudaw, Zaidi ordered an investigation on Monday into Mustafa Daeer Mohammedawi, the head of Maysan’s provincial council, after he threatened to block roads connecting the southeastern province with the rest of Iraq. Mohammedawi warned on Sunday that the province would resort to civil disobedience unless the Sheeb border crossing with Iran was reopened by Thursday.
“If it is not opened, then the people of Maysan province will be forced to resort to civil disobedience on all roads,” Mohammedawi said, according to Rudaw. He warned that Maysan could be effectively cut off from the rest of the country.
The crossing, known as Chazabeh in Iran and Sheeb in Iraq, is an important commercial route between the two countries. Baghdad closed it last Wednesday, citing the need to improve its technical and logistical infrastructure. Iraq government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi said the crossing lacked the necessary technical and technological preparations. Iraqi officials have also raised concerns about smuggling through the crossing. The wider story is likely related to Iranian influence on Iraq. It appears militias used an area near the crossing to target Saudi Arabia in September.
Iraq-Iran border closing enables review of security
An Iraqi border official told Reuters that the closure would enable authorities to review security arrangements and install detection equipment to prevent the smuggling of prohibited materials. Meanwhile, Abdul Amir Hassan Ali al-Taiban, an adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, claimed that drugs and currency were entering southern Iraq through crossings with Iran. Iraq referenced “uncontrolled groups,” which may be a euphemism for Iranian-backed militias.
Iran’s embassy in Baghdad rejected these allegations on Saturday, describing them as false and calling on Iraqi authorities to respond to statements that could damage bilateral relations. Maysan is a Shiite-majority province in southeastern Iraq. Its capital, Amarah, is an important commercial center near the Iranian border. The province’s location makes cross-border trade particularly significant for the local economy.
According to Rudaw, protesters gathered near the Sheeb crossing, including truck drivers whose livelihoods depend on trade with Iran. They claim they want to use the crossing for trade and regular reasons. Iraq appears to be facing pressure to keep the crossing closed.
Mohammed Jassim al-Khafaji, an Iraqi lawmaker, questioned whether Zaidi had the legal authority to investigate an elected provincial council chairman. According to Rudaw, Khafaji argued that only the provincial council could remove its chairman through a majority vote.
This has wider implications for the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella organization of pro-Iran armed groups, has accused the Iraqi government of yielding to Washington’s demands regarding border crossings and flights involving Iran.
Iraq sees demonstrations tied to Tishreen protest movement
At the same time, Iraq is witnessing renewed demonstrations connected to the Tishreen protest movement that began in October 2019. Protesters gathered in Baghdad on October 25. It’s worth recalling that in 2019 the Iranian-backed militias suppressed these protests and killed hundreds of people. The Badr Organization was one of the Iranian-backed groups accused of a role in suppressing the protests.
Shafaq News also reported on the demonstrations, noting that participants waved Iraqi flags and called for political and economic reforms. The Tishreen movement represented a major popular protest movement. Beginning in Baghdad and southern Iraq, the protests were driven largely by young Shiite Iraqis frustrated with corruption, unemployment, poor services, and the influence of political factions.
The demonstrators also opposed the system of sectarian political quotas known as muhasasa, which distributes political positions and resources among Iraq’s major communities.
According to figures cited by Rudaw from rights organizations, more than 600 protesters were killed, approximately 20,000 were injured, and around 3,000 were arrested during the movement. Badr leader Hadi al-Amiri, a senior figure in the Shiite-led Coordination Framework, recently defended the role of Iranian-backed armed groups in confronting the Tishreen movement. According to Rudaw, Amiri described the protests as “sedition” and said the Islamic Resistance in Iraq had helped preserve the political order. “The [Islamic] resistance [in Iraq] stood courageously against the Fitna [sedition] of Tishreen, maintaining the state and political order in the process,” he said at an event in late August. This shows how Iraq is divided between the militias and the ordinary people.
For protesters, accountability for the violence of 2019 remains a central demand. They have been angered by Badr’s appearance and its boasting of its role in killing Iraqis. Badr is the largest of the militias that are not sanctioned by the US. Most other groups, such as Kataib Hezbollah, are sanctioned as terrorist groups by Washington.
Shafaq News quoted activist and journalist Muntadhar al-Zaidi, who called for accountability over the killing of protesters and criticized the concentration of political power and misuse of public wealth.
According to Rudaw, the National House political party, which is associated with the Tishreen movement, called for peaceful demonstrations and reiterated demands to end corruption, reform the political system and bring weapons under state control.
For Zaidi’s government, the challenge is to demonstrate that state institutions can enforce the law, secure borders and respond to public demands without becoming hostage to competing political and armed factions. It remains to be seen if Iraq can free itself from Iran’s influence and control.

Attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have nearly emptied the skies over Riyadh this month, aviation data showed on Monday, with cancellations grounding almost nine out of every 10 scheduled flights at the Saudi capital's airport.
About 86% of scheduled flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, or 4,071 out of 4,736, were canceled between October 8 and October 25, according to the latest data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia this month, targeting airports, ports and oil facilities with ballistic missiles and drones. Riyadh's airport, the kingdom's second-busiest after Jeddah, has been struck repeatedly, including an attack on October 10 that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Saudi authorities partially reopened the airport on Sunday after a halt that had started on October 10. Domestic flights resumed from Terminal 1, while national carriers were allowed to operate international services from Terminal 2.
However, the Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh's airport again on Monday, calling it a "military target." The attacks have prompted international airlines to suspend services to the Saudi capital into November, while Delta Air Lines has postponed the launch of its Riyadh route until next year.
Riyadh events canceled, other airports face disruption
The disruption has forced several events in Riyadh to be canceled or postponed, including Saudi Arabia's marquee investment conference, as flight cancellations hamper travel to and across the kingdom.
The upheaval also spread beyond the Saudi capital. More than 7,800 flights, or 45% of all scheduled departures from Saudi airports, were canceled between October 8 and October 25, according to Cirium. The peak came on October 12, when cancellations exceeded 60% of scheduled flights nationwide.
Several major airports recorded severe disruption, including Riyadh at 86%, Dammam at 42% and Abha at 46.7%, where the Houthis have claimed strikes. A number of smaller regional airports saw the vast majority of flights canceled, including Najran, near the Yemeni border, where all flights were canceled.

Southern Syria is facing renewed security challenges. Armed groups have been attacking government security forces, tensions are on the rise in Sweida, and the Syrian government has been confronting threats from ISIS cells in the areas surrounding Damascus.
These developments illustrate the difficulties Syria’s government faces as it seeks to maintain security across the country.
Southern Syria is particularly complex for several reasons. One reason is the continued Israeli raids along the border. Syrians are becoming increasingly angry and frustrated with Israeli patrols into Syrian villages. Last week, a Syrian was killed, and this led to protests.
Another issue pertains to the Druze in Sweida. The Druze area is not under government control and has sought varying degrees of independence.
At the same time, ISIS cells and other threats appear to continue to pose problems in the areas between Damascus and Daraa and the Golan border. Israel has demanded southern Syria be demilitarized, which means that Syria can only deploy lightly armed Interior Ministry forces.
The situation is particularly serious in southern Syria, where instability in Daraa and Sweida has implications for the region near Israel’s border. Syria’s government is attempting to expand its authority, but local armed groups and other security threats might complicate these efforts.
Clashes with authorities, terrorists
Syria’s state-owned news agency SANA reported on Sunday that a highway security officer had been killed and another wounded when armed men attacked a security checkpoint in the Busra al-Sham area of the eastern Daraa province.
According to SANA, the Internal Security Forces said specialized units responded to the attack and arrested the perpetrators following an exchange of fire. Authorities said investigations were continuing to determine the circumstances and motives behind the incident.
The attack illustrates the challenges in Daraa, a province that played an important role in the uprising against the Assad regime that started in 2011.
This area has experienced years of division during the civil war, and the latest incident depicts how armed attacks remain a threat to government efforts to establish security.
In general, Daraa is known for supporting Damascus, but during the era when the former Syrian regime ran Daraa from 2018 to 2024, there were many mysterious killings. Some may have been linked to local feuds.
SANA noted that the attack followed another incident on October 13, when three highway security officers were killed in an attack on their patrol along the Salamiya-Sheikh Hilal-Athriya road in the eastern Hama province.
Although the incidents took place in different areas, they underscore the dangers facing Syrian security personnel.
Meanwhile, the situation in the neighboring Sweida province remains tense. SANA reported that armed groups in Sweida closed the main highway connecting the province to Damascus on Saturday.
Drug, weapon smuggling rampant
Notably, SANA represents the government’s stance. Druze authorities have rejected the claims. They were also angered by recent comments from US Special Envoy Tom Barrack, who slammed Sweida, describing it as an area rife with drug smuggling.
According to the recent Syrian state media report, the road was blocked in both directions at the Um al-Zaytoun checkpoint, which is controlled by what was called a “local armed group.”
Qutaiba Azzam, the director of media relations at the Sweida Media Department, said the groups had prevented traffic from passing through the area.
The report also said about 100 employees were prevented from reaching their workplaces earlier in the week. Similar restrictions had previously affected students seeking to leave the area to take national examinations.
On October 18, Sweida Gov. Mustafa al-Bakour warned that residents were suffering from difficult living conditions and deteriorating security. According to SANA, he accused armed groups of kidnappings, threats, and obstructing efforts to resolve the situation.
It is important to note, again, that SANA presents these developments from the perspective of the Syrian government, describing the armed factions as outlaw groups. Nevertheless, the continuing dispute exhibits the difficulties Damascus faces in extending its authority over Sweida.
Road closures and restrictions on civilian movement matter because they affect daily life and economic activity. Another dimension to this is the way in which local armed groups have clearly been exercising control even when the government seeks to restore normal administration.
In another development, Syrian security forces have continued operations against suspected ISIS cells around Damascus. Per Rudaw, two members of Syria’s Internal Security Forces were killed, and five were wounded during an operation targeting an ISIS cell in Rankous, approximately 45 kilometers north of Damascus.
The Internal Security Forces said the suspects refused to surrender and opened fire. The operation reportedly ended with five suspected ISIS members killed, six arrested, and weapons and explosive belts seized.
ISIS plots to attack government forces
SANA also reported the operation, saying it was carried out in cooperation with the General Intelligence Service.
The operation followed an October 16 announcement that Syrian intelligence and security forces had disrupted an alleged ISIS plot to attack a police patrol in the Damascus countryside. Two suspects were arrested, and an explosive device was seized.
Rudaw noted that ISIS continues to operate in parts of Syria despite a decline in its attacks. It cited an August 27 report by the US Lead Inspector General for Operation Inherent Resolve monitoring office that described a reduction in ISIS attacks following the withdrawal of American forces in April, while noting continued attacks on Syrian government forces.
Taken together, the developments point to several overlapping security challenges.
In Daraa, armed attacks threaten government personnel. When it comes to Sweida, the situation is unlikely to be resolved any time soon. Druze accuse the government of complicity in a massacre of more than 1,000 people in July of 2025. Around Damascus, ISIS cells remain a security concern.
These are not necessarily connected threats. However, they demonstrate the fragmented security environment confronting Syria’s new government.
For Israel, developments in Daraa and Sweida are particularly relevant because both provinces are part of the wider southern Syrian region bordering or close to the Golan Heights. Instability in these areas could complicate efforts to establish predictable security arrangements along the frontier.
The larger question is whether Damascus can consolidate security without creating new confrontations with local communities and armed groups.
Based on the incidents reported over the past week alone, restoring government authority seems to remain a difficult process, particularly in southern Syria, where local tensions intersect with broader regional security concerns.

The Kurier (Courier) ground robotic system of the Berkut special mining battalion of Russia’s Battlegroup South’s 11th Engineer Brigade is capable of withstanding a series of hits from FPV drones and remaining operational thanks to its anti-drone armor, the Zvezda TV channel reported.
"They’ve already withstood about four, five, or six hits from FPV drones <…> from the rubber all the way down to the base of the vehicle itself - about 40-45 cm. The TV program also featured the brigade’s proprietary development - the Shadriki demining robots. These robots can remotely detonate mines, shells, and other ammunition lying on the ground using a TNT pressure charge. "Once we’ve confirmed that we’ve positioned ourselves directly over the target, we drop the charge. As the charge falls, the fuse cord is ignited. We withdraw to a safe distance on the ground robotic platforms and conduct live recording," said a military engineer from the special demolition unit with the call sign Shadr, after whom the robotic platform is named.

Van der Burg plans to use more AI so government can cut payroll
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Deputy home affairs minister Eric van der Burg has set out plans to cut the number of civil servants by 16% by 2035 in a wide-ranging efficiency drive.
Van der Burg said he wanted to take 25,000 government officials off the payroll by standardising IT systems and using other tools to make government more efficient, including AI.
The VVD minister, whose official title is State Secretary for Decisive Government, also plans to reduce the number of advisory bodies and committees, currently 28 and 150 respectively, he wrote in a letter to parliament.
It is the first time Van der Burg has put a number on the civil service cuts, which the cabinet hopes will save €3.5 billion a year by 2035. The announcement confirms earlier reports in the Telegraaf that the cabinet plans to use AI technologies to streamline the apparatus of government.
The minister has not said which departments will have to bear the brunt of the savings, but the police and the defence budgets are expected to be excluded.
However, government agencies that are currently under strain such as the tax office and the employment benefits agency UWV are not likely to be spared.
Simpler regulation
Van der Burg said some of the savings could be made by having fewer regulations and “exceptions to exceptions”. The cabinet has committed to scrapping 500 rules a year under the coalition agreement drawn up by the D66, VVD and CDA parties.
But he admitted that not all the reductions could be compensated by more efficient methods. “Some choices will have to be made regarding what the government should be doing less or not at all,” Van der Burg said.
He also said the government wanted to tighten the rules around the freedom of information law Woo, which citizens and journalists rely on to access public information.
“The requests for information are frequently so broad that it is no longer clear what information we are supposed to provide,” he wrote.

A US Pivot Toward Commercial Espionage?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

Washington has spent three decades lecturing the world about intellectual property protection. Now it looks as if the United States wants to start stealing economic secrets from China and elsewhere.
According to the Washington Post, the Pentagon is standing up an intelligence unit geared toward the acquisition of economic secrets from foreign companies to benefit American companies. Although details remain hazy, the unit is expected to use operatives disguised as private business persons in order to infiltrate foreign companies and appropriate their commercial secrets. This shift was presaged in a Foreign Affairs article by David Cohen, former deputy director of the CIA.
This represents a significant, if not necessarily unwarranted, change in U.S. commercial espionage policy. In its recent history the United States has refrained from direct theft of economic secrets. During the Obama administration the United States attempted to establish norms of commercial espionage that rejected thefts of intellectual property that would award private firms with stolen secrets. The theft of information in order to improve the strategic position of the U.S. was fine; handing stolen goods to an American firm was across the line. This was in accord with a broader U.S. diplomatic effort to improve intellectual property protection across the world.
That the Trump administration would reject such norm-building efforts is unsurprising. The administration has made it clear that it does not believe that anything approaching a “fair” system of global trade exists; the United States has leverage over its trading partners and should use that leverage in order to generate favorable trade arrangements. It is also clear that while Chinese trade policy and practice has become more complex, especially with respect to intellectual property protection, Beijing never accepted anti-espionage norms. China would of course be a primary target for such espionage, especially in fields such as artificial intelligence.
But the effort also suggests that the Pentagon has no confidence that U.S. firms will remain ahead of Chinese and other foreign firms on the innovation curve. The Obama administration’s policy reflected the convenient reality that U.S. companies were, by and large, well ahead of most of their international competitors. Playing “fair” thus benefitted the United States more than it benefitted anyone else. The Pentagon now believes (probably correctly) that America’s technological advantage is not as secure as it would like.
While aggressive industrial espionage is obviously in contrast with some of the norms of the liberal international order, it is not exactly unprecedented for liberal democratic states to play hardball on technology theft. France, for example, has long conducted espionage to benefit French firms, to the endless frustration of French partners. South Korea and Japan have long made light technology appropriation a key part of their industrial strategies. And at its inception, even the United States undertook aggressive steps to steal foreign intellectual property, a practice that paused only when the US achieved a dominant technological position.
In any eventuality, this change in U.S. espionage policy, however justified or inevitable it might be, represents a major shift in how the United States has thought about intellectual property for the last three decades. Moreover, given the technological challenge that China represents to the United States, it seems unlikely that a future administration will reverse this effort.

How Japan's Reforms on Imperial Succession Affect Its Monarchy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:06:55 UTC
21:06:55 KST

Japanese lawmakers are reforming the country’s more-than-a-millennia-old continuous hereditary monarchy in an effort to keep it alive amid a shrinking imperial family.
Amendments to Japan’s Imperial House Law that passed in July took effect on Saturday. One allows Japanese princesses to keep their royal status even if they marry non-royals, though their future children are not considered royals. The other amendment is an apparent roundabout way to preserve patrilineal succession: members of the royal family may adopt a male from former imperial branch families, and those adoptees’ future male offspring can be considered legitimate successors to the throne.
The revisions aim to expand the future pool of eligible heirs to the throne while reinforcing the shutting out of women from leading the Japanese monarchy, which staunch conservatives including the country’s first female Prime Minister, Sanae Takaichi, have repeatedly advocated against upending.
Before the revisions took effect, Emperor Naruhito only had a few viable successors: his younger brother Akishino, followed by his 20-year-old nephew Prince Hisahito, then his 90-year-old uncle Prince Hitachi.
The small pool had raised concerns about the future of the Japanese imperial family. The Japanese public has shown support for female monarchs, signaling a preference to keep the renowned family on the throne. Fans of Princess Aiko, the emperor’s sole daughter, have marched in Japan’s streets in recent weeks in support of her eligibility to become empress.
But extreme right-wing factions in Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party have insisted that maintaining only males from the male imperial line as eligible to become emperor preserves the authority of the Chrysanthemum Throne. The revisions were ultimately borne out of the coalition agreement signed in October last year by the LDP and its junior partner, the Japan Innovation Party.
While the Imperial Household Agency has said it will study how to implement the measures, critics are already studying how to turn the policy over, arguing that it violates the country’s anti-discrimination law. Manga artist Yoshinori Kobayashi filed a lawsuit against the government that called the amendment “unconstitutional.”
Experts say the amendments could affect how the Japanese public views the imperial family.
“It could dilute the feeling of closeness or the feeling of holiness that some people might feel towards the royal family,” Jeffrey J. Hall, a lecturer at Kanda University of International Studies, tells TIME, “because they're more used to the royals that they already know.”
Welcoming back the former imperial family branches
The amendments allow members of the imperial family to adopt a male who is 15 years of age or older and is also a legitimate descendant of a male member of the imperial family before it was trimmed down after World War II. That adoptee should not be married or have children.
Several branches of the Japanese imperial family renounced their royal status in 1947 to cut down on costs the monarchy incurred after the war. Government officials previously said that these 11 families split from a common male-line ancestor some 600 years ago, and are now at least 36 degrees of kinship from Naruhito.
However, the adopted males would not be eligible for the throne—only their eligible male offspring would be. The law would be reviewed every 30 years.
Jeff Kingston, a professor of Asian history at Temple University’s Japan campus in Tokyo, tells TIME the government’s offered solution to the dwindling pool raises questions about the legitimacy of the potential heirs. “Would these people be taken as legitimate by the public?” he says remains an open question, especially as reports surface about who those potential additional successors to the throne might be. “The problem of a monarchy is it’s sort of based on—I don't know—a collectively held myth, belief, faith; and a sausage maker probably isn't going to have that magic.”
Hall, from the Kanda University of International Studies, echoes that the Japanese government will find it difficult to convince the public, especially since the move would introduce unfamiliar faces. “It will be a very difficult problem for the Japanese government to try to basically build up an ideology or a PR program that convinces people that the new royal adoptees are just as royal as the other ones that we all know.”
Snubbing the nation’s popular princess
Kingston says that conservatives proposed the amendments to ensure that a female-led monarchy wouldn’t happen in Japan, even when many Japanese people appear fine with it and some even seem to prefer it. Past media surveys have shown that more than 80% of Japanese respondents favored a female emperor.
Protesters took to central Tokyo’s streets on Oct. 10 to call for further debates on the Imperial House Law, claiming that Princess Aiko, who is 24, should be eligible for the throne.
The other amendment that took effect allows Aiko and the four other single princesses to retain royal status if they get married to people outside the imperial family. Before, princesses who did so lost their royal status, meaning their children are ineligible for the line of succession; the most recent being Mako, one of Naruhito’s nieces. Mako married her college boyfriend in 2021 and has since moved to the U.S.
Hall describes the recent amendments as “very strange” and suspects “many Japanese people won't really fully grasp” them. An August poll from the Social Survey Research Center came to a similar conclusion that the revisions to the Imperial House Law “have not gained the understanding of the Japanese public.”
While Naruhito and the royal family have largely ceremonial duties and do not weigh in on the country’s politics, they have even hinted at what they think should be done. In June, the emperor said he hopes any decision to expand the imperial family should have public support: “I hope it will be something that gains the understanding of the people.”

Royal Navy frigate crisis deepens as old warships wear out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:03:21 UTC
21:03:21 KST

- Two of the Royal Navy’s five remaining Type 23 frigates are expected to be declared unseaworthy, Navy Lookout reported, citing industry insiders.
- That could leave three frigates in service in 2027, with only one available for operations at a time.
Britain’s Royal Navy could be left with just one frigate available for operations at any given time next year, as two more of its five remaining Type 23 frigates are expected to be declared unseaworthy within months, leaving three ships in service in 2027 with one at sea, one in training and one in maintenance, British tabloid The Sun reported, citing a report by naval news site Navy Lookout.
Navy Lookout said industry insiders had told it that two of the five Type 23s will almost certainly have to be declared unseaworthy in the next few months, without naming the ships. The fleet now consists of HMS Kent, which has been in refit for more than two years, along with HMS Portland, Somerset, St Albans and Sutherland, which cover the navy’s main anti-submarine tasks. The youngest of the four was commissioned in 2002, in a class designed for an 18-year service life, and the ships are being retired because their light steel hulls are corroding beyond economic repair.
The frigates hunt Russian submarines in the North Atlantic, protect the Royal Navy’s nuclear-armed ballistic missile submarines as they leave and return to port, and guard undersea communications cables around the British Isles. Former frigate captain Cmdr. Tom Sharpe told The Sun that two tasks cannot be dropped, the towed array patrol ship that tracks Russian submarines in the North Atlantic and the Fleet Ready Escort that responds to threats in British waters, and that keeping even one ship available from a fleet of three becomes harder as the hulls age.
“If we are down to three frigates there will be times when none are available. We are wide open,” said Cmdr. Tom Sharpe.
The warning followed a House of Commons Defence Committee report on defense in the High North, published last week, which found that the navy’s readiness and ship numbers fall far short of the government’s own requirements. The committee cited an internal NATO assessment that reportedly ranks Britain 31st of 32 allies on the speed of rearmament, ahead only of Iceland, and recommended that no further towed-array Type 23 leave service until a new Type 26 frigate replaces it on a one-for-one basis.
“The current reality could hardly be bleaker,” the committee said.
The Royal Navy has had a minimum requirement for 19 frigates and destroyers since 2010, but now operates 11: six Type 45 destroyers and five Type 23 frigates. HMS Richmond and HMS Iron Duke were retired in July, Iron Duke less than three years after a £103 million (about $138 million) life-extension refit, and The Sun reported that around half of the remaining escorts have not sailed for two years.
Replacements are running late. The first Type 26 anti-submarine frigate, HMS Glasgow, is now expected to start contractor sea trials in the first half of 2027, almost a decade after construction began, with initial operating capability planned for October 2028, while the Ministry of Defence says only that the first Type 31 general-purpose frigates will arrive “by the end of the decade.” According to Navy Lookout’s reading of the committee report, the combined frigate force could fall to two ships in 2031 and not recover to eight until 2037.
The warnings come as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said Russia could be ready to attack by 2030 and that Britain must prepare accordingly.
“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The Ministry of Defence said the Royal Navy continues to meet its operational commitments around the world while bringing new maritime capabilities into service, and that it is spending £8 billion (about $10.7 billion) on new ships. The government has two months to respond to the committee’s call for a plan to raise frigate, destroyer and submarine availability before 2030.

Zaporizhzhia teenager develops smart bracelet for people with autism and will present it in Brazil
A school student in Zaporizhzhia has developed a smart bracelet designed to help people with autism detect sensory overload.
Source: Osvitoria, citing Mykhailo Semikin, acting Head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration
Details: Kyrylo Pavliuk is set to present his project at an international science and technology fair in Brazil.
The teenager, who is in 11th grade at the Science Lyceum of the Khortytsia National Academy in Zaporizhzhia, is working on a prototype of a device that will help people to notice the signs of sensory overload in advance.
Kyrylo has named his project Safe Space. The bracelet tracks physiological indicators using sensors, and the data is transmitted to a linked app. The system then analyses it and issues an alert if it detects signs of overload.
The device is primarily intended to help a person with autism realise when stimuli (sounds, bright lights, touch, crowds) become overwhelming, meaning it is time to take a break to calm down.
Safe Space is only a prototype, so it requires testing, verification and refinement. However, on 26-30 October Kyrylo will be presenting it in Brazil at Mostratec 2026, an international science and technology fair for young researchers.
Background: Earlier, Mykhailo Bilous, a school student from Kyiv, took third place at the European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS). He was commended by the judges for developing a neural network that can be used to design antibacterial drugs.

Videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel exilenova+ appear to show several drone strikes and burning buildings in what seems to be Voronezh. It is not clear whether the reported drones were affected by Russian air defense fire.
Neither Ukrainian nor Russian officials have confirmed the attack on Voronezhsintezkauchuk. Ukrainian defense company Fire Point claimed that its FP-1 deep-strike drones had been used in the attack on the chemical plant. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claim. Verifying reports of attacks inside Russia has become difficult due to Moscow's digital censorship.
The reported attack comes as Ukraine has intensified its long-range strikes inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories since the summer, hitting targets such as oil refineries, military-industrial plants, and airfields, aimed at degrading Russia's military-industrial capacity.
Ukraine previously reported hitting Voronezhsintezkauchuk in September. Ukraine's General Staff said at the time that the facility was involved in the production of solid rocket propellant, including for Iskander ballistic missiles.

Face-Offs at India-China Border Are Continuing at Multiple Points, ITBP Chief Confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:02:00 UTC
21:02:00 KST

Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.
At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”
Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.
In a letter dated June 26, 2026, to the deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri, the Nah Welfare Society (NWS) said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) had occupied Indian territory in and around Taksing, including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar in the Chujarta area, Marpan in Marnafe, Portrang Lake, and Tingdingtang. In addition to establishing a military camp in the area, the PLA has also built roads, bridges, and military camps in several locations traditionally used by local communities for grazing, hunting, and collecting forest produce. A Taksing-based tribal organization, the NWS expressed “deep grief” over the PLA’s gradual occupation of ancestral lands, which it said, has intensified since 2020.
Soon after the contents of the NWS’ memorandum became public, the Indian Army categorically dismissed the “reports” as “incorrect and without any basis.” Then came videos claiming the PLA had advanced 50-60 km into Indian territory. The Indian government’s Press Information Bureau Fact Check unit dismissed the reports as ” fake;” the videos did not pertain to the India-China border, it said. This was followed by reports and videos of “skirmishes” in the Taksing Circle on July 25-26. The “confrontation” reportedly “continued for nearly a week before the situation was brought under control following intervention by senior commanders from both sides.” However, Arunachal Pradesh’s Home Minister Mama Natung dismissed the reports of Chinese encroachment as “just rumors.”
Now, for the first time, there is official confirmation of confrontations at multiple locations along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh. And this confirmation has come from the head of the ITBP, the force that guards the India-China border.
The entire India-China border is disputed. The two countries not only have differing perceptions of where the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, runs, but they also claim swathes of territory under the other’s control. China claims 90,000 sq km of territory that roughly coincides with Arunachal Pradesh. India claims 38,000 sq km of territory in Aksai Chin that China occupied during the 1962 border war, and another 5,300 sq km in the Shaksgam Valley of Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan occupied in 1947-48 and gifted to China in 1963.
Besides the war in 1962, which China won, the two sides have engaged in skirmishes and standoffs several times over the decades, including at Samdurong Chu in Arunachal in 1986-87, at the Doklam trijunction of China, India and Bhutan in 2017, and at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, which resulted in the death of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.
Interestingly, China’s interest in Arunachal Pradesh has waxed and waned over time. After occupying Arunachal, then known as the North East Frontier Agency, for several weeks during the 1962 war, the PLA pulled out. Indeed, it did not seem interested in pressing any claims here, and under a swap proposal, was willing to give up claims in the eastern sector, in return for India accepting its control over Aksai Chin in the western sector.
It was only from the mid-1980s that China began reasserting claims over what it calls “Zangnan” or “South Tibet,” at bilateral talks, through military intrusions, by pushing back Indian patrol teams, objecting to visits of Indian leaders to Arunachal Pradesh, refusing to issue visas to Indian passport holders from the state on the argument that they are not Indian, and announcing “standardized” or Chinese names for places and geographical features in the state. According to a 2025 Pentagon report, Arunachal Pradesh is among China’s “core interests.”
In recent months, India and China have engaged in a slew of talks. On August 6, the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs was held in New Delhi. Then on August 26, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the Boundary Question in Beijing. On September 6, the Indian Army and the PLA held their first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh.
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands and chatted at the SCO Summit at Bishkek on August 31, and held a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12.
If the India-China face-offs are continuing, as the ITBP Director General Kapur said they are, it is clear the talks have had little impact in deterring the PLA.
One obvious reason is that Prime Minister Modi’s China strategy is guided more by his interest in beefing up his image among his supporters than taking a strong position against China. His government has repeatedly denied PLA encroachment into Indian controlled territory. “Neither is anyone inside our territory nor is any of our post captured,” Modi grandly declared at an all-party meeting days after the Galwan clashes. The recent spate of denials by the government over PLA’s encroachments in Arunachal is part of the same short-sighted vision. It has weakened India’s hand at talks.
Even more baffling is the Modi government’s withdrawal of ITBP companies from the border. Since June-July, massive anti-government protests in the capital have rattled the Modi government. In response, it has pulled out ITBP personnel from the India-China border and redeployed them in Delhi at a time when the border situation is volatile. Clearly, using the ITBP to crush unarmed civilian protestors in Delhi is more important to Modi than using the force to push back PLA advances at the Arunachal border.
Under the BJP government, almost every Indian state/union territory bordering China is roiled in unrest. Arunachal’s civil society has strongly opposed a mega dam being constructed in the state’s Upper Siang district. The state’s inept handling of public concerns raised over displacement, environmental impact, and loss of livelihoods, and its use of force to deal with protests have resulted in the escalation of the conflict. On October 23, Upper Siang witnessed unprecedented scenes of violence.
Already, Arunachalis are upset with the government for not acting on their apprehensions over PLA encroachment into their traditional lands and hunting grounds. Delhi’s use of the iron fist now to put down their protests will fuel further anger. This will only add to India’s troubles in a sensitive border region.

Poland’s rapid military expansion is running into a growing personnel problem, with the country lacking enough trained pilots to make full use of its F-16 fighter fleet.
The Polish Air Force has 47 F-16 fighter jets but only around 40 trained pilots, while at least 70 would be needed for effective operation of the fleet, the daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Monday.
The figures are unofficial because the Defense Ministry considers information on the number of trained pilots and instructors classified.
Training a new F-16 pilot takes around two years, making the shortage difficult to resolve quickly. 
Only a small number of jet pilots were trained at Poland’s military aviation academy in Deblin last year, according to the newspaper.
The problem has also been aggravated by the transfer of some experienced F-16 pilots to Poland’s incoming F-35 fleet.
The shortage highlights a broader challenge for Poland as it tries to convert one of Europe’s fastest military buildups into operational capability.
Warsaw has sharply increased defense spending since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine in 2022, with military expenditure expected to reach around 4.8% of GDP in 2026. 
Poland has bought or ordered US F-35 fighters, Abrams tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, Patriot air-defense systems and HIMARS rocket launchers as part of its modernization program.
In August 2025, Poland also signed a $3.8 billion (€3.390 billion) agreement to modernize its F-16 fleet to the Viper standard, improving radar, electronic warfare, communications and interoperability with the F-35 and other new weapons systems.
But the pilot shortage suggests that personnel and training capacity may not be keeping pace with equipment purchases.
According to Rzeczpospolita, a similar problem could emerge with Poland’s planned fleet of AH-64E Apache helicopters, for which the armed forces could eventually require as many as 400 pilots.

Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws critcism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:00:41 UTC
21:00:41 KST

Locals in a rural area of California were recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.
Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.
The night-time light demonstration, near the town of Lone Pine in the Sierra Nevada region, was conducted by a US startup called Reflect Orbital, which has an almost sci-fi aim to launch 50,000 satellites into space in the next decade to illuminate parts of the world at night.
In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Reflect Orbital’s proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year, which will orbit the Earth and, via a 59ft-diameter mirror, reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the sun at noon.
The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground, to the bewilderment of locals, one of whom called the lights “blinding”. Large mobile lights were erected near Mount Whitney, with Reflect Orbital comparing the radiance to that of a full moon.
This provided, the company said, a realistic simulation of one of the benefits of this technology: to help search-and-rescue teams and other emergency responders at night. Other planned uses include bathing crops in sunlight, replacing broken streetlights and even providing solar power for military operations, all summoned by the tap of a button on an app.
“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” said a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, which partnered with a local search-and-rescue team for the demonstration.
“We’ll keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever we operate, and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives.”
A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions, however. These groups have criticized the company and the FCC for threatening a harmful change to the separation of night and day that will affect everything from people’s sleep to wildlife and the ability to see the stars from Earth.
“This is an idiotic project,” said Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, an environmental group. “There are a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts. Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”
“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”
In August, four groups represented by Earthjustice asked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.
Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.
Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plans to place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth – that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.
There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’s health by disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.
Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.
But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals for solar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it, have also prompted fierce opposition.
“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.
“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”
Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.
“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”

Why do people with psychopathic traits enjoy fear? New psychology research offers a clue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

People with elevated psychopathic traits tend to find frightening scenes less distressing and more exciting than other people do, according to a new study published in Psychological Reports. The findings suggest that a heightened belief in one’s own invincibility helps explain why these individuals feel less afraid when watching scary footage, while a tendency to become easily bored does not appear to explain why they find it enjoyable.
Psychopathy is a personality profile characterized by two distinct sets of traits. The first dimension involves interpersonal and emotional features, such as superficial charm, manipulation, and a lack of empathy or guilt. The second dimension encompasses an impulsive lifestyle, sensation-seeking, and antisocial behavior. Early psychological theories proposed that individuals high in these traits take reckless risks simply because they have a fundamental deficit in the ability to feel fear.
More recent work has challenged the notion that psychopathic individuals are completely incapable of experiencing fear. While these individuals often show muted physical reactions to threat, a 2016 meta-analysis found little evidence that they lack the conscious, subjective feeling of fear. Psychological theories of emotion note that fear and excitement share nearly identical physical symptoms, such as a racing heart, meaning that how a person experiences a high-stakes moment depends heavily on how their mind interprets that physical arousal.
Building on this distinction, members of the team behind the new study developed the Fear Enjoyment Hypothesis, which proposes that people with psychopathic traits actually interpret frightening situations as pleasurable. Experiencing fear as enjoyable requires two simultaneous reactions: a dampened negative response, such as feeling less panicked, and a heightened positive response, such as feeling exhilarated.
In a 2020 experimental study by the same group, participants with higher psychopathy scores watched scary video game footage and reported fewer negative emotions and stronger positive emotions than their peers, and a 2026 study covered by PsyPost found that individuals higher in psychopathic traits interpret an elevated heart rate during scary moments as pleasurable excitement rather than distress.
What remains uncertain is why people with psychopathic traits evaluate threatening situations so positively. One possibility draws on horror filmmaker Alfred Hitchcock’s observation that audiences can enjoy suspense when they feel safe from actual threat. Psychopathic individuals may possess a strong sense of invincibility, defined as the belief that one is immune to danger and personal harm, which could make frightening scenarios feel safe enough to enjoy, much like riding a roller coaster.
Another possibility is boredom proneness, the tendency to become bored easily, which has been tied to sensation-seeking and was linked to sadistic behavior and bullying in research covered by PsyPost in 2023, and which might drive individuals with psychopathic traits to seek out fear for an emotional rush. To test whether invincibility and boredom proneness help explain the link between psychopathy and fear enjoyment, study author Angela Book, a professor and director of the forensic psychology and criminal justice program at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ontario, and her colleagues conducted two studies.
“Much of the research on psychopaths and fear has focused on a deficit in feeling fear, but we didn’t think this told the whole story,” Book told PsyPost. “Instead, we thought that people with psychopathic traits likely feel something, but maybe it is different from other people. More specifically, we think they actually enjoy fear-inducing situations. This particular study tried to examine why they might enjoy fear.”
In the first study, the researchers recruited 825 participants across two distinct groups to test the role of invincibility. The first group consisted of 425 undergraduate students from two Canadian universities, who had an average age of about 21 years and were predominantly female (75 percent). The second group included 400 adults from Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, an online crowdworking platform, who had an average age of about 38 years and were mostly male (59 percent).
All participants completed the 64-item Self-Report Psychopathy Scale, rating their agreement with statements such as “People sometimes say that I’m cold-hearted” on a five-point scale. They also completed the Invincibility Belief Index, which presents 20 hypothetical scenarios, such as being confronted by a vicious, angry dog, and asks respondents to rate the probability from 0 percent to 100 percent that they would escape unharmed.
Next, participants watched two three-minute first-person video clips in random order: a SeaWorld roller coaster ride designed to induce excitement, and a suspenseful sequence from the horror video game Outlast designed to induce fear. After each clip, participants rated how strongly they felt nine negative fear-related words, including “alarmed” and “panicked,” and nine positive excitement-related words, including “exhilarated” and “delighted,” on a scale from 1 to 5.
Across the combined sample, participants rated the roller coaster clip as more positive and less negative than the horror game clip, confirming that the videos triggered the intended emotions. Compared to the university students, the online adult group scored higher on perceived invincibility (averaging 6.08 versus 5.68 on an 11-point scale) and rated the horror video more positively (averaging 26.30 versus 24.36 out of a possible 45) and less negatively (averaging 28.99 versus 31.49 out of 45). Although statistical tests indicated that neither age nor biological sex altered the underlying links between personality traits and emotional reactions, the authors analyzed the student and adult groups separately to account for these baseline differences.
To evaluate why psychopathy relates to fear enjoyment, the researchers used mediation analysis, a statistical technique that tests whether an intermediate factor accounts for the connection between two variables. The analyses predicting negative reactions controlled for positive reactions, and vice versa.
In both groups, higher psychopathy scores were linked to a stronger sense of invincibility, which statistically accounted for the link between psychopathic traits and lower negative emotion during the scary clip. In the student sample, the direct link between psychopathy and reduced fear was no longer statistically significant once invincibility was considered; in the online sample, that link had not been statistically significant to begin with. By contrast, invincibility did not explain why participants with higher psychopathy scores reported heightened excitement during the horror clip.
The links were modest. Correlations between psychopathy scores and positive reactions to the horror clip were about 0.26 to 0.32, while the correlations with reduced negative reactions were about 0.07 to 0.10. On the usual scale, about 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium, and 0.5 large.
Because feeling invincible appeared to explain why individuals with psychopathic traits were unbothered by threat, but not why they found it actively thrilling, the researchers conducted a second study examining boredom proneness. They recruited a new sample of 425 undergraduate students from two Canadian universities, with an average age of 21 years and a majority of women (74 percent). These participants followed the exact same procedure as the first study, with the addition of the Boredom Proneness Scale, in which they rated items such as getting restless while waiting in line on a seven-point scale.
Across the sample, participants averaged 22.94 out of 45 on positive ratings of the horror clip and 29.99 on negative ratings. Psychopathic traits were positively correlated with both boredom proneness and a sense of invincibility (correlations of about 0.3), as well as with more positive and less negative ratings of the horror clip (correlations of about 0.2).
When both potential explanatory factors were tested together in a mediation model, invincibility again partially accounted for the link between higher psychopathy scores and reduced negative fear responses, and unexpectedly also partially accounted for the positive excitement response, though both effects were small and statistically borderline. Contrary to the authors’ expectations, the indirect pathway linking psychopathic traits to heightened positive reactions through boredom proneness was not statistically significant.
“First, we did find that people with psychopathic traits not only have less of a negative response to fear-inducing situations, they also have a larger positive reaction,” Book explained. “Essentially, they enjoy fear. Importantly, this appears to be due to a sense of invincibility. As Alfred Hitchcock famously pointed out, we only enjoy fear when we don’t feel like we are in danger.”
The researchers also broke the psychopathy scores down into the two main trait dimensions. Both were linked to fear enjoyment, though results for the impulsive-antisocial traits were less consistent, particularly in the online sample. In the second study, accounting for boredom proneness made their link to enjoying the scary clip stronger rather than weaker, a result the authors say may be a statistical fluke. Overall, the findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which similarly found that higher psychopathic traits, especially interpersonal and emotional features, were associated with more positive and fewer negative reactions to scary video clips.
“The relationship between psychopathic traits and fear enjoyment is of medium size, which is a relatively large effect in psychological research,” Book noted. “It has been found in multiple studies by multiple researchers and appears to be fairly robust.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because the studies measured personality traits and emotional reactions at a single point in time using self-report questionnaires, the data cannot establish that feeling invincible directly causes people to feel less fear. The researchers also did not publicly record their predictions before collecting data. In addition, the participants were university students and online workers rather than clinical patients or incarcerated offenders, meaning the findings reflect variations in psychopathic personality traits within the general population rather than a diagnosed personality disorder.
Another point to keep in mind is that the frightening stimulus was a three-minute video game clip rather than a real-life physical danger. Previous neurological research suggests that individuals high in psychopathic traits often fail to notice subtle threat cues in their environment, so their reduced distress might reflect inattention to danger rather than a conscious belief that they are invincible. Because boredom proneness failed to explain why scary situations feel exciting to people with elevated psychopathic traits, the authors suggest that future studies should investigate the brain’s dopamine-driven reward system, as the anticipation of a high-stakes situation may itself act as a powerful reward for these individuals.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to test how people with elevated psychopathic traits respond to more immersive threats that go beyond standard video clips. “Our next step will be to use virtual reality horror games/scenarios to look at the relationship in more realistic situations,” Book said.
The study, “Psychopathy and Fear Enjoyment: The Role of Invincibility and Boredom Proneness,” was authored by Angela Book, Beth Visser, Tori Wattam, and Kirkland Johnston.

Linguistic​ and Conceptual Justice in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

“Driven by the de facto dominance of English, AI multilingual alignment shows a form of cross-linguistic deference, a systematic tendency to resolve cross-linguistic disagreement by treating the English judgment as authoritative, rather than acknowledging the natural cross-linguistic inconsistency of human natural language.”
That’s from the “Cagliari Statement on Linguistic and Conceptual Justice in AI“, which objects to correcting such inconsistencies” in ways that “suppress legitimate semantic plurality and progressively establish English (spoken natively by only about 6% of the world’s population) as the de facto standard for what meanings should remain equivalent across languages.”
Rather, according to the statement, “language models require language-specific alignment, grounded in rich data on how ordinary speakers actually use their words in each language.”
The statement, which is currently open for signatures, includes distinct recommendations for AI developers, researchers in linguistics and philosophy, institutions and funders, and standard-setting bodies, among others.
It was originally drafted by Çağla Çimendereli (Old Dominion), Filippo Contesi (Cagliari), and Masaharu Mizumoto (Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) and worked on during the Linguistic Justice Society Satellite Workshop at the 6th European Experimental Philosophy Conference.
The statement provides some background on the issue:
While the capabilities of current frontier AI models have shown remarkable progress in areas such as mathematical ability, their semantic competence in natural languages—including, in particular, lower-resource languages—fails to accurately reflect basic human semantic intuitions (i.e., how ordinary speakers actually use their words in diverse contexts). This gap is what this statement addresses.
Multilingual AI systems now answer questions about foreign facts, reports, opinions, etc. in local languages without explicitly indicating that translation mediates the response. Moreover, because these systems acquire meaning from patterns of usage, they inherit the semantic norms of the larger corpora they are trained on—which are predominantly English. We therefore hold that decisions about how such systems behave across languages are not merely technical, but normative.
The full statement is here.
(via Çağla Çimendereli)

“I want to send a loud and clear message to the parties. We need maximum restraint and diplomatic solutions,” he said.
“If the sabre-rattling we are witnessing now translates itself into a major escalation, the situation in the region can get out of control.”
Moreover, navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea – critical maritime corridors for global trade.
He commended Egypt for its mediation role in helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the sides.
‘Keep the channels of diplomacy open’
The Secretary-General was speaking alongside Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty following meetings focused on this and other crises in the Middle East and Africa.
“Egypt is a pillar of multilateralism,” he said. “And at a time when divisions are deepening, it is critical to keep the channels of diplomacy open.”
On Gaza, Mr. Guterres expressed profound appreciation for Egypt’s indispensable role, noting that the country has been central to mediation and humanitarian efforts since the beginning of the conflict.
Lift Gaza aid restrictions
He commended continued support in facilitating life-saving aid, medical evacuations and the work of humanitarian partners such as the Egyptian Red Crescent.
The Secretary-General called for Israeli restrictions on humanitarian assistance to be lifted and obstacles blocking implementation of the UN Security Council-endorsed comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict to be removed.
“Civilians must be protected and international law must be respected,” he said.
Alarm over West Bank
The UN chief said he was also deeply alarmed by Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank, pointing to expanding settlements, “unrelenting” evictions, surging violence, assaults, and attacks against journalists and diplomats.
“We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment with the spectre of ethnic cleansing looming ever larger. This must end,” he said.
Moreover, there can be no durable peace in the Middle East without the realization of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination, he said, once again upholding the two-State solution.
Sudan and Libya
The Secretary-General also addressed the war in Sudan. He said that “the fighting must stop”, adding that the country’s future “must belong to the Sudanese people through an inclusive pro-political process that preserves its unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity”.
Regarding Libya, he said that “it is time to build on political momentum, unify institutions and pave the way for national elections, finally bringing the prolonged transition to an end.”
The UN chief leaves office at the end of the year and this marked his ninth visit to Egypt since being appointed in 2017.
Mr. Guterres began his remarks by explaining that he has come back repeatedly “because when this region and our world have faced some of the most difficult moments, Egypt has consistently worked to open space for diplomacy”.

Ebola: UN officials condemn killing of nurse in DR Congo
The UN’s Ebola coordinator and the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) have deplored the killing of a nurse working to halt the spread of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The nurse was killed by protesters in Bafwasende, a rural town in Tshopo province, on Saturday while responding to an Ebola alert. 
A health worker was also severely injured in the attack and remains in hospital.
Call for probe
Julien Harneis, UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, issued a statement extending condolences to the nurse’s family and colleagues.
“I strongly condemn this attack and call for a thorough investigation,” he said. “I urge communities to protect health workers and allow them to carry out their work safely”.
The WHO Director-General, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, expressed his condolences in a post on social media. He also wished a swift and full recovery to the injured health worker.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety,” he wrote on X. “Healthcare must always be protected.”
Historic outbreak
The deadly incident occurred amid ongoing efforts to contain the spread of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus for which there currently is no approved vaccine.
More than 9,760 cases and some 4,727 deaths have been recorded in the DRC since the outbreak was declared on 15 May, according to recent WHO figures.
The outbreak is the deadliest in the country’s history. It was first reported in the volatile eastern region and has now reached eight provinces: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi, Tshopo and Nord-Ubangi.
Uganda also confronted a smaller Ebola outbreak which was declared defeated in August, while France, Kenya and Nigeria have reported cases.
‘Remarkable achievement’ in Nigeria
Nigeria confirmed its first case last week – a woman who had travelled from Uganda.
She and a contact, who is her husband, were medically evacuated to Switzerland on Monday morning, WHO said, explaining that both are Swiss citizens and that the patient is clinically stable.
“The Nigerian medical team successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilized her condition,” the WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Janabi, wrote on X.
‘Vigilance remains critical’
He congratulated the Nigerian Government, health workers, clinicians, emergency responders and all those involved in the response.
“This is a remarkable achievement and a testament to what Africa can accomplish when we work together,” he said.
Dr. Janabi noted that the evacuation means Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases, “however, vigilance remains critical”.
Nigeria will continue to monitor 52 contacts, he said, while Switzerland will assume responsibility for the patient’s continued care and follow-up of her husband.
