====================================================================================================

A choice between debt and inflation: As protests rage, the French government has no good option for solving its financial problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:46:47 UTC
15:46:47 KST

Protests in France have brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets demanding higher wages, lower inflation, and more funding for hostpitals and schools. The government, meanwhile, is trying to cut spending on benefits, pensions, and public-sector salaries as part of an effort to curb the growth of a record-high public debt that has already reached 119% of GDP. Borrowing costs are rising, with investors now demanding higher yields on French debt than on Italian or Greek bonds. And although France’s social spending is indeed burdensome — the highest among OECD countries — the problem lies less in the spending itself than in the near-stagnation of the economy. France appears to be stuck in a vicious circle: the more aggressively Paris cuts spending, the more the economy will slow, making it even harder to reduce the debt. Before long, the problem could spread throughout the eurozone — after all, France is too big to bail out.
After a demonstration in Paris on Oct. 17, the statue of Marianne in the Place de la République was left bearing the inscription “Those who sow poverty reap anger.” According to the Interior Ministry, 550,000 people took to the streets across the country that day, though the protest organizers put the figure at 800,000.
The public discontent began in late September with a blockade of a high school near Paris, where students complained of teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and crumbling buildings. A month later, trade unions and the Yellow Vests joined the students, expanding the list of demands to include more funding for hospitals, higher wages, lower fuel prices, and wealth redistribution. In Limoges, the historic city hall was set on fire; in Marseille, protesters stormed a government building; and in Paris, stores were looted.
President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on television, speaking of “anger and shame” and insisting that the protesters’ demands had been heard. However, he said nothing about money — after all, parliament is debating the 2027 budget, which must convince France's creditors that Paris can rein in its growing debt.
Debt is growing, but the economy is not
France’s public debt stands at nearly €3.6 trillion — or 119% of GDP, an all-time high — and it is rising rapidly. A year ago, it stood at 115%, and the government expects it to reach 122% by the end of 2027.
Servicing the debt is becoming increasingly expensive. Next year the public sector will pay €91.2 billion in interest, up from €79.2 billion this year. Debt-servicing costs in the central government budget will rise by €10.3 billion. No other spending item is growing as fast. Excluding civil-service pensions, interest payments are becoming the government’s largest expenditure item, surpassing both defense (€64 billion) and education (€62.2 billion).
Excluding civil-service pensions, which are allocated across ministries, interest payments are becoming the government’s largest spending item
The average yield for French bonds sold in 2025 was 3.4%, Fitch notes, but earlier this month yields on French 10-year bonds topped 5% — the first time since 2002. The difference between the interest rate investors demand from France is now more than 1.4% higher than that demanded of Germany — wider than at any point since 2012, when the eurozone was in the midst of a debt crisis.
By mid-October, markets had calmed somewhat, but France was still paying more to borrow than countries that had been at the heart of that previous crisis: 4.8%, compared with 4.5% for Italy and 4.05% for Spain. (During the 2011 debt crisis, Italy paid as much as 7% — a rate that ultimately cost Silvio Berlusconi his job.)
Even with its new measures, the government projects a budget deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027. Without them, it estimates, the deficit would have reachd 6.4%. To keep public debt from rising relative to GDP, France needs to cut its deficit by around 3.5 percentage points of GDP, Fitch estimates.
A comparison with other countries shows how unusual France’s situation is. Sweden demonstrates that a generous welfare state can coexist with low public debt. The United States has a similar debt-to-GDP ratio to France’s, but it borrows in its own currency and controls its monetary policy. As a member of a currency union, France has no such option.
France spends more on healthcare as a share of GDP than any of the other countries in the comparison, and almost as much as Italy on pensions. It also spends a larger share of GDP on education than Germany, Italy, or Spain, though considerably less than Sweden.
Sweden shows that generous social spending does not necessarily lead to high public debt. It spends more than the EU average on old-age benefits and more than any of the other countries on education, yet its debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly one-third of France’s. France, by contrast, spends heavily on pensions without standing out for its education spending.
The growth picture is more complicated. In 2025, the French economy grew more slowly than those of Spain, Sweden, and the United States, but faster than Germany’s and Italy’s. However, Germany’s public debt is just 63% of GDP.
Spain presents the opposite picture. In the first half of 2026, its public debt rose by 4.3% in nominal terms, but its debt-to-GDP ratio fell by 1.8 percentage points, to 101.4%, as the economy grew faster than the debt. In the second quarter, Spanish GDP rose by 0.7%, while French GDP stagnated.
France may be much harder to rescue than the countries bailed out during the debt crisis, and experts like Nobel laureate Paul Krugman believe a bailout may no longer even be feasible. “France may have crossed the line between ‘too big to fail’ and ‘too big to save,’” he wrote earlier this month. France’s economy is far larger than those of Greece or Portugal, making a bailout much more expensive. Eurozone countries would also be likely to argue far more bitterly over who should foot the bill.
How France got to this point
The French economy is hovering on the brink of stagnation. Growth is being held back by weak consumer spending, rising borrowing costs, a decline in construction, the the hesitancy of businesses to commit to investment.
The main source of uncertainty is energy prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The Bank of France expects the purchasing power of wages to fall by 0.7% in 2026 and unemployment to rise to 8.4% by the end of the year.
The weak economy is putting pressure on public finances. The projected 2026 budget deficit has risen to 5.4% of GDP — already in excess of its 5% target. Fitch attributes this to two factors: the economic and labor-market slowdown is weighing on tax revenues, while interest payments on the debt are rising. In effect, the economy itself is contributing to the budget problem.
There are two familiar explanations for France’s troubles. The first is that the state spends too much. The second is that it allocates money, failing to turn government outlays into effective public services.
Two familiar explanations for France’s troubles: excessive public spending and poor allocation of funds
According to the IMF, France's public spending will reach a whopping 57.6% of GDP in 2026, and social spending exceeds 30% of GDP, one of the highest levels among OECD members. It is important to note that this OECD measure excludes schools and universities, covering only childcare and care for children under six. France’s exceptionally generous social spending is therefore not inconsistent with high school students’ complaints about teacher shortages.
A special OECD study put France’s social spending at 31.6% of GDP in 2022, compared with 26.7% in Germany. Pensions alone account for 24.3% of all public spending. France does collect significant amounts of tax revenue — but this fact means that there is little room to raise them further, as government revenue is already among the highest in the eurozone, the IMF notes.
Public money is also poorly allocated — at least, that's what citizens themselves say. In a 2022 survey conducted by the OECD, respondents in France were, on average, less satisfied with access to high-quality, affordable public services than respondents in Germany and the UK.
Where the government plans to make savings
On Oct. 1, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government presented its 2027 budget. New measures are expected to directly save €43 billion, and the government puts the total expected impact at €54 billion once the lingering effects of past measures are factored in. Overall, the plan calls for cuts to spending and in increase in tax revenues.
The main puzzle with this budget is the arithmetic. The €43 billion in new measures amounts to roughly 1.4% of GDP, yet the deficit is expected to fall by just 0.4 percentage points, from 5.4% to 5% of GDP. Without the new measures, however, the deficit would have been expected to rise to 6.4%.
Two possible scenarios: both are worse
France faces a choice between two strategies: continuing to borrow or rapidly cutting the deficit. Neither guarantees the desired outcome.
Continuing to pile up debt is the least painful option for those in power. Pensions, benefits, and public-sector salaries would continue to be indexed, consumption would hold up, and the protest wave would likely subside. However, every year of deficit spending adds to public debt, and each new loan becomes more expensive.
Debt accumulated when interest rates were near zero now has to be refinanced at significantly higher rates. Eventually, interest payments will crowd out other spending, including on education and healthcare. Fitch estimates that debt-servicing costs as a share of GDP are rising by 0.2–0.3 percentage points a year.
France could face another problem even sooner: a loss of investor confidence that sees them demand higher interest rates that in turn widen the deficit and thereby further reduce the market's faith in the French government. Unlike the United States, France cannot unilaterally devalue its currency or print money. In the event of a true debt criis, Paris would simply have to impose much harsher spending cuts.
For now, however, this remains a theoretical risk, and the eurozone also has a safety net in place in the event that creditors panic. Since 2022, the European Central Bank has been able to buy a country’s bonds when their yields rise unjustifiably, with no predetermined limit on purchases. The instrument is intended to counter market panic unrelated to a country’s economic fundamentals, and before using it, the ECB assesses whether the country complies with EU fiscal rules and whether its debt is sustainable.
“The first and foremost solution lies within France itself — in its fiscal policy,” as ECB President Christine Lagarde said on Oct. 14.
The alternative — radically cutting spending to reduce the deficit — would be painful. Sharp austerity would mean reductions in pensions, public-sector salaries, and government procurement. Such a move would increase the likelihood of even larger protests and greater instability while also weakening demand. As an IMF review of fiscal consolidation programs shows, spending cuts have a particularly severe impact during economic downturns, with low-income people hit hardest due to the fact that they have little access to credit to help them weather a loss of income.
If GDP contracts sharply enough, the debt-to-GDP ratio can even rise despite the presence of a smaller deficit. According to the IMF, austerity programs have frequently relied on overly optimistic growth forecasts, with debt ultimately rising rather than falling. The French Pensions Advisory Council illustrated this mechanism using economic models: cutting pension spending by 0.2% of GDP in the short term reduces economic activity by about 0.1 percentage points.
In practice, Paris is unlikely to choose either extreme, instead gradually reducing the deficit by reviewing spending and phasing out tax breaks. This is the approach the IMF recommends: bring the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2029 while protecting the most vulnerable members of society.
France will take a middle path, gradually reducing the deficit by reviewing spending and phasing out tax breaks
In May, IMF staff recommended scrapping ineffective tax breaks, eliminating duplicate spending, and developing a “credible pension reform strategy.” Still, even if the plan goes ahead, the IMF forecasts that public debt will continue to rise in 2028, reaching 121% of GDP.
The current budget, however, may pass more easily than its predecessor, as the approaching presidential election in April 2027 gives parties an incentive to leave the next government with the current budget, which it will then have to revise.
“We inherit the mistakes of our leaders, and they fall on our children’s shoulders,” read one placard in Place de la République captured by Euronews. The central question for France now is how to distribute the inevitable costs among generations and social groups.

Gloom in Moscow as Vucic's defeat in Serbia deprives Russia of an ally
MOSCOW, Oct 26 - Aleksandar Vucic's crushing election defeat by a student-backed protest movement has cast gloom over Moscow, which has lost another important partner in Europe just six months after ally Viktor Orban was ousted in an election in Hungary.
Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow who had been prime minister or president since 2014, suffered a defeat on Sunday that prompted nationwide celebrations, although few had any idea of how the Balkan country's new student-backed leaders would govern.
Russia saw Vucic's Serbia as a crucial ally in Europe, and as a bulwark against what Moscow has cast as the European Union's aggressive attempts to contain and punish it over its war in Ukraine.
Serbia buys large quantities of gas from Russian energy giant Gazprom, and although it has aspirations to join the European Union, it has not signed up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Instead, under Vucic — who enjoyed close ties to President Vladimir Putin — it continued to develop close economic, political and military links to Moscow.
The Kremlin put a brave face on Vucic's defeat, saying it had taken note of the result and that Vucic — whose contribution to bilateral ties it warmly praised — was moving into opposition.
"As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
"For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango."
GEOPOLITICAL SETBACK
Russia can still count EU member Slovakia, under Prime Minister Robert Fico, as a friendly country. It has also been closely watching unrest in France, where far-right politician Marine Le Pen has said she would cut financial aid to Ukraine if she won next year's presidential election.
Recent regional electoral successes for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have been welcomed in Russia, where Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has begun to speak about the possibility of one day reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia which were blown up in 2022.
But for now at least, the potential loss of Serbia as a close ally — after setbacks to Russia's geopolitical influence in the South Caucasus region and parts of Central Asia — is being seen as a serious blow in Moscow by Kremlin-aligned politicians, media and analysts.
Before Sunday's election, the Student List party said it would not introduce sanctions on Russia over Ukraine, that it would retain Serbia's military neutrality, and that it would not seek to join NATO.
Vucic has cast doubts on those pledges, suggesting the party would renege on them and impose sanctions on Moscow as soon as March or April.
Jovo Bakic, a representative for Student List and university lecturer, on Monday denied his party would U-turn.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector. There will be no changes there (in the country’s foreign policy),” Bakic told Russia’s RT Balkan TV outlet.
Members of Russia's political elite fear Serbia's EU aspirations could see it put under serious pressure to align itself more closely with EU foreign policy however and that Moscow could find itself betrayed by a traditional ally in the process.
"Brussels, for its part, is keen to see Belgrade align itself more closely with the common European position on Russia. The main indicator of Serbia's actual course will not be Vucic's statements or his opponents’ electoral pledges, but rather the first decisions taken by the new cabinet," said the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper.
Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of the influential Russia in Global Affairs journal, said it was clear that a new political era was under way in Serbia that could sharply reorient the country towards the EU, in the same way that Orban's loss of power in Hungary saw Budapest and Brussels become much closer.
"In this sense, the Hungarian case is quite telling," said Lukyanov. "And Russia has nothing good to look forward to." REUTERS

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:42:48 UTC
20:42:48 KST

Zelenskyy said the planned visit would gather Ukraine, the US, EU and NATO in high-level talks on security guarantees and diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's planned visit to Brussels this week for high-level talks with the US, EU and NATO has reportedly been cancelled.
Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's communications adviser, told reporters on Monday that Kyiv could no longer confirm the visit because of changes to the American side's plans.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Sunday, Zelenskyy said the talks were being planned for 27 or 28 October, bringing together representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU, as well as NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
Asked by Euronews about the planned talks, the European Commission said it remained engaged in diplomatic efforts but offered no further details.
"The Commission continues to participate in talks and efforts with allies and partners to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
"At this stage, we have no further information to share."
The Brussels meeting was intended to follow a series of diplomatic discussions in Oslo last week, including talks between Zelenskyy and US special envoy Steve Witkoff attended by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
According to Zelenskyy, wider discussions also involved security advisers to the leaders of Britain, France and Italy, alongside Björn Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The US subsequently briefed its partners following Witkoff's talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, Zelenskyy said.
"We had a briefing from the Americans, and now they want not just a briefing, but to discuss security, guarantees, the EU and its involvement more broadly," Zelenskyy said.
"They want a meeting in Brussels this week. The Americans, Ukraine, the EU at presidential level and NATO at secretary-general level. I don't know whether anyone else will be part of this group in Brussels."
The development comes ahead of another round of negotiations between Ukrainian, American and Russian teams, which Zelenskyy said was being planned for the first half of November.
Abu Dhabi has been mentioned as a possible venue, although the date and location have yet to be confirmed.

Israeli army chief clashes with Netanyahu over toppling Iran&#8217;s regime

Unknown Publisher

20:42:40 KST

Israeli media reports have highlighted growing divisions between Israel’s political and military leadership over how to deal with Iran, with security officials and allies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu believing that Iran’s regime cannot be toppled through direct military action.
Israel’s Channel 12 reported an “unprecedented” confrontation between army chief Eyal Zamir and Netanyahu, which escalated in recent hours over their positions on Iran and related developments.
According to the report, Zamir and several senior security officials fear that the political leadership’s approach could lead to a serious miscalculation and trigger a dangerous military escalation with Iran ahead of Israel’s elections. Concerns are also growing within the military that the Iran issue could be used for political purposes.
Meanwhile, Israel’s public broadcaster Kan 11 quoted sources close to Netanyahu and senior security officials as saying that regime change in Iran cannot be achieved through military strikes. They said such operations could weaken the regime but would not bring about its collapse.
These assessments contrast with remarks made by Netanyahu in recent days, in which he called for the mission to be “completed” and Iran’s regime to be toppled during the remainder of US President Donald Trump’s term in office.
About six months ago, however, Netanyahu said that the decision to topple Iran’s regime rested with the Iranian people themselves.

Elena Teslova
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted Monday to extend martial law and general mobilization until Jan. 29, 2027.
According to data published by the Rada, 293 lawmakers voted in favor of extending martial law.
The vote followed a proposal by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Before the final vote, lawmakers agreed to consider the bills under an expedited procedure.
It is the 21st time the current parliament has voted to extend martial law and mobilization.

Ukraine Wants EU Representative at Russia Negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:40:38 UTC
20:40:38 KST

Ukraine is seeking to move up planned trilateral negotiations with the United States and Russia by at least a week and bring an EU representative into the talks, Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing sources close to the negotiation team.
The next round of discussions between Ukraine, the US and Russia is tentatively scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on November 10, after the US congressional midterm elections. Kyiv and Washington are working to persuade Moscow to agree to meet at least a week earlier.
A source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's team told Ukrainska Pravda that the timing was critical because of the coming winter. “in December, every week will be important. When you have no power, water or heating, every single day plays a role”, the source said.
As of the evening of October 25, Moscow had not provided final confirmation of a change to the date.
Kyiv does not anticipate a breakthrough at the initial meeting, believing that several rounds of negotiations will be needed to reach substantive agreements. A source from the President's Office said Moscow still believed it “will be able to break us this winter”.
A member of Zelensky's team who has taken part in similar negotiations said the delegations might change, meaning the first meeting would be used to familiarize the participants with one another. “We have a feeling that there will be updates to the composition of the groups. Therefore, at the first meeting, the new delegations will get used to each other. At the second, substantive work will begin. And somewhere around the third, there may already be some real decisions,” the source said.
Ukraine also wants the sides to begin by discussing what peace should look like after the war, rather than immediately negotiating which villages should belong to each side.
A source close to the negotiation team told Ukrainska Pravda that Kyiv wanted to outline a future security arrangement for the region, including how Ukraine would be protected and what cooperation with NATO or other partners might entail. The source also pointed to low public confidence in the US president. “In Ukraine trust in Trump is only 6% higher than trust in Putin. Nobody here is going to do anything purely on Trump's assurances,” the source said.
Kyiv continues to push for European partners to participate in the negotiations despite resistance from Russia and, frequently, the United States.
Sources in Zelensky's diplomatic team told Ukrainska Pravda that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had conveyed to Russian President Vladimir Putin the idea of discussing a new security model, and that Putin had reportedly agreed.
Over the past two meetings, a potential EU representative has also emerged: Björn Seibert, head of cabinet and close aide to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to a source cited by Ukrainska Pravda, Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, told US officials that any final peace arrangement must be acceptable to people living in Kharkiv and Dnipro. “After Donbas, they are next, and if the residents of these regions look at our 'peace formula' and say, 'Okay, this suits us,' then that will truly be a work in progress,” the source said, relaying Arakhamiia's message.
US government sources have said the next round of talks involving American, Ukrainian and Russian delegations could take place in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Russian leader's aide Yuri Ushakov has said Moscow is ready to resume trilateral negotiations on ending the war after November 4.
Zelensky has said Ukraine will not accept restrictions on the size of its armed forces or neutral status under any potential peace agreement.

Ukrainian regulator stalling EBRD-backed capital market plan – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:40:21 EET
20:40:21 KST

Implementation of an integrated capital markets infrastructure model, developed jointly by the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), the Ministry of Economy and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), is currently being held up by the position of the head of the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC), NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"We are being asked what is happening with the capital markets. We explain the capital markets infrastructure model that has been developed jointly by the NBU, the Ministry of Economy and the EBRD. Unfortunately, its implementation is currently being held up by the position of the head of the NSSMC," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
In the NBU governor's view, the proposed model takes the state's interests into account in building a vertically integrated system, and therefore confidence in it should not be undermined.
"The key idea is to bring the entire capital markets infrastructure chain together under a single holding company. The strategic investor in this infrastructure holding company should be an entity trusted by global private capital: Deutsche Börse, Euroclear, Clearstream… Naturally, it should be selected through a competitive process. But in the current circumstances, national security requirements must also be taken into account. Our model provides for all of this. So why is the process being held up?" Pyshnyy concluded.
As reported, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso expressed hope at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group that Ukraine would pay greater attention to the capital market development project.
"Despite all the short-term challenges, we have indeed managed to move this process forward, and I hope this issue will soon become a priority," she said.
In July last year, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Rome by the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance, the NBU, the NSSMC and the EBRD on supporting integrated capital markets infrastructure in Ukraine. Its signing was preceded by the Financial Stability Council's approval of a plan for the practical implementation of the target capital markets infrastructure model.
In early September 2025, the National Bank announced the launch of the memorandum's implementation. The first stage involved optimizing the ownership structure and corporate governance of the National Depository of Ukraine (NDU) by transferring management of the state-owned stake, previously managed by the NSSMC, to the NBU.
The next stage envisages the creation of a holding company involving a reputable international strategic investor selected through an open tender, an operator of trading and post-trading infrastructure, international financial institutions, local market participants, and the state and state-owned banks. The holding company, in turn, will establish a new stock exchange in Ukraine, which will become the majority owner of the Central Counterparty Clearing Institution, the Settlement Center (SC), replacing the National Bank in that role. In addition, the exchange will own a minority stake in the NDU, while the National Bank will hold a majority stake.
The final stage is to consolidate depository services under the NDU, which is to operate as a single central securities depository, by transferring to it the functions of recording and servicing the circulation of government bonds from the National Bank.
In early June this year, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a bill on establishing a capital markets infrastructure holding company with the participation of a foreign strategic investor. However, due to a change of government, the document was submitted to the Verkhovna Rada only on September 4. The NSSMC subsequently proposed substantial amendments to the government's bill, including tightening the conditions for attracting a foreign strategic investor.
In addition, an alternative bill (No. 16038-1) was registered on September 21. Its authors include 12 members of parliament, among them Serhiy Taruta, first deputy head of the Verkhovna Rada's economic committee; Andriy Nikolaienko, head of the capital markets subcommittee of the parliament's finance committee; Oleksandr Fediyenko, head of a subcommittee of the parliament's security committee; and Anton Yatsenko.

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Despite growing interest in engineering, Estonia faces a shortage of more than 800 young engineers in the next decade as 40 percent retire. Changes to math teaching may help.
Interest in engineering has grown sharply, but according to OSKA, the Estonian Qualifications Authority's labor market forecasting system, the sector will still be short more than 800 young engineers over the next decade as 40 percent retire. There are no quick solutions, but efforts are being made to alleviate the shortage by changing how mathematics is taught.
Interest in studying at Tallinn University of Technology's (TalTech) School of Engineering has increased by 25 percent over the past three years. According to Fjodor Sergejev, dean of the School of Engineering, students are enrolling in a variety of programs, from energy and construction to mechanical and industrial engineering, but there will not be enough graduates to fill the gap.
"We need replacement workers because many engineers from previous generations are retiring and need to be replaced, but we also need to ensure the development of the sector, and for that we need even more engineers. Even the substantial demographic support we currently have is unfortunately unable to meet all our needs, because the replacement demand is indeed very high, in some fields even numbering in the thousands."
Cathy-Liis Põlluveer, president of the Estonian association of engineers (Eesti Inseneride Liit), also acknowledged the shortage: "We currently have a situation where it depends somewhat on the field, but when an engineer, particularly an experienced engineer, is being sought and a recruitment competition is held, there is practically no queue of applicants or diversity among candidates. Instead, engineers are being sought like needles in a haystack."
According to Anneli Leemet, an analyst at OSKA, demand will grow most for electrical and energy engineers, mechanical engineers and electronics engineers. Leemet said the issue is not only meeting the numerical demand but ensuring engineers have a diverse range of skills.
One possible solution experts see is strengthening mathematics education in basic schools (grades 1–9) — making mathematics teaching more relevant to everyday life, more integrated with other subjects, and delivered in a way that supports all children's motivation to learn. According to Tiina Kraav, a lecturer in mathematics education at the University of Tartu, there are no quick solutions, but mathematics teaching is being continuously developed.
"Making mathematics more interesting to learn, making mathematics learning more visible, making mathematical thinking more visible to students, making mathematics learning more creative, improving how problem-solving skills are taught in the classroom, getting students to talk about what they think and how they think when solving mathematics problems – all of this will certainly help in the longer term," Kraav said.
Põlluveer believes subjects that help connect natural sciences and mathematics could be beneficial.
Priit Laats, a teacher of technology education, arts and technology at Tartu Raatuse School, confirmed that schools are increasingly moving toward theme-based learning: "For example, in the first stage of basic school, there is integrated learning. It is theme-based, with Estonian, mathematics, nature studies and creative subjects all together all the time. In fact, other grades should already be structured in a similar way. But again, who is going to develop all of this? It is a huge amount of work. If I take how I, in turn, support mathematics, we introduce 3D modeling as early as fourth grade: the spatial world, shapes, symbols, symmetry, reflection, all the faces and planes – it is all mathematics all the time, and we do this right through ninth grade."
OSKA will publish a new cross-sector study of labor and skills needs in engineering in early November, which will show that competition for hybrid competencies is increasing in the labor market. This means engineers must have in-depth specialist knowledge combined with digital, data analysis, artificial intelligence, business or management skills.

Italy sees progress in well-being indicators, but poverty remains above EU average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:35 UTC
20:38:35 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Italy has made progress in several areas of equitable and sustainable well-being, including health and the environment, but continues to face challenges related to poverty, disposable income and households’ ability to make ends meet, according to the latest report by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT).
The report, which examines 132 indicators of equitable and sustainable well-being, found that 54 indicators improved, 55 remained stable and 23 deteriorated.
Despite the overall progress, Italy’s at-risk-of-poverty rate remains 2.3 percentage points above the EU average.
Compared with the EU, Italy performs better in health and safety, while significant challenges persist in education and training, employment, work-life balance, and innovation, research and creativity.
More than 5.4 million people were living in absolute poverty in Italy in 2025, with large families and households with at least one minor child facing particularly difficult conditions.
According to the report, 8% of households were living in absolute poverty, affecting 9.3% of the country’s population.
The incidence of individual absolute poverty remained highest in southern Italy, although it declined to 11.5% in 2025 from 12.5% in 2024.
In northern Italy, the rate fell to 8.5% from 8.8% a year earlier, while central Italy continued to record the lowest incidence, at 7.4%, down from 7.6% in 2024.

How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:32 UTC
20:38:32 KST

Article
Presidential election 2026
How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Monday 26 October 2026 14:05
Monday, 26 October 2026, 14:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The boundary between geographical distance and national identity often fades on election day. For our compatriots living thousands of kilometres from their homeland, presidential elections are not merely an administrative procedure, but an expression of belonging, hope and the desire to have their voices heard. How do Bulgarians around the world view the role of the head of state, and what makes them feel close to their homeland despite the physical distance?
Principles, Unity and International Standing: What matters most in a President
The question of whether the head of state should primarily uphold principles, unite the nation or defend the country’s standing on the international stage prompted a range of nuanced responses in our conversations with fellow Bulgarians on election day on October 25. For many, however, these three roles are inseparable.
40 thousand Bulgarians abroad register to vote in presidential election
“Personally, I think that if one person embodies all three of these qualities, that might sound a little utopian, but it would be the best possible outcome,” says Marina Tomova, who lives in Nettuno, Italy. “The president is the face of a country. We Bulgarians would identify with this representative figure in a number of ways: how they present themselves on the international stage and how they defend Bulgaria’s interests. At the same time, the president should serve as a unifying figure and a corrective force in both domestic and foreign policy.”
“People want to see a president who stands up for Bulgaria’s interests and is not afraid to take a position. They also want someone who protects their interests, is educated and well-informed, can speak eloquently at international events and is not afraid to express their views clearly and openly.”
Estela Encheva, from Munich, Germany, emphasises the importance of international law and domestic dialogue.
“For me, it is also important that the president respects international law and insists that our country abide by it, while also bringing the nation together. We live in a time when society is so divided that political measures alone can hardly bridge the divide. In our particular situation, it is important for the president to be able to act as a check on those in power.”
Marin Kachamakov, from Geneva, Switzerland, stresses that the head of state should unite people around moral principles and integrity, while also having the strength and voice to hold those in power to account.
“I believe the president should unite fellow Bulgarians around integrity and a shared moral compass, and help ensure that Bulgaria is not seen as a country that disregards principles, a country where anything goes and where signed treaties are not honoured. In short, the president should bring people together, set a moral example and ensure that the agreements and treaties signed by the state are respected.”
Milena Baeva, from Kuwait, says that, for her, it is equally important for the next presidential ticket to unite people in Bulgaria and defend the country’s interests:
“I imagine them as people whose actions, both at home and on the world stage, will make me proud to be Bulgarian.”
Viktoria Vlahovska, from Reading, United Kingdom, points out that Bulgarians abroad want a steady hand as commander-in-chief and a representative figure they can be proud of.
Adriana Dimitrova, from Berlin, Germany, sums up her expectations by saying she wants a competent leader who can hold their own with dignity on the world stage, someone Bulgarians will not be ashamed of.
When do Bulgarians abroad feel represented and heard?
For Bulgarians living outside the country to feel represented by the presidential institution, they need genuine attention, not merely formal gestures.
The role of the presidential ticket is to seek common ground and represent all Bulgarian citizens, regardless of their political beliefs or place of residence, stresses Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia:
“I would feel represented if the president regarded Bulgarians abroad as an integral part of the nation. This is not just about official visits or statements, but about genuinely understanding the problems faced by Bulgarian communities around the world and the contributions they make. What matters is that people abroad know their voices and experiences also count in shaping Bulgaria’s future,” says our compatriot from the other side of the world.
Martina Shopova-Yanev, from Vienna, Austria, is adamant that she has yet to see genuine concern from the presidential institution for the problems faced by Bulgarians abroad, and hopes this will change:
“I hope for a president and vice-president who will be present in the lives of Bulgarians abroad, not just on paper or during election campaigns, and who will help address our problems. These often concern the exercise of our right to vote and making voting easier. We hope the next presidential ticket will take a more active approach in this regard and demonstrate genuine interest, rather than merely campaigning for support.”
“I think the president should visit as many different countries as possible and make time for Bulgarians abroad,” suggests Marin Kachamakov from Geneva. “Although there are only 24 hours in a day, the president should also try to listen to the views of these Bulgarians. Let us not forget that some of them left Bulgaria not because they wanted to, but because they decided they could build a better life abroad, or because they were driven out of the country. I am referring to the period before 1989-1990.”
Marinela Koleva, from Kraków, Poland, proposes a concrete way to show support: the president could serve as patron of initiatives organised by Bulgarians abroad, demonstrating through action and policy that their concerns matter.
Ties to the Homeland and Faith in the Power of the Vote
Despite the distance and fluctuations in voter turnout, the bond with Bulgaria remains strong. In Melbourne, for example, 77 people voted, compared with 149 in the previous parliamentary elections in April 2026. Bulgarians abroad continue to express a desire for change in their homeland. This is reflected in the decisive victory of the Andrey Gyurov-Georgi Kandev presidential ticket among voters abroad, while in Bulgaria the advantage went to incumbent head of state Iliana Iotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev.
Gyurov wins 45.79% of overseas vote, well ahead of Iotova
“Wherever we live, we always feel close to our homeland,” says Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia.
“We keep ourselves informed through social media and the news, and we watch Bulgarian television. We will always remain Bulgarians, no matter how far away we are from our homeland. Every one of us cares deeply about Bulgaria, which is why you see such strong engagement abroad. People vote, they take an interest and they are not indifferent to what is happening, because we all care about Bulgaria.”
The organisation of polling stations abroad demonstrates the strength of the community and its commitment to developments in the homeland. In this sense, voting is not simply a civic duty, but a powerful expression of an enduring connection with Bulgaria. This is also evident in a video sent to us by Nadia Ullman from the Bulgarian Centre in Boston, USA. Voter turnout in New England was lower than in the previous vote in April 2026, but for her, taking part in the electoral process is a personal mission.
“As the mother of two grown-up children who have attended Bulgarian school in Boston for years, I see it as my mission to raise them as informed and engaged Bulgarian citizens. I teach them to love Bulgaria and value their right to vote. By actively participating in the life of the Bulgarian community abroad, they are learning to preserve their roots and traditions. I believe that this is how we raise responsible individuals who will always carry Bulgaria in their hearts and contribute to its future.
For me, voting is not simply an obligation, but a way of helping shape a better and more prosperous Bulgaria. Every vote cast from abroad sends a clear message that Bulgarians living outside the country are not indifferent to what is happening at home. The organisation of polling stations demonstrates the strength of our community and our desire to make Bulgaria a more attractive place for us and our children to return to.”
The conversations conducted by the Radio Bulgaria team with Bulgarians living in different parts of the world make one thing clear: liviging at a distance from Bulgaria does not diminish their expectations of the country’s institutions. Bulgarians abroad want their president to act as a check on those in power, unite the nation and serve as an authoritative representative of the country on the international stage. They want a leader who shows genuine concern for Bulgarian communities around the world and makes them proud of their origins.

As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:27 UTC
20:38:27 KST

Breadcrumb
As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
It has become almost customary for Palestinians, whenever we speak about Palestine, to begin by telling the story of our suffering. We are expected to explain how we became refugees, how our parents and grandparents were displaced, and which members of our families were killed, imprisoned or disappeared under Israeli occupation.
We are expected to expose our deepest wounds, relive generations of trauma, and to offer our grief as evidence that our demands for justice deserve to be heard.
This is nothing but emotional labour.
And today, I refuse to audition for anyone’s sympathy.
I refuse to bare my wounds for the world to see, simply to validate the decisions and actions we take on the path towards our liberation.
Palestinian rights are not conditional upon our ability to move an audience to tears.
This is why when Green Party members voted to adopt the historic motion declaring Zionism to be racism and calling for a free Palestine from the river to the sea, it felt like a historic movement in UK solidarity efforts.
As a Palestinian and a Green Party member who co-authored and helped develop and advance this motion, I saw this as more than a political victory. It was also an affirmation that Palestinian voices could shape the policies of a major British political party without having to surrender their own understanding of their oppression or dilute their demands to be palatable.
Yet what should have been a moment of collective reflection and celebration quickly became overshadowed by opposition from several Green Party MPs and figures within the party leadership.
A democratic victory that some refuse to accept
The motion did not emerge overnight. Outsiders did not impose it, nor was it the product of some mysterious group of extremists, as some have suggested.
It was drafted and championed by ordinary Green Party members, including Palestinians and anti-Zionist Jews, who spent months organising workshops, seminars, discussions and fringe events to engage fellow members.
Even after the motion was denied a hearing following procedural delays and filibustering during the party’s spring conference, we continued organising, discussing and engaging.
We believed in the Green Party’s commitment to grassroots democracy, even when its procedures appeared to work against us.
Nevertheless, once the motion finally passed, some elected representatives responded not by acknowledging the democratic outcome, but by questioning the motivations of those who brought the motion forward, portraying our organisation and determination as something threatening.
MP Ellie Chowns called for protecting the party from extremists and entryists.
Ironically, only months earlier, party leadership was enthusiastically celebrating a remarkable surge in membership.
Apparently, welcoming new members is something to celebrate until those members organise, exercise their democratic rights and successfully influence party policy.
Even my own MP, Sian Berry, whom I personally contacted to engage with the motion and its arguments, did not respond. Yet, once the media attacks started, Berry weighed in by publicly distancing herself from the motion, describing it as seriously flawed and accusing its Palestinian proposers of being unwilling to compromise.
She has even called on the party to revisit a decision reached through its own democratic processes.
MP Adrian Ramsay, the party's former co-leader, has publicly encouraged Green council groups to distance themselves from the democratically adopted policy. In a recent public statement
Ramsay praised council groups that rejected the motion, described the conference decision as a distraction from their work, and said it did not reflect the views of most party members.
It is deeply disappointing to see a former party leader effectively encouraging a division between elected council groups and the democratic decisions of the party’s own membership.
Selective silencing
Whilst disagreement is a legitimate part of political life, actively encouraging local representatives to distance themselves from a policy adopted through the party’s highest democratic forum raises serious questions about whose voices are ultimately respected.
What message does this send to party members who invest their time, energy and conviction in the democratic process, only to see its outcome publicly undermined by those elected to represent them?
What makes this particularly painful is that these Green MPs are now among the most vocal opponents of a motion written by Palestinians, for Palestinians, and supported through the party’s democratic process.
Not long ago, Palestinians within the Green Party extended a gesture of solidarity and goodwill to those very MPs. After Israeli authorities imposed entry bans on them, we sent a letter replacing that exclusion with an invitation to visit a Free Palestine, to stand alongside us and to hear directly from Palestinians about our aspirations for freedom, dignity and self-determination.
It was an invitation to listen, to engage and to recognise that Palestinians are not merely subjects of political debate, but people with voices, histories and a right to determine their own future. Judging by some of the responses to the motion, it feels like the invitation was buried under a pile of political calculations and selective solidarity.
Palestinians are also not the only ones who’ve been silenced by opposing MPs and the subsequent media storm.
A leading accusation against the motion is that it threatens the safety of Jewish members of the Green Party. But Jewish safety is not at risk from a motion that defines and confronts Zionism as a settler colonial ideology, examining its historical and contemporary manifestations, and reaffirming the Palestinian struggle for liberation, including ending occupation and confronting the structures of displacement and dispossession.
Not only is this argument, which conflates Zionist views with Jewish identity, antisemitic in itself, but it also completely ignores anti-Zionist Jewish members. Many of those members participated in drafting the motion and organising discussions and public meetings in support of it, but opponents have shown they’re not interested in this part of the story.
No one’s safety should ever come at the expense of another people’s freedom, dignity or right to self-determination.

He has lived in the UK since 2014 and is actively involved in grassroots campaigns for Palestinian liberation, social justice and environmental sustainability. A member of the Green Party and Greens for Palestine, he was recognised as one of The Big Issue’s 100 Changemakers in 2026 for his work in politics and activism.

Kondratov, 52, was reportedly hospitalized at the Botkin hospital last Friday for an undisclosed ailment. The cause of his death has not been made public.
Russian law enforcement authorities charged Kondratov with treason on Aug. 5, though he had been held for more than 70 days under so-called “carousel arrests,” a practice of consecutive detentions on charges of disorderly conduct.
Born and raised in Moscow, Kondratov moved to Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2012, where his family currently resides.
Russian border guards at Vnukovo International Airport detained him on May 5, when he arrived to renew his international passport.
His defense attorney Natalia Tikhonova said the treason charges, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison for men, stemmed from “at least six” online posts Kondratov had made. The nature of those posts has not been disclosed.
Kondratov was best known for his work as an art and production designer for the 2007 post-World War II detective drama “Liquidation.” His work on the series earned him two of Russia’s highest honors in television production — the TEFI and Golden Eagle awards.
Perviy Otdel reported that Kondratov’s death marks at least the 11th known case of someone dying in Russian custody this year while standing trial on charges widely viewed as being politically motivated.

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:37:32 UTC
20:37:32 KST

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
The system analyzes heart activity recorded during overnight sleep studies. Researchers found that it could identify patterns linked to future health problems, including risks that standard medical checks might not fully capture.
The study, published in the journal Sleep, used data from more than 35,000 patients at three US medical centers. Researchers trained an AI model to analyze heart signals alongside information about patients' sleep stages.
The team then tested the system on two independent groups, including 9,810 patients at Emory University Hospital and 12,576 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
The model predicted 5 outcomes: atrial fibrillation, a condition that causes an irregular heartbeat; stroke; heart attack; heart failure; and death from any cause. Researchers tracked health outcomes for up to 10 years in one group and 7 years in the other.
The strongest results came from predictions of irregular heartbeat, heart failure and death. Adding the AI's analysis improved the accuracy of risk assessments for these outcomes beyond estimates based on established risk factors, such as age, smoking, high blood pressure and diabetes.
For heart failure, the researchers reported an improvement of about 8% to 9% in the model's ability to distinguish between people who later developed the condition and those who did not.
However, the AI did not significantly improve predictions of stroke or heart attack beyond existing risk factors. The researchers said these conditions may be harder to predict years in advance using heart signals alone.
The approach could make better use of information already collected during sleep studies, which doctors commonly use to diagnose sleep disorders. These studies typically record an electrical signal from the heart, but clinicians do not routinely use it to assess long-term cardiovascular risk.
The researchers said the system could eventually help doctors identify patients who need closer monitoring or preventive care. It is intended as a screening tool, not a stand-alone diagnosis, and any concerning prediction would require further medical assessment.

One possible demand, according to the report, would be for NATO to return to its 1997 configuration, before former Soviet bloc countries began joining the alliance. Such a move could mean withdrawing NATO forces from Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Finland – all of which border Russia.

Moscow seeks a wider security discussion

It’s About Security, Stupid!

That said, NATO membership remains a key point of disagreement. Ukraine has said it needs strong security guarantees to prevent future Russian attacks, while Putin has rejected Ukrainian membership in the alliance. Kyiv has also rejected Russia’s demands that it surrender territory as a condition for ending the war.
The talks’ agenda, any Russian proposal on NATO, and the degree of European participation remain unsettled.

From China to Germany: HUR identified foreign equipment at Russian ballistic missile production facilities

From China to Germany: HUR identified foreign equipment at Russian ballistic missile production facilities
Kyiv • UNN
HUR released data on 30 units of foreign equipment in the Russian military-industrial complex. They are used to produce Iskanders, Kinz hals, and Zircons.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine published information on 30 units of foreign-made technological equipment used by Russian enterprises to manufacture ballistic missiles and their components. This was reported by UNN with reference to data from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Despite sanctions restrictions, Russia’s military-industrial complex continues to depend on foreign technologies.
Details
On the War&Sanctions portal, Ukrainian intelligence published data on equipment manufactured in China, Germany, Taiwan, the United States, Turkey, Switzerland, and Italy, which is used by Russian enterprises to manufacture missiles, altimeters, aerodynamic control surfaces, gyroscopes, and other weapons components. The Main Directorate of Intelligence notes that Russia is still unable to fully replace the industrial equipment of the world’s leading manufacturers with domestic analogues.
At the same time, the number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones, is increasing at Russian defense enterprises. Chinese equipment also depends on foreign components, including European, Japanese, and Taiwanese numerical control systems, servomotors, high-precision spindles, bearings, and measurement systems.
Among the equipment identified by intelligence:
-  the GX-650 five-axis universal machining center manufactured by the Chinese company Hyper Machine Tool, which is used by the Votkinsk Plant. The enterprise manufactures 9M723 "Iskander-M" ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 "Kinzhal" air-launched ballistic missile; 
-  turning and milling machining centers manufactured by the Chinese company Shtral, which are used by the "PEMZ \"Molot\"" enterprise to produce electronic equipment units for "Iskander-M" missiles; 
-  measurement equipment manufactured by the German company Rohde & Schwarz, installed at the "UPKB \"Detal\"" enterprise, which manufactures altimeters for "Zircon" missiles. 
The Main Directorate of Intelligence emphasizes that, in order to limit Russia’s ability to continue producing weapons, it is necessary to strengthen international control over the supply of industrial equipment and components. In particular, intelligence calls for checking the end users of products and the actual locations where they are used, controlling the supply of spare parts, software, and consumables, and regularly auditing distributors and intermediaries.
They propose paying particular attention to investigating cases in which foreign products reach Russia’s military-industrial complex and identifying their supply chains.
In addition, Ukrainian intelligence calls for restricting the supply of numerical control systems, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers whose equipment is delivered to Russian defense industry enterprises.
We remind you
On October 24, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy imposed sanctions against those involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles.

Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:35:53 UTC
20:35:53 KST

Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bristol
- Summary:
- Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.
- Share:
Exercise does more than make the heart stronger. New research suggests it also physically reshapes the nerves that control the heart, revealing an unexpected difference between the left and right sides of the body.
Scientists at the University of Bristol (UK) discovered that moderate aerobic exercise changes the structure of nerve cells involved in regulating heart activity. Even more surprisingly, the changes were dramatically different on the two sides of the body. The findings, published in Autonomic Neuroscience, could eventually help doctors develop more precise treatments for irregular heartbeats, chest pain, angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.
The discovery was made in rats, so further research is needed to determine whether the same changes occur in humans. Nevertheless, it offers a new perspective on how physical activity influences the nervous system that keeps the heart functioning.
Exercise Changes the Heart's Hidden Control System
The heart is regulated partly by the autonomic nervous system, a network of nerves that automatically manages essential functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and digestion. One branch of this system helps the heart beat faster when the body needs more oxygen, such as during exercise or stressful situations.
Small clusters of nerve cells called stellate ganglia play an important role in this process. Located on both sides of the lower neck and upper chest, these nerve hubs send signals that influence heart rate and other aspects of heart function.
The new research suggests that regular exercise changes these nerve clusters in ways scientists had not previously recognized.
Study lead author Dr. Augusto Coppi, Senior Lecturer in Veterinary Anatomy at the University of Bristol, said: "The discovery points to a previously hidden left-right pattern in the body's 'autopilot' system that helps run the heart.
"These nerve clusters act like the heart's dimmer switch and we've shown that regular, moderate exercise remodels that switch in a side-specific way. This could help explain why some treatments work better on one side than the other and, in future, help doctors target therapies more precisely and effectively."
Just 10 Weeks of Exercise Produced Striking Nerve Changes
To investigate how exercise affects these nerve clusters, the researchers examined rats that underwent 10 weeks of moderate aerobic training. Aerobic exercise is physical activity that increases heart rate and breathing, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
The study involved researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK, the University of São Paulo (USP), and the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP) in Brazil.
The team used advanced three-dimensional analysis techniques known as stereology to examine the nerve cells. This approach allows scientists to estimate the number, size, and distribution of cells within tissues.
The results revealed an unusual imbalance between the two sides of the body. In the trained rats, the cardiovascular nerve cluster on the right contained roughly four times as many neurons as the cluster on the left, a striking difference from the pattern observed in untrained rats.
The nerve cells also changed in size, but in opposite directions. Neurons on the left nearly doubled in size, while those on the right became slightly smaller.
These findings suggest that exercise does not affect all the nerves controlling the heart equally. Instead, it produces distinct structural changes on each side, potentially providing clues about how the nervous system adapts to regular physical activity.
Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Treatments?
The findings may have important implications for treating conditions involving abnormal nerve activity around the heart.
Arrhythmias occur when the heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or irregularly. Angina is chest pain or discomfort typically caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle. Another condition, commonly called 'broken-heart' syndrome, involves a sudden weakening of the heart muscle that is often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.
In some patients, doctors treat these problems by reducing excessive nerve signals reaching the heart. Procedures such as stellate ganglion nerve blocks temporarily interrupt nerve activity, while denervation involves disrupting certain nerve pathways.
Understanding how the left and right nerve clusters differ could eventually help physicians determine which side should be targeted for the greatest benefit.
Dr. Coppi explained: "Irregular heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome, and certain types of chest pain are often treated by dialing down overactive stellate ganglia -- the paired small nerve hubs in the lower neck/upper chest area that send 'go faster' signals to the heart.
"By mapping how exercise changes these ganglia on each side, the study offers clues that could one day fine-tune procedures like nerve blocks or denervation to the side most likely to help. The findings are early-stage and in rats, so clinical studies would need to follow."
What's Next for Exercise and Heart Research?
Although the structural changes were substantial, scientists still need to establish exactly how they affect heart function.
The research team plans to investigate whether the differences between the left and right nerve clusters influence how the heart behaves during rest and physical activity. They also intend to look for similar patterns in other animal models and eventually in humans.
For human studies, the researchers hope to use noninvasive markers, which could provide information about nerve activity without requiring surgery or tissue removal.
If the same left-right differences are found in people, the discovery could help guide more personalized treatments for arrhythmias, difficult-to-treat angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.
Dr. Coppi added: "Understanding these left-right differences could help us personalize treatments for heart rhythm disorders and angina. Our next step is to test how these structural changes map onto function and whether similar patterns appear in larger animals and humans."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bristol. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Fernando Vagner Lobo Ladd, Aliny Antunes Barbosa, Renato Albuquerque de Oliveira Cavalcanti, Larissa Freitas, Reinaldo Barreto Oriá, Ricardo Mario Arida, Mariana Pereira de Melo, Andrzej Loesch, A. Augusto Coppi. Asymmetric neuroplasticity in stellate ganglia: Unveiling side-specific adaptations to aerobic exercise. Autonomic Neuroscience, 2025; 262: 103338 DOI: 10.1016/j.autneu.2025.103338

Netanyahu faces reckoning for October 7 in Israel's first vote since attack

Netanyahu faces reckoning for October 7 in Israel's first vote since attack
BE'ERI, Oct 26 - Gal Cohen walks along a memorial wall engraved with the names of the men, women and children slain in the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on his kibbutz. For him, the idea that the man leading Israel, then and since, may be re-elected on Tuesday is painful.
One-in-ten residents of his kibbutz, Be'eri, were among the 1,200 people killed in Hamas' surprise attack. Dozens were among the 251 taken hostage to Gaza. It was Israel's deadliest single day.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should have taken responsibility and stepped down, said Cohen, 61, and the fact that he has fulfilled a full term in office is a slap in the face. Tuesday's election, he said, is critical for Israel.
"If this government will stay, many hearts and minds will be broken. It will be really hard to continue," said Cohen.
Many of Netanyahu's opponents see the election as an opportunity at last to deliver a long-postponed reckoning for the worst security failure in generations. But even if Israel's longest-serving prime minister loses his majority, he could well escape the decisive verdict his foes are seeking.
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. He maintains that Israel's wars against Hamas in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran will result in a more peaceful Middle East.
The task will be complete only with the downfall of Iran's clerical rulers, Netanyahu has said on the campaign trail, and only he has the conviction and standing to deliver.
Opinion polls have for months predicted a sharp drop for Netanyahu's Likud party. But a rival alliance of parties on the right, left and centre looking to unseat him also has no clear path to power, suggesting months of political stalemate with Netanyahu potentially at the helm of a caretaker government.
'TWO CLICKS TO THE RIGHT'
In the days after October 7, Be'eri was crawling with Israeli soldiers patrolling through burnt and shattered homes, floors stained with blood, doors pierced with bullet holes. In some spots, the stench of dead bodies still hung in the air.
The sounds of shelling and Israeli war planes flying over Gaza were incessant.
Three years on, the kibbutz is up and running and the sounds of construction of brand-new houses are heard all around the leafy green grounds. Most members, now residing in another kibbutz, are expected to return by summer.
A collective community established in 1946, now with around 1,000 residents, Be'eri exemplifies the socialist values that dominated Israel's politics in its early decades. Nearly all its votes went to the centre-left in the previous 2022 election, when only around 4% voted for parties in Netanyahu's nationalist-religious coalition.
The attack has made residents question longstanding views that there could be peace with the Palestinians in this generation.
"Everyone in Be'eri has made two clicks to the right. But I still think that most of us will stay with the opposition, the parties that want to replace this government," he said.
Miri Gad Messika, 48, third generation in Be'eri, hasn't yet decided how to vote. But it won't be for Netanyahu.
"He failed as a leader so many times. And he shouldn't be in politics anymore," she said. "I'm looking for a leader. Unfortunately, it's hard for me to see any leader in Israel at the moment."
"I want to be optimistic," she added, "and I can only hope for a better change."
'HOPE IS STRONGER THAN PAIN'
Through much of the past three years, opposition to the Netanyahu government gravitated around families of hostages taken to Gaza, some of whom accused the government of dodging responsibility and doing too little to secure their freedom.
A Tel Aviv open space came to be known as "Hostages Square", site of constant rallies and vigils. Although the last of the hostages were released under a US-brokered ceasefire reached a year ago, the families are still among those most prominently calling for accountability now.
"I don't see any legitimate reason why this government is running again for election," said Ofri Bibas, whose young nephews, a 4-year-old and a 9-month-old, were slain in captivity in Gaza along with their mother. Their father, Ofri's brother Yarden, was released in an early 2025 truce.
Bibas said her goal now is to make every Israeli remember October 7, "to take it with them to the day of the election and remember what happened here and who still hasn't taken responsibility."
On Saturday, thousands of Israelis rallied in Hostages Square. One of the speakers was Danielle Alony, who was kidnapped from Nir Oz with her 5-year-old daughter and freed from Gaza in a brief truce weeks later.
"Go vote," Alony urged the crowd. "In three days we can start writing a new chapter for our children. One in which truth is stronger than fear, responsibility stronger than dereliction and hope is stronger than pain." REUTERS
