2026-10-26
11:35:00 UTC
20:35:00 KST

Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of Bengali Hindus, ended on October 21, and Hindus celebrated the festival peacefully in the Muslim-majority country without any major incidents. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government passed its first major test of communal harmony since taking office in early 2026. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also drew attention by visiting puja pandals in several divisional cities outside Dhaka, becoming the first Bangladeshi prime minister to do so.
Beyond the celebrations, this year’s Durga Puja highlighted a significant shift in Bangladesh’s political landscape. The long-held perception that religious minorities are safer under the Awami League now appears to be on the verge of breaking down.
A Test for the BNP
Durga Puja is celebrated on a large scale in both Bangladesh and the neighboring Indian state of West Bengal. West Bengal has around 70 million Hindus among its population of roughly 100 million, and nearly 58,000 puja pandals were set up across the state this year. Bangladesh, meanwhile, has about 13.1 million Hindus but hosted 33,851 puja pandals, around 1,500 more than last year. This means Bangladesh had more puja pandals relative to its Hindu population than West Bengal.
This was the first Durga Puja celebrated under the BNP government, which came to power in February this year. As a result, the festival carried significance beyond that of a religious celebration. In particular, it represented a test of the new government’s ability, political will, and commitment to ensure the security of religious minorities.
Some untoward incidents have occurred during the festival over the years. This year was no exception in the period leading up to the formal commencement of the festivities, with several incidents reported in different parts of the country. Given the precarious law and order situation, there were concerns that such incidents might escalate.
Nevertheless, the BNP government successfully met the challenge of ensuring that Durga Puja was celebrated peacefully.
Representatives of the Hindu community had long demanded three days of public holidays for Durga Puja. During the Awami League’s rule, there was one public holiday on Bijaya Dashami. Following the political transition in 2024, the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus increased the holiday to two days.
This year, the BNP government extended it to three days. With public holidays from October 20 to 22 followed by the weekly holidays on October 23 and 24, people enjoyed a continuous five-day break.
The government also allocated more financial assistance than requested to encourage a festive atmosphere during the celebrations. While the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust sought 40 million Bangladesh taka for Durga Puja, the government allocated 50 million. Similarly, for the Buddhist community’s Kathina Civara Dana, the government allocated 30 million taka against a request for 20 million. The significance lay not in the amount of money but in the message conveyed by the government.
Netizens described this year’s Durga Puja as having been celebrated with unprecedented security arrangements and a festive atmosphere.
The End of the Hindu Vote Bank?
On October 20, during Durga Puja, Rahman visited puja pandals in the capital, Dhaka, and three other divisional cities: Rangpur, Rajshahi, and Chittagong. Rahman exchanged greetings with members of the Hindu community and listened to their concerns.
Earlier, in his Durga Puja greetings message on October 16, Rahman urged Hindus to celebrate the festival with joy and confidence, free from fear. He emphasized religious harmony, mutual respect, and equal rights for all citizens, regardless of their faith. “Religion belongs to individuals, while the state belongs to all,” Rahman said, stressing that ensuring everyone’s security is a responsibility of the state. He also spoke of building a safe and inclusive Bangladesh where people of all religions and communities can live with dignity.
These comments were significant in Bangladesh’s political context. Many have historically viewed a large section of the Hindu community as supporters of the Awami League. In contrast, there have long been attempts to portray the BNP as a relatively conservative political party, which has previously formed alliances with Jamaat-e-Islami, though the BNP, as a party, believes in liberal democracy.
On October 16, while visiting a puja pandal in Dhaka’s Banani area, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told members of the Hindu community, “You do not need to be anyone’s vote bank.” He urged them to make political decisions based on their civil rights, religious freedom, and constitutional entitlements. Ahmed also remarked that various political parties had exploited the Hindu community for political gain in the past.
His statement carries considerable significance in Bangladesh’s political landscape. Although the Awami League has been perceived as a relatively safe political refuge for minorities, numerous instances of attacks and discrimination against minority communities occurred during the party’s long tenure in power. These include the attacks on the Buddhist community in Ramu, Cox’s Bazar, in 2012; the attacks on Hindu homes and temples in Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, in 2016; and the communal violence that spread from Cumilla during Durga Puja in 2021. According to the U.S. State Department’s human rights report, six people were killed in the 2021 violence. These incidents demonstrated that the Awami League was not necessarily effective in protecting religious minorities.
According to the 2022 Population and Housing Census, Hindus accounted for 7.96 percent of Bangladesh’s total population, down from 8.54 percent in the 2011 census. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) identified migration, alongside a lower fertility rate, as a factor behind the declining proportion of Hindus in the population.
Following the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, allegations emerged of attacks on minorities, vandalism of homes and businesses, and assaults on places of worship in different parts of the country. Although the fact-finding team of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) found political rather than communal motives behind most of these incidents, neighboring India has continued to express concern over the situation.
According to the OHCHR’s 2025 fact-finding report, the violence was driven by several factors, including religious and ethnic discrimination, political revenge against people seen as Awami League supporters, land disputes and personal conflicts. The report also found that some local BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists were involved in the attacks. However, it found no evidence that either party had organized the attacks as part of party decision.
The Bigger Picture
The Awami League was banned from taking part in the national election held on February 12 this year. Of the 300 elected parliamentary seats, the BNP won 209, while Jamaat-e-Islami secured 68. The results showed that the BNP gained strong support in many Hindu-majority areas that were traditionally considered Awami League strongholds.
Netra News analyzed results and voter records from more than 40,000 polling stations. Of these, 1,088 were in areas where more than half of the voters were inferred to be Hindu, based on their names in the electoral rolls. The BNP led in 984 of these polling stations, securing 69.1 percent of the valid votes cast, compared with 14.9 percent for Jamaat-e-Islami. These figures suggest that minority voters migrated to the BNP after the Awami League was banned.
In this year’s election, only four candidates from religious and ethnic minority communities – two Hindus and two Buddhists – were elected to parliament, all nominated by the BNP. Four more women from minority communities were later nominated to parliament through reserved seats, also representing the BNP. This brings the total number of minority lawmakers to eight. Their representation remains low compared with the share of religious and ethnic minorities in Bangladesh’s population. It shows that more needs to be done to ensure meaningful political representation for minority communities, beyond symbolic inclusion.
The peaceful conclusion of Durga Puja should not overshadow concerns about incidents reported before the festival. On October 15, the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee reported 34 alleged incidents across the country, including damage to idols, attacks on temples and other violence. The organizations said arrests had been made in 11 of these cases.
Bangladesh Police later said that investigations into some of the incidents found no evidence of plots to disrupt communal harmony. Instead, they pointed to local leadership disputes, theft, and other causes. Even so, transparent and credible investigations into all the allegations remain important, and those responsible must be brought to justice.
According to the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council, 257 incidents of communal violence were reported across Bangladesh between January and June 2026 (a period covering both the interim government and the BNP government). The organization said 44 people were killed in 40 of these incidents.
The India Dimension
The changing political situation of religious minorities in Bangladesh also has implications for relations with India. Minority security has long been a sensitive issue between the two countries.
During Sheikh Hasina’s rule, close ties between Dhaka and New Delhi were shaped not only by security and strategic cooperation but also by the Awami League’s self-claimed secular political image.
However, Bangladesh-India relations became strained after Hasina fled to India and took refuge there in 2024. Even under Bangladesh’s current elected government, disagreements over Hasina, border issues, trade and water sharing remain unresolved.
Still, this year’s Durga Puja celebrations have drawn approval even from some Indian critics who have long raised concerns about minority security in Bangladesh. Among them is Kolkata-based journalist Mayukh Ranjan Ghosh, who praised the scale and grandeur of the celebrations. Such reactions suggest that perceptions of Bangladesh may be beginning to change across the border.
Whether this will lead New Delhi to reconsider its longstanding political suspicion of the BNP. Much will depend on whether the BNP government can sustain the same sense of security and confidence among religious minorities beyond the festival.

Health Expo Iraq to offer prime opportunity for Iranian medical sector
Unknown

Health Expo Iraq to offer prime opportunity for Iranian medical sector
TEHRAN – The sixth edition of Health Expo Iraq, the country’s annual international health exhibition and congress, will offer Iranian health-sector manufacturers a valuable opportunity to enter the Iraqi market and expand their business in the neighboring country.
The event is scheduled to take place from October 28 to 31 at the Baghdad International Fair.
The expo will feature a wide range of products and services, including medical equipment, laboratory devices, pharmaceuticals, hospital supplies, and healthcare services. Additionally, seminars, workshops, and panel discussions are organized for participants, encouraging industry professionals to share knowledge and experiences and establish new business connections.
Iranian delegation will set up their pavilions to feature the products and achievements of the Iranian knowledge-based firms, establish connections between Iranian and Iraqi experts and stakeholders, hold B2B meetings, and identify the needs of Iraq market in the field of health.
Iran’s ambassador to Iraq and embassy advisors will visit Iranian pavilions and hold meetings with companies to explore potential and capacities for the expansion of ties between the two countries.
With a population of over 46 million and the pharmaceutical market valued at 4 billion dollars, Iraq is one of the biggest health markets in West Asia. The country is planning to meet 70 percent of its pharmaceutical needs through domestic production by 2027.
Boosting academic ties to meet domestic, regional priorities
On October 19, Iran’s scientific counselor in Iraq, Mohammad-Javad Najafi, and Iraqi Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, Haider Abd Dahed, discussed ways to strengthen academic cooperation between universities in the two countries, with a focus on problem-solving approaches and addressing domestic and regional needs.
Collaboration on problem-oriented research, the provision of scholarships, the facilitation of educational issues for students, and preparation for the ‘Third Iran-Iraq Science Week’ were the key topics discussed during the meeting, IRNA reported.
The officials also discussed conducting collaborative research projects, supervising joint dissertations for postgraduate degrees, and publishing joint scientific articles in globally reputable magazines.
Addressing the challenges and educational problems faced by the students in reciprocal countries was the other issue raised by the two sides.
In September, the chancellor of Shiraz University, Alireza Afsharfar, and Najafi explored the potential to expand academic ties with Iraqi universities.
The officials met on September 26, discussing ways to develop collaborative educational courses, exchange students and professors, attract international students, and conduct joint research projects, msrt.ir reported.
Establishing dual degree programs, holding summer schools and educational courses in English and Arabic languages, and participating in Iran-Iraq Science Week were among other issues highlighted by the officials.
The officials also highlighted the need to share the scientific and educational capacities and the capabilities of Shiraz University with Iraqi students, and to implement research projects on shared challenges like dust storms and the environment. They also discussed ways to foster ties with universities and scientific centers in Lebanon and Kurdistan.
Iran regional leader in health system
In May 2025, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) director for the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) said Iran is a leading country in expanding its healthcare system and providing access to universal health coverage.
Lauding the country’s achievements in recent years, Hanan Balkhi said that by expanding primary health care services, increasing access to health coverage in rural areas, maintaining high vaccination rates, and reducing maternal and newborn mortality, Iran has managed to become a successful role model in the region, the health ministry’s website reported.
The official made the remarks in a meeting with Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi. The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly (WHA).
The issue of medicine and medical equipment production and self-sufficiency in these areas is one of the government’s priorities, Zafarqandi said in March 2025.
Medicine and medical equipment are two important areas related to people’s health, he said, adding: “We are trying to reach self-sufficiency for the supply of medicine and medical equipment,” IRNA reported.
According to the head of Iran’s Union of Medical Equipment Manufacturers and Exporters the medical equipment is exported to more than 60 countries annually.
More than 70 percent of medical equipment and 100 percent of normal hospital beds are domestically made, IRNA quoted Abdolreza Yaqoubzadeh as saying.
Also, over 95 percent of specific ICU and CCU beds and more than 85 percent of operating room medical equipment, such as anesthesia machines and other equipment, are manufactured with cutting-edge technology in the country, he added.
Some 600 medical equipment companies are operating in the country, producing around 99 percent of the medicine supplied to the domestic market.
Medical equipment manufacturers in the country produce and supply over 10,000 types of medical equipment to domestic and foreign markets. Now, various pieces of laboratory equipment are manufactured at prices much lower than the same foreign products.

Syria says UN aviation agency withdraws 13-year-old airspace warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:34:17 UTC
20:34:17 KST

Sahin Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has withdrawn a safety warning concerning Syrian airspace that had been in place for more than 13 years, Syria’s civil aviation authority said Monday.
Omar al-Hosari, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, said the withdrawal marked an important step toward reintegrating Syrian airspace into the international aviation network, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
He said ICAO had confirmed that its previous warning, issued in 2013, would no longer serve as a basis for operational decisions concerning Syrian airspace.
Instead, risk assessments would be based on updated international aviation safety and security standards, he added.
Al-Hosari said the development would allow countries, civil aviation authorities and international airlines to reassess their decisions regarding flights crossing Syrian airspace, as well as those arriving at and departing from Syrian airports.
The move could help increase overflight traffic and encourage additional international airlines to consider resuming operations to Syria, he said.
However, he stressed that the withdrawal would not automatically lift operational restrictions imposed by individual countries or aviation regulators.
He said the decision would support ongoing technical and diplomatic efforts to address such restrictions based on internationally recognized aviation safety and security assessments.
The Syrian aviation authority continues to coordinate with ICAO and international civil aviation authorities to strengthen confidence in the safety of flight operations and expand connectivity with regional and international markets, he added.
The original ICAO warning, dated March 22, 2013, concerned the safety of civilian aircraft operating in the Damascus Flight Information Region.
Separately, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) maintains a conflict-zone information bulletin concerning Syrian airspace, which was revised on Oct. 1 and remains valid until Nov. 30, 2026.
Syria had previously reopened its air corridors and resumed flight operations at Damascus International Airport in April following temporary closures linked to regional tensions.
Al-Hosari said restoring Syria’s role in international air navigation remains a strategic priority, citing its potential to increase air traffic and support economic activity and investment in the country’s civil aviation sector.

Belarusian national guilty in enforced disappearance case, Swiss court rules
The Cantonal Court of St. Gallen in northeastern Switzerland has sentenced a Belarusian man to a 24-month suspended prison term for enforced disappearance. He is alleged to have been involved in the murder of politicians in 1999 while serving in a special unit of the regime of President Alexander Lukashenko.
The court quashed the acquittal handed down by the lower court in one case. It based its decision on statements made by the man during the preliminary investigation, in which he had described his involvement in the enforced disappearance of three people in a credible and detailed manner.
More
‘Hope never dies’: Swiss help Mexicans tackle enforced disappearances
However, the defendant was acquitted on two counts. In the first case, the court did so because the accused, who was 20 years old at the time, was unaware that the abductee would later be killed. In the second case, the court ruled that the private prosecutors lacked standing. Relatives of the politicians who disappeared had lodged an appeal against the first instance decision as private prosecutors.
The trial centred on an offence based on a United Nations convention that allows for the prosecution of acts committed abroad.
The defendant can appeal the decision.

Israel’s election result unlikely to shift Palestine, Mideast policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:31:00 UTC
20:31:00 KST

As Israel votes in a pivotal election Tuesday, political analysts and regional policymakers caution that no matter who emerges victorious, the country’s core policies toward the Palestinians, Iran and its position within Middle East are unlikely to experience any significant change.
With polls showing a close contest between incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, both figures are campaigning on hard-line security platforms and share a host of strategic priorities – most notably, maintaining military pressure on Iran and denying Palestinian statehood.
That consensus, analysts argue, stems at least in part from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion and the Israeli genocidal war it triggered, while neighboring Lebanon and Iran became increasingly embroiled on the periphery.
"If Netanyahu is elected, he'll do whatever he thinks he wants to do," said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. "Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue. What you see now is what you'll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively. As long as Iran is in such a situation, it's a waste of time talking about Palestine."
In Bushinsky’s view, echoed by many in Israel’s security establishment and its political class, the electoral contest is less about opposing visions for Israel’s future and more about how far and how fast to push longstanding priorities: confronting Iran, deepening control over the West Bank, and maintaining military deterrence.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot – a former military chief now leading the centrist Yashar party – have publicly opposed the establishment of an independent Palestinian state, a stance now shared by nearly all major Jewish-led parties.
This shift away from the internationally backed "two-state solution” has defined the rightward tilt in Israeli politics. "The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement," said Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib.
The West Bank, occupied by Israel since the 1967 Middle East War, has seen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements under Netanyahu. Critics argue that the government has overlooked or outright enabled increasing violence by terrorist Israeli settlers against Palestinians, as hundreds of thousands of settlers have established themselves in the territory.
While Eisenkot, in contrast, favors settlement "in principle,” he calls for compliance with Israeli law and says that settlements built without official authorization should be dismantled. He has pledged to curb settler violence and opposes building in the contested E1 area of the West Bank, which, if developed, would cut the West Bank in two and sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory – an outcome seen by many as the death knell for Palestinian statehood aspirations.
Despite these stylistic differences, Eisenkot supports the continuation of Israeli security control "from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea.” The only notable exception among mainstream parties are the Democrats, the reconstituted center-left faction – and even they appear diminished as the center of political gravity has moved right.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out forming a government with Palestinian-led Israeli parties, which represent about a fifth of the population, foreshadowing the unlikelihood of significant policy reform from any new coalition.
Three years into Israel’s genocidal and a year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire, Israeli troops now control roughly two-thirds of Gaza, while an estimated 2 million Palestinians remain crowded into the remaining third of the strip. Most live amid the ruins of previous fighting – displaced, under siege, and with little prospect for reconstruction.
Both leading candidates say Israeli forces will remain in Gaza until Hamas is stripped of its weapons and political power, with Eisenkot pledging to replace Hamas’ rule within 18 months, either by international agreement or force of arms. Attempts at negotiating a handover to the Palestinian Authority or a third party have so far failed.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu say Israeli troops will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is disarmed, and that Israel is prepared to restart fighting to achieve this, according to a Reuters analysis.
Arguably the most intractable aspect of Israel’s future for any new government is its stance toward Iran. Oct. 7 and the subsequent genocide further entrenched the prevailing doctrine: maintaining "forward defense” and using overwhelming force as deterrence against regional adversaries.
Prime Minister Netanyahu has repeatedly made clear his ambitions extend beyond containment: "There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran,” he declared at a recent graduation for military officers, describing Iran as the "head of the venomous octopus” that threatens Israeli and regional security.
Eisenkot, though less fiery in his rhetoric, has promised no dramatic departure from this approach.
As the U.S. continues its policy of pressuring Tehran, a State Department spokesperson reiterated, "as long as Iran devotes its energy revenues to financing attacks on our allies, supporting terrorism around the world, and pursuing other destabilizing actions, we will use all the tools at our disposal to hold the regime accountable.”
The Trump administration also reiterated its opposition to the annexation of the West Bank, describing a "stable West Bank” as crucial to Israeli security and regional peace.
Despite the alarm Netanyahu provokes among Arab leaders – many of whom fear his expansionist agenda – there is a begrudging acknowledgment that his hard line against Iran aligns with their own security calculations.
"Netanyahu’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging,” said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Center. "As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran’s role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony.”
Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center notes that underlying Israeli consensus "reduces the scope for big policy shifts.” Recent years have seen the emergence of a rough stalemate: Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza weakened, but not eliminated, and Iran’s broader regional influence endures. The Iranians, he argues, bet they can outlast their opponents and retain their ambitions, including pursuit of a nuclear deterrent.
"This is a quagmire,” Young said. "The Iranians can outlast Trump.”
The contours of likely government coalitions reinforce the direction of policy. Netanyahu’s current government depends on support from far-right parties led by settler activists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who openly promote annexation and have been sanctioned in some Western capitals for encouraging settler violence. The coalition also includes ultra-Orthodox parties, who demand broad exemptions from military service.
Eisenkot, by contrast, would need to rely on right-wing parties less radical than Netanyahu’s allies, and possibly the Democrats’ small center-left faction. Neither candidate, however, is expected to seek support from Arab-led parties, and Eisenkot’s opposition to military exemptions further complicates coalition arithmetic.
For the region – whether in Tehran, Riyadh, or Ramallah – Tuesday’s ballot is viewed not as a potential turning point, but as a test of whether a long confrontation is becoming permanent. "From Tehran to Riyadh, Tuesday's election is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved,” said one observer.
The coming days may deliver a new Israeli prime minister – or reaffirm Netanyahu’s long rule – but the strategic posture toward Palestinians, Iran, and the wider Middle East, will likely remain unchanged. For many, the only open question is whether the next government chooses to escalate existing conflicts or simply maintain the status quo.

Over 355 earthquakes hit Iran in a month

Over 355 earthquakes hit Iran in a month
TEHRAN – A total of 356 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from September 23 to October 22, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 322 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, 30 earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and four earthquakes with a magnitude between 4 and 5 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, two had a magnitude of 4.2 on the Richter scale which occurred on October 16 and 20 in Kerman province.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 44, followed by Kerman with 40, and Yazd with 30 earthquakes.
During the same period, 10 earthquakes hit Tehran, the biggest one had a magnitude of 3.3 on the Richter scale.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Stone-covered roof provides "absolute camouflage" for Gamaya Farms eco-resort in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Stone-covered roof provides “absolute camouflage” for Gamaya Farms eco-resort in India
Architecture studio Biome Environmental Solutions has used a hill-like roof covered in local stone and walls of compressed earth bricks to conceal this eco-resort within its site in India.
Named Gamaya Farms, the resort is located in the town of Vikarabad, near Hyderabad and has a total built area of 854 square metres.
It comprises a series of individual guesthouses and farm plots organised around a shared amenities block at its centre.
Biome Environmental Solutions designed each building to offer a different spatial experience of the surrounding landscape, from the hill-like vaulted roof of the central pavilion to a mixture of elevated and subterranean guesthouses.
“Gamaya Farms redefines architectural iconism not through bold geometry, but through absolute camouflage and tectonic erasure,” director Anurag Tamhankar told Dezeen.
“Rather than treating the program as a monolithic footprint, the master plan deconstructs the traditional resort layout into distinct, site-specific architectural typologies,” he added.
“Taking cues from the surrounding hills and forest to create an intervention that transitions out of the ground, the design disperses the program across decentralised pockets of the land, offering distinct sensory experiences.”
The curved, single-storey pavilion at the centre of Gamaya Farms contains the main entrance and reception at its western end. This leads into a large multi-purpose hall and dining room, as well as utility areas and bathrooms.
Large, circular windows set in exposed earth-block walls fill these spaces with light, and are shaded by the vaulted form of the pavilion’s hill-like roof, which extends to shelter a paved terrace to the north.
Punctured by rows of large, arched openings, this roof was constructed using shotcrete, or sprayed concrete, applied over chicken and weld mesh and topped with a layer of unworked local rubble.
In front of the central pavilion, four guesthouses are partially sunken into a slope, with narrow, dark entrance stairs opening out into bedrooms with large, north-facing windows.
Further toward the wooded edges of the site are two Forest Pavilions – cylindrical structures that are perched atop concrete stilts and accessed via spiral staircases in yellow-painted steel.
The lower levels of these guesthouses contain bathrooms lined in smooth, curved plaster, while above, their circular bedrooms are wrapped by glazing and a balcony with yellow-painted railings.
“The subterranean cottages, sunk into the ground, preserve the expansive view from the pavilion, while getting their own private views,” Tamhankar eplained.
“The isolated forest cottages are tucked into the woodland perimeter, with a 360-degree view of the forest canopy,” he added.
Another resort in India recently featured on Dezeen is The Earthen Retreat by AKSH Architects, which comprises a cluster of small abandoned buildings coated in mud and lime plaster, and Serenity by Ma+rs, which is distinguished by its thatched roofs.

Iran-China project to restore wetlands, curb dust storms enters implementation phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:28:50 UTC
20:28:50 KST

Iran-China project to restore wetlands, curb dust storms enters implementation phase
TEHRAN – A joint Iran-China project to restore Salehiyeh and Allahabad wetlands, located west and southwest of Tehran, and curb dust storm sources has entered the implementation phase, with planned measures covering more than 48,000 hectares.
The wetlands are important ecosystems that help sustain local biodiversity and regulate environmental conditions. However, declining rainfall, drought, excessive water extraction, and drainage projects have contributed to their degradation and the shrinking water bodies.
A specialized webinar to review the operational aspects of the memorandum of understanding for the joint project was held on Saturday with the participation of University of Tehran faculty members and representatives of relevant organizations.
Coordinated by the Secretariat of the National Dust Storm Headquarters, the project involves the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the University of Tehran, and the Plan and Budget Organization. It aims to curb active dust storm sources, improve the hydrological regimes of the two wetlands, and enhance the livelihoods of local communities.
Under the plan developed for the first phase, rehabilitating drainage systems and reopening waterways, establishing living and non-living windbreaks, implementing biological measures, using environmentally compatible mulches, and empowering local communities have been envisaged, Mehr news agency reported.
According to the Department of Environment (DOE), in accordance with President Masoud Pezeshkian’s directives and to follow up on the resolutions of Iran’s National Headquarters for Dust Storm Policy and Coordination, a specialized webinar was held on Saturday, reviewing the operational aspects of the tripartite memorandum of understanding (MOU) of the Iran-China joint project. Officials from the University of Tehran and other related organizations attended the webinar.
Addressing the event, Behzad Raygani, secretary of the National Secretariat for Sand and Dust Storms, outlined the parameters for joint effort while highlighting the need for integrated water resources management, restoration of wetland ecosystems, development of conservation agriculture, and stabilization of soil in critical dust hotspots.
The initiative serves as an example of national synergy, and proactive environmental diplomacy will be pursued across the short-term, medium-term, and long-term.
Pezeshkian pushes for drafting action plan to combat desertification
In September, President Pezeshkian highlighted the need to draft a five-year Iranian-Chinese action plan to manage airborne dust and combat desertification in line with a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by the two countries.
The MOU was inked in the last month of spring in 2025, in Lanzhou, China, to promote scientific cooperation and address sand and dust storms (SDSs) challenges, IRNA reported.
Following specialized meetings and an assessment of scientific and operational indicators, a five-year action plan is scheduled to be developed, and two regions have been designated as pilot sites for implementing joint efforts.
The selected areas include Salehiyeh Wetland, a major dust source affecting Alborz, Qazvin, and Tehran provinces, and Tabas desert, another main dust hotspot in the country, chosen due to their roles in the expansion of desertification, sandstorms, and their impacts on agriculture and infrastructure.
Highlighting the importance of protecting natural resources and the environment, Pezeshkian called for taking action against unauthorized construction and illegal activities that undermine regulations and lead to environmental consequences, as well as benefiting from the capacities and expertise of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in implementing pilot projects.
The official made the remarks in a meeting held on September 13 to give an account of the progress in the bilateral MOU.
Moreover, the president urged the University of Tehran to maintain constant collaboration with the Chinese Academy of Sciences and develop a joint action plan to be assessed and discussed in the next meetings. The official also asked the Plan and Budget Organization to secure funds required for the studies and measures in the five-year action plan.
Dust storms are significant environmental challenges that adversely affect food security, human health, and the sustainable development process at national and regional levels.
Being located in an arid and semi-arid area, Iran has been negatively impacted by climate change. The rise in temperatures, drop in precipitation, intensified droughts, and frequent SDSs have not only threatened the ecosystem and biodiversity but also jeopardized the country’s food security by exacerbating soil erosion, expanding desertification, and declining agricultural productivity.

Serbia after Vucic: Who will be PM and when will a government be formed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:28:25 UTC
20:28:25 KST

Serbia after Vucic: Who will be PM and when will a government be formed?
Uncertainty remains over key positions after student-led movement deals blow to longtime leader’s political dominance.
A student-led opposition movement has emerged victorious in Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, ending former President Aleksandar Vucic’s long grip on power.
The Student List’s win on Sunday followed nearly two years of youth-led protests triggered by the death of 16 people in a railway station canopy collapse in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
Demonstrations demanding accountability quickly evolved into a wider political campaign against alleged corruption and capture of democratic institutions. In its electoral programme presented in September, the Student List said fighting corruption and organised crime were among its main priorities. It also pledged to raise living standards, boost employment, improve education, ensure media freedom and the independence of Serbia’s institutions.
After declaring victory on Sunday, the movement also said it would work to improve relations with neighbouring countries following a period of tension during Vucic’s more than decade-long rule.
Here’s what you should know:
What are the latest results?
The Republic Election Commission (RIK) announced on Monday that the Student List had won 52.54 percent of the vote, based on 8,077 processed polling stations out of 8,392.
The figures also showed the United Serbia list, led by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party, had secured 39.29 percent of ballots cast.
Voter turnout stood at 68.78 percent, a record high in more than 30 years, according to RIK data on Sunday.
What’s next?
While the final election result is not yet known, the figures mean that the Student List will be able to form a majority in Serbia’s 250-seat parliament on its own.
The bloc is projected to win 140 seats, well ahead of the 126 mandates required for a majority, while United Serbia is expected to have 103.
The remaining seats are set to go to the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (three); the Albanian political bloc (two); and the Rasim Ljajc-Ljudski and SDA Sandzak lists, with one each.
Who could be the new prime minister?
Unlike United Serbia, which named Vucic as its candidate for prime minister before the election, the Student List made no such announcement during the campaign.
Since its formal creation, the list has avoided highlighting single candidates, eager to emphasise the collective nature of the movement that brought together academics, doctors and workers.
During the campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Novi Sad. The cardiologist is now seen as the most likely candidate to become the next prime minister, but it remains unclear who will take over key ministries, including those of internal affairs, finance and justice.
When will the new government be formed?
This depends on when the final election results will be announced and when parliament convenes.
The new National Assembly must be established within 30 days of the final results being announced.
A government must be formed within 90 days after that – but the Student List’s clear majority removes the need for lengthy coalition talks.
What about the president?
Vucic has dominated Serbia’s politics – first as prime minister and then as president – since 2014.
Following his call for the snap parliamentary vote last month and his resignation as president, the post has been held temporarily by Ana Brnabic, the president of the National Assembly.
Brnabic is obliged to call for an extraordinary presidential election which must be held no later than three months after the end of Vucic’s mandate.
Vucic resigned on September 27 , so the deadline to hold a vote is December 27 .
The president of Serbia is elected directly by the citizens, not by the representatives in the assembly, but the post is largely ceremonial.

Israeli voters head to polls for pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:28:20 UTC
20:28:20 KST

A woman walks past a Likud Party campaign billboard featuring U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with a Hebrew message reading, "We have one opportunity to win," in Tel Aviv, Israel, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (AP Photo)
Israelis will vote on Oct. 27 in the first national elections since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack in what is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership.
The deadliest day in Israel’s history features prominently in the campaign, but not in the way many outsiders might expect.
There’s been almost no debate over Israel’s wartime conduct in Gaza, which led to an international arrest warrant against Netanyahu, its occupation of much of southern Lebanon and parts of Syria, or its two wars launched against Iran, all of which have broad support.
Instead, candidates have focused on Netanyahu’s leadership and moral character; his role in the security breakdown on Oct. 7, 2023,; his efforts to exempt ultra-Orthodox Jews from military service and a 2023 judicial overhaul seen by critics as an assault on Israel’s democratic institutions.
Both of the main electoral blocs are dominated by parties that support Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state, and no major candidate is advocating a return to the long-moribund peace process.
A poll published by public broadcaster KAN found that out of 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, 52 would go to Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with
Netanyahu and 50 to the Israeli premier, with the rest going to non-aligned parties, including Arab ones.
People heading to the polls will pass the faces of fallen soldiers peering from stickers on train station walls and faded yellow ribbons honoring the hostages, the last of whom were returned in a ceasefire deal last year.
Around 68 percent of Jewish Israelis say their attitudes toward the 2023 attack are a central factor in deciding which party to support, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. 
Among the Arab minority, just 32 percent said it factored prominently, with most citing crime as the main issue.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has sought to shift blame for the failures surrounding the attack to security officials while touting Israel’s military achievements against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and their patron, Iran.
Critics accuse him of evading responsibility by blocking an official inquiry into the attack, of not reaching a deal to bring back the hostages sooner, and of failing to win a decisive victory against any of Israel’s foes.
Netanyahu’s governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties that demand exemptions from military conscription for young men engaged in religious studies. That policy has infuriated
Israel’s secular majority as reservists have been repeatedly called up in the various wars.
Israelis vote for parties, not specific candidates, and no single party is expected to win anywhere close to a 61-seat majority in parliament, known as the Knesset. Whoever can cobble together a majority coalition will become the next prime minister.
If no one is able to, Netanyahu’s government will continue to serve as caretaker until another round of elections in the coming months.

Pakistani Mustafa Prize laureate explores nanotechnology in fight against breast cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:26:45 UTC
20:26:45 KST

Pakistani Mustafa Prize laureate explores nanotechnology in fight against breast cancer
TEHRAN - Nanotechnology is opening new avenues for breast cancer treatment by improving drug delivery, overcoming resistance to chemotherapy, and reducing damage to healthy cells. Pakistani medicinal chemist Muhammad Iqbal Choudhary, a 2021 Mustafa Prize laureate, is among the researchers exploring how advanced drug-delivery systems can make cancer therapies more precise and effective.
Breast cancer remains a major global health challenge, with patients often facing recurrence, drug resistance, and severe treatment-related side effects. Conventional chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells but can also damage healthy tissues, including hair follicles, the gastrointestinal lining, and bone marrow. Meanwhile, cancer cells can develop multidrug resistance (MDR) by activating molecular pumps that expel drugs before they can take effect.
“Cancers are very difficult, complex, and diverse diseases,” Choudhary said. He explained that chemotherapy drugs often affect both cancerous and healthy cells, making it challenging to target tumors without causing significant side effects.
Choudhary, who heads the International Center for Chemical and Biological Sciences (ICCBS) at the University of Karachi, serves as vice president of The World Academy of Sciences (TWAS) and coordinates the Standing Committee on Scientific and Technological Cooperation of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (COMSTECH).
Receiving the Mustafa Prize marked a turning point in his scientific career, providing renewed motivation and focus. Since then, his research group has increasingly concentrated on innovative breast cancer treatments and smarter drug-delivery technologies.
Nanocarriers offer one promising approach by encapsulating therapeutic compounds in microscopic particles that protect drugs from premature degradation and release them more effectively at tumor sites. These systems can use passive targeting, which exploits the increased permeability of tumor blood vessels, or active targeting, in which antibodies, peptides, or other molecules help nanoparticles bind to cancer-cell receptors.
According to Choudhary, nanoparticles can contribute both to drug discovery and to delivering existing medicines more precisely, potentially improving their effectiveness while limiting harmful side effects.
One promising strategy involves poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer widely investigated for controlled drug delivery. Adding vitamin E-derived TPGS may further help counter drug resistance by interfering with the energy-dependent mechanisms that cancer cells use to expel chemotherapy drugs.
Researchers are also investigating nanoparticles coated with natural cell membranes to help them evade immune clearance and accumulate more effectively in tumors. Platelet membranes are particularly promising because their surface proteins may support tumor targeting. A 2025 preclinical study reported greater uptake of platelet-membrane-coated, bufalin-loaded PLGA nanoparticles by tumor cells than that of uncoated particles.
These advances could be particularly valuable against triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype lacking estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors, which limits conventional targeted treatment options. Nanoparticle-based systems that respond to local tumor conditions may offer alternative ways to deliver drugs without relying on these receptors.
Despite the promise, significant challenges remain. Producing platelet-membrane-coated nanoparticles consistently at clinical scale is difficult, and incomplete membrane coverage remains a concern. Such technologies must overcome manufacturing and regulatory hurdles before routine clinical use becomes possible.
Choudhary emphasizes that, although increasingly selective therapies are available, no drug can yet deliver absolute disease-specific precision. Integrating molecular biology, nanotechnology, and medicinal chemistry could nevertheless bring researchers closer to safer, more effective treatments for cancers that have long resisted conventional therapies.

Koretsky urges business to plan for worst case, warns of $1.5 bln budget gap
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:26:04 EET
20:26:04 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky has called on the business community to prepare in advance for the most critical scenarios regarding enemy attacks and economic challenges.
"When we talk to founders and top management, I’ve sensed a certain attitude that 'it will somehow blow over.' Perhaps I won't be targeted by missiles or drones, perhaps my sector won't be touched. Therefore, first: I would strongly ask and recommend thinking according to the most critical scenario of events. Thinking ahead about alternative production sites: who you can cooperate with, where you can make a private label if we are talking about consumer goods, if your enterprise is hit. How to talk in advance with suppliers, perhaps even for imported goods, how to conclude framework contracts and be ready rather than doing it all later. Looking at alternative premises for relocation, for restoration. In other words, think in the most critical scenario. It is better to be ready for this and have it not happen than to find oneself in an unexpected situation," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to the Prime Minister, enemy strikes have already caused over $7.7 billion in losses, with more than 1 million square meters of various types of real estate, both state and private, destroyed or damaged. Significant destruction has hit energy, metallurgy, logistics, processing enterprises, retail, and other sectors.
"Considering these losses, considering the strikes, we already see that by the end of the year the state budget will underfulfill its plans and forecasts by about $1.5 billion. That is the baseline forecast we have today," he stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that despite all this, the country's economy continues to function.
"If we think in terms of PnL (Profit and Loss statement), allocating a lot of funds to support business is impossible. There is no such PnL, because we can only cover one-third of the budget. Even realizing, clearly realizing this, we live even on a cash flow principle and in a certain way go all-in, allocating certain funds to support programs, to various subsidies, to grant programs. Because we realize that without this support, business – small, medium, and large in particular – cannot be sufficiently resilient to counter enemy attacks. And this is the conscious logic and tactics of the government," Koretsky noted.
The Prime Minister stressed that the government will continue programs that have proven their effectiveness, notably the "Affordable Loans 5-7-9%" program. He noted that since the program's inception, UAH 580 billion has been issued, with the current loan portfolio principal standing at around UAH 200 billion. He recalled the recent decision allowing large businesses to receive about UAH 2 billion "in one hand per group of companies" at a preferential interest rate of around 10%.
"The 2026 budget allocated Hr 18 billion. We are expanding this program and see that by the end of the year it will be Hr 22 billion. We currently have a certain deficit on four billion, but one way or another we will cover it, because we consider this to be one of the fundamentally important, correct programs that genuinely supports business," the Prime Minister said.
He also pointed out the necessity of establishing a war risk insurance and damage compensation system. Koretsky recalled the proposal to create a special fund in the budget with an initial state contribution of $1 billion, which partners would double or triple.
"How will this work further? A simplified procedure. Compensation within 30 days after processing. And the tariff for this insurance risk must be very basic, symbolic, we are aiming at approximately 2%. And the maximum damage compensation will be about $5 million in one hand," the Prime Minister detailed.
Koretsky also stated that there is currently no consensus or support for increasing the Value Added Tax (VAT) from 20% to 21% to fund this special fund.
"There is no consensus among big and medium business, there is no support in parliament yet. We are looking for other mechanisms, we will see how the budgetary process proceeds in parliament and build from that. But we have no other path, we must find the instrument. Together we will see what we can contribute," Koretsky emphasized.

"The next military aid package is already ready, and we will
send it to Kyiv as soon as possible."

minister Massimo Garavaglia to retain the leadership of the

Ambassador Sabbatucci presents his credentials to the President of the Swiss Confederation
The excellent relations between the two countries were highlighted during the meeting
ROMA,
26 October 2026, 12:25
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The Italian Ambassador to Bern, Luca Sabbatucci, presented his credentials to the President of the Swiss Confederation, Guy Parmelin, at the Federal Palace.
During the meeting, which took place on the sidelines of the ceremony, Ambassador Sabbatucci conveyed greetings from the President of the Republic, Sergio Mattarella, to President Parmelin, highlighted the excellent relations between Italy and Switzerland at both the bilateral and multilateral levels, and expressed his hope that these relations would be further strengthened.

PKK-linked group in Iraq’s Sinjar begins disarmament, integration process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:23:30 UTC
20:23:30 KST

Iraqi security forces on Oct. 26 have taken control of key military positions held by the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS), a group affiliated with the PKK terrorist organization, as the group prepares to disarm and integrate into Iraq’s security institutions.
The handover is part of a broader process to bring the group’s members, weapons and military positions under state control, according to statements by Iraqi authorities.
Iraq’s Security Media Cell announced that the transfer of military positions in the Sinjar district began, confirming that Iraqi security forces took over several key sites previously held by the YBS. Additional positions were expected to be handed over later on Oct. 26.
A ceremony scheduled for Oct. 26 on Mount Sinjar will mark a new phase in the process, with around 2,000 YBS members expected to lay down their arms.
A further 3,000 to 4,000 members are expected to disarm in subsequent stages, while YBS personnel will be distributed among the Iraqi army, police and the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi, an Iraqi state-sponsored paramilitary umbrella organization.
Sabah al-Numan, military spokesman for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, said the process would also involve reorganizing the group’s military ties with Iraqi security forces and transferring responsibility for security on Mount Sinjar to the relevant federal authorities.
Al-Numan said the initiative was part of the government’s policy to bring all weapons under state control, adding that Iraq’s Constitution prohibits the formation of armed groups outside the country’s official armed forces.
The developments come amid broader efforts by Ankara and Baghdad to strengthen state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of unauthorized armed groups.
Türkiye and Iraq agreed on Sept. 23 to restore full state authority in Sinjar and end the presence of banned foreign armed groups, according to a joint statement issued after Turkish President Recep Tayyip 
Erdoğan met Iraqi al-Zaidi on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Under the agreement, Turkish forces are to gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan military compound to Iraq’s federal government, in line with progress on Baghdad’s security measures and an agreed mechanism and timetable.
The move also comes as Türkiye continues its “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, aimed at ending the PKK’s terror in the country. While the disarmament process is ongoing, Ankara has called for a broader regional approach, urging that all groups affiliated with the PKK across the region should lay down their arms.

Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

British premier says revising UK’s Brexit deal with EU could ‘bring people together’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:22:23 UTC
20:22:23 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
British Premier Andy Burnham has said that revising the UK’s relationship with the EU could help bring people together, while insisting that any decision to rejoin the bloc would be for the British public to make.
Speaking in an interview on Monday on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, hosted by Susanna Reid and Richard Madeley, Burnham said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime but stressed that he would not impose his personal views on the public.
“I’ve said – I’m going to be honest – in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the British public are the bosses here,” he said.
Asked whether he saw himself as the prime minister destined to take Britain back into the EU, Burnham replied: “Honestly, I don’t.”
He said his priority was to take a pragmatic approach to the country’s challenges, adding: “I see it as my job to be pragmatic about the whole situation. Can I make it work better? Can I add growth to the British economy?”
Burnham rejected suggestions that he was reopening the Brexit referendum debate in breach of a promise made during the Makerfield by-election campaign.
Instead, he reiterated his argument that the UK should reconsider its post-Brexit arrangements with the EU, saying the current settlement was not working.
He also argued that a more practical and open discussion about Brexit could help bridge political and social divisions that have persisted since the 2016 referendum.
“And [to] go back to Brexit, by just talking about it in a more practical way, by being honest about it … that can start to bring people together who voted in different ways,” he said.
“The divides that we’ve lived through in the last decade really do need to end, and we need to pull people together …”
Burnham said addressing the UK’s relationship with Europe was necessary to provide the country with a clear direction.
“I’m trying to give the country a direction and there is no way I can do that without coming back to the relationship with Europe and saying, ‘Look, here are some options as to how we got this right.’”
He again ruled out seeking to rejoin the EU before the next general election.
 
Rules out early election
During the interview, Burnham also dismissed speculation about an early general election, saying there would be no election “anytime soon.”
Asked whether he was preparing the public for an early election, he replied: “No, I’ve ruled that out.”
Pressed on whether that was definite, Burnham said he had made his position clear before the Labour Party conference.
“I just don’t think people want another backward-looking squabble. I think they want me to get on with the job,” he said.
Reid returned to the issue towards the end of the interview, prompting Burnham to reiterate that an early election was not on his agenda.
“My mind is not on that [an early election]. I don’t know if that is coming over here, but it genuinely is not on that. There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well just put that out of their mind,” he said.

Agricultural Year Recap and Spring Planting Scenarios: UCAB to Host #DoAgro26 Conference
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:22:21 EET
20:22:21 KST

On December 4, the 18th International Conference “Agribusiness in Ukraine” (#DoAgro26) will take place in Truskavets (Lviv Oblast). The event will be attended by government officials, market leaders, and leading agricultural producers.
This was reported by the press service of the organizers—the “Ukrainian Agribusiness Club” and the UCABevent agency.
This year, the event is completely revamping its format and usual location to take stock of the past year and develop a roadmap for the upcoming season.
This isn’t about monologues or dry reports—those are a thing of the past. What lies ahead is the search for new operating models: open dialogue with government officials, collective brainstorming, and making strategic decisions right here and now. The main goal is to find effective operating models under the new rules of the game.
Participating in #DoAgro26 means:
- Pre-conference fireside chat: an evening meeting with a guest expert, an informal conversation, and quality networking on the eve of the conference.
- Open agropolitical debates: no imposed topics or pre-written scripts. Participants themselves choose the direction of the discussion and the most pressing issues right here and now.
- Collective brainstorming and roundtables: a format where everyone becomes a co-creator of the event, joins the discussions, and collaboratively shapes effective strategies.
- Direct access to solutions: the opportunity for open dialogue with government officials and market leaders.
The program will focus on key issues:
- 2026 in Review: How the agribusiness market (did NOT) adapt to challenges.
- Checkmate to the season’s challenges: scenarios for the 2027 spring planting season and strategic moves for agribusiness.
- A macroeconomic overview above and below the line—from global trends to the financial realities of agribusiness.
The “Agribusiness in Ukraine” conference will be held in cooperation with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and in partnership with the Ministry of Finance of the Czech Republic. Valtra, part of AGCO Corporation, is the exclusive technical partner, and Credit Agricole is the gold financial partner.
Agricultural producers and participants in previous UCAAB events are eligible for a 20% discount off the base price, while association members receive special terms.
For more information about the event, follow the links: https://cutt.ly/9yQmTlnY
Interfax-Ukraine is the conference’s media partner.

Engagement Altitude of Up to 9 km: Helsing Unveils AD-2 Ambush Counter-UAS Interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:21:38 UTC
20:21:38 KST

German company Helsing has presented the new AD-2 Ambush interceptor missile, designed to engage high-speed and low-observable aerial targets.
Militarnyi reports this from a presentation by the company’s co-founder, Gundbert Scherf, in Berlin.
The AD-2 Ambush is primarily designed to neutralize high-speed threats that exceed the capabilities of standard counter-drone systems.
“Thanks to rocket motors, an affordable all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, these interceptors deliver autonomous fire superiority at altitudes of up to 10 kilometers, at an affordable cost and on an industrial scale,” company president Niklas Köhler reported.
The interceptor is equipped with a solid-fuel rocket motor that lets it reach speeds over Mach 2.5. Its combat radius exceeds 20 km.
The AD-2 Ambush has a maximum target engagement altitude of over 9 km. This allows it to intercept objects flying at altitudes beyond the reach of most low-cost air defense systems.
For target guidance, the missile uses an onboard radar seeker with artificial intelligence capabilities. During the midcourse phase, ground-based radar stations correct its trajectory with commands.
The missile can effectively engage targets at night and in adverse weather conditions.
The seeker is designed for mass production without relying on exclusive components.
The AD-2 Ambush launches from dedicated transport-launch containers, each holding 20–40 missiles. They can be mounted on vehicles or railway platforms.
Helsing will manufacture the missiles at its Resilience Factories.
In July, Helsing announced that Andrii Shevchenko would head the company’s office in Ukraine.

Drone strikes cut power across southeast Sudan, operator says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:20:31 UTC
20:20:31 KST

Drone strikes cut power across southeast Sudan, operator says
CAIRO, Oct 26 - Paramilitary drone strikes hit power stations in southeast Sudan on Monday, cutting power across the region, the state electricity company said.
The operator accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces — which have been fighting a civil war with the army for around 3-1/2 years — of knocking out power in four states, which cover about half the territory currently held by the military.
The Rapid Support Forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the account from the Sudan Electricity Holding Company.
Power was cut in Sennar, Al Qadarif, White Nile and Gezira states, threatening the stability of the whole national grid, the operator said.
The attacks hit stations in the towns and areas of Sinja, El Hawata, Al Fao and Mashkour, as well as Al-Junaid in Gezira State, causing "severe damage" and "major destruction" to equipment, it added.
The United Nations has warned that attacks on power infrastructure threaten health and other services for millions of people already hit hard by the conflict.
Sudan's army has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule.
Both sides have stepped up drone strikes, with a series of attacks on Nyala, held by the RSF, and Khartoum airport, held by the army, this month. REUTERS

Koretsky: government must deliver new mobilization social contract by Dec 1
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:19:28 EET
20:19:28 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky predicts that following changes to the reservation system, over 90-95% of employees in the fuel-energy and defense-industrial complexes will be re-reserved.
"We are separating the concept of criticality from economic reservation criteria. This is very important. Why? Because salary and the absence of tax debt are not the same as an enterprise's criticality. This is important, it indeed brings transparency, cleanup, and additional revenues, but it does not equal criticality. Critical means energy, the defense-industrial complex, communications, housing and communal services, pharmacies, groceries, logistics, and so on. But there are enterprises, a large number already, that got there largely due to salaries and a lack of tax debts. Therefore, we are separating criticality from the economy," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He emphasized that workers currently in the energy sector or the defense-industrial complex have nothing to worry about, as over 90-95% will be re-reserved.
"However, creating a large number of enterprises, whether IT or conditionally defense industry, where three drones are made and hundreds of people are reserved – I am conditionally simplifying, hyperbolizing in a certain sense, but that is how it is. And there are very many such cases. Contracting organizations. And it grows, grows, grows," he added.
According to the Prime Minister, changing the rules is designed, on the one hand, to cut down on unfair reservations without letting the economy collapse, and on the other hand, to give active military personnel a clear understanding regarding rotations.
"To say that these mobilization and reservation rules will produce a super-effect – no, there is no such thing, but we are at least stopping the endless growth of sometimes unfairly reserved individuals. And now, most importantly, what I am appealing to enterprises, business, and the economic sector about: we need to jointly come up with a new social model where, even if everyone is reserved, enterprises provide predictable mobilization of people into the army. This is an idealistic model. If such a solution could be found, the need to search for people on the streets would disappear. And if a business, entrepreneur, manager, or head takes on such a commitment – then nothing else is needed at all, this is a new social contract. But not thinking about it, not preparing for it, is a super-strategic mistake," Koretsky stated.
He stressed that failing to prepare in advance for a potential tightening of mobilization in Russia, which could reach 300,000–500,000 troops, would mean being forced to make unpopular decisions in manual mode once again.
"Then it won't be about reservations, or percentages. The issue is the survival of the state, and therefore this must be taken into account. Seeking to increase accountability for those who hide is also on the agenda – this is all a comprehensive story. By December 1, we must deliver a new social contract," he added, announcing a meeting with businesses on this issue.
As reported, on October 23, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky stated that the Cabinet of Ministers had finalized changes to the reservation system – an enterprise's criticality is being separated from its economic indicators, sectoral and regional criticality criteria will be updated, and enterprises will be checked for abuses.
The second change is that the maximum reservation level, particularly for the energy sector and defense industry, will no longer be 100% (dropping to 95%). The government will not weaken the work of those manufacturing weapons or maintaining critical infrastructure, and if uninterrupted operation requires reserving more, the enterprise can submit a justified appeal to a special Coordination Center.
The third change involves the Ministry of Defense strengthening liability for draft evasion. The fourth is the preparation of a mechanism for 100% reservation provided mobilization obligations are fulfilled: an enterprise will be able to fully reserve employees if it regularly and voluntarily recruits a portion of them for military service.
The Cabinet has also initiated a review of sectoral and regional criticality criteria, taking into account new requirements within 10 days.
