Not just Iran: Netanyahu defies IDF chief over continuing Hebron operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:54:41 UTC
19:54:41 KST

The military operation in Hebron, launched after a deadly shooting attack near the West Bank city killed two IDF soldiers, has become another point of contention between the military leadership and Israel's political leadership, just a day before Tuesday's election. While troops from the IDF's 98th Division continue intensive operations involving searches for weapons, arrests of suspects, the evacuation of Palestinian residents and the demolition of unauthorized structures, military officials believe that the limited operational results so far warrant reassessing whether the operation should continue in its current form.
According to sources familiar with the discussions, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir presented his position during a meeting with the political leadership, attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, arguing that the time had come to end the operation. Netanyahu and Katz, however, rejected that assessment and instructed the military to continue. Ultimately, the chief of staff's recommendation was not accepted, and the decision was made to keep the operation underway.
The IDF has pointed, among other concerns, to the legal difficulties involved in keeping Palestinian residents away from their homes for extended periods, particularly when the operation is not producing significant military gains. So far, troops have made arrests and located a limited number of weapons, but have not uncovered unusual weaponry or large weapons stockpiles.
The political leadership, however, presents a different assessment. Officials argue that the two terrorists who carried out the deadly attack were armed with automatic weapons and substantial quantities of ammunition, making it necessary for the IDF to continue searching for additional weapons in the area. They also maintain that prolonging the operation will strengthen deterrence. Security officials explain that the very presence of large IDF forces operating inside Hebron creates a psychological impact among Palestinians, particularly because the troops have entered a major Palestinian city rather than refugee camps, as they did during previous operations in Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem.
The current disagreement recalls an IDF operation in the Qalandiya refugee camp in August. At the time, the military defined its objectives as targeting terrorist operatives and infrastructure. Katz also pushed for a large-scale operation and again raised the possibility of taking control of another refugee camp, similar to the operations carried out in Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams.
IDF officials said the military had operational plans for every refugee camp but had not mobilized forces to carry them out because there was no operational necessity. There was also tension over contingency planning for a scenario known in the military as a "turning of the guns," involving a possible armed escalation in which Palestinian security forces turn their weapons against Israel. Katz presented the IDF's extensive and aggressive plan for such a scenario, although intelligence assessments at the time did not indicate that an escalation of that kind was imminent in the West Bank.
It is important to note that the prolonged military operations in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, which Katz was among those pushing for and which were conducted under Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, led to a significant decline in terrorist activity in the area, according to Israeli security assessments. 
However, the Qalandiya operation ended after just two days and, based on the information available so far, did not produce significant operational results. Now, in Hebron, the question is once again whether continuing the operation is likely to yield further results or whether it has already achieved its main objectives.
But the debate over the Hebron operation is unfolding against a broader and more complicated security backdrop. The IDF is currently also focused on preventing the next attack, particularly attacks carried out by lone assailants inspired by previous incidents. Security officials are concerned about copycat attacks that could develop following exposure to incitement on social media and military activity on the ground. Central Command is therefore concentrating its efforts on identifying threats early, thwarting potential attackers and preventing an escalation that could emerge from several directions.
The IDF stresses that such conditions require precise, targeted counterterrorism operations, accompanied by constant assessments of their operational value and their consequences on the ground. The concern is that an escalation could develop rapidly, making it necessary to consider not only existing threats but also the reactions military operations themselves could provoke.
Against this backdrop, the Hebron operation illustrates the tension between the political leadership's demand to continue military activity in pursuit of deterrence and additional weapons discoveries, and the IDF's position that the operational benefits must be weighed against the consequences of prolonging the operation for the local Palestinian population.

Ukrainian drone plot against Moscow air defenses foiled – FSB (VIDEO)
Unknown

Ukrainian drone plot against Moscow air defenses foiled – FSB (VIDEO)
A Ukrainian plot to damage a key component of Moscow’s air defense system has been thwarted, according to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
In a statement on Monday, the agency accused the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) of organizing the operation and recruiting a man in Ukraine’s Dnepropetrovsk Region to carry it out. The SBU allegedly supplied him with small drones and improvised explosive devices.
The suspect recruited another person, and the pair retrieved the equipment in Russia’s Smolensk and Kaluga regions before heading to Moscow Region, the FSB said. They were allegedly tasked with assembling the drones, fitting them with explosives and positioning them near two targets: an air defense site and an energy facility.
Russian investigators were reportedly aware of the operation in advance and intervened at a time of their choosing.
A video released by the FSB includes footage apparently recorded by a third person as equipment was retrieved from a cache and one of the drones assembled in the field, with instructions relayed live over a phone.
The agency did not identify that person, but said alerting the authorities to a planned crime could exempt an informant from criminal liability.
The two suspects, identified only as foreign nationals from the Caucasus region, face up to 15 years in prison on terrorism charges.
Moscow is among the most heavily defended parts of Russia. During the record Ukrainian drone attack on the capital on September 19–20, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 1,600 drones were intercepted across defensive lines, including 450 which were approaching the city.
Kiev has previously used infiltrators in attempts to deploy short-range quadcopters carrying explosives for sabotage or targeted assassinations.

Hsiao calls for cooperation to support aging Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:52:27 UTC
19:52:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) on Monday urged businesses, organizations, and experts to work with the government to improve care for older adults.
Speaking at the Super-Aged Society Action Summit, Hsiao said Taiwan became a super-aged society last year, creating challenges for health care, the workforce, and family support that require diverse solutions, per CNA.
She said population aging could become an opportunity for social innovation if older adults share their experience, younger generations contribute their creativity and technological skills, and families and workplaces strengthen support networks.
Hsiao said annual government funding for long-term care had risen from about NT$5 billion (US$153 million) when former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) took office in 2016 to more than NT$110 billion. She also highlighted President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) Healthy Taiwan Promotion Committee and the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s “888 Plan,” which targets high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and high blood lipids.
She said government policies focus on maintaining older adults’ independence, preventing chronic diseases, and building age-friendly communities. Community health assessments cover cognition, mobility, and emotional well-being, with follow-up care designed to delay functional decline, she added.
Hsiao thanked businesses and experts for supporting older adults through technology, insurance, and senior housing. She urged continued cooperation to build a healthier and more caring country.

Taiwan air cargo rates climb as AI shipments grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:52:06 UTC
19:52:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China Airlines and EVA Air expect the approaching holiday shipping season to push airfreight rates higher as AI cargo keeps capacity stretched.
Shipping costs for urgent US-bound shipments have reached their highest level this year after a short-term increase of more than 10%, per UDN. Some shipments now cost more than NT$400 (US$12.30) per kilogram.
Customers seeking priority space, guaranteed arrival windows, or a particular flight pay extra, according to the report. Standard US-bound quotes total NT$357–387 per kilogram, comprising a NT$77 fuel surcharge and a base rate of NT$280–310.
Semiconductor equipment and AI servers are among the goods driving demand. Nearly 100 US charter flights arrived in Taiwan in September, with American electronics companies arranging flights to collect items.
EVA Air General Manager Sun Chia-ming (孫嘉明) linked the disappearance of the usual seasonal lull to year-round AI shipments. He said profitable AI companies could absorb higher freight costs.
The airlines expect the November pickup in European and US holiday orders to sustain the capacity shortage through the fourth quarter.
Cargo revenue at EVA Air grew 42.55% year on year in September, per CNA. Sun cautioned that fuel prices were still the biggest wild card for profits despite the airline raising both passenger fares and freight rates.

Unknown Publisher

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) opened his campaign headquarters on Monday, with both KMT and TPP chairs attending the event.
The rally was held at Taipei Municipal Dun Hua Junior High School, 33 days before the local elections. Supporters wore white shirts to show their support for Chiang, according to UDN.
KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文), TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌), former Interior Minister Lee Hong-yuan (李鴻源), and former National Taiwan University President Kuan Chung-ming (管中閔) attended the event. Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜), and Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) were also present, according to Yahoo News.
Television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永), who recently attended the campaign headquarters launch of DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋), was at the rally. Wearing a white shirt, Tsai sat in the front row of the audience.
Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), the KMT's New Taipei mayoral candidate, and Wu Tsung-hsien (吳宗憲), its Yilan County magistrate candidate, also attended. They entered with Chiang, Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政), and Hsinchu City Mayor Kao Hung-an (高虹安), who are both seeking reelection.
In his speech, Huang Kuo-chang said Taiwan had fundamental values and priorities that should transcend party divisions and personal interests. He called on the public to defend Taiwan's democracy and rule of law.
Cheng Li-wun urged voters to judge Chiang based on his work and achievements over the past four years. The incumbent KMT mayor is seeking reelection against Shen and four others in the Taipei mayoral election, according to FTNN.

Kremlin reacts to Serbian election outcome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:51:41 UTC
19:51:41 KST

Kremlin reacts to Serbian election outcome
Russia is willing to maintain mutually beneficial relations with Serbia after the opposition Student List movement forms a new government following its election victory, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Outgoing Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic has conceded defeat for his United Serbia coalition in Sunday’s vote. Peskov on Monday hailed Vucic for playing a constructive role in maintaining ties with Moscow amid pressure by the European Union.
“We express hope that their actions will similarly be aimed constructively at further development of our relationship and that these new political forces realize that cooperation with Russia meets Serbia’s interests,” he said.
“But, as you know, it takes two to tango,” the official added.
Vucic, who Peskov noted intends to remain involved with Serbian politics, previously claimed that Student List candidates intend to bend to Brussels’ pressure and impose anti-Russian sanctions as soon as next spring. The movement has denied such plans on the campaign trail.
The Student List is projected to secure a majority in the parliament, positioning it to form a single-party government.
Serbia has been on the road to join the European Union for over a decade, having been granted candidate status in 2012. Following the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict, Brussels made alignment of foreign policy mandatory for nations seeking EU membership, forcing Belgrade to choose between making progress on its path or maintaining its traditionally good relations with Russia.

Revolut to launch platform for investing in private tech companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:50:46 UTC
19:50:46 KST

Revolut announced on Monday the launch of Revolut Ventures, a new platform developed with Carne Group to give eligible investors access to private technology companies, an investment market traditionally reserved for wealthy individuals and large institutions.
Private technology companies are taking longer to go public, with the median age at listing rising from 6.9 years in 2014 to 11 years in 2025, according to figures cited by Revolut in an announcement released on Monday.
This means more of their growth takes place before shares become available on public markets and can be accessed by retail investors.
"With Revolut Ventures, we're aiming to dismantle one of the final barriers in wealth management: retail investor exclusion from non-listed companies," Rolandas Juteika, Head of Revolut Wealth and Trading (EEA) at Revolut stated.
"Value creation happens long before an IPO, and by managing our own platform, we're giving everyday investors the opportunity to access tomorrow's market leaders right from the Revolut app," Juteika added.
The new platform is expected to become available in 2027 and will be integrated into the Revolut app alongside existing investment options, including stocks, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bonds and money market funds.
The announcement follows the introduction of private market investment products in selected European Economic Area (EEA) countries in July 2026.
However, investments in private companies carry significant risks.
Unlike publicly traded shares, they are more difficult to sell and investors could lose a substantial portion or all of their invested capital.
The launch comes as Revolut continues to expand its operations, having secured full banking licences in the UK and France earlier this year.
The UK fintech, which is seeking to diversify its revenue streams, is also considering a dual stock market listing in London and New York, although no date has been confirmed.

Parliament supported the extension of martial law in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:50:18 EET
19:50:18 KST

Parliament supported the extension of martial law in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
A total of 293 deputies voted to extend martial law from October 31, 2026. Earlier, Zelenskyy submitted the relevant bill.
On October 26, the Verkhovna Rada supported extending martial law for 90 days from October 31, 2026, UNN writes.
Details
"The Verkhovna Rada extended the period of martial law in Ukraine (No. 16182). A total of 293 members of parliament voted in favor. The document extends the period of martial law in Ukraine from October 31, 2026, for 90 days," the parliament reported.
As MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak clarified, "The Verkhovna Rada supported No. 16182 on extending martial law for 90 days—until January 29, 2027. This is already the 21st time the current convocation has voted on these issues."
Additional information
Earlier, on October 26, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted bills to the Verkhovna Rada proposing to extend martial law (No. 16182) and general mobilization (No. 16183) in Ukraine for another 90 days.
The first bill, according to the explanatory note, "proposes extending the period of martial law in Ukraine for 90 days from 5:30 a.m. on October 31, 2026."
The second, according to the explanatory note, provides that "the period of general mobilization is extended from October 31, 2026, for 90 days."

Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years

Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.
- Share:
Scientists exploring the forests of Yunnan, China, have discovered an extraordinary giant fungus that is challenging previous assumptions about how large certain fungi can grow. The newly identified species, Dianjunus rex, produces upright reproductive structures that can reach 50 cm (20 inches) in height and weigh as much as 2.2 kg (4.9 pounds). These are the largest known fruiting bodies among fungi belonging to the phylum Ascomycota.
"This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae, and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms," said Dr Indunil C Senanayake, an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China and corresponding author of the study, published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology.
"The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests."
A Giant Fungus Hidden in China's Forests
Researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany encountered the unusual fungus while surveying several forest environments in Yunnan. Their fieldwork included temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang, along with tropical rainforest near Nanbang.
The team spotted unusually large, whitish reproductive structures, known as 'stromata', growing from the woody roots of Chinese cork oak trees. These structures emerged from the rhizosphere, the region of soil surrounding plant roots, and appeared to belong to an unidentified member of the ascomycete fungi.
Ascomycetes make up the largest major group of fungi, with more than 64,000 recognized species. Unlike familiar mushrooms, these fungi do not produce true mushroom structures. Instead, they generate spores within tiny sac-like structures found inside or on the surfaces of their fruiting bodies.
To investigate the discovery, the scientists collected samples and preserved reference specimens in the Kunming Institute of Botany's collections. They also cultivated spores under laboratory conditions to examine the fungus's physical characteristics and sequenced its genome, including its protein-coding genes.
Meet D-Rex, a Record-Breaking Fungal Giant
The genetic analysis, together with a close examination of the fungus's physical features, revealed that the discovery represented much more than a previously unknown species. It was sufficiently different from known fungi to require the creation of a new genus and an entirely new family (Dianjunaceae) within the order Xylariales.
The researchers named the species Dianjunus rex, drawing inspiration from its impressive size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Its nickname, 'D-rex', reflects its exceptional stature among related fungi.
Its closest known relative is Graphostroma platystoma, a fungus that grows on dead hardwood throughout the Northern Hemisphere. That species is the sole representative of its own family, Graphostromataceae.
Members of the order Xylariales are known for producing a variety of specialized chemical compounds and enzymes capable of breaking down complex molecules in plants. Researchers believe similar enzymes may allow 'D-rex' to decompose dead wood and obtain nutrients from it.
A 65-Million-Year Connection to Dinosaur Extinction
One of the most intriguing findings concerns the ancient evolutionary origins of the newly identified fungal family.
Using a technique known as a 'molecular clock', the scientists compared the fungus's DNA with genomic information from hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary histories have been established. This analysis allowed them to estimate when the Dianjunaceae family first appeared.
Their results suggest that the lineage originated approximately 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. That catastrophic event eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs along with countless other animal and plant species.
The timing raises the possibility that the enormous environmental changes following the extinction helped create favorable conditions for the ancestors of this unusual fungus.
"This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material," said Senanayake. "For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities."
Why Does This Fungus Grow So Large?
Another mystery is how and why Dianjunus rex evolved such an extraordinary size.
Before its discovery, the tallest known ascomycete fruiting bodies measured approximately 20 to 30 cm. The newly identified fungus can reach 50 cm, making it substantially taller than the previous record holders.
One possible explanation involves how the fungus releases and spreads its spores. By extending high above the forest floor, its reproductive structures may be better positioned to catch moving air and distribute spores through dense vegetation.
However, growing such a large structure also requires considerable energy. The researchers suggest that this unusual evolutionary strategy would be advantageous only in environments where the benefits of greater spore dispersal outweigh the resources needed for growth.
"A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs," hypothesized Senanayake.
China's Forests May Harbor More Undiscovered Fungi
The discovery also highlights how much remains unknown about fungal diversity in China's subtropical forests.
Researchers believe the region is particularly well suited to the evolution of unusual fungal species because it contains a wide variety of habitats, has experienced relatively stable climatic conditions, and supports intricate relationships among living organisms.
Despite these favorable conditions, many fungi in the region have received little scientific attention. Remote and difficult terrain complicates fieldwork, while the seasonal appearance and often hidden nature of fungal reproductive structures make some species especially difficult to locate. Historically, research has also concentrated heavily on fungi with commercial or practical value.
The scientists expect that continued exploration of these forests will uncover additional species, potentially revealing more unexpected forms and evolutionary histories.
"This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification. Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi," said Senanayake.

Output from 3 western oilfields exceeds contractual target
TEHRAN – Daily oil production from Iran's East Paydar, Cheshmeh Khosh and Dalpari fields has risen to 127,000 barrels, exceeding the 120,000-barrel daily target set under a contract with a Russian company, the head of the Petroleum Engineering and Development Company (PEDEC) said on Monday.
Nasrollah Zarei said production from the three fields stood at about 41,000 barrels per day when the current administration took office, before increasing to the current level through development projects carried out with Russian companies.
The Aban and Paydar West development project is nearing completion and is expected to require about another year, Zarei said. A second, larger project covering the Cheshmeh Khosh, Dalpari and East Paydar fields is progressing according to schedule, with about two years of work remaining.
Zarei described the Russian company's performance in implementing the projects as satisfactory, adding that plans were underway to increase production beyond contractual commitments while maintaining output levels.
He said all PEDEC projects include environmental assessments and that no work begins before the required permits are obtained. The company is also committed to environmental standards, with support from oil ministry officials helping advance compliance efforts.
Zarei said the company had also undertaken social responsibility initiatives, including social studies conducted under two contracts with universities and the production of a film highlighting its activities.
The Cheshmeh Khosh, Dalpari and East Paydar oilfields are located in western Iran within the operating area of the West Oil and Gas Production Company. They began production in 2011.
A contract to develop the three fields was signed in February 2020 with the participation of Russian and Iranian companies and entered the implementation phase in 2020 after the necessary permits were obtained.
The project aims to increase and sustain crude oil production and improve the utilization of reservoir capacity.

More than half of Swiss worried about disinformation, study finds

Unknown Publisher

More than half of Swiss worried about disinformation, study finds
Some 56.5% of the Swiss population view fake news as a major social problem – significantly more than five years ago. More than half regularly come across misleading content, particularly on social media, video platforms and via AI chatbots, the Research Centre for the Public Sphere and Society (fög) revealed in a new study.
According to the fög’s 2026 Quality of the Media Yearbook, published on Monday, the quality of news media remained stable in 2025, but diversity declined. Nearly one in three articles in the German-speaking Swiss press appeared in several publications; in the case of national political reporting, the figure was as high as 44.7%.
According to the centre, which is based at the University of Zurich, 42% of those surveyed are “news-deprived”, meaning they either do not keep up with current affairs or obtain their information in a piecemeal fashion via social media. This group is therefore particularly susceptible to conspiracy theories, which are perceived as a growing risk.
More
How Switzerland and other states are navigating disinformation
Consuming quality media is considered the most effective protection against disinformation. Social media platforms, on the other hand, offer no protective effect. According to the study, those who obtain their information exclusively via TikTok or Instagram are just as susceptible to conspiracies as people who do not consume news at all.
Support for public broadcaster, crisis among private outlets
With regard to the licence renewal for the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (Swissinfo’s parent company) in 2029, the study reveals strong public support: 57.7% consider public broadcasting, as provided by the SBC, to be important or very important. Contrary to the SBC’s current cost-cutting plans, they expect the corporation to provide a comprehensive range of news, education, culture, sport and entertainment, according to the study findings.
More
Swiss Broadcasting Corporation unveils cost-saving measures for 2027
While tech platforms siphoned off up to CHF2.5 billion ($3 billion) in Swiss advertising revenue annually, revenue for the domestic media fell to CHF1.94 billion, according to the fög. The researchers are therefore calling for counter-measures, such as media vouchers for young adults.

Agricultural output rises despite water cuts, reduced cultivated area

Agricultural output rises despite water cuts, reduced cultivated area
TEHRAN – Iran's agricultural production reached 137 million tons in the past crop year despite a 15 billion-cubic-meter reduction in water allocated to the sector, a deputy agriculture minister said.
Majid Anjafi, deputy agriculture minister for crop production, said cultivated areas for vegetables, summer crops and many melons and other field crops had declined, but higher productivity and yields per hectare had helped increase overall output.
He said the Ministry of Energy allocated 15 billion cubic meters less water to agriculture than planned in the previous crop year, leaving little scope to expand cultivated land with available water resources.
Of the approximately 65 billion cubic meters of water scheduled to be supplied to agriculture under official plans, only a limited amount was allocated as water available for planned use, Anjafi said.
He warned that without improvements in productivity and a shift away from traditional farming practices, the water shortfall could have reduced agricultural output by at least 30 million tons. Production could have fallen to 100 million tons from a projected 130 million tons, he said.
However, official figures showed that total agricultural production reached 137 million tons, which Anjafi described as an exceptional achievement for the country's farmers and agricultural sector.
The gains came despite reduced water availability and smaller cultivated areas for several crop categories, highlighting the role of improved yields in sustaining and increasing production.

====================================================================================================

“Strasbourg Calling” EU should increase funding for investigative journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:48:46 UTC
19:48:46 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
Investigative report exposes investment funds channeling money to arms industry under the banner of “sustainability”
“Strasbourg Calling” EU should increase funding for investigative journalism
Interview with Voxeurop’s editor-in-chief Gian-Paolo Accardo on billions invested in defence companies through ESG funds
Interview with Gian-Paolo Accardo
Monday 26 October 2026 11:15
Monday, 26 October 2026, 11:15
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
Can a tank be green, and can a bomb manufacturer be part of an investment portfolio marketed as sustainable and responsible? An investigation by Voxeurop traces how nearly €50 billion in investments reach defence companies through investment funds.
Meanwhile, the European Commission maintains that defence financing is compatible with social sustainability, provided certain conditions are met.
Where does Europe’s need to rearm end and the rebranding of the arms industry as a public good begin? And do investors in these funds know what their money is financing?
The investigation entited "War made sustainable: how green investment funds bankroll the arms industry with EU backing" documents a rise in investments in military companies held by funds classified as sustainable. The amount flowing directly into the arms industry rose from €14.5 billion in 2021 to €49.8 billion in 2025.
The investigation was one of the finalists for the 2026 Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for Journalism, whose winner was announced on October 21 at the European Pariament in Strasbourg.
Speaking to Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) on the special live programme “Strasbourg Calling", Gian-Paolo Accardo, editor-in-chief and co-founder of Voxeurop, explains the findings:
“My two colleagues Giorgio Michalopoulos and Stefano Valentino, who are also Italian journalists, examined data on 118 companies, including the largest publicly traded defence industry companies whose shares are held in the portfolios of 3,037 investment funds. We analysed data covering the period from 2021 to 2025, which is freely available from the London Stock Exchange.”
Gian-Paolo Accardo and Irina Nedeva on “Strasbourg Calling” programme at the European Parliament, 21 October 2026
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
European regulations distinguish between funds covered by Article 8, which promote environmental and social characteristics, and Article 9 funds, which must have sustainable investment as their objective. Gian-Paolo Accardo explained:
“The investment funds we investigated operate under both Article 8 and Article 9. These are the green funds we looked into. The problem is that there are no legal restrictions preventing such green funds from investing in defence and arms companies. The only exception is when they manufacture weapons deemed unethical, such as chemical or nuclear weapons. This means they can quite legitimately finance the production of tanks, drones, ammunition and what are known as conventional weapons.”
According to Accardo, ordinary investors are often unaware that by investing in these funds, their money may be used to support weapons production. At the very least, they should be informed, he believes.
“Investigative journalism is very expensive, and we are forced to rely on private funding. The European Union provides some funding, but it is not enough, so our goal is to see it increased,” Accardo said.
The full interview of Irina Nedeva with Gian-Paolo Accardo was aired on BNR's Horizon channel on October 21 and can be heard HERE.

New copper, gold mines set to begin production next year
TEHRAN – Iran's Mines and Metals Development Company has more than doubled estimated reserves across 14 mineral exploration areas, with development work at selected copper and gold deposits expected to begin next year after exploration is completed, its chief executive said.
Morteza Aliakbari said on Monday that the company had focused exploration on 14 of its original 31 mining areas after technical assessments identified greater potential for further exploration.
Direct exploration work has more than doubled the estimated reserves in those areas, he said, adding that the company was pursuing formal registration of the reserves with the Ministry of Industry, Mine and Trade.
The selected areas are mainly focused on copper and gold deposits. Under the company's plans, one or two mines could each support the construction of a dedicated processing plant, Aliakbari said.
He also outlined a shift in the company's investment strategy, saying it began reducing its exposure to commercial steel production in 2026, with the transition expected to continue through 2031.
Energy constraints, carbon-related costs and the prospect of lower profitability in commercial steel were among the factors behind the change, he said. Copper and gold, alongside rare earth elements and critical metals, are expected to play a greater role in the company's future development plans.
Aliakbari said much of the company's current investment in local-currency terms was directed toward projects including Sarmad Abarkuh Steel, Kurdistan Steel and Khorasan Steel East. By 2031, copper and gold are expected to account for the largest share of its investment portfolio.
Rare earth reserves estimated at 121m tons
Iran has identified 121 million tons of rare earth reserves across two mines, Aliakbari said in response to a question about the latest exploration activities.
The country currently has the capacity to produce 17 rare earth oxides, he said, adding that domestic technical expertise had been developed to process and separate rare earth elements from mining waste.
He said reserve assessments and completion of exploration work were prerequisites for decisions on developing mining projects, with deposits containing medium to large reserves given priority for investment.
Regarding overseas operations, Aliakbari said the company had been pursuing development opportunities at two iron ore mines in Afghanistan, but regional developments and security conditions had delayed progress.
Efforts to advance the plans have since intensified, and work is also underway through one of the company's subsidiaries, he added.

International credit rating agency Fitch Ratings has affirmed Lithuania's long-term foreign-currency issuer default rating at A+ with a stable outlook, the Finance Ministry said on Saturday.
The rating is currently the highest long-term debt rating assigned to Lithuania by the three major credit rating agencies.
According to Fitch, the rating is supported by a credible policy framework, membership of the European Union and eurozone, resilient economic growth, moderate government debt and high institutional quality.
It is constrained by heightened geopolitical risks and the small size of the Lithuanian economy.
The agency also said consistent fiscal policy should help consolidate public finances, although the budget deficit is projected to widen in the near term.
The government plans to run a deficit exceeding the Maastricht limit of 3 percent of gross domestic product.
Government debt is projected to reach 54.3 percent of gross domestic product in 2029, remaining below the 60 percent threshold set by the Maastricht criteria.

Iran, Turkey explore trade opportunities, export potential
TEHRAN – Iran and Turkey should strengthen trade ties by identifying competitive Iranian export products, assessing market demand and verifying potential buyers, Iran’s commercial attaché in Turkey said at a seminar on bilateral trade opportunities and challenges.

Davari Niko said none of Turkey’s border crossings with Iran had been closed, expressing hope that trade between the two countries would continue. He also highlighted direct engagement and bilateral consultations as important tools for strengthening commercial relations, referring to a meeting between Qazvin Chamber of Commerce board members and Turkish counterparts in Istanbul.
The seminar examined Iranian goods with export potential in the Turkish market, as well as opportunities for imports from Turkey. Participants emphasized the importance of assessing market needs, evaluating products’ competitive advantages, calculating production costs and determining profitability before entering new business sectors.
Other topics included estimating operating costs, assessing mutual benefits, checking the commercial credibility of trading partners and understanding formal and customary contractual practices. Participants also discussed required regulations and permits, tariffs, transportation costs and payment methods as part of efforts to reduce trade risks.
Earlier in June, the representative of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce Ibrahim Dogan Salman stated that in 2025, the trade between Iran and Turkey surpassed $5.6 billion.

The Istanbul Chamber of Commerce representative emphasized: "To strengthen the bond between the chambers of commerce on both sides, we are prepared to hold joint meetings, bilateral talks, and specialized exhibitions."

Jordan unites as victims' families recount Karak church massacre

Breadcrumb
Victims' families recount Karak church massacre as tragedy unites Jordanians
Grief, anger and shock have consumed the village of Hammoud in Jordan's southern Karak governorate following the deadly attack on St George's Church on Friday 23 October which saw nine lose their lives.
Relatives recalled the moment gunfire erupted and desperate attempts to rescue the wounded, while stressing the deep-rooted relationship between Muslims and Christians in Karak and insisting the attack will not undermine social cohesion or national unity.
Jordan's Public Security Directorate announced early on Monday that the three gunmen who carried out the massacre had been arrested following an armed confrontation with security personnel.
Sultan al-Khitan, a Hammoud resident who witnessed the horrific scenes on Friday, told The New Arab that the incident began as people gathered in the church courtyard and exchanged greetings. Heavy gunfire suddenly rang out, sending people scrambling for cover.
The attackers continued firing from the street behind the church, while those present attempted to assist the wounded and get them out of the area.
Al-Khitan said he helped transport two people to safety, one wounded in the shoulder and the other in the neck. The gunfire continued for a while before gradually subsiding, and residents used their cars to take the injured to hospitals before returning to help evacuate others, he said.
He described seeing a blue Dyna pickup truck carrying two people, one of whom was armed with what looked like a Kalashnikov rifle.
Al-Khitan said the attack was unprecedented, with life in Hammoud characterised by close ties, regular visits and shared celebrations and condolences. To his knowledge, there had been no previous disputes or feuds that could explain the violence.
Waad al-Halsa, a relative of some of the victims, told The New Arab that those inside the church had been attending the funeral of their uncle's wife when the firing erupted without warning, leaving those present confused and initially unsure how to act.
He insisted that the massacre will not affect relations between Karak's Muslims and Christians, describing their bonds as strong and deeply rooted in everyday life.
Al-Halsa said one example was his friend Louay al-Halalmeh, who contacted him immediately after the attack to offer help transporting the injured—such gestures reflected the genuine solidarity between residents, which was demonstrated through practical action, particularly during times of hardship.
Khaled Barqan, a cousin of one of the victims, told The New Arab that Jordan had lost young people and skilled professionals in an immense tragedy without precedent in the country's history.
The victims were peaceful residents of Hammoud who had gone to a funeral, never expecting that a social obligation would turn into a scene of violence and bloodshed, he said.
Barqan described the attack as an act of terrorism that was difficult to comprehend, and condemned its violation of all laws, customs and human values.
Ehab Haddadin, another relative of a victim, said the tragedy extended far beyond the bereaved families to encompass the whole country.
"No matter how much a person tries to speak, there are no words that can express the scale of this tragedy," he told The New Arab.
He said relations between Muslims and Christians in Jordan were based on fraternity and solidarity, with no history of religious division, adding that he was shocked that such an attack had taken place.
Lina al-Halsa, whose cousins were among the dead and wounded, called for the harshest possible penalties against those responsible, so they would serve as a warning to anyone contemplating attacks on places of worship or peaceful civilians.
Sarah Haddadin said residents were still struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy. She saw the targeting of the church as an attempt to sow discord between Muslims and Christians, but believes it will fail to change the nature of relations between Jordanians.
The scenes of mourning and solidarity at the funerals in the village had demonstrated national unity and rejection of discrimination and division, she said, expressing confidence that security forces would pursue those responsible and bring them to justice.
Tribal figures in Karak also stressed that the attack had struck the entire country.
Firas Madallah Ali al-Assasfeh told The New Arab that Jordanians shared a commitment to national unity and social cohesion. He pointed to members of the Habashneh tribe, including Saed Mahmoud Ahmed Faleh al-Habashneh and Raji al-Aroud al-Habashneh, who were wounded alongside Christian victims outside the church church.
The scene embodied the shared fate of Jordanian communities and underscored the importance of safeguarding the country's security and stability.
Tribal figure Ismat al-Majali likewise called the attack a "painful tragedy" for Karak and Jordan as a whole, insisting that it would not damage the longstanding bonds between Muslims and Christians in the governorate.
Karak had historically been a unified community in which religious affiliation did not divide its residents, he said, pointing to the family and social ties reflected in shared celebrations, condolences and regular visits.
Some of the victims had worked in humanitarian professions, particularly medicine, and were accustomed to treating patients and helping those unable to afford healthcare, al-Majali added.

Andrey Gyurov attracted 12.3% of voters who backed Progressive Bulgaria in the April parliamentary elections, while 30% of that electorate did not support Iliana Yotova in the first round of the presidential election, according to exit poll data from Trend Agency.
Gyurov also won the support of 86.2% of voters who had backed PP-DB in April and 47.6% of those who voted for GERB-SDS. Yotova, meanwhile, received 71.2% of Progressive Bulgaria’s voters and 76.9% of those who supported BSP-United Left. She also secured 22.9% of the GERB-SDS electorate.
Trend’s analysis found clear socio-demographic differences between the leading candidates’ supporters, particularly in terms of age, education and place of residence.
Gyurov performed best among younger voters. In the 18-to-29 age group, he received 42.5% of the vote, compared with 27.1% for Yotova. Among voters aged 30 to 39, Gyurov led with 40.5%, against Yotova’s 27.8%.
The two candidates were almost evenly matched among people aged 40 to 49, with Yotova receiving 34% and Gyurov 34.1%. Support shifted increasingly toward Yotova among older voters, reaching 56.8% among those over 70, compared with 22.2% for Gyurov.
More than 40% of Yotova’s voters were over 60, while that age group accounted for 22.6% of Gyurov’s electorate. Conversely, voters under 40 made up 36.1% of Gyurov’s supporters, compared with 21.4% of Yotova’s.
Geography also divided the two electorates. Gyurov won decisively in Sofia, receiving more than twice as many votes as his rival. Yotova led in regional centers, with 34.8% against Gyurov’s 30.8%, and held a much stronger advantage in small towns and villages.
Sofia residents accounted for 31.8% of Gyurov’s voters, compared with 12.2% of Yotova’s. In contrast, 45.8% of Yotova’s electorate lived in small towns and villages, compared with 26% of Gyurov’s supporters. The figures point to a concentration of Gyurov’s support in the capital and major urban areas, while Yotova performed better in smaller settlements.
Education was another significant factor. Among voters with university degrees, Gyurov led with 39%, compared with 31.7% for Yotova. Among those with secondary education, Yotova received 41.3%, while Gyurov won 24.7%.
University graduates accounted for 65.5% of Gyurov’s electorate and 47.1% of Yotova’s.
The profile of Kostadin Kostadinov’s supporters differed from those of the two leading candidates. People aged 40 to 69 made up 65.9% of his electorate, while voters under 30 accounted for 9.1% and those over 70 for 10.2%.
Trend’s findings also showed differences in when supporters of the two leading tickets decided whom to vote for. Two-thirds, or 66.3%, of Yotova’s voters had made their choice before the campaign began, compared with 53.1% of Gyurov’s supporters.
During the campaign, 25.4% of Gyurov’s voters decided to support him, compared with 16.7% of Yotova’s electorate, suggesting that Gyurov gained relatively more support as the campaign progressed.
Across the electorate as a whole, 55.7% had decided whom to support before the campaign started, while 20.9% made their choice during the campaign. Another 10.4% decided in the final days before the vote, and 9.3% made their decision on election day.

Trade flows continue despite temporary border closures, higher logistics costs

Trade flows continue despite temporary border closures, higher logistics costs
TEHRAN – Goods continue to enter Iran despite restrictions on transport routes, with shipments being redirected through alternative corridors when individual routes are disrupted, a trade official said.
Seyed Ali Emami, director general of the Trade Logistics and Support Office at the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO), said maritime restrictions had prompted a shift toward alternative transport routes but had not halted seaborne shipments into the country.
The level of restrictions varies according to cargo type and vessel conditions, with some ships facing tighter controls than others, Emami said.
He said importers were increasingly using multimodal transport and changes to shipping documentation, including a practice known as “switching bills of lading.” Some goods are also entering Iran on smaller vessels or via rail and road networks.
Restrictions may temporarily affect land crossings with Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, Emami said, adding that the psychological impact of reports about border closures can sometimes exceed their practical consequences.
A border may close for two days before operations gradually resume, he said. Such reports can trigger significant concern even when cargo movements restart after a short disruption.
Goods continue to enter Iran through various routes despite the restrictions, Emami said. When one border becomes inaccessible, shipments can be redirected through other crossings, although detours may lengthen transport distances and increase costs.
The main downside is higher logistics expenditure, he said, noting that the additional costs depend on the type of goods, country of origin and mode of transport.
Restrictions have affected road, rail and maritime transport, but they have not brought the country’s commercial logistics to a complete standstill, Emami said. Shipments are continuing, although they may take longer and cost more than before.
Regarding trucks held up at border crossings, he said such delays had occurred even before the current wartime conditions, though the situation could exacerbate existing constraints.

GECF ministerial meeting opens in Moscow ahead of leaders' summit
TEHRAN – The 28th ministerial meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) opened in Moscow on Monday, bringing together representatives of member states to discuss gas market developments, energy security and ways to strengthen cooperation.

The agreement was discussed at a previous meeting between the Iranian and Russian presidents in Turkmenistan, Bovard said. He added that a pipeline project Russia is pursuing through Azerbaijan could enable gas exchanges between the two countries in the near future.
Cooperation in the oil sector is also continuing, with Russian companies involved in the development of four major Iranian oilfields. Bovard said the projects had made satisfactory progress and that discussions on advancing the contracts would continue during his visit.
Iran plans to use the GECF meetings to discuss production plans, expand cooperation with member states, particularly in the gas sector, and address international developments and damage to its energy infrastructure, Bovard said.
Ahead of the ministerial meeting and summit, the GECF executive board held an extraordinary session in Moscow on Sunday, chaired by Seyed Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, Iran's deputy oil minister for international affairs and trade. The session focused on coordinating the two gatherings and finalizing key documents, including the summit's closing declaration.
During his visit, Bovard also toured the monitoring center of Russian oil company Zarubezhneft and was briefed on its operations and technical capabilities.
He welcomed the participation of Russian companies in Iranian oil industry development projects, saying Iran's national oil and gas companies had also established a similar monitoring center to oversee operations across the country.
Zarubezhneft Chief Executive Sergei Kudryashov said the center consolidates data from the company's onshore and offshore operations, allowing production volumes and other operational parameters at individual wells to be monitored.
The GECF has 12 full members, including Iran and Russia, and represents countries that hold about 70 percent of the world's proven natural gas reserves, account for 38 percent of global marketed gas production and supply 42 percent of global gas exports. Member countries also account for an estimated 47 percent of global liquefied natural gas exports.
The forum holds its leaders' summit every two years. Previous meetings have been hosted by Doha, Moscow, Tehran, Santa Cruz in Bolivia, Malabo in Equatorial Guinea and Algiers, which hosted the seventh summit in 2024.

Saudi-led coalition says it struck Houthi missile facilities
Coalition says it destroyed ballistic missile launchers as well as tunnels and a depot used by the Houthis to store missiles.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it carried out a military operation “aimed at neutralising sources of threat”, as the armed group claimed attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on Monday its forces destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.
In a post on X, he also said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.
The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.
The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have carried out a wave of strikes in recent weeks against Saudi airports and other infrastructure. This follows a major escalation in fighting in Yemen’s war, in which Saudi Arabia is supporting the internationally recognised government fighting the Houthis.
A Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport this month killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.
The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.
The airport reopened and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target.”
Houthis claim new attacks
The Houthis later claimed they attacked the airport “with a ballistic missile, striking the target with precision”, according to a post by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on social media on Monday.
Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”
Saree also said that the Houthis had struck oil pumping stations in Saudi Arabia with drones.
In a separate statement, Saree also claimed responsibility for more ballistic missile attacks on “enemy” forces and weapons depots in Yemen.
He said the attacks targeted positions in the Salah al-Din area of Aden governorate and the al-Wahat area of Lahij governorate.
Yemen’s war reignited in the summer when the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, which intervened in 2015 to lead a coalition aimed at restoring the internationally recognised government that was ousted from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis in 2014.
A 2022 truce that had halted most fighting collapsed last month, as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government forces and also attacking Saudi energy facilities and airports.
Yemen’s government forces this month launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.
‘Everything is shaking’
As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and discussed a key air defence system.
Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said, referring to a battery of the US-made air defence system deployed by Greece to Saudi Arabia in 2021, which protects energy infrastructure in Yanbu, on the Red Sea coast.
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.
The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.
Images released by the kingdom’s official press agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

Ukraine proposes new pathway to attract foreign workers to address labor shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:38:53 UTC
19:38:53 KST

Ukraine proposes new pathway to attract foreign workers to address labor shortages
Ukraine’s government has proposed a new mechanism to attract foreign professionals and skilled workers in sectors facing labor shortages — in a bid to help employers fill vacancies and support the economy amid Russia's ongoing invasion.
The draft resolution, published by the Economy Ministry, would establish an annual list of in-demand professions and standardize the assessment of foreign applicants’ qualifications. The proposal is not yet in effect, and its provisions could change.
The plan could help Ukrainian businesses fill critical jobs needed to keep the economy running during war by making it easier to recruit qualified workers from abroad. While still in its early stages, its effectiveness will depend on which jobs are available, how easy the application process is, and whether Ukraine can realistically attract foreign professionals despite the security risks.
The State Employment Service would compile the list each year, drawing on information from employers, government agencies, and regional employment centers. Employers would be able to report their staffing needs by Oct. 1, with the proposed list published by Dec. 31.
Foreign applicants would need to demonstrate their education and work experience and provide an employment contract, job offer, or other evidence of an employment arrangement in Ukraine.
Volodymyr Landa, who has led investment screening at the Economic Security Council of Ukraine since September 2025, welcomed the government’s recognition that foreign recruitment may be necessary to address labor shortages.
"Ukraine is not the number one destination for international labor migration, so we need to make this journey as simple and clear as possible," he said.
But Landa said the draft leaves practical barriers unresolved. He sees it as excessive bureaucracy, including document translation requirements, and the potential need to use the government online platform Diia.
He also questioned how foreign professionals would find vacancies and navigate the recruitment process, noting that the proposal focuses on submitting documents rather than attracting candidates in the first place.
Further changes would be needed to connect international professionals with Ukrainian employers and reduce administrative barriers, he said.
The government's plan includes running a pilot project during martial law while the war continues, for three months after it ends or is lifted, and a maximum of two years from the resolution’s entry into effect.

Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:36:48 UTC
19:36:48 KST

Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria
Governorate’s Druze majority in deadlock with Syrian government.
United States special envoy Tom Barrack recently spoke with a popular X personality about Syria and, in particular, Suwayda, which has been a hotbed of tensions between the government and Israel.
The southern governorate, which is majority Druze, is one of the last places in the country where the Syrian government does not have full control.
Barrack referred to “a particular Druze sheikh”, thought to be Hikmat al-Hijri, a leading political and religious figure in Suwayda. The National Guard, a Druze armed group linked to al-Hijri, has been accused of receiving support from Israel with separatist ambitions.
Barrack’s comment on al-Hijri is perceived by many as a firm message to Israel, which has attacked Syrian ministries and soldiers and tried to curry favour with Syria’s Druze community with the National Guard accused of acting as an Israeli proxy.
US President Donald Trump has built a strong relationship with his counterpart in Damascus, Ahmed al-Sharaa, and perceives any instability in Syria as dangerous for a country trying to rebuild after 13 years of war.
“[Barrack’s] message was totally clear,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies, told Al Jazeera. “Israel backing [al-Hijri] does not equal American backing. Washington has prioritised an agreement with Damascus while Israel retains its own security demands and relationship.”
Divergent views on Syria
Since the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, the US has slowly rebuilt relations with Damascus and its new leader.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has received strong US support for his assaults in Lebanon, Palestine and Iran, has a view of the new Syrian government that is very different from Trump’s.
In the days immediately after the collapse of al-Assad’s government, Israel invaded Syria and seized land in Quneitra governorate and other strategically important areas of the country.
Israel has threatened President al-Sharaa’s government in Damascus, bombed the Ministry of Defence, and harassed and arrested Syrians in southern Syria. Israel has drawn an outcry from Syrian officials due to its repeated incursions into Syria.
Barrack, a Trump confidant who is the US ambassador to Turkiye and a special envoy to Syria and Iraq, has built a reputation for his direct approach to diplomacy, at times without regard to caution, as evidenced when he called some members of the media in Lebanon “animalistic” last year.
On Friday, Barrack spoke to Australian X personality Mario Nawfal and addressed the situation in southern Syria. He appeared to take the view that Washington favoured Damascus having control over Suwayda rather than a group aligned with al-Hijri and linked to Israel.
“[Barrack’s] remarks expose differences with Israel,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian analyst told Al Jazeera. “Washington is building a partner in Damascus while Israel appears to prefer a Damascus that is too weak to assert itself in the south.”
Israel and al-Hijri
Having grown tired of their worsening living conditions, residents in Suwayda, including many in its Druze majority, rose up against the al-Assad regime in 2023. They maintained their protests until the regime collapsed in December 2024.
Many in Suwayda celebrated this moment, which ended more than five decades of Baathist rule, although they were also hesitant to throw their support behind the new government.
That hesitancy turned to blatant opposition to al-Sharaa after fighting between Bedouin tribes and Druze in Suwayda turned into deadly sectarian killings in July 2025. Forces reportedly connected to the government joined the fighting on the side of the Bedouins. While there was violence and death on both sides, the casualties were overwhelmingly Druze.
Israel intervened in the fighting at one point, attacking what it said were Syrian government forces entering Suwayda. Since then, Israel has reportedly been trying to curry favour with locals there, including al-Hijri, who has been fervent in his opposition to Damascus’s new leadership.
“Israel appears intent on a lasting military presence in southern Syria, and it uses Suwayda as a lever against Damascus, offering enough support to keep the province reliant on Israeli protection and too little to secure its future,” Hawach said. “Along its line in Quneitra and Daraa [areas of southern Syria that Israel has invaded], Israel treats neighbouring communities differently, reviving wartime grievances between Syrians that any future Syria-Israel arrangement would struggle to undo.”
In Suwayda, analysts said, al-Hijri’s support is not universal but he benefits whenever the Druze community feels under attack.
“Sheikh al-Hijri’s authority rises with the community’s sense of threat and opens to debate as that threat recedes, so pressure from Damascus tends to strengthen the leadership it aims to weaken,” Hawach said. “Each side points to the other’s hard line to justify its own. That keeps Suwayda’s future framed in security terms and crowds out the many residents, clerics and local figures seeking a path between central rule and separation.”
Accountability needed for reconciliation
After the events of July 2025, the US began talks with the Syrian government hosted by Jordan to resolve the crisis. A trilateral agreement was signed in Amman in September 2025 that said Syria would invite an independent international commission to investigate what happened in Suwayda and perpetrators would be brought to justice.
While major fighting has not resumed between Damascus and Druze factions, the situation in Suwayda remains in a deadlock with many in the province having no trust in the government.
“Distrust has hardened, partly because Damascus has sought to bring Suwayda back by pressuring its leadership, and residents feel that pressure first, in their salaries, their children’s exams and the road to the capital,” Hawach said. “Trust tends to return through what the state delivers. Damascus stands a better chance of winning people back by serving residents directly and pursuing accountability for July 2025.”
Analysts said accountability is crucial if Damascus wants to bring Suwayda back into the Syrian fold.
“A durable settlement needs credible accountability for what happened in 2025,” Saban said. “The Druze need to be guaranteed protection of movement, education and security. Neither weakening Hijri, nor restoring government institutions alone will rebuild the trust.”

European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.
Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.
The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.
Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.
Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.
It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.
Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.
European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

LG B6 OLED TV Review (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Low price for an OLED. Deep and rich blacks. Easy setup and install. Great refresh rate for video games. The skintone test was better than average.
TIRED
Did not perform as well as a Micro RGB for brightness and contrast.
It’s amazing what can happen in just one year. The LG B6 is the cheapest LG OLED model around (priced lower than the LG C6 and LG G6), but it also has some stiff competition. New art televisions like the Amazon Ember Artline (which costs under $1,000) use a matte display that renders masterpiece paintings in convincingly realistic glory. RGB televisions like the LG Micro RGB Evo and those from Samsung and Hisense have also burst onto the market, making a convincing argument for choosing an RGB screen over an OLED one.
Last year around this time, we reviewed the LG B5 and ranked it a solid 8/10, but there was less competition. The LG B6 is still a good budget OLED TV, it’s just beset on all sides by better, brighter options, including from LG’s own LG C6.
Sleek Angles, Less Sleek Remote
Photograph: John Brandon
The first thing that struck me while setting up the LG B6 is that it’s incredibly thin—just 1.8 inches at the base and about a quarter-inch at the top and around most of the bezel. The OLED panel doesn’t need any backlighting like most LED or RGB televisions, so it can be extra thin. The lower portion of the TV is thicker because of the four HDMI ports (all of which support a 120-Hz refresh rate), an optical audio out, two USB 2.0 ports, and one LAN port. The TV only supports Wi-Fi 5, certainly not the latest standard.
The B6 comes with two legs that are easy to install (two screws each), though I generally prefer a single pedestal stand design. The 65-inch model I tested fit comfortably on two 38-inch IKEA SPIKSMED TV benches set side by side that measure 76 inches long.
Like all LG TVs, setup involves LG’s own WebOS interface or ThinQ app, not built-in Google TV or Fire TV. It was easy to complete the setup using the LG ThinQ app on my iPhone—in minutes, I was loading my usual assortment of apps like Prime Video, Disney+ and Apple TV+.
The B6 is packed with features too. A few of my favorites include a gaming mode that helps improve low latency gaming, AI picture enhancements that actually work and make a discernible difference, an artwork mode called LG Gallery+ that costs $5 per month, and an LG music app in case you don’t like Spotify or other music apps. It also has settings for audio dialogue sync, similar to what you can do with powered speakers like the Klipsch The Fives II. A desktop mode means you can mirror your laptop screen and even run a Gmail app.
Photograph: John Brandon
I have mixed feelings about WebOS, though. My main gripe is that you cannot disable the pointer on the LG remote, and it jumps around a lot. When you press the center dial on the remote, it turns off temporarily as though LG user interface designers are admitting it isn’t that great. I also have mixed feelings about the remote—it’s hard to use in the dark by feel. The Home button is offset so it’s hard to find, and shortcuts for Netflix and other apps are situated at the bottom, but not backlit.
OLED Strengths, OLED Weaknesses
Based on the pricing, it’s obvious LG has positioned the B6 as the entry-level OLED in their line-up. That became crystal clear once I started testing movies and TV shows.
In the official specs, LG only lists “wide color gamut” and not a percentage for the specific BT.2020 spec, nor a specific brightness rating. This is where the benchmark testing comes in handy, and what I tested right away.
One win for the B6 is blacks and grays, which have great texture and clarity, a surprise given how many midrange televisions make dark, shadowy scenes look washed out. Scenes from Awake and The Creator, very dark movies, were clear and detailed, after tweaking a few picture quality settings (namely changing to Vivid mode).
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
Contrast and brightness are more of a mixed bag. I watched House of the Dragon and Game of Thrones (yes, the infamously dark season eight, episode three) to stress test these specs, and the B6 struggled. On better TVs (and home theater projectors), you can see trees in the background of a scene where a character emerges on a frozen lake. On the B6, they are completely black—e.g., a contrast problem.
Color saturation and luminance could be better too, especially compared to RGB TVs I’ve tested recently. The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, with its various blooming effects, wasn’t exactly terrible looking, but certainly not as crisp as on something like the LG Micro RGB Evo. (The less technicolor The End of Oak Street fared better.) During a demo reel benchmark, green grass by a fence in winter looked a bit too brown for my taste (again, color saturation issue), but skin tone variation was surprisingly good.
LG is not the first brand I think of for playing video games (it’s Sony), but the B6 deserves some extra credit here. The 120-Hz refresh rate screen does its job, and made all my movements playing Crimson Desert on PC crisp and responsive. Resident Evil: Requiem looked almost photo realistic, with gleaming statues and surprisingly good color quality, even zooming in on crumpled leaves.
Watching sports and news didn’t yield any surprises—a Baltimore Orioles baseball game looked rich and textured, but not very bright.
Affordable, But Outclassed
LG B6 may be an entry-level OLED, but, like an entry-level BMW, it has a lot of the bells and whistles of a flagship, with plenty of ports, features, and premium finishes. My main issue with it is brightness and contrast, both could be better. And LG’s WebOS is still not my favorite interface in the world.
The main issue might actually be price. At the time of writing, the LG B6 is on sale for $1,300. The superior midrange LG C6 is also on sale for $1,500. That’s only $200 more for a much better, brighter TV (both 65-inches). That’s not even discussing buying an older (but still brighter) model like the LG C5 (which I found on sale for less than the B6). It all depends on how much you want to spend.
John Brandon is a contributing writer for WIRED. He reviews televisions, projectors, speakers, and other AV staples. He started writing full-time in 2001 and has been featured in Forbes, Popular Mechanics, The Telegraph, Minnesota Monthly magazine, and many other publications. He lives in Minneapolis–Saint Paul.
