It’s About Security, Stupid!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:46:01 UTC
18:46:01 KST

Transitioning from Ukraine to the West exposes significant shifts in perspective. My most recent reentry into Europe and the US, after a stint in Ukraine, brought to light a perceptual disconnect around one crucial issue – especially as peace talks and potential deals appear in the news. That issue is security.
Outside of Ukraine I’m often asked the question: “Would Ukrainians accept a land-for-peace deal?”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The simple answer is: “Yes, definitely. As long as they get a real security guarantee.”
In an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour aired on Thursday, Oct. 22, President Volodymyr Zelensky insisted: “The most important thing [is] security guarantees.”
Of course, the full answer to the question of “land-for-peace” is very complex.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology indicated that 61 percent of Ukrainians consider handing Moscow all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region in exchange for security guarantees completely unacceptable.
However, like all such polls, the survey needs to minimize the contingencies surrounding any given issue. In this case, giving up the so-called “fortress belt” of cities in the remainder of the Donbas region that Ukraine still controls would be “unacceptable,” as it would require Kyiv to pull troops away from what constitutes its “Maginot line” against a Russian blitz toward Kyiv. In terms of security, such a land giveaway would be tantamount to capitulation – something obvious to Ukrainians on the ground there.
Russia Won’t Negotiate Seriously While It Thinks It Can Force Ukraine to Surrender, Sybiha Says
Focusing on the issue
When I consider the question, I keep hearing the refrain of Bill Clinton during the 1992 US presidential elections, when he was running against the incumbent George H.W. Bush.
Bush had just won a quick war, liberating Kuwait and manhandling the Iraqi army, which was supposed to be the third strongest in the world. Yet, despite his undisputed foreign policy success, economic figures were beginning to hint at recession, and the young candidate Clinton jumped on them with the rally cry: “It’s the economy, stupid!”
Clinton’s success lay in his ability to simply focus on the obvious, rather than getting sidetracked by ancillary issues and spectacles.
In a sense, that’s how Ukrainians feel. Everything depends on security. And security for Ukrainians has never been easy.
3 options for security guarantees
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has sought three basic types of security guarantee.
The most desirable for Kyiv, at least initially, was NATO. But as Zelensky pleaded for some sort of NATO membership, it became clear that this would never happen as long as Ukraine was under attack. And even after a ceasefire, opposition to Ukraine’s full membership would be virtually insurmountable.
That left Ukraine with the hope of a watered-down alternative to NATO: separate bilateral security agreements with partners that could help in the event that any future peace deal were breached by Moscow. Preferably, the partner should be a NATO member with nuclear capabilities. (Only the US, the UK, and France fit that bill).
The key to any such agreement would be what’s referred to as an “Article 5-type” clause that would oblige the partner to come to Ukraine’s assistance in case of attack. But Article 5 is ambiguous enough to have even NATO members questioning what would happen if Russia attacked (ironically, the very scenario that NATO was designed to deter and/or defend against).
This second scenario is fraught with problems. What about foreign boots on the ground to monitor the ceasefire? What about foreign military bases in Ukraine? What about tripwires? It’s not surprising that most nations have diplomatically eschewed committing to Ukraine’s security beyond money and materiel.
The third scenario – at least from the perspective within Ukraine – is fast proving to be the only viable solution: Ensure that the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) become so strong and capable that any invasion of Ukrainian territory would be too costly for the aggressor. And this is exactly what’s happening.
As with any promising solution to an intractable problem, the positives tend to snowball with momentum. As the nature of warfare becomes increasingly determined by drones and artificial intelligence, all the world’s military powers are studying the tactics and technologies employed in Ukraine. Even NATO military officers understand that in order to defend against a hypothetical attack, Ukraine’s know-how – acquired and developed out of necessity – is essential.
At this stage, though, Ukraine still can’t go it alone. Kyiv is currently parlaying its battlefield experience and willingness to sacrifice blood into a flood of treasure coming from the rich countries to its west. Security autonomy will take time, so Ukrainians have little choice but to hold the line, have faith in the AFU, and hope for the best in the West.
What this means for negotiations
As Zelensky continually insists: It’s about security. All the mineral and gas deals, all the talk of Donbas lines and territorial integrity, these are sideshows – important only inasmuch as they determine Ukraine’s security.
The Donbas issue – which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio disingenuously claimed on Oct. 22 was what “the war is about” – offers a perfect example:
It’s not that Ukraine is so attached to some holy notion of land or the mineral wealth beneath it. Zelensky has publicly repeated that he would accept a ceasefire on the current line of contact. But to give away land Russia has been unable to grab in 12 years for the sake of a dubious guarantee? That would be worse than naiveté – it would be disastrously criminal negligence on the part of Ukraine’s negotiators – especially as US President Donald Trump and his cohort, most notably Elon Musk, are so quick to double-cross friends for the sake of personal (not even national) interest.
As such, any proposed peace deal, if it is to be taken seriously, must offer real security guarantees. Given the current climate of distrust, “Article 5-like” guarantees will and should be met with a politely diplomatic “Thank you very much, but…” followed by hardnosed inquiries into details of commitments and tripwires.
The view from Ukraine, now nearly five full years into Moscow’s failed full-scale invasion, is rather clear. From the front line, where Russians are dying at a 10:1 ratio in many places and being fed into a drone buzzsaw in a maniacal effort to claim ruined Donbas villages as “conquered,” to cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, where inhabitants are bracing for a winter rife with power outages and ballistic missile attacks, no one is talking about surrendering, which is what Trump is effectively trying to coerce.
With each passing day, Ukraine’s only real security hope grows in strength, and many of its European partners have begun to realize that in terms of security they cannot do without a strong Ukraine.
Ultimately, though, Ukrainians know their security will hinge on two ineluctable facts – one biological, the other political – all dictators die, and all empires disintegrate.
This is a generational fight that can’t be framed by American or European election cycles. And the existential security problem Ukraine has with Moscow is centuries old.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron
Israel’s assault on the West Bank city has forced thousands of people to flee their homes.
The Farsh Al-Hawa area in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank is unrecognisable after Israeli forces demolished a three-story building and industrial facilities there. Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds the West Bank portfolio in the Ministry of Defence, said he ordered their destruction.
It all started on Friday, when two Palestinians attacked an Israeli military checkpoint in Farsh Al-Hawa, killing two soldiers and injuring others.
Since then, Hebron, the West Bank’s economic capital, has been attacked and put under lockdown by Israeli forces.
Israel has announced a sweeping military assault in the city, targeting the neighbourhood of the gunmen, who were killed on Friday. Israeli forces have already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians. City officials say almost half of the displaced are babies and children under 18, along with 81 pregnant women and 204 elderly.
Fahd Ahmaro was forced to leave his home, along with his family. He told Al Jazeera that he planned to stay but felt compelled to seek shelter outside his neighbourhood because the women and children were terrified.
“We left with nothing but the clothes on our backs. Our savings, belongings and documents are all in the house,” he said. “I tried to go back after I got my family out safely, but I couldn’t. It’s not safe any more.”
Palestinian authorities in Hebron have declared a state of emergency and created a crisis group, bringing together government agencies, the private sector and civil society, to respond after thousands of people in the city were forced to flee their homes.
Riyadh Khamis, who serves on the committee, told Al Jazeera that philanthropists who could not bear the thought of fellow Palestinians staying in temporary shelters opened their homes to the displaced.
“Hebron is known for its social solidarity and generosity. Our city was the first to provide aid during the COVID lockdown and during the genocide,” Khamis told Al Jazeera. “Today, our neighbours needed help so we all rallied.”
Real estate developer Mohamed Al-Rujoob is one of the philanthropists who sprang to action at the start of the assault on the city.
Al-Rujoob, who owns several apartments in Dura, a town close to Hebron, announced that the properties would be made available for displaced families, prompting other owners to do the same. He now hosts three extended families in his apartments, including 30 children.
“We must preserve people’s dignity. Today, we host these good people. Tomorrow, who knows? It might be us who need shelter. We’re all under the same occupation and we’re all vulnerable,” he said.
The Israeli army says Hebron is on lockdown, which affects nearly 1 million Palestinians who live in the city and the rest of the district.
Restrictions on movement have had a severe impact on the West Bank’s largest district. Schools have moved to online classes, while Hebron’s universities have made similar arrangements for their 18,000 students until the Israeli operation ends.
The measures are essential for Palestinian students who are stuck in their homes and neighbourhoods, including the besieged Fawwar refugee camp in Hebron, home to nearly 8,000 Palestinians. Israeli soldiers closed the camp’s entrance gate on Saturday, barring residents from entering or leaving, even on foot.
Abdel Fattah Al-Ttitti, a school teacher who lives in the camp and works in a Hebron school, said “we are locked in”.
“If, God forbid, somebody needs medical attention, we may be able to get them to the clinic in Masafer Yatta, but that clinic is poorly equipped. If there’s a medical emergency, they can’t help,” Al-Ttitti told Al Jazeera.
He is glad that schools announced online classes. “Until this campaign is over, there’s no other way,” he said.
Many in Hebron believe that Israel’s military campaign in the city has a political dimension, with Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday for a general election.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition is vying for every right-wing vote. Violence against Palestinians has proved an expedient campaign tactic for politicians such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Minister of Settlement Affairs, Orit Strook.
Both right-wing ministers have homes in illegal settlements in the Hebron area and support the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank and Gaza, which they refer to as “encouraging voluntary migration”.

in the fitting rooms, the aluminum curtain maps the city’s running paths, while photographic carpets document local sneaker-collecting culture across the footwear department.

[FEATURED]
SPACON designs installations for ADIDAS store in COPENHAGEN
Copenhagen-based architecture and design practice Spacon has developed two site-specific installations for the Adidas flagship store in Copenhagen. Intervening in two distinct retail zones, the fitting rooms and the Originals footwear area, the custom installations draw reference from the city’s urban running culture and the material archives of local sneaker collectors.
overview of the Adidas store in Copenhagen | all images ©Spacon
- SINE-WAVE PERFORATED ALUMINUM CURTAIN screens FITTING ROOMS
In the fitting room area, Spacon Studio installed a perforated aluminum curtain formed into a continuous sine-wave profile. The corrugated metal surface is calibrated across three viewing distances using varying perforation densities to project three nested graphic motifs: an aerial satellite view of Copenhagen centered on its central lakes with a crosshair indicating the store’s coordinates, a silhouette of a runner mid-stride, and a close-up profile of an Adidas Adizero shoe. The undulating surface of the aluminum sheet reflects ambient retail lighting while translating local running topography into a kinetic metallic partition.
detail of the custom seating installation
- PHOTOGRAPHIC CARPETS INTEGRATE ARCHIVAL VINTAGE SHOE BOXES
In the Originals footwear section, the studio placed three oversized photographic carpets across the floor. The textile prints depict an expansive field of vintage Adidas shoe boxes shown in various states—sealed, open, and empty. Embedded within the photographic field are rare archival sneakers sourced directly from the private collections of local sneaker collectors Joachim Idestrup Friis and Alexander Cummings, turning regional footwear archives into large-format floor graphics.

Can Latvia still afford Rail Baltica? Latvian Transport Minister warns current approach is no longer sustainable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:44:25 UTC
18:44:25 KST

Latvia's next government will have to assess whether and how the country can afford to continue implementing the Rail Baltica railway project when preparing the next state budget, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis of New Unity (JV) said on TV3's programme 900 Seconds.
He explained that Russia's war in Ukraine and other geopolitical developments mean the issue will require serious consideration and difficult decisions.
According to Kozlovskis, it is clear that Latvia can no longer continue implementing the project in the same way as before.
Furthermore, there is currently no clarity regarding funding from the European Union in future planning periods or financing from the European Commission.
Kozlovskis pointed out that a funding shortfall already exists within current contractual commitments, while financial obligations continue to increase.
At the same time, it is impossible to predict how much project costs may rise.
Consequently, there is also uncertainty about the financial burden on the state budget if existing contracts continue.
The minister stressed that the government must take these circumstances into account when preparing the budget and establish a clear expenditure plan for Rail Baltica.
As previously reported, the first phase of Rail Baltica's main railway line in Latvia is planned to proceed within its existing scope.
This includes establishing a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction work at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station.
These developments are intended to make it possible to connect Rail Baltica with Latvia's existing railway network.
The cost of the first phase of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 14.3 billion euros, including 5.5 billion euros in Latvia.
However, after adjusting for cost increases, Latvia's share could rise to six billion euros.
According to the project's cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros.
By comparison, the previous cost-benefit analysis, conducted in 2017, estimated the entire project would cost 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica aims to establish a European standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, connecting the Baltic states by rail with the rest of Europe.
The project envisages constructing 870 kilometres of new European standard-gauge railway track, with a gauge of 1,435 millimetres, across the Baltic states.
Trains on the new railway are expected to be capable of reaching a maximum speed of 240 kilometres per hour.

Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
More than 2,600 Palestinians have been displaced as the Israeli army continued a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank city of Hebron for a fourth consecutive day on Monday, amid raids, closures, and assaults on residents.
The army has shut all entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Local sources told Anadolu that additional Israeli forces accompanied by military vehicles entered Hebron around midnight through the Farsh al-Hawa entrance, while troops raided the southern part of the city near Jabal Karbaj.
Military reinforcements and large trucks arrived in the Al-Jilda area early Monday, where Israeli forces seized several Palestinian vehicles, the sources said.
Anadolu footage showed Israeli forces stopping and searching Palestinians at military checkpoints near Al-Jilda Roundabout and mistreating a young man.
Additional army forces also arrived in the Deir Bahha area, where Israeli forces seized several Palestinian vehicles, witnesses said.
Separately, Israeli forces divided a street in the Jabal al-Rahma area between Palestinians and Israeli occupiers, restricting Palestinians’ movement in the area, according to witnesses.
Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jabari told Anadolu on Sunday that the Israeli army had forced around 2,200 Palestinians from their homes and demolished five commercial and industrial structures and a three-story residential building since the operation began.
A local relief committee in the area on Monday updated the number of displaced Palestinians from the area at around 2,649.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner Society, the Israeli army arrested 50 Palestinians in Hebron since Friday.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz acknowledged Saturday evening that around 2,000 Palestinians had been forcibly displaced from their homes in Hebron, saying they would not be allowed to return until what he described as “Hamas infrastructure” in the city was dismantled.
The operation comes amid intensified Israeli army attacks and violence by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since Israel’s war on Gaza began in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings and arrests of Palestinians, demolitions of homes and other structures, the burning of mosques and vehicles, bulldozing farmland, preventing farmers from reaching their fields, displacing Palestinian communities and expanding illegal settlements.

Starvation in Gaza becomes Israeli election campaign issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:43:42 UTC
18:43:42 KST

Hardline Israeli rhetoric toward Palestinians has increasingly become part of campaigning ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections, while humanitarian conditions in Gaza have worsened amid tighter restrictions and continued Israeli violations.
Last week, extremist Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir released an AI-generated campaign video depicting Gaza completely destroyed by 2030 as part of his far-right Jewish Power party’s election campaign.
Four developments have emerged among the most pressing crises facing Gaza: the loss of food assistance for half a million Palestinians, the threat of vital hospital services shutting down because of depleted generator fuel, the expansion of areas under Israeli military control, and rising numbers of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces.
The developments come amid continued Israeli bombardment, gunfire, and restrictions on the entry of supplies despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since October 10, 2025.
The following are four crises that have worsened in Gaza during Israel’s election campaign and their impact on Palestinians.
Food aid cuts
On October 19, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced a one-third cut in food assistance in Gaza, leaving around 500,000 Palestinians without support and reducing beneficiaries from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
It halved food rations, cut daily hot meals from 250,000 to 150,000 and reduced deliveries to hard-to-reach areas.
The WFP blamed funding shortages, saying it needed $450 million to sustain operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank from October to March 2027.
Around 1.4 million Palestinians in Gaza face high levels of food insecurity.
Meanwhile, Israeli restrictions, inspection procedures and limited crossing capacity continue to hinder aid deliveries, according to the UN.
Gaza’s government media office warned that aid cuts were worsening famine conditions, while the Palestinian government raised concerns over rising malnutrition among children and pregnant women.
Hospitals at risk of shutdown
On October 21, Gaza’s Health Ministry said stocks of fuel needed to operate hospital electricity generators had run out, warning that the remaining generators could fail and life-saving medical services could be forced to stop.
Hospitals require more than 2,500 litres of fuel each month to keep generators running for extended periods amid a lack of electricity, the ministry said.
On September 13, Mazen al-Araishi, director general of engineering and maintenance at the ministry, said the quantities of fuel allowed into Gaza were limited and insufficient to meet generator operations and maintenance needs.
The ministry did not say when the last shipment of fuel entered Gaza or how long the generators could continue operating.
Gaza hospitals have depended on generators since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023 and its sole power plant stopped operating after running out of fuel, while the war destroyed large sections of electricity lines and distribution networks.
The generators power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators and dialysis machines, making their failure a direct threat to patients’ lives.
Expansion of Israeli-occupied areas
The Israeli army has continued expanding areas under its occupation in Gaza by moving “Yellow Line” markers westward, contrary to the ceasefire agreement’s gradual withdrawal plan. The line separates areas under Israeli military control from those where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
On October 11, Israeli forces advanced into Gaza City’s Shujaiya neighbourhood, moving concrete markers westward and forcing scores of families to flee.
The UN’s OCHA agency confirmed the changes on October 19, warning of further forced displacement.
The expansion restricts Palestinian access to homes, farmland and public facilities while complicating aid deliveries.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in June that the army occupied around 70 percent of Gaza and ruled out withdrawing from the Yellow Line.
He has linked further withdrawal to Hamas’s disarmament, while the group says the issue of its weapons can be addressed alongside a gradual Israeli withdrawal.
Palestinian deaths
Alongside the expansion of Israeli military control, the number of Palestinians killed by Israel from October 2-21 rose by around 40 percent compared with the same period in September, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry figures.
The data showed that 95 Palestinians were killed during that period in October, compared with 68 during the corresponding period in September, an increase of 27 deaths.
The number of Palestinians killed by Israel since the ceasefire agreement took effect reached 1,534 as of October 21, according to Health Ministry figures.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed 74,494 Palestinians and injured 175,604 others in Gaza, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Drive reindustrialisation from No 10 North or risk failure, MPs tell Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:42:48 UTC
18:42:48 KST

Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said.
The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode”.
John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”.
However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work.
“The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says.
The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues.
The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy.
And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry.
Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.”
Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.”
He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel, adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education.
Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.”
A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.”
In its industrial strategy, published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence.
In his conference speech, to which Healey had invited a young apprentice who had worked on building a new Mersey ferry, the chancellor said Labour would “get Britain growing. With hope for our young people. With good work, good jobs and a new age of industrialisation.”

Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:42:21 UTC
18:42:21 KST

Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova narrowly led the first round of presidential elections Sunday, exit polls showed, in a vote held amid security concerns following a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, scored between 35 and 36.5 percent of the vote, according to three polls.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
She will face Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition who came second with between 32.2 and 32.5 percent, in the November 1 runoff.
The result was closer than expected, with surveys ahead of the vote predicting a comfortable win for Iotova.
Turnout was only around 20 percent, according to the polls.
After casting her vote, Iotova said she wanted to address “the dire issue of poverty” in the EU’s poorest member state, “alongside inequalities and regional disparities”.
“I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security,” added the 62-year-old, who has made the war in Ukraine a central theme of her campaign, promising to be a “president of peace”.
Gyurov meanwhile said he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud... and where the state works as it should”.
- Ship attacks -
Four vessels were struck off Bulgaria’s coast this month, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
Serbia’s Student Movement Ousts Longtime Leader in Parliament Poll
While Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking Moscow to them.
Iotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state, when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman ever elected president in the country of 6.4 million people.
A win for Iotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Without questioning Bulgaria’s membership of the EU or NATO, she opposes military aid to Ukraine and advocates negotiations.
Gyurov, 50, has sharply criticised Radev’s foreign policy and is a strong supporter of Bulgaria’s Euro-Atlantic ties.
At his final campaign rally in Plovdiv on Wednesday, Gyurov said he wanted Bulgaria to be “a reliable ally within NATO, defending its interests through solid preparedness, strong diplomacy and clear positions”.
- ‘Unconvincing response’ -
Parvan Simeonov, founder of polling institute Myara, said Iotova “did not step out of her presidential role” during the campaign, “which prevented her from engaging in sharper debate”.
He added that the low turnout showed “that we don’t have a problem with the polls, but with the very functioning of democracy”.
Casting his vote earlier, Radev blamed the low turnout on the “significant lead between the first and second according to surveys, which gives reassurance in one camp and perhaps a sense of doom in the other”.
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Moscow.
Twenty-seven pairs of candidates for president and vice-president were competing in the first round, nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.
Teodor Slavev, a political analyst and programme director at the Bulgarian Institute for Legal Initiatives, told AFP the results were “a resounding electoral slap in the face for Rumen Radev’s administration and their inability to address people’s problems”.
He also said voters were giving their verdict on “Iotova’s unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea”.

EU forced to seek seat at talks on Ukraine settlement — news portal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:40:45 UTC
18:40:45 KST

ROME, October 26. /TASS/. After years of confrontation with Russia, the European Union is now urgently seeking a way to secure a place at the negotiating table for talks on resolving the conflict in Ukraine, the Italian news portal L’AntiDiplomatico reported on Sunday.
"How has it come to pass that one of the world’s largest economic powers now finds itself having to ask for a seat at the negotiating table in a military conflict that directly affects its own security?" the portal’s columnist asked.
According to the report, Brussels has spent recent years tightening sanctions on Russia and providing military and financial assistance to Ukraine in an effort to isolate Moscow politically. Yet the EU is now being forced to "desperately seek diplomatic channels with the very government with which it had vowed never to normalize relations," the publication noted.
Politico previously reported that EU member states are concerned about their role in potential negotiations on Ukraine and are seeking a representative capable of advancing the bloc’s interests. According to The Telegraph, potential candidates include Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Czech President Petr Pavel, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Moscow has repeatedly expressed its readiness to engage in dialogue with European countries on the continent’s security architecture, taking into account the interests of all parties.
On October 22, Russian President Vladimir Putin, responding to questions from Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin, endorsed the US position that discussions on future security guarantees for both Ukraine and Russia should also address the broader European security architecture.
Russia will closely monitor developments over the coming days, Putin added.

Israel loses two key allies in Brazil and Serbia, putting strategic ties at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:39:51 UTC
18:39:51 KST

Israel is facing two significant foreign policy setbacks following election results in Brazil and Serbia, where political figures regarded as close allies of Jerusalem suffered defeats over the weekend. While the outcome in Brazil has dashed hopes of ending a prolonged diplomatic crisis, the political upheaval in Serbia raises more immediate questions about Israel's defense cooperation with one of its most important European military partners.
In Brazil, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured another term after defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. In Serbia, former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that emerged from nearly two years of anti-government protests.
For Jerusalem, the results have created the impression of a diplomatic gamble that failed. Both politicians had cultivated close relationships with Israel, but their defeats carry different consequences. Brazil represents a missed opportunity to restore diplomatic relations, while Serbia poses a potential challenge to an established strategic partnership involving weapons supplies, defense technology and military cooperation.
Neither election result automatically means that existing agreements will be canceled or diplomatic relations will deteriorate further. However, both demonstrate how quickly Israel's international relationships can become uncertain when they depend heavily on individual leaders.
Brazil: Hopes of moving the embassy to Jerusalem collapse
In Brazil, the disappointment is primarily about the diplomatic opportunity Israel has lost rather than fears of a dramatic new deterioration in relations.
Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to reverse the policies of the Lula administration, deepen Brazil's military and diplomatic cooperation with Israel and move the Brazilian Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.
He had also pledged to receive the credentials of a new Israeli ambassador on his first day in office, signaling his intention to restore diplomatic representation between the countries.
His defeat means those promises will not be implemented under his proposed administration, leaving Israel facing another presidential term under Lula, whose relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been openly hostile.
Relations between Israel and Brazil are already at a historic low. Israel declared Lula persona non grata following his remarks comparing the war in Gaza to the Holocaust and likening the conduct of Israeli soldiers to that of the Nazis.
Neither country currently has an ambassador serving in the other's capital, reflecting the depth of the diplomatic breakdown.
Netanyahu had openly supported the possibility of a change in Brazil's leadership. Following the first round of voting, he congratulated Bolsonaro on his electoral performance and wished him success in the runoff.
The prime minister is not expected to telephone Lula to congratulate him on his victory. The two leaders remain completely estranged, and Netanyahu's public support for Bolsonaro has only deepened the divide.
Bolsonaro's defeat therefore closes off, at least for now, the possibility of a rapid diplomatic reset involving restored ambassadors, closer defense cooperation and a Brazilian Embassy in Jerusalem.
For Israel, the immediate consequence is not the loss of an existing close partnership, but the disappearance of an opportunity to rebuild one.
Serbia: The more serious challenge to Israel's defense interests
The consequences of the Serbian election could be more substantial because the relationship between Jerusalem and Belgrade has already developed into a strategic partnership.
Under Vučić, Serbia became an important defense partner for Israel, particularly during the war against Hamas and Hezbollah.
As several countries imposed restrictions or embargoes on weapons exports to Israel, Serbia continued supplying military equipment and munitions.
Serbian deliveries increased dramatically during the fighting, with an extensive airlift helping Israel replenish stocks depleted by the IDF's heavy consumption of explosives, artillery shells, missiles, bombs and interceptors.
This cooperation took on additional significance in September, when Serbia inaugurated a factory to assemble Israeli-made drones in partnership with Israeli defense company Elbit Systems.
The facility marked a further expansion of military-industrial ties between the countries, moving their relationship beyond weapons purchases and shipments toward joint defense production.
Vučić had cultivated a close relationship with Israel, making Serbia an important partner at a time when other European countries were increasingly critical of Israeli military operations.
His electoral defeat now raises questions about whether the new Serbian leadership will maintain that same level of cooperation.
The incoming student-backed political movement has not yet established a clear position toward Israel. Existing defense contracts are not automatically canceled because of a change in government, and there is no indication that the new leadership has decided to terminate them.
Nevertheless, Israel will have to assess whether the political relationship that supported those agreements can survive without Vučić.
Another consideration is Serbia's relationship with the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already welcomed the student movement's electoral victory and expressed the EU's willingness to support democratic reforms and Serbia's accession process.
Closer integration with European institutions could potentially bring Belgrade under greater pressure to align itself with European positions on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Such a shift is not inevitable, particularly given the uncertainty surrounding the incoming government's foreign policy. But it creates a potential challenge for a bilateral relationship that has been unusually close.
For Jerusalem, the central concern is therefore not simply the departure of a friendly politician, but whether Serbia will continue serving as a dependable source of military equipment and a partner in Israeli defense manufacturing.
A wider problem for Netanyahu's foreign policy
Taken together, the election results highlight a vulnerability in the way Netanyahu has built many of Israel's international relationships.
His foreign policy has frequently relied on personal and ideological connections with individual leaders rather than broader, institutional relationships between states.
As long as those leaders remain in power, the ties can appear exceptionally strong. But when they lose elections, some of the political foundations supporting those relationships can weaken along with them.
The same challenge extends beyond Brazil and Serbia. It has implications for Israel's relationships with European countries and the United States, where changes of government can alter policies even when strategic interests remain unchanged.
The electoral defeats do not necessarily establish a broader international trend against Israel.
In Latin America, Lula's victory runs counter to the gains made by several right-wing politicians associated with U.S. President Donald Trump, including in Colombia.
The reasons for the results also appear overwhelmingly domestic.
In Serbia, the election followed nearly two years of protests against Vučić's rule. In Brazil, the presidential contest was decided by voters divided between two political camps of roughly comparable size.
Israel was not a central issue in either campaign, and the outcomes should not be interpreted as evidence of changing public attitudes toward Israel in those countries.
Nevertheless, the results underscore the strategic importance of building institutional alliances that can withstand changes in political leadership.
Lapid attacks Netanyahu, Saar responds: ‘Turning your back on friends of Israel’
The developments have also become part of Israel's domestic political debate, with Tuesday's Knesset election just hours away.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid used the defeats of Bolsonaro and Vučić to criticize Netanyahu's relationships with foreign leaders.
"Another two people close to Netanyahu lost elections last night because of high voter turnout and national pride among people who refused to accept dictates from abroad," Lapid wrote Monday morning.
"Tomorrow, the people of Israel will begin the process of putting things right, returning Israel to a path of hope and success."
Lapid subsequently clarified that he did not welcome Lula's victory.
"And let me be clear: I am very unhappy about Lula's victory. I always support the pro-Israel candidate. That is the most important criterion," he wrote.
"But today, being close to Netanyahu is a political liability everywhere in the world. In Israel too."
Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded with a sharp attack on Lapid, accusing him of belittling politicians who have supported Israel.
"For the good-for-nothing Lapid, two great friends of Israel, such as Serbian President Vučić and Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, are simply 'two Netanyahu associates,'" Saar wrote.
"Turning your back on Israel's friends and currying favor with those who act against it is contemptible and a moral low, even before considering the level of foreign policy thinking on display."
He concluded with a warning directed at voters: "Anyone with any sense should stay away from the clowns' ballot paper at the polling station."
The exchange reflects competing interpretations of the election results. Netanyahu's opponents may point to the defeats as evidence of weaknesses in his foreign policy, while his supporters can argue that the outcomes demonstrate the risks posed by the rise of governments more critical of Israel.
However, the foreign election results are unlikely to become a decisive issue for Israeli voters, who face a wide range of more immediate domestic and security concerns.
Can Israel rebuild its alliances elsewhere?
Despite the setbacks in Brazil and Serbia, Israel may still see opportunities to develop closer relationships with other governments in the coming years.
In France, Marine Le Pen has been leading in several polls ahead of the next presidential election, while in Spain, recent surveys have placed right-wing opposition parties ahead of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's governing party.
Both political environments could offer potential openings for Israel if future governments adopt more favorable diplomatic positions, although election outcomes and subsequent policies remain uncertain.
But the immediate lesson from Brazil and Serbia is not about which political camp may prevail in the next election.
In Brazil, Israel has lost the prospect of a rapid normalization of diplomatic relations and a symbolic embassy move to Jerusalem. In Serbia, a proven defense relationship now faces a period of political uncertainty.
The two setbacks differ in scale and practical consequences, but they point to the same strategic challenge: Friendly leaders can help build important partnerships, yet the durability of those partnerships ultimately depends on whether they can survive the leaders themselves.

Iran accuses US of 'lacking seriousness' in talks, imposing demands on Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:39:43 UTC
18:39:43 KST

Iran accused the US on Monday of lacking seriousness in negotiations, saying Washington has repeatedly confused diplomacy with imposing demands on Tehran.
“The American side is not serious about negotiations,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said during his weekly news conference, as cited by the state-run IRNA news agency.
He accused Washington of repeatedly making false claims, recalling that US President Donald Trump had expressed support for negotiations shortly before the US military attacks on Iran in June 2025.
“What do you call this? Do you see any goodwill in this approach?” he asked.
Baqaei said Tehran had not received any new European proposal for negotiations beyond a political statement, criticising Britain, France and Germany for their positions during the conflict.
He accused the three countries of following Washington’s lead on the restoration of UN sanctions and failing to condemn military attacks against Iran.
No nuclear weapons
Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed nuclear weapons or sought to acquire them, accusing Washington of using allegations about Tehran’s nuclear program to justify military action.
He said Iran had negotiated in good faith and signed the 2015 nuclear agreement, but the US withdrew from it three years later.
The spokesman accused the US administration of being influenced by Israeli claims about Iran’s nuclear program, describing allegations that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb as a justification for military aggression.
Missing Iranian pilot
Baqaei said Iran continued to hold Qatar responsible for offering a clarification on the fate of three Iranian pilots whose aircraft were hit in the Gulf country.
“Until we have evidence of their deaths or receive precise information and documentation, we assume that the country where their aircraft were hit must be held accountable,” he said.
He added that Tehran was pursuing the matter in coordination with its military leadership and through technical delegations and legal discussions.
Baqaei also confirmed that a Qatari delegation recently visited Tehran, saying the trip involved bilateral cooperation and regional mediation efforts.
He described such visits as normal during regional conflicts, noting that Qatar had sought to convey messages and present its positions.
Commenting on Israel’s upcoming elections and threats of military action against Iran, Baqaei accused Israeli politicians of competing over who could commit more crimes.
“It makes no difference to us who takes charge of a regime with a history of violence and killings,” he said.
Russia visit
The spokesman confirmed that President Masoud Pezeshkian would travel to Russia on Monday night to attend a summit of gas-exporting countries.
He said the visit would provide opportunities to strengthen energy cooperation with Moscow and hold consultations with other major energy-producing countries.
Baqaei also addressed border-related difficulties with Pakistan and Iraq, saying discussions with Islamabad were progressing positively.
He said Pakistan had described the issue as technical while also raising security concerns, including reports of planned attacks.
Regarding Iraq, he said Iranian diplomatic missions were pursuing the matter, warning that US pressure on Baghdad could harm the Iraqi population and bilateral relations.
Baqaei said Iran summoned the Italian ambassador on Sunday to express concern over the authorities’ handling of protests in European countries.
He accused France, Belgium and Italy of using excessive force and restricting the right to protest, saying such measures were inconsistent with their human rights obligations.
The French ambassador had also been summoned previously, he added.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen
On the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said regional security was interconnected and instability in one country could affect others.
He stressed that the dispute should be resolved between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, reiterating Tehran’s readiness to help facilitate a settlement.
“Military approaches make problems more complicated and cause extensive damage,” he said, expressing hope that Saudi Arabia would pursue a negotiated solution.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a regional conflict and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, Trump and Pezeshkian signed a Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding, aimed at ending hostilities, reopening the strategic waterway and paving the way for a broader agreement.
However, disagreements over the implementation of the understanding, including the US naval blockade, sanctions and navigation through the strait, have continued to hinder diplomatic efforts.
Earlier this month, Iran said restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz remained central to negotiations with Washington, insisting that the US must take specific steps to resolve the standoff.

Strike on Tolyattikauchuk Damages Production of Rocket Fuel Feedstock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:39:31 UTC
18:39:31 KST

The October 24 attack on the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant damaged at least two production facilities linked to isobutylene production, a feedstock for synthetic rubber.
According to an Exilenova+ analysis, Ukrainian drones particularly struck the isobutane dehydrogenation unit, where isobutane is converted into isobutylene.
The external unit No. 2 of the BK-4 workshop, which produces and purifies high-purity isobutylene, was also damaged.
The damage could delay synthetic rubber production and the supply of feedstock for further industrial processes, including solid rocket fuel manufacturing.
The Tolyattikauchuk plant is one of Russia’s largest petrochemical facilities, with an annual synthetic rubber production capacity of around 260,000 tonnes.
The plant also produces butadiene, isoprene, hydrocarbon fractions, and methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), which increases gasoline octane ratings.
The attack on the plant took place on the morning of October 24. By 6:30 a.m. local time, residents reported a large fire at the facility.
This is not the first attack on the facility. On the night of April 4, 2026, drones sparked fires on the plant’s premises, including the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 units, which produce butyl rubber.
The strike also hit the D-12 unit, which houses tanks for storing liquefied products, and the D-1 unit, through which isobutane is fed for further processing.
The next attack took place on September 12.
At the time, Militarnyi reported that the strike had disabled the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 units, which support butyl rubber production. Equipment damage halted the manufacture of the isobutane-isobutylene fraction, which is required to produce methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a high-octane fuel additive.

Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:39:07 UTC
18:39:07 KST

Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
The Swiss woman in Nigeria who has been infected with the Ebola virus is being brought back to Switzerland for treatment. She was flown out of the Nigerian capital, Abuja, on Monday morning, Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate announced on X.
The patient’s condition has improved significantly. She is stable, conscious and responsive. Her laboratory results had also returned to near-normal levels, Pate said.
The woman’s husband, a Swiss diplomat, was also flown out with her. He continues to show no symptoms. Despite the improvement in her condition, the patient may still be infectious. Strict protective measures are therefore being observed. The Nigerian Minister of Health indicated that further information would be provided on Monday afternoon, once the patient and her husband had arrived safely at their destination.
More
Exploitation and misinformation hinder DRC Ebola response
The couple had travelled to Uganda before returning to Nigeria. First signalled last week, this infection remains the only one recorded in the country to date. Nigerian health authorities have identified 53 close contacts.
The Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) did not initially confirm the information on the repatriation when contacted by the Keystone-SDA news agency.
A ‘more complex’ outbreak
The World Health Organization (WHO) recently warned that Africa was facing a “more complex” Ebola outbreak, as the virus has been detected in the west of the continent, while it is also present in the east and centre.
Nigeria had previously faced Ebola in 2014, during the outbreak that struck West Africa. That outbreak claimed more than 11,000 lives between late 2013 and 2016.
Two competent Swiss hospitals
Since 2019, Switzerland has had two reference hospitals equipped to treat diseases such as Ebola: the University Hospital of Zurich (USZ) and the University Hospital of Geneva (HUG).
+ WHO declares Ebola an international health emergency
To date, two people who had contracted Ebola in Africa have been treated in Switzerland. In 1995, a Swiss anthropologist was treated in Switzerland after contracting Ebola while working with monkeys in Africa. In 2014, a Cuban doctor was admitted to the Geneva University Hospital (HUG). He had become infected while on a humanitarian mission in Sierra Leone and was part of a medical team combating the Ebola epidemic in West Africa. Both patients survived, according to the public health office.

Why are Elvis Presley rightsholders suing AI company Anthropic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:37:19 UTC
18:37:19 KST

Anthropic could face more than $40million in damages over the alleged unauthorised use of Elvis' music catalogue.
Anthopic, the company behind AI assistant Claude, is being sued by Elvis Presley rightsholders over alleged copyright infringement of 274 of the King's songs.
They have launched legal action against AI company, accusing it of using Elvis' songs to train its models without permission.
The lawsuit was filed on Friday (23 October) in the US District Court for the Northern District of California by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, the company that controls much of Presley’s intellectual property and trademark rights.
The suit states 274 songs, including 'Can’t Help Falling in Love', 'Don’t Be Cruel', and 'A Little Less Conversation', were copied without permission and used to train Anthropic’s Claude AI models.
The plaintiffs have claimed that Anthropic infringed their copyrights without a licence or payment, and the company retained copies in an internal library for training future versions of its models - all without obtaining permission or paying the relevant rights.
Anthropic could face more than $40million (approx. €36m) in damages.
“The Elvis Plaintiffs’ iconic collective catalog contains some of the most groundbreaking, revolutionary, influential, and enduring musical compositions in human history,” the lawsuit reads.
“The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in a statement, according to Pitchfork. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.”
Anthropic told NBC News that they “disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully”. The company has previously maintained that training AI models on copyrighted material can be protected under US fair use law.
In October 2023, Universal Music Publishing Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO sued Anthropic, alleging that Claude had reproduced copyrighted lyrics without authorisation.
This year, Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell also filed a lawsuit against Anthropic, accusing the company of using copyrighted lyrics and sheet music from artists including The Beatles and Michael Jackson to train Claude.
Anthropic has also faced a lawsuit from authors who accused it of using pirated books to train Claude. The company agreed to a $1.5bn settlement in July.
Last month, the company told would-be shareholders that the technology it sells could threaten humanity itself. Anthropic listed risk factors including the possibility that increasingly advanced AI models could manipulate, blackmail or behave in other unpredictable ways. Anthropic's own research has shown autonomous models sabotaging code, assisting fraud and manipulating information in controlled tests.

Russia’s Yak-130M aircraft fitted with President-S130 active defense system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:35:37 UTC
18:35:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Yak-130M combat training aircraft has been equipped with an active defense system against anti-aircraft missiles, which emits electronic jamming signals and releases heat decoys, Russia’s state tech corporation Rostec told reporters.
"The third Yak-130M prototype aircraft of our United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) has recently successfully completed its maiden flight. Its integration will accelerate testing of the new aircraft. The first deliveries to customers are planned as early as 2028. The aircraft is equipped with the President-S130 onboard system," the statement said.
The system operates in three stages: it automatically detects the launch of an enemy missile, instantly jams the detection and guidance systems with electronic countermeasures, and then deploys special decoys to neutralize infrared and radar homing heads.
The Yak-130M is a modernized combat trainer based on the Yak-130 aircraft, featuring improved combat capabilities. The aircraft can engage ground and air targets, including unmanned aerial vehicles.

Ukrainian Drone Barrage Against Voronezh Kills At Least 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:34:42 UTC
18:34:42 KST

At least three people were killed in a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Voronezh in southern Russia, local authorities said early Monday, with another 29 people being reported injured.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defense systems destroyed 113 drones in the skies above the region overnight. He said most unmanned aircraft were intercepted directly over the regional capital.
“Unfortunately, two people were killed,” Gusev initially wrote in a post on Telegram, identifying the victims as two men born in 1960 and 1973. At an emergency meeting later in the day, he said the death toll had risen to three people.
Gusev said most of the people wounded in the overnight attack were on a passenger train that was hit.
Falling drone debris also sparked fires at multiple industrial and commercial sites, the governor added, as well as residential buildings and a school’s sports arena.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of black smoke rising over Voronezh to identify one of the targeted industrial sites as a synthetic rubber plant owned by the Sibur petrochemical corporation.
The facility makes rubber and polymers used in military aircraft tires, armored vehicles and solid rocket fuel components for Iskander ballistic missiles.
If confirmed, the strike in Voronezh would mark the third attack on a Russian synthetic rubber factory in as many days, following strikes on rubber plants in the cities of Tolyatti and Omsk this weekend.
Elsewhere, Bryansk region Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said a drone attack killed a train driver on Sunday night.
A passenger train bound from the southern resort town of Anapa to Moscow was also hit in an overnight strike, with Russian Railways reporting that at least five passengers were wounded.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 290 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Civil aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights across all Moscow airports.
Reuters contributed reporting.

'Democracy has won': Europe celebrates Lula's surprise victory in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:33:58 UTC
18:33:58 KST

European leaders have greeted Lula's re-election in Brazil. "Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," Ursula von der Leyen said.
European leaders have hailed Brazilian President Lula da Silva's re-election for a fourth term, defying predictions of a right-wing surge in Latin America's most populous country and securing a key ally for the EU.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa were among the first to congratulate Lula, with whom they worked closely to secure the EU-Mercosur trade deal.
The agreement, signed in January with the South American trading bloc comprising Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, was seen as a rebuke to US President Donald Trump's punitive tariffs. Brussels had feared that Lula's right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, would jeopardise the deal after calling on Brazil to break free of Mercosur's "shackles" and pursue independent trade agreements, including with the US.
"Congratulations to my friend, Lula," von der Leyen said on social media.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil. Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," she went on.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Costa spoke with Lula on Sunday night to personally congratulate him.
"The Brazilian people have spoken," Costa said.
"We will continue to work together to deepen our ties, tackle global challenges and build a more peaceful and prosperous world."
French President Emmanuel Macron, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro also joined the chorus.
"In the face of the great challenges of our time, let us strengthen our strategic partnership and bring to life the friendship between our two countries in service of a more just world," Macron said.
Pedro Sánchez, the most prominent left-wing leader in Europe, hailed Lula's re-election as a "great victory" and drew a parallel with his country, where the conservative opposition leads the polls ahead of snap elections next month.
"What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain," Sánchez said. "The comeback of global progressivism has just begun."
The European reactions poured in as the results from Brazil showed Lula with a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote.
Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, is in jail for leading a coup attempt, has contested the tally and said the election should be annulled.
Bolsonaro claimed the order by Brazil's judiciary to extend voting hours due to public transportation delays and torrential rains was a "dirty trick".
A win for Bolsonaro, as many opinion polls had predicted after the first round, would have consolidated Latin America's right-wing turn. The Trump administration has tried to assert dominance in the region under the so-called "Donroe Doctrine".
Trump has been credited with bringing the EU and Brazil closer together, as the two searched for reliable partners in an increasingly volatile world.
The EU and Brazil have found common ground on areas that Trump has challenged, such as free trade, the multilateral order and climate action, with a focus on the Amazon.
Some crucial differences remain, most notably on Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Brazil, as a member of the BRICS, maintain close ties with Russia.

Oil spill off UAE widens, prompting more beach closures
- An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the UAE has widened, satellite images show, and is now close to Umm Al Quwain’s coast.
- Authorities have closed beaches in Umm Al Quwain, Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah while they assess the leak and try to contain it.
- Experts warn the spill is a serious environmental threat to Gulf marine life, with risks rising after recent attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
AI generated
DUBAI – An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union’s Copernicus satellite observation network dated Oct 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict’s environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Oct 23 that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.
However, experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile in September, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
The images provided by the EU’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Oct 23 that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
“The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed,” Nidal Hilal, professor of Engineering and director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Water Research Center, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Oct 24 that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice.
The UAE’s marine life “is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters”, including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature says on its website. REUTERS

Brexit deal is not good enough for British public, says Andy Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:30:10 UTC
18:30:10 KST

Brexit has not “played out” like it was promised to the public, has weakened the economy and the current deal is not good enough, Andy Burnham has said, while ruling out any major changes in the current parliament.
The prime minister said Britain had ended up with a “harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign” and it had not helped to control the small boats crisis. Backing the home secretary’s tougher immigration rules, he said Brexit had weakened the UK’s ability to control its borders as it could no longer send people back to Europe.
When asked directly on Monday whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, Burnham told Good Morning Britain: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”
Explaining why he even brought up the possibility of “going all the way” in terms of closer relations with the EU, Burnham said: “Looking back at Brexit … I don’t think it has played out as people said it would at the time. We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign.
“It’s weakened our economy. It’s also weakened our control of immigration, and that might surprise people because that was the big issue, but the small boats crisis has risen since and we have a different form of immigration now.”
He added: “I am not going to say at the moment that the deal we’ve got is good enough for Britain. I don’t think it is good enough.”
Burnham said he would not “move away from the red lines in Labour’s manifesto”, adding: “I’m not proposing rejoining [the EU] in this parliament. We’re way, way away from that at this particular point in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better.”
There are concerns among Labour MPs who represent leave-voting constituencies in the north of the England and the Midlands that reopening the Brexit debate could create opportunities for Reform UK.
Asked about the fact that 65% of his constituents in Makerfield voted to leave the EU, the prime minister said: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing. The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit … What I can do though is make practical steps to make the arrangements work better.”
Emphasising the negative impact Brexit had had on Britain’s control of immigration, the Labour leader said: “I think we’ve got weaker control now. The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can’t return people, and people know we can’t do that in the same way that we used to be able to.”
Burnham said he hoped the UK-EU summit on 20 November could yield a deal “which would be good for British food manufacturers, because they’ve been hit hard by Brexit”.
He said he backed “the principle” of the home secretary’s controversial plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Burnham said Shabana Mahmood was right to pursue the plans based on the principle that “settlement is a right to be earned not just something that is granted automatically”.
He also ruled out calling an early general election, despite polling suggesting Labour was still enjoying a “Burnham bounce”. “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.”
On Wednesday’s budget, Burnham said it would offer people and businesses “breathing space”, claiming it would give Britain “a little bit of light at the end of the tunnel”.

Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.
Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”
Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.
Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.
Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.
Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.
It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.
“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.
The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.
But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”
Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”
That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”
