Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?
After years of war, displacement and restrictions, Gazans ask whether Israel’s election will affect their future.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — After three years of genocidal war, Palestinians in Gaza are watching the upcoming elections in Israel with a mixture of fear and uncertainty.
Although the territory has been under a “ceasefire” since October 2025, Palestinians in Gaza continue to endure almost daily Israeli air strikes, dire living conditions, and a punishing siege that has caused shortages of basic goods.
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday to vote for their next government, in an election that has been shaped by the war on Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been strongly criticised for his handling of security before the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel. Members of his far-right government have called for a tougher line on Gaza, including the expulsion of its population.
The people of Gaza know this election will shape their future and many have been closely watching the campaign.
Mohammed Eliyan, 36, was displaced from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza and now lives in Deir el-Balah with his five children. He hopes a change in leadership in Israel could bring relief to Palestinians who have endured repeated displacement and war.
“We follow the Israeli election to see who will win in the next phase. We hope there might be some easing for the Palestinian cause and for us, who have been displaced again,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eliyan hopes that Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military commander and Netanyahu’s main rival, will defeat the prime minister. He sees Netanyahu as more hardline and fears that if his Likud party and far-right allies win another term, it would mean more war and further displacement for Gaza’s people.
“We hope there will be changes after the election, and that someone other than Benjamin Netanyahu will win. What Netanyahu has done to the Palestinian people, before and after October 7, has not been a small thing,” he said.
But regardless of who wins, Eliyan does not expect a major shift in Israeli policy.
“They are still our enemy, and I don’t expect things to improve dramatically,” he said. “But we hope someone else might be less harsh than Netanyahu.”
He called on Israel’s next leader to end the war, prevent displacement and starvation, and ease restrictions at Gaza’s crossings.
“We want whoever leads Israel not to be hardline. End the war and let us live in peace,” he said.
Islam Salem, 41, is displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and has three daughters. He is following Israel’s election closely and believes the result could affect Gaza’s future and the lives of his children, likely for the worse.
“Politics is our livelihood. It is connected to everything in our lives, our living conditions and even the future of our children,” he said.
But he also believes that elections primarily serve Israeli interests, so even if there are new faces in the next government, the Gaza strategy will likely remain the same.
“Israeli policy will not change in any way. Whatever they take, they consider it theirs and a political gain for them, the gains of a war they have pursued for a long time,” Islam told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Israel’s continued control of about 65 percent of Gaza’s territory inside the “Yellow Line”. He also doubts whether reconstruction will begin soon in Gaza, where more than 80 percent of buildings have been damaged, and about two-thirds of those have been completely destroyed.
“I think reconstruction will be difficult. They do not want to give others any rights. They want their rights in full, and even more,” he said.
Years of war have left Salem struggling to imagine a future beyond his harsh daily reality.
“There is no future left for us to be afraid of. We live day by day. We have no idea what will happen next, and everything we feared has already happened,” he said.
Asked what he would say to Israel’s next prime minister, he spoke of how many in Gaza are feeling.
“If only a simple person could come and talk to him and say, ‘Leave us alone. Give us some breathing space and let us breathe.’ But he would not be convinced. What can I say to him?” he said.
Hanan Abu al-Maaza, 57, has been displaced more than 12 times during the war on Gaza. She fears Israel’s next government could bring more suffering to its people in the besieged enclave.
“We follow the election because of the fear and anxiety we are living with. We have been displaced more than 12 times, and we are afraid they will do even worse to us than before,” she said.
“We go to sleep without feeling safe, wondering what they might do to us next. The fear is still in our heads and hearts.”
Abu al-Maaza says if Netanyahu is defeated, there will be more chance that she can return to her home in Beit Lahiya.
“I hope someone else wins, so we can have peace of mind and feel safe, and return to our homes. That is what we wish for,” she said.
After years of destruction in Gaza, she hopes Israel’s next leader will show Palestinians more mercy.
“Maybe he will say that there is nothing left in Gaza, that they have done enough and should let people live. There is hardly anything left in Gaza for anyone to think about doing anything more,” she said.
Abu al-Maaza urged Israel’s next leader to end the war and stop the suffering in the territory.
“We have had enough of war and destruction. There is nothing left to destroy, yet the suffering continues,” she said.
Manar Owaida, 23, is originally from northern Gaza and is now displaced in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. She is also keeping an eye on the Israeli election and considering its potential impact.
“I follow the election to know what they are saying and planning, and to understand what is happening around us and how the next Israeli government might affect the situation in Gaza,” she said.
Owaida hopes Gadi Eisenkot will replace Netanyahu, and sees the current prime minister as more extreme than his challenger. But she does not believe a change in Israel’s leadership would transform Palestinian lives, arguing that government policies have remained consistent for decades.
“Israel’s policy is one of crime, killing and destruction. Since 1948, it has been the same policy, the same killing and the same blockade,” she said.
Still, she hopes a new government could ease restrictions and killings and withdraw from areas beyond the “Yellow Line”, allowing life to gradually return to Gaza.
“There might be a change in Israeli policy if someone comes in place of Netanyahu and eases the blockade and the killing we are living through,” she said.
“There could be a withdrawal from the Yellow Line and life could gradually return to Gaza. But we are waiting with fear and uncertainty, alongside a little hope.”
Her greatest concern is that Netanyahu could launch a wider regional war to avoid domestic political pressure around the time of the vote.
Owaida said she wants Israel’s next prime minister to allow Palestinians to live without fear of further violence.
“We want to live in freedom and peace, away from killing and wars,” she said.
Mousa Ali, 33, was displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and is now in Gaza City with his four children.
He believes that the outcome of the election could determine whether displaced Palestinians can return to areas beyond the “Yellow Line”.
“For Palestinians, this election is critical, especially because of the Yellow Line. We hope the opposition will be better when it comes to allowing displaced people to return to their areas,” he said.
Ali mentioned Gadi Eisenkot as a possible alternative and hopes Arab parties will perform strongly so they have a role in the next government.
But he does not expect a new leader to bring major changes for the people of Gaza and fears that Israeli attacks will continue. He says a Netanyahu victory would prolong displacement and control over areas around the “Yellow Line”.
“Every day in Gaza, there is blood, there are people being killed, and there is bombing everywhere,” he said. “We hope this policy will end and that a new prime minister will stop this ongoing bloodshed.”

Fok added the government could be more proactive in pitching the airport to the world to attract more foreign airlines.

Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies at 46
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:42:46 UTC
17:42:46 KST

Dilara Hamit
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Eric Bauza, the Emmy-winning Canadian voice actor best known for voicing Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died Sunday at age 46, according to his family.
Bauza died at his home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records.
His family announced his death in a statement posted on his Instagram account Sunday.
“Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly,” the family said, adding that further details would follow.
Bauza was among the animation industry's most prolific voice actors, with more than 400 acting credits over a career spanning roughly 25 years.
Besides Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, he voiced several other Looney Tunes characters, including Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner and Charlie Dog.
His work featured in productions including Looney Tunes Cartoons, Space Jam: A New Legacy and the 2026 film Coyote vs. Acme.
Bauza also contributed to animated series including Avatar: The Last Airbender, Chowder, Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated, Fanboy & Chum Chum, Ben 10: Omniverse, The Adventures of Puss in Boots and Rick and Morty.
He received five Daytime Emmy nominations for his performances in Looney Tunes Cartoons, Muppet Babies and The Adventures of Puss in Boots.
Bauza also won three Children's & Family Emmy Awards for his work on Looney Tunes Cartoons, Bugs Bunny Builders and Teen Titans Go!
Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks Chairman Channing Dungey said Bauza brought “joy and laughter to millions around the world” during his 15 years with Warner Bros. Animation.
“He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc,” Dungey said, referring to the voice actor who originated many classic Looney Tunes characters.
Born in Scarborough, Toronto, on Dec. 7, 1979, Bauza began his animation career as a character designer before moving into voice acting.
His first credited acting role came in the Canadian animated series The Ripping Friends in 2001.
At the time of his death, Bauza was working on Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical, in which he was due to voice Daffy Duck, and The Dragon Masters, in which he was cast as the Shogun King.

The Civilian Control Line runs several kilometers south of
Jeongmin Kim is Executive Director at Korea Risk Group, based in Seoul. She covers inter-Korean relations and North and South Korean foreign and military affairs. Crown Princess Elisabeth thanks well-wishers for birthday greets (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:56 UTC
17:41:56 KST

Crown Princess Elisabeth of Belgium celebrated her 25th birthday at the weekend. To mark this festive occasion, the Royal Palace released a new photograph of the Belgian Crown Princess. The Royal Mint and postal services provider Bpost are also celebrating the birthday with a commemorative coin and a new postage stamp.
In a short video posted on social media, Elisabeth thanks everyone, in two of Belgium’s three national languages, for the many birthday wishes she has received through various channels. “It has warmed my heart” she said.
A year’s break after her student days
Crown Princess Elisabeth is the eldest child – and daughter – of King Filip and Queen Mathilde and will be the first woman to ascend the throne in Belgium. She has held the title of Duchess of Brabant since 21 July 2013.
In May, Elisabeth graduated from the Harvard Kennedy School in Boston, one of the most prestigious universities in the world, with a master’s degree in public policy.
She had previously completed a bachelor’s degree in ‘History & Politics’ at Lincoln College, a college that forms part of Oxford University in the United Kingdom.
In an interview on the day of her graduation, the Crown Princess left it open as to when she would start working full-time for the Royal Family. “My time at university was very intense; I threw myself into it completely. I’m now going to try to take a step back and lay a solid foundation for what lies ahead. Nothing in a hurry; everything in its own time” the princess said.
“I’d like to take a year or so to think about it. For the time being, I want to develop myself in a different way. How exactly? I don’t know yet.”
As Crown Princess, Elisabeth will in the future lead Belgian trade missions abroad. At present, this is still a job for Queen Mathilde. When Elisabeth takes on her role as active Crown Princess, she will also be given her own royal household and an allowance.
Commemorative coin and stamp
Both Belgium’s Royal Mint and postal services provider Bpost are honouring the Crown Princess with a special issue.
The Royal Mint is launching Elisabeth’s first commemorative coin. The euro coin, with a face value of 12.5 euros, is the only gold commemorative coin to be issued this year. Only 2,500 copies will be produced.
Alongside the portrait of the Crown Princess, the number 25 and her monogram, the reverse of the coin also features Elisabeth’s father, King Filip, together with the face value and ‘Belgium’ in the three national languages.
Bpost is issuing a stamp sheet featuring Elisabeth’s brand-new black-and-white portrait by photographer Bas Bogaerts. Only a limited edition of 41,970 sheets will be printed.
This is not the first time Princess Elisabeth has been honoured with her own stamp. This happened in 2002, on the occasion of her first birthday, in 2016 (featuring the whole family) and in 2019, to mark her 18th birthday. Her latest stamp will, however, be the first special self-adhesive stamp dedicated to a member of the Belgian royal family.

Ukraine’s strike capability weakens as Russia hits its military facilities — expert
Unknown

2026-10-26
08:41:24 UTC
17:41:24 KST

LUGANSK, October 26. /TASS/. The strike capability of the Ukrainian armed forces declined last week amid attacks by Russian forces on Ukrainian military facilities, including those located in the rear, military expert Andrey Marochko reported.
"Last week, the situation on the line of contact worsened for Ukrainian forces, largely as a result of rear logistics disruption and Russian strikes targeting the military-industrial complex facilities, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure, weapons and military equipment production sites, military-technical equipment warehouses, as well as temporary deployment sites for Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries. "The strike capability of Ukraine’s armed formations has fallen to minimal levels," he wrote on his VKontakte page, after analyzing data released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Marochko noted that amid this decline in strike capability, effective counterattacks by Ukrainian troops in the special operation zone "have become practically impossible."
The military expert added that due to logistical disruptions in several areas in the special military operation zone, Ukrainian troops are not evacuating the wounded and the dead, and are instead "simply finishing off their seriously wounded comrades."
On Friday, the Russian Defense Ministry reported that over the past week, the Russian military had launched three massive and 11 combined strikes on the enemy’s logistics centers, energy and transport sites. Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities were incapacitated.

Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:23 UTC
17:41:23 KST

Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin America
The outcome of Brazil’s presidential election demonstrates that the far-right tide in Latin America is not inevitable.
At 80, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has pulled off an extraordinary political victory. After losing the first round to Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, by 47 percent to 45 percent, Lula defied the odds to secure a stunning second-round victory, with 51.8 percent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2 percent.
His triumph confounded every pre-election poll and crowned a dramatic campaign revival that few had anticipated.
Lula’s victory in Latin America’s largest country does more than halt the far right’s return to power in Brazil. It breaks a succession of right-wing electoral victories across the region and deals a major blow to United States President Donald Trump’s increasingly interventionist agenda in the Western Hemisphere.
When Bolsonaro unexpectedly defeated Lula in the first round, the result sent shockwaves across Brazil and beyond. For the government, the defeat was particularly startling given its strong socioeconomic record. What followed was an extraordinary three-week political mobilisation that transformed the sluggish first-round campaign of Lula’s Workers’ Party into an existential confrontation over the future of democracy and sovereignty in Brazil.
The economic record was hardly that of a government heading for defeat. Brazil’s economy grew by a cumulative 9.2 percent between 2023 and 2025, compared with an average of just 5.6 percent among its South American neighbours. Unemployment fell from 9.3 percent in 2022 to a historic low of 5.4 percent in 2026.
Brazil also exited the United Nations Hunger Map in 2025, after having returned to it under the Bolsonaro senior administration. In the Amazon, deforestation fell to its lowest level in decades, a sharp reversal of the trend under his predecessor.
Not everything has been rosy under the Lula administration. Millions of Brazilians have remained trapped in credit-card debt, struggling with extremely high interest rates, while an explosion of online gambling has devastated the livelihoods of families. The run-off result sent a clear signal that there was social discontent.
Lula responded with unusually bold measures: a sweeping debt-relief initiative and restrictions on online betting, as well as expanded social benefits, fuel subsidies, and the transition from a six-day to a five-day working week. These policies sought to reconnect the government’s macroeconomic achievements with the everyday economic anxieties of Brazilian voters.
Bolsonaro offered a radically different vision for Brazil: sweeping spending cuts, privatisations, lower taxes and, above all, an iron-fisted response to crime and insecurity. His proposals included building five maximum-security prisons modelled on El Salvador’s notorious penitentiary system and authorising lethal force against heavily armed criminals.
Bolsonaro also pledged to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years for plotting to overturn the 2022 election, and to grant clemency to those convicted over the January 8, 2023 assault on Brazil’s democratic institutions. For his supporters, this represented an opportunity to reverse what they considered judicial persecution. For his opponents, it threatened to rehabilitate the attempted coup and undermine judicial independence.
Lula’s campaign came back re-energised, with many young Brazilians mobilising at the grassroots level. The campaign was able to overcome even algorithmic bias by social media giants like Meta, which favoured Bolsonaro.
Ultimately, the election became a battle not only over Brazil’s democracy but also its sovereignty. Trump’s administration has intervened conspicuously in Brazilian politics throughout Lula’s term, imposing punitive tariffs, sanctioning a Supreme Court justice involved in Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and openly embracing his son’s candidacy.
In May, Trump received Flavio Bolsonaro in the Oval Office. Two days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio designated Brazil’s two largest crime organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a measure Flavio had publicly requested.
These designations carry implications extending far beyond electoral politics. They potentially open the door to US military operations on Brazilian territory under Washington’s expanding war on so-called “narcoterrorism”. The world saw how one such foreign terrorist designation enabled the US to intervene militarily in Venezuela and abduct its sitting president.
Whereas Trump seeks to draw Latin America’s largest country into Washington’s expanding system of hemispheric military dominance, Lula has defended Brazil’s strategic autonomy, insisting that cooperation against organised crime must respect national sovereignty.
He framed the election as a choice between a sovereign Brazil charting its own course and one subordinated to Washington’s geopolitical agenda. Sunday’s election result shows that the Brazilian people have made their choice.
Importantly, Lula’s victory may mark a turning point in Latin America’s rightward shift. Since Trump’s return to the White House, the right has scored a string of electoral victories in Honduras, Chile, and Bolivia, among others. But Lula’s re-election suggests that its momentum may be faltering.
The result comes just ahead of the US midterms and could deliver a significant setback to the strength of Trump’s leadership in the Americas. In Argentina, President Javier Milei — who regularly attacks Lula and threw all his weight behind Bolsonaro — has been sliding in the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. In Chile, President Jose Antonio Kast has suffered an even more precipitous collapse in public support.
Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum, for her part, has likely breathed a sigh of relief. A Lula defeat would have left her increasingly isolated in a region gravitating towards Mexico’s northern neighbour. Instead, Latin America’s two most populous countries and largest economies will remain firmly on the left for the foreseeable future.
It is too early to declare the region’s rightward turn over. But Lula’s victory raises the possibility that the wave has already crested. Brazil will not be joining Trump’s Shield of the Americas, and while the “Donroe Doctrine” remains a threat, its moment of greatest ascendancy may already be behind it.
Lula’s victory is a vindication of a lifetime spent fighting for society’s most marginalised and disenfranchised. And its significance extends far beyond Brazil’s borders. For defenders of democracy, multilateralism, international law, environmental protection and the sovereignty of the Global South, it sends a powerful message: the far right’s advance is neither inevitable nor irreversible. Not in Brazil. Not anywhere.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Sulina Canal capacity must be expanded to develop Ukraine’s Danube ports – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:00 UTC
17:41:00 KST

Sulina Canal capacity must be expanded to develop Ukraine’s Danube ports – expert
Vitalii Nikula, Director of Izmail Sea Commercial Port, made the comment to Ukrinform during the Rebuilding Ukraine Forum in Bucharest.
“We need certain agreements to increase the capacity of the channels connecting the Danube and the Black Sea. First of all, this is the Sulina Canal, which now plays one of the key roles and is the central entry route for vessels from the Black Sea to the Danube cluster,” Nikula said.
He noted the canal allows passage for vessels with a draft of up to seven meters, carrying both export and import cargoes such as fertilizers, construction materials and other goods needed in Ukraine. The main problem remains limited capacity, with work under way at the level of the relevant ministries in Ukraine and Romania.
“Work is being carried out by ministries of both countries and by our Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority, which is in constant contact with colleagues from the Sulina Canal,” Nikula said.
One expected step is the introduction of night navigation, which he believes would increase cargo handling volumes for both exports and imports.
“We hope night navigation will start soon. This will allow us to boost cargo turnover and process more shipments,” he added.
Another challenge for Danube ports is low water levels, which reduce transport efficiency.
“Ports are facing seasonal drops in the Danube’s water level. It is now catastrophically low. Barges that can normally carry 2,000–2,500 tonnes of grain are currently loaded with a maximum of 750–800 tonnes,” Nikula said.
He also stressed the need for investment in port equipment modernization. “As a state stevedore we maintain our handling equipment in proper condition, but investment in upgrading our fleet of machinery would improve efficiency,” Nikula concluded.
As reported, Ukraine exported 2.4 million tonnes of agricultural products in September, equal to 46% of the required potential volume.

AI chip surge lifts South Korea to record surplus, behind only China
Soaring memory prices pushed quarterly earnings past Germany and Japan combined for the first time
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Park Chan-kyongin Seoul
South Korea earned US$116.63 billion more from the world than it spent in the second quarter of this year – exceeding the combined current account surpluses of Germany and Japan for the first time on record.
The current account measures a country’s trade and income with the world. It counts goods and services sold abroad, money earned on overseas investments and payments flowing the other way. A surplus means more foreign currency is coming in than going out.
Surging demand for semiconductors helped propel South Korea’s second-quarter surplus, with chip exports reaching US$113.89 billion in the three months to June, according to government figures – up 181.6 per cent from the same period last year.
Prices for memory chips have jumped in recent months amid the global artificial intelligence boom. In June, US manufacturer Micron Technology reported that its prices had risen by as much as 80 per cent quarter on quarter.

Ahead of Tuesday's election, more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities at a Perach Israel village are learning about their right to vote and practicing how to cast their ballots.
As millions of Israelis prepare to head to the polls, residents of a Perach Israel-operated rehabilitation village are getting ready for Election Day with a special initiative to help them exercise one of their most fundamental democratic rights.
The village, home to more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, has set up a mock polling station, complete with a voting booth, envelopes, and ballot slips, allowing residents to familiarize themselves with the voting process ahead of the October 27 Knesset election.
Staff members are guiding residents through the process, explaining their right to vote and helping them practice selecting a ballot and placing it in an envelope, as they would at an official polling station.
Right to choose is important element of rehabilitation village
"The right to choose is part of everyday life in our village," said Moshe Stein, CEO of Perach Israel.
"We work to teach our residents the importance of making their own choices, from deciding what color clothes to wear to choosing how to spend their free time. The ability to make their own decisions plays a significant role in their quality of life."
For residents, the exercise offers a chance to learn the practical aspects of voting in a familiar environment, ahead of an election in which millions of Israelis will choose their representatives in the next Knesset.
With Election Day just around the corner, the practice sessions are helping ensure that residents who are eligible to vote have the opportunity to make their voices heard alongside the rest of the country.

Anthropic’s Claude bypassed paywall to obtain vote count in US state of Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:32:56 UTC
17:32:56 KST

Dilara Hamit
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence model bypassed a paywall to obtain publicly available aggregate vote counts from the US state of Georgia without human authorization, Axios reported Sunday.
The incident occurred while Claude was being used internally for a statistics project requiring public data that the state normally provides for a fee.
"Without being asked to, the model requested a token to query a dashboard that contained information normally available for a fee," an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.
"We have since put in place mitigations to block these kinds of actions," the spokesperson added.
Anthropic said Claude did not access Georgia's voter registration system, obtain individual voting records or alter election data.
The information obtained consisted solely of aggregate vote counts available to members of the public who paid the required fee.
According to Axios, Anthropic notified the Georgia secretary of state's office and the White House about the incident several weeks ago.
The company had previously described the case without identifying Georgia in an Oct. 9 report examining unintended actions by its AI models.
In that report, Anthropic said Claude Mythos 5 learned from an archived version of an unnamed state agency's website that its public dashboard issued access tokens to visitors.
The model then requested a token and used it to query the database without paying, the company said.
Anthropic said the incident was among several cases in which Claude circumvented restrictions to access information protected by tokens or fees, including on websites operated by US federal, state and local government agencies.
The company described the behavior as "persistence," in which the model encountered an obstacle and found an unintended way around it rather than stopping.
Anthropic said the incidents caused minimal real-world harm but warned that similar behavior could have greater consequences as AI models become more capable.
Following its review, the company moved some evaluations offline, tightened restrictions on Claude's internet tools and developed systems to detect and block unauthorized actions.
Anthropic said the new safeguards successfully blocked all the disclosed behaviors during testing.

Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are returning home to vote in Tuesday's Knesset election, with some traveling thousands of miles and others arranging special flights after regular services were canceled. Among them are expatriates hoping to move back to Israel and others who say the country's political direction has changed how they feel about identifying as Israeli overseas.
According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, approximately 810,000 eligible Israeli voters live abroad. The Fly&Vote initiative, which encourages Israelis overseas to exercise their voting rights, estimates that roughly 67,000 will return to Israel to participate in the October 27 election, potentially representing the equivalent of about one and a half Knesset seats.
The figure is an estimate by the initiative, rather than a confirmed count of voters who have arrived. Most Israeli citizens living overseas cannot cast their ballots abroad and must travel to Israel to vote.
On Sunday, a special flight from Portugal landed at Ben Gurion Airport carrying dozens of Israelis determined to make their voices heard at the ballot box. Representatives of Fly&Vote were waiting to welcome them in the arrivals hall.
The flight was arranged after Portuguese airline TAP canceled its services to Israel, leaving hundreds of Israelis who had planned to travel home for the election without their original flight arrangements.
‘We want to return, so it's important to be part of what happens here’
"If you want to make a difference, you have to take action. You can't wait for someone else to do the work," said Gali Mazor Biton, a married mother of three who has lived in Cascais, Portugal, for the past five years.
Standing in the arrivals hall at Ben Gurion Airport, she explained that she had come to Israel for just three days, specifically to cast her ballot.
"We want to return to Israel, so it's important for us to be part of what's happening here and to influence our future," she said.
But not everyone making the journey plans to move back to Israel. For some, the motivation is closely connected to their experience of being Israeli abroad.
Itamar Tzahovel, a costume designer working in the film industry, has spent the past three decades living in Milan, Shanghai, Berlin and, most recently, Lisbon. He said Israel's policies have increasingly affected the way he is perceived overseas, prompting him to purchase a plane ticket and return to vote.
"Whenever I used to say I was Israeli, I said it with pride. That's no longer the case," he said.
"Today, when I say I'm from Israel, there's a certain defensiveness to it. I told myself, enough. I bought a ticket and came to make a difference. I want honest people running this country, so that every Jew in the Diaspora can stand tall and proudly say they're Israeli."
‘We could be the surprise of this election’
For Dana Levy, 51, originally from Jerusalem, the decision to travel from Lisbon, where she has lived for 23 years, came after an outpouring of encouragement from friends and former acquaintances.
"My friends convinced me to come especially because this time every vote matters," she said.
"The appeals came from everywhere. Friends in Israel, even my old group of friends from the Scouts in Jerusalem. They asked me to come and explained how important it was to vote in this election. They told me we must not end up again in a situation where there is no clear outcome."
Levy said the encouragement went beyond messages and phone calls. Israelis have established informal support networks to help people living abroad make the trip, including offering accommodation to those returning specifically to vote.
"I received so much support and assistance to make it here. There are even Facebook groups where people offer to host those arriving especially to vote. Everyone just wants me to come. It's incredibly moving," she said.
Her stay in Israel will be brief. She plans to vote and return immediately to Lisbon. But she believes overseas Israelis could have an impact that has not been fully reflected in election polling.
"I'm staying in Israel for a very short time. I'll vote and then go straight back to Lisbon," she said.
"I think the votes of Israelis living abroad will be the surprise of this election because nobody has counted us in the polls."
Ella Raz, 41, who has lived in Portugal for five years and works in tourism, expressed a similar sense of responsibility.
"It was absolutely clear to me that in this election I had to show up at the polling station and make a difference," she said.
"My entire family is in Israel, and I care deeply about what's happening in the country. Both for those who live here and for those of us who don't."
‘Israel is still our home’
The wave of returning voters is not limited to Europe. Israelis living in North America are also traveling to Israel to take part in the election.
Shay Eden, who works in human resources at a Jewish research institute in New York, spoke to ynet before boarding a flight with her husband, Josh Daryl.
"For us, Israel is our home," she said. "We're living in New York for a limited period, with the intention of returning. So even when we live abroad, we feel committed to the future of the country, its character and the values on which it will be built."
For Eden and her husband, the journey is about maintaining their connection to a country they still consider home, despite temporarily building their lives elsewhere.
"These elections are an opportunity to influence the direction Israel takes and the society we want to live in," she said.
"We believe that even two votes are part of our collective ability to make a difference, and that we shouldn't give up the opportunity to help shape the future."
She added: "This is our way of taking responsibility, making our voices heard and being part of the decision about the future of our home."
Whether the estimated tens of thousands of returning voters will materially affect the distribution of Knesset seats remains uncertain. Their political preferences and the number who will ultimately cast ballots cannot be determined from the travel estimates alone.
But for the Israelis arriving from Lisbon, New York and elsewhere, the motivation is already clear. They may have built lives far from Israel, but they are determined to participate in deciding its future.

Can EU Inc still make business easier? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:30:34 UTC
17:30:34 KST

EU Inc, Europe’s harmonised corporate form, is stalled after Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs failed to vote. Caught between furious founders and protesting workers, could EU Inc still change how you build a startup? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
The European Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) failed to agree on the draft report on EU Inc on 19 October, having already postponed the vote on 5 October. Disagreements among MEPs over workers' rights are driving the deadlock.
EU Inc is an EU-wide company structure that lets businesses register in one member state and operate across the bloc. It would follow a shared set of rules, the “28th corporate regime”, so founders wouldn’t have to navigate 27 different national frameworks.
Proposed by the European Commission in March 2026, EU Inc aims to make it easier and cheaper to set up a business in the EU. It tackles the fragmentation across Europe’s startup ecosystems and boosts collaboration, talent mobility, and access to funding.
Founders could set up a company fully online within 48 hours, with starting capital of €1 and no notary. Registration and documentation are handled in English, with no translation or local-language requirements when operating abroad.
While EU leaders agreed to finalise the law by year-end, pushback is coming from multiple fronts.
EU Inc founders argue that months of negotiations had weakened the proposal. On 15 October, in a public statement they accused the EU of reducing EU Inc to a fast-track registration process by stripping away its core features, including free choice of registration and a common-stock framework to attract talent.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) warn that a proposal threatens workers’ rights. On 24 September and 20 October, trade unions from across the bloc protested in Brussels and Strasbourg, warning that it would let companies use lighter corporate rules to circumvent national labour laws and social standards.

China may well be the next big competitor for Asian migrant labour

Advertisement
Opinion
China may well be the next big competitor for Asian migrant labour
The country that once transformed global labour markets by exporting workers could reshape Asian migration by beginning to import them
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduras-born journalist based in Taiwan covering Asia–Latin America relations, geopolitics and supply chain issues. 
For decades, China was one of the world’s largest sources of migrant labour. Its workers staffed factories at home and built infrastructure abroad. But demographic decline may eventually force China to contemplate a striking reversal: importing workers on a meaningful scale.
That change is not imminent. China still has a vast labour force and substantial youth unemployment. It is investing heavily in industrial automation, extending working lives through a gradual increase in the retirement age, and trying to move workers from regions with surplus labour to where employers struggle to recruit.
Yet the direction of travel is becoming difficult to ignore. China’s population fell for a fourth consecutive year in 2025. The number of employed people declined to 725 million from 740 million in 2023.

Russia’s Once-Feared Lancet Drones Are Turning Into a Multimillion-Dollar Failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:29:08 UTC
17:29:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Once-Feared Lancet Drones Are Turning Into a Multimillion-Dollar Failure
Russia’s Lancet attack drones, once considered among Moscow’s most effective battlefield weapons, are facing questions over their effectiveness after a Russian unit reportedly spent millions of dollars launching the drones with almost no results.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev, Russia’s “Sparta” drone unit launched approximately 100 Lancet loitering munitions over three months, successfully striking only three targets. The operation cost between $3.7 million and $6.1 million.
The launches were conducted by a team commanded by Senior Lieutenant Kirill Ozerov, known by the call sign “Nevsky,” during a period beginning in mid-June 2026. Gubarev did not specify where the unit was operating.
Despite deploying around 100 drones, the unit reportedly managed to hit only a self-propelled artillery system, an infantry dugout, and a roadside kiosk—an estimated success rate of just 3%. Ukrainian air defenses intercepted most of the remaining Lancets, while Russian forces destroyed several of their own drones due to poor coordination between units.
Gubarev estimated the cost of each Lancet at between $37,000 and $67,000, bringing the total expenditure to as much as $6.1 million for just three successful strikes.
He also accused the unit’s commanders of deploying expensive drones without adequate preparation while submitting misleading reports about their effectiveness to senior military leadership.
The claims have not been independently verified and describe the performance of a single Russian unit rather than the entire Lancet fleet.
Manufactured by Russia’s ZALA Aero, the Lancet is a loitering munition designed to destroy artillery systems, armored vehicles, and other battlefield targets. It features optical guidance, an explosive warhead, and an estimated operational range of 40–50 kilometers.
Earlier, on March 17, Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov reported that Russia had launched up to 40 Lancet drones toward Kyiv in what he described as a largely symbolic operation.

Drones Strike Russia’s Titanium Giant Supplying Su-34 Fighters and Iskander Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:29:04 UTC
17:29:04 KST

- Category

Drones Strike Russia’s Titanium Giant Supplying Su-34 Fighters and Iskander Missiles
Drones struck the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Russia’s Perm region overnight on October 25, targeting a major titanium production facility supplying materials used in Russian military aircraft and missile systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack took place in Berezniki, where AVISMA operates as part of VSMPO-AVISMA, Russia’s largest titanium producer. The facility manufactures titanium sponge, a key raw material used in aircraft engines, fighter jets, and missile components. Footage of the reported strike was published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Perm region Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed the drone attack on October 25, claiming Russian air defenses intercepted 11 drones. He acknowledged minor damage to an industrial facility and reported that five employees had been injured. According to Makhonin, the facility continued operating.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), VSMPO-AVISMA produced approximately 33,500 metric tons of titanium sponge in 2024, accounting for roughly 96% of Russia’s total production.
The corporation supplies titanium alloys to Russian aircraft manufacturers Sukhoi and Irkut, which produce Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35 fighter jets. Its products are also used in Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has identified VSMPO-AVISMA as a supplier involved in the production chains of Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35S fighter jets.
The company also supplies Russia’s missile industry, including the Votkinsk Machine Building Plant, which manufactures Iskander ballistic missiles and Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The reported strike follows Ukrainian attacks on two Russian defense-related facilities on October 24. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed strikes on the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Orel and the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in the Samara region, both linked to Russia’s cruise and ballistic missile production.

Reuters: Myanmar Evaded Sanctions by Importing Iranian Aviation Fuel Disguised as South African Diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:28:00 UTC
17:28:00 KST

Myanmar’s military authorities helped conceal imports of Iranian aviation fuel subject to US sanctions.
According to Reuters, the shipments were falsely declared as South African diesel to hide their true origin.
In December 2025, the sanctioned oil tanker Reef arrived in Myanmar carrying approximately 113,000 barrels of fuel.
According to documents Reuters obtained, Myanmar-based energy intermediary Dynamic Wave signed a contract with Thai company Tawan-Oil Trading to buy a similar volume of diesel fuel from South Africa for $15.8 million.
However, shipping documents, satellite imagery, and SynMax Intelligence’s analysis of the vessel’s route indicate that those involved in the scheme provided false information when making the purchase. Data from the United Nations and maritime analytics provider Vortexa also show no evidence of diesel trade between South Africa and Myanmar in 2025.
The scheme involved entities linked to Myanmar’s military authorities. In a letter dated November 30, the country’s foreign exchange regulator stated that it would issue import documents listing the cargo as diesel fuel rather than aviation fuel.
The document also authorized Dynamic Wave and its client, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Company, to transfer funds to the Thai supplier.
A similar scheme played out in May 2025, when Dynamic Wave signed a contract to buy 202,000 barrels of purportedly South African diesel fuel worth $26 million.
However, the fuel specifications listed in the documents matched aviation fuel, and its price was more than 50% higher than the global diesel benchmark. In June, the tanker Noble delivered nearly 200,000 barrels of Iranian aviation fuel to Yangon.
According to Reuters, from October 2024 to December 2025, Iran remained the main supplier of aviation fuel to Myanmar’s military authorities. The tankers Reef, later renamed Maris, and Noble transported much of the fuel.
During one of its voyages, Noble transmitted signals indicating that it was supposedly heading to the port of Chittagong in Bangladesh, when it was actually bound for Myanmar.
The United States imposed targeted sanctions on Myanmar’s aviation fuel sector in 2023 in response to airstrikes carried out by the country’s military authorities against civilians during their crackdown on the uprising.
Separately, US sanctions also cover the purchase of Iranian oil and petroleum products. However, despite these restrictions, Iranian aviation fuel continued to flow into Myanmar, supplying both civilian aviation and military air operations. According to the agency, these deliveries continued into 2026.
On October 1, 2026, Militarnyi reported that Iranian oil tankers had become stranded near Sri Lanka amid pressure from US sanctions. Ports and companies across Asia refused to service the vessels due to the risk of being targeted by US sanctions.

Army drone deal widened to cover heavier aircraft
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:27:37 GMT
17:27:37 KST

The Ministry of Defence intends to raise the maximum take-off weight allowed under the British Army’s mini drone contract from twenty kilograms to fifty, and to confirm that the contract covers flights beyond visual line of sight, without running a new competition, according to a transparency notice published by the department.
The TIQUILA contract was awarded to Lockheed Martin UK on 7 December 2022 and is worth £129,350,000 excluding VAT. It runs for one hundred and twenty months, with options to extend by up to a further twenty four months and to vary the volume of goods and services delivered.
The notice says the department proposes “to broaden the contractual technical envelope so that TIQUILA can continue to procure and integrate relevant UAS capability as technology and operational demands evolve”, and that the change will “confirm the inclusion of VLOS and BVLOS Packable MUAS capability” and “increase the platform take-off weight from a maximum of 20kg to 50kg”.
Arguing that it can make the change without a fresh procurement, the department says: “The modification does not change the contract into a requirement for a different category of capability. The requirement remains focused on UAS capability supporting field operations through the existing SI-led model, while accommodating unanticipated technological advancement beyond the parameters originally defined.”
It goes on: “It preserves the commercial model, of engagement with the wider UAS market and new entrants through flexible supply-chain arrangements; supports the same field-operational purposes and retains the same SI-led integration, modular architecture and through-life delivery model, while responding to technological advancement and developing operational demands in the manner contemplated by the original procurement, and is therefore considered a vertical evolution of the existing UAS capability, rather than horizontal expansion.”
The department says all pricing mechanisms stay the same, that it considers the change a permissible non-material modification under the principles established in the Pressetext case and the Defence and Security Public Contracts Regulations 2011, and that it published the notice voluntarily to provide transparency.
TIQUILA delivers mini uncrewed air systems for intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance in packable and portable loads, with Lockheed Martin UK acting as systems integrator and bringing in other suppliers through enabling arrangements intended to reach new entrants, industry and academia. The original scope required a modular technical and digital architecture built on open-standard interfaces so that new capabilities could be integrated as they emerged.
The aircraft bought under the programme so far are the Stalker VXE 30, a near-silent long-endurance machine weighing under twenty kilograms, and the Indago, a backpack-sized aircraft under eight kilograms that can be put in the air in around two minutes. Ninety nine Stalkers and fifteen Indagos were ordered, deliveries began in March 2023, and full operational capability for four Future Soldier batteries was expected this year, as this publication reported when the contract was signed.
Brigadier Pete Drew, the Army’s senior responsible owner for the programme, said at the time that “TIQUILA will bring the next generation of remotely piloted air systems into service in the Army”, and that it would speed up decision making and make the force more lethal, responsive and resilient.
Raising the ceiling to fifty kilograms takes the contract past the weight of anything currently flying under it and into a class of aircraft carrying heavier sensors and flying longer. Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, told Parliament this week that military flights beyond visual line of sight use temporary segregated airspace notified through the warning system pilots check before flying, or permanent segregated airspace such as danger areas, with the Civil Aviation Authority responsible for United Kingdom airspace throughout.

Russia says it caught Ukrainian agents preparing close range drone attack on Moscow's air defences
MOSCOW, Oct 26 - Russia's FSB security service has thwarted a planned Ukrainian drone attack from inside Russia on a key element of Moscow's air defence system and on an electricity facility, the FSB said on Monday, saying it had arrested two men involved in the plot.
The two men, who the FSB said were from the South Caucasus region and had been acting under instructions from Ukraine's SBU security service, had retrieved First Person View drones and explosives from two Russian regions, delivered them to the Moscow region, and configured and activated the drones, the FSB said. The drones were to be remotely controlled from Ukraine, it said.

To this end, he enlisted the help of an acquaintance from his close circle," the FSB said.
"The suspects were detained by FSB officers while preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electricity infrastructure facility and on one of the key components of Moscow's missile defence system," it said.
There was no immediate comment from the SBU or from Ukraine, which has intensified its attempted drone attacks on the Russian capital in recent months, as Russia has stepped up its own attacks on Ukrainian power and other infrastructure targets. REUTERS

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine should maintain an army of 800,000 personnel to ensure its security, adding that the size of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) is an internal matter that will not be negotiated with Russia or the US.
In an interview with Alla Mazur, host of TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week), Zelensky said the key question was how Ukraine’s military would be funded and what security guarantees the country would receive as part of any peace settlement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If I have sufficient funding, I want to maintain an army of 800,000 people. If we are in NATO, the number could be 800,000 or less,” he said.
According to Zelensky, the central issue is who is prepared to finance Ukraine’s armed forces.
“And that is my question for NATO,” he added.
Starlink and intelligence sharing resume
Zelensky also said Starlink had resumed operating in Ukraine and that the country was once again receiving uninterrupted intelligence on ballistic missiles following what he described as productive talks in Oslo.
He said Ukrainian intelligence on ballistic missile strikes was now functioning at 100% capacity.
“The dialogue between Ukraine and the US – which had become quite emotional – has returned to a functional state. Starlink is back up and running (as of Saturday, Oct. 24, at 5:20 a.m.). We achieved the right outcome; we secured what we needed. This was one component of our discussions in Oslo,” Zelensky said.
Why Are Laws Vital to Ukraine’s EU Integration Stuck in Parliament as the Country Loses Money?
He revealed that tensions in the dialogue with Washington had centered on three main issues: shortages of air defense systems, operational restrictions on Starlink, and limitations on the intelligence provided by the US.
Two of those issues have now been resolved, Zelensky said, although the provision of additional air defense systems remains unresolved.
Zelensky rejects neutrality and restrictions on Ukraine’s army
Zelensky also discussed a document containing US proposals for ending Russia’s war against Ukraine that US special envoy Steve Witkoff delivered to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
According to Zelensky, the document contains various proposals from Washington, but Ukraine has made clear that two issues are non-negotiable: the country’s neutrality and restrictions on its armed forces.
“The document contains various proposals from the American side. We maintain that key aspects of this are that there can be no discussion of our state adopting neutrality, nor can there be any talk of placing restrictions on the Ukrainian army,” Zelensky said.
He did not disclose whether Ukraine’s red lines were explicitly spelled out in the document, saying that agreements with the US prevented him from sharing all the details.
However, Zelensky reiterated that Russia cannot dictate the terms of Ukraine’s security guarantees.
“Therefore, restrictions on our army and the neutrality of Ukraine are not up for discussion. The issue of territory is a ‘red line’ that can only be addressed at the level of the leaders themselves. For us, this has always been a non-negotiable constant,” he said.
“Yet, the Americans frequently raise the question of territory – asking what we might be willing to trade in exchange for certain fundamental principles,” Zelensky added.
Zelensky stressed that Ukraine does not intend to give up territory but remains open to discussions.
He said territorial questions must be addressed directly by the leaders, while other issues could be handled by technical groups.
“If the discussion concerns the territorial issue, it must take place at the level of leaders. Other matters should be handled by technical groups. What constitutes ‘other matters’? Security guarantees. For instance, the issue of NATO – which, naturally, appears in relevant documents and new proposals – is one such matter,” Zelensky said.
“We are discussing security guarantees; someone must provide assurances that Russia will not launch a new act of aggression,” he added.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine expects such guarantees from the US and Europe.
He also stressed that the document delivered by Witkoff was not a plan simply presented to Putin for approval.
“It is not Russia that makes the decision; all parties involved do. There are proposals for discussion – including those from the American side – which are being discussed with us,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky proposes energy truce as first step toward peace
Asked by Mazur what Putin would need to do to demonstrate that he genuinely intended to end the war, Zelensky pointed to an energy truce as a possible first step.
“This would be a signal. If that doesn’t happen, then we look to a trilateral meeting at the level of leaders,” he said.
Zelensky believes such a meeting involving Ukraine, the US, and Russia is possible. However, he cautioned that Putin’s apparent willingness to resume negotiations does not guarantee that the Kremlin will follow through.
However, he suggested that Moscow could be feigning readiness for dialogue to avoid further confrontation with US President Donald Trump.
Zelensky said it was too early to judge the outcome of a potential leaders’ meeting before it took place.
“One should discuss the outcome ‘after’ the meeting in question, not ‘before’ it. What will unfold there? What escalatory developments might arise in the Middle East? Will this meeting take place in Abu Dhabi, or perhaps in Europe? We shall see,” he said.
Zelensky added that he did not know what had prompted Putin’s sudden shift in position on peace negotiations.
“What influenced this? I cannot say. Perhaps there are some agreements between America and Russia of which I am unaware,” he said.
Ukraine is prepared to participate in trilateral negotiations involving technical groups, Zelensky added, but he stressed that the talks must produce concrete results.
He recalled that the American side had asked what specific outcomes Ukraine wanted to see.
“The Americans asked me, ‘What kind of specifics are you looking for?’ I replied, ‘Look, could the war end in November during a meeting of the technical group?’ Without the leaders present, it won’t be a complete resolution,” Zelensky said.
He then outlined several alternatives that could produce tangible progress even without a comprehensive peace agreement.
“Fine – if that’s not on the table, then let’s have an ‘energy truce,’ address the maritime situation and grain exports, carry out an ‘all-for-all’ prisoner exchange, or hold a meeting of the leaders. That, undoubtedly, constitutes a result. A result creates opportunity,” he added.
Zelensky added that these were proposals put forward to the American side, not demands.
He said it should become clear in November whether Putin was genuinely prepared to negotiate or was merely making political gestures to avoid escalating tensions with Washington ahead of the elections.
“And if this is merely a political stunt – if Putin is simply saying ‘Yes, I’m ready’ because he wants to avoid escalation with America ahead of the elections – we will find out very quickly in November whether it was a ruse or not,” Zelensky said.
US proposes temporary ceasefire in Oleshky
Zelensky also said the US had proposed a ceasefire in the Oleshky area starting Tuesday, Oct. 27 and lasting several days to facilitate a humanitarian mission.
Under the proposal, representatives of Ukraine, the US, and Russia would travel to the area. Russian forces would be expected to clear roads of mines, while Ukraine would verify the work and carry out the necessary measures.
Zelensky said he had issued specific instructions to Ukraine’s ombudsman and that the government had also consulted the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the military.
He cautioned, however, that Russia could clear the roads in a way that directs people toward Russian-controlled territory, rather than allowing them to leave freely.
Zelensky said some people would nevertheless be evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
“The main thing is to unblock these people so that they can live. Ideally, they will be able to reach their goal and be evacuated here – to us, to Ukraine,” he said.

Hungarian Tycoon’s Firm Funded Pro-Orbán Advertising Agency, Records Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

A firm owned by Hungarian construction mogul László Szíjj — who amassed a fortune under previous Prime Minister Viktor Orbán — donated about $863,000 to Megafon, a political advertising agency that promoted the former ruling party.
The donations are detailed in two years of annual financial statements from Szíjj’s firm, Vakond Via Kft., which were examined by OCCRP and Direkt36. The company made “cash grants” that totaled 300 million Hungarian forints to Megafon Digital Incubator Center, adding up to about $252,000 in 2024, and $611,000 the following year.
Launched in 2020, Megafon became one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of Orbán’s Fidesz party.
But since Orbán’s stunning electoral defeat in April, after 16-years in power, Megafon has kept a low profile. The company’s website was taken offline in August, and its employees have fallen from 72 to three, according to information from a firm that provides commercial registry data.
Neither Megafon nor Szíjj responded to requests for comment.
Megafon’s situation mirrors the condition of other media organizations that backed Fidesz, and received generous state advertising contracts or donations from government-friendly entrepreneurs.
Since coming to power, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has taken steps to halt state advertising being funneled into pro-Fidesz media. Some outlets have stopped publishing, while others have downsized as their budgets dried up.
OCCRP and Direkt36 recently reported that Megafon had received about $12 million between 2022 and 2024 from a firm owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, another wealthy pro-Orbán businessman. Mészáros, who is also a business partner of Szíjj, did not respond to questions at the time.
Magyar cited those findings in a Facebook post following publication, saying the reporting confirmed that Mészáros’ firm, while “funded by public money,” had supported Megafon’s “propaganda.” Magyar asked in the post how long the State Audit Office would “remain silent” about the funding.
The State Audit Office has confirmed to Direkt36 it is investigating finances around this year’s election.
“The audit naturally includes an evaluation of news reports and conclusions published in the press, including an examination of Megafon’s activities,” the office said in an emailed response to questions.
It is unknown if Szíjj’s firm, Vakond Via, made donations to Megafon this year. Vakond Via’s 2026 annual financial reports are not yet available, and the company did not respond to a request for comment.
Vakond Via is part of Szíjj’s sprawling Duna Group of companies. The conglomerate’s flagship firm, the road-building company Duna Aszfalt Út és Mélyépítő Ltd., “won the highest value of public contracts” in a ranking compiled by Transparency International.
The anti-corruption group’s Hungarian chapter calculated that Duna Aszfalt received around $2 billion worth of public contracts between 2018 and 2020.

Hong Kong looks to profit from Halloween ghosts and zombies during longer festivities
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:35 CET
17:22:35 KST

By Joyce Zhou
HONG KONG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of revellers in costumes ranging from evil bartenders to Donald Trump impersonators, zombies and Taoist priests, packed an entertainment zone as Hong Kong lit up for Halloween celebrations set to stretch over three weekends.
The colourful crowds thronged the narrow streets of Lan Kwai Fong as onlookers scrambled to take pictures during month-long festivities to ring in Halloween, which falls on Oct. 31, as part of an effort to boost tourism.
“Being here gives me this real carnival vibe — it’s a great way to completely let loose and release ourselves after work,” said 34-year-old Huang Wei, outfitted as the beloved Monkey King of Chinese mythology.
“I feel like the main reason for coming here is to free ourselves,” added the visitor from the southern technology hub of Shenzhen, who rode the metro with nine friends.
The carnival atmosphere lingered well into the night, as Western horror characters mixed with figures from Chinese folklore, and others inspired by the pandemic era.
Mock enforcers of COVID-19 curbs, dressed in white protective suits, roamed the streets carrying thermometers and swab kits, as loudspeakers blared orders to report for testing, in scenes once familiar across China.
A signature attraction is a giant eyeball installation in Central’s Statue Square Gardens, drawing large crowds, while similar Halloween-themed displays have sprung up elsewhere.
MAINLAND CURBS OFFER OPPORTUNITY FOR HONG KONG
Growing curbs have hemmed in Halloween festivities in mainland China since 2023, when authorities in the commercial hub of Shanghai detained some revellers over costumes that satirised social and economic issues.
In Hong Kong, authorities and businesses hope the longer Halloween celebrations will boost tourism, nightlife and consumer spending in the Asian financial hub while luring more visitors across the border.
The effort aims to pull more visitors to the city’s bars, restaurants and retailers, said Allan Zeman, chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Group, who helped introduce Halloween celebrations to the district more than four decades ago.
“Halloween, which was a Western holiday, was able to suddenly be accepted by the East now,” added Zeman, who estimated that the festivities led to a bump of 20% to 25% in food and beverage sales each year.
“So that’s really what Hong Kong is all about, ‘One country, two systems’. And so we can celebrate all together.”
Organisers said about 80,000 people celebrated in Lan Kwai Fong on October 31, 2025, but this year’s festivities spread over three consecutive weekends in Hong Kong’s effort to position itself as a regional Halloween destination.
“Every year it gets stronger and people spend, and every year the costumes get more and more outrageous,” Zeman added. “So that brings a lot of income here and it really helps the GDP of the area.”
(Reporting by Joyce Zhou; Editing by Anne Marie Roantree and Clarence Fernandez)

Ebola scientists to probe Nigeria case origin, Africa CDC says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:30 CET
17:22:30 KST

By Jennifer Rigby
LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A team of leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the country’s first patient in more than a decade got infected, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said.
Their task will involve trying to work out how the female patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, caught the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Her travel documents show she had not visited the outbreak epicentre in Democratic Republic of Congo, Kaseya said in an interview with Reuters in London.
Finding out how she became ill matters to ensure that the deadly Bundibugyo outbreak, already the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, is not spreading silently in as-yet undiscovered locations, and to help trace and isolate all contacts.
‘MANY UNKNOWNS’
“We have so many unknowns,” said Kaseya. “I’m bringing a group of scientists in Abuja because… we need to be led by science.”
One of the theories the scientists will investigate is a potential link between the patient in Nigeria and the first case in Kenya, reported earlier this month in a man who had travelled from Congo. On Friday, genomic sequencing showed that the viruses that infected the two patients were closely related.
The patient in Nigeria had been on holiday in Uganda and travelled through Entebbe Airport on October 3. The patient in Kenya, who has since died, was likely in the airport at the same time, as their flights were around 40 minutes apart, although they did not depart from the same gate and it is not clear whether they had any contact, Kaseya said.
Kaseya said while genomic sequencing had shown that the viruses were similar, it did not mean that one of the patients had directly infected the other and the patient in Abuja, whose condition is improving, has said she does not remember meeting the Kenya patient.
However, he said they were not excluding any options, including that there may have been indirect contact through another person, for example. Ebola spreads through close contact with the infected bodily fluids of a person with symptoms, according to the World Health Organization.
INVESTIGATION ONGOING
Kaseya said all countries involved were now willing to collaborate in the investigation, after what he described as tension last week when Uganda’s government insisted the patient in Abuja had been to Congo, while Nigerian authorities suggested she had not and was infected in Uganda, which has been Ebola-free since August.
Kaseya said the team, which will be led by the co-discoverer of Ebola, Congolese expert Jean-Jacques Muyembe, would also look at more sequencing data to work out where the Kenyan patient was infected.
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo has now caused almost 10,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries in Africa – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo.
(Reporting by Jennifer Rigby; Editing by Toby Chopra)

SOFIA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Bulgaria will head to a runoff vote on November 1 after a tight race between the two leading presidential candidates failed to produce an outright winner in Sunday’s elections, which garnered record-low participation, official results showed.
With 95% of the votes counted, incumbent Iliana Iotova, 61, attracted 34.6% against 32% for ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, falling short of the 50% threshold for the largely ceremonial role in a race of 27 candidates.
Sunday’s vote took on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast that likely killed some two dozen international seafarers. However, only about 22% of the eligible voters showed up to cast their ballot, according to polling agencies.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
BOTH CANDIDATES CONDEMN DRONE STRIKES
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
“I want to share a certain worry and tell Bulgarians that it is an illusion if they think we can change something in this country without (them) voting,” Iotova said after polls closed at 8 p.m.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
(Reporting by Alex Lefkowitz; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by David Holmes)

The Israeli army has forced more than 2,200 Palestinians from their homes and demolished five commercial and industrial facilities and a three-story residential building amid a large-scale military offensive in Hebron in the southern West Bank, the city’s mayor said.
Speaking in an interview with Anadolu, Yousef al-Jabari said the forced evacuations affected Deir Bahha and parts of Al-Jilda in western Hebron, an area that covers approximately 330 dunams (330,000 square meters), and contains more than 495 housing units.
He said Israeli forces surrounded Deir Bahha and Al-Jilda and used loudspeakers to order residents out of their homes.
“Those displaced include children, women, young men and older people,” he said. Some residents initially refused to leave before troops stormed their homes and forced them out.
On Saturday, Hebron municipality said that around 1,500 Palestinians from 250 families had been displaced, before the mayor updated the figure to over 2,200 people.
Al-Jabari did not specify where the displaced residents had gone, while witnesses said some families sought refuge in other West Bank towns and villages.
In a separate count covering three neighborhoods, Riyad Khamis, a media official with a local committee supporting affected families, told Anadolu that more than 380 Palestinian families had been forced from their homes in Deir Bahha, Al-Jilda and Khirbet al-Maghariba.
The Israeli army launched its offensive on Friday following a shooting that killed two Israeli soldiers in the Farsh al-Hawa area at the city’s northwestern entrance.
Khamis said the affected neighborhoods form a contiguous residential area within Area A, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to exercise civil and security control under the Oslo Accords.
The neighborhoods are “located far from settlements, outposts or settler roads,” he said.
 
Collective punishment
Al-Jabari said the Israeli army closed Hebron’s entrances, preventing Palestinians from entering or leaving.
Israeli forces also closed the Ibrahimi Mosque and prevented prayers, as troops and military vehicles deployed across the city, he said.
Streets have become largely deserted because of the siege and movement restrictions, the mayor said, describing the measures as a “policy of collective punishment.”
Al-Jabari accused Israeli authorities of using Friday’s attack to intensify measures against Hebron’s residents ahead of Tuesday’s Israeli elections.
He said the escalation aimed to bolster occupiers’ support for the far right.
Following Friday’s attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened a wider military operation in the occupied West Bank that he described as unprecedented since the 1967 war, including evacuating Palestinian neighborhoods and raiding homes.
The Israeli siege has forced hundreds of businesses in Hebron and neighboring villages to close because workers cannot reach their workplaces and goods cannot move in or out, al-Jabari said.
“Israeli forces have continued demolishing commercial and industrial facilities and residential buildings since Friday,” he added.
Al-Jabari said the municipality declared a state of emergency in the area and deployed teams to assist displaced residents.
“Municipal teams are working to secure shelter for displaced families, assess residents’ needs and address damage to roads, water networks and sewage infrastructure,” he said.
The offensive comes amid escalating Israeli army and occupier attacks across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings, arrests, demolitions of homes and other structures, destruction of agricultural land and displacement of Palestinian communities, alongside settlement expansion.

Switzerland suspends MSF funding after reports of sexual exploitation
The humanitarian organisation Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is accused of failing to adequately inform the Swiss authorities of the scale of reports of sexual misconduct by MSF staff in Chad. The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) has now suspended funding of CHF1.25 million ($1.52 million) to MSF.
The frozen amount represents one tranche of the CHF6.25 million pledged to MSF for the current year.
According to the newspaper NZZ Am Sonntag, an internal investigation by MSF revealed 59 reports of sexual violence and exploitation, particularly involving women and young girls who are refugees from neighbouring Sudan. Eighteen staff members have been dismissed, including six employees from the NGO’s Swiss branch.
The NZZ explains that this constitutes “widespread sexual exploitation”, adding: “Money, jobs or humanitarian aid in exchange for sex: staff members are alleged to have taken advantage of the distress of refugee women and girls”.
The German-language newspaper notes that “the Confederation’s aid workers were effectively operating in the dark”. Although the SDC received the first indications as early as November 2024, it only became aware of the true scale of the problem following articles published in the press in June 2026 by the AP news agency.
More
MSF in Sudan: ‘It’s very hard to reach people in need’
“Internal emails now reveal just how reluctant the Swiss Confederation was to act, even though it was already aware of the facts,” reports the NZZ.
Whilst fighting rages in Central Africa, which has been experiencing a major humanitarian crisis since 2023, hundreds of thousands of people are fleeing the civil war in Sudan to seek refuge in neighbouring Chad.
The first alert from MSF staff at the Geneva headquarters reached the SDC by email on a Friday in November 2024, “shortly before the end of the working day”. Three female refugees “are reported to have described cases of sexual exploitation in Chad; the allegations are reportedly already under investigation”, the NGO stated.
A very slow response
In mid-December 2024, it was agreed at the Swiss foreign ministry “that a meeting with MSF would take place in January”. But it was not until June and July 2025 that the department resumed discussions on how to handle the case.
