Myanmar rebels destroy Chinese-made armored vehicles with FPV drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:22:57 UTC
16:22:57 KST

- A Myanmar resistance group destroyed several Chinese-made ZSL-92 armored vehicles of the Myanmar Army using FPV drones, analyst Jesus Roman reported.
- The strikes were attributed to Monywa Scout, a local armed group, but the exact number, date and location of the losses were not disclosed.
Fighters from a local armed group in Myanmar have destroyed several Chinese-made ZSL-92 infantry fighting vehicles belonging to the Myanmar Army using first-person-view (FPV) drones, open-source analyst Jesus Roman reported on Oct. 24, attributing the strikes to Monywa Scout, a resistance group named after Monywa, the main city of Myanmar’s Sagaing Region in the country’s northwest, though he did not say exactly how many vehicles were hit or when and where the attacks took place.
The ZSL-92, also known as the Type 92, is a Chinese six-wheeled armored vehicle that carries infantry and is armed with a 25 mm cannon in a small turret, and Roman noted that this version is seen less often in Myanmar than the WMA-301, a wheeled vehicle built on the same family of chassis and armed with a 105 mm gun, of which Myanmar’s armed forces operate about 100, according to Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi.
FPV drones are small, cheap quadcopters flown by an operator watching a live video feed through goggles or a screen, which lets them steer an explosive charge into a precise weak point on a target such as a vehicle’s roof, engine deck or open hatch, a tactic that became widespread during the war in Ukraine before spreading to other conflicts, including Myanmar’s civil war.
Myanmar’s resistance groups first used drones in combat in December 2021 in Pale township of Sagaing Region, less than a year after the military seized power in a coup, and the conflict monitor ACLED had recorded more than 2,100 drone strikes by resistance groups across more than 600 locations in the country by mid-2025, most of them carried out with commercial and agricultural drones converted to drop small explosives, although both resistance fighters and government forces have since adopted FPV drones.
Chinese-made armor has been a frequent target: in December 2023, Roman reported the destruction of a Chinese Dongfeng Mengshi armored vehicle belonging to the Myanmar Army during fighting in the north of the country, alongside BTR-3 and MT-LB armored vehicles, and earlier this year footage showed resistance fighters destroying a Myanmar Army WMA-301 that had been fitted with a metal grille, a type of improvised drone protection that also first spread during the war in Ukraine.
The drones are now reaching beyond the battlefield, as on Sept. 10 anti-junta fighters launched FPV drones at Myanmar’s Tada-U Air Base, about 35 km (22 miles) south of Mandalay, where video posted online showed one striking the nose of a Russian-made Yak-130 jet.

U.S. Prepares Bases for Three Months of Combat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:21:16 UTC
16:21:16 KST

The Pentagon has started preparing U.S. military bases to operate independently for at least 90 days in the event of a major war.
According to Fox News, the preparations are part of the FORTRESS military initiative, which aims to ensure that U.S. military bases can continue operating without relying heavily on civilian infrastructure.
Major U.S. military installations on the mainland must be able to meet their essential needs for electricity, water, fuel, and communications independently for at least three months.
To ensure energy independence, the initiative includes the use of portable small nuclear reactors, large-scale energy storage systems, and local power grids.
This will allow military bases to operate independently if civilian power infrastructure is disrupted.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell stated that the U.S. military can no longer rely solely on the protection provided by the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
“We do not want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to support our national defense. That is an unacceptable risk,” he emphasized.
Other aspects of the program include establishing strategic reserves of ammunition, fuel, critical minerals, electronics,spare parts, and medical supplies.
The Pentagon also aims to ensure at least two independent supply or production channels for the most critical defense components, so that the loss of a single factory or supplier does not disrupt military operations.
Particular attention is being given to preparing U.S. industry for large-scale wartime production. Through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, the Pentagon plans to identify civilian companies in advance that could quickly switch to manufacturing defense products during a war.
To achieve this, the military will need to coordinate technical requirements, contracts, production conversion procedures, and cybersecurity measures. The initiative also includes regular industrial capacity tests and exercises to practice mobilizing manufacturing capabilities.

The nuclear-armed neighbors remain in communication through diplomatic and military channels, a ministry spokesperson said as per the report.
Last week, India's China border police chief, Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, said that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops are continuing at multiple locations along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, despite ongoing talks between the two countries.
The face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh underscore the challenges of maintaining peace along the border even as the two countries have held several rounds of military and diplomatic talks this year.
India has over the years reiterated that the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh is an integral part of the country, while China considers it to be a part of Tibet.
Gandhi acquitted in defamation case
An Indian court acquitted Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi in a defamation case on Monday, local media reported.
Gandhi was accused of calling India's Home Minister Amit Shah an "accused murder" during a state election campaign speech in 2018. The case was filed in Sultanpur town of Uttar Pradesh by a BJP member. Sultanpur is less than an hour away from New Delhi by road.

India hosts prince of Liechtenstein for state visit
Prince Alois of Liechtenstein arrived in Mumbai today, on the second day of his four-day state visit to India.

Liechtenstein is an independent principality nestled between Austria and Switzerland. With a population of about 40,000 people, the country is about the size of the Indian city of Varanasi.
This is Prince Alois's second visit to India this year. Before that, he has visited the country in 2010 and 2018, India's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"Prince Alois will hold bilateral meetings to discuss cooperation in various areas including trade and investment, science, technology and innovation and people-to-people exchanges as well as exchange views on regional and global developments," the statement said.

Caught in the act: Italy and Africa join forces against art trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:16:01 UTC
16:16:01 KST

Cooperation between Italy and Africa is focused on training, traceability and the restoration of cultural heritage.
Cultural heritage is safeguarded not only by recovering stolen works, but also by reconstructing their history, spotting suspicious movements on the market and training those tasked with protecting them.
It is on this front that Italy and African countries are strengthening cooperation against the illicit trafficking of cultural property, with a new professional training programme included in the Piano Mattei.
The initiative stems from a three-year agreement between Italy's National School for Cultural Heritage and Cultural Activities and the École du Patrimoine Africain (EPA), an institution based in Porto-Novo, in Benin, specialising in the conservation and promotion of African cultural heritage.
The first course began earlier this month and brings together professionals from nine French-speaking African countries. The Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage (TPC) is also contributing to the activities, sharing its investigative expertise and the experience gained in international cooperation.
Provenance and digitisation to stop illicit trafficking
The programme aims to strengthen the technical skills of people working in museums and cultural institutions, with a particular focus on documenting collections, digitising inventories and researching the provenance of works, known as provenance research.
Reconstructing provenance means establishing where an object was located, who owned it and through which transactions it reached the market. Incomplete documents, unclear changes of ownership or exports lacking the necessary authorisations can help identify items that have been stolen or excavated clandestinely.
Traceability is also crucial in preventing artefacts originating from looting or from unstable areas entering private collections and international commercial circuits. Up-to-date inventories and shared digital archives can make it easier to recognise sought-after objects and provide the authorities with the information they need to launch investigations.
The course involves professionals from Algeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon, Morocco, the Republic of the Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Senegal and Tunisia. The goal is to build lasting skills and relationships among operators, administrations and institutions on both continents.
From the Axum obelisk to the Benin Bronzes: the impact of restitutions
Cooperation on heritage protection takes place against a backdrop marked by looting, illegal exports and disputes over the restitution of works. A particularly significant case for relations between Italy and Africa is that of the Axum obelisk in Ethiopia.
The monument, a stele dating back around 1,700 years, was removed by Italian troops during the fascist occupation in 1937 and taken to Rome. After decades of requests and negotiations, Italy returned it to Ethiopia in 2005. The monument, transported in three large sections, was reassembled at its original site in 2008, with the involvement of UNESCO and Italian funding for the operation. It is an example of international cooperation that required not only a political agreement but also complex technical and logistical work.
Another emblematic case is that of the Benin Bronzes, now part of Nigeria's heritage. In 1897, during the British military expedition against the Kingdom of Benin, thousands of objects were looted from the royal palace and later dispersed into Western collections.
In 2022, Germany embarked on a restitution process of historic scope: the foundation overseeing Berlin's state museums transferred ownership of 512 objects from the Ethnological Museum collection to Nigeria, under a broader agreement that also covered other artefacts. Some of the works remained on temporary display in Berlin on loan, while ownership passed to Nigeria.
These cases show why the protection of cultural property requires different, complementary tools. Restitution addresses the claims of countries of origin, while prevention and documentary research can help identify removed works, trace their journeys and curb new trafficking. The historical episodes linked to colonial plunder, however, do not automatically coincide with contemporary offences: each case calls for a specific documentary and legal reconstruction.
The role of the Art Carabinieri and international cooperation
Italy's experience in tackling crimes against cultural heritage also rests on the work of the Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, set up in 1969. This specialised unit conducts investigations into thefts, illegal excavations, unlawful exports and the sale of works of illicit origin, also by working with judicial authorities and foreign police forces.
International cooperation is already a tangible tool in recovery operations. In 2022, for instance, the TPC Carabinieri worked with the Manhattan District Attorney's Office and the US agency Homeland Security Investigations to recover Italian archaeological artefacts that had reached the United States via international trafficking networks. The operation led to the return of 58 objects, including works from the Etruscan, Roman and Magna Graecia periods.
The guiding principle behind these activities also applies to collaboration with African countries: sharing information, documentation and expertise can facilitate the identification of items, support investigations and make recovery and restitution procedures more effective.
At international level, a key point of reference is the 1970 UNESCO Convention, which commits states to combat the illicit import, export and transfer of cultural property and promotes cooperation for their recovery. The Convention also encourages preventive tools such as national inventories, export certificates and controls on the trade in works.
Piano Mattei, culture and partnerships between the two continents
The new training path is part of the cultural cooperation promoted by Italy as part of thePiano Mattei for Africa. The Directorate-General for European and International Affairs of the Ministry of Culture is supporting the programme, which aims to create opportunities for training, professional exchange and collaboration between institutions.
For Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli, the fight against illicit trafficking is a shared responsibility that calls for highly qualified skills and cooperation between institutions. He stressed that the agreement is based on reciprocity, the exchange of knowledge and respect for cultural identities.
The goal is to build a partnership that does not simply transfer know-how from Europe to Africa but fosters ongoing collaboration between professionals. The protection of collections, the conservation of artefacts and the reconstruction of their provenance thus become part of a common strategy, in which safeguarding cultural heritage is also a matter of historical memory, identity and the rights of communities.

Experts consider Estonia's plan to register AI agents dangerous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:16:00 UTC
16:16:00 KST

Experts consider Estonia's plan to register AI agents dangerous
Estonia wants to lead the regulation of AI agents and has prepared a corresponding bill, but experts see no point in the plan, with some even calling it dangerous.
An AI agent is not the same as a conversation with ChatGPT or another AI chatbot. While AI provides answers to questions in a conversation, an agent is given a task and can find its own way to complete it.
The agent can be compared to a robotic vacuum cleaner, which tidies a room but is not told exactly how to do it. People are increasingly using AI agents to make their lives easier.
"For example, they file tax returns, have analyses carried out on their bank account balances and also analyze their mobile plans. They have an agent look at their phone bill, for example, to see where they could save money," Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Liina Vahtras said.
There are also cases where agents have been instructed to look for and buy airline tickets. The user has handed over their credit card details, which poses a potential security risk.
One Estonian e-resident has openly shared how he uses Anthropic's AI platform Claude to conduct business with the Tax and Customs Board and manage bank accounts. He only occasionally enters the necessary codes in Smart-ID.
Vahtras said these cases demonstrate the need for national regulation of AI agents.
The idea for creating identifiers for AI agents came from the IT sector, and have informally been referred to as personal identification codes. Vahtras stressed that agents will not actually be given their own identities.
"We are creating an opportunity for people to register an additional code for themselves, which we call an agent code, so that when they use an agent's assistance in private or public information systems, they can distinguish between themselves and the machine acting on their behalf," she explained.
The codes would be entered into a central database where it would be possible to check which agent is acting on whose behalf. While the initial plan was to allow both individuals and companies to register agents, and for one person to register several agents, this has now been abandoned. Initially, only private individuals will be able to register agents, with one agent per person.
The minister said they will see how this works and then discuss how to move forward.
Cybernetica: Adopting such a bill is dangerous
Although the idea of agent codes came from the IT sector, there are also many critics.
Cybernetica, an information technology company that helped build Estonia's e-government infrastructure, submitted 11 pages of feedback on the bill. It said the text is deficient and contradictory and that insufficient work has gone into its preparation.
Adopting the bill in its current form would not achieve its objectives and would, in the company's assessment, be dangerous. It recommended that the bill should not be approved in its current form.
In fact, none of the ministries approved the bill by the deadline. The Government Office was the only institution to do so.
Speaking to ERR, Cybernetica's development manager Arne Ansper highlighted one important aspect: a security risk arises if an agent does not have the same kind of secure authentication available to Estonian residents through ID cards and their PIN codes.
"This issue has not been addressed at present. There has been talk of registering agents, but registration alone gives us nothing if we do not have a strong authentication or signing tool to provide to that agent. The security level must actually be equivalent to what we currently have with ID cards, Mobile-ID or Smart-ID. If it were lower and someone granted all their authorizations to that tool, we would be lowering the overall level of security," he said.
Ansper stressed that the development principles behind Estonia's e-government system and digital identity have served the country very well, enabled efficient governance and must not be undermined.
He also highlighted that the legislative amendment has been completed before a technological solution has been developed. Ansper said legislation should not be developed in isolation from technology.
However, Vahtras said the work is taking place in parallel.
"The very first working group that was established was the legal working group, but the communications and technical solutions working groups also began operating in parallel. We do not yet know exactly what the technical solution will be, and we want to involve more parties. But in order for us to have at least some basis and opportunity to amend the law by the end of the year, given the very tight deadline we were set for working on this project, this was made a priority," she said.
There has also been considerable criticism from legal experts, the Competition Authority and the Data Protection Inspectorate.
Responsibility is unclear
The Estonian Association of Information Technology and Telecommunications (ITL) also said the bill should not proceed in its current form.
However, speaking to ERR, ITL President Ats Albre said the government is moving in the right direction, but feedback needs to be taken into account.
One important issue is responsibility.
"If, for example, as an entrepreneur you ask an AI agent to submit various data of yours that it has access to to Statistics Estonia, it is not yet sufficiently clear who is responsible for what, and we at ITL would like to be certain that ultimately the person themselves remains responsible," Albre said.
He also drew a parallel with a robot vacuum cleaner.
"If you also have a dog and the dog leaves a mess on the floor and the robot spreads it everywhere, then ultimately you are still responsible. It cannot be that the robot is responsible or the dog is responsible," the association president explained.
Albre said not everything needs to be regulated. Some issues are technological and do not require legislation, and many other experts share this view. Albre said members of the association will meet with the minister next week to discuss the feedback and get on the same page on these issues.
Amid the criticism, the question of why this process needs to be rushed has arisen. Some experts have said the whole bill drafting process should start again. But Vahtras does not agree that work should be abandoned.
"From my previous work experience, I have seen that major innovations are often held back precisely by legislative amendments. For the state to innovate, so that we can quickly develop a technical solution on top of this, the law needs to be amended, and that is precisely why we started with it, so that once we have the technical solution, it will not be held back by legislative amendments," she said.
It is hoped the legislative amendments will reach the Riigikogu by early November.
Vahtras said there are plans to revise the bill further. She stressed that registering AI agents is only one option. It entails no obligations and that if the plan fails, it can be abandoned.
"All we are doing is creating an opportunity for people to register this code for themselves. They do not have to do so. It creates no obligation for anyone, not for any service provider or any individual. It simply creates an opportunity. If, for example, after the legislative amendment, our technical working group finds that it cannot be implemented, that it is not possible to give agents their own authentication and signing functions — for example, because it is too complicated or too expensive — then nothing happens as a result of the law having been amended. It causes no harm to anyone. The costs to the state are minimal," the minister said.

Ukraine war lessons show up on Chinese armor in Pakistan drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:15:54 UTC
16:15:54 KST

- Chinese Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles with anti-drone roof cages took part in Karakoram 2026, the first China-Pakistan joint army training, in Xinjiang.
- The drill included drone swarm strikes and robotic dogs scouting buildings, with all equipment supplied by China.
Chinese Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles fitted with anti-drone roof cages and side grilles carried assault troops during Karakoram 2026, the first joint army training between China and Pakistan, now under way in Korla in China’s northwestern Xinjiang region, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Oct. 21.
The exercise has moved into its main drill phase, in which mixed Chinese and Pakistani units rehearse a full raid on a mock terrorist camp, from reconnaissance and strikes to clearing buildings. Footage aired by CCTV also showed drone swarms carrying out suicide strikes and robotic dogs scouting building interiors ahead of the troops.
The drill opened with reconnaissance vehicles and drones watching the camp to track the mock enemy’s positions and movements. Snipers then took up firing positions, drone swarms struck exposed targets, and armored vehicles followed with direct fire. When the strikes ended, Type 08 vehicles carried the assault team forward, and more of them brought in clearance teams that dismounted and pushed deeper into the camp, with the robotic dogs going ahead to check buildings.
The Type 08 is an eight-wheeled armored vehicle family used by the People’s Liberation Army. The vehicles seen in the drill had a metal grille fitted over the roof and additional grilles on the sides, which CCTV said were designed specifically to counter drone attacks.
Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs commentator, told the Global Times that the roof cage was a rapid tactical adaptation to the drone threat, drawing on lessons from the war in Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East. He said that even in counterterrorism training, units in high-altitude areas rely on drones, and that the PLA needs ways to counter militant groups that might use drones for sabotage.
Such cages, often called “cope cages,” first spread widely on Russian armor during the war in Ukraine, where first-person-view drones have repeatedly hit the thinner roof, rear and engine areas of tanks and armored vehicles. Chinese forces have adopted them before: the PLA has fitted cages to ZBD-09 infantry fighting vehicles and showed Type 15 light tanks with anti-drone cages during a high-altitude exercise in October 2024.
Chinese soldiers said they had picked up tactics from their Pakistani counterparts, whose army has extensive counterinsurgency experience.
“What impressed me most about this joint training is that the Pakistani military has real combat experience, so many of their lessons are worth learning. When we enter a building and throw a grenade, we throw it far; they throw it at the ground so it bounces at speed, ricocheting two or three times instead of staying in one place. That effectively stops the enemy from picking it up and throwing it back,” said Pan Li, a member of a unit under the Xinjiang military command, CCTV reported.
China’s Ministry of National Defense announced the exercise on Oct. 10, saying it would focus on joint counterterrorism operations at high altitude and include training in drone operations, firing on the move and long-range sniping, as well as joint command and live-force drills. All weapons and equipment are being provided by China, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and drone and counter-drone systems, CCTV Military reported.

Climate-driven farm losses push agricultural insurance payouts higher in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:14:42 UTC
16:14:42 KST

Extreme weather events linked to climate change are taking an increasing toll on Türkiye’s agricultural sector, with crop damage reports and insurance payouts rising sharply in recent years, according to data from the Agricultural Insurance Pool (TARSİM).
The number of crop insurance damage notifications increased by 51.2 percent year-on-year in 2025, while compensation payments surged from 8 billion Turkish Liras in 2023 to 12 billion liras in 2024 and 35 billion liras in 2025. In the first 10 months of 2026, producers received 13 billion liras in compensation payments, bringing total payouts over the past four years to nearly 70 billion liras.
TARSİM data showed that damage notifications in crop insurance rose from 284,357 in 2024 to 430,076 in 2025. In the January-October period of this year, total damage notifications across all agricultural insurance branches reached 478,000, including 311,000 related to crop and greenhouse insurance.
The main causes of agricultural losses have changed over time. Hail, frost, wild boars, floods and storms were the leading sources of damage reports in 2023, while hail dominated in 2024. Agricultural frost became the primary cause in 2025, whereas floods and water inundation emerged as the most damaging events in 2026.
In crop insurance, hail accounted for 123,239 damage notifications, or 43.3 percent of the total in 2024. In 2025, frost-related claims rose to 171,558, representing 39.8 percent of all notifications. This year, floods and water inundation became the most significant source of losses, while frost damage remained more localized.
The provinces recording the highest number of claims in the January-October period were Malatya, Manisa, Diyarbakır, Amasya and Tokat. Hazelnut-producing areas in Samsun, Ordu and Giresun were affected by floods, water inundation and landslides, while reports of damage caused by wild animals and birds increased in corn- and sunflower-growing regions.
This year, lentils, wheat and barley were hit by floods, hail and storms, while peaches and nectarines suffered hail-related damage. Grapes and apricots were also affected by lighter hailstorms and frost.
Under the TARSİM system, insured agricultural land totaled 33 million decares in 2023, 35.6 million decares in 2024, 44.3 million decares in 2025, and 27 million decares as of October 2026. According to TARSİM, insurance coverage in crop and greenhouse insurance stood at around 30 percent at the end of 2025.

According to him, the enemy suffered the heaviest losses as a result of operations conducted by Russia’s Battlegroup Center.

The greatest losses in manpower were inflicted on Ukrainian armed formations in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup Center, which operates in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) and in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the expert wrote on his VKontakte page after analyzing data released by the Russian Defense Ministry.
Marochko added that during the week, the Russian military also destroyed nearly 5,600 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), 15 marine vessels, 43 field artillery guns, 43 electronic warfare and counter-battery stations, as well as 805 different combat vehicles.

Renewables account for 63 percent of Türkiye’s installed power capacity

16:13:04 KST

Türkiye’s total installed electricity generation capacity reached 127,355 megawatts (MW) as of the end of September, according to a statement by the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry.
The country’s renewable energy capacity rose to 80,315 MW during the same period, bringing the share of renewables in total installed capacity to 63.1 percent. Domestic energy sources accounted for 72.1 percent of total installed capacity.
Installed solar and wind power capacity increased to 43,762 MW in September, with the two sources representing 34.4 percent of Türkiye’s total installed electricity capacity.
Türkiye generated 31.79 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity in September. Hydropower remained the largest source of electricity generation, producing 8.27 billion kWh, equivalent to 26 percent of total output.
Solar power generation reached 4.32 billion kWh, accounting for 13.6 percent of total electricity production, while wind power generation stood at 3.84 billion kWh, representing 12.1 percent. Combined solar and wind generation totaled 8.16 billion kWh during the month.
Electricity generated from renewable sources amounted to 18.10 billion kWh, corresponding to 56.9 percent of total production. Electricity generated from domestic resources reached 22.35 billion kWh, accounting for 70.3 percent of the total.
As of the end of September 2026, hydropower accounted for 32,332 MW of installed capacity, followed by solar power with 28,222 MW, natural gas with 25,009 MW, wind power with 15,540 MW, domestic coal with 11,565 MW, imported coal with 10,466 MW, biomass with 2,423 MW, and geothermal energy with 1,798 MW.

Elbit wins $200 million from unnamed Asia-Pacific country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:12:33 UTC
16:12:33 KST

- Elbit Systems won about $200 million in contracts from an unnamed Asia-Pacific country for helicopter targeting sensors, head-up displays and training system support.
- The deal includes Elbit’s new SPECTRO 12 compact surveillance and targeting payload, with work running up to five years.
Israel’s Elbit Systems has won contracts worth about $200 million from an unnamed country in the Asia-Pacific region to supply helicopter targeting sensors, cockpit head-up displays and support for airborne combat training systems, the company announced on Oct. 26.
The work will be carried out over up to five years. Elbit did not identify the customer, the aircraft types involved or how many systems it will deliver.
The largest element is the SPECTRO 12, a new multispectral surveillance and targeting payload that will be integrated on the customer’s helicopters. The turret-style sensor combines high-resolution imaging channels with a laser designator and artificial intelligence-based image processing, allowing crews to detect, identify and track targets at long range, at night and in bad weather, and to mark them for precision-guided weapons.
The SPECTRO 12 is the newest and smallest member of Elbit’s SPECTRO family. The company describes it as a 12-inch-class payload derived from its larger 15-inch-class systems, designed for aircraft where size, weight and power are tightly limited, such as light and medium helicopters.
The contracts also cover follow-on support and upgrades for airborne live training systems already installed on the customer’s aircraft. The systems let pilots fly realistic air-to-air and air-to-ground training sorties, including mixed live and simulated scenarios, with real-time combat simulation, weapon scoring and mission debriefing.
Elbit will also deliver head-up displays, the transparent screens in front of a pilot that project flight and targeting data so the pilot can keep looking outside the cockpit. The company said the new displays offer higher resolution, improved video and lower power consumption for day and night flying.
“Elbit Systems’ airborne solutions combine advanced technologies with extensive operational experience across a wide range of mission environments. We are proud to provide our customers with innovative capabilities that enhance mission effectiveness, situational awareness and operational readiness across a broad spectrum of airborne missions,” said Bezhalel Machlis, president and CEO of Elbit Systems.
The award follows a roughly $270 million deal for SPECTRO family payloads that Elbit signed with another unnamed international customer in September, covering systems that combine mid-wave infrared, visible and short-wave infrared channels with laser designation, along with the AMPS NG airborne surveillance payload. Earlier customers of the family include Romania, which ordered SPECTRO XR sensors for its IAR 330 Puma helicopters in 2023.
Elbit, based in Haifa, reported revenue of $2.29 billion for the quarter ended June 30 and an order backlog of $32 billion.

Brazil's Lula wins, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:12:05 UTC
16:12:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Brazil's Lula wins, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to recognise results
Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father's lead by refusing to concede defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential election.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for corruption charges and a coup attempt, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled.
"It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.
Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.
Still, Bolsonaro's refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say.
Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.
Lula defies expectations
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. The result will disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
Financial markets also expressed initial concerns at the shock result. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory, while analysts expected the Brazilian real to fall against the US dollar.
Lula had trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Speaking at a hotel in São Paulo late on Sunday, he took a conciliatory tone.
"I won’t speak of national unity, because that doesn’t always fit the reality of this country. No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," Lula said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will have to work alongside a Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast Brazil's legislature in favor of the president's enemies.
"The challenges are countless," said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper in São Paulo.

Chinese carmakers lose ground in Türkiye as Europe drives growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:11:32 UTC
16:11:32 KST

Chinese automotive brands, which have been among the main drivers of growth in the European market, suffered sharp declines in Türkiye amid additional customs duties and stricter import requirements.
Chinese brands sold a combined 36,245 vehicles in Türkiye in January-September 2026, down 43.8 percent year-on-year, according to data compiled from the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD). Their combined market share fell to 5.77 percent during the period.
Chery remained the largest Chinese brand in the Turkish market with 17,357 units sold, although its sales declined 23 percent from a year earlier. Omoda-Jaecoo followed with 9,717 units, posting a 64.4 percent increase, while BYD sold 6,886 vehicles, marking an 80 percent decline. MG recorded sales of 2,266 units, up 36.2 percent, and Hongqi sold 19 vehicles, an increase of 46.2 percent.
BYD’s steep sales decline played a significant role in the overall contraction, as the company was unable to import vehicles due to its investment plans in Türkiye. Chinese brands collectively sold around 30,000 fewer vehicles in Türkiye compared with the same period a year earlier, highlighting the slowdown in the local market.
Türkiye’s overall passenger car market contracted 15 percent in January-September from a year ago.
By contrast, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) showed that the European passenger car market expanded 6.3 percent in January-September, surpassing 10.5 million units. Car sales across Europe increased by 626,903 units from a year earlier.
Of that increase, 510,976 units came from five major Chinese-owned automotive groups. In other words, Chinese companies accounted for 81.5 percent of the growth in the European car market during the period.

Can you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of math
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:10:24 UTC
16:10:24 KST

Today’s puzzle is set by Terence Tao, who may be the world’s most famous mathematician.
Tao, aged 51, has been a global phenomenon since the age of ten, when he became the youngest competitor at the International Maths Olympiad, a record he still holds. For the last three decades he has been a professor at UCLA, where he has been garlanded with prizes, and where one of his colleagues famously said: “Terry is like Mozart: mathematics just flows out of him.”
Tao is a very visible leader of the field, not only because of his scientific contributions and collaborations, but also because he writes the most widely-read blog in research level maths. When Open AI earlier this month stunned the community with the release of hundreds of proofs of long-standing open questions – the “mathpocalypse” – his blog has become one of the most important forums for the community’s response.
This week Tao publishes Six Maths Essentials, his first work aimed at a general audience. The puzzle below reflects ideas in the book.
He said: “I like this puzzle in that it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve the problem: working out small examples by hand can give some valuable initial intuition, but it will be algebra that lets you solve the entire problem in a civilized amount of time.”
The magic money plant
In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant:
- a regular plant produces a single coin per day
- a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.)
At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each.
Suppose that I begin on Day 1 with a mother plants, b regular plants and c coins.
1. How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3?
2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X.
3. At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What are a, b and c?
I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solutions – and Tao will explain what it all means.
PLEASE NO SPOILERS Instead discuss the mathpocalypse.
UPDATE: The solutions can be read here.
Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at the Guardian Bookshop.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

'Tyranny of distance' weighs against big cycling call
Unknown

Cadel Evans says an Australian Grand Tour start is possible but he wouldn't want to ride it
In short:
Cadel Evans has said one of cycling's three great stage races could start here, but the tyranny of distance would make it unlikely.
Australia's only Tour de France winner, Evans said some Grand Tour races were considering starts in America, and that he would be open to them coming to the Southern Hemisphere.
Evans's Great Ocean Road Race will take place in late January.
Cadel Evans is intrigued by the revolutionary idea of Australia hosting a Tour de France stage, especially given he's long retired as a pro cyclist.
The 2011 Tour champion, the only Australian to win cycling's most famous event, remains heavily involved in his sport as a race promoter and commentator.
Cycling's three-week Grand Tours, the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España, regularly start with stages outside their own borders.
Next year, the Tour's "Grand Depart" will be three stages through Scotland, England and Wales.
But it would be something else entirely to bring a Grand Tour start to the other side of the world.
The San Francisco 49ers and LA Rams faced massive logistical challenges last month to stage their NFL game at the MCG and they didn't have to play again until several days later.
"It would be possible — I wouldn't want to be the one telling the riders," Evans said on Monday.
"But it's never out of the question. There's been talk before … some Grand Tours are maybe considering stages in America.
"I'd be totally open to it, but I wouldn't want to ride it myself. Australia — as we all know, the tyranny of distance — it's pretty far."
There was speculation last summer that the WA government was sounding out Giro organisers.
While a Grand Tour start remains at long odds, the likelihood of cycling superstar Tadej Pogačar returning to race in Australia may well be firming.
Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta in late August, ending his season early.
Tour Down Under race director Stuart O'Grady has been trying to lure Pogačar to Adelaide for several years. The project took a step forward this year when Pogačar's manager visited and spoke highly of the race.
If Pogačar returned to Adelaide, he would most likely also race at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race in Geelong the following weekend.
Pogacar competed at the two events in 2019 and last raced in Australia at the 2022 Wollongong world road championships.
"He wants to start his season early, apparently. If he would like to come back to our race, that would be amazing," Evans said.
"When you have the opportunity to see the greatest of all time in any sport, it's pretty unique for any sporting fan."
The Slovenian's stunning run of sustained success has invited comparisons with Belgian Eddy Merckx — until now, cycling's all-time greatest rider.
Evans gives the nod to Pogačar.
"It's unfair to compare periods, but it's a far more competitive environment that we race in now," he said.
"There are so many more specialists in our sport now and he's been an all-rounder, winning everywhere, It's just remarkable, and at such a young age as well [28].
"One thing that's so great about Pogačar, other than that he's just an amazing rider, is he wants to win everything."
Evans, at 174 centimetres, was standing alongside Max Gawn, at 209cm, to announce the Melbourne captain as an ambassador for the People's Ride, held on January 30 before the women's road race at Geelong.
"Particularly someone like Pogačar, he goes beyond our sport — and of course, that's having Max part of it [as well]," Evans said.

The directorate said, "Terrorism has no place among us," and that the three had met their "just fate," according to the Reuters news agency. The directorate didn't name the suspects or point to any possible links to any Islamist militant groups, Reuters added.

Missiles Strike Energiya Defense Battery Plant in Yelets
Another monitoring channel, Supernova+, reported that the Severny Bridge in Voronezh may also have been targeted, citing reports that the bridge was closed and smoke was visible nearby.
Industrial and aviation facilities possibly targeted
Supernova+, citing their own open-source intelligence analysis, suggested that the Voronezhsintezkauchuk synthetic rubber plant and the Voronezh Aircraft Joint-Stock Company (VASO) may also have been targeted.

Killed and injured in Voronezh drone attack, governor says

The attack also sparked fires at several industrial facilities, a business center, an apartment building, two dacha settlements, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative, according to the governor. He said the industrial fires had no major consequences.

The Sverdlovsk Railway said traffic on the Reshety-Aramil section had been suspended after the derailment compromised clearance of an adjacent track. Firefighting and recovery trains were dispatched to the scene.
Local residents reported seeing flames and thick black smoke, with one witness telling media that an explosion had illuminated the area near the Chusovsky Tract.
Russia’s consumer rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it would test air quality in nearby residential areas.
The derailment comes amid a series of reported disruptions to Russian railway infrastructure in recent months.
The Moscow Times reported that Ukrainian drone attacks on railway infrastructure in the Bryansk Region on Sept. 28 caused 10 railcars to derail after a railway bridge section collapsed, while a separate incident derailed 18 empty freight cars.
Other reported railway incidents in September and July caused train delays and damage, although the causes differed.
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian officials have publicly attributed the Sverdlovsk derailment to an attack.

Discovering Almaty: Mountain mornings, street art and market flavours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:08:20 UTC
16:08:20 KST

Kazakhstan’s former capital marked its birthday with music, markets and apple fairs. Beyond the celebrations, mountain breakfasts, colourful architecture and art hiding in plain sight offer reasons to linger.
The first thing many newcomers notice about Almaty is the skyline. Snow-capped peaks of the Trans-Ili Alatau rise beyond the rooftops, close enough to shape everyday life. They even influence the way people give directions. In a city laid out largely on a grid, locals may tell you to head “up”, meaning towards the mountains, or “down” - away from them.
You can start with coffee in the city centre and head towards the foothills for a walk or a late breakfast. The mountains are close enough to be part of an ordinary morning, and not just a weekend escape.
To explore the mountains, head to the Medeu base station and take the cable car up to Shymbulak Mountain Resort. In winter, skiers and snowboarders come for the slopes, but you can also visit simply for the views or a meal in the mountains. There are opportunities for walking and hiking all year round.
Art on the walls, and a city shaped by history
Almaty was Kazakhstan’s capital until 1997, and its cultural reputation runs deep. Look closely at older buildings and you’ll find layers of the city’s artistic history: brightly coloured mosaics embedded in facades.
Many date from the 1960s to the 1980s, when monumental artists from across the Soviet Union worked in the city. Some have since been damaged or lost, making the surviving works worth seeking out.
Almaty’s buildings tell other stories too. The colourful wooden Ascension Cathedral, completed in 1907, survived a major earthquake just four years later.
For a contemporary contrast, visit the Almaty Museum of Arts, which opened last year. Designed by the British architectural firm Chapman Taylor, its two interlocking forms represent the mountains and the city, one clad in limestone and the other in aluminium. Inside, the collection brings together modern and contemporary art from Kazakhstan, Central Asia and beyond.
Come hungry
The Green Bazaar is a good place to discover another side of Almaty. Apples share space with dried fruit, nuts and local produce, while the surrounding food scene moves easily between Kazakh staples and dishes familiar across Central Asia.
Try beshbarmak, a dish of meat served over flat pieces of pasta, or kazy, a traditional horsemeat sausage. Dairy specialties are worth sampling too: kurt (salty dried curd balls) and kumys (fermented mare’s milk with a tangy flavour).
Make room for plov, a rice pilaf, lagman noodles or steamed manty dumplings. The range of flavours offers a glimpse of the different communities and traditions that have shaped the city.
Almaty’s appeal changes with the seasons: winter brings skiing, warmer months invite mountain walks, and the city’s museums, markets and varied food scene offer plenty to explore throughout the year.
It can also be the starting point for a longer journey. With flight connections to Europe and East Asia, as well its location next to neighbouring Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan and Tashkent in Uzbekistan, Almaty lends itself to a stopover for a wider Central Asian itinerary. Before moving on, though, leave a few days for the city itself.

Zelenskyy proposes parliament extend martial law and mobilisation until 29 January
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has submitted bills to the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) on extending martial law and mobilisation for another 90 days – until 29 January 2027.
Source: bills No. 16182 and No. 16183 on the Verkhovna Rada website
Details: Currently, martial law and general mobilisation in Ukraine are in force until 05:30 on 31 October 2026.
Zelenskyy proposes extending both terms for another 90 days – until 29 January 2027.

Without security guarantees, this war will not truly end; we will not be able to recognise that it has ended, because there would remain a risk of renewed aggression from such a neighbour."
Background:
- According to previous decisions, martial law and mobilisation are in force from 2 August until 31 October 2026.

Discovery of baby orangutans in India exposes booming illegal pet trade
India is emerging as an important market in the global illegal wildlife trade, estimated to be worth US$34 billion annually
The three males and two females, aged six to eight months – were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700km (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India. They are now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been playing classical music to soothe them.
Wild orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they sustain rainforests by spreading seeds across vast areas, allowing trees to regenerate and store carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. The species is critically endangered, threatened by severe habitat loss. There are about 119,500 orangutans left in the wild, according to conservation organisation WWF.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Riyaz ul Khaliq
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
North Korea has told the UN Security Council that a mine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone was a "fabrication" by South Korea, state media reported Monday.
North Korea's permanent representative to the UN sent a letter to the Security Council president Sunday, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency, or KCNA.
The letter came amid tensions on the Korean Peninsula after three South Korean soldiers were wounded in a mine explosion on Sept. 21.
Seoul blamed Pyongyang for the incident and called for the restoration of military talks. North Korea rejected the accusations and has yet to respond to the South Korean Defense Ministry's offer to resume communication.
Pyongyang's letter followed a similar communication from South Korea to the Security Council, demanding an apology from the North over the incident, the Korea Herald newspaper reported.
The exchange came as South Korea and the US began joint air drills Monday, a day after Yonhap News reported that North Korean troops were seen conducting drills with a self-propelled howitzer in coastal border areas of Hwanghae province.
North Korea's letter described the mine explosion as a "sinister obstructive move" by South Korea aimed at portraying Pyongyang's border fortifications as a military invasion.
It also accused Seoul of attempting to delay the fortification work and evade responsibility for escalating tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
The letter said the fortification of North Korea's southern border was a "legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty" in accordance with the UN Charter and international law.
Pyongyang described the work as a defensive measure against external threats of aggression.
"If the RoK violates the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DPRK despite our warnings, the former will be held wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences," the letter said.
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is North Korea's official name, while the Republic of Korea is the official name of South Korea.
 
South Korea, US launch joint air drills
South Korea's Air Force said Monday that joint air drills with the US were focused on "counter-air and air interdiction missions aimed at enhancing wartime joint operations."
The two-week Freedom Flag exercise is being held at Kunsan Air Base in Gunsan, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) southwest of Seoul.
The 1950s Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
Some 39,000 US military personnel are stationed in South Korea under a mutual defense pact.

Arnab, which formed over the Bay of Bengal, has intensified since Monday, India's weather office said on Tuesday.

Nearly 50,000 people had been moved to shelters from vulnerable areas by Monday night, out of 400,000 estimated to need evacuation, Prakhar Jain, Managing Director of Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told Reuters.
"Evacuation is continuing," Jain added.
There have been no evacuations in Odisha so far, Rajesh Prabhakar Patil, Special Relief Commissioner of Odisha, told Reuters. The state had already announced closure of schools and colleges in five districts for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Televison showed waves crashing on deserted beaches and shuttered shops lining the streets along affected areas.
At least 12 trains were cancelled in the east, while rail services on 53 routes along the southern coast were suspended for Tuesday and Wednesday, regional railway authorities said in social media posts.
The Bay of Bengal is one of the world's major regions for tropical cyclones, which makes India's eastern coast particularly vulnerable to sea-linked weather disasters.

Other precautions include a ban on sea fishing and keeping rescue teams on standby to ensure safety.

The One About Matthew Perry Is More Than the Typical Saga of Fame and Addiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:01:02 UTC
16:01:02 KST

When it comes to representing the famous and addicted, Hollywood seems to know only two stories. Both begin with a passionate talent who longs to make an impact on the world. Then, as no less an expert on this subject than Courtney Love memorably put it, they get what they want and they never want it again. Afflicted by affluenza or impostor syndrome or the newfound knowledge that success can’t heal their internal wounds, they escape into substance abuse. It’s only in their final chapters that the two narratives diverge. Some lucky souls hit rock bottom, get clean, and live happily ever after. The rest die young.
It would be easy to slot Matthew Perry, the Friends star who died from ketamine and drowning in October 2023, into the latter category. But in the intimate three-part Netflix documentary The One About Matthew Perry, director Mary Robinson (Quiet on the Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV) honors his memory by resisting that simplistic binary. Yes, addiction (and a cadre of enablers who are now serving time for their roles in his death) killed Perry at 54. It’s also true that he spent more than 25 years surviving it, fighting to act and write and enjoy his friendships and make his family proud and fall in love. Instead of hiding that struggle, he used his fortune to aid others in their recoveries and his platform to advocate for a broader understanding of addiction as the illness that it is.
Robinson captures all of this in straightforward, chronological order, through emotional interviews with family and longtime friends, as well as Perry’s own startlingly frank reflections in media appearances and his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing. The absence of major celebrities, whether by design or otherwise, limits the fond platitudes. In their place are vivid behind-the-scenes anecdotes and candid memories of who he was offscreen—the ambition, charm, humor, and magnanimity, but also the pain he was capable of inflicting on those who loved and needed him. His sister Mia Perry Bowick, a psychotherapist, is the most insightful presence, embracing grief and ambivalence as she ties her big brother’s highs and lows to early family dynamics.
With all due respect to Chandler Bing, Perry’s greatest contribution was his vulnerability, even when the image of him it exposed wasn’t flattering. In its honesty, this documentary continues that work.

====================================================================================================

Scientists uncover new clues to the actual night sky behind Van Gogh’s The Starry Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:07:52 UTC
16:07:52 KST

Researchers led by South Korean scientist Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim argue that Vincent van Gogh's painting may show the Taurus constellation rather than Aries, challenging the accepted timeline of the impressionist masterpiece.
More than a century after Vincent van Gogh painted one of the most recognisable night skies in art history, scientists believe they may have pinpointed the real celestial scene that inspired it - and the answer could change the accepted date of his masterpiece.
Their findings indicate that rather than being a product of Van Gogh’s imagination, The Starry Night may have been inspired by what he saw as he gazed heavenward from his French asylum 137 years ago.
A South Korean team recently reported that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France’s Saint-Remy de Provence right around 22 July 1889.
That’s a month later than the long-accepted time frame for the post-impressionist painting which depicts a sky with swirling ribbons of blue, blazing stars and luminous crescent moon, with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.
Art historians have long dated the painting to June 1889, soon after Van Gogh checked into the asylum. He'd cut off his left ear several months earlier during an argument with painter Paul Gauguin.
A team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.
"No two skies are the same. Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting," Kim said in an email. He added: "I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date."
The latest study addresses "a real puzzle" that in mid-June 1889, the moon was not the thin crescent painted by van Gogh, said Jose Luis Aragon at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He has studied The Starry Night as a physicist, but did not take part in the new research.
"Still, I would see the July date as an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer," Aragon said in an email to AP.
Kim and his team discovered that around 22 July 1889, the shape of the moon before dawn appeared like the one in the painting, with the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus rising in the east alongside Venus. The sky should have been clear enough for Van Gogh to see all this, based on their weather analyses.
The researchers tested and verified their methods on night skies in other paintings, making for what Aragon considers "a careful and genuinely interdisciplinary study."
There is another important complication: Van Gogh did not simply stand at his window and reproduce the sky exactly as he saw it. He worked on The Starry Night in a studio at the asylum, drawing on sketches and memory to construct its extraordinary landscape.
That means the painting’s celestial elements may not correspond to a single night at all, and that "the sky is likely a composite of many nights as the authors themselves acknowledge," Aragon said.

Kyrgyzstan keeps key interest rate at 12% as inflation slows
The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic has kept its key interest rate at 12% amid ongoing inflationary pressures and global economic uncertainty. The decision was made on October 26 and took effect on October 27, 2026, Qazinform News Agency cites the bank’s press service.
Annual inflation slowed to 10.8% in October, down from 12.2% in September, while cumulative inflation since the beginning of the year reached 8.5%, according to the central bank.
The regulator attributed inflationary pressures to fluctuations in global food and raw material prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. However, tight monetary policy and government measures to ensure sufficient supplies of essential goods have helped slow price growth.
Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan’s economy expanded by 10.8% in real terms during the first nine months of 2026. Growth was driven by strong investment, particularly in construction, rising domestic consumption, tourism, and major international events.
The central bank said maintaining the key rate would help limit inflationary pressures and support its medium-term target of bringing inflation within the 5-7% range. It added that monetary policy could be adjusted if risks to price stability increase.
The next scheduled meeting to review the key interest rate will take place on November 30, 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade rose 13.3% to 12 billion US dollars in the first eight months of 2026.

These measures are contributing to increased investment activity. In the first nine months of 2026, investment in fixed capital in Alatau rose 1.6 times to reach 70.3 billion tenge. Overall, the city’s investment portfolio includes 67 projects worth nearly 6.9 billion US dollars, with the potential to create around 55,000 jobs.
Urban infrastructure is also being developed to support the implementation of investment projects. Work is currently underway on 28 projects, with 35.3 billion tenge allocated from the reserve fund. Key initiatives include the reconstruction of the Kokpa-1 substation, the construction of water supply facilities, and road repairs. These improvements are expected to provide the necessary conditions for launching new businesses and supporting further construction.
The deputy prime minister placed particular emphasis on the quality and safety of Iconic Complex. He stressed the importance of meeting construction deadlines, complying with seismic safety and energy efficiency requirements, and involving Kazakhstani companies and specialists in the project.
As part of the special legal regime, a mechanism for independent technical review of project documentation has also been introduced, involving international experts. The initiative is intended to bring international best practices into the assessment of complex construction projects.
We expect Iconic Complex to set a new standard for design and construction quality and contribute to Alatau’s development as a modern city. The project must be completed on schedule while meeting stringent quality and safety requirements, said Bozumbayev.
China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC) is serving as the project’s general contractor, while the architectural concept was developed by the US-based firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM).
Construction of Iconic Complex is scheduled for completion by the end of 2029.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the KAIST branch would open in Alatau.

Kazakhstan to open official consular office in Houston
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:14:36 UTC
16:14:36 KST

Kazakhstan to open official consular office in Houston
Kazakhstan celebrated its Republic Day in Houston, bringing together members of the Kazakhstani community, local officials and representatives of business and cultural organizations. The evening opened with the national anthems of Kazakhstan and the United States, setting a solemn and friendly tone for the event, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
During the celebration, representatives of the Houston city administration, on behalf of Mayor John Whitmire, presented the organizers, Texas Qazaq Foundation, with a proclamation recognizing Kazakhstan’s national holiday.
One of the evening’s key announcements came from Kazakhstan’s Consul General in Houston, Gabidulla Ospankulov, who said that an official consular office of Kazakhstan would open in the city in the near future.
On the instructions of President of the Republic of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, an official consular office of Kazakhstan will be opened in Houston. Its opening and the commencement of operations are expected in the near future, said Ospankulov.
The new office is expected to strengthen ties between Kazakhstani citizens living in the United States and their homeland while creating additional opportunities for cooperation.
Jason Wilson, director at the U.S. Commercial Service Office in Houston, noted that bilateral trade in goods and services between the United States and Kazakhstan exceeded $7 billion for the first time in 2025.
The celebration also highlighted efforts to preserve the Kazakh language, culture and national traditions abroad.
Children from Houston Qazaq School, described as the first Kazakh school in the United States, performed traditional Kazakh dances and songs and played the dombra.
The school, which has been operating for nearly 15 years, began with just 10 students and now brings together around 80 children. Young members of the community are also developing initiatives to strengthen connections among Kazakh Americans and preserve their cultural heritage.
Twelve Kazakhstani entrepreneurs played an important role in supporting and organizing the celebration.
Texas Qazaq Foundation, which works to unite Kazakhstanis living in Texas, continues to develop business and educational initiatives, including the Steppe Business Club and a student forum. Among the foundation’s long-term plans is the establishment of its own Kazakh community center to host cultural events and support future generations.
The evening culminated in a concert by Kazakhstani singer Miras Zhugunusov, which attracted a large audience.
The celebration served as an occasion to reaffirm national identity, pride in Kazakhstan and the friendship between Kazakhstan and the United States. The official recognition of Republic Day and the announcement of the forthcoming consular office opening marked significant milestones for the Kazakhstani community in Houston, which continues to preserve its roots and introduce American society to Kazakhstan’s rich cultural heritage.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported, in its review for Republic Day, that Kazakhstan had achieved significant socio-economic progress and demographic growth following a seven-year period of national transformation.

Book of Wills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:09:55 UTC
16:09:55 KST

“In Gaza, where the world wavers between silence and forgetting, the written word becomes a final sanctuary – a fragile, luminous act of survival,” Reem Ghanayem writes in the Editor’s Note to the bilingual edition of Book of Wills (Akoya Publishing, 2026). Both erasure and preservation are recorded in this collection of brief writings from Gaza during the genocide. As the writers in this anthology address various people, including the readers themselves, there is no escaping the importance of language.
“Language is a feeble tool,” Alberto Manguel writes in the foreword. “And yet, despite the impossibility of finding language adequate to address a victim’s suffering, when confronted with that suffering, our human condition impels us to speak.”
The book opens with a strong denunciation by Saleem al-Naffar, killed in December 2023 by an Israeli airstrike. Al-Naffar’s contribution is written just 25 days into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and his words are directed at the Arabs who failed to stand with Palestinians: “They and their leaders are part of the conspiracy that aims to exterminate us.”
In most of the writings in this anthology, extermination becomes a personal reckoning imparted to various audiences. Several contributions impart the final wishes of a person expecting death, because death became an inescapable reality during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, rather than a natural termination of life. However, the book also forces the world outside Gaza to a reckoning with its own oblivion, as Amal Abu Assi al-Yazji writes of the aftermath of genocide: “Tear Palestine out of the notebook of your memory, since you’ll have no need for it.” The reader cannot help but contemplate the various levels of oblivion, and al-Yazji’s use of language is particularly striking when she writes, “That worry of yours is gone for good.” How much did all the people outside Gaza worry about Gaza, and what form did that worry take from a sheltered distance? This is perhaps one of the book’s deepest moments, as no one outside of Gaza can truly comprehend the imminent threat of erasure Palestinians have experienced. What would the Palestinian people’s erasure mean, from a distance?
What significance does a will have when military power supports erasure? As the writers in this anthology ponder their last wishes, some create ambivalence through imaginings of survival, even as forced displacement and airstrikes limit areas of safety. Others ponder a will and testament from the hypocritical lens of the humanitarian paradigm, such as Hussein Hazrallah who writes, “I’m nearly certain that the world has seen nothing but a tiny fraction of what’s happening in Gaza, less than the trickle of crumbs that have reached the people here under the label of ‘humanitarian aid’.” The same humanitarian aid also carries death with it, as the author remembers “the death we carried away in sacks marked with United Nations logos, or with the propaganda of the Arab and Islamic nations.”
BOOK REVIEW: Every Moment Is a Life: Gaza in the Time of Genocide
Hazrallah also connects the past to the present when he notes of Palestinians’ ancestors, “They died after escaping death previously, and we were born to them in an attempt to restore the rights that are now slipping through our fingers.” Colonialism, however, made sure that rights and Palestinians are separated by the coloniser’s violence.
Layan Osama Abu al-Qumsan narrates the story of her family’s death by an Israeli airstrike, reflecting upon the fact that her father, a doctor, was unable to live up to his promises of keeping her safe: “I realise that the doctor, with his medicine and medical knowledge, couldn’t avert the disaster that had come upon us.”
Ni’mah Hassan also reflects on her inability to keep her children safe from Israel’s genocide. “I keep trying to put off writing my will,” she writes, while she imagines futures in Gaza despite the absence of futures. Turning to the present scenario, she writes of looking at her children’s fingers: “I never thought of writing their names on them, to prevent death from noticing them. May death leave their limbs intact.”
Other writings take a completely opposite direction – the normalcy in the abnormal life during genocide also speak of having abandoned the fear of death. “Death no longer concerns us as much as the question of how to get a bag of flour or a gas cylinder the next morning,” Nasser Rabah writes. Yet death also occurred during the search for necessities such as flour or gas. The mind filters out the fear of death to accommodate the human instinct to survive.
Writing provides testimony in the face of annihilation. The imagined audiences for each testament in this book vary – from loved ones to the global population away from Gaza. It is through reading from the point of view of the latter that the pain sears through in a different way. Language testifies not only to the lived experiences of the writers, but also as to how much all those not living in Gaza do not know. Under the threat of erasure, language is a tool of preservation.
